en: Now begins the first section, the Setumāhātmya, within the Brāhmakhaṇḍa. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Salutations to Śrī Vedavyāsa. For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, who is moon-colored, four-armed, and has a gracious countenance. (1)
The sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, headed by Śaunaka, were devoted to the eightfold yoga and solely intent upon the knowledge of Brahman.
Great-souled seekers of liberation, free from the sense of "mine," exponents of Brahman, knowers of dharma, devoid of malice, and devoted to truthfulness. || 2 ||
Having conquered their senses and subdued their anger, they were compassionate toward all living beings, worshipping the eternal Viṣṇu with supreme devotion.
They performed austerities in the highly meritorious Naimiṣa forest, which bestows liberation; once, those great-souled ones held an excellent assembly.
Possessing great merit, they spoke stories that destroy sin, while inquiring among one another about the means to both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Of those twenty-six thousand sages of purified souls, as well as their disciples and grand-disciples, it is impossible to calculate the number.
In the meantime, the great sage Sūta, a highly learned disciple of Vyāsa and the best among those who know the Purāṇas, arrived at the Naimiṣa forest.
Seeing that sage who had arrived, blazing like a fire, the sages headed by Śaunaka honored him with offerings of water for the feet and other traditional rites.
When the Sūta was seated comfortably upon an excellent and auspicious throne, they questioned him regarding a supreme secret, out of a desire to benefit the world.
O Sūta, knower of the true principles of dharma and artha, welcome, O bull among sages! You have heard the Purāṇas from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī.
Therefore, O great sage, you are a knower of the meaning of all the Purāṇas; which sacred fields and which holy fords exist upon the surface of the earth? (11)
Or how will liberation from the ocean of worldly existence be attained by living beings? And how is devotion to Hari or even to Hara produced in men? (12)
By what action is the threefold fruit of the self accomplished? O son of Sūta, please tell me all of this and whatever else [is required] out of compassion. (13)
"Teachers may indeed speak even the secret [teachings] to a devoted disciple. Thus was Sūta questioned at that time by the inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest.
Having first bowed to Vyāsa, his own guru, he began to speak. Śrī Sūta said: "O Brahmins, this which you have asked is excellent and for the welfare of the world."
I shall tell you this secret; listen with reverence. O best of sages, I have never before spoken this to anyone.
O best of Brahmins, restraining your minds, listen with devotion: there exists on Rāmasetu a place sanctified by the name Rāmeśvara.
Among all sacred fields and even among all holy fords, Rāmasetu is the most excellent; by merely beholding it, one attains liberation from the ocean of worldly existence.
There shall be devotion to Hari and Hara, as well as an abundance of merit; there will be success in all three kinds of action—of this there is no doubt. (19)
O best of sages, listen as I describe the fruit of the merit of that man who, during his lifetime, beholds the Setu with devotion. (20)
Accompanied by twenty million kinsmen on both the mother’s and father’s side, he enjoys [the fruits of his merit] for a kalpa with Śambhu, and thereafter attains liberation.
The grains of dust on the earth can be counted, and the stars in the sky can be counted; yet the merit born from seeing the Setu cannot be counted even by Śeṣa.
The Setubandha is proclaimed to be the embodiment of all the deities; who is capable of calculating the merit of a person who beholds it? (23)
O Brahmins, having seen the Setu, a man is considered to have performed all sacrifices; he has bathed in all sacred fords and has practiced every form of austerity.
O twice-born ones, whoever says to any man whatsoever, "Go to the Setu," he too obtains that same fruit; what is the use of other lengthy speeches? (25)
A mortal who performs the ritual bath at Setu, accompanied by seventy million members of his lineage, reaches the abode of Viṣṇu and is liberated right there.
A person who meditates upon the Setu, the Rāmeśvara Liṅga, and the Gandhamādana mountain is truly liberated from all sins.

Accompanied by a hundred thousand million kinsmen on both his mother’s and father’s side, he reaches the abode of Viṣṇu and is liberated right there; having remained at the feet of Śambhu for three kalpas, he is liberated in that very place. || 28 ||
One who bathes at Setu does not behold the state of being a rat, the pit of fat, nor the Vaitaraṇī river, nor the devouring of dogs, nor the drinking of urine.
One who bathes at Setu does not behold the heated trident, the heated stone, the city of Puṣkara, nor the pit of blood.
Climbing the silk-cotton tree, eating blood, eating worms, eating one's own flesh, and entering the flames of fire. || 31 ||
One who observes the bridge would not lead [beings] through a rain of stones, a rain of fire, the Kālasūtra hell, the alkaline waters, or the hot water.
O Brahmins, even a man who has committed the five great sins, along with his hundreds of millions of ancestors on both the maternal and paternal sides, [is purified] by bathing at Setu.
Having remained there at the foot of Viṣṇu for three kalpas, one is liberated right there; [otherwise, there is] the hell of drying with head downwards and the immersion in alkaline liquid.
The crushing by stone-machines, as well as falling from a precipice, being smeared with excrement, and likewise being sawn apart—these [are the torments]. (35)
Eating excrement, drinking semen, burning at the joints, wandering upon a bed of coals, and likewise being crushed by a pestle. (36)
One who bathes at Setu truly does not see these hells, provided he reflects with the thought, "I shall perform the bath at Setu. (37)

Even one who is a perpetrator of a great sin (mahāpātaka) shall go [to heaven] if he walks a hundred paces; likewise, those who drag many wooden machines or pierce with weapons [attain the same]. (38)
Falling and leaping up, the crushing of clubs and staffs, striking with elephant tusks, and the biting of various serpents. (39)
Inhaling smoke, binding with nooses, being tormented by various piercing pains, and the sprinkling of alkaline water into the mouth and the nose. (40)
Drinking alkaline water, the hell of heated iron, and the consumption of iron needles—these hells a person whose sins have departed certainly does not go to.
The entry into cavities filled with alkaline water, the consumption of filth, the cutting of tendons, the burning of tendons, and likewise the breaking of bones; || 42 ||
Consuming phlegm-inducing substances, drinking bile, frequenting great bitter [herbs], drinking excessively hot oil, and drinking alkaline water; 43.
Drinking decoction-water, eating heated stones, bathing in extremely hot sand, and likewise the grinding of the teeth; 44.
There was also a bed of heated iron, immersion in boiling water, and the thrusting of needles into the eyes and the joints of the mouth. (45)
Indeed, there shall be the binding of his penis and testicles with an iron weight, as well as falling from the top of a tree into a place filled with foul odors. (46)
One who bathes at Setu does not behold such terrible hells as the bed of sharp-edged weapons, nor the drinking of semen, and so forth. || 47 ||

O best of Brahmins, as many particles of dust as cling to the body of him who lies in the midst of the sandy banks of the Setu, smeared with that very dust— [so many years shall he dwell in heaven]. (48)
The destruction of that many sins of killing a Brahmin shall occur; there is no doubt about this, for one whose entire body is touched by the wind situated in the middle of the Setu.
Ten thousand instances of drinking liquor perish for him at that very moment, provided his hair remains after the shaving performed in the middle of the Setu.

The sin of violating the teacher’s bed perishes for him at that very moment, if his bones are placed within the Setu by his sons and grandsons; likewise, the sin of stealing gold perishes for him at that very moment. (51)
O best of the twice-born, by remembering it and performing a bath in the middle of that bridge, the fault of association with great sinners shall go to its dissolution for him.
One who deviates from the path, one who consumes his own wealth, one who reviles ascetics and Brahmins, one who eats excessively, and a seller of the Vedas—these five are slayers of Brahman.
He who, having summoned Brahmins with the words "I shall give you wealth and so forth," later says "there is nothing," is also proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin.
O Brahmins, he who, having fully understood the teachings, harbors hatred toward them or treats the Brahmins with contempt, is likewise proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin.
O Brahmins, he who drives away a herd of cows that has come to a water reservoir for the purpose of drinking is also proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin.
But having come to Setu, all of them—O best of the twice-born, including those who are equal to killers of Brahmins and others—are liberated from their accumulations of sin. (57)
All of them, having come to Setu, are liberated; there is no doubt in this. [This applies even to] one who has abandoned the *aupāsana* fire and one who eats the food of a deity. (58)
One who associates with women who drink liquor, one who eats the food of a courtesan, one who eats the food of a group, and he who delights in the food of outcasts; (59)
These are declared to be drinkers of liquor, excluded from all religious rites; yet they are all liberated from their sins by bathing at the Setu.
Others who are equal to drinkers of *surā* are also liberated by bathing at the Setu, as are those who deal in bulbs, roots, fruits, musk, and fine silk garments.
Likewise, [the scent] of milk, sandalwood, camphor, and betel nuts; as well as that of honey, clarified butter, copper, bronze, and rudrākṣa beads.
But those who are thieves, equal to those who steal gold, should be fully recognized; having come to Setukṣetra, they are liberated—of this there is no doubt. (69)
And all others who are thieves, O twice-born ones, are indeed liberated from all sins by bathing at Setu; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
A sister, a daughter-in-law, and likewise a woman in her menses; a brother’s wife, a friend’s wife, a woman who drinks liquor, and the wife of another. (65)
He who, out of passion, approaches a low-caste woman who trusts him should be known as one who has violated the bed of his guru; he is excluded from all religious rites.
These and others who exist, equal to those who violate the teacher’s bed—all of them, O twice-born ones, are indeed liberated by bathing at the Setu.
Those Brahmins who associate with these, as well as others who are sinful, shall also attain liberation by means of the great bath at Setu.
Desiring enjoyment with Ghṛtācī, Menakā, and others in the world of the gods without performing sacrifice, the Brahmins went to bathe at Saṃtāpahanāpa.
Without having served the Sun or worshipped the supreme deities, a person desiring auspiciousness should perform a bath with devotion at the Setu.
Without giving sesame seeds, land, gold, grain, and even rice, those twice-born ones desire heaven; yet they go to bathe at the Setu.
Without having tormented their own bodies through all manner of fasts and vows, let men who long for heaven bathe at the Setu, which grants liberation.
Indeed, bathing at the Setu bestows liberation as well as purity of mind, [surpassing] even the results of chanting, fire-offerings, charity, sacrifice, and austerity.
Indeed, bathing at Setu is proclaimed as preeminent in the Purāṇas; a bath performed at Setu, which destroys sin, even when done unintentionally, [yields great merit]. (74)

O best of the twice-born, it has been declared that this truth has been spoken: that man who joyfully bathes at the Setu with the aim of attaining prosperity [shall attain] the state of non-rebirth. (75)
O best of the twice-born, he attains abundant prosperity; if he bathes at the Setu for the sake of purification, then he shall attain purity. (56)
If a man bathes for the sake of pleasure with the Apsarases in heaven, then he obtains delight with the celestial women in the world of Svarga. (77)
And if one should bathe on the Setu that bestows liberation for the sake of liberation, then one attains liberation from which there is no return. || 78 ||
Through bathing at the Setu, righteousness is attained; from bathing at the Setu, the destruction of sin occurs. O best of the twice-born, bathing at the Setu bestows the fruits of all desires. (79)

It is remembered as a merit superior to all vows, declared to be greater than all sacrifices, proclaimed to be superior to all yogas, and remembered as being more excellent than all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 80 ||
O best of the twice-born, those in whom attachment toward the enjoyments of the worlds of Indra and the other gods arises must bathe at least once at the bridge built by Rāma.
Those who desire to sport in the world of Brahmā, in Vaikuṇṭha, or even on Kailāsa, the abode of Śiva, should bathe with devotion at the Setu.
[He attained] abundance of longevity and health, and was enriched with beauty and virtues; he became one who has reached the further shore of all four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches.
He who bathes at the Setu, which grants the accomplishment of all goals, with the aim of mastering all scriptures and attaining proficiency in all mantras, [attains those very things].
He shall attain each respective siddhi; this is the truth, there is no doubt in this matter. Those men on earth who fear poverty and hell [shall likewise attain it]. (85)
Let them all perform their ablutions at Rāmasetu, which bestows liberation; whether the mortal is endowed with faith or even devoid of faith. (86)
One who bathes at the Setu does not experience suffering either in this world or in the next; by bathing at the Setu, the entire accumulation of sins of all beings is destroyed. (87)
The mass of dharma increases like the moon in the bright fortnight, and just as various kinds of jewels increase within the ocean. 88.
Likewise, O twice-born ones, merits indeed increase by bathing at the Setu, just as the wish-fulfilling cow in this world bestows all desired objects.
Just as the cintāmaṇi jewel grants the heart's desires of men, and just as the celestial wish-fulfilling tree (amaratara) grants whatever is desired by men; || 90 ||
Likewise, bathing at the Setu shall grant all desired objects to men; even a person who is unable to undertake the pilgrimage to the Setu due to poverty [shall obtain the fruit]. || 91 ||
Having requested wealth from the virtuous, he should perform a ritual bath at the Setu; the donor there obtains merit equal to that of bathing at the Setu. (92)
Likewise, even when accepted [as a gift], it yields its full fruit; one should accept a gift from a Brāhmaṇa with the specific intention of performing a pilgrimage to Setu.
One may accept [gifts] even from a Kṣatriya if the Brāhmaṇas do not give them; or one may accept from a Vaiśya if the kings do not bestow them. (94)
A man should not, under any circumstances, accept food from a Śūdra, nor should he accept wealth or even grain from one who goes to the Setu.
Furthermore, the person who, having given clothing and other such gifts, causes [this work] to be set in motion, attains the unsurpassed fruit of sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha. (96)
One shall obtain the fruit of reciting all four Vedas in their entirety; one enjoys the fruit of the foremost gifts, such as the Tulāpuruṣa.
There shall be the destruction of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. What is the use of much talk? One attains all desires. 98.
Even though she has accepted [the gift] in this way, she enjoys a fruit equal to that; for one who asks for the purpose of a pilgrimage to Setu, there is no taint of acceptance.
He who entices someone by saying, "Go to Setu, I will give you wealth," and later says, "There is nothing," him they call a slayer of a Brahmin.
If a man, though endowed with wealth for the purpose of a pilgrimage to Setu, should beg like a pauper out of greed, the wise call him a thief. (101)
That man who, having taken wealth with the thought "I shall go to Setu," does not go to Setu due to greed, him they call a slayer of a Brahmin.
By whatever means possible, a man should go to Setu with joy; if he is unable, he should either give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) or cause an excellent brahmin to go there.
Just as no fault is found in performing a sacrifice after having made a request, so too no fault is found in undertaking a pilgrimage to a sacred bridge after having made a request. 104.

Even if one procures the materials from elsewhere, one should proceed with the ritual bath at the Setu; that person also obtains the same fruit as the man who performs the bath at the Setu himself. (105)

In the Kṛta Yuga, people attain liberation through knowledge; in the Tretā Yuga, sacrifice alone bestows liberation. Likewise, in the other two ages, they say that charity is supreme. Indeed, for men everywhere, the construction of a bridge and the performance of sacrifices are the highest virtues.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Fruits of Going to the Setu," in the Setumāhātmya, within the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O highly fortunate Sūta, how was the bridge built by Rāma, whose actions are effortless, across the lord of rivers, that fathomless abode of Varuṇa?
O best of those learned in the Purāṇas, tell us—who are full of faith—how many sacred fords (tīrthas) exist at Setu and on Mount Gandhamādana.
Śrī Sūta said: O best of sages, I shall now fully relate to you how the bridge was indeed constructed by Rāma across the abode of Varuṇa.
Indeed, by his father's command, Rāma dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forest at Pañcavaṭī, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, with a composed mind.
O twice-born ones, while that high-souled Rāghava was as if present there, his wife was carried off by Rāvaṇa through the disguise of Mārīca.
Searching for his wife in the forest, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, went to the bank of the Pampā, overwhelmed by grief and delusion.
There, the son of Daśaratha saw a certain monkey; then this Rāghava was asked by the monkey, "Who are you? (7)
From the beginning, he related his own story to him in accordance with the truth; then, questioned by Rāghava, [the monkey asked], "Who are you? (8)
He too made his representation to the high-souled Raghava: "I am a monkey named Hanuman, the minister of Sugriva. (9)
Impelled by him, who desires friendship with you both, I have come; therefore, may it be well with you, come quickly indeed to the presence of Sugrīva.
"So be it," said that Rāma; and together with him, O lords of sages, he went to Sugrīva and formed a friendship with fire as witness.
Then, O twice-born ones, Rāma also pledged himself to the slaying of Vālin, and Sugrīva likewise promised the recovery of Vaidehī.
Having thus made this agreement and inspired mutual confidence, the lord of men and the lord of monkeys were filled with supreme joy.
Likewise, those best of brahmins sat upon Mount Ṛṣyamūka, having quickly brought the body of Dundubhi for the sake of convincing Sugrīva.
With his big toe, Rāghava hurled it many yojanas away; the seven palm trees were shattered by the high-souled Rāghava.
Then, with a joyful mind, the heroic Sugrīva said to Rāma: "O Rāghava, I have no fear even of the gods, beginning with Indra."
Since you, who possess such great prowess, have been obtained by me as a friend, I shall slay the Lord of Laṅkā and bring back your wife.
Then the mighty Rāmacandra, accompanied by Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa, went quickly to Kiṣkindhā, which was protected by Vālin.
Then Sugrīva roared, longing for Vālin’s arrival; and Vālin, unable to endure the roar of his own younger brother, likewise roared.
Having emerged from the inner apartments, he fought with his younger brother; struck by Vālin’s fist-blow, he became utterly overwhelmed.
Sugrīva quickly went forth to where the mighty Rāma was; then the long-armed Rāma [placed his hand] upon Sugrīva’s neck.
Having fastened the sign upon the creeper, Sugrīva then challenged Vālī to battle once more, summoning him with a roar.
Then, at Rāma’s urging, he engaged in a hand-to-hand struggle; thereafter, Rāghava struck Vālin with a single arrow. (23)
When Vālin had been slain, Sugrīva took possession of Kiṣkindhā; then, when the rainy season had passed, Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, [prepared for his expedition].
Taking with him a great army of monkeys to quickly bring back Sītā, he arrived in the presence of the two princes.
He dispatched the monkeys with the desire to search for Sītā; and when Vaidehī had been discovered in Laṅkā by the son of the Wind-god, [he sent them forth].
And when that crest-jewel was given, Rāghava was filled with both joy and sorrow, along with Sugrīva, his younger brother, and the wise son of the Wind.
O twice-born ones, being followed by other monkeys led by Jāmbavat and Nala, that Rāma [set out] during the Muhūrta called Abhijit.
Having traversed various regions, he went to Mount Mahendra; then, having gone to Cakratīrtha, he made his dwelling there.
Right there, that righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, the brother of the lord of the Rākṣasas, arrived together with four ministers.
Rāma received him with a great-souled welcome; however, Sugrīva felt apprehensive, thinking, "Could this man be a spy? (31)
Rāghava, having perceived through his actions and his own beneficial conduct that he was indeed free from malice, honored him accordingly.
He consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa as the sovereign over the entire kingdom of the Rākṣasas and made him his chief minister, a peer to the son of the Sun.
Having reached Cakratīrtha and dwelling there, the illustrious Rāghava, the joy of the Raghus, spoke to Sugrīva and the others while reflecting.
In the midst of the monkey leaders, this word appropriate for the occasion was spoken: "What means, indeed, do you have for crossing this ocean? (35)
And here is this great army, and also the ocean, difficult to cross—this dark mass of waters, agitated by restless waves. (36)
It was crowded with leaping fish, great crocodiles, conchs, and shells; in some places it was overtaken by the submarine fire (aurvānala), foaming and exceedingly terrifying.
Accompanied by dark clouds drawn forth by powerful winds, it possessed the roar of the clouds at the time of universal dissolution and was driven by a violent gale. || 38 ||
"How shall we cross the unshakeable ocean, reaching the abode of Varuṇa, all of us surrounded by the armies of these monkeys of great prowess? (39)
"By what means shall we reach the lord of rivers and streams? How can we, together with our army, suddenly cross over to the abode of Varuṇa? (40)
"Extending for a hundred yojanas and difficult to approach even by thought, there are indeed many obstacles here; how then can Maithilī be reached? (41)
Today we have reached a state more miserable than misery, left without refuge, like those in a vast ocean with great waters and fierce winds, truly without support.
What means shall we devise for the sake of providing sustenance to the forest-dwellers? Deprived of our kingdom, we have reached the forest; Sītā has been abducted and our father is dead. (43)
Even this is unbearable suffering: the leaping across the ocean! Fie, fie upon the roaring of the sea! Fie upon this state of being a mass of water! 44.

How could that word of the great seer born from a jar be false, when it was declared: "Having slain the wicked Rāvaṇa on the pure Gandhamādana mountain, you must go quickly for the pacification of your sin"? (45)
Śrī Sūta said: Having heard these words of Rāma, those led by Sugrīva then—
With palms joined in reverence, they spoke with excitement to that mighty Rāghava: "We shall cross over this by means of boats and various kinds of rafts."
Then, in the midst of the millions of monkeys, Vibhīṣaṇa spoke: "King Rāghava ought to seek refuge with the ocean."
This ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, was dug by the Sāgaras; therefore, the sea ought to perform that service for Rāma, who is their kinsman. (49)
Thus addressed by the wise Rākṣasa Vibhīṣaṇa, Rāghava spoke these words to all the monkeys, consoling them.
All the monkeys were unable to cross this most terrifying ocean, which was a hundred yojanas in width, by means of rafts or boats.
O bulls among monkeys, there are no ships for this vast army; moreover, how could one such as I cause harm to merchants? (52)
Moreover, our army is vast, and the enemy might strike at our vulnerabilities; therefore, crossing by means of rafts or floats does not appeal to me at all.
"O monkeys, Vibhīṣaṇa has spoken this very truth which brings me joy; however, I myself shall attend upon this ocean for the sake of achieving my path. (54)
"If he had not shown me the way, I would have then consumed him with irresistible great missiles, blazing more fiercely than fire and wind."

Having spoken thus, Rāghava, together with the son of Sumitrā, performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya) and lay down according to the prescribed rites upon a bed of kuśa grass facing the ocean.
Then the mighty-armed Rāma lay down upon the bank of the lord of rivers and streams, which was strewn with kusha grass, like a sacrificial fire upon the altar.
Resting his right arm, which resembled a remaining serpent’s hood, as a pillow, the scion of Raghu, the most skillful, reclines upon the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters.
As that Rāma lay sleeping on the surface of the earth covered with kusha grass, three nights passed by while he remained vigilant due to his religious observances.
Having stayed there for three nights, Rāma—skilled in policy and devoted to dharma—then paid homage to the ocean in order to achieve success on his journey.
And at that time, the ocean did not show itself to the dull-witted Rāma, even though it had been worshipped by the diligent Rāma with all due honor.
Even so, Sāgara did not show himself to Rāma; thereupon, Rāma, his eyes red at the corners, became enraged with the ocean.
And he addressed Lakṣmaṇa, who was standing nearby: "Today, with the sea-monsters pierced by my arrows, let the ocean be filled."
O Saumitri, I shall gradually cause this water, along with its shells, pearl-oysters, schools of fish, and crocodiles, to cease flowing in an instant.
Today, with my unerring arrows, I shall dry up the ocean; for this abode of sea-monsters has treated me, who am endowed with patience, with contempt.
He recognizes his own powerlessness and thinks, "Shame on my patience toward such a person; Sāgara does not reveal his true form to me through conciliation. (66)
"Bring my bow, O Saumitri, and arrows resembling venomous serpents! I shall dry up the ocean so that the monkeys may pass on foot. (67)
"I shall, with my arrows, render this abode of Varuṇa—which has transgressed its bounds, which is agitated by a thousand waves, and which is itself lawless—subject to my own discipline."
I shall dry up the great ocean, which is teeming with mighty dānavas, filled with huge sea-monsters and crocodiles, and agitated by vast waves.
Having spoken thus, with bow in hand and eyes agitated by anger, Rāma became invincible like Śiva, the destroyer of Tripura.
Drawing his bow and shaking the world with arrows in his wrath, he released fierce shafts upon the Triple Cities, just as Bhava did.
The blazing and terrible arrows, illuminating the ten directions, entered the waters of the ocean which were crowded with proud Dānavas.
Then, O brahmins, the Ocean, terrified and trembling, with palms joined in reverence and having no other refuge, rose up himself from the netherworld (pātāla).
She sought refuge with Rāghava, the cause of the state of absolute liberation; O brahmins, she praised Rāghava with enchanting words.

The Ocean said: I bow to your lotus feet, O Rāghava, Lord of Sītā, which bestow happiness through their service; I bow to the dust of your glorious feet, worshipped by the hosts of gods, which brought about the liberation of Gautama’s wife. (76)

Salutations, salutations to you who tore apart the body of Sundapriya; salutations to you, the protector of the sacrifice of Kauśika; salutations to the piercer of Mahādeva’s arrow; salutations, salutations to the destroyer of the hosts of Rākṣasas. || 76 ||
O Rāma, Rāma, I bow to you, the bestower of desires upon your devotees, who have descended into the lineage of Raghu with the intent of accomplishing the work of the gods. (77)
O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one! Protect me, who have come to you for refuge—Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning or end, the giver of liberation, auspicious, and infallible.
"Restrain your anger, O lord of kings; forgive us, O abode of compassion! O descendant of Raghu, earth, wind, space, water, and the luminaries [are yours]. (79)
Whatever natures were created by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, those very natures they continue to possess; for my own nature is indeed unfathomability.
But the transformation would be profound; this I tell you as the truth, O scion of Raghu—whether it be from greed, desire, fear, or even passion. (81)
I shall not, under any circumstances, abandon the virtue born of my lineage; moreover, I will provide assistance to your army in crossing over.
To the ocean, lord of rivers, who had spoken thus, Rāma replied: "Accompanied by my army, I shall go to Laṅkā, which is ruled by Rāvaṇa. (83)
"May you now become dry for the sake of my crossing. Thus addressed, the abode of Varuṇa spoke again to Rāghava.
Listen attentively, O Rāma; having heard, perform what must be done. If, by your command, I am to wither away while you, together with your army, desire to depart. (85)
Others too shall command me thus by the power of their bows; I shall, however, tell you another means for the crossing of your army.
For here there is a monkey named Nala, esteemed for his craftsmanship; O descendant of Kakutstha, he is the powerful son of Tvaṣṭṛ, the Viśvakarman. (87)
Whatever wood, grass, or even stone he shall throw upon me, I will sustain it all; that shall become your bridge.
"Go by that bridge to Laṅkā, which is protected by Rāvaṇa. Having spoken thus, when he had vanished, Rāma addressed Nala.
"O high-minded one, you are indeed capable; build a bridge across the ocean. Then Nala spoke these words to Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma.
"I shall indeed construct a bridge over the bottomless abode of Varuṇa; for I have been granted a boon by my father, and I am equal to him in capability. (91)
On Mount Mandara, a boon was granted to my mother by Viśvakarman: "A son shall be born to you who will be equal to me in the art of craftsmanship. (92)
"I am his legitimate son, indeed equal to Viśvakarman; let the monkey-men build the bridge this very day according to their desire."
Then, dispatched by Rāma, those exceedingly powerful monkeys [seized] mountains, mountain peaks, creepers, grass, and trees.
Those of massive bodies, possessing the speed of Garuḍas and the wind, gathered [the materials]; Nala constructed a great bridge in the middle of the lord of rivers and streams.
Rāma, the beloved of Jānakī, thus caused a bridge to be built ten yojanas wide and one hundred yojanas long.
Indeed, having reached that very bridge, it was caused to be built by Rāmacandra through Nala, the lord of monkeys and the son of Viśvakarman. || 97 ||
All mortal sinners are liberated from all their sins; yet Śiva is not so pleased by vows, gifts, austerities, or burnt offerings. (98)
Just as Śaṅkara is satisfied by merely bathing at the Setu, there exists no splendor equal to the splendor of the Sun. 99.
There is nothing equal to bathing at the Setu anywhere; that root of the Setu is at Laṅkā, where Rāma [stayed] with the desire to depart.
The monkeys began the construction of the bridge, which is meritorious and destructive of sins; it later became renowned throughout the worlds by the name Darbhaśayana.
O Brahmins, thus was the construction of the bridge over the ocean described by me; here there are many sacred fords (tīrthas) and numerous meritorious sites. (102)
The remainder is not capable of being counted by number or named; however, I shall today proclaim some of the sacred fords (tīrthas) therein. 103.
There are twenty-four principal holy sites on the Setu; the first is Cakratīrtha, and after that is Vetālavarada.
Then there is the world-renowned holy site for the destruction of sins; then the meritorious Sītāsaras; and then Maṅgalatīrthaka.
Then there is the one that destroys all sins, known by the name Amṛtavāpikā; after that is the Brahmakuṇḍa tīrtha, and then the Kuṇḍa of Hanumān.
For after that is the Āgastya-tīrtha, and beyond that is considered the Rāma-tīrtha; then there would be the Lakṣmaṇa-tīrtha, and beyond that the Jaṭā-tīrtha.
Beyond that is the supreme sacred site of Lakṣmī; after that is Agnitīrtha; then the meritorious Cakratīrtha; and beyond that is Śivatīrtha.
Then there is the holy site named Śaṅkha, followed by the Yāmuna-tīrtha; after that is the Gaṅgā-tīrtha, and immediately thereafter the Gayā-tīrtha.
Then there is the one called Koṭitīrtha, then the nectar of the Sādhyas, then the tīrtha called Mānasa, and after that, Dhanuṣkoṭi.
O best of the twice-born, these principal holy sites situated within the Setu, which remove great sins, have indeed been described.
O best of Brahmins, it has likewise been told how that great bridge was built by Rāma across the ocean—a meritorious act that destroys all sins.
Having heard and having recited this, a person on earth is liberated. || 113 ||
O best of the twice-born, the man who reads this chapter or listens to it with devotion attains infinite victory in the hereafter; he shall never again undergo the suffering of rebirth.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Construction of the Setu and Other Matters," in the Setumāhātmya of the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: "O Sage, regarding those twenty-four holy places (tīrthas) which were mentioned by you at the Setu that destroys sin, among those preeminent tīrthas—"
O Sūta, tell us who ask you: how did the first of these sacred sites come to be renowned as Cakratīrtha? || 2 ||
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, regarding these twenty-four principal holy places (tīrthas), that which was declared to be the first is renowned throughout all the worlds.
By the mere remembrance of that holy place (tīrtha), dwelling in a womb no longer occurs; even sins committed over a hundred thousand lifetimes go to their destruction.
O best of the twice-born, by bathing even once at that sacred ford, or even by remembering it or praising it, there is no other sacred ford in the world superior to it, nor indeed equal to it.
O best of sages, this which I have spoken is the truth: there exists no [other river] equal to the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, the Revā, the Paṃpā, or the river Godāvarī.
The Kālindī, the Kāverī, the Narmadā, and Maṇikarṇikā, as well as whatever other sacred fords and holy rivers exist upon the surface of the earth.
O best of Brahmins, there is nothing equal to this sacred ford even by a ten-millionth part; for those who know the past call that sacred ford "Dharmatīrtha."
I shall now relate how it became renowned as his Cakratīrtha; listen, O best of sages. (9)
For that is declared to be the root of the bridge (Setumūla), and it is considered the bed of Darbha grass; right there is Cakratīrtha, which crushes even the greatest of sins.
For in ancient times, a sage named Gālava, who was devoted to Viṣṇu, lived on the shore of the southern ocean not far from Hālāsya.
Near Phullagrāma and likewise beside the Kṣīrasaras lake, on the bank of the Dharmapuṣkariṇī, he performed great penance.
Chanting the eternal Brahman for ten thousand ages, the sages were endowed with compassion, abstaining from food, truthful, and having their senses conquered. (13)
Beholding all beings as himself, free from longing for sense objects, devoted to the welfare of all beings, self-controlled, and devoid of all dualities; || 14 ||
For several years he subsisted on withered leaves; for some time he lived on water, and for many years he sustained himself on air alone.
In this manner, for five thousand years, that great sage performed severe penance, which was exceedingly difficult even for the gods to perform.
Then, for five thousand years, that bull among sages remained without food, without light, without breath, and without support.
During the rainy seasons he endured the downpours, in the winters he lay in the water, and in the summers he stood amidst five fires, solely devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu.
Chanting the eight-syllabled mantra and meditating on Janārdana within his heart, Gālava, the preeminent sage of great splendor, performed intense austerities.
In this manner, ten thousand years passed for that sage; then the Blessed Lord, the Master of Kamalā, was pleased by his ascetic penance.
The wielder of the conch, discus, and mace appeared before him, with eyes like the petals of a full-blown lotus and a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Mounted upon the son of Vinatā, adorned with an umbrella and chowries, and decorated with necklaces, armlets, a crown, bracelets, and other ornaments.
He was surrounded by his servants, such as Viṣvaksena and Sunanda, as well as by Nārada and others who played instruments like the lute, the flute, and the drum.
His victory being sung by bards, he was resplendent in yellow garments; his chest was adorned by Lakṣmī, and his complexion was like that of a dark blue cloud.
Madhusūdana, served on both sides by great yogis such as Sanaka and others, shook a lotus with one hand.
O Brahmins, enchanting the entire three worlds with a gentle smile and illuminating all ten directions with his own radiance, he shone forth.
He was adorned with the Kaustubha gem resting upon his neck, and attended by numerous chamberlains holding golden staffs in their hands.
The Lord Himself, Hari, the beloved of Lakṣmī, whose own wonders are sung in ways inconceivable and unattainable by others, is easily accessible to those who possess true devotion.
They placed it before that great sage Gālava; then, seeing him manifested with his chest marked by the Śrīvatsa, [he was filled with wonder].
The great sage attained satisfaction upon seeing the god wearing yellow garments; endowed with supreme devotion, he praised the Lord of the Universe.
Gālava said: Salutations to the God of gods, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace; salutations to the eternal, the pure, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.

Salutations to you, the destroyer of the distress of devotees, whose very nature is the sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors; salutations to you, the triple-formed one, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.

Salutations to the Supreme Lord, salutations to the All-pervading One; let there be salutations to the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Ordainer. Salutations to Him whose eyes are the sun and the moon, salutations to Him who is worshipped by Viriñci and the other gods.
Salutation to that destroyer of the Daityas, who is free from conceptual constructions such as name and genus, who is devoid of all defects, and who removes the fear of the entire cycle of existence.

Salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇa, whose prowess is immeasurable, who is to be known through the Vedāntas, who is the Lord of Ramā, who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha, who is the father of the Creator, and who removes the suffering of the virtuous. || 35 ||
Salutations to you, the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; salutations to you again and again, who reclines upon the couch of Śeṣa.
Having thus praised Hari, O brahmins, that Gālava remained silent; and Hari, having heard the praise of that high-souled one, which was pleasing to the ears.
The wielder of the conch, discus, and mace attained supreme satisfaction; then Śauri embraced the sage with his four arms.
Filled with affection, he spoke: "O Gālava, choose a boon; I am pleased today by your asceticism and also by your hymn of praise. (39)
"Delighted by your salutation, I, the giver of boons, have come to you. Gālava said: "O Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of Ramā, O wearer of yellow garments, O you who pervade the universe! (40)
O Janārdana, abode of the universe, Govinda, slayer of Naraka! By the sight of you, I have achieved my life’s purpose; indeed, it is superior to all else. (41)
The most unrighteous do not see you, because you are the protector of dharma; that which neither Bhava nor Brahmā knows, and likewise that which the three Vedas do not know—[that you are]. (42)
I know him as the Supreme Self; what boon could be greater than this—that the yogis do not see him, nor do the ritualists see him? (43)
I behold him as the Supreme Self; what boon could be greater than this? O Janārdana, Lord of the World, by this I have achieved my life’s purpose.
I behold that Janārdana, by the mere remembrance of whose name even great sinners attain liberation, O sages.
"May my devotion to the pair of your lotus feet be unwavering. Hari said: "O Gālava, may you now possess firm and disinterested devotion toward me. (46)
Listen further, O sage, to these words being spoken by me: one who performs action for my sake, whose meditation is on me, and who is devoted to me; || 47 ||
At the end of this body, which has been commenced by past karma, you shall attain my own nature; O best of sages, dwell in this very hermitage.
This Dharmapuṣkariṇī is meritorious and the destroyer of sins; performing penance upon its bank, one shall attain perfection through austerity.
In ancient times, Dharma, having arrived at the shore of the southern ocean, then performed penance while meditating upon Mahādeva in his mind.
O great sage, Dharma also created one sacred bathing place for the purpose of ritual ablution; because it was made by him, it became renowned as Dharmapuṣkariṇī.
O best of sages, just as you have now performed penance, so too has he performed penance through that dharma which serves Hara.
Pleased by his ascetic penance, Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident, appeared, illuminating the ten directions with your own splendor.
Then, as Mahādeva, the treasury of compassion, arrived at the hermitage, Dharma, being supremely satisfied, praised the Supreme Lord.
Dharma said: I bow to the Lord of the Universe, the Sovereign whose essence is the Praṇava, who is the embodiment of all deities and is devoid of beginning, middle, or end. (55)
I bow down to Virūpākṣa, whose vital seed is drawn up, who possesses universal forms, who is the support of the entire world, and who is infinite, unborn, and immutable.
I bow to that Increaser of Prosperity whom the lords of yogis proclaim; salutations to the Sovereign of the World, who deceives and utterly deceives. 57.
Salutation be to Nīlakaṇṭha; salutation to the Lord of Creatures. Salutation to the destroyer of taints, and salutation to the most bountiful.
Homage to the god Rudra, to the benevolent Rudra, the wise one; homage to you who hold the Pināka bow in hand, to you who hold the trident in hand. 59.
Salutation to the one whose form is consciousness; salutation to the Lord of nourishments. Salutation to the five-faced God; salutation to the Lord of sacred fields.
Thus praised, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, attained supreme satisfaction regarding Dharma and spoke to him.
Maheśvara said: "O Dharma, O high-minded one, I am pleased with this hymn of yours; choose a boon from me and do not delay."
Thus addressed by Īśvara, Dharma then spoke to the god: "O Lord of Pārvatī, I shall always be your vehicle."
"O Destroyer of Tripura, this alone should be granted as my boon; by the mere act of marrying you, O Lord, I shall have achieved my life's purpose."
Thus addressed by Dharma, the god then spoke of righteousness. Īśvara said: "O Dharma, honored by the world, always become my vehicle."
My power of carrying you shall be unfailing; those who serve you shall always possess devotion toward me—of this there is no doubt. (66)
When Śaṅkara had spoken thus, O Gālava, Dharma, assuming the form of a bull, has carried the Supreme Lord from that time until now.
Having mounted Dharma, who was indeed in the form of a bull, Mahādeva, shining most brilliantly, spoke this supreme nectar of truth to Dharma.
Īśvara said: "This sacred site (tīrtha) which has been established by you on the shore of the southern ocean shall become famous in the world as Dharmapuṣkariṇī."
On its bank, recitation, burnt offerings, charity, and even the study of sacred texts, as well as other multitudes of religious duties, are joyfully performed by men. (7)
"It should be known that it yields infinite fruit; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. Having thus granted the boon to that Dharmatīrtha, Śaṅkara—
Having mounted the bull Dharma, he went to Mount Kailāsa; O Gālava, you too have now gone to the bank of the Dharmapuṣkariṇī.
"O tiger among sages, dwell here with a concentrated mind, performing austerities until the fall of your body; thereafter, you will certainly attain me."
Whenever fear arises within you, I shall destroy it in an instant with my weapon, the discus, impelled by me.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu vanished right there. Śrī Sūta said: When Viṣṇu had disappeared, Gālava, the bull among sages— || 75 ||
On the bank of the Dharmapuṣkariṇī, devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu, he worshipped Viṣṇu three times a day at Śālagrāma, which bestows liberation.
The wise, steadfast, dispassionate, and self-controlled sage dwelt there; once, during the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, on a day sacred to Hari (77).
Having observed the fast and kept a vigil at night, he worshipped Viṣṇu; then, on the following day, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), he bathed in the waters of the Dharmapuṣkariṇī.
He performed his daily obligatory rites preceded by the twilight prayers (saṃdhyāvandana); thereafter, he proceeded to perform the worship of Hari.
Having gathered flowers such as tulasī and having performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa, Gālava recited this hymn of praise. (80)
Gālava said: I bow to Viṣṇu of a thousand heads, to Hari who assumed the form of a fish, to Hṛṣīkeśa who possesses the forms of the tortoise and the boar. 81.
I bow down to Viṣṇu as Nārasiṃha, the one named Vāmana, Jāmadagnya, and Rāghava; to Balabhadra, Kṛṣṇa, and Kalki. (82)
I bow to Janārdana, Vāsudeva, who is without support, the destroyer of the suffering of those who prostrate before him, and the support of all living beings. 83.
I bow to Janārdana, the omniscient, the creator of all, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, who is inconceivable and indefinable. 84.
Praising him in this manner, the great yogi Gālava, the best among sages, stood on the bank of the Dharmapuṣkariṇī pond, devoted to meditation. || 85 ||
In the meantime, a certain terrible Rākṣasa, severely oppressed by hunger, came to devour the sage Gālava.
Then that Rākṣasa swiftly seized Gālava; having been thus quickly captured by that Nairṛta, Gālava [was held fast]. (87)
He cried out repeatedly, "Protect me! Protect me! to Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the discus, who is the ocean of compassion and the ultimate refuge for those who have fallen into distress.
O Supreme Lord, O Ocean of Bliss, O Protector of those who seek refuge! Save me, O Ocean of Compassion, for I have fallen into the power of a demoness. 89.
O Lakṣmīkānta, O Hari, O Viṣṇu, O Vaikuṇṭha, O Garuḍadhvaja! Protect me, who am seized by a rākṣasa, just as you protected the elephant seized by a crocodile.
O Dāmodara, O Jagannātha, O crusher of the demon Hiraṇyāsura! Protect me, who am being severely oppressed by the Rākṣasa, just as you protected Prahlāda.
O best of the twice-born, as Gālava was thus offering praise, the bull among monkeys, Cakrapāṇi, perceiving the fear of his devotee, [acted].
He dispatched his own discus for the sake of protecting his devotees; that discus of Viṣṇu was sent by the all-powerful Viṣṇu himself.
Then he arrived with speed at the bank of the Dharmapuṣkariṇī, [a place] resembling infinite suns and possessing a splendor equal to infinite fires.
Upon seeing Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana—blazing with great flames, emitting a great roar, and crushing the great asuras—the Rākṣasa then fled.
As that Rākṣasa was swiftly fleeing, Sudarśana suddenly severed his head, which was difficult to approach due to its garland of flames. 96.
Then Gālava, seeing the Rākṣasa fallen upon the ground, was filled with supreme joy and praised Sudarśana.
Gālava said: O Discus of Viṣṇu, salutations to you who are consecrated for the protection of the universe; salutations be to you, the ornament upon the lotus-hand of Nārāyaṇa. (98)
O Mahārava, O Sudarśana, salutations to you who are skilled in destroying the asuras in battles and who destroy the suffering of your devotees. 99.
Protect me, who am agitated by fear, from every sin; O Lord Sudarśana, O All-pervading One, may you always be my refuge in the sacred ford of Dharma.
"Stay for the benefit of the world that longs for liberation. O lords of sages, when Gālava had spoken thus, that Discus of Viṣṇu spoke to the sage Gālava as if to please him out of friendship.
Sudarśana said: "O Gālava, this is a place of great merit, an unsurpassed sacred site of dharma. (102)
I dwell here constantly out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds; yet, having considered the suffering caused to you by that evil-minded Rākṣasa, [I have come]. (103)
"O Brahmin, urged by Viṣṇu, I arrived here in haste; this lowest of Rākṣasas, who was tormenting you, has now been slain by me. (104)
"You have been liberated from this fear, for you are always a devotee of Hari; O bull among sages, I am indeed Dharma here in this lotus pond. (105)

"Indeed, for the sake of constantly protecting the world, I maintain my presence here; O twice-born one, because of my presence in this place, [the powers] of you and others shall likewise be effective. (106)
From this point forward, there shall be no suffering arising from spirits or rākṣasas; for this is the Dharmapuṣkariṇī, the destroyer of all sins.
"O bull among sages, in former times this region as far as Devīpaṭṭana was indeed established by Dharma; here, everywhere, I shall dwell forever. (108)
Because of my presence here, this place shall be renowned as Cakratīrtha. Those who perform their ablutions here at Cakratīrtha, which bestows liberation, [shall attain it]. (109)
Indeed, their sons, grandsons, and all those born in their lineage shall have their sins shaken off and go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O Gālava, those who offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) here for the sake of their ancestors all go to heaven, and their ancestors, too, are fully gratified.
Having spoken thus, O twice-born ones, that discus of Viṣṇu suddenly [struck], while Gālava was looking on, as were the other brāhmaṇas.
He entered that Dharmāpuṣkariṇī, which destroys all sins. Śrī Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, the Dharmatīrtha is renowned as Cakratīrtha. (113)
Just as it was attained, so has it been joyfully described by me to you: there has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford equal to Cakratīrtha.

Men and Brahmins who bathe here become partakers of liberation; of this there is no doubt. One who recites this chapter or listens to it with a concentrated mind obtains the supreme fruit of bathing at Cakratīrtha. Having attained happiness in this world, one shall obtain happiness in the next as well. (116)
Whoever remembers Dharmatīrtha, as well as Gālava, Kurvāṇaga, Ugrasamādhiya, Sudarśana, and Rākṣasanāśana—even once—that person shall not be a partaker of sin. || 117 ||

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of Dharmatīrtha’s Attainment of the Renown of Cakratīrtha," within the Gālava Narrative of the Setu-māhātmya, in the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O Blessed One, O Sūta, best among those versed in the Purāṇas, who was that Rākṣasa who harassed the high-souled Gālava, a devotee of Viṣṇu?
The venerable Sūta said: O Brahmins, listen with respect as I relate the story of that cruel Rākṣasa, and how that Rākṣasa was born through the power of the sages' curse.
Formerly, on the peak of Kailāsa, in the temple of Śiva at Hālāsya, there were twenty-four thousand sages who discoursed upon Brahman.
All those of great luster, headed by Vasiṣṭha and Atri, were devotees of Śiva; their entire bodies were smeared with ashes, and their foreheads were marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra).
Adorned with garlands of rudrākṣa beads and devoted to the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra, they [worship] Hālāsyanātha, Bhūteśa, Candracūḍa, and Umāpati.
The inhabitants of Madhurāpurī sat in worship for the sake of liberation. Once, there, the powerful Gandharva, the son of Viśvāvasu, [arrived].
O best of Brahmins, there was one named Durdama who was devoted to the company of harlots; accompanied by a hundred women, he was naked in a body of water.
Vasiṣṭha, together with the sages, sported joyfully at that holy site of Hālāsyanātha with those young women who were naked.
Intent on performing the midday rites, he departed from the temple of Śaṅkara; then, beholding those sages, the women became overwhelmed with fear.
They covered him with garments, but the irrepressible one, devoid of shame, did not act out of rashness; thereupon Vasiṣṭha, being enraged, cursed that shameless man.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O Gandharva Durdama, because you did not quickly cover yourself with a garment out of shame upon seeing us, therefore go henceforth to the state of a Rākṣasa."
Having spoken thus, Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages, said to those women: "O excellent ladies, because you saw us and covered [us] with your garments... (12)
"Therefore, I shall not grind you; go hence to the third heaven. Having been addressed thus by Vasiṣṭha, the women then stood with palms joined in reverence.
Having prostrated before Vasiṣṭha with minds bowed in devotion, they spoke thus to that Vasiṣṭha in the midst of the circle of sages.
The women said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, son of the four-faced Brahmā! O ocean of compassion, having looked upon us, you ought not to show anger. (15)
For a husband alone is said to be the supreme ornament of women; O sage, a woman who is deprived of her husband, even if she has a hundred sons, [is truly wretched]. (16)
In this world, the term "widow" is known as the death of those women; therefore, O Sage, out of respect for our husbands, please grant us your favor. (17)
"A single offense should be forgiven by sages who perceive the ultimate truth; O ocean of compassion, grant forgiveness for this difficult-to-tame disciple of yours. (19)
O best of the twice-born, having been thus entreated by the women of Durdama, Vasiṣṭha, being pleased, spoke these words once more.
"O fair-browed ones, my word shall never be false; I will tell you a means—listen with faith. (20)
"The curse upon your husband will certainly last for sixteen years; and at the end of those sixteen years, this one of demonic form will become difficult to restrain. (21)
"O celestial nymphs, he will go to the Ācakra-tīrtha by chance; there dwells the great yogi Gālava, who is devoted to Viṣṇu."
This Rākṣasa will approach that sage for the sake of devouring him; therefore, the supreme discus was dispatched for the protection of Gālava.
"Rāma, an incarnation of Viṣṇu, will take his head; of this there is no doubt. Thereafter, having regained his true form, the one who was so difficult to subdue will be released from the curse. (24)
Your husband will go again to the third heaven; there is no doubt about this. For once he has reached the third heaven, this Durdamana shall indeed be your husband.
"Clad in beautiful attire, he will delight you, O beautiful women. Śrī Sūta said: Having spoken thus to those excellent women of Durdama, Vasiṣṭha—
Devoted to Hālāsyeśvara, he quickly returned to his own hermitage; then the distressed wives embraced their difficult-to-restrain husband, Rāma.
Agitated by grief and immersed in an ocean of sorrow, they wept; even as they were looking on, he became the Rākṣasa Durmada. || 28 ||
Having large fangs and a massive body, with red beard and hair, they saw him and, agitated by fear, went to the triple heaven, O Rāma.
Then this one, disguised as a Rākṣasa, difficult to subdue and of terrifying form, devoured all living beings, wandering from country to country and forest to forest.
Wandering with a blue-colored speed, he then went to Dharmatīrtha; in this manner, sixteen years passed while he was thus wandering.
Then, O lords of sages, at the end of sixteen years, this Rākṣasa went to devour the sage Gālava, who was dwelling at Dharmatīrtha.
Attacking with the speed of the wind, he praised Janārdana; then Viṣṇu, being lauded by Gālava, urged forth his discus.
To protect the sage Gālava who was being tormented by the Rākṣasa, the Discus of Hari arrived and struck off the head of the Rākṣasa.
Then, having cast off this demonic body and assuming a divine form, Durdama ascended an excellent celestial chariot while being showered with flowers.
Bowing down with palms joined in reverence, he paid homage to Sudarśana and, with great devotion, praised him with foremost words as pleasing to the ear as the Vedas.
Durdama said: "O Sudarśana, salutations to you, the sole ornament of Viṣṇu’s hand! Salutations to you, the destroyer of the asuras, who possesses the splendor of a thousand suns! (37)
By a mere fraction of your compassion, O Viṣṇu, wielder of the discus-weapon, I have abandoned my demonic body and regained my true form; salutations be unto you!
"O beloved of Viṣṇu, grant me permission to go to the third heaven; my wives are grieving, their minds distressed by separation. (39)
O Discus, grant me your grace so that I may remain devoted to you for as long as I live; salutations be unto you.
O lords of sages, when Viṣṇu’s discus was thus praised with devotion by Durda, it immediately granted its favor, saying, "So be it."
Permitted by the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), Durdama bowed to the sage Gālava; having been granted leave by him, the Gandharva departed for the third heaven.
When Durdama had gone to heaven, Gālava, the bull among sages, requested the discus, the unsurpassed weapon of Viṣṇu.
O wielder of the discus, crusher of the great asuras, I bow to you at the unsurpassed Dharma-tīrtha on the outskirts of Devīpaṭṭaṇa.
Establish your presence here, which destroys all sins; for by your presence, all the sinners who bathe here [shall be purified]. (45)
"Effect the destruction of sins and grant eternal liberation; establish for yourself the renown among the world as 'Cakratīrtha'. (46)
O Noble One, wielder of the discus, by your presence the fear of the sages here has been dispelled; henceforth let it be so—salutations unto you! (47)
"O Lord, let there be no fear from ghosts, spirits, or demons"—thus was the Discus entreated by Gālava, O lords of sages. (48)
Having spoken thus, "So be it," he vanished at that sacred ford. Śrī Sūta said: "O Brahmins, in this manner has that account of Bhava as a Rākṣasa been narrated to you by me."
The majesty of Cakratīrtha, which removes impurities, has been told; by hearing which, a person on earth is liberated from all sins.
The sages said: O Sūta, disciple of Vyāsa, possessed of great wisdom, best among those learned in the Purāṇas! [Describe] starting from Darbhaśayana up to Devīpattana.
Tell me now: how did that unsurpassed Cakratīrtha, which was joined with great effort, come to be severed in its middle? 52.
"You ought to sever this doubt that dwells within your mind. Śrī Sūta said: "In ancient times, all the mountains possessed wings and were as swift as thought. (53)
Moving through the path of the sky together with the peripheral mountains, they traveled through cities, kingdoms, villages, and forests.
Leaping again and again, the mountains stand everywhere upon the earth; wherever there are mountains, they stand having repeatedly stepped over them.
Here and there, men, cattle, and other multitudes of living beings suddenly met their death, being crushed by the mountains.
Immediately after the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, had perished, the deities suddenly fell into calamity due to the absence of sacrifices and other rites. || 57 ||
Then Indra, greatly incensed and impetuous, took up his thunderbolt and suddenly severed the wings of those powerful mountains. (58)
All the mountains, their wings being severed by Vāsava, having found no other refuge, entered the ocean out of fear.
And as all those who were immovable fell into the salt ocean, some even fell at Cakratīrtha, mistaking it for the sea.
With its interior filled by those fallen mountains, the highly meritorious Cakratīrtha was severed in its middle. || 61 ||
By chance, the great mountains did not fall there upon his two sides; for this reason, indeed, it was likewise [chosen] for the bed of darbha grass and for Devīpura as well.
With its middle portion severed, it appears as if divided in two; Cakratīrtha has been turned into dry land by the mountains fallen from the center. 63.

The venerable Sūta said: O lords of sages, I have thus related to you how this sacred site was established from the midst of that place, and how the lofty mountains, their wings suddenly severed by Viḍaujas (Indra), fell down here.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Liberation from the Curse of the Gandharva Durdama," in the Setumāhātmya of the Brahmakhaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
The venerable Sūta said: O lords of sages, having introduced the meritorious Cakratīrtha which destroys all sins, I shall now relate something else that is truly wonderful.
For the Vasu named Vidhūma and the goddess Alambuṣā attained the state of humanity in former times due to a most terrible curse from Brahmā.
Having bathed at the highly meritorious Cakratīrtha, the two were liberated from the curse. The sages said: "O Sūta, O Sūta of great wisdom, you who are expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas! (3)
Because of your wisdom and because you are a disciple of Vyāsa, there is nothing unknown to you. By what offense was Brahmā cursed along with Alambuṣā and Vasu?
Long ago, the Four-faced One (Brahmā) cursed one named Vidhūma; by that terrible curse of a Brahmin, those two attained the state of being his sons. (5)
How did the end of the curse come about for those two who were cursed by Brahmā? You ought to tell this in detail to us who are full of faith.
The venerable Sūta said: In ancient times, indeed, the Lord Brahmā, the self-born one with four faces, was resplendent on both sides by Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī.
By the eternal sage Sanaka, the wise one, and by the high-souled one named Sanatkumāra and Nārada.
He was being attended by Sanandana and other lords of sages, and was being praised by Indra, who was himself joined by hosts of gods.
His lotus feet were being praised by the planets beginning with the Sun, and he was surrounded by Siddhas, Sādhyas, Maruts, and Kinnaras.
It was surrounded by hosts of kimpuruṣas and the eight vasus, and was as enchanting as the celestial courtesans headed by Urvaśī.
Once, in the assembly hall of Satyaloka, while repeatedly watching a dance accompanied by instrumental music, he held a conversation in the midst of the gathering.
Deep as the roar of clouds and repeatedly delighting the people, the sound of lutes, flutes, and drums spread forth there.
Then a breeze, cool from the touch of the spray from the garlands of Ganges' waves and pleasant to the touch, blew very gently.
Then, in turn, all the celestial women danced; when the courtesans had become exhausted by the fatigue of dancing, they were respectfully replaced by others.
Alambusā, a celestial woman endowed with beauty and youth, gladdening all the people, indeed danced in the midst of the assembly. (16)
At that moment, as she was dancing in the assembly, O twice-born ones, the wind playfully blew away her inner garment.
When that garment was cast off, the root of her thighs became clearly visible. Seeing her in such a state, all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, were overcome with shame.
Seated in the midst of the assembly, they closed their eyes; however, the Vasu named Vidhūma was tormented by the arrows of desire.
Seeing her in that very same palace of Brahmā, her garment carried away by the wind, his eyes blossomed with joy and his hair stood on end.
Seeing that Vasu, named Vidhūma, had conceived a lustful desire for Alambuṣā, the Four-faced One (Brahmā) cursed him. || 21 ||
"Since you have performed such a deed, O Vidhūma, you shall therefore attain the state of a human being in the world of mortals."
"And this celestial maiden shall become your wife there. Thus was Vidhūma cursed by Brahmā, his mind distressed. (23)
Having prostrated before Brahmā, Vasu sought his favor. Vidhūma said: "O Blessed One, who is compassionate toward your devotees, [grant me grace] regarding this terrible curse. (24)
"I am not worthy of this, O Lord of Gods; protect me, O ocean of compassion! Thus was the imperishable Lord of Bhāratī propitiated by him.
Filled with supreme compassion, he spoke soothingly to Vidhūma. Brahmā said: "This curse has indeed been bestowed upon you, yet I do not speak an untruth. (26)
Therefore, I shall now fix the limit for this curse of yours: having attained mortal state along with this Alambusā, [you shall remain so]. (27)
Having been born there, O Great King, and having ruled the earth for a long time, he begot upon that queen an incomparable son who became a lord of the earth.

And having consecrated him, who was skilled in protecting the kingdom, in the sovereignty, [he went] to the great Cakratīrtha situated near Phullagrāma on the shore of the southern ocean, for the sake of pacifying this curse.
When you perform your bath together with this wife, then you shall cast off your human state, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.
Having departed together with your wife, you shall return to your own world; for without bathing at Cakratīrtha, such a curse as this cannot be destroyed.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Vidhūma was not particularly delighted; he took leave of the four-faced one and quickly entered his own abode.
There he reflected: "As I am about to attain the state of a mortal, who will be my father on earth, and who will be my mother? (33)
Having reflected deeply on this in many ways, Vidhūma reached the conclusion that there was a king known as Śatānīka in the city of Kauśāmbī.
There was a fortunate hero, and his wife was devoted to her husband; she was named Viṣṇumatī, as beloved to him as Śrī is to Viṣṇu. (35)
Making him my father and appointing her as my mother, I shall be born in the world of mortals through the ripening of my own karma. (36)
Then, having summoned his three servants—Mālyavān, Puṣpadanta, and Balotkaṭa—he related this account to them.
"O servants, listen; may it be well with you! Out of great fear of a Brahmin's curse, I shall be born as a son from Viṣṇumatī by Śatānīka. (38)
Having heard these words, all her servants, whose very lives were departing and whose faces were filled with tears, spoke these words like smokeless fire: 39.
The attendants said: "We three cannot endure separation from you; therefore, O Lord, you shall go with us into the state of humanity. (40)
This Yugandhara, who is the minister of the royal sage Śatānīka, and this Senānī Vipratīka, who is the foremost in battle; (41)
The great one named Vallabha, who is a dear friend in jestful affairs—these three shall all become his sons; of this there is no doubt.
"To you, who have entered into the state of being the son of the royal sage Śatānīka, we shall provide service in various tasks. To those speaking thus, Vidhūma replied with these words: || 43 ||
Vidhūma said: "I am aware of your unsurpassed affection for me."
Nevertheless, I shall speak today; listen to these beneficial words concerning that which was brought about by my own evil deed and by a terrible curse of a Brahmin. (45)
I alone am following this contemptible human condition; for this following of a curse was not ordained for you.
Therefore, do not set your minds now upon this loathsome human state; until the end of the curse, endure this separation from me.
When he had spoken thus, all of them, headed by Mālyavat, bowed their heads and spoke, entreating him again and again.
Having protected us out of compassion, do not commit such a rash act; today you are abandoning all of us, your innocent devotees. (49)
"O Lord, because of our separation from you—a most terrible thing—we even hold this contemptible human state in high regard; therefore, protect us now. (50)
Thus he granted leave to those three servants who were entreating him; accompanied by those three, he desired to go to Kauśāmbī.
At that very time, however, one who increased the Lunar dynasty was born into the lineage of Arjuna, originating from Janamejaya.
King Śatānīka protected the earth; he was intelligent, ethical, eloquent, and devoted to the protection of his subjects.
Endowed with a fourfold army and possessing valor as his sole wealth, that young great king indeed resided in the city of Kauśāmbī.
Yugandhara was born as his minister, a knower of the secrets of mantra; and Vipratīka became his general, the foremost in battle.
In his jesting activities, he had a friend, a twice-born man named Vallabha; his beloved wife was named Viṣṇumatī, who was like Śrī to Viṣṇu.
That high-minded Śatānīka, endowed with all virtues, did not find a son equal to himself through that wife.
Realizing that he was childless, he was deeply distressed; he summoned his minister Yugandhara, the most eminent among those skilled in counsel.
"How might I obtain a son?"—thus he deliberated on this matter. Gladdening King Yugandhara, who was distressed by his failure to obtain a son, with his own words, he spoke these sentences: || 59 ||
Yugandhara said: "There is indeed a great sage named Śāṇḍilya, who is truthful in speech and pure. (60)
Equal toward enemy and friend, self-controlled, and devoted to austerity and sacred study—having approached that very sage, who was like a blazing fire, [he spoke]. (61)
"O King, you should request a son equal to yourself from that compassionate great seer with humility; he will certainly grant you a son."
Having heard those words, his eyes blossoming with joy, he went to the hermitage of the sage accompanied by that minister.
The lord of the earth bowed down to him as he sat in the hermitage; and the highly effulgent Śāṇḍilya [greeted] the king who had arrived at the hermitage.
Having seen him and honored him with water for the feet and other offerings, he spoke words of welcome. Śāṇḍilya said: "Śatānīka, for what purpose have you come to my hermitage? (65)
"Tell me now what must be done by you; I shall perform it. To the sage who was speaking thus, Yugandhara replied:
"O Blessed One, this king is indeed distressed by his failure to obtain a son; he has now come to you for refuge for the sake of a son. (67)
"You ought to dispel this sorrow born of his sonlessness. Having heard these words of his, Śāṇḍilya, the best of sages, [acted].
He indeed promised that boon of obtaining a son to the king; that glorious giver of boons, having arrived respectfully at Kauśāmbī, [honored] the king. (69)
The great sage became the officiating priest for one desiring sons through the Putreṣṭi sacrifice; then, by the grace of the sage, [he became] like King Daśaratha.
Like a performer of sacrifices obtaining his son Rāma, Sahasrānīka obtained his son; thus was Vidhūma born from Śatānīka, the best of kings.
In the meantime, the chief minister, the commander-in-chief of the king, the brahmin, and the companion in jest obtained sons worthy of their lineage. (72)
The son of Yugaṃdhara was a servant named Mālyavat; he was known by the name Yaugandharāyaṇa and was an expert in the sciences of counsel.
The son of Vipratīka was indeed Puṣpadanta, who became renowned as Rumaṇvān, the crusher of enemy armies. || 74 ||
At that time, a son was born to Vallabha who was indeed fierce in strength; he was known as Vasantaka, skilled in the arts of jesting.
Then all of them, led by the princes, grew up; immediately after they had reached the age of five years.
The celestial nymph Alambuṣā was born as a maiden named Mṛgāvatī in the great city of Ayodhyā, the daughter of King Kṛtavarman.
In this manner, Vidhūma and the others were born upon the circle of the earth. In the meantime, there was a powerful and great being accompanied by wicked followers.
A great Daitya named Ahidaṃṣṭra, fierce in his strength, was joined by a wicked companion named Sthūlaśiras. (79)
He besieged the city of the gods and oppressed the deities as well, while a great battle between the gods and the Rākṣasas was taking place in heaven.
Puraṃdara brought Śatānīka for the sake of assistance; that king, having duly installed his son in the position of crown prince (yauvarājya), [departed].
Having ascended his chariot, that wielder of the bow set out for battle with the sons of Diti; Mātali approached him and respectfully escorted him there.
Having made the gods spectators, he slew the sons of Diti in battle; then that lord of the Daityas was also slain in the conflict in heaven.
Then, at the word of Śakra, Mātali quickly placed that bull among kings, who had passed away, upon the chariot and departed for Kauśāmbī.
Having brought him to the surface of the earth, he presented him to his son; then Sahasrānīka, having lamented, was deeply afflicted by grief.
Having consulted with his ministers, he performed the funeral rites; and learning that her husband was dead, the queen followed him in death.
When the king, together with his queen, had met his end and remained as nothing but a memory, Śatānīka’s son assumed the sovereignty at the word of the ministers.
When Yugandhara, Vipratīka, and Vallabha had died, all of their sons, headed by Yaugandharāyaṇa, [remained]. || 88 ||
While his son Śatānīka performed those various duties, that powerful prince protected the earth in this manner.
When some time had passed, during the great festival of Sanandana, he was invited by Mahendra and heard the account of what was to happen as told by him.
Due to the curse of a Brahmin, Alambuṣā, the celestial nymph, was born as Mṛgāvatī, the daughter of King Kṛtavarman, in Ayodhyā.
And formerly, you were the Vasu named Vidhūma; having seen that very celestial maiden in the abode of Brahmā with her garment carried away by the wind, [you were struck with desire].
At that very moment, overcome by passion, he fell into the state of a mortal due to a curse; O King, my friend, she alone shall soon become your beloved wife.
But when you, O King, having established your son in the kingdom, [go] together with your wife Mṛgāvatī to the shore of the southern ocean—
When you perform a bath at the highly meritorious Cakratīrtha near Phullagrāma, you will then be liberated from the curse.
Thus spoke the Grandfather in the world of truth, O Blessed One; and having heard these words of Indra, King Sahasrānīka [acted accordingly].
Likewise, having made preparations for the wedding and taken leave of the Lord of Śacī, he set out joyfully for Kauśāmbī, accompanied on the way by Tilottamā.
Remembering that beloved woman as she spoke, with his mind fixed on nothing else and meditating upon the words of Indra, the lord of the earth did not perceive anything at all.
Disregarded with contempt, that fair-browed woman cursed the king: "O King Sahasrānīka, even though you were summoned by me! (99)
"Meditating on Mṛgāvatī in my heart, why do you disregard me? Proud women intoxicated by their own good fortune cannot endure being treated with contempt. (100)
"O King, disregarding me, she whom you now meditate upon in your heart—you shall be separated from her for fourteen years. (101)
To Tilottamā, who had thus uttered a curse, the king said: "If I may obtain that very daughter of Kṛtavarman... (102)
"I shall endure the suffering born of separation from him for fourteen years," having said this, the king, with his mind fixed on him, departed for his own city. (103)
Then, in the course of time, the beloved daughter of King Kṛtavarman, who was the very life-force of the flower-bowed god of love, came to him.
Having attained Mṛgāvatī, who was like a graceful creeper on a tree of charm and a wave from the ocean of amorous grace, Madanadyuti rejoiced.
She conceived a child from him, just as Bhavānī did from the moon-crested Lord; she shone with such paleness that she appeared like a digit of the moon washed in nectar.
Then, with her pregnancy-longings manifesting, the beautiful queen of the king shone like the eastern quarter pregnant with the moon.
Driven by her pregnancy-longings, whatever desire that queen cherished—even if it were very difficult to obtain—he brought all of it to her out of love.
Once, while her husband was fulfilling her desires, that Mṛgāvatī spontaneously formed the intention to immerse herself in the Red Pond.
Having understood Mṛgāvatī’s desire, the lord of the earth had a pond filled with safflower water constructed in an instant.
In that blood-red water, the queen respectfully performed her bath; then, she was seen drenched in the crimson liquid, resembling a blossoming *kiṃśuka* tree. || 111 ||
A monstrous bird born of the Suparṇa lineage, mistaking her for meat, carried off the innocent queen due to the power of a cruel fate.
Having carried her a great distance through the sky, he, who was like a mountain, abandoned her—who was helpless under the sway of delusion—in a cave of the Eastern Mountain (Udayācala).
Having regained consciousness, her slender vine-like body trembling slowly, she repeatedly shed tears from her eyes that resembled blue lotuses.
"Alas, O Lord! I am ill-fated and tormented by separation from you. What is my refuge? Where indeed shall I go? When shall I behold your face? (115)
Having spoken thus, she stood before the elephants and lions, desiring their slaughter; yet, though abandoned by all the maned beasts and elephants, she did not meet her death.
"In times of calamity, death is surely not obtained by men. Hearing her exceedingly piteous lamentation, they looked up [in astonishment]. (117)
The deer, their movements paralyzed, did not even consume grass; then the son of the sage, that ocean of compassion, [beheld] her remaining in such a state.
Having compassionately brought the weeping queen to his own hermitage, he presented that queen to his preceptor Jamadagni; and the righteous-souled Jamadagni consoled her in his presence.
Jamadagni said: "Know me thus, O blessed lady, as Kṛtavarman is to you."
Thus consoled there by Jamadagni out of compassion, she made her dwelling right there in that hermitage crowded with sages.
Then, after a short time, the young woman gave birth to a son endowed with the qualities of heroism and fortitude, just as Pārvatī gave birth to Viśākha.
