The wives of the sage performed for Mṛgāvatī all the duties pertaining to the lying-in chamber that are usually carried out by kinswomen, treating her as if she were their own mother.
A certain incorporeal voice addressed that well-born prince, and because he was born on the Mountain of Sunrise (Udayācala), gave him the name Udayana.
In that hermitage, having had the rites of tonsure and other initiations performed by the lord of sages, he mastered all branches of knowledge under the great sage Jamadagni.
Once, while devoted to hunting, that young prince saw a serpent firmly bound by a hunter. (126)
Filled with compassion, he said, "Hunter, release the serpent! What will you do with him? You ought not to harm him."
Then the hunter said to him: "O man, by means of this serpent, I shall obtain wealth, grain, and other riches in villages and cities. (128)
"Therefore, for the sake of my livelihood, I shall by no means release him," saying this, the lowest of Śabaras bound him in a chest.
Seeing that the serpent was bound, he gave the bracelet given by his own mother to the Śabara who desired wealth, and thereby set it free.
That serpent, having been liberated by him, assumed human form and, with palms joined in reverence, immediately formed a friendship with him and led him to Pātāla.
Accompanied by the Naga named Kinnara, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he entered Pātāla and dwelt there happily, being duly honored.
The prince took as his beloved wife Lalitā by name, the daughter of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the sister of the Kinnara, who was endowed with every virtue. || 133 ||
She gave birth to a son of incomparable splendor from him; then Lalitā spoke in haste to Udayana.
Lalitā said: "Formerly, I was a Vidyādharī named Sukarṇī by name; through a curse I attained the state of a serpent, and this embryo within me is the end of that curse."
"Therefore, accept this son of incomparable splendor, as well as this betel-leaf plant, this unfading garland, and this resonant lute. (136)
"So be it," replied the prince, accepting all of that; and while all the serpents looked on, she ascended into the sky.
Then he too, taking his lute, his garland, and his little son, was filled with haste, desiring to see his own distressed mother.
Having taken leave of his father-in-law and the others, he went suddenly to his own hermitage, where his mother, who was consumed by grief, had been consoled by Jamadagni.
Having approached her, he pleased her and reported his conduct to her; then Mṛgāvatī became joyful at heart. (140)
In the meantime, that Śabara went to Kauśāmbī to sell the jeweled bracelet marked with the name Sahasrānīka.
Having observed the royal seal upon the bracelet, that excellent merchant went with the Śabara and reported everything to the king. || 142 ||
Then Sahasrānīka, having obtained that jeweled bracelet, was tormented by the fire of the poison of separation from Mṛgāvatī.
Placing that bracelet—cool with the showering spray of nectar from contact with her arm—upon his heart, he lamented, deeply afflicted by grief.
And he asked, "O Śabara, how was the bracelet obtained by you? Being thus addressed, he reported to him the sequence of its acquisition. (145)
Having heard the words of the Śabara, King Sahasrānīka set out together with his ministers, eager for the sight of his beloved.
He suddenly approached that very mountain, upon which the moon, the sun, and other luminaries attain their simultaneous rising.
Having traversed a short distance along the path, he stood there with his troops resting; he remained sleepless, intent on meditating upon the union with his beloved.
Vasantaka indeed told various stories; by listening to those very stories, he passed that night.
Then, in the course of time, having reached the region protected by Indra, he went to the hermitage of Jamadagni, where lions and elephants lived without enmity toward one another.
Seeing the sage engaged in ascetic penance, he bowed his head in salutation; the sage received the king with a blessing.

He worshipped him according to the prescribed rites with water for the feet, the guest-offering, and water for sipping; and he spoke words endowed with righteousness and purpose to the protector of the earth.
O Lord of Men, this son born to you from Mṛgāvatī is a treasure-house of glory and possesses great splendor, like another Rāmacandra. (193)
O highly fortunate one, this grandson of yours, the son of Dyutidhana, will be a youth with the powerful build of a lion and a conqueror of the quarters. (154)
This wife Mṛgāvatī is devoted to her vow of fidelity; therefore, O Great King, accept these three without delay. (155)
Having spoken thus, the lord of the earth accepted those gifts given by the sage and, accompanied by his beloved wife and surrounded by his ministers, set out for his own city. || 156 ||
Then, having entered the city of Kauśāmbī, that best of kings, remembering the words of Śakra, despised his human birth.
He gave the earth to his wise son Udayana; while that son Udayana was capable of protecting the kingdom... (158)
Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to Vasanta and Karumaṇvat for the sake of averting the curse, he [departed] along with his wife Mṛgāvatī.
Accompanied by the minister’s son Yaugandharāyaṇa, he went to the highly meritorious Cakratīrtha on the shore of the southern ocean.
He went quickly on vehicles with the speed of the wind to the salt ocean, the most excellent among all supreme holy fords (tīrthas), in order to perform his ablutions. 161.
Having reached Cakratīrtha, they performed their ablutions according to the prescribed rites; and as soon as those kings and others had bathed in Cakratīrtha—
That most contemptible human state was destroyed at that very moment; thereafter, their sins shaken off, they regained their own original forms.
All of them, wearing celestial garments and adorned with divine garlands and unguents, mounted highly precious celestial chariots and were thus embellished.
Regarding that sacred ford as the cause for severing their own curse, they then departed for the heavenly world while all the people looked on.
From that time forward, having realized the majesty of that sacred ford, they all constantly perform their ablutions here at this purifying Cakratīrtha.
Those men who, having come to that holy ford of such power, perform a bath even once, all of them become dwellers in heaven.

Thus, O brahmins, has the great life-story of Vidhūma been narrated to you. Whoever should read this chapter or listen to it with a concentrated mind shall quickly attain whatever desire he may wish for. (168)
The sages said: O Sūta, disciple of Dvaipāyana, best among those versed in the Purāṇas! [Tell us of] the unsurpassed Cakratīrtha, extending as far as Devīpattana.
Thus you spoke to us in the past; therefore, we ask something: where indeed is that Devīpura, which is the limit of Cakratīrtha?
How did it come to be known by the name Devīpattana? And likewise, [what is the result] for even sinners who have bathed at the base of the Śrī Rāma Setu? (3)
And what kind of merit might there be at Cakratīrtha as well? O best of those learned in the Purāṇas, tell me this and other particulars.
The venerable Sūta said: O best of sages, I shall relate all of this; listen, for this narrative destroys the sins of those who read and hear it.
There, having established nine stones, the descendant of Raghu, the lord of Maithilī, first bound a bridge across the ocean.
Devīpura is located right there at the very end of Cakratīrtha; this is how its name "Devīpattana" came to be.

Therefore I say this, O best of sages: listen with faith. Long ago, during the war between the gods and the asuras, Diti, whose sons had been destroyed by the gods and who was overwhelmed by grief and delusion, spoke to her own daughter.
Diti said: "Go, my daughter, to perform penance in the unsurpassed forest of asceticism."

O lady of beautiful hips, for the sake of a son, you have remained self-restrained with your senses controlled; yet by that son alone, the gods, including Indra and the others, will surely not be surpassed.
Having been addressed thus by her mother, she bowed to her; then, assuming the form of a buffalo, she entered the forest situated amidst five fires.
She performed severe penance, by which the worlds trembled; while she was engaged in that austerity, the three worlds became stricken with fear.
O best of the twice-born, Indra and the hosts of gods fell into a state of delusion; then the sage Supārśva, agitated by her ascetic penance, spoke to her.
Supārśva said: "I am well-pleased, O fair-hipped lady; you shall have a son who has the form of a buffalo in his face, but possesses a human body."
A son named Mahiṣa shall be born to you, possessed of exceeding prowess; he will afflict heaven and the Lord of the Gods along with his armies.
Having spoken thus to her and dissuaded her from that asceticism, Supārśva took leave of the female ascetic and returned to his own world.
Then that Mahiṣa was born exactly as previously described by Brahmā; possessing great heroism, he grew like the great ocean during the full moon.
Then, O twice-born ones, there was the son of Vipracitti, Vidyunmāli, the leader of the asuras, as well as other excellent asuras who were on the surface of the earth.
Having heard that this Mahiṣa had been granted a boon, all those best of sages joyfully assembled and addressed Mahiṣāsura.
"O Great-minded One, sovereignty over heaven formerly belonged to us; however, relying upon Viṣṇu, the gods forcibly seized our kingdom. (20)
O Mahiṣāsura, seize that kingdom of ours by force; display today both your valor and your own power.
Possessing incomparable strength and valor, and emboldened by the boon granted by Brahmā, slay the Lord of Pulomajā in battle along with the hosts of gods.
Thus addressed by the Danujas, the immensely powerful Mahisha, desiring to fight with the immortals, then set out for Amaravati.
O best of Brahmins, in ancient times there occurred a tumultuous battle between the gods and the asuras for a hundred years, which caused the hair to stand on end.
Then, O Brahmins, placing Purandara at their head out of fear, the host of gods became bewildered as to where to go and fled to Brahmā.
Brahmā, taking all those immortals with him, went once again to where Nārāyaṇa and Śiva, the protectors of the universe, reside.
Having gone there, paid homage, and praised her with numerous hymns, Brahmā reported the deeds of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
[He described] the affliction of the gods by the asuras, and [the state] of the two deities Śambhu and Kṛṣṇa, as well as Indra, Agni, Yama, Sūrya, Indu, Kubera, Varuṇa, and the others.
Having set aside their respective offices, he himself remains there; he also remains in the offices of other hosts of gods.
That host of gods, driven from their own world to the surface of the earth, wanders like mortals, oppressed by the demon Mahiṣāsura.
I have come here with the hosts of gods to inform you both of this; therefore, protect those who have assembled here.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Rameśvara and Maheśvara became terrible-faced and difficult to behold due to their anger. || 32 ||
Then, O twice-born ones, from the mouth of Viṣṇu, which was blazing with extreme anger, a great splendor issued forth, as did that of Śambhu and likewise of the Creator.
From the bodies and other parts of certain other gods, a fierce splendor emerged; that became one single entity.
But that mass of their splendors, resembling a blazing mountain, was seen by those hosts of gods as its flames pervaded the intermediate quarters of space.
O twice-born ones, that collection of splendors then became a certain woman; the splendor of Śiva became her face, and the splendor of Viṣṇu became her two arms.
Her two feet were formed from the splendor of Brahmā; her waist from the splendor of Indra; her hair from the splendor of Yama; and her breasts from the splendor of the Moon.
O Brahmins, his shanks and thighs were fashioned from the splendor of Varuṇa; his hips from the splendor of the Earth, and his toes from the splendor of the Sun.
Likewise, the fingers of the hand were fashioned from the splendor of the Vasus; O Brahmins, the nose was fashioned from the splendor of Kubera.
The rows of her teeth were produced by the splendor of the nine Prajāpatis, and her two eyes were born from the brilliance of the fire-god Agni.
The two eyebrows were born from the two twilights, and the ears from the energy of Vāyu; and [the rest] from the exceedingly fierce energies of the other gods. (41)
The woman, whose limbs were fashioned [by him], became Durgā, supremely radiant and more difficult to overcome than even all the gods and asuras. || 42 ||
Arising from the collective splendor of the entire host of gods, those deities, who had been oppressed by Mahiṣa, felt great joy upon seeing her.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the gods beginning with Rudra extracted their own weapons and gave those weapons, such as the trident and others, to her.
They gave her ornaments, garments, garlands, and sandalwood paste; and then that goddess [was adorned] with those garments, ornaments, sandalwood paste, and other such things.
Adorned with flowers as weapons and with necklaces by her attendants, that Bhairavī, possessing a terrifying voice, let out a loud, boisterous laugh.
She roared, as if making heaven and earth tremble, which are served by the gods; by the goddess’s terrifying sound, the entire world shook.
Then the gods, sages, Siddhas, and Gandharvas praised that Goddess, who was mounted upon a lion, with shouts of "Victory! (Jaya).
Seeing the three worlds agitated by the exceedingly terrifying roar of the Goddess, the Daityas, the enemies of the gods, rose up with their weapons raised.
Mahiṣa too, with great fury and his mighty weapon raised, hearing that sound, then advanced surrounded by the Asuras.
Then he beheld the Goddess, who pervaded the three worlds with her splendor, endowed with weapons and infinite arms, and who caused the earth to tremble with her roar.
Beholding the Goddess who had agitated the entire succession of great nāgas beginning with Śeṣa, the asuras armed themselves and raised their weapons.
Then a battle took place between the goddess and the asuras, fought with missiles, weapons, arrows, discuses, maces, and even clubs.
There, the mighty Mahisha, the subduer of enemies, fought together with the Goddess, accompanied by countless elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
There were thousands of lakhs and koṭis of chief leaders of the asura hosts; indeed, no one could calculate the number of their individual armies.
They all simultaneously assailed the Goddess with weapons by their might; then that formidable Goddess [neutralized] the multitude of missiles discharged by the Daityas.
He effortlessly pierced [the enemy] with arrows discharged from his own bow, discharging numerous volleys of shafts upon the bodies of the Daityas. (57)
By the power of the Goddess as their refuge, the gods fought fearlessly with the leaders of the Daityas in battle, using weapons, missiles, and various other armaments.
Then the gods, intoxicated by their strength and bolstered by the power of the Goddess, utterly annihilated all the asuras with their weapons.
When his own army had perished, Mahiṣāsura became greatly agitated; taking up his bow and drawing it with speed, he made a great sound.
O brahmins, aiming at the divine armies, he released arrows: ten thousand at Indra and five thousand at Yama.
Eight thousand [oblations] for Varuṇa, six thousand for Kubera, and [the same number] for Sūrya, Candra, Vahni, Vāyu, the Vasus, and the Aśvins. || 62 ||
Moreover, against the other gods as well, Mahiṣa, the lord of the Dānavas and the best among the strong, released ten thousand arrows at each one.
Then the gods, oppressed by Mahiṣāsura, fled from there; crying out, "Save us! Save us!", they came to the Goddess for refuge.
Then the Goddess commanded her own hosts of Bhūtas, Vetālas, and others: "Destroy the demonic army quickly! (65)
But I shall fight the arrogant Mahiṣa in battle; thereafter, the entire host of Asuras shall be swiftly destroyed by the Goddess and her Gaṇas.
Then, once his army had been brought to destruction by the Gaṇas impelled by the Goddess, Mahiṣa stood ready to fight with the Gaṇas.
In the meantime, Mahānāda, Sucakṣus, Mahāhanu, Mahācaṇḍa, Mahābhakṣa, Mahodara, and Mahotkaṭa [arrived].
He has five faces and hair upon his feet; he has many eyes and many arms; he has one eye and one foot, yet he also has many feet and is footless.
These and many other ministers of Mahiṣāsura, desiring to fight, stood before the Goddess in the battle.
Then the goddess, having mounted her lion vehicle which was as swift as thought, took up a formidable bow that resounded like the thunderclouds at the time of universal dissolution.
Having burst them open, he released arrows equal in speed to lightning in the battle; [he was accompanied] by ten lakhs of elephants and also by a hundred lakhs of horses.
The Daitya Mahāhanu, who was joined by a hundred lakhs of chariots and ten million foot soldiers, was struck down in battle by the Goddess. (73)
And in his army, O best of the twice-born, thousands of lakhs and crores of the foremost asura leaders were slain by the goddess with her arrows. (74)
For each of Mahiṣa’s principal commanders possesses a fourfold army endowed with great strength and prowess. (75)
O Brahmins, just as Mahāhana possessed great strength, so too did he have immense power; all of that was destroyed by the Goddess with her gold-feathered arrows.
O best of Brahmins, within just one watch of the night, that became as if a miracle.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between the Goddess and Mahiṣāsura," within the "Account of the Name Devīpura," in the "Praise of Cakratīrtha" section of the Setumāhātmya, in the third part (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: Then, beholding his own army slain by the Goddess, Mahiṣa, the lord of the Dānavas, spoke with great wrath to Caṇḍakopa.
Mahiṣa said: "O Caṇḍakopa of great heroism, fight this wicked-souled woman! Having replied, "So be it," the powerful Caṇḍakopa then [prepared for battle]. || 2 ||
He showered the Goddess with volleys of arrows at the forefront of the battle; and she, with ease, [cut down] the nets of arrows of Caṇḍakopa instantly.
Sāṃbikā struck Caṇḍakopa with her weapon after cutting [his bonds]; she also severed his horses, as well as his charioteer, banner, and bow.
He shattered the chariot as well and struck him in the heart with arrows; thus, his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed, he [stood there]. || 5 ||
Then Caṇḍakopa, bearing a sword and a shield, approached the Goddess; the great Asura struck the lion, the vehicle of the Goddess, with his sword.
He also struck the Goddess on her left arm with a sword; that sword shattered into a thousand pieces upon the Goddess's left arm.
Then Ambikā struck Caṇḍakopa in the heart with a great trident; he fell down and died.
When that Caṇḍakopa, possessed of great heroism and great strength, had been slain, Citrabhānu, mounted upon an elephant, rushed toward the goddess.
Then she discharged a divine spear, tumultuous with the sound of a great bell; the Goddess, with her "huṃ" cries, warded off that spear which was otherwise irresistible.
Then, with her trident, that goddess tore apart Citrabhānu; when he was dead, Karāla then swiftly approached in the battle.
Struck by a blow from the fist of his hand, he too was felled by the Goddess; thereafter, she deprived the one intoxicated with pride of his life with her mace.
O best of the twice-born, the goddess Durgā dispatched Bāṣkala to the realm of Yama with both her spear and her discus.
In this manner, having impaled other ministers of Mahiṣa who possessed massive bodies with his trident, he then dispatched them to the abode of Yama.
When his own army had been thus destroyed by Durgā, Mahiṣāsura then assumed the form of a buffalo and devoured the attendants of the Goddess.
Enraged, he struck some with his snout, others with blows from his tusks, and still others he caused to fall with the breath of his nostrils.
Having thus struck down the host of spirits by the Goddess, Mahiṣāsura grew enraged and roared in order to kill the Goddess's lion. || 17 ||
Then the lion became enraged, possessing great heroism and great strength; he shattered the surface of the earth and the mountains with his blows against the gods. || 18 ||
As Mahiṣāsura approached, she tore him apart with her claws; then Caṇḍikā, becoming enraged, set her mind upon his slaughter.
Overwhelmed with rage, Caṇḍikā bound Mahiṣa with nooses; then, having released him from those nooses, he abandoned his buffalo form.
The Daitya, possessed of great strength and prowess, assumed the form of a lion; meanwhile, the Goddess resolved to sever his head.
Then that man appeared with a sword in his hand; thereupon the Goddess [struck] that man, who held a sword, with volleys of arrows.
He struck him with sharp-edged tips that tear open the vital organs; then, O Brahmins, that man became an elephant possessing trunk and tusks.
He seized Durgā’s vehicle, the lion, with his hand; thereupon, the lion tore at his hand with the tips of its claws.
Once again, the great Asura was born, having assumed the form of a buffalo; thereupon, the enraged Bhadrakālī partook of a great draught of wine.
Then, intoxicated by the power of the drink, she laughed with reddened eyes; and that Mahiṣa, out of pride, [threw] heaps of mountains with his two horns.
She hurled the image of Caṇḍikā at him, and she [the goddess] cut it to pieces with her arrows; then the Goddess, the Mother of the World, spoke to Mahiṣāsura.
The Goddess said: "O fool, indulge in your pride for a moment while I drink the honey; once I have finished my drinking, I shall lead you to the abode of Yama. (28)
Now that you, an invincible thorn in the side of the gods, have been slain by me, let the Siddhas, Sādhyas, and hosts of Maruts return each to his own abode. (29)
Having spoken thus, she struck Mahiṣāsura with her fist; then, being struck by the Goddess, Mahiṣa became utterly overwhelmed.
He fled in great haste to the shore of the southern ocean; the Goddess, mounting her vehicle, the lion, pursued him.
Then, pursued by the Goddess, Mahiṣa, the lord of the Dānavas, fled for ten yojanas into the waters of Dharmapuṣkariṇī.
Having entered, he remained there invisible, overwhelmed by the blow from Durgā; then Durgā reached the bank of the Dharmapuṣkariṇī pond.
Then Caṇḍikā beheld the Asura Mahiṣa there; subsequently, an unembodied voice addressed the goddess Durgā.
O Bhadrakālī, Great Goddess, O auspicious one, the Dānava Mahiṣa was struck by you with your fist in the waters of the Dharmapuṣkariṇī.
"He lies hidden within this [cave], afflicted by fear; kill him! By whatever means possible, deprive him of his life. (36)
When Caṇḍikā had thus been addressed by an incorporeal voice, she, intent on slaying the lord of the asuras, spoke to her own vehicle, the lion.
O Lion among beasts, possessing the prowess of a lion and great strength and valor, drink up this water from the Dharmapuṣkariṇī until it is entirely exhausted.
O Brahmins, having been addressed thus by the goddess, the five-faced one drank the water of the Dharma-puṣkariṇī until it was entirely exhausted, so that not even a speck of dust remained.
Then the wretched buffalo emerged from that body of water; as the demon approached, the Goddess stepped upon his head with her foot.
Enraged, she tormented his throat with a sharp spear; then the Goddess, seizing a sword, severed his great head.
Thus, O brahmins, that buffalo, together with his servants, forces, and vehicles, was struck down by Durgā; he fell to the ground and died.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and supreme Ṛṣis, having praised the Goddess with hymns, were satisfied and rejoiced at that time.
Then, permitted by the Goddess, the gods departed as they had come. Thereafter, the Goddess, the Mother of the World, [established] an excellent city in her own name.
Then, on the northern shore of the southern ocean, those gods, led by Śakra, were instructed by the Goddess.
They then filled the Dharmapuṣkariṇī with nectars; consequently, that supreme sacred site received the name Amṛtatīrtha.
Then the Goddess, filled with joy, granted a boon to her own city, saying: "May this city be conducive to cattle and free from disease. (47)
And she granted a boon to the holy ford, saying, "For men who bathe here, let there be success according to their desires," and having spoken thus, she departed for heaven.
Śrī Sūta said: Because the Goddess established this unsurpassed city under her own name, that supreme city of the Goddess is called Devīpattana.
O twice-born ones, beginning from Devīpattana on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment, one should first pay obeisance to Vighneśvara and likewise to Salilasvāmin.
Permitted by Mahādeva, the exceedingly righteous Rāmacandra joyfully established nine stone slabs with his own hand.
O brahmins, having ascended the auspicious throne fashioned by Nala, Rāma began the construction of the bridge toward Laṅkā without weariness. || 52 ||
He caused a bridge to be built across the ocean by the monkeys, headed by Nala and others, using mountains, branching trees, logs, stones, and heaps of timber.
And the monkeys gathered grass from the midst of the forest.
Nala, having taken those [reeds], constructed a bridge over the great ocean; in five days, the bridge reached as far as the vicinity of Laṅkā.
Ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long, a meritorious bridge was built by Nala across the ocean, which destroys all sins.
Near Devīpura, at the base of the Setu in the form of the Navapāṣāṇa, a man should bathe for the complete purification of his own sins.
Likewise, one should bathe at Cakratīrtha and worship Hari, the Lord of the Setu—the construction of the bridge which was built beginning from Devīpattana.
O best of Brahmins, that root of the Setu is thus designated according to its true nature; the western extremity of the Setu is proclaimed as Darbhaśayyā.
Devīpurī and Prākkoṭi—both of which have their base at the Setu—are declared to be meritorious, purifying, and destructive of sins.
By whichever path men go to the root of the Setu, they, having traveled along those respective paths, attain liberation in each and every one of them.
Having first bathed at the base of the Setu and likewise at Cakratīrtha, they should thereafter proceed to Setubandhana after making a formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
Likewise, O Brahmins, at Devīpura and also at Darbhaśayyā, as well as at Cakratīrtha, there is an auspicious bath that destroys both merit and sin.
O twice-born ones, by the mere remembrance of Cakratīrtha in both cases, even the sins committed over a hundred thousand lifetimes are reduced to ashes.
Even birth shall go to destruction, and liberation itself shall rest in the palm of one's hand; there has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford equal to Cakratīrtha.
O best of the twice-born, whatever holy places exist on the earth, such as the Gaṅgā and others, they truly do not equal even a sixteenth part of Cakratīrtha.
First, one should perform a bath in the ocean amidst the nine stones; thereafter, one should likewise do so at Kṣetrapiṇḍa and at Cakratīrtha.
One should worship Hari as Setunātha for the complete purification of one's own sins; indeed, those who have traveled by that path should likewise perform this on a bed of darbha grass.
Whatever person pays homage to the lion-throne made of reeds, which was ascended by Rāmacandra, for him there is no fear of hell.
At the outset, one should pay homage to the Setu while meditating on Rāma within the heart—that [Setu] whose dust has been purified by the treading of the feet of the hero of the Raghus.
Salutations to the Setu, the cause for the severing of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa's heads; salutations to the banner of Rāmacandra, the sole cause for the path to liberation.
O twice-born ones, having first prostrated with all eight limbs using this mantra, [one should worship] the Setu, which is like the sun to the lotus of Sītā’s mind. (72)
Thence one should go to the very powerful Vetālavarada Tīrtha; by bathing there, a man attains supreme perfection.

O best of the twice-born, for that man who reads this chapter or hears it with devotion, heaven and other realms shall not be difficult to attain; even liberation (kaivalya) shall be as if already held in his hand.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of the Asura Mahiṣa," within the "Narration of the Name of Devīpura" in the "Praise of Cakratīrtha," in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O Blessed One, O omniscient Sūta, dear friend of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana! Having heard from your own mouth these stories that rain down the nectar of the ears...
No satiety arises for us who drink the nectar of your words; therefore, speak further auspicious stories to us who are desirous of hearing them.
"You previously stated that there is a most meritorious sacred site named Vetālavarada to the south of Cakratīrtha. (3)
How did this holy place (tīrtha) come to be known by the name Vetālavarada? And what is the power of that tīrtha? You ought to tell us this.
Śrī Sūta said: O lords of sages, you have indeed asked well regarding this most secret matter; listen with your minds as I relate this most wonderful narrative.
Even the most ignorant rejoice upon hearing this auspicious tale; this story of great merit was [first told] of old on Mount Kailāsa.
O twice-born ones, I shall relate to you this most wonderful story which was told by Śambhu to Pārvatī during their times of play.
Formerly, indeed, a great sage named Gālava, truthful in speech and pure, performed penance in his own hermitage while meditating upon the Supreme Brahman.
His daughter was highly fortunate, endowed with beauty and youth; the young girl, named Kāntimatī, used to move about near her father.
And she would gather flowers for the sake of that sage’s sacrificial offering, as well as perform the sweeping of the altar and the fetching of sacrificial fuel.
The young girl served her father with perfect devotion; once, she set out to gather flowers for the sake of an offering.
Then Kāntimatī went very far into that forest; having gathered beautiful flowers there, she placed them in a basket.
The young woman, devoted to the service of her father, quickly turned back. As that maiden was returning, two Vidyādhara youths [beheld her].
Sudarśana and Sukarṇa, seated in their celestial chariot, beheld her, the daughter of Gālava, endowed with beauty and youth. (14)
The eldest son of the Vidyādharas, named Sudarśana, [beheld] Rati, the graceful consort of Kāma, as if she were the goddess herself in bodily form. || 15 ||
With eyes blossoming with joy, he, deluded by passion, desired her as he gazed again and again at that woman whose face was like the full moon.
Desirous of sporting with her, he descended from the top of his celestial chariot; approaching that maiden of the sage, Sudarśana spoke to her thus: (17)
Sudarśana said: "Who are you, blessed lady? Whose daughter are you, endowed as you are with such beauty and youth? Indeed, this incomparable form gladdens my heart. (18)
"Seeing you, who resemble Rati herself, the god of love torments me; I am the wife of the Vidyādhara lord named Sukaṇṭha. (19)
My son is endowed with beauty and is named Sudarśana; O blessed lady, accept me and protect me with a compassionate glance. (20)
"Having obtained me as your husband, you shall enjoy all pleasures. Having heard these words of that son of the Vidyādhara, she—
Then Kāntimatī spoke these words consistent with dharma: "O Sudarśana, illustrious one, son of the lord of the Vidyādharas! (22)
"Know me to be the daughter of the high-souled Gālava; I am an unmarried maiden, devoted to the service of my father. (23)
"For I have come here to gather flowers for my father's funeral offering; while I was gathering the flowers, one watch of the day has passed away. (24)
O Lord, because of my delay, that ascetic sage, the best among munis, who is intent on the worship of the gods, will surely become angry. (25)
Therefore, I shall go quickly today; flowers have already been gathered by me. Furthermore, maidens are always dependent upon their fathers and are never independent.
"If you desire me, then ask my father," Kāntimatī then said to the son of the Vidyādhara.
Apprehensive of her father, she quickly prepared to go to the hermitage; seeing her as she was departing, a young Vidyādhara—
Afflicted by passion, he ran forward and quickly seized him by the hair; seeing him grasping her own hair, she [restrained him]. || 29 ||
The sage’s daughter suddenly cried out loudly like a female osprey: "O Father, O Lord, save me from this son of a Vidyadhara! (30)
"Today this evil-minded son of a Vidyadhara seizes me by force! Thus he cried out loudly, not far from his own hermitage.
Hearing that cry, the sages dwelling on Mount Gandhamādana placed Gālava, the bull among sages, at their head.
Desiring to know what this was, they went quickly to that place; having arrived at that place, all those bulls among sages [beheld it]. (33)
They saw that hermit maiden held by the Vidyadhara, and another son of a Vidyadhara standing nearby.
Having seen this, the great yogi Gālava, the bull among sages, fell somewhat under the sway of anger and cursed that wicked-minded one.
"O lowest of Vidyādharas, since you have performed such a deed, go now to a human womb as the fruit of your own evil karma! (36)
Having attained a human birth that is beset by manifold sufferings, within a very short time, indeed in that very same life— (37)
"You shall go to that state of being a vetāla which is censured even by men; you shall always devour flesh and blood. (38)
Vetālas, who are mostly Rākṣasas, seize women by force; therefore, having become a human, you shall attain the state of a Vetāla. (39)
That youngest brother of yours who was the consenter to your evil deed, he too shall become a human being known by the name Sukarṇa.
But because he did not perform such an act directly, his state remains merely that of a human; let him not become a *vetāla*. (41)
When he beholds the lord of the Vidyādharas known as Vijñaptikautuka, then that youngest one shall be liberated from the curse.
But you, who are the perpetrator of such a great sinful deed, having attained human birth, shall [reap its fruit] in that very same life.
"Having attained birth as a Vetāla, you shall wander in this world for a long time. Having spoken thus, Gālava took the girl and departed with the sages.
Having cursed the two sons of the Vidyādhara, he departed for his own hermitage; then, when that illustrious bull among sages had gone forth, [the following occurred]. 45.
The two sons of the lord of the Vidyādharas, named Sudarśana and Sukarṇa, being afflicted with suffering due to the sage’s curse, reflected deeply.
Having decided upon what must be done, Sudarśana and Sukarṇaka [went] to the one named Govindasvāmin, who dwelt on the bank of the Yamunā.
Having conceived that brahmin, who was perfected in virtue, as their father, the two of them abandoned their own forms and were then born as his sons.
He had two sons named Vijaya and Aśokadatta; the eldest son, Sudarśana, was born as the one called Vijayadatta.
The one named Aśokadatta and Sukarṇa, the youngest, both Vijaya and Aśokadatta reached youth in due order. (50)
At that very time, on the auspicious bank of the Yamunā, there occurred a twelve-year famine due to drought.
A Brāhmaṇa named Govindasvāmin, who had mastered the Vedas, then saw his own city afflicted by famine.
He set out for Kāśanigara with his son and his wife; having reached Prayāga, he beheld the two [sages] and the great banyan tree.
He saw before him an ascetic adorned with a garland of skulls; Govindasvāmin then paid homage to that sage.
The sage pronounced blessings upon him, along with his wife and son, and spoke these words to Govindasvāmin: || 55 ||
O best of Brahmins, you will now soon be separated from this eldest son, Vijayadatta. (56)
Having heard these words of his, the one named Govindasvāmin, after the sun had set, completed the evening rites there.
Accompanied by his wife and son, the Brahmin, distressed by the long journey, stayed that night in a deserted temple.
Then Aśokadatta and the brahmin woman, both deeply distressed, spread their garments upon the ground and fell asleep during the night. (59)
Then Vijayadatta, due to having traversed a long distance, became exceedingly weary and was severely afflicted by a cold fever.
Although he was being tightly embraced by his father Govindasvāmin to ward off the affliction of the cold, he did not abandon that sensation of cold.
"O father, a cold fever afflicts me excessively now; bring fire without delay for the sake of relieving this affliction. (62)
Having heard these words of his son and searching for fire everywhere, he, finding no fire, returned and spoke again to his little son:
"O son, though I have searched everywhere, I do not find the fire; for the middle of the night has arrived and the gates are closed. (64)
"The citizens, overcome by sleep, will certainly not give us fire," said his father thus to Vijayadatta, who was afflicted with fever.
Afflicted by the suffering of cold arising from a feverish chill, he entreated his father, Agni, with a piteous voice.
"The wind, laden with sprays of snow, torments me doubly today; 'the fire has not been found'—this which you said, O father, was indeed false. (67)
Look! From afar, in the space before us, this fire is seen, filled with garlands of flames and licking the sky with its crests. (68)
"Bring that fire quickly, dear son, for the cessation of the cold. To him who had spoken thus, his father replied: || 69 ||
"I do not speak a falsehood, my son; today I speak only the truth. This place is filled with fire, as can be seen from afar. (70)
"O son, know that this place before you, where this fire with flames licking the clouds blazes forth, is now the region of the ancestral forest (pitṛkānana). (71)
"O son, know that to be the fire of the funeral pyre, which causes terror; this inauspicious fire of the pyre, defiled by touch, must not be approached."
And he who serves the fire of the funeral pyre undergoes the exhaustion of his lifespan; therefore, my son, I have done this so that there may be no loss of your life. (73)
"This funeral fire is inauspicious, untouchable, and has not been brought here," said his father; to him who spoke thus, the son replied in distress: || 74 ||
"This may be either a funeral fire or a sacrificial fire; by all means, let it be brought here, otherwise my death will surely occur. (75)
Then, overcome by affection for his son, one named Govindasvāmin went quickly to the cremation ground to collect the funeral fire.
When Govindasvāmin had departed to collect the funeral pyre, Vijayadatta also quickly followed after him as he went. || 77 ||
Having reached the vicinity of the funeral pyre where bones were scattered, he attained peace slowly, as if anxiously embracing it.
Then he said to his father: "What is this round object, shining intensely in the fire, resembling a red lotus? (79)
Having heard these words of his son, that best of Brahmins examined him closely and spoke these words once more: (80)
Govindasvāmin said: "This skull is circular, encircled by a wreath of blazing fire; it is rich with fat, bone, and flesh, and resembles a red lotus. (81)
Having heard this, the son of the twice-born struck it with the tip of a wooden stick, whereby it burst open and he became one whose face was drenched by the spilling fat that gushed forth.
Then, as he repeatedly licked with his tongue the blood that had adhered to his mouth from striking the skull, he savored that very blood.
Having thus tasted it and taken up that skull, he became greatly agitated; having drunk the fat, his body grew massive and he became most terrifying.
Then, at night, the sharp-fanged Vetāla instantly attained his form; by the sound of his boisterous laughter, the cardinal and intermediate directions were then filled.
The sky, the atmosphere, and the earth seemed to crack apart on all sides as he, having violently dragged his father toward him, prepared to kill him.
"Do not commit a rash act!"—such a voice arose in the sky. Hearing that divine speech, the Vetāla became exceedingly terrifying.
Leaving his father behind, endowed with great speed, he quickly entered the sky and proceeded with unimpeded motion.
Having traveled a long distance, he encountered the Vetālas; and seeing that he had arrived, all those Vetālas [beheld him]. (89)
Because he attained the state of a Vetāla by means of the sound of splitting skulls, they thereafter called him by the name Kapālasphoṭa.
Then that Kapālasphoṭa, surrounded on all sides by Vetālas, [was brought] immediately before the king of the Vetālas named Narāsthibhūṣaṇa.
Endowed with great strength, he quickly reached his presence and, adorned with human bones, appointed him as his commander-in-chief.
Once, however, a powerful Gandharva named Citrasena struck him down in battle; he too was adorned with human bones, and he remained standing [in that state].
When that Gandharva, who was adorned with human bones, was slain in battle by him, Kapālasphoṭa then attained that state.

Sudarśana, the son of the lord of the Vidyādharas, having first entered the human state, attained the form of a Vetāla due to the curse of a great ṛṣi, and in due course became the lord of the Vetālas. (95)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Sudarśana’s Attainment of the State of a Vetāla," within the Praise of the Vetālavarada Tīrtha, in the Setu Māhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Then, at dawn, that brahmin, afflicted by grief for his son and accompanied by Aśokadatta and his wife, lamented.
O twice-born ones, seeing Govindasvāmin lamenting in this way, a merchant named Samudradatta brought him to his own home.
Having brought him back and comforted him, the compassionate and excellent merchant appointed him as the guardian of all his wealth.
Remembering the words of the great ascetic and longing for the sight of his son, he remained in the house of the merchant together with his wife and son.
The second son of the brahmin was named Aśokadatta; he became exceedingly proficient in both weaponry and sacred scripture.
Likewise, among other sciences as well, there was no one on earth equal to him; the son of a twice-born man, having completed his studies, became renowned throughout the city.
In the meantime, a certain powerful wrestler, the ruler of the land of Kāśī, approached King Pratāpamukuṭa.
King Pratāpamukuṭa, for the sake of victory over this wrestler, summoned that powerful son of a Brahmin by means of his servants.
Seeing him arrive, Pratāpamukuṭa said: "O Aśokadatta, [confront] this wrestler, who is suddenly and excessively powerful."
"O best among the powerful, slay Durjaya in battle; once this great champion of the South has been conquered by you—"
"Whatever is desired by you, all that I shall give; of this there is no doubt. Having heard these words of his, the powerful son of the twice-born [replied]: || 11 ||
He struck the great wrestler-king of the South; though struck by the son of the twice-born, that wrestler was powerful even against the powerful.
With his eyes rolling, he fell dead upon the ground; that deed of the brahmin’s son was difficult to accomplish even for the gods. (13)
Seeing this, Pratāpamukuṭa became delighted at heart; he then gave him much wealth and villages and established him nearby.
Once, O Great King, accompanied by the son of a brahmin, he indeed traveled on horseback in a secluded place at the time of twilight.
There, accompanied by the son of the twice-born, he then heard the piteous voice: "O King, I have committed only a slight offense, repeatedly instigated by my enemies. (16)
"I have been impaled upon a stake by the executioner with a heart devoid of compassion; today is the fourth day that I have remained alive upon this stake. (17)
The vital breaths do not depart easily for those who have performed evil deeds; O King, intense thirst oppresses me greatly, so please quench it. (18)
Having heard these piteous words, the king spoke to the son of a brahmin named Aśokadatta, who was endowed with fortitude.
"O son of a brahmin, you must give water to this innocent creature, who has been impaled upon a stake and is tormented by thirst."
Thus commanded by the king, the son of the twice-born quickly took up a jar filled with water and departed with great speed.
Having reached that cremation ground, which was teeming with spirits and vetālas, he was eager to offer water to him who had been impaled upon a stake.
Then the twice-born one beheld a woman standing there, radiant with fresh youth; he gazed upon her of great splendor, as if she were Rati incarnate.
Beholding her, the steadfast son of a brahmin then said: "Who are you, O blessed lady of beautiful limbs, staying here in this desolate cremation ground? (24)
"Why do you stand beneath him who is impaled upon the stake? Hearing these words of his, she of the beautiful countenance replied:
"This man, my beloved, has been delivered by the king to the stake; behold him, like a miser with his wealth, he does not relinquish his life. (26)
Standing here, I am waiting to follow him who is near his death; he, being thirsty, asks me for water, and he suffers repeatedly.
With his neck impaled on a stake, this leader of living beings stands there eager for death; standing below, I am not able to make him drink water.
Having heard that, Aśokadatta, an ocean of compassion, then spoke these words appropriate for the occasion to his bride.
Aśokadatta said: "Mother, climb onto my shoulder and give him cool water. Having replied to him, "So be it," the young woman, filled with haste, [did so].
The son of the twice-born indeed climbed with his feet upon the shoulder of that [elephant], whose body was bent low; he then beheld fresh blood falling.
"What is this? he asked, suddenly lifting up his face; and having recognized that he was being devoured by her, that son of a brahmin—
Aśokadatta seized her anklet; then she departed, leaving behind that anklet which was set with jewels and fastened to her foot.
Taking that anklet, which was enriched with many inlaid gems, Aśokadatta departed from that cremation ground and went into the presence of the king.
Having reported all that had occurred at the cremation ground to the king, he then presented him with an anklet inlaid with highly precious jewels.
Having learned of that heroic deed, so difficult for other heroes to perform, the lord of the earth gave his daughter, named Madanalekhā, to him.
Then, on one occasion, having seen that divine anklet, the king thought: "Indeed, there must be another anklet equal to this excellent anklet. (37)
"Ashokadatta then reflected with reverence on where it might be obtained; having understood what the king desired," (38)
He reflected in his mind for the sake of recovering the anklet: "Since this anklet was previously obtained by me in the cremation ground... (39)
"Where shall I see her now, so that I may reach the interior of her anklets? Having reflected thus in many ways, the high-minded one reached a conclusion.
"I shall go to the cemetery and sell human flesh there, among all the rākṣasas, vetālas, piśācas, and others. (41)
When she is summoned by means of mantras, that Rākṣasī will also arrive; seizing her by force upon her arrival, I shall take that anklet from her.
Whether it be a thousand rākṣasas, or ten thousand piśācas, or even ten million vetālas, they are no match for my strength.
Having thus resolved in his mind, he went quickly to the cremation ground, selling human flesh after summoning the rākṣasas with mantras.
"Take it!"—thus he moved about, making it heard in all directions with a loud voice: "Human flesh is for sale; take it, take it! (45)
There, Rākṣasas, Vetālas, skeletons, Piśācas, and other hosts of spirits arrived, filled with great joy.
"We shall all eat meat that is most delicious. While they were all approaching there, she was surrounded by Rākṣasa maidens.
That rākṣasī also arrived, eager for the consumption of flesh; then the brahmin, searching about, beheld that rākṣasī.
"This is the very one seen before"—thus he attained recognition. To her, the son of the brahmin said: "Give me another anklet. (49)
Having heard his words, she was delighted and then spoke these words: "O Lord of Heroes, you previously took away my very anklet. (50)
"Take this second anklet, as beautiful as a jewel," he said, and having spoken thus, he gave him the anklet and his own beloved daughter.
Having obtained that beloved wife named Vidyutprabhā, who was endowed with beauty and youth, the brahmin rejoiced at being given her by Vidyutkeśī.
Vidyutkeśī gave her son-in-law a golden lotus; having obtained the golden lotus, as well as Vidyutprabhā and the anklet, he [departed].
Having addressed his mother-in-law, he quickly departed once more to the presence of the king; then Pratāpamukuṭa was delighted by the recovery of the anklet.
He praised the son of the twice-born for his endowment with heroism and fortitude; then that brahmin spoke in private to his beloved Vidyutprabhā.
"O Mother, O beloved, from where did you obtain this golden lotus? For I shall obtain others like it from somewhere, O fair-faced one. (56)
Then, in private, Vidyutprabhā said to her husband, the son of a twice-born: "O Lord, [I belong to] the king of Vetālas named Kapālavisphoṭa. (57)
"There is a certain divine lake adorned with golden lotuses; this was brought here by your mother-in-law while she was engaged in water-sports. (58)
Having heard these words, he said, "Lead me there. Then she suddenly led the Brahmin to that golden lake.
Then that son of a brahmin, desiring to seize the golden lotuses, slew all those who had wronged him, including the vetālas and others.
He himself beheld the lord of the Vetālas, Kapālavisphoṭa, who had slain his entire army, and he set about to kill him.
In the meantime, the lord of the Vidyādharas, possessed of great splendor and named Vijñaptikautuka, arrived by means of a celestial chariot and spoke to him.
"O best of Brahmins, do not commit such a rash act against Aśokadatta. Having heard that, the son of the twice-born [beheld] him seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
He beheld the lord of the Vidyādharas endowed with splendor in the sky; by the mere sight of him, the son of the twice-born was released from his curse.
Having cast off his human form, he attained a divine form; he was mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot and adorned with divine ornaments.
To Sukarṇa, who had been released from the curse, he spoke with curiosity and a desire to inform him: "O Sukarṇa, this brother of yours belongs to the great sage Gālava."
Having committed the sin of touching his daughter, he attained the state of a Vetāla due to that curse; and you too were cursed by him in the past, as you were a consenter to that sin.
"This curse of yours, who have committed but little sin, shall end upon my sight; however, that sage did not ordain an end to his own curse."
"Therefore come, O Sukarṇa, you are now freed from the curse; ascend to heaven. Then Sukarṇa spoke to that lord of the Vidyādhara clan: (69)
"O Lord of the Vidyādharas, without my elder brother present now, I have no desire at all to go to heaven, even though it is endowed with every enjoyment. (70)
"Tell me how the end of the curse may come for my brother. To him, the one of great splendor, who was eager to grant his request, replied: ||| 71 ||
Who else could possibly ward off this curse that is so difficult to avert? However, I shall now tell you something most secret.
In ancient times, this was narrated by Brahmā to the sages headed by Sanaka on the meritorious shore of the southern ocean, which is the refuge of all sacred fords.
Near Cakratīrtha, however, there is a most excellent sacred site; by the mere sight of which, even the multitudes of great sins [are destroyed]. (74)
They perish at that very moment; I do not know the fruit born of bathing there! If your elder brother were to go there and bathe, O most excellent one, [the merit would be immeasurable]. (75)
He would surely then abandon his state as a Vetāla born from the curse of Gālava. Having heard those words from his brother in the form of a Vetāla, Sukarṇa—
Accompanied [by his followers], he quickly proceeded to the shore of the southern ocean, which lies south of the holy ford known as Cakratīrtha and north of Gandhamādana.
Having approached the sacred ford described by Brahmā to Sanaka and the others, he reached the bank of that ford and spoke thus to his brother: || 78 ||
O brother, for the cessation of this terrible curse of Gālava, bathe soon in this sacred ford, the most excellent among all sacred fords.
On that day, O Brahmins, the sprays of that sacred bathing place, brought there by the wind, fell upon his limbs.
Then, by the touch of that spray, he abandoned his state as a vetāla and regained his human form as the son of a brahmin.
Then, having made a solemn resolve at that most excellent of holy places, the son of the twice-born suddenly immersed himself for the sake of ending his human state.
Rising up suddenly, he attained a divine form; mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, he was surrounded by celestial women.
Adorned with all ornaments, Sudarśana, together with his brother, praised that sacred ford and paid homage to it again and again.
And having honored the curiosity of the conscious beings, he departed for heaven; from that time forth, that holy ford was known by the name Vetālavarada.
The state of being a vetāla was destroyed merely by the touch of his spray for one who reached this sacred ford (tīrtha) located to the south of Cakratīrtha. || 86 ||
Those who occasionally perform their ablutions there become liberated while living; a merit equal to this sacred ford has never existed, nor will it ever exist.
Having abandoned his terrible state as a Vetāla, he then attained divinity. || 88 ||
Having made a formal resolve here and bathed at this auspicious place, O bestower of boons, one should, endowed with self-restraint, offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors.
Thus, O Brahmins, the majesty of that sacred site has been recounted to you, as well as how it acquired the name "Vetālavaradā."
Whoever recites this chapter or hears it shall be liberated.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Sudarśana and Sukarṇa from their Curse," within the Praise of Vetālavarada Tīrtha, in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 9 ||
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having bathed at the Vetālavarada Tīrtha, a man should then proceed very slowly toward Mount Gandhamādana.
This Gandhamādana mountain, which exists in the ocean in the form of a bridge, is the path to the world of Brahmā fashioned by the Creator of the Universe.
Thousands of lakhs of crores of lakes and rivers, as well as oceans of great merit, forests, and hermitages.
Meritorious fields such as Kṣetraja, Vedāraṇya, and others; and sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, along with Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras. || 4 ||
The Blessed Madhusūdana was there with Lakṣmī and Dharaṇī, and the four-faced one (Brahmā) together with Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī.
Heraṃba and Ṣaṇmukha, as well as the gods headed by Indra, the Ādityas and other planets, and likewise the eight Vasus, O twice-born ones.
The Pitṛs, the world-protectors, and likewise other hosts of deities [are present] for the destruction of multitudes of great sins and for the purification of the world.

Day and night they dwell here on Mount Gandhamādana; here Gaurī always remains, ever contented in the company of Hara. Here the play of the beloveds of the Kinnaras is perpetually awake. By the mere sight of it, men attain happiness of mind. (9)
The wives of the Siddhas and Cāraṇas, having made their dwelling upon his summit, constantly worship Śaṅkara, the husband of the Mountain-born Goddess.
Tens of millions of sins of Brahman-slaughter and tens of millions of sins of incestuous unions perish by the winds of Gandhamādana that touch one's body.
In ancient times, that Gandhamādana mountain stood in the midst of the great ocean with its surging waves, and it was indeed frequented by hosts of sages.
Then, once Nala had constructed the bridge, it became accessible to all human beings as well, being situated within its range by the command of Rāma.
One should pray to that mountain Gandhamādana, which is in the form of a bridge: "O mountain, O greatly meritorious one, saluted by all the gods! (14)
O best of mountains, even those gods beginning with Viṣṇu who serve you with faith—I am treading upon you with my feet. (15)
Forgive the blow of my foot out of compassion for me, who am evil-minded; show me Śaṅkara, who has made his dwelling upon your head.
Having thus prayed to that best of mountains, which is like a bridge, a man should then proceed with gentle steps toward the purifying Gandhamādana.
Having bathed there in the ocean at Mount Gandhamādana, one should then perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), even if it be only the size of a mustard seed.
The ancestors of that person attain satisfaction until the end of the eon; or he may offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors equal in size to śamī leaves.
Those dwelling in heaven attain liberation, and those residing in hell go to heaven; therefore, there is a great sacred site (tīrtha) above that, renowned throughout the worlds.
O Brahmins, on Mount Gandhamādana there exists a most meritorious and holy place, the best of all sacred sites, known by the name Pāpavināśana.

Merely by remembering it, one is no longer subject to dwelling in a womb; having reached that place, a man should bathe, which destroys the impurities of his own body. By bathing there, a man goes to Vaikuṇṭha—of this there is no doubt.
The sages said: O Sūta, tell us the majesty of the holy site named Pāpavināśa; for you, O great sage, having been instructed by Vyāsa, know everything.
The venerable Sūta said: O best of Brāhmaṇas, I shall relate to you this auspicious narrative concerning what occurred at the hermitage of Brahmā on the beautiful slopes of the Himavat.
His holy hermitage is situated on the auspicious slopes of the Himavat, within the beautiful Brahma-hermitage, and is filled with various groves of trees.
It was filled with many shrubs and creepers, frequented by deer and elephants, resounded with the voices of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, and was a delightful forest in full bloom.
It was filled with many enclosures and graced by ascetics, as well as by highly fortunate Brahmins who resembled the blazing sun and fire.
It was crowded with ascetics endowed with restrictive vows and observances, who were initiated for the sake of sacrifice, moderate in diet, and self-controlled.
It was surrounded by Vaidikas perfected in the study of the Vedas, and by those in the stages of studentship, householders, forest-dwellers, and mendicants. (29)

[He was attended] by the Vālakhilya sages, who were devoted to the conduct of their own stages of life and performed the duties prescribed for their respective castes, as well as by the Marīcis who had arrived there.
O twice-born ones, formerly in that hermitage, a certain Śūdra named Dṛḍhamati, impulsive and filled with joy, approached the presence of a Brāhmaṇa.
Having arrived at the hermitage and being honored by the ascetics, a Śūdra named Dṛḍhamati indeed prostrated himself with all eight limbs.
Seeing those hosts of sages, who were like gods and possessed of great majesty, performing various sacrifices, that Śūdraka was filled with joy.
Then the thought occurred to him to perform unsurpassed austerity; thereupon, having approached the sage Kulapati, the ascetic, he spoke to him.
Dṛḍhamati said: "O ascetic, salutations to you; protect me, O ocean of compassion! By your grace, O bull among the twice-born, I wish to practice righteousness. (35)
Therefore, O observer of noble vows, initiate me, who have come to you for sacrifice. O Brahmin, O best of beings, I am of inferior caste; by birth I am a Śūdra.
"I wish to perform service; be gracious to me who have sought refuge. When the Śūdra had spoken thus, the Brāhmaṇa then said to him:
The Kulapati said: "A Śūdra, being of low birth, cannot be initiated for a sacrifice; listen, if such is your intent, then devote yourself to service. (38)
Instruction should never be given to one of low birth; in giving instruction, a great fault accrues to the teacher. (39)
A wise man should not teach a Śūdra, nor should he perform sacrifices for him; likewise, he should not instruct a Śūdra in the scriptures, such as grammar and the like.
One should never cause a Śūdra to recite poetry, drama, or even the science of poetics (alaṃkāra), nor the Purāṇas or the Itihāsas. || 41 ||
And if a Brahmin should ever instruct a Śūdra in these [matters], the other Brahmins should expel that Brahmin from the village inhabited by the Brahmanical community.
One should abandon a twice-born man who instructs a Śūdra, treating him like a Caṇḍāla; and one should avoid from afar a Śūdra who is possessed of the syllables of the Veda.
Therefore, may prosperity be yours; serve the Brahmins with faith. For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born has been proclaimed by Manu and others.
"For you ought not to abandon your innate duty. Thus addressed by the sage, that Śūdra then reflected.
"What should I do today? For my faith in the vow was indeed firm from before; I shall strive this very day so that true knowledge may arise within me. (46)
Having thus resolved in his mind, the Śūdra Dṛḍhamati then went far from the hermitage and constructed an auspicious leaf-hut.
There indeed are temples for the deities, sacred shrines, flower gardens and the like, as well as the digging of tanks and similar works. || 48 ||
With faith, he performed rites for the sake of his own success in austerity, including ritual ablutions, observances, fasts, and so forth. (49)
Having performed the bali offering and offered oblations, he worshipped the deities; endowed with resolve and self-restraint, subsisting on fruit and having his senses conquered.
He constantly honored guests who arrived according to custom with bulbs, roots, flowers, and likewise fruits.
In this manner, indeed, a very long time passed for him; then, one named Sumati by name came to his hermitage.
A twice-born man born of Garga’s lineage, truthful and with senses subdued, honored the sage with a welcome and gratified him with fruits and other offerings.
While recounting meritorious stories, he inquired after his welfare; thus was he honored with prostrations and other marks of respectful service.
Having greeted him with blessings and accepted his hospitable reception, he, with a joyful heart, took leave of him and returned once more to his own hermitage.
Thus, day after day, the Brahmin, full of partiality toward this Śūdra, would come to his hermitage to see that one born of a Śūdra womb.
For a long time, that brahmin had association with one born of a Śūdra womb; having fallen under the sway of affection, he did not transgress what was spoken by the Śūdra.
Then the Śūdra, overcome by affection, spoke to the arrived twice-born man: "O Lord of Sages, tell me the entire procedure for the offerings to the gods and the ancestors. (58)
For the purpose of performing the rites for the ancestors and likewise for the rites for the gods, please instruct me in the mantras as well as the procedure for the Mahālaya ceremony.
"Tell me all this secret—the performance of the Aṣṭakā śrāddha and whatever else is Vedic—for you are indeed considered my guru. (60)
Thus addressed by the Śūdra, he instructed him in all of this; likewise, he caused him to perform the ancestral rites and other such duties.
When the ancestral rites had been performed by him, that twice-born man was dismissed and departed; then, after a long time, he was nourished by one of Śūdra birth.
Abandoned by the hosts of brahmins, that twice-born man met his death; led away by the soldiers of Vaivasvata, he was cast even into the hells.
Having experienced the hells in succession for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of kalpas, he finally became a sovereign lord at their conclusion.
Then he was born as a donkey, and after that as a village pig; then he was born as a dog, and afterwards he attained the state of a crow.
Then he attained the state of a Caṇḍāla, and after that he entered the womb of a Śūdra; subsequently he became a Vaiśya, and immediately thereafter a Kṣatriya.
Oppressed by powerful beings, he then indeed became a Brāhmaṇa; that twice-born one was invested with the sacred thread by his father in the eighth year from conception.
While living in his father’s house, devoted to the practice of virtuous conduct, he was once seized by a Brahma-rākṣasa while wandering in the forest.
Weeping, wandering, stumbling, bewildered, laughing, and lamenting, he constantly cried out "Alas! Alas! and thus abandoned his Vedic duties.
Seeing his son in such a state, the father was tormented by grief; taking his son with him out of affection, he went to Agastya for refuge. (70)
Having bowed to the sage with devotion, the father indeed informed him of the conduct of his son.
And then the Brahmin spoke to that preeminent sage born from a jar: "O Brahmin, this son of mine has been seized by a Brahma-rākṣasa. (72)
O Brahmin, do not resort to pleasure; protect him with a compassionate glance. I have no other son for the sake of liberating my ancestors from their debt. (73)
O Pot-born One, tell me the means for the destruction of his suffering; in the three worlds, no one is found who possesses ascetic power equal to yours.
"You have indeed been declared by the great sages to be the foremost among the devotees of Śiva; without you, there exists no protection for this son of mine. (75)
"Have mercy upon my father; for the virtuous are indeed compassionate by nature. Śrī Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by him, the one born from a water-jar (Agastya) then resorted to meditation.
Having meditated for a very long time, Agastya then spoke to the brahmin. Agastya said: "O high-minded one, this son of yours was a brahmin in a previous birth. (77)
This brahmin named Sumati indeed gave his wisdom to a śūdra; he taught him all the Vedic rites.
Therefore, after having experienced the hells for ten million times a thousand kalpas, he was born on earth at the end of that period in the wombs of immobile beings and the like.
Now, O son, by the remainder of your karma you have been born as a Brāhmaṇa; here you were seized by a Brahmarākṣasa sent by Yama.
"Indeed, because of a cruel sin committed in a previous birth, I shall tell you the means for the destruction of this Brahma-rākṣasa. (81)
Listen with faith, O Brahmin, and with a concentrated mind: in the southern ocean there is a great mountain in the form of a bridge.
The purifying Gandhamādana mountain, which is to be served by the deities, exists there; upon it is a great sacred ford (tīrtha) named Pāpavināśana.
There exists a well-known merit that destroys great sins, [and protects against] ghosts, spirits, piśācas, vetālas, and brahmarākṣasas. (84)
That holy ford is known as the destroyer of even great diseases; taking your son, go to that ford situated in the middle of the Setu.
"Being self-restrained, bathe your son at this sin-destroying holy ford; by bathing there for three days, the Brahma-rākṣasa will perish. (86)
No other means for its destruction exists on earth; therefore, go quickly to Rāmasetu, which bestows liberation.
"There, at the sacred ford named Pāpavināśa, have your son bathe; do not delay here, O twice-born one, but go with all haste."
Thus addressed, that twice-born man prostrated himself on the ground like a staff before Agastya; and having been permitted by him, he departed for Gandhamādana.
Accompanied by Suta, the lord of brahmins went to Pāpavināśana; having first made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), he performed ritual ablutions for three days on behalf of his son.
O best of Brahmins, the father himself bathed at Pāpavināśana; then his son was there liberated from the state of a Brahma-rākṣasa.
He was born free from disease, healthy, and possessing a beautiful form; enriched with all prosperity, he enjoyed manifold pleasures. || 92 ||
At the end of his body's life, he attained liberation through bathing at Pāpavināśana; his father also attained liberation at the end of his body by bathing there.
That Śūdra who is thus instructed, having experienced hells in succession and having been born in many contemptible wombs, [attains his state].
Thereafter, you were born as a vulture on Mount Gandhamādana; once, he went to the Pāpavināśana Tīrtha to drink water.
Having arrived, he drank the water and sprinkled his own body; at that very moment, possessing a divine form and adorned with all ornaments, [he stood there].
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with red sandalwood paste, he ascended a celestial chariot, adorned with umbrellas and chowries.
Surrounded by the most excellent women, he proceeded to the abode of the immortals.

Śrī Sūta said: Such indeed is the power of this holy place (tīrtha), which destroys sins, bestows heaven and liberation, is meritorious, and likewise serves as an expiation; it is frequented by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, and served by the gods.
O Brahmins, because it destroys sins, that place is indeed called Pāpanāśa; therefore, a man seeking his own welfare should bathe at Pāpavināśana.

Thus, O lords of sages, has this secret been told—the majesty of that destroyer of sins—by virtue of which, through ablution there, both the twice-born and the śūdra were instantly liberated despite their censurable deeds. (101)

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Power of the Destruction of Sins," within the Praise of Gandhamādana, in the Setu-māhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: Having bathed at Pāpanāśa, which destroys all sins, a man should then proceed to Sītāsaras to bathe according to the prescribed rules.
Whatever meritorious holy places exist within the universe, such as the Gaṅgā and others, they are for the complete purification of one's own sins.
The highly precious sacred fields, such as Kāśī and others, remain day and night within the Sītā lake, which destroys great sins.
They resort to the Sītāsaras lake for the pacification of their respective sins; there, a foolish [creature], drawn by the quality of its music, [enters] that lake.

Even the five-faced one (Śiva) dwells there as the destroyer of the five great sins. O Brahmins, in ancient times, having come to this very holy place and bathed with faith, Purandara was indeed liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
The sages said: O sage, how did the murder of a Brahmin come to pass for Vāsava in ancient times? And how was he liberated from it by bathing in the Sītā lake?
Śrī Sūta said: O twice-born ones, in ancient times there was a Rākṣasa named Kapālābharaṇa.
By virtue of a boon from Brahmā, he became invulnerable to all the gods; his best minister was named Śavabhakṣaṇa.
He possesses a hundred akṣauhiṇīs teeming with horses, elephants, and chariots; he also has a city known as Vaijayanta.
O twice-born ones, that powerful one adorned with a skull-dress resides in this city; having summoned Śavabhakṣa, his minister, he spoke to him.
O eater of corpses, O one of great heroism, you who are skilled in the mantra-śāstras! Having gone to the city of the gods and having utterly defeated the deities in battle, [we shall prevail]. (11)
We shall dwell with our soldiers in the delightful palace of Śakra; we shall sport in his Nandana grove with hosts of Apsarases such as Rambhā.
O brahmins, having heard those words of Kapālābharaṇa at that time, Śavabhakṣa spoke there, saying, "So be it."
Then the powerful Kapālābharaṇa, having established his heroic son Durmedhasa in the city, surrounded him with an army.
Desirous of fighting with the immortals, he set out for Amarāvatī with elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, amidst rising clouds of dust.
O Brahmins, drying up the oceans and rivers, pulverizing even the mountains, and likewise making heaven and earth resound with the noise of his war-drums.
By the neighing sounds of horses, the trumpeting of elephants, the fierce clatter of chariot wheels, and the lion-like roars of the infantry; (17)
Making the ears of the elephants of the quarters deaf, he went to the city of the gods, desiring to fight with the immortals.
Then, O twice-born ones, having heard the tumultuous sound of the army, Indra and the other gods, intent on battle, marched out from the city.
Then a battle took place between the gods and the Rākṣasas, such as had never before been seen in the world, nor even heard of.
Then Indra and the other gods struck down the Rākṣasas in battle, and the Rākṣasas, desiring victory, struck down the gods in the fray. (21)
A duel took place between the gods and the rākṣasas, and in that battle, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra fought with Kapālābharaṇa.
O best of brahmins, Śavabhakṣa fought with Yama, Kauśika with Varuṇa, and Rudhirākṣa fought with Kubera. || 23 ||
Fond of meat, addicted to liquor, cruel of gaze, and terrifying—these four valiant ones are the younger brothers of Kapālābharaṇa.
The Aśvins fought with Agni and Vāyu against one another in battle; then the highly powerful Yama, moving with great speed, [struck] with his staff of death (kāladaṇḍa).
Having slain Śavabhakṣa, Yama sent him to his abode; in that battle, Yama struck down thirty akṣauhiṇīs belonging to him.
In the battle, Varuṇa struck off the head of Kauśika with a javelin; Kubera struck off the head of Rudhirākṣa with a spear.
O brahmins, those younger brothers of Kapālābharaṇa, who were like the Aśvins, Agni, and Vāyu, were slain in battle and went to the abode of Yama.
O twice-born ones, even a hundred akṣauhiṇīs were slain by the Lord of the Gods in battle; within half a watch, they departed for the abode of Yama.
Then Kapālābharaṇa, beholding his own army slaughtered, took up his bow and sharp arrows of great velocity.
He rushed at Śakra in battle and cried out, "Stay! Stay! Then he struck Śakra’s head with five arrows.
Before they could reach him, that slayer of Vṛtra cut them down with arrows in the battle; then, in the fray, he who was adorned with a skull-garland took up a trident.
He hurled it at Devendra, and he struck him with that spear; then [the Lord], adorned with a skull-ornament, [threw] a mace a hundred cubits long.
He took up an iron [mace] fashioned from the weight of five thousand *tulās* and struck Śakra in the region of the chest during the battle.
Then Śakra, having fainted, sat down on the seat of the chariot; thereafter, Bṛhaspati, having recited the Mṛtasañjīvinī mantra, [restored him].
He performed the wonderful feat of reviving the husband of Pulomajā in battle; then, having mounted Airāvata, he went into the presence of Kapālābharaṇa.
Then Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka and lord of Śacī, arrived to strike him with his thunderbolt in a single blow. (37)
In battle, he [struck] the one adorned with skulls—along with his chariot, horses, bow, banner, quivers, and armor—with the thunderbolt. (38)
Enraged, he reduced him to pieces like sesame seeds and even to fine particles; thus was that great hero, Kapālābharaṇa, slain in battle.

Happiness came to the entire world, which had long been suffering; yet the terrible sin of Brahman-murder arising from the slaying of the Rākṣasa then pursued Purandara, making the ten directions resound with its roar.
The sages said: "O Sūta, O sage, that one adorned with a skull was not a Brāhmaṇa-rākṣasa; so how did the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa pursue Indra because of his slaying? (41)
The venerable Sūta said: O lords of sages, I shall declare the supreme secret, which is most wonderful.
Listen with faith, having composed your minds: formerly, in the regions of the Vindhya mountains, there was a Rākṣasa named Trivakra.
His wife was endowed with virtues and possessed of the quality of beauty; named Suśīlā, she had beautiful hips and was marked by all auspicious characteristics.
Once, that graceful woman, lovely-limbed, well-attired, and sweetly smiling, wandered about in the forest regions at the foot of the Vindhya mountains.
In that forest there lived a great sage named Śuci, who was devoted to austerity and meditative absorption, and intent upon the study of the Vedas.

That woman of excellent complexion went near his hermitage; seeing her, the sage, tormented by the god of love, lost his self-control. Approaching that lady of beautiful hips, the best of sages spoke to her. (47)
Śuci said: "O beautiful woman, welcome to you! Whose wife are you, O lady of radiant smiles? (48)
What is the purpose of your coming to this most terrifying forest? You are weary, O lady of beautiful hips; stay here in my hermitage.
Thus addressed, that woman of beautiful hips replied to the sage: "O sage, I am the wife of the Rākṣasa Trivakra; my name is Suśīlā. (5)
"Desiring to gather flowers, I have come to this forest, O Sage; I am childless, sent by my husband who longs for a son. (51)
"By propitiating the pure sage, you shall obtain a son from him"; having been thus instructed by her husband, she has come to you. (52)
"O Sage, show compassion toward me and procreate a son for me. Thus addressed, the pure sage spoke to that virtuous woman: || 53 ||
Śuci said: "O lady of excellent character, upon seeing you, great joy now arises within me; please fulfill the vast ocean of my heart's desire. (54)
Having spoken thus, that sage sported there with her for three days; then the sage, being pleased, spoke to her, who possessed a beautiful form and an excellent complexion. (55)
In your womb, O one of great heroism, there shall be one named Kapālābharaṇa; he will protect the kingdom for a long time and rule the earth. || 56 ||
For a thousand years, the calf gratified Brahmā through his ascetic penance; consequently, he was not subject to death at the hands of any gods other than Indra.
"May such a son as this be yours, with prowess equal to Indra. Having spoken thus, the sage went to Kāśī, the city of Śiva.
Suśīlā also gave birth to a son adorned with a skull-ornament; O best of sages, Śakra struck him down in battle with his thunderbolt.
Because Indra had slain him who was born from the seed of Śuci, Śakra Puraṃdara was seized by the sin of Brahman-murder.
Then Śakra, overwhelmed by fear, fled through all the worlds; as he ran, the personified sin of Brahmin-slaughter pursued him, running right after him.
O best of sages, for he was pursued by the sin of Brahman-slaughter, Śakra reached the assembly of the Grandfather with an exceedingly distressed heart.
That Purandara reported the Brahman-slaying to Brahmā, saying: "O Blessed One, O Lord of the World, this Brahman-slaying is most terrifying."
