"O Knower of Beings, she afflicts me; tell me how she may be destroyed. Thus addressed by Purandara, Brahmā spoke to the Lord of Heaven: bādhate māṃ prajānātha tasyā nāśaṃ bravīhi me | puraṃdareṇaivamukto brahmā prāha divaspatim || 64 || "O Knower of Beings, she afflicts me; tell me how she may be destroyed. Thus addressed by Purandara, Brahmā spoke to the Lord of Heaven:
Brahmā said: "O Indra, go to Sītākuṇḍa on the Gandhamādana mountain; having worshipped Sadāśiva with sacrifices on the bank of Sītākuṇḍa," (65)
And you should bathe in that auspicious lake which removes all sins; then, O Śakra, being purified and released from the murder of a Brahmin, you shall become cleansed.
One shall go again to the world of the gods, freed from all suffering; Sītākuṇḍa bestows liberation and is a meritorious site that removes all sins.
It is the supreme nectar that destroys the multitude of great sins, pacifies all sufferings, and eliminates all poverty. (69)
O slayer of Vṛtra, since it bestows wealth and grain, is pure, and grants such stations as Vaikuṇṭha, perform your sacrifice there at the Sītā lake.
Thus addressed, that king of the gods departed for Gandhamādana; having reached Sītāsaras, O Brahmins, he bathed and performed sacrifices in its vicinity.
Having been liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin, he returned once more to his own city. Such is the power of that supreme holy site, the Kuṇḍa of Sītā. 71.
For the sake of providing proof to Rāghava, Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, entered the fire in the presence of all the gods.
Having emerged again from the fire, she who was beautiful in all her limbs established an excellent sacred site (tīrtha) in her own name for the sake of protecting the world.
Sītā herself bathed there; therefore, it is remembered as Sītāsaras. Whatever man bathes there shall obtain all his desires.

O best of the twice-born, having touched the waters there, having given various kinds of gifts, and having performed sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees, a man shall go to the world of the Supreme Lord.

O lords of sages, this greatness of the Sītā lake has been thus proclaimed by you; indeed, by hearing or reciting it, one shall enjoy pleasures even in this very world and obtain happiness in the hereafter as well. (76)

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Liberation of Indra from the Sin of Brahmin-Slaughter," within the Praise of Sītāsaras, in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having bathed in the highly meritorious Sītākuṇḍa, a man should then, with a concentrated mind, proceed to the Maṅgala Tīrtha.
In that lake, Kamalā, the beloved of Viṣṇu, always resides; indeed, it is there that the gods resort for the removal of misfortune.
All the sages, headed by Śatakratu, constantly assemble at this very tīrtha which purifies the world. (3)
I shall proclaim this meritorious history that destroys all sins: in ancient times, there was a king named Manojava, born of the lunar dynasty.
He protected the earth, girt by the oceans, according to righteousness; he worshipped the gods with sacrifices and honored the Brahmins with heaps of food.
Every year he gratified the ancestral deities with the kavya offerings; he constantly studied the three Vedas and recited the meaningful scriptures.
He conquered his enemies by his valor; Prāṇa, Sīda, Īśa, and Keśava took their seats; he delighted in the treatises on political ethics and likewise studied the great Mantras.
Thus that king protected the earth according to dharma; while that king was ruling, his kingdom became free of all thorns.
Egoism arose for him, which brought about the destruction of his wealth of sons; wherever there is egoism, there also arise greed and pride.
O best of Brahmins, lust, anger, violence, and likewise envy that causes delusion—these become the causes for the destruction of prosperity.
The man in whom these are found perishes in an instant, along with his sons, grandsons, and all his wealth.
And there was always in him a malice that caused him to be hated by people; likewise, for one whose mind is agitated by malice and who possesses vain pride, [there is no success]. (12)
The mind of that greedy man, corrupted by lust, became thus resolved: "I shall impose taxes upon the village of brahmins. (13)
Having thus resolved in his mind at that time, the king indeed seized the wealth and grain of the brahmins out of greed.
Out of passion, he seized the wealth belonging to the gods such as Śiva and Viṣṇu, as well as that belonging to the high-souled Brahmins of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the other deities. (15)
"This man, his intellect deluded by egoism, has seized the fields; thus he is one joined with injustice and an adversary of the gods and the twice-born. (16)
O best of the twice-born, due to the ripening of his evil karma, a powerful enemy, the ruler of a foreign land, besieged the city with cruelty.
O best of Brahmins, the wicked-minded Golabha, joined by a fourfold army, fought for six months. Thus the battle with Golabha took place. (19)
Then, King Manojava, whose soul was devoted to egoism, was defeated in battle by Golabha and deprived of his kingdom.
Accompanied by his sons and wife, that Manojava entered the forest; meanwhile, Golabha remained for a long time protecting the city of Manojava.

O best of Brahmins, having driven him out in battle, that powerful one, though endowed with the speed of thought, was filled with grief along with his wife and sons, even though he possessed a fourfold army.
Emaciated by hunger and constantly stumbling, he entered a great forest resounding with swarms of crickets and terrifying with tigers and wild beasts.
In that most terrible forest, filled with the trumpeting of elephants and crowded with boars and buffaloes, he was tormented by hunger.
The infant son of Manojava begged food from his father: "O Mother, give me food; hunger oppresses me greatly. (24)
In this manner, the boy also made a request to his own mother; and there, his parents heard the speech of their son.
Overwhelmed by grief, they suddenly fell into a state of delusion; then the king spoke to his wife, who was known by the name Sumitrā.
Fainting again and again, with his throat, lips, and palate parched, he said: "O Sumitra, what shall I do? Where shall I go? What is my refuge? (27)
"This son of mine, tormented by hunger, will die before long. O beloved, for what purpose did the Creator create me, so ill-fated and in vain? (28)
"Who indeed shall deliver me from this suffering born of evil karma? Neither Śambhu nor Hari was worshipped by me in my previous births. (29)
Likewise, O beloved, other deities headed by Sūrya and Vibhāvasu [were cursed]; and because of that sin, O beautiful one, I am now in this birth.
Overcome by egoism, I seized the lands of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas; I also misappropriated the wealth belonging to the gods, such as Śiva and Viṣṇu. (31)
Thus, due to the abundance of my evil deeds, I was defeated by Golabha; I have come to this desolate forest together with you and my son.
"Without food, without wealth, miserable, hungry, and thirsty, how shall I give food to my hungry son? (33)
"O lady of pure smiles, I have not given food to the Brāhmaṇas; nor have I worshipped Śambhu, Viṣṇu, or any other deity. (34)
"Because of that sin, this suffering has come upon me today; previously, I neither offered oblations into the fire nor did I visit sacred fords. (35)
O beloved, on the anniversary of their deaths, the śrāddha for the mother and the śrāddha for the father should be performed according to the rules of either the ekoddiṣṭa or the pārvaṇa rite.
"O blessed lady, I have indeed not provided even abundant food; because of that sin, this suffering has come upon me today. (37)
O beloved, in the month of Caitra, under the asterism Citrā, I [offered] a refreshing drink made of sweet jackfruit or perhaps plantain fruit. (38)
Likewise, a parasol with its staff, a pair of beautiful sandals, betel leaves, flowers, sandalwood, and unguents; (39)
"No gift was given by me to those learned in the Vedas for the satisfaction of Citragupta; because of that sin, this suffering has come upon me today. (40)
Neither the Aśvattha nor the mango tree, nor the Nyagrodha, the Tiṃtiṇī, the Picumanda, the Kapittha, or likewise the Āmalakī tree [should be used]. (41)
"Or perhaps a coconut tree was planted for the relief of travelers; by that sin, this suffering has come upon me today. (42)
I have not performed the sweeping of the temples of Śiva and Viṣṇu; nor have I dug a pond, nor even a well or a lake. (43)
O beloved, neither a flower garden nor a grove of tulasī was planted by me; nor were temples dedicated to Śiva and Viṣṇu ever constructed by me.

"Because of that sin, this suffering has come upon me today. O beautiful one, during the month sacred to the ancestors, I did not perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha for the sake of my forefathers, nor even the Aṣṭakā Śrāddha. (45)
O beloved, the daily śrāddha, the optional śrāddha, and the occasional śrāddha were not performed, nor were sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees offered according to the prescribed rules.
The month-long fast was not performed, nor was the fast on the eleventh day; even during the month of Dhanus, at the hour of dawn, [he failed to worship] Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and the other deities.
"O auspicious lady, although I worshipped according to the prescribed rites, I did not offer an oblation of food (naivedya). Because of that sin, this suffering has come upon me today. (48)
I did not perform the chanting of the names of Hari and Śaṅkara, nor the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) according to the seven verses spoken by Jābāla. (49)
O blessed lady, neither have I worn ashes nor have I worn rudrākṣa beads; likewise, I have not performed the recitation of the Rudra-hymns nor the five-syllabled mantra. (50)
Likewise, O blessed lady, neither the recitation of the Puruṣasūkta nor that of the eight-syllabled mantra was performed by me, nor was any other accumulation of merit ever undertaken. (51)
"By that sin, this suffering has come upon me today. Thus lamenting, the king, dejected in mind, addressed his wife.
O Brahmins, he fell into a swoon and collapsed upon the ground; seeing her husband fallen, his wife Sumitrā [also fell].
Then, embracing him, she, together with her son, lamented in great distress: "O my lord, O great king, upholder of the lineage of Soma! (54)
"Leaving me behind in this desolate forest with my son, where have you gone—to me, who am now protectorless, following after you like a doe terrified by a lion? (55)
"O Indra among kings, if you are dead, then I too shall follow you immediately; as a widow, I shall not remain for even a moment. (56)
"Behold your father fallen on the ground, O son Candrakānta! Thus addressed, the king's son Candrakānta was also afflicted by hunger.
Then, embracing his father, he wept silently; in the meantime, O Brahmins, [a man] appeared, covered with matted hair and bark garments.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, his forehead marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra), adorned with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, and wearing a white sacred thread; || 59 ||
A sage named Parāśara arrived there by chance; perceiving that sound, he who was esteemed by the virtuous and the good [approached]. (60)
Then, seeing that Parāśara had arrived, Sumitrā, devoted to her husband, together with her son, paid homage at his feet.
Then Parāśara consoled this Sumitrā and comforted her with the words, "Do not grieve, O beautiful lady," and the great sage, the son of Śakti, questioned Sumitrā.
Parāśara said: "Who are you, O lady of beautiful hips, and who is this man who has fallen before me?"
"And who might this child be to you? Tell me the truth, O auspicious one. When she was thus questioned by the sage, the virtuous woman spoke to that great muni.
Sumitra said: "O best of sages, this man is my husband and I am indeed his wife; and this son named Candrakānta was begotten by us both. (65)
This king named Manojava is born of the lunar dynasty; he is the son of Vikramāḍhya, powerful and equal to Viṣṇu in valor.
I am his wife, named Sumitrā, devoted to my husband; King Manojava was utterly defeated in battle by Golabha.
O Brahman-sage, fallen from his kingdom and without support, he entered the forest—terrible with its fierce creatures—accompanied by me and his son.
Afflicted by hunger, our son indeed begged for food; the king, Vidhura, being himself without food, saw his son tormented by hunger. (69)
"O Brahmin, with a mind overwhelmed by grief, he fainted and fell to the ground. Having heard those words, spoken in syllables choked with sorrow, [he replied: 70.
The sage Śaktiputra spoke to that devoted wife Sumitrā, the consort of King Manojava, who was like a flame of fire.
Parāśara said: "O wives of Manojava, let there be no fear whatsoever; your misfortune shall truly come to an end before long. (72)
"O blessed lady, having abandoned her fainting fit, your husband will rise in an instant; then the brahmin Parāśara [will touch] that lord of men with his hand. (73)
While reciting the mantra and meditating upon the three-eyed god, he touched me; then King Manojava was touched by the hand of the great sage.

Suddenly rising there, having abandoned his swoon of darkness, the lord of the earth then bowed to the sage Parāśara and, being exceedingly delighted, spoke with palms joined in reverence to that best of Brahmins.
Manojava said: O Sage Parāśara, today, by virtue of serving your lotus feet— || 76 ||
My fainting has immediately vanished and my sin has been destroyed; the sight of you can never be attained by those devoid of merit. (77)
"Protect me with your compassionate gaze, for I have been driven from my city by enemies. Thus addressed, that sage spoke to the king, who was as swift as thought.
Parāśara said: O King, I shall tell you the means for conquering your enemies at the highly meritorious Rāmasetu on Mount Gandhamādana. (79)
There exists a sacred ford (tīrtha) that bestows all sovereign powers; for the benefit of all the worlds, Rāghava [performed his rites] in that lake. || 80 ||
O best of kings, you shall always be attended by Lakṣmī and Sītā; having gone there with your sons and wife, bathe with devotion. (81)
O King, perform the Śrāddha and other rites on its bank as well; for when this is done by you, O King, Alakṣmī, who causes distress, will depart.
"O King, by the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), it will undoubtedly meet its destruction; and you shall obtain all auspicious blessings before long. (83)
Having conquered your enemies in battle, you shall regain your kingdom; therefore, O Manojava, together with your wife and son, [you shall dwell there].
"Go to that Maṅgalatīrtha on Mount Gandhamādana; I too shall come, desiring to show you favor. (85)
Having spoken thus, Parāśara, together with those three chief kings, set out toward the Setu to bathe in the auspicious tīrtha.
Accompanied by the king and others, the sage traversed various forests, forest regions, and numerous villages of bandits.
He proceeded to the auspicious Maṅgala-tīrtha on Mount Gandhamādana; having made his formal resolve there according to the rules, that bull among sages bathed.
He also bathed the king and the others according to the prescribed rites; and there, O protector of the earth, the king performed a śrāddha ceremony for the satisfaction of his ancestors.
There, the king, along with his wife and son, bathed for three months; thereafter, the sage Parāśara bathed according to the prescribed rules.
In this manner, that bull among sages bathed for three months together with them at the highly meritorious place named Maṅgala, which destroys all inauspiciousness.
Then, at the conclusion of that, the sage Parāśara imparted to Rāma the single-syllable mantra which destroys all misfortunes.
There, at that sacred ford, the king recited the single-syllable mantra for forty days, following the very path prescribed by the sage.
O twice-born ones, as he was thus practicing the single-syllable mantra, by the grace of the sage, a firm bow appeared before him.
There were also two inexhaustible quivers and two swords with golden hilts; one shield, one mace, and likewise one excellent club.
A single conch shell, a great-sounding chariot yoked with horses, along with its charioteer and banner, rose up from the sacred ford and stood before them.
By the grace of the sage, a golden armor, radiant like the fire Vaiśvānara, appeared from that sacred bathing place.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, crowns, bracelets, and other ornaments, it rose up before the king from that most excellent of sacred fords.
Then, from the sacred ford, there appeared a thousand divine garments and a garland named Vaijayantī, adorned with golden lotuses.
Having observed all of this, he reported it to the sage; then the sage Parāśara took water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
They consecrated the lord of men with water purified by mantras; then the king, having been consecrated, was graced by the sage.
The youth was armored, wearing a breastplate and a sword, bearing a bow and arrows, and adorned with necklaces, armlets, a crown, bracelets, and other ornaments.
Wearing celestial garments and seated upon a chariot yoked with horses, the king shone exceedingly, like the sun at midday. || 103 ||
There, the great sage [bestowed] upon that king the Brahmā weapon, along with its ancillaries, its secret lore, its method of discharge, and its method of withdrawal.
Then the son of Śakti, Manojava, instructed King Sumitra with the blessings of the sage preceding his words. (105)
Urged on, he mounted his chariot, bowed to the bull among sages, circumambulated him, and was then granted permission by the great seer.
Accompanied by his wife and son, he set out for victory; having reached his own city, the king then blew that conch shell.
Then, hearing the sound of the conch, Golabha, together with his army, quickly set out for battle against King Manojava.
A battle took place between the king and Golabha for three days; then, on the fourth day, [he encountered] Golabha along with his army.
In battle, King Manojava destroyed [his opponent] with the Brahmāstra; thereafter, having reached his own city with his sons and wife, that king [reigned]. (110)
Protecting the entire earth, he enjoyed it together with his wife; from that time forward, this king indeed never again indulged in egoism.
The king likewise avoided such faults as envy; devoted to non-violence and self-controlled, he remained ever dedicated to righteousness. (112)
In this manner, that lord of the earth protected [the kingdom] for a thousand years; thereafter, O Indra among kings, having become dispassionate, he entrusted the kingdom to his son.
He went to the auspicious pilgrimage site on Mount Gandhamādana; there he performed penance, meditating upon Sadāśiva within his heart.
Then, after a short time, having cast off his body, King Manojava went to the world of Śiva by virtue of the majesty of that sacred ford.
O Brahmins, his wife Sumitrā also then embraced his body and ascended the funeral pyre; she attained that very same world.
Śrī Sūta said: Such is the power of that sacred ford named Śrīmaṅgala, where King Manojava bathed in that most excellent tīrtha.
Having conquered her enemies, she went to the world of Śiva with her wife at the end of her body; therefore, Maṅgalatīrtha should be resorted to with every effort. 118.

This sacred ford is exceedingly beautiful and auspicious, always bestowing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men; it is a fire that consumes heaps of sins like straw and cotton. O best of the twice-born, resort to it for the sake of emancipation. 119.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Manojavā and Lakṣmī," in the Praise of Maṅgalatīrtha, within the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: Having bathed in the great holy site named Maṅgala and become free from sin, a man should thereafter proceed to the sacred field known as Ekāntarāmanātha.
There, Rāma, the Lord of the World, was surrounded by Jānakī and Lakṣmaṇa, as well as by the monkeys headed by Hanumān.
O Brahmins, out of a desire to bestow grace upon the worlds, she always remains present there; indeed, a merit-bestowing well named Amṛtavāpikā exists in that place.
For those men who immerse themselves in it, there is no fear born of old age or death; for that man who bathes with faith in this pool of nectar.
By the grace of Śaṅkara, he attains immortality for those who immerse themselves in this pond, which destroys even the most grievous sins.
Hara always stands upon its bank to bestow the state of immortality. The sages said: "For what reason is this called the 'Pool of Immortality' (Amṛtavāpī)? (6)
O you who are instructed by Vyāsa, please tell this to us out of compassion, as well as the majesty of the pond named Amṛtā; for no satiety arises in us, who drink the nectar of your words. (7)
The venerable Sūta said: The name of this [goddess] is "Amṛtā," and her majesty is captivating.
I shall explain this in detail; listen, O best of the twice-born! Formerly, on the slopes of the Himavat, which were crowded with various sages... (9)
It was frequented by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Devas, and Kinnaras, and it was teeming with lions, tigers, boars, elephants, buffaloes, and other creatures.
It was densely filled with *tamāla*, *tāla*, *hintāla*, *campaka*, and *aśoka* trees, and graced by swans, cuckoos, *dātyūha* birds, ruddy geese, and other such creatures.

Surrounded by lakes abounding with lotuses, blue water-lilies, white lilies, and night-blooming water-lilies, [he saw] the younger brother of the pot-born [Agastya], who was truthful, virtuous, eloquent, and self-controlled.
Seeking liberation and beloved by Śaṅkara, he dwells constantly performing austerities, worshipping Śambhu three times a day with wild roots, fruits, and other offerings.
Dedicated to the performance of the twilight devotions, he honored and worshipped guests who arrived near his hermitage with forest-grown foods, and he tended the sacred fire.
Joyfully reciting the great mantras such as the Gāyatrī at the appropriate times, he should abandon sleep during the Brāhma-muhūrta, contemplating upon Viṣṇu.
O Brahmins, performing his bath at dawn, bowing to the twilight with a serene mind, chanting the Gāyatrī, and worshipping Hari and Śaṅkara; || 16 ||
He was a student of the Vedas and a reciter of the Shastras; he honored guests at midday, listened to the recitations of the Puranas, and was untiring in his fire-rituals.

O twice-born ones, he was constantly devoted to the five great sacrifices, offering the Vaiśvadeva and bali oblations; every year he performed the śrāddha for his parents as well as other ancestral rites.
Thus he passed his time, intent upon constant religious observances; and as he was thus engaged, performing supreme austerity, [the following occurred].
For a thousand years he passed with his mind fixed on Śaṅkara; nevertheless, Śaṅkara did not then manifest himself before him.
Then that brother of Agastya, during the summer, stood in the midst of five fires, fixing his gaze upon the sun and observing a vow of silence.
Standing motionless on his left little toe, with his arms raised and without support, he performed most rigorous penance.
Then Mahādeva, the ocean of compassion, with a serene soul, appeared, illuminating the ten directions with his own radiance.
Then the sage beheld Śambhu seated upon his bull together with Ambā; having seen him, he bowed down and praised the Lord, the husband of Bhavānī.
The sage said: Salutations to you, O Lord of Pārvatī, O Blue-throated One, O Maheśvara! O Śiva, O Rudra, O Mahādeva, salutations to you, O all-pervading Śambhu! (25)
O Śrīkaṇṭha, O Lord of Umā, O wielder of the trident, O destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, O imperishable one, O bearer of the Gaṅgā, O Virūpākṣa, salutations to you, O Rudra, to your wrath! (26)

O Bringer of the End, O Enemy of Kama, O God of gods, O Lord of the world! O Master, O Paśupati, O Śarva, salutations to you, the wielder of the hundred bows! Salutations to the destroyer of Dakṣa and Yakṣas; salutations to the Lord of the sinews! Salutations to you, the Wanderer; salutations to the Lord of the nourished. || 28 ||
Again and again, salutations to you, O Mahādeva, abode of compassion! O Three-eyed One, deliver me from the ocean of worldly existence, which is so difficult to cross. (29)
Thus praised by Agastya’s brother, Śambhu spoke, pleasing with his own words the sage who was the younger brother of the Pot-born one.
Īśvara said: O sinless one born from a jar, I shall tell you the means to liberation: there is a great sacred site (tīrtha) in the midst of the Setu on Mount Gandhamādana.
It is situated not far from the sacred ford named Maṅgala; go there, perform your ablutions, and then you shall attain liberation.
There is no other easier means for your liberation than resorting to that sacred ford; indeed, even I am unable to describe the specific excellence of that sacred ford.
O best of sages, you should not entertain any doubt in this matter today; therefore, go to that very place if you desire the destruction of worldly existence.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Īśa vanished right there; then, at the word of the God, the uterine brother of Agastya [arrived].
Having gone to the bridge over the ocean, he quickly reached that sacred ford on Mount Gandhamādana which had been described by Īśvara himself.
There, at that most meritorious holy site which bestows liberation upon those who bathe, there is the auspicious ornament of the sacred field known as Ekāntarāmanātha.
That twice-born one indeed bathed according to the prescribed rules for three years; then, in the fourth year, the great sage became established in meditative absorption.
By means of yoga, having ascended the vital breath through the Brahma-nāḍī to the crown of the head, he caused his life-breaths to exit there through the Brahma-randhra.
Then, by the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), this younger brother of Agastya cast off his body and attained supreme liberation.
Because of the power of bathing at that sacred ford, all his suffering was destroyed, and the younger brother of Agastya attained the state of deathlessness.
Therefore, O lords of sages, it acquired the renown as "Amṛtavāpī" (the Pool of Nectar). Those men who, at this sacred site, remain diligent for three years, [attain immortality]. || 42 ||

Those who perform their ablutions there truly attain immortality; thus, O Brahmins, its fame as the "Amṛtavāpī" (Pool of Nectar) and its majesty have been recounted to you. What more do you wish to hear?
The sages said: O sage, that sacred field is indeed known as Ekāntarāmanātha.
O Sūta, how did they come together? You ought to tell us this, O tiger among sages; our desire to hear it is very great. (45)
Śrī Sūta said: Formerly, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, accompanied by Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa, was joined by his brother Lakṣmaṇa and by Hanumān, who was skilled in counsel.
While the bridge was being constructed by the monkeys in the midst of the ocean, he, meditating on Sītā in his mind, consulted with her in private.
While those mantras were being recited for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa and the others, the ocean roared intensely with its waves surging even more violently.
As the ocean roared with a terrifying, great sound, they could not hear one another's words as they spoke to each other.
Then, slightly incensed, his eyes crooked with a frown, Rāma restrained the ocean at that time by the mere play of knitting his brows.
O best of Brahmins, he consulted with them regarding the slaughter of the Rākṣasas; for it was there in private that Rāghava deliberated together with them.
O twice-born ones, that sacred field became known as Ekāntarāmanātha; it was this very ocean that was bound by the playful knitting of Rāma’s eyebrows.
Even today, still water is seen in those regions; this is that most excellent sacred field known as Ekāntarāmanātha.
Having arrived and bathed in the Pool of Immortality (Amṛtavāpī) according to the prescribed rules, even those who worship Rāma and the other deities shall all attain liberation.

O best of the twice-born, those who are devoid of the discernment of non-dual knowledge, lacking dispassion, bereft of meditative absorption, and abandoned by the performance of sacrifices and other rites—having bathed here, they shall go to immortality.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Agastya’s Brother," within the Praise of Amṛtavāpī, in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 13 ||
The venerable Sūta said: Having bathed in the Amṛtavāpī and having worshipped Ekāntarāghava, a man who has conquered his senses should then proceed to the Brahmakuṇḍa to bathe.
In the middle of the Setu, on Mount Gandhamādana, there is a great sacred site (tīrtha) renowned as Brahmakuṇḍa, which is the panacea for all poverty.
There exists the sight of Brahmakuṇḍa, which destroys tens of millions upon tens of millions of sins of killing a Brahmin and annihilates the entire flood of all evils.
What need has he of many holy fords, what need of austerities, or what need of sacrifices? What need has he of great gifts who beholds the Brahmakuṇḍa? || 4 ||
O twice-born ones, bathing even once in Brahmakuṇḍa is the cause for attaining Vaikuṇṭha; likewise, by whomsoever the ashes produced from Brahmakuṇḍa have been worn— || 5 ||
His three attendant deities are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; he who [applies] the Tripuṇḍra with the ashes produced from the Brahma-kuṇḍa...

It bestows upon him absolute liberation, which is then held in the palm of his hand; of this there is no doubt. Even a single atom of that ash, if it should be worn upon the forehead, [achieves this].

At that very moment his liberation shall occur; no deliberation is required in this matter. Furthermore, that mortal who performs the smearing of ashes (uddhūlana) with the ashes from that sacrificial pit [attains the same]. || 8 ||
Śaṅkara may or may not know how to describe the fruit of the merit of one who does not wear the ashes produced from the Brahma-kuṇḍa.
He shall fall into the Raurava hell until the moon and stars perish—unless he applies the smearing of ashes or the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with the ash from the Brahmakuṇḍa.
That lowest of men who delights in reviling the ashes produced from the Brahma-kuṇḍa shall never experience happiness.
The wise man should infer its origin from the confusion [of elements] at the time of creation; this ash, produced from the Brahma-kunda, is the purifier of the world.
If a person says that [the lineage] is equal to other ashes or even inferior, a wise man should infer that there was a mixture of castes at its origin. (13)
Even while this ash produced from the Brahma-kuṇḍa remains present, the man who wears the Tripuṇḍra with other ashes [is at fault].
A wise person should infer its potential for confusion at the time of its origin: that there might be some mortal who would never wear this ash. (15)
A wise person should infer its impurity at the very moment of its origin; for he who gives to a twice-born man ashes produced from the *brahmakuṇḍa* [is guilty]. (16)
By him the earth, bounded by the four oceans, has been given; no doubt should be entertained here, for I swear this three times. (17)
"Truth, truth, and again truth—raising his arm, he declares: 'O best of the twice-born, wear the sacred ash produced from the Brahma-kuṇḍa!'"
For this purifying ash originates from the Brahma-sacrifice; indeed, in ancient times, the Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, [instituted it]. (19)
In the presence of all the gods, on Mount Gandhamādana, he performed all the sacrifices for the sake of removing the curse of Īśa.
O best of the twice-born, having duly performed all the sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees, Brahmā was suddenly released from the curse of Śambhu.
Those men who, having reached this sacred ford, perform their ablutions, attain union with Mahādeva; of this there is no doubt. || 22 ||
The sages said: O disciple of Vyāsa, O one of great wisdom, O expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas, [tell us of] the four-faced Creator of the fourteen worlds. (23)
"O Sage, tell us all this in truth and with due respect: for what offense did Śambhu curse the Lord of Bhāratī, and what kind of curse was indeed given to him by Hara in the past?"
The venerable Sūta said: In ancient times, a quarrel arose between Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Pointing to some cause or other, two who boast out of rivalry say: "I am the doer; there is no doer other than me upon the surface of the earth. (26)
Thus Brahmā spoke to Hari, and likewise Hari to Brahmā; in this way, a very great dispute arose between the two of them in ancient times.
In the meantime, O brahmins, for the sake of destroying the pride and awakening those two gods who were quarreling with one another, [the Lord acted].
In the middle, there appeared a self-luminous and stainless Liṅga. Seeing that Liṅga, Brahmā and Viṣṇu were both struck with wonder at one another.
In ancient times, O Brahmins, they made a compact in the presence of the gods regarding this great Liṅga without beginning or end which is seen here before us.
"Whoever shall behold the end or the beginning of this liṅga of ours, which resembles infinite suns and possesses a splendor equal to infinite fires," (31)
"He would become superior in the world, the creator of the world, and its Lord; as for me, I shall go upwards, searching for the end of the Liṅga. (32)
"Go down below, O Hari, for the sake of searching for the root. Having heard these words of his, the Lord of Ramā replied, "So be it."
Having thus made an agreement, the two set out on their search; Viṣṇu, in the form of a boar, went downwards to investigate.

Having assumed the form of a swan, the son of Bhāratī went upward; then, after searching through the worlds below for many groups of years, Viṣṇu returned to his proper place and spoke in the presence of the gods.
Viṣṇu said: "I did not see the beginning of this Liṅga," he spoke thus with truthful words.
Then, having searched upward, Brahmā also arrived there; having arrived, the four-faced one spoke these words with guile.

Brahmā said: "I have seen the end of this Liṅga"—this was false. Having heard those words of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, Maheśvara laughed and spoke thus to the four-faced one, the speaker of falsehood: 38. "I have seen the end of this Liṅga"—this was false. Having heard those words of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, Maheśvara laughed and spoke thus to the four-faced one, the speaker of falsehood: 38. [Note: The provided source text contains a repetition of verse 38; the translation reflects the content of that verse.]
Īśvara said: "O four-faced one, that which you have spoken before me is untrue."
"Therefore, there shall be no worship of you anywhere in the world at any time. Then the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, spoke again to Vishnu.
"O Hari, Lord of Kamalā, because you have spoken the truth, therefore your worship shall be equal to mine; of this there is no doubt. (41)
Then Brahmā, being despondent, addressed Śaṅkara: "O Lord, O ocean of compassion, please forgive my transgression. (42)
"A single offense should be forgiven by masters who are lords of the world. Then Maheśvara spoke to Brahmā, consoling him:
Īśvara said: "O Brahmin, my word shall not be false; I shall tell you, so listen. Go at once, my child, to Mount Gandhamādana."
In that regard, perform sacrifices for the sake of pacifying the fault of falsehood; then you will be cleansed of sin, of this there is no doubt. (45)
Therefore, O Brahmin, your worship shall always be directed toward the rites prescribed by the Vedas and those recorded in the Smṛtis; there shall be no worship for you in images.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Īśa vanished right there; then, O Brahmins, Brahmā went to Mount Gandhamādana.
And for eighty-eight thousand years, O best of sages, he, the performer of sacrifices, worshipped the Lord of Pārvatī with various rites.

With all the sacrifices beginning with the Pauṇḍarīka, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, he worshipped Śiva in the presence of Indra and all the other gods. Śambhu was pleased by that and granted him a boon.
Īśvara said: "The fault of your false speech has been destroyed here by these sacrifices you have performed."
O Four-faced One, O Brahmā, your worship shall be performed with purity in the rites prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis; there shall be no worship of you in images.
Today, this place of sacrifice shall attain fame throughout these three worlds as "Brahmakuṇḍa"—a meritorious site that destroys all sins.
O Creator, for one who performs a single bath at the holy site named Brahmakuṇḍa, the bolt on the door of liberation is shattered at that very moment.
Wearing on his forehead the ashes produced from the Brahmakuṇḍa, he shall pierce the door of illusion and proceed toward the gateway of liberation.
He who does not wear on his forehead the ashes arising from the Brahma-kuṇḍa is not a son born of his father’s seed; he is no son to his mother.
O Creator, by wearing the ashes produced from the Brahmakuṇḍa, ten thousand killings of Brahmins as well as ten thousand instances of drinking liquor are destroyed.

Ten thousand transgressions of violating the Guru's bed are destroyed, as are ten thousand thefts of gold; likewise, ten thousand instances of association with such sinners are destroyed—this truth has been spoken by me, O Brahmā. (57)
By the power of wearing the ashes produced from the Brahmakuṇḍa, ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and other such beings perish in a mere instant. || 58 ||
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Īśa vanished on that very spot; then, when the sacrifices were completed, the sages, whose senses were conquered, [departed].
Indra and the other deities, as well as the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras, and other hosts of gods, were on Mount Gandhamādana.
Having understood his majesty, they remained constantly at that sacrificial ground, which was personally frequented by Rudra himself.
Then, having completed the sacrifices according to the prescribed rites with abundant sacrificial fees, Brahmā went to Satyaloka, his heart's desire fulfilled by Śiva.
From that time forward, O best of the twice-born, the gods and the sages, having reached Brahmakuṇḍa, performed sacrifices according to the prescribed rites.
Therefore, mortals who desire [merit] should indeed perform sacrifices right here.

O twice-born ones, this auspicious Jalajasambhava-kuṇḍa is worshipped by kings, gods, and lords of sages; it destroys the entire cycle of worldly existence, removes all sins, and bestows all desired objects. (65)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation from Brahmā’s Curse," within the "Praise of Brahmakuṇḍa" section of the *Setumāhātmya*, in the third part, the *Brahmakhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having performed his ablutions with a concentrated mind in the highly meritorious Brahmakuṇḍa, a man should then proceed to the Kuṇḍa of Hanumān.
Formerly, when the Rākṣasas had been slain, the work of battle completed, and Rāma and the others had returned to Mount Gandhamādana; || 2 ||
For the benefit of the entire world, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, established an excellent holy site in his own name, the best among all sacred fords.
Having recognized its majesty, which is personally served by Rudra himself, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a holy place (tīrtha) equal to it.
In that most meritorious tirtha, which destroys great sins, men who bathe go to the eternal world of Śiva.
When he was created by the son of the Wind for the benefit of all the worlds, indeed, all the hells became empty for a long time.
Śaṅkara may or may not know the full majesty of that sacred ford, where the king named Dharmasakha, born of the Kekaya lineage, [resided].

"Having bathed previously with devotion, he obtained a hundred sons. The sages said: "O Sūta, you ought to recount today the life-story of Dharmasakha, who, having bathed at the holy site of Hanūmatkuṇḍa, obtained a hundred sons."
The venerable Sūta said: Listen, O sages, you all, to the life-story of that king.
Today, O Dharmasakha, I shall speak to you in brief: there was a king named Dharmasakha, who had conquered his enemies and was exceedingly righteous. (10)
In former times, he was possessed of statesmanship and was devoted to the protection of his subjects; O Brahmins, he had a hundred wives who regarded their husband as their deity.
While that king was protecting the earth with its mountains, forests, and groves, he did not obtain a son from those wives to perpetuate his lineage.
Then that protector of the earth made many efforts for the sake of obtaining a son.
And that lord of the earth performed great acts of charity for the sake of obtaining a son.
He performed sacrifices for the sake of the gods, such as the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha) and others, and he gave abundant gifts, chief among which was the Tulāpuruṣa.
Until midnight, the lord of the earth provided food for everyone without restriction—food accompanied by many soups and rich in grains. || 15 ||
He performed the Śrāddha ceremony for his ancestors according to the prescribed rules, and with his senses restrained, he recited the mantras that bestow progeny.
The king performed many such religious acts for the sake of a son, constantly performing the most excellent dharmas with his son in mind. || 17 ||
After a long time, the king reached old age; once, while that aged monarch was thus striving, [the following occurred]. (18)
A son named Candra was born to the eldest wife; he was beautiful and pleasing to the mind. When the son was born, all those mothers were indeed free from any partiality toward him.
Those most excellent women nourished him equally with milk and other foods, along with all the king's mothers, the citizens, and likewise the ministers.
This son was born as a source of delight for both mind and eye; cherishing his son, the king attained a joy greater than the greatest. (21)
Once, as that son was lying on a swing, a scorpion stung his foot with its tail, which emitted the fire of its rising venom.
From the crushing of the scorpion, the son cried out intensely; thereupon, all his mothers wept, overcome with grief.
Surrounding their son, O Brahmins, a tumultuous sound of lamentation arose; then King Dharmasakha heard that cry of distress.
Seated in the midst of the assembly together with his ministers and domestic priest, the king then dispatched an attendant to find out [the cause].
Having approached the outer gate of the inner apartments, that chamberlain summoned the elderly eunuchs and addressed them with these words: || 26 ||
"O eunuchs, why are the women of the inner apartments weeping now? Let the cause of their weeping be ascertained by going there."
"For this purpose indeed did the king urge me forward in the assembly. Having been addressed thus, they understood the cause of her weeping.
Having departed from the inner apartments, he reported everything exactly as it had happened to him; having heard the words of the eunuch, that chamberlain went to the assembly hall. (29)
He reported to the king that his son was suffering from a scorpion sting; then King Dharmasakha, having heard this account, [acted accordingly].
Rising up in haste, together with his ministers and his family priest, he entered the inner apartments along with the experts in mantras and those who remove poison.
He treated his son with various medicines and other remedies many times; then, once the son had regained his health, the king caressed him.
And having honored him with jewels, gold, pearls, and other treasures, the king, deeply overwhelmed with anxiety, departed from the inner apartments.

Accompanied by his sacrificial priests, family priest, and ministers, he entered that assembly hall. There, King Dharmasakha, seated upon an excellent throne, spoke these appropriate words to the sacrificial priests and the family priest: 34. "The king, seated upon a noble seat, addressed these fitting words to the officiating priests together with the domestic chaplain."
Dharmasakha said: "O best of Brahmins, having only one son leads only to sorrow. (35)

Indeed, for men, having no son at all is better than having only one son; because it is constantly free from misfortune, having no son is truly preferable. O Brahmins, after much reflection, I married a hundred wives. (36)
O twice-born ones, my youth has passed away along with that of my wife; my life and the lives of my wives are now centered entirely upon this son. (37)
Upon his destruction, the death of all my wives is certain; likewise, there would be the loss of my own life upon the killing of my only son. (38)
"Therefore, by what means indeed might I have many sons? O Brahmins, most learned in the Vedas, tell me that means."
"May each of you have a virtuous son from among your hundred wives; therefore, perform that rite according to dharma, having consulted the scriptures. (40)
Whether by a great or even a small deed, or by one that is difficult to perform—if that fruit is to be accomplished, I shall achieve it; of this there is no doubt. (41)
"What you have spoken, I shall perform; of this there is no doubt. Know that it is already accomplished, for I swear it by my own meritorious deeds. (42)
"If there exists such a deed by which a hundred sons might be obtained, tell me now where that deed must be performed by me. (43)
Thus questioned by the king at that time, all the officiating priests together with the family priest assembled and spoke these well-considered words to the king: || 44 ||
The officiating priests said: "O King, O Kaikaya, there exists a means by which, through great merit, you shall have a hundred sons born of your hundred wives; we shall explain it to you."
There is a certain mountain of great merit called Gandhamādana, which exists in the midst of the southern ocean in the form of a bridge.
It is crowded with hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and divine sages; by its sight and touch, it destroys the great sins of men.
Therein is the Hanumatkuṇḍa, renowned throughout the worlds, which pacifies great suffering and bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation. || 48 ||
It pacifies the afflictions of hell and likewise liberates one from poverty; it grants sons to those without sons and bestows wives upon men who have none. (49)
Having bathed there with self-restraint in that river which grants all desires, perform the *putrīyeṣṭi* sacrifice on its bank with a well-concentrated mind.
Therefore, O King, let there be one son for each of your hundred wives; let this happen quickly, and do not entertain any doubt in this matter.
Thus addressed by the brahmins, the officiating priests, and the family chaplains, the king, together with those priests, his wives, and the priest, at that very moment—
Accompanied by his ministers and servants, and provided with the materials for the sacrifice, he set out for Mount Gandhamādana on the southern ocean.
Having reached Hanumatkuṇḍa, he bathed there along with his army; for one month he dwelt upon its bank, performing his ablutions.
Then, when spring had arrived in the month of Caitra, that best of kings, together with his family priest, commenced there the sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son.
The officiating priests, together with the family chaplain, performed the rites correctly for that royal sage, who was accompanied by his wife and whose friend was Dharma.
When that sacrifice was completed, the royal priest had the remnants of the oblation consumed by the king’s wives on the bank of the Hanumat-kuṇḍa.
Then King Dharmasakha, accompanied by his hundred wives, duly performed the avabhṛtha bath at the waters of Hanumatkuṇḍa.
O best of the twice-born, the king bestowed countless and abundant sacrificial fees upon the officiating priests, and he also gave villages to the Brahmins.
Then that righteous king, together with his ministers, his retinue, and his wife, returned joyfully toward his own city.
Then, after some time had passed, in the tenth month, his wives gave birth to a hundred sons, each most excellent in virtue.
Then the great king Vīra Dharmasakha, with a joyful mind, having bathed and purified himself, made a formal resolve and performed the birth-rite (jātakarma).
He gave much to the Brahmins, including cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and other gifts. At that time, there were two sons of his senior wife: the elder and the younger.
O twice-born ones, all one hundred and one sons flourished; when they had reached maturity, the king divided the kingdom among them.
Having given [the gift], he departed for the Gandhamādana mountain via the bridge with his wife; reaching Hanumatkuṇḍa, he performed austerities on its bank.
A great length of time passed for that king as he performed austerities, while this King Dharmasakha remained absorbed in meditation upon the wielder of the trident.
Then, after a long time had passed, King Dharmasakha, who was righteous and possessed a peaceful mind, met his end there.
Then the wives of that royal sage also followed their husband; and the eldest son, Sucandra, having performed the funeral rites for his father, [proceeded].
The king, together with his wife, performed religious rites with faith until his death; consequently, he went from here to Vaikuṇṭha.
All those princes of great prowess, headed by Sucandra, enjoyed their respective kingdoms as brothers who had abandoned all envy.
Thus, O Brahmins, has the majesty of the Hanumat-kuṇḍa been recounted to you, as well as the most wonderful life-story of King Dharmasakha.
For the sake of accomplishing all those desires, one should bathe in the pool of Hanūmat.
O twice-born ones, the man who reads this chapter or listens to it with a well-concentrated mind attains infinite happiness in the hereafter and sports in heaven together with hosts of gods.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Dharmasakha’s Attainment of a Hundred Sons," within the Praise of Hanumatkuṇḍa, in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 15 ||
Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, having bathed in the pool of Hanumān, which was personally frequented by Rudra, one should then proceed with a concentrated mind to Agasti-tīrtha.
This sacred ford was indeed manifested by the Pot-born Sage himself in ancient times, during the conflict that arose between Mount Meru and the Vindhya range.
When the entire expanse of the world had ceased to exist and all living beings were breathless, the Vindhya mountain grew, and then the deities [acted].
Having gone to Mount Kailāsa, they informed Śambhu of this; at that time, he was eager and full of curiosity for the marriage ceremony with Pārvatī.
Having dispatched the sages Vasiṣṭha and others to request Pārvatī's hand in marriage, he commanded Agastya, "O Pot-born one, restrain the Vindhya mountain. || 5 ||
Then that pot-born one spoke to the Lord who wields the Pināka bow: "O God, O All-pervading One, how shall I not behold you in your attire for marriage?"
Thus addressed, Śambhu spoke again to the Pot-born (Agastya): "O Pot-born one, together with Pārvatī, I shall indeed assume the guise of a bridegroom for you."
"In the highly meritorious Vedāraṇya, I shall undoubtedly reveal [the truth]; therefore, O Lord of Sages, go quickly to the Vindhya mountain to subdue it."
Thus addressed, Agastya then restrained the Vindhya mountain, leveling the surface of the earth with a mere tread of his feet.
Having traveled through the southern regions, he followed toward Gandhamādana; and that great seer, having come to know the splendor of Gandhamādana, [proceeded].
There, the sage established a highly meritorious holy site (tīrtha) by his own name; even today, the pitcher-born Agastya dwells there together with his companion Lopāmudrā.
Having bathed there and drunk [its water], one shall not undergo birth again; O twice-born ones, even at the three times of day, there is nothing in this world equal to that sacred ford.
There exists no sacred ford (tīrtha) that bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, nor one that grants all the desires of men, as does the majesty of bathing in this sacred ford. (13)
The son of Sudīrghatamas, known by the name Kakṣīvān, obtained as his beloved wife the daughter of Svanaya, named Manoramā.
This is that sacred narrative of Kakṣīvān, which destroys both merit and sin; I shall relate that story to you, O lords of sages—listen to it! (15)
There was a sage named Dīrghatamas, most righteous; he had a son who became renowned as Kakṣīvān.
Having been initiated, that Kakṣīvān, a celibate student with his senses conquered, took up residence in the family of his teacher for the purpose of studying the Vedas.
Dwelling in the house of his preceptor Udaṅka, the son of Dīrghatamas studied the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (Aṅgas), as well as the six Śāstras.
Having resided for sixty years in the presence of his guru, Kakṣīvān mastered the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, and likewise the Upaniṣads as well. (19)
O Brahmins, as he was about to depart for his own home, he gave a sacrificial fee to his preceptor; then the learned preceptor Kakṣīvān, the best among the knowers of Brahman, spoke to him.
Kakṣīvān said: "O great sage, having looked upon me now with a compassionate glance, grant me permission as I shall depart for home. Then Udaṅka, being delighted, spoke to Kakṣīvān.
Udaṅka said: "I give you leave, Kakṣīvat; go now toward your own home."
"O child, I shall tell you the means for your marriage; listen to that. Go to Rāmasetu and to Mount Gandhamādana."
Therein lies the holy ford (tīrtha) created by Agastya, which bestows all desired objects, grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation to men, and destroys all sins. || 24 ||
Bathe there, O you who accomplish all auspiciousness; dwell there for three years, endowed with self-restraint and right conduct.
When three years have passed, then in the fourth year, a certain elephant will emerge from that most excellent sacred site.
Having bathed there, mount that elephant, which has four tusks, a massive body, a complexion like an autumn cloud, and resembles a mountain.
Mounting that elephant, my child, go to the city of Svanaya; seeing you mounted upon a four-tusked elephant like another Indra, [he will be amazed]. (28)
The wise royal sage Svanaya, his eyes agitated with joy, would surely cast away the sorrow dwelling in his heart for the sake of his daughter. (29)
For formerly, his daughter Manoramā had made a vow to [give him] an elephant with four tusks, of massive body, and entirely white in all its limbs.
Having heard that vow of his daughter—"He who shall arrive after climbing [this] would be my husband"—that king [acted].
With a mind agitated by sorrow, he reflected constantly; while he was thus reflecting upon his own policy, Nārada arrived.
Seeing that sage had arrived, the most righteous royal seer went out to meet him with joy and honored him with water for his feet, the arghya offering, and other rites.
Having bowed to Nārada, the king spoke these words: "O divine sage, this daughter of mine made a vow long ago. (34)
"May he who comes riding an elephant with four tusks, of massive body and entirely white in every limb, become my husband. (35)
An elephant with four tusks, a massive body, and entirely white in every limb might exist in the abode of Indra, but it is not found upon the surface of the earth. (36)
And this foolish woman has made this vow which is so difficult to fulfill; for this vow indeed constantly torments me exceedingly. (37)
"For an unmarried daughter always brings grief to her father. Having heard these words of his, Nārada spoke to Svanaya: || 38 ||
"Do not despair, O royal sage; such a husband as this shall belong to her before long—he who will be the best of Brahmins upon the earth. (39)
"One renowned as Kakṣīvān shall become your son-in-law"; having spoken thus, the sage Nārada departed by way of the sky. (40)
Having heard those words spoken by Nārada, Svanaya longed day and night for such a meeting.
Therefore, gentle and highly fortunate Kakṣīvat, ascetic from your youth, go now with haste to bathe at Agastya-tīrtha.
"Success in all auspicious matters shall be yours; of this there is no doubt. Having been addressed thus by Udaṅka, Kakṣīvān, the bull among the twice-born, [departed].
Permitted by his preceptor, he departed for Gandhamādana; having reached the Agastya-tīrtha, he, with his senses subdued, bathed there.
The lord of sages observed a fast at the sacred field for one day; on the following day, having bathed again, the twice-born performed the breaking of his fast.
There, Kakṣīvān, devoted to righteousness, slept that very night; such was the state of the sage Kakṣīvān as he remained bound by his observances.
Then three years, less by one day, passed away; and at the end of those three years, on that very same day, the sage [arrived].
Having performed his evening twilight rites, he slept soundly on that bank; when only one watch of the night remained, a great sound arose.
A sound arose, resembling the tumultuous roar of the waves of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution; by that great noise, Kakṣīvān was awakened.
Then the powerful king named Svanaya, the lord of Madhurā, accompanied by his followers and eager for the hunt, arrived there.
Slaying elephants, lions, boars, buffaloes, and deer, as well as other species of wild animals, that king struck them down with his arrows.
Accompanied by his ministers, devoted to hunting, and joined by chariots, horses, and elephants, he arrived near Agastya-tīrtha together with his soldiers.
Exhausted from hunting and surrounded by his weary army, that king, the lord of the earth, sat down on the edge of the bank of that sacred ford.
Then, at the clear dawn, Kakṣīvān, the best of sages, bathed in the Agastya-tīrtha and performed the morning twilight devotions.
On its bank, he remained engaged in the recitation of mantras, bound by his religious observances. In the meantime, a single elephant emerged from that excellent holy site.
Having four tusks and a massive body, like Mount Kailāsa personified, he rose from that sacred bathing place and went into the presence of Kakṣīvān.
Then, having observed him who had arrived, characterized by the signs described by Udaṅka, Kakṣīvān performed his ritual bath in order to mount [the horse]. (57)
Having paid homage to that sacred ford and praising it again and again, Kakṣīvān mounted the great elephant with four tusks.
Having mounted that four-tusked elephant, which resembled a mountain of silver, Kakṣīvān desired to go to the city of Svanaya itself.
Seeing him mounted upon that excellent white elephant with four tusks, the king concluded that he was indeed Kakṣīvān.
With a serene heart, the king approached him; having come near, the monarch then spoke to Kakṣīvān.
Svanaya said: "O Brahmin, whose son are you? Tell me, what is your name? Having mounted this elephant, where do you wish to go? Thus addressed by Svanaya, Kakṣīvān spoke these words.
Kakṣīvān said: "I am the son of Dīrghatamas, renowned by the name Kakṣīvān. (63)
"I am going toward the city of the royal sage Svanaya; I desire to marry his beautiful daughter Manoramā. (64)
Mounted upon the four-tusked elephant and fulfilling that vow, O lord of men, I shall take the hand of Svanaya’s daughter.
Having heard that speech of his, which was a rain of nectar to the ears, Svanaya, his eyes blossoming with joy, spoke these words: || 66 ||
"O Kakṣīvat, I have achieved my purpose; for I am indeed that very Svanaya, whose beautiful daughter you desire to marry. (67)
Welcome to you, O best of sages, Kakṣīvat, ascetic from childhood! O you whose wealth is penance, accept this daughter of mine, Manorama.

"Practicing the dharma together with her, maintain the life of a householder. Thus addressed by the king, Kakṣīvān, who was devoted to righteousness, then spoke to King Svanaya, the delighted resident of Madhurāpura.
Kakṣīvān said: "O Lord, my father, named Dīrghatamas, [resides] in the forest of the Vedas."
That gentle one dwells performing austerities, devoted to the practice of restraints; O Lord of the Earth, send a single brāhmaṇa to his presence.
Thus addressed, King Svanaya, with a joyful heart, dispatched his own priest along with a vast army.
To the place known as Vedāraṇya, he sent a Brahmin named Sudarśana; that Sudarśana was commissioned by King Svanaya.
Accompanied by a great army, he set out for the Veda forest; there, he [found] the sage Dīrghatamas seated within a hut.
Then the domestic priest saw him seated, performing austerities and meditating upon the Lord of the Veda-forest, as he was reciting an excellent mantra.
Sudarśana paid homage to that sage and spoke to the sage Dīrghatamas as if gladdening him.
Sudarśana said: "O Brahmin, is all well with you? Does your asceticism flourish? Is all well in the hermitage? Tell me, are you at ease in the practice of dharma?"
Thus questioned by Sudarśana, the sage Dīrghatamas then spoke these words to Sudarśana, preceded by the ritual offering of arghya and other honors.
Dīrghatamas said: "O Brahman, O Sudarśana of great intelligence, all is well everywhere; by the grace of the Lord of the Veda-forest, nothing inauspicious exists for me anywhere. (79)
"O Brahmin, is it well with you? Is your arrival likewise pleasant? And what is the purpose of your coming to my hermitage, O Sudarśana? (80)
"You are indeed the domestic priest of Svanaya and the best among those who know the Vedas; yet, O Great King, you have abandoned him who resides in the city of Mathurā. (81)
"Why have you come here with such a great army? Thus was Sudarśana addressed by Dīrghatamas at that time.
He spoke to that great-souled sage of blazing splendor: "O Brahmin, by your grace, I am always happy in every respect. (83)
O Blessed One, King Svanaya, having prostrated with his eight limbs, has addressed you with humble words; hear them through my mouth. (84)
Svanaya said: "O Brahmana, your son Kakṣīvān is currently staying on Mount Gandhamādana, performing his ablutions at the sacred bathing place of Agastya."
His form, his asceticism, his dharma, as well as his Vedic conduct, his proficiency in the Vedas and Shastras, and his noble birth were all of such a kind. (86)
"O Sage, having recognized that all this is transcendent, I desire to give my daughter Manoramā to him in your pleasure grove."
"O tiger among sages, being fond of the hunt, I came to Mount Gandhamādana and am now staying in the presence of your daughter. (88)
"O best of sages, your son Kakṣīvān says this: 'I will not marry your daughter without my father's permission.'"
"Grant me the favor of giving your daughter, who possesses those qualities, to him; and send Sudarśana to your presence along with an army. (90)
Sudarśana said: "O Blessed One, thus has the king sent me into your presence; may you therefore grant your approval for what that king intends to do."
Śrī Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the priest of Svanaya then ceased; thereupon Dīrghatamas spoke to the priest of Svanaya.
Dīrghatamas said: "O Sudarśana, let it be exactly as Svānaya has spoken; for this auspicious marriage ceremony is most desired by me."
"O Brahmin, I shall come to Mount Gandhamādana," having said this, O Brahmins, that sage, the great Dīrghatamas, departed.
Having bowed to the Lord of the Forest of the Vedas with a mind inclined toward devotion, he set out toward Setu accompanied by Sudarśana.
After six days, the sage Puṇya went to Gandhamādana; and having reached the bank of the Agasti-tīrtha, the sage Dīrghatamas [arrived]. (96)
Then the great sage saw his son Kakṣīvān before him; and Kakṣīvān, seeing his father, saluted him while proclaiming his own name.
Then the yogi Dīrghatamas, having placed his son upon his own lap and smelled the crown of his head, embraced him with affection, his body bristling with horripilation.
Then the seer Dīrghatamas inquired after his welfare: "O Kakṣīvat, my dear child, have you studied all the Vedas? (99)
"Did you study the scriptures? Or rather, my dear son, tell me everything. Thus questioned by his father, he related the entire account to him. (100)

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Kakṣīvān’s Preparations for Marriage," within the "Praise of Agastitīrtha" section of the Setumāhātmya, in the third part (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: O lords of sages, Kakṣīvān spoke again to his father: "Just as I have now been sent here by my elder brother Udaṅka."
O best of sages, I have arrived at this sacred site of Āgastya, impelled by my preceptor for the purpose of accomplishing the marriage of Svanaya’s son.
Employing the stratagem described therein, I returned at the end of three years, accompanied by a plan for our marriage.
While he was staying right here, Svanaya approached him by chance; having come to me, he spoke these words: "I shall give you my daughter. (4)
"Therefore, out of consideration for me, this king has summoned you"; having spoken thus to his father, Kakṣīvān fell silent.
Then Sudarśana, the best of brahmins and the domestic priest of Svanaya, went into the presence of the king to inform Svanaya [of the matter].

Having approached that king, Sudarśana announced that the sage Dīrghatamas had arrived. Then King Svanaya, having heard from his domestic priest that the sage had arrived, went forth with great splendor from his pavilion to see him.
On the bank of the Agastyatīrtha, King Svanaya beheld that most excellent sage together with his son, just as the king of the gods beholds Brahmā.
He paid homage at the feet of Dīrghatamas, which are auspicious for the world; then, O Brahmins, the sage Dīrghatamas raised the king up.
Then he offered a blessing to King Svanaya; at that moment, the great sage Udaṅka also arrived.
Surrounded by his circle of disciples, that lord of sages, accompanied by a multitude of one hundred thousand sages, went to bathe at Dhanuṣkoṭi on Rāmasetu.
The sage Udaṅka arrived at this Agastya-tīrtha to bathe; seeing that Udaṅka had arrived, Kakṣīvān bowed down to him.
Then the brahmin teacher offered a blessing to his disciple; thereafter, the brahmin Dīrghatamas [approached] that great sage Udaṅka.
He too inquired after the welfare of that bull among sages; both those tigers among sages were renowned throughout all the worlds.
There they both spoke stories that destroy all sins; then the king also bowed down to that lord of sages, Udaṅka.
Udaṅka also offered a blessing to that Svanaya; then King Svanaya, being pleased, spoke these words there.
"Let the marriage rite be performed for that sage Dīrghatamas"; then the sage Dīrghatamas replied, "So be it."
"O high-minded King, let it be done tomorrow at an auspicious hour; let the taking of hands take place right here on Mount Gandhamādana."
"Therefore, bring this maiden here quickly to the inner apartments. Thus addressed, King Svanaya went to his own tent.
Then, having summoned hundreds of elderly men of excellent years, he dispatched them to bring the girl to the inner apartments.
Then those chief ministers, urged by Svanaya, mounted horses swift as thought and went to Madhurā.
Having quickly gone to the inner apartments and reported everything that had occurred, they returned once more together with the maiden and the women of the inner court.
Then, on the following auspicious day, the sage Dīrghatamas duly performed for his son the rites beginning with the Godāna ceremony.
Then, when the rites such as the gift of cows had been completed, Kakṣīvān was joined by his father and his preceptor to marry the princess.
Mounted upon a four-tusked elephant of massive body, entirely white in every limb, he was filled with joy like a second King of the Gods.
Fulfilling the desire of the maiden Manoramā, he was accompanied by many thousands of Brahmins who were reciting benedictions.
O royal sage, having performed the auspicious rites, Kakṣīvān joyfully went to the cloth pavilion whose entrance was adorned with archways.
Then that daughter of Svanaya, adorned with auspicious ornaments, [ascended] a great-bodied white elephant with four tusks.
Seeing Kakṣīvān approaching, eager for his own marriage, he felt joy, thinking, "The vow made for my sake has now been fulfilled."
Accompanied by Dīrghatamas and Udaṅka, Kakṣīvān gradually arrived at the outer gate of the king's palace in the form of a mendicant.
Then Svanaya, seeing that Kakṣīvān had arrived, went out to meet him accompanied by his family priest Sudarśana.
Then, the maidservants of the bridegroom Kakṣīvanta’s daughter performed the rite of lustration with silver and golden vessels.
Summoned by his own method and surrounded by brahmins, the illustrious Kakṣīvān then entered the royal palace.
Then the king, filled with humility, led that sage Dīrghatamas, together with his son Vara, to his own home while shedding tears.
The king presented the water of honor (arghya) to Udaṅka and Dīrghatamas in the middle of the water-shed, which was adorned with cloths, chowries, and arches.
Then the excellent Dīrghatamas and other Ṛṣis bearing the *sodaṅka* mark sat down, as did Svanaya, together with his ministers and his family priest.
Then [he gave] his daughter, that maiden Sukeśī, who was pleasing to the mind, adorned with ornaments on her limbs, wearing divine garments, and auspicious.
They led her, who had bimba-red lips, beautiful limbs, and full, elevated breasts, through the midst of the thronged crowd of people.
Then, in the midst of the people, that auspicious and beautiful woman placed a garland made of campaka flowers around the neck of the bridegroom.

Then Udaṅka, having arrived and established the fire upon the ground, performed the rites beginning with the oblation of parched grain (lājāhoma) up until the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha). || 41 ||
And Udaṅka, having caused the hand of that maiden to be taken by the bridegroom, indeed performed all the rites there.
Then, O brahmins, they bestowed blessings upon the bridegroom and the bride; thereafter, King Svanaya [honored] the sage Dīrghatamas with a boon.
Udaṅka likewise fed three hundred thousand Brāhmaṇas—both those from the bridegroom’s side and those from his own side—with food possessing the six flavors.
Then he honored him in many ways with betel leaves and other offerings; thereafter, having taken leave of the best of sages, Udaṅka went to his own hermitage.
And all the other brahmins then departed for their own countries; thus was the marriage of Kakṣīvat and the princess concluded.
Having entered Agastyatīrtha, that best of elephants vanished; then, O brahmins, Dīrghatamas, together with his son and daughter-in-law, [remained there].
Having bathed in the great Tīrtha of Agastya, which bestows all desired objects, he praised that Tīrtha, renowned throughout all the worlds.
The best of sages, having taken leave of the king to come, set his mind upon going to his own meritorious hermitage, Vedāraṇya.
Then King Svanaya, filled with joy, gave his daughter a dowry of hundreds of thousands of gold pieces.
He gave away a thousand cows and a thousand female slaves; being devoted to his daughter, he also gave five hundred villages.
Out of affection for his daughter, he also gave her a hundred boxes of ornaments filled with divine garments, as well as a thousand necklaces.
Taking all of this with him, that sage, accompanied by his son and daughter-in-law and permitted by the king, departed for the Veda forest.
O brahmins, having reached Vedāraṇya, the sage Dīrghatamas then lived there happily with his son and daughter-in-law.
Having served the Lord of the Veda-forest, who bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, Kakṣīvān also dwelt there for a long time with his wife.
That royal sage Svanaya also, having bathed in that most meritorious sacred ford (tīrtha) made by the pot-born [Agastya], was accompanied by all his troops.

Then, taking his city with him, he went joyfully to his own capital. O Brahmins, it was solely through the greatness of Agastya-tīrtha that the marriage of the sage Kakṣīvata occurred in such a way as is not easily attainable by others.
The venerable Sūta said: O lords of sages, this history is meritorious and established in the Vedas.
O twice-born ones, this [work] bestows merit, fame, and long life, and increases renown and good fortune; it should be heard and recited in every way by human beings. (59)
For those who read or hear this ancient history, there shall be no affliction, nor even poverty, either in this world or in the next. (60)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Completion of Kakṣīvān’s Marriage," in the Setumāhātmya of the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: Having performed an ablution in this Kuṃbhasambhava Tīrtha, a person should then go to the meritorious Rāmakuṇḍa for the sake of liberation from sin.
O twice-born ones, the Raghunātha-saras is meritorious and likewise a destroyer of sins; a sacrifice was performed on the bank of the Raghunātha-saras even with meager sacrificial fees.
O twice-born ones, even the study of sacred texts and the recitation of mantras performed on the bank of the Raghunātha lake shall yield their full fruit, even if it be only the measure of a handful.
If a gift is given to one learned in the Vedas, it becomes infinite in merit; O best of sages, I shall now speak concerning Rāmatīrtha.
This history is of great merit and destroys all sins; it was [taught] by the eminent brahmin and sage named Sutīkṣṇa, whose mind was disciplined.
A disciple of Agastya who meditated upon the lotus feet of Rāma performed extremely difficult penance on the shore of the Rāmacandra lake.
He constantly and unweariedly recited five thousand times the six-syllabled mantra, which has Rāmacandra as its presiding deity and is the king of mantras.
Performing his ablutions in the waters of the Raghunātha lake, he muttered prayers, subsisting on alms with a restricted diet, having conquered anger and subdued his senses.
O best of Brahmins, thus Sutīkṣṇa lived for a long time. Then, on one occasion, that sage, always meditating upon Rāma in his heart, devoutly offered praise to Rāmacandra together with Sītā.
Sutīkṣṇa said: Homage to you, O Lord of Jānakī; homage to you, O beloved of Hanumān. (10)
Salutations to you, who are consecrated for the protection of the sacrifice of the sage Kauśika; salutations to you, the descendant of Kausalya and the beloved of Viśvāmitra.
Salutations to you, O breaker of Hara’s bow, served by the gods; O king of kings, destroyer of Mārīca and annihilator of Tāṭakā’s life!
O Kabaṃdhāri, O Hara, salutations to you, the son of Daśaratha; salutations to you, the conqueror of Paraśurāma, the destroyer of Khara. || 13 ||
Salutations to the Lord Sugrīva; salutations to you, the slayer of Vālin, who removes the fear and suffering of Vibhīṣaṇa and who takes away all impurity.
Salutations to you, the elder brother of Bharata, who removed the suffering of Ahalyā; salutations to that one who built the bridge across the ocean and thereby destroyed its pride.
Salutations to you, the Tāraka-Brahman, O elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa; salutations to you, the destroyer of the Rākṣasa, the crusher of Rāvaṇa.
"Obeisance to you, the wielder of the bow, the provider of all protection"—thus did that sage Sutīkṣṇa praise Rāma every day. (17)
With his mind fixed upon Rāmacandra, he spent his time incessantly; thus did he practice the six-syllabled mantra of Rāma. (18)
O you of excellent vows, for one who praises Rāmacandra with this hymn and performs the daily ritual bath at the sacred ford of the Lord of the Raghus, [there shall be great merit].
His devotion to Rāmacandra became unwavering and utterly pure; he attained the non-dual realization characterized by the oneness of the inner self.
O twice-born ones, he possessed knowledge of the three Vedas without having studied them, likewise the realization of what had not been heard, and the power to enter the bodies of others. (21)
The power to travel through the sky, proficiency in the arts, and the comprehension of scriptures never heard before, even without a teacher. (22)
Movement throughout all worlds without obstruction, the capacity to perceive objects beyond the senses, and likewise conversation with the gods. (23)
O twice-born ones, even the knowledge of the livelihood of creatures such as ants, as well as the ability to travel to the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva, [is attained]. (24)
O best of beings, the power to travel at will through the fourteen worlds, as well as all these other [powers], are attainable by the yogin. (25)
O brahmins, through the service of that sacred ford (tīrtha), Sūtīkṣṇa’s wives attained [liberation]. Such is the power of that sacred ford; it is the destroyer of great sins.
It brings about great accomplishment, is meritorious, and destroys untimely death; it bestows enjoyment and liberation upon men and annihilates the sufferings of hell. (27)

Bestowing eternal devotion to Rāma and being the cause for the destruction of saṃsāra, the scion of Raghu installed a great liṅga on its bank and worshipped that liṅga with the desire to show grace to the world. (28)
By bathing at the highly meritorious Rāmatīrtha and beholding that Liṅga, liberation itself shall be attained by men; what need then to mention other worldly prosperities? || 29 ||
O twice-born ones, having bathed there and beheld Śiva in ancient times, the son of Dharma was instantly liberated from the fault arising from his false speech.
The sages said: "O son of Sūta, why was an untruth spoken by the son of Dharma, that he bathed in the exceedingly purifying Rāmatīrtha for the sake of pacifying his transgression? (31)
The venerable Sūta said: O sages, I shall relate to you how that which was spoken in battle was rendered false by Dharmaputra through deceit at Rāmatīrtha.
Long ago, O Brahmins, the Pāṇḍavas, headed by Dharmaputra, and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, headed by Duryodhana, were at enmity with one another.
O best of Brahmins, having incurred a great enmity for the sake of the kingdom, they assembled at Kurukṣetra together with a vast army.
The heroes, who never retreated in battle, fought in the conflict; after fighting for ten days, the son of Gaṅgā fell to the earth.
Then, for five more days, the heroic preceptor Droṇa, possessed of great strength and prowess, fought with Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Discharging many missiles and weapons, the mighty and heroic preceptor Droṇa afflicted the Pāṇḍava army.
Then the mighty Dhṛṣṭadyumna, a hero skilled in divine weapons, pierced Drona’s army in many ways with a rain of arrows.
Then Droṇa overwhelmed Dhṛṣṭadyumna with showers of arrows; likewise, Pārtha’s army was severely afflicted by the rain of Droṇa’s shafts. 39.
Overcome by fear, the best of the twice-born fled in the ten directions; then Arjuna, the foremost of chariot-warriors, fought Droṇa in battle.
