The sky became completely filled with gods who had gathered there to witness the battle between Vijaya and Droṇa, both of whom were experts in combat.
O brahmins, there was no comparison for the battle on earth between Droṇa and Phālguna; then a combat took place between the preceptor and his disciple, both filled with indignation.
The battle between Droṇa and Phālguna was like that between Droṇa and Phālguna themselves; then, in his mind, Droṇa highly esteemed Arjuna’s prowess.
Then the valiant Droṇa, leaving behind the highly heroic Phālguna, his beloved disciple, engaged in battle with the Pāñcāla army.
In that battle, Droṇācārya slew thirty thousand kings, along with their elephants and horses.
Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, enraged, struck Droṇa with arrows; and Droṇa, seizing a sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa), struck Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
In that battle, he pierced him with sharp arrows resembling flames of fire; struck by those shafts, Dhṛṣṭadyumna turned his back there. || 47 ||
Then Vṛkodara, having approached Dhṛṣṭadyumna who was deprived of his chariot, placed him upon his own chariot and spoke to the preceptor Droṇa.
If those lowest of the twice-born, who are uncontent with their own duties and skilled in weapons, were not cruel and did not fight, these kings would not perish in battle. 49.
For non-violence is always remembered as the supreme duty of Brāhmaṇas; by means of violence, those of the hunter caste protect their wives, sons, and others. || 50 ||
For the sake of your only son, you have slain many kings by standing in battle; yet that son of yours, O Brahmin, lies slain upon the field of combat.
Nevertheless, you feel no shame, nor does grief arise within you here, even after hearing these truthful words from Bhīma and Yudhiṣṭhira.
O twice-born ones, Dronacharya, the knower of yoga, then cast aside his own weapon, descended from his chariot, and sat down in the vow of fasting unto death (prāya).
Having discerned that opportunity, he rushed from the side of Preceptor Droṇa toward the battlefield with sword in hand to sever his head.
Although being restrained by the sons of Pṛthā, he rose up to sever that head; yet, because Droṇa was a knower of yoga, a light from his head ascended to heaven.
It was witnessed in battle by Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna, Kṛpa, the son of Dharma, and others, that he severed the head from this lifeless body of Droṇa.
When Bhāradvāja was slain in battle, the Kauravas fled in fear; meanwhile, O brahmins, the Pāṇḍavas, headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, then rejoiced.
Seeing that army in flight, the son of Droṇa said to Suyodhana: "O King, why is this army fleeing, having abandoned its weapons? (58)
Then King Duryodhana, being unable to speak of the slaying of Droṇa in battle himself, urged Kṛpācārya to do so. Thereupon, Kṛpācārya spoke of his preceptor’s death to the son of Droṇa.
Kṛpa said: O Aśvatthāman, your powerful father, having slain hundreds of enemies in battle with the Brahmāstra, sent them to the abode of Yama.
O best of brahmins, seeing that prowess which was most difficult to overcome, Keśava, who is skilled in speech, then addressed these words to the Pāṇḍavas.
Keśava said: "O Pāṇḍavas, there is a means to conquer Droṇa, who is difficult to defeat in battle."
"O Droṇa, your son Aśvatthāman has now been killed in battle"—if an authoritative person were to speak thus, one who speaks the truth would indeed say this. (63)
"Then Droṇa would abandon his weapons and withdraw from the battle in an instant; therefore, let the King of Dharma now utter this false report. (64)
Droṇa, who is skilled in warfare, cannot be conquered by any other means; if he is impossible to defeat through righteousness, then one should conquer the enemy even by abandoning righteousness.
Having heard those words of Keśava, Bhīma approached your father while he was seated with Pṛthā and spoke these deceitful words: || 66 ||
"Aśvatthāman has been killed; O Droṇa, he has now fallen here in battle. Even the preceptor Droṇa accepted those words as being true.
Then, having regained his confidence, he approached the son of Dharma and said: "O son of Dharma, my son Aśvatthāman has now been slain in battle."
"Are you slain? Speak now! You are considered a speaker of truth; yet the son of Dharma was once afraid of untruth and eager for victory in battle. (69)
"What must I do now?"—thus his mind became unsteady, swinging like a swing, as he beheld the elephant named Aśvatthāman, who had been slain by Bhīma.
"The great Aśvatthāman has been slain today by Bhīma in the battle! Thus did that son of Dharma speak to Droṇa with deceitful words. (71)
Having heard that, your father cast aside his weapon and withdrew from the battle; then the son of Dharma said, "He is indeed a supreme elephant."
"Once I have cast down my weapon in battle, I shall not take it up again"—thus did your father, the mighty Droṇa, O child, make his vow once more.
Therefore, fearing the breach of his vow, he did not take up a weapon; for upon seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna, your father then beheld his own death.

Having resolved thus, that knower of yoga, having restrained his breath and controlled his speech, lay down upon the seat of the chariot, established in meditative absorption through fasting unto death. || 75 ||
Then, having pierced through his head, his life-breaths departed in an instant; O child, the head of the deceased Droṇa was then [severed] with a sword.

Seizing him by the hair with his hand, Dhṛṣṭadyumna cut him down in battle; "Do not kill him! cried all the sons of Pṛthā and the soldiers alike. Even while being restrained by everyone, he slew your father from his side.
Śrī Sūta said: O twice-born ones, having heard that his father had been slain, the son of Droṇa wept for a long time, along with Rudra.
Then, blazing with great anger, he spoke these words: "He who, having spoken a falsehood to his father, caused him to lay down his weapons. (79)
Today, having seized my father—that Pārtha—and likewise the other Pāṇḍavas by their locks of hair, he struck off their heads while they had laid down their weapons.
I shall slay that son of Pṛṣata by means of a stratagem before long; let the Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇa, witness my prowess.
Thus the son of Droṇa made that terrifying vow there before the twice-born; then, when the sun had set, all those kings [prepared for battle].
When both sides had been struck down by Droṇa, they entered the tent of cloth; thus, after eighteen days, the battle came to an end.
Then, having slain Śalya, Karṇa, and others headed by Duryodhana—the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—in battle, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, [attained his goal].
O Brahmins, he performed the funeral rites for his own deceased kin as well as those of others, according to the prescribed rules, together with Dhaumya and the other twice-born priests.
Having paid homage to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, all the Pāṇḍavas gathered together; permitted by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, they were surrounded by those people who had survived the slaughter.
Having reached Hastināpura, they entered their own palace; then, after some days had passed, it is said, the citizens [gathered].

Together with Dhaumya and other sages, the lords of munis began to perform the royal consecration of the high-souled son of Dharma. While the consecration of that son of Dharma was underway, an incorporeal voice then spoke to the delighter of Dharma.
O illustrious son of Dharma, who are compassionate even toward your enemies, do not perform the royal consecration; you are not fit for the protection of the kingdom.
Since you, O King, being shameless, spoke falsely to the preceptor—the best of the twice-born—and caused him, who had laid down his weapons in battle, to be slain by deceit. (91)
Therefore, O delighter of Dharma, there exists in you an abundance of sin; without performing expiation for this, [you have engaged] in the act of governing the kingdom.
"Since no atonement exists for an Arhat, therefore perform penance"; having said this, that bodiless voice then ceased.
Then King Dharmasuta, deeply distressed by those words, thought: "I am deluded, reckless, cruel, treacherous, and infatuated by greed. (94)
Out of a desire for a worthless kingdom, I have committed such an evil deed; for the purification of this sin, what shall I do? What is my recourse? (95)
"What gift shall I give, or where indeed shall I go?"—while that King, born of Dharma, was thus overwhelmed with grief. (96)
Then Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa arrived in his presence; thereupon, rising up with palms joined in reverence, he paid homage to that Vyāsa.

Having worshipped with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites with a mind full of devotion, that brahmin related everything in its entirety, exactly as it had been spoken by the bodiless voice.
The son of Dharma, being distressed, caused Vyāsa to hear it; having heard all those words of Dharmaja, the great sage meditated for a very long time and then began to speak.
Vyāsa said: "O King, do not be afraid; I shall tell you a remedy. Having heard it, let it be performed by you for the sake of pacifying this sin. (100)
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O great yogin, O son of Parāśara, O ocean of mercy, tell me that by which my sins may be destroyed; speak of it now so that it may happen without delay. (101)
Vyāsa said: On the bridge over the southern ocean, on Mount Gandhamādana... (102)
O Great King, on Rāmasetu there is a famous, meritorious, and perfected lake known as Rāmatīrtha, which destroys even the most heinous sins.
By the mere sight of whom ten million great sins (mahāpātaka) instantly go to destruction, just as darkness does at the rising of the sun.
When one beholds Rāmatīrtha, which was created by Rāma himself, at that very moment one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin; there is no doubt about this.
Having gone there, O Great King, bathe at Rāmatīrtha, which bestows liberation; your purification from sin will occur, as well as your fitness for protecting the kingdom.

"O Yudhiṣṭhira, perform acts of charity on its banks with gifts of cattle, land, sesame seeds, clothing, gold, and silver; by this, the purification of your sins will surely come to pass before long."
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, this son of Dharma was thus addressed by Vyāsa.
At that very moment, accompanied by Dhaumya and his younger brothers, the righteous son of Dharma then established Sahadeva in the kingdom.
Aiming for Rāmasetu, he set out on foot; in just a few days, he reached Rāmasetu.
Having reached Rāmatīrtha together with Dhaumya, the Pāṇḍava performed the ritual resolve according to the rules, following the path instructed by his priest.
He bathed at the sacred Rāmasaras-tīrtha, which destroys all sins; having bathed and sipped water (ācamana), his soul purified, he offered the piṇḍa for the field (kṣetrapiṇḍa).
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, gave all the gifts prescribed by Vyāsa; for one month he remained without food and bathed there.
O twice-born ones, he gave gifts every day without any greed for wealth; then, when one month had passed in this manner, on a certain day, [he continued].
Again, an incorporeal voice spoke to the son of Dharma: "O King Yudhiṣṭhira, all your sin has gone to destruction. (15)
O scorcher of foes, that fault which previously arose from your speaking a falsehood and from the slaying of your preceptor has also been destroyed.
Go to your own city, O King, and protect the earth; have yourself consecrated, for you possess the fitness to protect the kingdom.
Having spoken thus, that bodiless voice then ceased; thereupon the son of Dharma, being pleased, [looked] toward that direction.
Having paid homage to that bodiless Speech, he, along with his younger brother, set out for Hastināpura with a deeply joyful heart.
Then, having been consecrated in the kingdom, he protected the earth; thus, O Brahmins, did the son of Dharma [Yudhiṣṭhira] [attain his sovereignty] by bathing at Rāmatīrtha.
Having his sins gone and his soul purified, he became fit for the protection of the kingdom. Thus has the wonderful majesty of Rāmatīrtha been narrated to you.
It is meritorious, removing all sins, and bestowing devotion and liberation; by bathing there, that son of Dharma was liberated from the fault of falsehood.

Those best of the twice-born who recite this chapter, or those men who hear it and are freed from sin, shall go to Kailāsa, which is unattainable by others; having gone there, they do not undergo birth again.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pacification of the Fault of Dharmaputra’s False Statement," within the Praise of Rāmatīrtha, in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 18 ||
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having bathed in the holy ford of that Tārakabrahman, one should then proceed with a concentrated mind to the holy ford of Lakṣmaṇa.
Having bathed at the holy site of Śrī Lakṣmaṇa, they are liberated from sins and attain stainless liberation characterized by the absence of rebirth. || 2 ||
By bathing at Lakṣmaṇatīrtha, all poverty is destroyed; moreover, a son who is long-lived, virtuous, and learned is born to him.
Whoever chants that mantra on the bank of Lakṣmaṇatīrtha shall become a knower of all scriptures; he shall even be a master of the four Vedas.
On its bank, Lakṣmaṇa installed a great Liṅga; whoever bathes at that holy site and worships Lakṣmaṇeśvara, [attains the fruit].

O Brahmins, in ancient times, Balabhadra was liberated from poverty, disease, and from saṃsāra by bathing at Lakṣmaṇatīrtha and worshipping Lakṣmaṇeśvara; thus he was freed from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The sages said: "O son of Sūta, how did the murder of a Brahmin come to befall the son of Rohiṇī? And how was it destroyed in this matter? Tell us that, O great sage. (7)
The venerable Sūta said: O twice-born ones, in ancient times, the Lord Balabhadra was an incarnation of Śeṣa.
But having observed the preparations for war between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, Halāyudha was unable to endure the slaughter of his kinsmen.
The high-minded Balabhadra reflected thus: "If I were to provide assistance to the King of the Kurus... (10)
"If I were to do a favor for the Pāṇḍavas, an irresistible and most terrible anger would arise against me from the sons of Pāṇḍu. (11)
Perceiving that Duryodhana might become enraged, Halāyudha then set out for the middle region under the pretext of a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Then, having gone to Prabhāsa and bathed according to the prescribed ritual intention (*saṃkalpa*), he gratified the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors with water.
Then the wielder of the plow proceeded toward the west along the Sarasvatī river, reaching Pṛthūdaka, Bindusaras, Muktida, and Brahmatīrthaka.
Having reached the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sindhu, Śatadrū, and Sudarśana, this Balabhadra bathed according to dharma in those sacred fords.
He reached the Naimiṣa forest, which is frequented by the lords of sages; then, seeing him arrive, the ascetics of Naimiṣa [welcomed him].
Established in a long sacrificial session, perfectly self-restrained, and devoted to the Dharma, they rose up to meet the best of the Yadus, bowed down, and then rose from their seats.
Then they honored him with seats and other offerings, as well as roots and fruits; having accepted the seat, he was thus worshipped along with his attendants.
Having observed the disciple of Vyāsa seated on a high seat, not bowing, not rising, and sitting without his hands joined in reverence, he [spoke]. (19)
Seeing the brahmins bowing down and observing that he himself had arrived, the son of Rohiṇī became enraged at Sūta, the best of those learned in the Purāṇas.
"Among these sages, why does this sūta—a person of mixed caste born in the inverse order—sit upon a high seat? This is certainly not proper. (21)
Having utterly disregarded us, the protectors of dharma, he remains fearless, neither rising nor bowing down to us. (22)
Having studied all the Purāṇas along with their histories, as well as numerous treatises on Dharma, from the presence of Dvaipāyana; (23)
"Upon seeing me, they do not bow down, nor do they even leave their seats; such are the twice-born disciples of the great Dvaipāyana, headed by Paila. (24)
They would never have committed such an unrighteous act as this; therefore, I shall slay this evil-minded and senseless wretch.
Indeed, I have come to the world of mortals for the sake of subduing the wicked; for once that evil-minded one has been slain by me, he will undoubtedly attain purification.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Rāma—the wielder of the mace, the powerful wielder of the plow—wrathfully severed that head with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass held in his hand.
All the sages dwelling there cried out, "Alas, what misery! Then those sages, exponents of the Veda, spoke to Rāma.
O Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, a grievous unrighteousness has been committed by you toward Rāma; for we have granted this charioteer the great seat of Brahmā. (29)
"O Halāyudha, we have granted him an inexhaustible lifespan; yet today, by you acting without knowledge, a great Brahman-slaughter has been committed. (30)
For you, the Lord of Yoga, there is no one who can restrain you; however, regarding this act of Brahman-slaughter, please deliberate upon what ought to be done.
"O Blessed One, Rāma, perform the expiation yourself for the sake of gathering the world together; do not act prompted by anyone else. Thus addressed, the Blessed Lord Rāma spoke to those sages.
Rāma said: "O believers, I shall perform an expiation that purifies one of sin."
"For the sake of gathering the world together, and not out of any other desire, we must now observe such a vow as will bring about the pacification of sin. (34)
"Tell us today such a rule as this: 'Since you have granted this Sūta an imperishable lifespan, I shall, by means of my yogic power (yogamāyā), restore his senses and his vital strength. (35)
The sages said: "O Lord Rāma, you ought to act so that your word may become true—namely, regarding your prowess, your weapon, death, and ourselves. (36)
Rāma said: "The Veda always declares that the Self indeed exists in the form of a son. (37)
"O best of Brahmins, he proclaims: 'Therefore, from his body, let there be a son who is long-lived and endowed with strength, sensory faculties, and vigor. (39)
He will narrate to you the Purāṇas and other texts every day; through the power of my Yogamāyā, he shall become omniscient.
Having spoken thus, the son of Rohiṇī addressed them again with humility: "What is desired by your hearts? What may I do for you? (40)
"Therefore, speak, O sages; I shall do it without a doubt. O best of sages, tell me the expiation that will bring about the cessation even of this sin committed by me through ignorance."
The sages said: "There was a certain Dānava named Balvala, who was the son of Ilvala."
"He defiles our sacrifice by coming here on this auspicious day; slay that wicked and sinful Dānava, who is the sole thorn in the side of the world. (43)
"By this, a true worship has now been performed for us by you; for in the sacrifice, there were bones, excrement, urine, blood, liquor, and meat. (44)
That Dānava, having come here, always showers [rain] upon us; indeed, whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist in this region of Bhārata, [he rains upon them].
Bathe in all of them for one year with a well-composed mind; by that, there shall be the pacification of your sin—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Śrī Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, when the sacrificial rite of the sages had commenced at the time of the festival, there arose a most terrifying rain of dust and a fearsome tempestuous wind.
O best of Brahmins, there appeared a rain of pus and blood; thereafter, a rain consisting of excrement was also produced by Balvala.
Then, in an instant, that Balabhadra beheld an Asura with a trident in hand, possessed of great strength and prowess, within the sacrificial hall.
Beholding him at that time, possessed of a massive body resembling a scorched mountain, with a face made fierce by a beard and fangs glowing like molten copper; (50)
Rāma thought of the pestle that rends the enemies, the ploughshare that destroys the Dānavas, and the mace that shatters the Daityas.
Whatever weapons were thought of appeared before that Rāma; then, having dragged the sky-walker Balvala with the tip of his plow, he [struck him].
Enraged, he struck him on the head with force using the pestle; with his forehead crushed, he fell to the ground vomiting blood.
Trembling and speaking piteously, like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt, the sages then praised Rāma and uttered pure blessings.
They consecrated him with auspicious waters, just as the gods consecrated the enemy of Vṛtra; they gave him the Vaijayantī garland, adorned with glorious lotuses.
Wearing those auspicious garments and beautiful ornaments for Mādhava, the exceedingly powerful son of Rohiṇī put them all on.
O twice-born ones, accompanied by flowering trees like Mount Kailāsa, he was then permitted by the sages to visit all the sacred fords.
For one year he wandered about, endowed with the practice of religious observances; then, when the year was complete, Balarāma reached the divider of the Kālindī.
Having completed his pilgrimage, he set out to go to the city; then he beheld a thin, shadowy form consisting of darkness following behind him.
Baladeva beheld her crying out with a great roar; then he heard a report arising in the sky.
O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed son of Rohiṇī, you who possess a white radiance; O sinless one, by your pilgrimage to the sacred fords and by your conduct today—
"O son of Rohiṇī, your sin of Brahman-slaughter has not been destroyed; it remains without exception. Having heard these words, Balarāma indeed began to reflect.
"I have performed atonement for one year by resorting to sacred pilgrimage sites; nevertheless, I have heard these words: 'That sin of killing a Brahmin has not been destroyed.'"
Thinking, "What shall I do?", he went to the Naimiṣa forest; having arrived there, that subduer of enemies reported it to the sages.
The son of Rohiṇī reported everything—the words heard in the sky and that which was seen consisting of darkness—to the sages; having heard that, all the sages then spoke these words to Rāma.
The sages said: "O Rāma, if your Brahman-murder has not been entirely destroyed," (66)
"In that case, O illustrious one, go to Mount Gandhamādana, which pacifies great suffering and destroys great disease. (67)
On the highly meritorious Rāmasetu, on Mount Gandhamādana, there is a lake known as Lakṣmaṇatīrtha, which destroys all sins.
"Perform your bath there and bow down to that Liṅga; by that, the sin of killing a Brahmin will be destroyed without remainder—of this there is no doubt. (69)
Śrī Sūta said: Having been addressed thus, O best of sages, Rāma then went to Mount Gandhamādana and reached Lakṣmaṇatīrtha.
Having bathed at that sacred ford according to the prescribed ritual of formal resolve (saṃkalpa), Halāyudha bestowed wealth, grain, cows, and land upon the Brāhmaṇas.
At that moment, a bodiless voice spoke there to Rāma: "O Rāma, your sin of Brahman-murder has now been completely destroyed here. (72)
"No doubt should be entertained here; go happily to your own city. Having heard that, Balabhadra then praised that sacred ford.
Then, having bathed in all the holy fords there, and likewise having bathed at Dhanuṣkoṭi and worshipped Rāmanātha, Mādhava—his accumulation of sins destroyed—proceeded to his own city, Dvārakā.
The venerable Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, has the pure Śrī Lakṣmaṇasara been described to you.

Whoever should read or listen with a concentrated mind to this chapter—which is meritorious, purifying, destructive of sins, and a cleanser of even the murder of a Brahmin—[attains the highest goal]. || 76 ||
O best of Brahmins, he attains liberation from which there is no return. || 77 ||

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Balabhadra from the Sin of Brahmin-Slaughter," within the Praise of Lakṣmaṇatīrtha, in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 19.
The venerable Sūta said: Having bathed at the great tīrtha of Lakṣmaṇa, which destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin, one should then proceed to Jaṭātīrtha for the sake of purifying one's own mind.
O twice-born ones, for those whose minds are afflicted by the cycle of birth, death, and old age, there is no destroyer of ignorance other than the Jaṭātīrtha.
In this world, some seekers of liberation, desiring purity of mind, recite the Vedāntas with their speech but do not experience them through silence.

In this ocean of Vedānta, which is infested with the great crocodiles of prima facie arguments and teeming with the fish of established conclusions, the twice-born who have fallen therein become bewildered by ignorance.
Those who first study the Vedāntas for the sake of purifying the mind, after having studied them, engage in disputes and spread quarrels.
Purification of the mind does not arise from the Vedānta, for it is a cause of great delusion; therefore, O lords of sages, we do not hold the Vedānta in high esteem.
O ascetics, if you desire purification of the mind by an easy means, I proclaim it to you all: resort to Jaṭātīrtha.
In former times, for the sake of benefiting all beings, this sacred ford (tīrtha) that destroys ignorance was directly fashioned by Śambhu on Mount Gandhamādana.
O Brahmins, when Rāvaṇa had been slain, the righteous Rāma washed his matted locks in that water; therefore, it is called Jaṭātīrtha.
Sixty thousand years of immersion in the waters of the Ganges are equal to a single bath in the Godāvarī when Jupiter is situated in Leo.
When Jupiter has entered Leo, one obtains the merit of a thousand ritual baths in the Gomatī by merely beholding the Jaṭātīrtha for a year.
O best of the twice-born, for those humans who have bathed at Jaṭātīrtha, there shall be purification of the inner organ, and through that, ignorance is destroyed.

Upon the destruction of ignorance, knowledge shall arise; from that, you will attain liberation. Thereafter, you shall become completely filled with indivisible existence, consciousness, and bliss. 13.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history, a dialogue between father and son, between Vyāsa and Śuka.

O twice-born ones, in former times, Śuka, having bowed his head to Vyāsa—the best of sages, the infallible Kṛṣṇa who had realized the Self, who knew the distinctions of the traditional lineages, and who was skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures—indeed questioned him. (15)
Śrī Śuka said: O Blessed One, O Father, O Omniscient One, tell me the unsurpassed secret.
Thereby there shall be purification of the internal organ and the destruction of ignorance; and by that means, the arising of knowledge and, in the end, eternal liberation shall occur. || 17 ||
O great sage, out of affection for me, tell me today that means; for the Vedāntas, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas and other texts in their entirety [do not provide it].
"The subjects I have studied from you do not purify my mind; therefore, O father, tell me how my mental purity may be attained. (19)
O best of sages, having been thus questioned by Śuka, Vyāsa then recounted that secret by which ignorance is destroyed.
Vyāsa said: O Śuka, I shall tell you that secret which severs the knot of ignorance, which bestows purity of intellect upon men, and which destroys the fear of birth and other such states. (21)
On Mount Gandhamādana at Rāmasetu, there exists the highly meritorious Jaṭātīrtha, renowned as the destroyer of sins. || 22 ||
There, Rāma himself, the glorious Rāma, son of Daśaratha, purified his own matted locks and granted a boon to the sacred ford.
He thought, "May those who come here and bathe in this most purifying Jaṭātīrtha attain purity of heart. (24)
Without sacrifice, without knowledge, and without recitation or fasting, the purification of the intellect occurs for men merely by bathing at Jaṭātīrtha. (25)
The merit arising from bathing here shall be equal to all forms of giving; by this, one crosses over difficulties and attains the worlds of merit.
Through bathing in the auspicious waters of Jaṭātīrtha, one attains greatness; apart from Jaṭātīrtha, there is nothing else for the purification of the inner heart.
There is no other rule or recitation for another deity; it is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, and renowned throughout all the worlds. (28)
O Śuka, Jaṭātīrtha is now the purifier of purifiers; it pacifies all sins and is the most auspicious among auspicious things. (29)

O Śuka, in former times Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, asked his father Varuṇa about the auspicious and purifying means for attaining purity of intellect; Varuṇa then spoke to him concerning that auspicious means which bestows purity of intellect.
Varuṇa said: O Bhṛgu, on the meritorious Rāmasetu at the Gandhamādana mountain, || 31 ||
"By merely bathing at this sacred ford (tīrtha), the purification of the intellect will certainly occur. At his father's word, Bhrigu, the son of Varuṇa, immediately [acted].
Having gone and bathed at Jaṭātīrtha, Bhṛgu attained purity of intellect; by that purification, the continuity of his ignorance was then destroyed.
Having attained the realization of non-duality, Śuka became like his father Varuṇa, possessing a form that was the fullness of indivisible being, consciousness, and bliss.
Even Durvāsas, though a portion of Śaṅkara, attained purity of mind through ablution at Jaṭātīrtha and quickly became filled with the bliss of Brahman. || 35 ||
O Śuka, Dattātreya also, being a portion of Viṣṇu, having his inner self purified by bathing in this sacred ford, became one whose form was Brahman.
He who desires the destruction of ignorance should bathe at the most pure and meritorious sacred ford named Jaṭā, which destroys all sins.
Therefore, O Śuka of great intelligence, go from here to Jaṭātīrtha; perform a bath there, which bestows purity of mind and grants merit. (38)
O twice-born ones, having been thus addressed by his father Vyāsa, Śuka, his son, then [proceeded] to the highly meritorious Rāmasetu and Mount Gandhamādana.
Desiring to bathe, the sage Śuka went to the Jaṭātīrtha, which bestows purity; having bathed in the Jaṭātīrtha according to the prescribed ritual (saṃkalpa), he performed his ablutions.
Having attained purity of mind and, through that, the destruction of ignorance, he entered his own true nature, which consists of supreme bliss.
And those other best of the twice-born who desire purity of mind, they all should bathe at Jaṭātīrtha with devotion. (42)

Alas, people! Even though the auspicious Jaṭātīrtha, which is equal to the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), exists here, why do you, being deluded, take delight elsewhere in that which is trivial? 43.
O twice-born ones, one who desires enjoyment shall obtain enjoyment, and one who desires liberation shall obtain that; by merely bathing at Jaṭātīrtha, this has been truly spoken by me. (44)
Through the recitation of the Vedas, merit, sacrifice, charity, austerity, vows, fasting, chanting, and yoga, the purification of the mind occurs for human beings. (45)
O best of Brahmins, even without these [rites], by the mere act of bathing at the exceedingly purifying Jaṭātīrtha, the purification of the minds of Brāhmaṇas will certainly occur.
The majesty of Jaṭātīrtha cannot be described by me; Śaṅkara knows that tīrtha, as do Hari and Brahmā. (47)
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford equal to Jaṭātīrtha; whoever performs the offering of food for the ancestors at the bank of Jaṭātīrtha [attains the highest reward].

His merit shall be equal to that of performing a śrāddha at Gayā; of this there is no doubt. Having bathed at Jaṭātīrtha, a man is not defiled by sin; he does not encounter poverty, nor is he led into the ocean of hell.
The venerable Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, the majesty of Jaṭātīrtha has been narrated to you.
Where the yogi, son of Vyāsa, having bathed at Pāpavimocana, attained purity of mind, which is the means for the knowledge of non-duality.
But he who reads this chapter or listens to it with a concentrated mind, having shaken off his sins here, attains the state of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Purification of Śuka’s Mind," in the Praise of Jaṭātīrtha, within the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: Having performed an ablution at the holy site named Jaṭātīrtha, which destroys all sins, one whose soul is purified should then proceed to Lakṣmītīrtha.
O best of the twice-born, whatever desire a mortal may have in mind when he performs a bath at Lakṣmītīrtha, that very desire he attains.
It pacifies great poverty, bestows abundance of great grain, alleviates great suffering, and increases great prosperity. || 3 ||
Having bathed here, the son of Dharma attained great sovereignty; formerly, while residing at Indraprastha, he was impelled by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The sages said: O great sage, tell us how the son of Dharma obtained sovereignty by immersing himself in Lakṣmītīrtha according to the word of Kṛṣṇa.
The venerable Sūta said: O Brahmins, in ancient times, the five Pāṇḍavas, endowed with great strength and prowess, dwelt at Indraprastha, directed there by Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Once Kṛṣṇa went to Indraprastha to see them; seeing that he had arrived, those Pāṇḍavas were filled with eager anticipation.
Filled with supreme joy, they brought him to their own home; Kṛṣṇa dwelt there in that excellent city for some time.
Once, having summoned Kṛṣṇa and honored him, Yudhiṣṭhira questioned Vāsudeva, the lotus-eyed Lord of the universe.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O highly wise one, tell us that dharma by which human beings attain great sovereignty, O great-minded one. Thus addressed by the son of Dharma, Kṛṣṇa spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O illustrious son of Dharma, on Mount Gandhamādana...
There is a place renowned as Lakṣmītīrtha, the sole cause of sovereign power; perform your ablutions there, and you shall attain prosperity.
By bathing there, the abundance of wealth and grain increases; all rivals perish, and their kṣatriya power flourishes.
In ancient times, O son of Dharma, the gods bathed at the merit-bestowing holy site named Lakṣmī; by that merit, they obtained all sovereignty.
They swiftly slew the highly powerful Asuras in battle; and for those men who bathe in that sacred ford, there shall be the earth, prosperity, and righteousness.
It will happen very soon; do not entertain doubt in this matter, O Pāṇḍava, through austerities, sacrifices, gifts, and blessings.
Just as sovereignty is attained by immersion in the Lakṣmītīrtha, so too, O Brahmins, all sins are destroyed and always go to their dissolution.
Diseases are destroyed by resorting to Lakṣmītīrtha; one obtains very great welfare in this world—of this there is no doubt. (18)
O son of Dharma, by merely bathing in this sacred ford of Lakṣmī, the king Avadha obtained Rambhā, the most excellent of the Apsarases.
Having bathed here at this meritorious tīrtha, Kubera, whose vehicle is man, became the lord of the treasures, chief among which is Mahāpadma.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too, having bathed in the auspicious Lakṣmītīrtha, accompanied by your younger brothers headed by Vṛkodara, [should perform the rites].
"You shall attain great fortune and you shall also conquer your enemies; no doubt should be entertained in this matter, O son of my paternal aunt, O son born of dharma. (22)
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, this son of Dharma, whose appearance was wondrous, departed quickly for the Gandhamādana mountain along with his younger brothers.
Then, having gone to Lakṣmītīrtha, the cause of great sovereignty, Yudhiṣṭhira bathed there along with his younger brothers, observing the prescribed restraints.
In the waters of Lakṣmatīrtha, which destroy all sins, he, together with his younger brothers, bathed for one month according to the prescribed rules.
He gave many gifts of cattle, land, sesame seeds, gold, and other riches to the Brahmins; then that son of Dharma, accompanied by his younger brothers, departed for Indraprastha.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, desiring to perform the Rājasūya sacrifice and wishing to offer it, summoned Kṛṣṇa. || 27 ||
Summoned by the messenger of Dharmaja, Kṛṣṇa, filled with haste, mounted a swift chariot yoked with four horses.
Accompanied by Satyabhāmā, he arrived at Indraprastha; seeing him arrive, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) was filled with joy.
He then informed Kṛṣṇa of his preparations for the Rājasūya sacrifice; Kṛṣṇa also gave his consent, saying, "Let it be done exactly so."
And he spoke these words, consistent with reason, to the son of Dharma: "O righteous nephew of my father's sister, listen to my beneficial words. (31)
This Rājasūya sacrifice is difficult to perform even for all the lords of the earth, involving many hundreds of foot-soldiers, chariots, elephants, and horses.
Only this lord of the earth is worthy to perform this sacrifice, and no other; first, the ten directions must be conquered by you while you possess strength.
Having extracted the highest tribute from the conquered enemies, this supreme sacrifice must be performed with that gold.
I do not delight in this reasoning, nor indeed do I intend to frighten you, sir; therefore, before the commencement of the sacrifice, perform a conquest of the quarters.
Then the son of Dharma, having heard the beneficial words of Kṛṣṇa, praised the son of Devakī and summoned his own younger brothers.
Having summoned his four brothers, the son of Dharma spoke to them, gladdening them: "O Bhīma of mighty arms, O Dhanañjaya of great prowess! (37)
And the twins, with their delicate limbs, are consecrated for the destruction of enemies; I desire to perform the unsurpassed great sacrifice, the Rājasūya. (38)
Having conquered all the lords of the earth in battle, he must then conquer even those four kings along with their armies. (39)
"Go forth to the four directions, O most heroic ones! With the materials procured by you, I shall perform a great sacrifice. (40)
Having been addressed thus with respect by all those headed by Vṛkodara, the younger brothers of Dharmaputra then became cheerful of countenance and departed from the city.
For the victory of the kings, the Pāṇḍavas set out in all directions; having conquered all those many monarchs stationed in the four quarters, they returned. || 42 ||
Having brought those kings under their control, the sons of Pāṇḍu received from them vast and incomparable wealth in manifold quantities.
Taking him with them, those who had taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa quickly returned to their own city; Bhīma, endowed with great strength and prowess, also arrived there.
Having taken up a hundred bhāras of gold, Arjuna then took a thousand bhāras of gold from that supreme city.
Then Nakula, possessed of great strength and prowess, arrived at Śakraprastha, carrying with him a hundred bhāras of gold.
The one of great splendor arrived at Śakraprastha, the most excellent city; then, fourteen golden palm trees were presented by Vibhīṣaṇa.
Having seized the accumulated wealth of the southern kings, Sahadeva also quickly returned to his own city.
The Yādava Kṛṣṇa gave thousands of lakṣas of koṭis and even hundreds of lakṣas of koṭis of gold pieces to the son of Dharma.
Thus, with the countless great riches brought by his own younger brothers, and also with the countless riches given by Kṛṣṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira [performed the sacrifice].
Taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa, the Pāṇḍava performed the Rājasūya sacrifice; at that sacrifice, he gave wealth to the Brāhmaṇas according to their desire.
There Yudhiṣṭhira gave food to the Brāhmaṇas; likewise, he gave garments, cows, land, and ornaments.
With whatever gold and other riches the seekers were satisfied, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, caused twice that amount to be given to them.
"Such various riches as these have been given to supplicants; even tens of millions of Brahmās are not able to measure this extent. (54)
Seeing the wealth being given there by seekers, the people indeed said: "Aha! Even his entire possession has been given away by the king! (55)
Having seen those countless treasuries filled with infinite jewels and gold.
"People said at that time, 'Very little indeed has been given to those who asked,' after the son of Dharma, along with his younger brothers, had thus performed the Rājasūya sacrifice. (57)
Abounding in great wealth, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, took delight there in that excellent city by virtue of the majesty of Lakṣmītīrtha.
O Brahmins, he obtained all of this; oh, what majesty belongs to this sacred ford! This holy place is of great merit and is the destroyer of great poverty. (59)
It bestows wealth and grain upon men, destroys great sins, eradicates the great hells, and turns back great suffering. || 60 ||
It eternally bestows liberation and heaven, grants release from great debts, and provides virtuous wives and noble sons to men.
A holy place equal to this has never existed, nor will there ever be; O Brahmins, I have thus described to you the majesty of Lakṣmītīrtha.
Whoever reads this chapter or listens to it with devotion attains merit that destroys evil dreams and accomplishes all desired objects. (63)
That man shall be prosperous with wealth and grain; of this there is no doubt. Having enjoyed all pleasures here in this world, he shall attain liberation at the end of the body.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Dharmaputra’s Attainment of Unsurpassed Prosperity," within the Praise of Lakṣmītīrtha, in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 21 ||
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having bathed in the auspicious Lakṣmītīrtha—the sole cause of all sovereignty for men—a man should then proceed to Agnitīrtha.

The Agnitīrtha is immensely meritorious and the destroyer of great sins; it is the supreme among all holy sites and the sole means for accomplishing every desire. A person should bathe there with devotion for the complete purification of their own sins.
The sages said: O Lord of Sages, how did he acquire the renown of being "Agni" (Fire)?
Where is this Agnitīrtha, and what is its majesty? You ought to describe this in detail to us who are full of faith.
The venerable Sūta said: You have indeed asked well; listen, O best of sages. Formerly, Rāghava, having slain Rāvaṇa along with his retinue, [proceeded].
Having established his lord Vibhīṣaṇa in Laṅkā, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, joined by Sītā and the son of Sumitrā, [departed].
Being praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, gods, and hosts of Apsarases, as well as by groups of sages, he was one whose blessings were true and who took delight in sacred fords.
Holding his bow with ease, Rāma, whose prowess was irresistible, acted thus to establish his own purity and likewise to vindicate Jānakī.
Accompanied by Indra and the hosts of other gods, as well as the sages and the ancestors, and together with Vibhīṣaṇa and all the monkeys; || 9 ||
He arrived at Mount Gandhamādana by way of the Setu bridge; having stationed himself on the bank of Lakṣmītīrtha, he remained there for the sake of purifying Jānakī.
He invoked Agni in the presence of the celestial sages and the ancestors; then, from the Lakṣmītīrtha, not far away, he rose up from the great ocean.
While all the worlds were looking on, the Fire-god, licking the waters, with copper-red eyes, clad in yellow garments, and bearing a bow, appeared.
Licking the ten directions with seven tongues, he beheld the heroic Lord of the Raghus, who appeared in the playful form of a human.
For the sake of Janaki’s purification, he spoke these charming words: "O Rama, Rama, O mighty-armed one, who brings fear to the Rakshasas! (14)
By means of Jānakī’s devotion to her husband, you slew Rāvaṇa; this is true, true, and again true—there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (15)
This Kamalā is the Mother of the World, assuming a human form through her divine play; she possesses a celestial body when in the state of a deity, and is a human being when in the state of a mortal.
O Lord of the World, O God of gods, O Janārdana, whenever he assumes a body for himself in accordance with the form of Viṣṇu’s own body.
You take incarnations, and she is your companion in this; when you were Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, then this earth was her form.
Now she has become Jānakī, and thereafter Rukmiṇī; in other incarnations as well, she is the companion of Viṣṇu. (19)
"Therefore, O Raghava, accept her on my word. Having heard those words of the Fire-god, the gods and the great seers [applauded].
The Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, humans, and likewise the Pannagas, as well as other multitudes of beings, [honored] Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
They praised Jānakī, the princess of Mithilā, again and again; and Rāma, following the words of Agni, accepted the stainless Sītā.
Thus, for the sake of Sītā’s purification, when the invocation was performed by Rāma of unwearied deeds, the Fire-god appeared at a distance from Lakṣmītīrtha.
O best of the twice-born, know that unsurpassed region from which I rose up from the ocean to be Agnitīrtha. || 24 ||
Because the fire emerged from there, it is called Agnitīrtha; having bathed here with devotion in this fire-tīrtha which bestows liberation, a person [attains release]. 25.
Having observed the fast, one should also feed Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas; to them one should give clothing, wealth, land, and a decorated maiden.
Completely liberated from all sins, he shall attain union with Viṣṇu; on this bank of Agnitīrtha, the gift of food is especially distinguished.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford equal to Agnitīrtha; for even one who is ill-famed and a great sinner attains the state of a Piśāca through bathing there.
Having abandoned his most terrible form, he attained a divine body; formerly, in Pāṭaliputra, he was a Vaiśya named Paśumān.
He was indeed constantly devoted to righteousness and intent upon honoring the Brahmins; he practiced agriculture incessantly and always protected his cattle.
And he was selling gold and other goods righteously in the marketplace of that excellent merchant named Paśuman.
There were three wives, devoted to the service of their husband; the eldest gave birth to three sons who increased the lineage of the Vaiśyas.
Madhyamā gave birth to two sons, Sukosha and Bahukosha, who were excellent merchants, possessed of great wealth, and likewise possessed of beautiful merchandise.
On the third [wife], three sons were born to that Vaiśya, renowned as Mahāpaṇya, Mahākośa, and Duṣpaṇya.
O best of the twice-born, in this manner that Vaiśya Paśumān had eight sons born from those three wives. (35)
All those sons, whose faces were like fine merchandise, grew up in due course; playing with dust, they brought joy to their parents.
Gradually, those sons of the Vaiśya attained the age of five years; and the lordly Vaiśya Paśumān likewise [reared] all those sons.
From childhood onwards, he constantly instructed them in their respective duties; they were gradually trained in the occupations of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade.
The seven foremost merchants, disregarding the words of their father, immediately carried out whatever task Paśumān commanded. || 39 ||
They attained extreme proficiency even in the arts of goldsmithing; however, the eighth son, Duṣpaṇya, from his very childhood, was constantly... [40]
Having become devoted to evil ways, he did not listen to the words of his father; beginning with playing in the dust, he became intent on wicked paths. (41)
Even while still a child, that son oppressed other children; seeing him thus intent on evil deeds, his father, Paśumān, likewise [restrained him].
Saying, "This man is a fool; he has shown only indifference toward me," the eight sons of the Vaiśya then reached their youth. (43)
Then this eighth son, Duṣṇaya, the best among the strong, seized the children residing in the city by their hands and necks.
He threw [them] into wells, rivers, and even lakes; no person whatsoever knew of this wicked conduct of his. (45)
As long as those children died, he continued to cast them into the water; and for those deceased children, their fathers and mothers likewise [grieved]. (46)
They searched for all of them throughout every city; and seeing those sons dead, which people indeed wept aloud? (47)
Then, seeing the corpses in the waters, the people performed what was appropriate. In this manner, Duṣpaṇya continued to kill children in the city every day.
Thus he continued for a long time, unknown even to the people, due to the karma of the Vaiśya’s son while the children were dying. (49)
Due to the lack of growth among the subjects, the city became almost empty; then the citizens gathered together and reported that matter to the king.
Having heard those words, the king summoned the village guards and commanded them: "Consider the cause of this child's death."
The village guards, having replied "So be it," stationed themselves here and there and thoroughly investigated the cause of the boy's death.
Though they searched diligently, they did not find Bālāmāraka; returning once more to the king, they spoke these words in fear.
O King, although we have been searching for him, we do not find him—this one who, staying within the city, constantly slays even children.
Furthermore, all the citizens, having approached the king in their distress, spoke again of the death of the subjects, their voices choked with tears. (55)
The king, however, remained silent after reflecting on the reason for this; then, at one time, this son of a Vaiśya was with five other boys.
Then Duṣpaṇya approached the edge of the lake under the pretext of gathering lotuses; seizing those boys by force while they were crying out, he took them away. || 57 ||
The cruel-hearted Duṣpaṇya submerged them in the lake water up to their necks; thinking they were dead, he quickly went to his own home.
The five fathers, searching for their sons in the city while they were thus searching, [found] those five very young children by him.
Although they were cast into the waters, by chance they did not die; slowly reaching the shore, all five had their heads drenched.
Unable to go to the city due to their childhood, they wandered right there while their kinsmen called out their names from afar.
Having heard this, all five of those boys made a reply; then their father, having heard it, arrived there at the edge of the lake.
Seeing their sons still alive, they were filled with incomparable joy; then those boys were asked by their father and the others, "What is this? (63)
Then the kinsmen reported Duṣpaṇya’s evil deed to them; thereafter, the citizens, having learned the facts of the matter, approached the king. (64)
They reported the account of Duṣpaṇya as it had been told by the five; then the king, having summoned Paśumant, the best of merchants, spoke these words while the citizens were listening.
The king said: "This city, named Duṣpaṇya, possesses many cattle and a great multitude of offspring."
Behold how it has been made almost empty by your evil-minded son; now he has indeed caused these innocent ones to drown in the water.
And by chance, those endowed with life have returned once more to the city. Now that matters have come to this pass, tell me what must be done.
"Today I ask you alone, since you are so devoted to dharma. Thus addressed by the king, Paśumān, who was himself a knower of dharma, spoke what was appropriate. (69)
Paśu said: "He by whom the city has been utterly destroyed deserves nothing but death; for in this matter, O King, there is nothing further to be asked. (70)
For this cannot be my son; he is surely an enemy who has committed a most heinous crime. I see no atonement for him, by whom the city has been utterly destroyed.
"This wicked-souled one must indeed be put to death; I speak the truth. Having heard these words of Paśumān, all the citizens [agreed]. (72)
Praising the excellent merchant, they said this to the king: "Let this wicked man not be executed; let him be quietly banished from the city. (73)
Then that king, having summoned Duṣpaṇya, spoke as follows: "O evil-minded one, depart from this country immediately! (74)
"If you remain right here, I shall surely punish you with death!"—having thus rebuked him, the king had him banished from the city by messengers.
Then Duṣpaṇya, filled with fear, abandoned that region and went instead to the forest crowded with circles of sages. (76)
There, seeing that the sage’s son had died, the sons of the sage who had come for the sake of sport submerged one of the sage’s sons in the waters. (77)
Approaching him, they, being deeply afflicted by grief, told it to his father; then Ugraśravas, having heard from them that his son was dead in the water, [acted].
By the power of his asceticism, Ugraśravas perceived that evil conduct; he then cursed Duṣpaṇya, the son of the Vaiśya.
Ugraśravas said: "O Mārī, since you have cast my son into the water, may your own death likewise come about by drowning in water. (80)
"And having died, you shall become a Piśāca for a very long time. Upon hearing this curse, Duṣpaṇya immediately became distressed in mind.
Having abandoned that forest, he went to another, terrible forest abounding in cruel creatures such as lions; when he had reached that other part of the forest, [the following occurred].
A great tempestuous wind blew, raining down a heavy shower of dust and repeatedly uprooting trees; its touch was like the stroke of a thunderbolt.
With great force, the rain shattered his body and was exceedingly difficult to endure; seeing that, Duṣpaṇya became deeply distressed as he reflected upon it.
He saw a single large-bodied elephant that was dead and dried up; at that time, it was unable to endure the great wind and heavy rain. (85)
He entered the depths of the belly through the very opening of the elephant's mouth; as soon as he had entered it, there was a most abundant rain.
Then, from all those rains, a very great torrent arose; that torrent became a certain river in that forest. (87)
Then, with his belly filled by those rains, that elephant, floating upon the great flood, became completely submerged.
Then, because the elephant was without any opening and its belly was filled with water, he was unable to emerge from its stomach.
Then, a torrent of rainwater with terrifying velocity carried the elephant, who had Duṣpaṇya within his belly, to the ocean.
Dūṣpaṇya, submerged in the water, was deprived of his life in an instant; having died, that Dūṣpaṇya attained the state of a piśāca.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, he took refuge in an impenetrable forest; during the terrible heat of the summer season, he cried out in a terrifying manner.
He remained in the dense forest, experiencing many sufferings for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas.
That Piśāca, suffering great misery, dwelt in the terrible forest; he ran from forest to forest, and likewise from region to region.
Experiencing suffering everywhere, he gradually reached the Daṇḍaka forest; while wandering not far from the holy hermitage of Agastya, he proceeded onward.
Uttering a terrifying roar, he spoke these words aloud: "O all you whose wealth is asceticism, listen to my words! (96)
For you, sirs, are compassionate and devoted to the welfare of all beings; favor me, who am excessively tormented by sufferings, with your merciful glance. (97)
Formerly, in Pāṭaliputraka, I was a Vaiśya named Duṣpaṇya; as the son of Paśumant, I killed many children. (98)
Then, banished by the king from that country, he went to the forest; there, in the water, he killed the son of the sage Ugraśravas.
That sage granted my wish for death in the water, but he also bestowed upon me a terrible state as a Piśāca, filled with excessive suffering. (100)
For thousands of millions of eons, and even for hundreds of millions of eons, this state of being a piśāca has been experienced by you in the regions of empty forests. (101)
"I am not able to endure this thirst and hunger; therefore, out of compassion, protect me, who am beset by great suffering. (102)

"O ascetics, act in such a way that I may be liberated from this state of being a Piśāca. Having heard these words of the Piśāca, those whose wealth was their austerity spoke to Agastya, the son of the Jar (Kumbhasambhava), who was accompanied by Lopāmudrā. The ascetics said: "O Blessed One, tell us the supreme means of atonement for this Piśāca. (4)
"You are indeed capable of protecting against such evils; Agastya, who is learned in the scriptures and endowed with supreme compassion, summoned his dear disciple Sutīkṣṇa and spoke these words. (5)
Agastya said: "O Sutīkṣṇa, go quickly to Mount Gandhamādana."
There exists a very great sacred bathing place called Agnitīrtha, which destroys sins; O high-minded one, bathe there for the sake of liberating the Piśāca.
When you have bathed there for the sake of the Piśāca according to the prescribed ritual resolve (saṃkalpa), he shall cast off his state as a Piśāca and attain divinity.
"I see no means of atonement for him except by resorting to that sacred ford; therefore, out of compassion, O Sutīkṣṇa, protect this Piśāca."
Thus addressed by Agastya, Sutīkṣṇa, that ocean of compassion, reached Gandhamādana and, at the Agnitīrtha, made a formal vow for the sake of the Piśācas.
Having worshipped Rāmanātha and the other deities, and having accepted that sacred water, he bathed there for three days according to the prescribed rule for the sake of the Piśāca.
Then, having returned to his own hermitage, Sutīkṣṇa, the best of brahmins, immediately freed him from the state of being a piśāca by sprinkling that sacred bathing place (tīrtha) with water.
By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), he immediately attained divinity; mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, he was surrounded by divine women.
Having repeatedly paid homage to Sutīkṣṇa, Agastya, and other ascetics rich in penance, and having taken leave of them, he was filled with great joy.
By the greatness of Agnitīrtha, Duṣpaṇya, the son of a Vaiśya, quickly ascended to heaven, honored even by the gods.
Having abandoned the state of a Piśāca born of a curse, he thus attained divinity. Thus, O Brahmins, the majesty of Agnitīrtha has been recounted to you.
Whoever should read this chapter or listen to it with devotion—the narrative known as "The Liberation of the Piśāca"—is liberated from all sins. (17)
Having enjoyed great pleasures here, one shall obtain happiness even in the next world. || 119 ||

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Liberation of Duṣpaṇya from the State of a Piśāca," in the Praise of Agnitīrtha within the Setumāhātmya, in the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The venerable Sūta said: Having performed a bath at the sacred ford named Agnitīrtha, which destroys all sins, one whose soul is purified should then proceed to Cakratīrtha.
O best of the twice-born, whatever desire a mortal may have in mind when he performs a ritual bath at Cakratīrtha, that very desire he attains.
Formerly, a great sage named Ahibudhnya, firm in his vows and devoted to asceticism, worshipped Sudarśana here on Mount Gandhamādana.
O Brahmins, while the sage was performing penance there, Rākṣasas of terrible form, who were solely intent on obstructing his asceticism, constantly harassed him.
Then Sudarśana, having arrived with the desire to protect his devotees, effortlessly slew the harassing Yātudhānas in ancient times.
O twice-born ones, from that time forward, at the request of his devotees, that discus has always maintained its presence at the sacred site established by Ahirbudhnya.
From that time onwards, that holy ford has been called Cakratīrtha; by virtue of the grace of Sudarśana, through immersion in that sacred site, [one attains liberation].

There is never any affliction caused by Rākṣasas or Piśācas here at all. In ancient times, the Sun-god, whose hands had been severed, bathed in this purifying holy site (tīrtha) and, through the majesty of that sacred place, regained his golden hands.
The sages said: "O son of a Sūta, how did Āditya become one whose hand was severed? And how did he regain two golden hands? Tell us that."
The venerable Sūta said: In former times, Indra and the other gods were constantly oppressed by the Daityas.
"What shall we do?"—having thus reflected, the gods gathered together and consulted one another; having placed Bṛhaspati at their head, they deliberated for a long time.
Placing Turāsāha at their head, they went to the abode of Svayambhū; having approached Brahmā, they beheld him and praised him with devotion. (12)
Then they informed him of the reason for their arrival. The gods said: "O Blessed One, O Lord of Bhāratī, the Daityas are indeed arrogant with power. (13)
"O Lord, they constantly afflict us; tell us the remedy for that. Thus addressed by the gods, Brahmā spoke these words out of compassion: ||| 14 ||
Brahmā said: "Do not fear, O gods; I shall tell you the means for that: the great sacrifice to Maheśvara, which brings about the destruction of the asuras. (15)
"O gods, you must begin this undertaking together with the sages who perceive the truth; and this has been undertaken by all the deities without any desire for worldly gain. (16)
"O bulls among the gods, let the great Māheśvara sacrifice be performed on Mount Gandhamādana; for if they were to perform that sacrifice elsewhere, [it would not be successful]. (17)
Then those evil-minded enemies of the gods would create obstacles to the sacrifice; however, if this sacrifice is performed on Mount Gandhamādana, [they will not succeed].
Then, by the grace of Sudarśana, no obstacle whatsoever shall arise for the great seer named Ahirbudhnya on Mount Gandhamādana.
For the sake of bestowing grace, Sudarśana remains present at that sacred ford; therefore, O sages, perform that sacrifice on Mount Gandhamādana.
Not far from Cakratīrtha was the place that brought about the destruction of the Asuras; then, by the word of Brahmā, they quickly went to Gandhamādana.
Placing Bṛhaspati at their head, they went forth with the desire to perform a sacrifice; having bowed down to the high-souled Ahirbudhnya, the lord of sages.
They then established the sacrificial enclosure not far from that hermitage, together with those ascetics rich in penance who were highly skilled in the rituals of sacrifice.
The gods commenced a sacrifice intended for the destruction of the Asuras; at that rite, Bṛhaspati himself served as the Hotṛ priest.
Jayaṃta, the son of Indra, became the Maitrāvaruṇa priest; and the eighth Vasu among the Vasus became the Acchāvāka priest there.
There, Parāśara, the son of Śakti, became the Grāvastut priest; and the highly resplendent Aṣṭāvakra took up the office of the Adhvaryu.
There, the great sage Viśvāmitra was the Pratiprasthātṛ; Varuṇa was the Neṣṭṛ, and Dhaneśvara was the Unnetṛ. || 27 ||
Brahmā became Savitṛ, bearing half the yoke of the sacrifice; Vasiṣṭha, the best among Brahmins, became the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest. || 28 ||
Śunaḥśepa became the Āgnīdhra priest, and Jātapāvaka became the Potṛ; Vāyu became the Udgātṛ, and the King of the Dead (Yama) became the Prastotṛ. || 29 ||
The Pratihartṛ there was Agastya, born from a water-jar; the Subrahmaṇya was the great Madhucchandas, the son of Viśvāmitra.
The sacrificer himself became Devarāja Purandara; there, the sage Śuka, son of Vyāsa, was the witness.
Then all those officiating priests duly initiated Purandara, the king of the gods, in that sacrifice dedicated to Maheśvara.
Thus did that great sacrifice proceed on Mount Gandhamādana; [the demons] were indeed excessively tormented, being unable to endure the power of Sudarśana.
The Asuras did not find any flaw there while the sacrifice was being performed; thus, that great ritual proceeded without any obstacles.
And there, while consuming [the offerings], Hari blazed like the fire; the Adhvaryu priest, performing the various ritual acts according to rule without any agitation, [proceeded].
He offered the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), purified by mantras, into the fire; then the Adhvaryu priest respectfully divided the remainder of the offered cake.
He bestowed that destroyer of sins upon the officiating priests, headed by the Hotṛ; and he gave one of even more fierce splendor to Savitṛ and Brahmā.
There, he offered the portion of the sacrificial cake known as the *prāśitra*; then Savitṛ received that *prāśitra* with both hands.
As soon as it was touched by Savitṛ, that *prāśitra* portion became difficult to approach; while all the officiating priests were looking on, he cut off his two hands.
Then, his hand severed by that Prāśitra of fierce splendor, he became terrified and dejected of countenance, wondering, "What is this? (40)
Savitṛ summoned all the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and spoke this: Savitṛ said: "This portion of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), known as the *prāśitra*, is mine. (41)
Datta severed my hands even while you all were looking on; therefore, all of you priests together must indeed act.
"Prepare these two hands; otherwise, I shall destroy that sacrifice. Hearing the words of Savitṛ, they all reflected together.
There, in the midst of the lords of sages and all the gods, the highly effulgent Aṣṭāvakra addressed those officiating priests.
Aṣṭāvakra said: "Listen, all you officiating priests, to my words with focused minds; while I, the best of Brahmins, am alive, a hundred cycles of Viriñcas have passed. (45)
Tens of millions of four-faced Brahmās were born and died; even as I beheld them all, I sustained my vital breaths.
At that time, while Prajāpati was known by the name Lokeśvara, a Brahmin named Harihara lived in the city of Śyāmalāpura.
Having come into the middle of the target, his feet were pierced by arrows shot for sport by a forest-dwelling hunter skilled in hitting the mark. (48)
Having reached Gandhamādana, he was then urged by the sages; and having bathed in this Munitīrtha, he formerly attained the feet [of the Lord]. (49)
At that time, this meritorious holy site was called Munītīrtha; now it is known as Cakratīrtha, having acquired the name "Cakra."
Therefore, if it pleases you, let a bath be taken here at the Muni-tīrtha by Savitṛ, whose hand was severed by Prāśitra. (51)
Having been thus addressed by the great sage Aṣṭāvakra, all the officiating priests (ṛtvijas), filled with great joy, spoke to Savitṛ.
"O Sāvitra, bathe in this sacred ford; your two hands shall become [as those of] Aṣṭāvakra. Act with a concentrated mind, just as he has instructed."
Then that Sāvitra went to the great Cakratīrtha and bathed there in that place which bestows desired boons, for the sake of regaining his hands.
Rising up right there after bathing with devotion, he was seen endowed with two golden hands.
Seeing him with golden hands, all the officiating priests rejoiced; then, having completed that sacrifice and having conquered the hosts of Daityas, [they departed].
All the gods, beginning with Indra, having attained happiness, went to heaven; therefore, this holy place (tīrtha) should be visited by all human beings.
It should be served with effort for the attainment of one's own desired goal, even by those who are blind, those with withered arms, the mute, the deaf, and even the hunchbacked. (58)
By those who were humpbacked, by the lame, by others likewise deprived of limbs, by those with severed hands and feet, and by those with various other members of their bodies cut off—59.
This holy ford, which bestows all desired objects, should be resorted to by humans and others alike for the fulfillment of any physical deficiency. (60)
Thus, O Brahmins, the majesty of Cakratīrtha has been described to you; having bathed there in ancient times, Prabhākara regained his two severed hands.
Whoever should read this chapter or listen to it with a concentrated mind, his deficient limbs shall undoubtedly become complete.
For a mortal desiring liberation, there shall be liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Śrī Sūta said: Having bathed at Cakratīrtha, a person should then proceed to Śivatīrtha, where indeed, by merely bathing, millions of great sins [are destroyed]. || 1 ||
And by that very contact, O ascetics, those [sins] perish at that very moment; having bathed here, Kālabhairava was released from the murder of a Brahmin.
The sages said: O great sage, for what reason did the sin of killing a Brahmin befall Kālabhairava-Rudra? O Sūta, you ought to tell us that here.
The venerable Sūta said: O all you sages, I shall relate an ancient account that bestows liberation; by the mere hearing of which one is released from all sins.
In ancient times, a quarrel arose between Prajāpati and Viṣṇu on account of a certain cause, in the presence of all people.
I alone am the creator of the world; there is no other creator whatsoever. I am the bestower of both restraint and grace upon all the manifestations of the universe.
In ancient times, Brahmā thought thus in the presence of the gods: "There is no one superior to me, nor even equal to me, even among the deities. (7)
Then, O best of the twice-born, Nārāyaṇa spoke with a smile: "Why do you speak thus now out of egoism?"
O Brahmā, you ought not to speak such words again; I alone am the creator of the universe, the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa, the sacrifice itself.
Without me, the continued existence of this phenomenal world would be impossible; by my grace, the entire universe, both stationary and moving, was created by you.
While Brahmā and Viṣṇu were thus engaged in a dispute, each desiring victory, the four Vedas arrived there before the gods and spoke these truthful words that reveal the supreme reality: ||| 11 ||
The Vedas said: "O Viṣṇu, you are not the creator of the world; nor are you, O Brahmā, Prajāpati. (12)
However, the Lord is the creator of the world, the all-pervading one who is higher than the highest; this entire realm of moving and non-moving beings is fashioned by His power of māyā. (13)
For Sāmba, whose characteristics are truth and the like, is indeed worthy of salutation by all the gods; he alone is the Lord of the worlds, the creator, the protector, and the destroyer. (14)
O best of the twice-born, having heard these auspicious words thus uttered by the Vedas, Brahmā and Viṣṇu then spoke there.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu said: "How can Śambhu, embraced by Pārvatī, the embodied lord of the Pramathas, be the Supreme Brahman, which is devoid of all attachment? (16)
When they had spoken thus, O twice-born ones, the Praṇava then addressed them there, assuming a form with a great resonance.
Praṇava said: This Śambhu, the Great God, does not at any time sport with a Pārvatī who is distinct from himself; rather, he sports with her who is his own essential nature.
That Śambhu is without a superior, self-luminous, and stainless; Mahādeva is greater than the universe, and thus he is heard to be "greater than the universe. (19)
He is the soul of all, the creator of all, independent, and the source of all beings; O Brahmā, at the time of creation, he impels you by means of the quality of rajas.
O Keśava, Śambhu sends you forth for the protection of beings through the quality of sattva; he impels the one called Kālarudra for the purpose of dissolution through the quality of tamas.
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, independence never belongs to you two, nor does it belong to Prajāpati; rather, independence belongs only to Śambhu.
O Brahmā and Viṣṇu, for what reason is Maheśvara—not known by all the worlds, the creator, and likewise superior to the universe—not recognized by you two? || 23 ||
That power, the goddess Umā, is never separate from Śaṅkara; being the very essence of Śambhu’s bliss, that goddess is not considered adventitious.
Therefore, Rudra is superior to the universe, independent, and free from conceptual construction; this Śaṅkara is to be worshipped by all the gods, and by you two as well.
There is no creator of this Rudra, nor is there anyone superior to him; even his equal does not exist in the worlds, even by the hundreds.
"Therefore, O Brahmā and Viṣṇu, do not act in vain out of delusion. Having heard this spoken by the Praṇava, both Brahmā and Keśava [reflected].
Deluded by the Māyā of Śambhu, they did not abandon their ignorance; in the meantime, Brahmā beheld a great wonder.
Pervading the entire sky, resembling infinite suns, it was a circle of splendor situated in the midst of space, facing every direction.
To determine that, Brahmā created an upward-facing mouth; he did so with a fifth mouth, emitted through the power of his asceticism.
The Lord gazed repeatedly at that orb of splendor; it blazed up with anger from the sight of his brilliance.
Resembling infinite suns, that fifth head blazed forth like the submarine fire at the dissolution of the worlds, as if desiring to consume them.
And that splendor appeared as a man, blue and red; having seen him, the creator Brahmā then addressed the Supreme Lord.
"I know you, O Mahādeva; formerly you emerged from my forehead, O Śambhu, as my son named Rudra. (34)
Having heard these words filled with such pride, Maheśvara then dispatched a man named Kālabhairava.
Kālabhairava, born from a portion of Mahādeva and bearing a trident, an axe, and a mace, fought with Brahmā for a long time.
Having fought for a very long time with Brahmā, Kālabhairava gazed upon the fifth, auspicious face of Brahmā.
Beholding the fifth face of the Lord of Bhāratī turned upward and filled with great pride, he blazed up, exceedingly incensed.
Then Bhairava, in a rage, severed that fifth face; thereupon Brahmā died, slain by Kālabhairava.
By the grace of the Lord, he regained his life once more; then he beheld Śaṅkara, adorned with the moon.
Having seen Mahādeva Śaṅkara together with Pārvatī, adorned with the ornaments of the eight serpent-lords beginning with Vāsuki, the Creator (Brahmā) beheld him.
He obtained the knowledge of Maheśvara through the grace of Mahādeva; thereupon, he praised Giriśa, the most excellent Śiva, the bestower of boons. 42.
Brahmā said: Be gracious to me, O Giriśa, whose crest is adorned with the moon; O Śambhu, O ocean of compassion, forgive whatever offense I have committed against you. (43)
"Forgive my arrogance," he said repeatedly, "O Śaṅkara! and he paid homage to that Soma, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Then the Lord Śambhu, being pleased with this Brahmā who was born from his own portion, said, "Do not fear," and addressed Bhairava.
Īśvara said: "This eternal Brahmā is worthy of worship by the entire world; now, you must carry the head of this slain Viriñca."
"For the sake of purifying the murder of a Brahmin and out of a desire to maintain the welfare of the world, O Bhairava, wander for alms with a skull-bowl at my command. (47)
Having spoken thus, O Brahmins, Śaṅkara, the blue-throated Mahādeva, whose body is half-formed by the Daughter of the Mountain, vanished right there.
O twice-born ones, he caused Bhairava to take on the face of Brahmā, saying: "Wander indeed for the sake of purifying your sin and for the purpose of gathering the world."
"Let Bhairava, the bearer of a skull, receive alms with his hand!"—having spoken thus, Giriśa [sent] a certain terrifying maiden.
Having dispatched that cruel [power] named Brahmahatyā, which resembled the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), Giriśa spoke again to Bhairava.
Īśvara said: "O Bhairavī, perform this vow for one year for the purification of the sin of killing a Brahmin; bathe in all the sacred fords (tīrthas) for the sake of your own purification."
Therefore, go to Vārāṇasī for the pacification of the sin of killing a Brahmin; by entering Vārāṇasī, that most base sin of Brahmin-slaughter shall be removed from you.
If it is destroyed with only a quarter remaining, one-fourth does not perish; O Bhairava, I shall describe its destruction to you—listen to that.
On the shore of the southern ocean, on Mount Gandhamādana, I have established this auspicious sacred site for the benefit of all living beings.
Go there with reverence to that place of great merit known as Śiva; by merely entering it, your inauspicious sin of killing a Brahmin shall be destroyed.
"By the majesty of Śivatīrtha, [all sins] will certainly perish without remainder. Having spoken thus to Bhairava, Rudra departed for Kailāsa in an instant.
Then Bhairava, skull in hand and impelled by Śiva, wandered through the worlds of the gods, dānavas, yakṣas, and others.
As he went, the most terrifying Brahmahatyā followed him; Bhairava [followed] all the holy fords (tīrthas) and sacred shrines (āyatanas).
Having wandered about at his ease, the Lord then went to Vārāṇasī; indeed, when Bhairava, born from a portion of Śaṅkara, had entered Vārāṇasī.
Without a fourth part, the most loathsome Brahman-slaughter was destroyed; with a fourth part, it fled toward Bhairava, who is born from a portion of Śaṅkara.
Then that god Bhairava, trident in hand and bearing a skull, went afterwards to Mount Gandhamādana by the command of Śiva.
Then, O twice-born ones, Bhairava went to Śivatīrtha and bathed; by the mere act of bathing there in that most excellent Śivatīrtha, [he was purified].
The most terrifying sin of killing a Brahmin was completely dissolved. At that moment, Śambhu appeared before him; having manifested, Mahādeva spoke these formidable words: || 64 ||
Īśvara said: "By immersing yourself in Śivatīrtha, your sin of killing a Brahmin shall be entirely removed. (65)
"It is lost, O Bhairava; there is no doubt about this, O you of noble vows. You must place this skull somewhere on a spot in Kāśī. (66)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Śambhu vanished right there; O Brahmins, Bhairava too was then liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
Due to the greatness of Śivatīrtha, he went to the city of Vārāṇasī; O twice-born ones, he established the skull in a certain place, and that spot then received the name Kapālatīrtha.
Śrī Sūta said: Such is the power of that meritorious Śivatīrtha, which bestows liberation.
It pacifies great suffering, destroys great sins, alleviates the afflictions of hell, and likewise bestows heaven as well as liberation.
I have proclaimed the majesty of Śivatīrtha, which bestows liberation; by constantly reciting this, a mortal is released from the multitude of sufferings. (71)

The venerable Sūta said: Having bathed at Śivatīrtha for the sake of liberation from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa, a man should then proceed to Śaṅkhatīrtha for the purpose of pacifying the entire web of his own sins.
Where even an ungrateful person is liberated merely by immersion, [yet those] who, deluded, do not honor their mothers, fathers, and teachers.
And whatever other evil-minded people there may be—ungrateful and shameless—they all become purified merely by bathing in this Śaṅkha-tīrtha.
Formerly, on Mount Gandhamādana, a sage named Śaṅkha dwelt performing austerities, meditating on Viṣṇu with a concentrated mind.
There he fashioned an excellent holy ford for the purpose of bathing; the holy ford created by Śaṅkha is known as Śaṅkhatīrtha.
Having bathed there even once, a mortal is liberated, even if he be ungrateful.
In this regard, I shall relate an ancient history that destroys all evil.
