Merely by hearing it, a person may attain liberation. In ancient times, there was a lord of brahmins, the great sage Vatsanābha.
Truthful, virtuous, eloquent, and devoted to compassion for all beings; equal toward enemy and friend, self-controlled, ascetic, and having conquered his senses.
Expert in the Supreme Brahman and taking sole refuge in the reality of Brahman, that sage of such power performed austerities in his own hermitage.
Remaining right there on the ground with all his limbs motionless, he did not move from his own position even by the measure of an atom.
While he remained in one place performing austerities for many hundreds of years, a termite hill covered his body, and she desired him and made it so.
Although his body was covered by an anthill, the great sage Vatsanābha continued his ascetic penance and did not even notice the anthill.
And while he was performing penance there, O best of sages, Vāsava [perceived it]. || 1 ||
Having released masses of clouds, he, full of speed, caused rain to fall.
In this manner, he rained continuously for seven days; yet even while being drenched by that exceedingly great downpour, the sage remained steadfast.
With his eyes closed, he received that rain, quickly deafening his ears with a great roar.
A great thunderbolt fell directly upon the anthill while the rain-god was pouring down rain amidst cold winds that were exceedingly difficult to endure.
The summit of the anthill became shattered, struck by the thunderbolt; when that anthill had its peak destroyed by the strike of the thunderbolt, [the serpent emerged]. || 17 ||
Vatsanābha endured that most unbearable rain, reflecting deeply as the great sage was oppressed by the torrents day and night.
An exceedingly great compassion arose in the mind of Dharma; that Dharma then reflected upon Vatsanābha as he was performing austerities.
Even though it rains excessively, he does not desist from his asceticism; oh, how Vatsanābha’s mind is solely intent upon dharma! 20.
As he was reflecting thus, this thought arose in his mind: "I shall indeed assume a very large and beautiful buffalo form."
Having assumed the form of a buffalo, I shall stand above the yogi, bearing his rugged hide as he endures the falling torrents of rain.
"For even a rain accompanied by great force shall not overwhelm him"; having thus resolved upon his duty, he held the streams upon his back. (23)
Then, having covered his body with the vatsanābha [poison], he remained there; thereafter, at the end of seven days, that rain indeed ceased.
Then that Dharma, assuming the form of a buffalo and filled with great compassion, left that anthill and stayed at no great distance.
Then, when the year had passed, the great sage Vatsanābha, having ceased his austerities, quickly looked out toward all the quarters.
I stand here amidst the falling rain, performing great penance today; the earth is seen drenched with water in every direction. (27)
The peaks of the mountains, the forests, the groves, and the hermitages of the great seers were all drenched with fresh waters.
Having seen all these things and more, the righteous-souled great sage Vatsanābha became joyful and reflected: || 29 ||
"I have surely been protected by someone in this great rain; for while this great rain falls, how else could my life remain? (30)
Having reflected thus, the best of sages looked everywhere; then he saw a massive-bodied being standing not far away in front of him.
The ascetic Vatsanābha, having sighted a dark-colored buffalo, reflected upon it in his mind.
How is it that even among those of animal birth the nature of righteousness is seen? For by a buffalo I was protected from the great rain. (33)
"May he have long life, since he has protected me here"—having reflected thus, and so forth, he set out once more for asceticism.
Furthermore, seeing him engaged in ascetic penance, he who had assumed the form of a buffalo experienced intense joy, his entire body covered with horripilation.
Furthermore, as the sage Vatsanābha was engaged in ascetic penance, his mind did not become one-pointedly fixed upon the Supreme Brahman as it had been before.
Becoming despondent in mind, Vatsanābha reflected: "If there were no purity, then the mind would be fickle. (37)
When there is an abundance of evil, the mind does not become pure at all; yet I do not possess even a trace of evil—how then is my mind so restless? (38)
Vatsanābha reflected again and again on the cause of his misfortune; having deliberated and reached a firm conclusion, he immediately censured himself.
"Fie on me, this evil-souled one! Alas, I am utterly deluded; the great fault of ingratitude has come upon me today. (40)
If I remain without worshipping Mahiṣottama, who is the savior from such a great rain, then I shall be guilty of ingratitude.
Ungratefulness is a great fault; for the ungrateful, there is no atonement. For the ungrateful, there are truly no worlds, and for the ungrateful, there are no kinsmen. (42)
My mind is defiled by the fault of ingratitude; for those who are ungrateful and those who betray the trusting go to hell. (43)
"I see no means of atonement whatsoever for the ungrateful, except for the renunciation of life, according to the words of those who know the Dharma. (44)
Having failed to support one's parents, having failed to give the teacher’s fee, and having incurred ungratefulness—for these, indeed, atonement ends only with death. (45)
"Therefore, having renounced my life-breaths, I shall perform penance. Having thus resolved in his mind, the great sage Vatsanābha [acted accordingly]. (46)
Disregarding his own life with a detached inner self, he ascended the peak of Mount Meru, desiring to perform an act of atonement.
From that peak of Mount Sumeru, the sage sought to throw himself down; as he was about to fall, Dharma himself, having abandoned his buffalo form, restrained him, saying, "Do not hasten! (48)
Dharma said: "O Vatsanābha, O highly wise one, may you live for many years! (49)
I am well-pleased; may it be well with you, for you desire to renounce the body. Indeed, there is no one in this world who is equal to you in the domain of dharma.
Although the sacrifice of one's life might serve as expiation for an ungrateful person, nevertheless, because of your virtuous character, I shall prescribe another form of expiation for you. (51)
There is indeed a sacred ford named Śaṅkhatīrtha on Mount Gandhamādana; for the sake of pacifying this sin, bathe there with a concentrated mind.
From this, you shall attain purity of mind and be freed from defilement; thereafter, having gained higher knowledge, you shall attain the eternal state.
"I am Dharma, O lord of yogis; I tell you the truth. Having heard these words of Dharma, the great sage Vatsanābha—
Desiring to bathe at Śaṅkhatīrtha, the great sage went toward Gandhamādana; having reached Śaṅkhatīrtha, he bathed there.
Then, his mind having become free from evil, it attained purity; thereafter, in a short time, the sage reached the state of Brahman.
Thus, O Brahmins, the majesty of Śaṅkhatīrtha has been recounted to you; for by merely bathing there, even an ungrateful person is liberated.
A betrayer of mother, a betrayer of father, a betrayer of teacher, and likewise others who are a multitude of ungrateful persons—these are all liberated by immersion here.
Therefore, this [place] should always be resorted to by ungrateful men; oh, how great is the majesty of this holy site (tīrtha), that even an ungrateful person is liberated! 59.
Having failed to provide for one's parents, having failed to give the teacher’s fee, and having incurred ungratefulness—for these, indeed, atonement ends only with death.
But here, by mere bathing, even an ungrateful person finds atonement; even the state of ingratitude perishes through merely bathing at that sacred ford.
What then need be said now regarding all other trivial sins? || 62 ||

O mortals, even one who is ungrateful, if he recites this chapter with devotion, shall be liberated from sin; with his inner self purified, having gone to Satyaloka, he shall quickly attain liberation together with Brahmā.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pacification of the Fault of Ingratitude by Vatsanābha," within the Praise of Śaṅkha Tīrtha, in the Setu Māhātmya, in the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having performed their ablutions at Śaṅkhatīrtha, mortals should proceed in due order to the Yamunā, the Gaṅgā, and Gayā as well. || 1 ||
The great holy site named Yamunā, the unsurpassed Gaṅgā-tīrtha, and Gayā-tīrtha—these destroy the great sins of mortals.
This triad of holy fords is meritorious and renowned throughout all the worlds; it pacifies all obstacles and eradicates all diseases.
For this triad of sacred fords (tīrthas) destroys all ignorance; when ignorance has been destroyed, it likewise bestows knowledge upon men. (4)
In ancient times, O great king, Jānaśruti bathed in these sacred fords and obtained supreme knowledge from Raikva, the best of the twice-born.
The sages said: O Sūta, knower of the truth of all matters, high-minded disciple of Vyāsa! It is well known that there are the Yamunā, the Gaṅgā, and Gayā as well. (6)

O Sūta, tell us this: from where did these three holy fords (tīrthas) originate on Mount Gandhamādana? And how was the attainment of knowledge from Raikva obtained by the royal sage Jānaśruti after bathing in all three of those holy fords?
Śrī Sūta said: In ancient times, indeed, there was a great sage named Raikva on Mount Gandhamādana.
Performing difficult austerities, that great sage Raikva, a treasury of ascetic power, dwelt there for a long time practicing penance.
By the great power of his asceticism, the great sage named Raikva attained a long life, even though by birth he was indeed lame.
Due to his lameness, that sage became unable to go to those holy places (tīrthas) which exist on Mount Gandhamādana.
He proceeded toward them by traveling in a chariot itself; for that eminent sage Raikva was traveling together with a pair of draft animals.
In this world, an ascetic who possesses the Vedic [knowledge] is called a *sayugva*; for "yugva" is said to mean a cart, and he exists together with that. (13)
Indeed, that best of sages, the sage named Sayugvān, possessing complete knowledge, performed austerities on Mount Gandhamādana.
In the summer, he performed great penance while standing in the midst of five fires; during the rainy season, he remained immersed in water reaching up to his neck.
When his body was withered by asceticism, scabies arose upon him; that lord of sages scratched the scabies day and night. (16)
While merely scratching his itch, this sage Sayugvā did not abandon his austerity; such was the state of mind that arose within him.
"I must indeed bathe right now in these three meritorious holy places: at the Yamunā, the Gaṅgā, and Gayā. (18)
Having reflected thus, that sage then formed another thought: "For I am lame by birth; therefore, bathing is indeed difficult for me to achieve. (19)
"It is not possible for me to go too far by cart; what shall I do now?"—thus did that highly intelligent man reflect. (20)
He indeed resolved that he must go to the three sacred fords (tīrthas) for the purpose of bathing, thinking: "The power of my asceticism is irresistible and invincible."
"I shall invoke those three sacred fords right here. Having thus resolved in his mind, he, with his senses restrained, faced the east.
Having sipped water three times, Sayugvā meditated for a moment without weariness; by the power of his mantra, that great river Yamunā [was brought under control].
The Gaṅgā, the daughter of Jahnu, and that Gayā which destroys sin—all three of them suddenly rose from the netherworld (pātāla) after piercing through the earth.
Assuming human form and approaching Sayugvā, they spoke with great joy, gladdening that sage.
O Sayugvan Raikva, may it be well with you; desist from this meditation. We have been drawn here by your mantra and have assembled at this place. (26)
"What must be done for you by us? Tell us that, O Lord of Sages. Having heard these words of theirs, the great sage Sayugvān [replied].
Quickly withdrawing from his meditation, he saw them standing before him; having honored them according to the prescribed rites, Raikva spoke these words.
O Goddess Yamunā, O Gaṅgā, O Gayā, destroyer of sins! Grant me your presence here on Mount Gandhamādana.
"Wherever you have emerged here after piercing through the earth, those sacred fords (tīrthas) shall be known by your names."
Saying "So be it," they then vanished instantly from that place; and from that time forward, those three became sacred fords (tīrthas) upon the earth.
By that very name, she is always sung of by people, where at that time the Yamunā emerged after bursting through the earth.
That place is indeed called Yamunātīrtha by the people, because from that very fissure in the earth the Gaṅgā suddenly rose up.
That place is renowned in the world as Gaṅgātīrtha, the destroyer of sins; for Gayā indeed went forth after assuming a human form.
That very opening in the earth is proclaimed as the sacred site of Gayātīrtha; thus, these three unsurpassed sacred sites possess great merit.
By the power of the Raikva-mantra, [the earth] rose up suddenly; here, those best of men who perform their ablutions in these three sacred fords (tīrtha), [attain liberation]. || 36 ||
The ignorance of those [beings] shall be destroyed and knowledge shall arise; for the sage has drawn them there by his own mantra to those three sacred sites.
He spent his time constantly performing his daily ablutions; at that very same time, however, there was a great king named Jānaśruti.
The grandson of that royal sage, who regarded him as his own son and was solely devoted to righteousness, would then give food and other necessities to seekers with nothing but faith. (39)
Therefore, they declare that this gift of faith is not to be given in the light of day; for the speech regarding the food of a king is far more extensive [in its consequences]. (40)
He dwells in his home for the sake of satisfying those who are needy and hungry; therefore, he is called "Bahuvākya" (the one with many words) by all supplicants.
That powerful King Jānaśruti, the son of Pautrāyaṇa, was a lover of guests and likewise became a great giver of gifts. || 42 ||
In cities and kingdoms, in villages and forests, at all crossroads and on every great highway. || 43 ||
He indeed prepared hospitality consisting of abundant food and drink, along with soups, vegetables, and other items, for the satisfaction of those who came as supplicants.
"O seekers, enjoy all things here, such as food and drink!"—thus he proclaimed in various inhabited places. (45)
The virtues of that king—who was fond of guests, who gave much, and who was renowned for his generosity toward supplicants—were celebrated everywhere. (46)
Then, as this Pautrāyaṇa lived amidst a multitude of virtues, the highly fortunate celestial sages desired to bestow their grace upon him.
Assuming the form of a swan during the night in the summer season, he quickly formed a beautiful row and ascended into the sky.
Flying up again and again with great speed and force, they soared high above that lord of the earth who was standing at the window of his palace.
As those swans were flying swiftly, one swan, traveling behind them, then addressed the lead swan.
While the king was listening, he spoke these words with derision: "O Bhallākṣa, Bhallākṣa! O swan-like one walking ahead! (51)
"Right here in the middle of the palace stands the king, the son of Jānaśruti; he is worthy of worship—do you not see him, like one who is blind? (52)
His splendor, which is invincible from the abode of Brahmā down to this world, blazes intensely before us like infinite suns.
Do not go swiftly past that royal sage; if you proceed further, his splendor will instantly consume you.
To that swan who had spoken thus, he replied in front of him: "Oh, you are truly knowledgeable; you are worthy of praise by the wise. (55)
Since you praise this man who is unworthy of praise and a mere gambler, for what purpose do you praise this person who is so insignificant? (56)
Like a bellows or like a beast, he merely breathes; for this lord of the earth does not know the secret of dharmas.
The knower of reality is like Raikva Sayugvān, the best of Brahmins; for the great light of Raikva is a secret even from the gods.
Indeed, this mere living being possesses no such splendor; there is simply no limit to the masses of merit belonging to Raikva. (59)
The grains of dust of the earth may be counted, and the stars in the sky may be counted; but the mass of merit belonging to Raikva, which is like Mount Meru, cannot be counted at all.
Moreover, let these perishable phenomena remain as they are; that sage is indeed praiseworthy because of his unassailable knowledge of Brahman.
But for Jānaśruti, such a dharma does not exist at all; since even that which is difficult to attain for the lords of yogis is absent, how could there be the majesty of such knowledge? (062)
"Abandoning that wicked-souled one, leave this wretched person behind; you yourself should praise that sage Raikva Sayugvān. (63)
O Lord of Sages, even one who is lame by birth, desiring to perform his ablutions, [goes] to the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and even to Gayā.
He summoned, by means of a mantra, the great sage Raikva, a knower of Brahman, from the vicinity of his own hermitage for the sake of the accumulation of dharma.
The floods of merit belonging to those dwelling within the three worlds are contained therein; however, the domain of merit belonging to Raikva is not indeed contained within the three worlds.
When the swan, who was thus speaking as their leader, had finished and become silent, [the king] entered at some point into the enclosure of the dharma for living beings. 67.
Those lords of sages, having assumed the form of swans, returned once more to the world of Brahmā. Then King Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, the subduer of enemies—
And having heard that Raikva had reached the pinnacle of excellence, the ultimate limit, he became exceedingly despondent, like a wretched man defeated at dice. (69)
Sighing repeatedly, that king reflected: "Ha! By exalting Raikva, he has here spoken of me as inferior."
Oh, how great is the majesty of Raikva, whom even the birds praise! Having abandoned this entire worldly existence and his kingdom here and now—|| 71 ||
Seek refuge in that very same high-souled Sayugvā; for Raikva, that treasure-house of compassion, will surely protect me who have come to him for refuge.
"He will accept my self-knowledge and teach it to me"—thinking thus, O twice-born ones, he somehow or other [proceeded]. (73)
Remaining awake, he passed that night which had overflowed its bounds; when the end of the night arrived, it was heralded by the songs of a multitude of bards.
He heard the sound of auspicious music accompanied by the resonance of trumpets; having heard that, the great king remained right there upon his couch.
Having quickly summoned the charioteer, he spoke these respectful words: "O charioteer, go swiftly and, mounting the chariot, proceed with speed. (76)
In the hermitages of the great seers, in sacred forests, in secluded regions, and in the dwelling places of the virtuous; || 77 ||
On the banks and sandbanks of sacred fords and rivers, and in other regions where the lords of sages reside. || 78 ||
Among all of them, he saw the lord of yogis named Raikva, who was lame and seated in a cart, the sole refuge of all dharmas.
"O charioteer, seek out Sayugvāna, the sole abode of the knowledge of Brahman; having found him, return quickly for my pleasure. (80)
Saying "So be it," he departed and, mounted upon a swift chariot, searched everywhere for the sage Raikva, the knower of Brahman.
He wandered over the entire earth, searching here and there in mountain caves and in the hermitages of sages.
Having searched through various regions with great haste, the charioteer eventually reached Mount Gandhamādana, which was densely crowded with great sages.
Searching there as well, he beheld that lord of sages standing upon the wooden seat of a cart, scratching an itch.
Seeing that great sage Sayugvān there, constantly meditating upon the partless Brahman of non-duality, the charioteer [spoke]. (85)
Thinking, "This is Raikva," he approached him, prostrated before him, and having sat down near that sage, questioned him with humility. (86)
"O Brahmin, who indeed are you, Sayugvān by name, the son of Raikva? Having heard his words, that sage replied:
"I am indeed Sayugvā Raikva by name"—having heard these words of the sage, as well as his many gestures, [the king understood]. (88)
Having understood the king's desire for wealth for the sake of maintaining his family, he returned from Gandhamādana and reported everything to the king.
Then Jānaśruti, having heard the words of the charioteer with respect, [gave] six hundred cows and a load of gold coins as wealth.
Taking a chariot yoked with mules, that royal sage Pautrāyaṇa, filled with haste, approached Raikva.
Having gone there, that lord of the earth spoke these words to Raikva: "O venerable Raikva Sayugvan, please accept what has been given by me."
"Accept from me also six hundred cows, a load of gold coins, wealth, and a chariot yoked with mules. (93)
"O Brahmin, having accepted all this, please instruct me; let the knowledge of non-dual Brahman be imparted to me. (94)
Having heard these words of his, spoken with longing and agitation, Raikva, who possessed the chariot-yoked cart, replied to Jānaśruti, the subduer of enemies.
Raikva said: "Let these cows be yours, as well as the weight of gold coins and the chariot; what use have I for this meager thing, living as I do through many kalpas?"
"This [amount] is not truly sufficient for the maintenance of my family, even if you were to give me a hundredfold of this. (97)
"O Indra among kings, even that is not sufficient for the maintenance of a family. Having heard these words of Raikva, Jānaśruti spoke: (98)
Jānaśruti said: "O Sage, for this knowledge of Brahman being taught by you, O Brahmin, neither this wealth of cattle nor even the chariot is the price. (99)

"Whether you accept it or not, here is this [gift] of mine, such as the cow and so forth; O Brahmin, please instruct me in the knowledge of partless non-duality. Having heard those words of his, Sayugvā spoke these words: (100)
Raikva said: "He who has detachment toward worldly existence, as well as toward merit and demerit... (101)

And there is the destruction of those two [karmas] already set in motion; he indeed is a recipient of the instruction of knowledge, even though detachment from worldly existence has arisen within you. (2)
Nevertheless, there is indeed no destruction of merits and demerits for one who acts with deceit; for the accumulated masses of merit and demerit are the causes for rebirth. (3)
O King, for their destruction does not occur without the loss of their enjoyments; nevertheless, I shall now tell you the means for their destruction.
Since you have come to me for refuge, listen with a concentrated mind: here there exists a triad of meritorious sacred sites that bestows all desired objects.
For indeed, for all those seeking liberation, this Yamunā-tīrtha as well as the Gaṅgā-tīrtha effects the destruction of all commenced karma (prārabdha). || 6 ||
This is also Gayātīrtha; bathe in these without delay. Then there will be the destruction of all *prārabdha* karma; of this there is no doubt.
"Therefore, I shall impart knowledge to you whose mind is purified. When this was said by the sage Raikva, [Janaka's] eyes blossomed with joy.
Approaching with great haste, he bathed in all three sacred fords; by the mere act of bathing in those holy waters, the king’s mind became pure.
That king again attended upon his teacher Sayugvā; and that Sayugvā Raikva [bestowed] that which is difficult even for the lords of sages to attain.
Out of compassion, he imparted knowledge for the sake of the learning and wisdom born therefrom; and as soon as that knowledge, which is the very form of Brahman, had been taught by him— || 11 ||
That best of kings became possessed of uncontradicted experience through the grace of the yogi Raikva, who had attained the nature of Brahman.
The phenomenal world, consisting of jars, walls, and granaries, did not manifest; having suddenly pierced through illusion (māyā), there remained only Brahman alone.
Thus, by bathing in these three sacred fords, King Jānaśruti—oh, what a king!—attained the state of becoming Brahman, which is difficult even for hosts of yogis to achieve.
Thus, O Brahmins, the majesty of those three sacred fords has been recounted to you; whoever reads this chapter concerning the majesty of the triad of holy places, [attains the fruit]. || 15 ||
Having pierced through the darkness of ignorance, it leads to becoming Brahman. || 116 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Jānaśruti’s Attainment of Knowledge," within the "Praise of the Yamunā, Gaṅgā, and Gayā Tīrthas" of the Setu-māhātmya, in the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 26 ||
Śrī Sūta said: Having joyfully performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites at the Yamunā, the Gaṅgā, and Gayā, a man should then proceed to Koṭitīrtha.
Koṭitīrtha is of great merit, renowned throughout all the worlds; it bestows all prosperity, is pure, and destroys all sins.
For this indeed destroys bad dreams, destroys great sins, pacifies great obstacles, and brings about great peace for men. || 3 ||
That which destroys all the sins of men by mere remembrance was fashioned by Rāma himself, as if in sport, with the tip of his bow.
Formerly, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, having slain Rāvaṇa in battle, went to the Gandhamādana mountain for the sake of liberation from the sin of killing a brahmin.
Desiring to bestow grace upon the worlds, he installed a single *liṅga*; meanwhile, he searched for pure water for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of this *liṅga*.
The son of Daśaratha did not find water there on the bank, reflecting, "What water is there suitable for the consecration of the Liṅga? (7)
Having resolved in his mind, "The Liṅga must be bathed by me with fresh water," that scion of Raghu's lineage [proceeded] there to Dhanuṣkoṭi.
Quickly piercing the earth while remembering the Ganges in his mind, that tip of Rāma’s bow then reached the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Then that best of archers drew forth that bow from the surface of the earth as it was being raised by Rāghava.
Recalled by the descendant of Kakutstha, Gaṅgā emerged from that opening; with that water, the scion of Raghu’s lineage consecrated that liṅga.
Since it was fashioned of old by the very tip of Rāma’s bow, that sacred site is renowned throughout the three worlds as Koṭi.
Having first bathed in whichever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist here on Gandhamādana, one becomes cleansed of all impurities.
Then, for the sake of liberation from all remaining sins, a man should bathe at Koṭi; for that flood of sins which is not destroyed by bathing in other holy places [is destroyed there].
Indeed, all that has been accumulated over many millions of births and remains stored within the bones perishes entirely through ten million ritual baths; of this there is no doubt. (15)
For if a man bathes here at this Koṭi first, O twice-born ones, then for him who is liberated, all other holy places are indeed rendered useless. (16)
The sages said: O Sūta, knower of the truth of all matters, disciple of Vyāsa, lord of sages, best among the knowers of the Purāṇas, please sever some doubt of ours.
If for a mortal who has bathed at Koṭi, other sacred sites (tīrthas) are in vain, for what purpose do men bathe in sacred sites such as Dharmatīrtha? (18)
Tell me this: why indeed do men, having bypassed all those other holy fords, not perform their ablutions right here at Koṭi?
The venerable Sūta said: O lords of sages, this secret which you have asked about is that very thing which Śambhu formerly spoke to Nārada when he questioned him.
Therefore I speak, O best of sages; listen with faith: whether one goes by chance or is intent upon a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrtha), [one should act as follows]. (21)
O best of the twice-born, that lowest of men who, upon seeing or even hearing of a sacred ford or a temple along the way, does not visit it out of delusion, is the most base of persons.
"The supreme sages have declared that there is no atonement for him; therefore, if a man goes to the Setu and does not bathe in the other [tirthas], [he incurs that sin]. (23)

On account of the fault of bypassing sacred fords (tīrthas), he should be expelled by the twice-born as one who has transgressed; therefore, O twice-born ones, one must certainly bathe in these [sites] such as Cakratīrtha and others.
And having bathed in these sacred fords (tīrthas) for the sake of liberation from remaining sins, men here, being self-restrained, should bathe in Koṭitīrtha.
Having performed the extraction [of Soma] at Koṭitīrtha, one should not remain on Gandhamādana; freed from sin, one should return from Gandhamādana at that very moment.
For in ancient times, Rāma himself, having bathed there, consecrated Rāmanātha with the waters produced from Koṭitīrtha.
Freed from the sin of killing a Brahmin at that very moment, he, along with his younger brother, ascended the Puṣpaka chariot and departed for Ayodhyā, surrounded by monkeys.
Therefore, having bathed at Koṭi and being liberated from the remainder of his sins, a man should return at that very moment, just as Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, did. || 29 ||
For this is the most excellent of sacred fords, renowned throughout all the worlds, which was created by Rāghava for the consecration of Rāmanātha.
Where the Blessed Goddess herself is present, and where the Ganges flows; where Rāma, the Tāraka-Brahman, performed his ablutions with devotion.
Who indeed can describe the greatness of that Koṭitīrtha, where in ancient times Kṛṣṇa bathed with the desire for the welfare of the world?
Having been liberated from the sin of killing his maternal uncle Kaṃsa, by whom indeed can the greatness of that Koṭitīrtha be described? || 33 ||
The sages said: For what reason did Kaṃsa, the joy of the Yadus, kill his maternal uncle? O Sūta, for the pacification of whose fault did that high-minded one bathe at Koṭitīrtha?
Śrī Sūta said: In the lineage of Yadu, there was one known as Vasudeva, the son of Śūra; he [married] Devakī, the daughter of Devaka, who was widely renowned by that name. (35)
Having married and mounted his chariot, he formerly set out for his own city; then Kaṃsa became the charioteer of Ānakadundubhi.
Then an incorporeal voice spoke to Kaṃsa, the charioteer, as well as to his sister and to Bhāma, who was driving that excellent chariot.
"O subduer of enemies, that woman whom you are carrying here in the chariot—her eighth pregnancy will slay you; of this there is no doubt. (38)
O best of the twice-born, having heard these divine words, Kaṃsa took up his sword and made an effort to kill his sister.
Then Vasudeva, consoling him, spoke to Kaṃsa. Vasudeva said: "O Kaṃsa, I shall give to you whatever sons are born of her."
"Do not harm this sister; for she has no fear of you. Having heard those words, Kaṃsa then desisted from killing her.
Accompanied by Devakī and Vasudeva, he went to his own city; meanwhile, Devakī and Vasudeva had their feet bound with fetters.
Then the evil-minded Kaṃsa imprisoned her in a dungeon; thereafter, after a long time, Devakī [bore sons] from Vasudeva.
O best of sages, she gave birth to six sons in succession; however, Kaṃsa killed those who were born and handed over by Vasudeva.
O best of the twice-born, while his six sons born from the womb of Devakī were yet infants, the cruel-minded and merciless Kaṃsa [persecuted them].
Then the seventh embryo remained in the womb of Devakī; thereafter, Māyādevī, impelled by Viṣṇu, [took] that embryo.
He placed Devakī’s seventh embryo, which had fallen from her womb, into Rohiṇī, who was staying at the house of Nanda the cowherd. || 47 ||
A great renown arose in the world through the divine play of Viṣṇu; subsequently, Viṣṇu entered the womb within the belly of Devakī.
Then, when ten months had passed, the imperishable Hari was born from the womb of Devakī, renowned by the name Kṛṣṇa.
His four arms were resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, and sword; he wore a crown and a forest garland, and was the destroyer of his parents' grief. (50)
Having seen that Lord Hari, Ānaka-dundubhi offered him praise.

Vasudeva said: You are the universe, you alone are the Lord of the universe; you are the source of the universe, and the universe rests within you. O Blessed One, you are the Great Principle (Mahat), the Primal Matter (Pradhāna), the Cosmic Man (Virāṭ), the Self-Radiant (Svarāṭ), and the Universal Sovereign (Samrāṭ)—you are everything.

Thus, salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇa, the abode that is the cause of the universe, whose prowess is immeasurable, who bears the glorious Śārṅga bow, the discus, the sword, and the mace, and who has assumed a human form by his own will.
O best of the twice-born, while Vasudeva was thus praising him, Hari then spoke to him and to Devakī, gladdening them both.
Hari said: "I shall slay Kaṃsa; do not fear, O parents. On the previous day, Yaśodā, the wife of the cowherd Nanda, gave birth to a daughter—my own Māyā, who deludes all the worlds. (55)
"O best of the Yadus, having placed me upon her bed, take that daughter of Yaśodā and bring her to the bed of Devakī."
O twice-born ones, having been addressed thus by Kṛṣṇa, she did exactly so; the illusory daughter wept while remaining on Devakī’s bed.
Then, hearing the sound of a child’s cry, Kaṃsa, his mind agitated, came to the lying-in chamber and took up that infant girl.

The merciless and shameless one pounded her against a stone. Then, seizing his hand, the Great Goddess, possessing eight great arms equipped with weapons, summoned Kaṃsa and spoke to him in extreme anger.
Māyā said: "O Kaṃsa, you sinful soul, evil-minded one of deluded intellect! (60)
"O Kaṃsa, wherever that life-taking enemy of yours may be, seek out that enemy who is your own death; do not delay!"
Having spoken thus, that goddess attained divine abodes; having received worship from humans, she became the bestower of desired boons.
Having heard the words of the goddess, Kaṃsa too became deeply agitated; he [summoned] the child-seizing spirits such as Pūtanā and others to afflict his enemy, who was the cause of his own death.
He dispatched other children to various regions to cause affliction; and all those child-seizing spirits (bālagrahas) went to Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
Slain by Kṛṣṇa, they then departed for the abode of Yama; thereafter, O best of the twice-born, after some days had passed...
Then the two boys, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, grew up in Gokula; those subduers of enemies played with many kinds of childhood games.
For some time they were cowherd boys playing the sound of the flute; for some time they were cowherds adorned with *guñjā* berries and *tāpiccha* leaves.
Rāma and Keśava remained for a long time in Gokula. Once, Kaṃsa [sent] Akrūra to Gokula to fetch Rāma and Keśava.
O best of Brahmins, he dispatched messengers to bring them quickly; and Akrūra brought Rāma and Kṛṣṇa from Gokula.
By Kaṃsa’s command, he went to Mathurā, which was adorned with golden archways.
Then, having brought Rāma and Keśava along, the son of Gāndinī went before the city; and having seen Kaṃsa and reported his purpose to him, he subsequently entered his own home.

Then, on another day, in the afternoon, the two sons of Vasudeva, together with their beloved cowherd boys, approached the city of Mathurā, which was fortified with ramparts and moats and possessed gate-towers and watchtowers.
Hearing the praises of the young women, Kṛṣṇa went together with Rāma; he saw the place where the bow was kept and that great bow with its firm string.
Having routed all the guardians of the bow, he quickly and effortlessly took up the bow; as he bent it to fix the string upon it, it snapped in two right there.

O best of the twice-born, having quickly heard the sound arising from the breaking of the bow, those two powerful ones seized fragments of the bow and struck down the mighty Pālas who had rushed forward to kill them.
Then, having slain the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa stationed at the gate in an instant, those two, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, possessed of great strength and prowess—|| 76 ||
Having uprooted his two tusks and holding them in both hands, they placed those tusks upon their shoulders and went to the arena in an instant.
Having slain the wrestlers Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, and Tośala, as well as other preeminent wrestlers, they sent them to the abode of Yama.

Then the two of them quickly ascended the lofty platform; having approached Kaṃsa as he sat there upon his high seat, they stood before him, treating him with contempt like two lions regarding a small deer. (79)
Then Kṛṣṇa, having dragged Kaṃsa who was standing upon the couch, seized his feet and whirled him with great force in the air.
Then, O twice-born ones, he dashed him to the ground so that he lost his life; Balarāma also struck down the eight brothers of Kaṃsa with his fist.
Having thus slain Kaṃsa, Kṛṣṇa, the crusher of enemy forces, released his two parents, who were exceedingly distressed, from their fetters.
Mādhava stationed them all together with Balarāma; having heard that Kaṃsa had been slain by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they then arrived at the city.
Those kinsmen who had previously been oppressed by Kaṃsa in Mathurā—Keśava likewise established Ugrasena upon the throne.
O twice-born ones, unable to endure such treatment from his parents, he killed his maternal uncle Kaṃsa, who had committed offenses against them and was a thorn to the gods and the brāhmaṇas.
Then once, that most excellent being, Kṛṣṇa, asked all the sages led by Nārada who had come to see him this: (86)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O brāhmaṇas, this maternal uncle Kaṃsa, who was a perpetrator of great sins, has been slain by me. Regarding the killing of a maternal uncle, a fault is proclaimed by those most learned in the scriptures. (87)
"Therefore, speak of an expiation for the removal of that fault. O brahmins, thereupon Nārada spoke to Kṛṣṇa of wondrous valor with sweet words, preceded by devotion and affection. (88)
Nārada said: You are eternally pure, liberated, and always auspicious. (89)
The eternal Supreme Self is of the nature of truth, consciousness, and bliss; O Kṛṣṇa, delight of the Yādavas, merit and sin do not exist for you.
Nevertheless, O Mādhava, whose banner is Garuḍa, you must perform an expiation according to this rite for the sake of instructing the world.
"For now, you must perform the gathering of the world at the highly meritorious Rāmasetu on Mount Gandhamādana."
In ancient times, Rāma established the Liṅga named Rāmanātha; for the purpose of its consecration water, the descendant of Raghu [performed the bath] at Dhanuṣkoṭi.
Having pierced the earth, he established the holy site renowned as Koṭitīrtha, by means of your former incarnation, Rāma, whose actions are performed without effort.
Perform your bath there in that righteous place, which destroys sin and was created by the Lord himself for the purpose of purifying the murder of a Brahmin.
By that, the fault arising from the killing of your maternal uncle will quickly perish; bathing in Hari at Koṭitīrtha is the purifier of even the slaughter of a Brahmin and other such sins. (96)
"Bestowing heaven and liberation upon men, and increasing longevity and health"—having heard these words of the sage Nārada, that Mādhava [acted accordingly]. || 97 ||
O twice-born ones, having dismissed all those sages at that very moment, he went quickly to Rāmasetu for the purification of his own faults.
After traveling for several days, the scion of the Yadu dynasty reached Koṭitīrtha; there he bathed according to the prescribed ritual and gave various gifts many times over.
He was instantly liberated from the sins arising from the murder of his maternal uncle; and having worshipped Rāmanātha, he went to his own city, Mathurā. || 100 ||

Śrī Sūta said: O lords of sages, such is the power and merit of Koṭitīrtha; a human being is instantly liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. There is no other holy place on the surface of the earth equal to this.
O twice-born ones, by bathing here, the three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—become pleased, as do all other deities; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Thus has been narrated to you the wondrous majesty of Koṭitīrtha, by hearing which a human being on earth is liberated from all sins.
O lords of sages, by hearing and reciting this meritorious chapter, a person is truly liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Pacification of the Sin of Killing His Maternal Uncle by Kṛṣṇa," within the Praise of Koṭitīrtha, in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 27 ||
Śrī Sūta said: Having visited the highly meritorious Koṭitīrtha alone, a man who has conquered his senses should then proceed to the Sādhyāmṛta Tīrtha to bathe.
The Sādhyāmṛta, a great sacred ford that bestows the fruit of great merit and pacifies great suffering, is located on Mount Gandhamādana.
There exists [a place] that removes the sins of men and bestows all desired objects; having bathed there with devotion, a person may attain all their wishes.
Neither by austerity, nor by celibacy, nor again by sacrifices or by charity, can a mortal attain that goal which is obtained through immersion in the Sādhya-amṛta.
The sin residing in the bodies of those whose limbs have been touched by the auspicious waters of the Sādhyāmṛta perishes at that very moment.
That man who performs the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra penance in the waters of the Sādhyāmṛta, having shaken off his sins here, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
That man who, having committed sinful deeds in the earlier part of his life, later resorts to the nectar of spiritual practice while filled with remorse; || 7 ||
A man who has bathed at Sādhyāmṛta is liberated in his final years; of this there is no doubt. Having bathed at Sādhyāmṛta, a man is released from the bondage of the body.
Indeed, even those men of sinful deeds who bathe in the waters of the Sādhyāmṛta do not go to the hells that are terrible with manifold afflictions.
O twice-born ones, that destination which men attain by bathing in the waters of the Sādhyāmṛta cannot be reached through sacrifices, nor through the Vedas, nor through meritorious deeds.
As long as the bones of humans remain situated in the water of the Sādhyāmṛta, for that many years they shall dwell in the world of Śiva, highly honored.
Just as the sun shines at its rising after having dispelled the intense darkness, so too one who bathes in the nectar of the sādhya shines, having pierced through all evils.

A man who bathes here always obtains his desired objects; having bathed in this place of great merit, King Purūravas in ancient times abandoned his separation from Urvaśī, which had arisen from the curse of Tumburu.
The sages said: O highly fortunate Sūta, how did he [dwell] together with Urvaśī, the celestial woman?
King Purūravas, a mortal who first attained yoga, abandoned the separation from Urvaśī that had arisen from the curse of Tumburu. (15)
"O bull among sages, explain all of this in detail: for what reason did the sage Tumburu curse the king?"
Sūta said: In ancient times, there was a king named Purūravas, whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra; he was like the king of kings and was indeed honored by the immortals. || 17 ||
That best of kings protected the earth according to righteousness; he worshipped with many sacrifices and gave gifts at all times.
While that high-minded king was ruling the entire earth, O twice-born ones, Urvaśī reached the earth due to the curse of Mitra and Varuṇa.
There, in the vicinity of that king's city, Urvaśī wandered and sang in the grove upon her lute, which was as sweet as the song of the cuckoo.
Once, filled with curiosity to enjoy himself in the royal garden, he mounted his horse and set forth, surrounded by hundreds of women.
To such an Urvaśī, whose waist was as slender as a palm, that king spoke there, saying, "Become my wife."
She too, afflicted by desire, replied to the king there: "Let it be so, O best of men, if you will agree to my condition. (23)
"I shall do it; I will dwell near you with joyful anticipation," he said, "O fair-browed one, I shall fulfill my promise to you. (24)
Then Urvaśī, full of longing, spoke to Purūravas: "If you will protect these two young fawns, who have become like my own sons... (25)
"O King, if you are never seen naked, and if you do not give me food remnants, then I shall dwell in your presence. (26)
"O best of kings, I shall subsist on only ghee. Having been told "So be it" by the king, he led her to his own home. (27)
That king took delight in Alakā, as well as in the Caitraratha forest and on the banks of the Sarasvatī, which were delightful with clusters of lotuses.
He spent sixty-one years enjoying himself with her; because of that, Urvaśī’s affection increased day by day. (29)
The slender-waisted woman felt no longing even for the world of the gods; without her, that world of the gods was no longer beautiful.
"Therefore, O twice-born ones, I shall lead her to the world of the gods"; having reflected thus, Viśvāvasu departed for the earthly realm (bhūrloka) in an instant.
Having learned of the agreement between Urvashi and the king, this Viśvāvasu, together with the Gandharvas, assembled during the middle of the night.
From near Urvaśī’s bed, he quickly seized the quail; and as it was being carried into the sky, Urvaśī heard her husband’s voice.
My son said: "By whom can he be seized? Let him be abandoned! Destitute and deprived of my senses, to what man shall I go for refuge? (34)
Having heard her words during the night, Purūravas did not go out at that time, thinking, "May the goddess not see me naked."
Then, having taken another ram, those Gandharvas departed; Urvaśī also heard the sound of that ram.
"My son is being seized by thieves while I am helpless," the queen cried out harshly; "To what man shall I go for refuge? (37)
Having heard those words, the king, overcome by indignation and believing everything to be shrouded in darkness, took up his sword.
"O wicked one, wicked one! Where are you going? he cried out, rushing after him; at that moment, a brilliant flash of lightning was intensely produced by the Gandharvas.
Seeing the king stripped of his garments by the circles of light emanating from her, the goddess, her time having expired, departed at that very moment.
Having abandoned the two rams there, even the Gandharvas departed; the king, taking the two rams, went joyfully to the side of his own bed.
Having arrived there, he saw Urvaśī, the large-eyed one; and not seeing her, he wandered naked upon the ground like a madman.
Having gone to Kurukṣetra, the king beheld her sporting with four celestial nymphs in a lake crowded with lotuses.
"Go! Stay! O you of terrible mind!"—thus repeatedly uttering these words, the king indeed lamented that hymn in many ways. (44)
And while sporting with the hosts of Apsarases, Urvaśī said to him: "O sinless one, this conduct of yours is not worthy of a great king."
"Previously, at the end of this year, you shall indeed come here while I am pregnant; a son, most righteous, will be born to you. (46)
"O King, I shall indeed dwell with you for one night. Having been addressed thus, O twice-born ones, the king entered his own city filled with joy.
She then spoke of that king to those Apsarases: "This is that best of men by whom I was [approached] while I could assume any form at will. (48)
"O friends, out of longing overcome by passion, I have dwelt for so long with this king, Mahākāla, for such a great length of time. (49)
Having been addressed thus, her friends then said to her, "Excellent, excellent! O friend, we shall sit with him at all times."
Thus did the Apsarases then speak to their friend Urvaśī there; and when the year was complete, the king also came to the edge of the lake.
Seeing that King Purūravas had arrived, Urvaśī, with a heart full of affection, gave him the prince Āyu.
Having stayed with him for one night, that passionate Urvaśī quickly conceived a fetus from him that was to grant five sons.
And Urvaśī, that supreme woman, said to the king: "O lord of the earth, out of affection for me, the Gandharvas will grant you a boon."
"O best of royal sages, let a boon be requested from them by you. Thus addressed by her, the king spoke to those foremost of Gandharvas.
I possess full treasuries and have conquered the circle of my enemies; there is nothing else remaining for me to attain except the same world as Urvaśī. (56)

"Therefore, I choose to spend my time with that Urvaśī. When the king had spoken thus, the Gandharvas, their minds filled with satisfaction, then gave him a vessel of fire and said this to the monarch: (57)
The Gandharvas said: "O best of kings, you who follow the Vedas, divide the fire into three parts. (58)
"O King, having sacrificed with this oblation, go to the same world as Urvaśī. Thus addressed by them, the king took the vessel of fire and departed. (59)
"Alas! How utterly deluded I am," thought the king in the midst of the forest: "Urvaśī was not obtained by me; what indeed is the fruit of this vessel of fire? (50)
Having left the cooking pot in the forest, the king departed for his own city; when midnight had passed, he, unable to sleep, reflected within himself: || 61 ||
"For the sake of attaining the world of Urvaśī, the Gandharva leaders gave me this fire-vessel; however, it was abandoned by me in the forest. (62)
"I shall fetch the vessel again," saying this, he rose and went to the forest; however, Purūravas did not see the fire-vessel there in the forest. (63)
Then, seeing an Aśvattha tree with a Śamī tree at its core at the site of the fire-altar, he reflected: "In the past, I deposited a cooking pot here in this forest."
And that [fire] has now become this Aśvattha tree with a Śamī at its core; therefore, taking it in the form of fire, I shall go to the city.
Having gone there and properly prepared the fire-drill (araṇī), the king resolved, "I shall reverently attend to the fire produced from it," and returned to his own city.
O twice-born ones, at the time of its construction, the king measured that beautiful araṇī with his own fingers and muttered the Gāyatrī mantra.
The king made the araṇī wood as many finger-breadths in measure as there are syllables in the Gāyatrī being recited. (68)
There, having produced the three fires by friction, the king performed the rite, aiming for the desired fruit of attaining the world of Urvaśī. (69)
In accordance with the Vedas, the king joyfully offered oblations into the three fires; by that very same fire-ritual, he then performed many sacrifices.
Having reached the worlds of the Gandharvas, O best of the twice-born, that lord of the earth rejoiced for a long time with Urvaśī in the realm of the gods.
Then, once, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, accompanied by all the immortals, beheld the dance of the celestial nymphs in the assembly hall.
Then King Purūravas also came to the assembly of Devendra to behold the captivating dance of the celestial nymphs of the gods.
Those women danced one by one before Śakra; then Urvaśī, having arrived, danced before Hari.
Then Urvaśī, filled with pride in her skill at dance and dramatic gesture, beheld Purūravas and laughed, she who was exceedingly enchanting. (75)
When the king also laughed upon seeing Urvaśī there, Tumburu, the master of dance, became enraged by that laughter and, out of anger, cursed both her and the best of kings.
Tumburu said: "Whatever was done here in this assembly hall filled with many gods,"
"You both laughed in the midst of the dance without cause and in vain; therefore, O Indra among kings, your separation shall occur instantly, in a moment. (78)
"May it be so! he cursed him in the presence of all the deities. Then the king, having been cursed there by the dance teacher, was filled with grief.
Thereupon Purūravas went for refuge to the wielder of the thunderbolt, crying out, "Protect me! Protect me! and spoke to Puruhūta with a piteous voice. (80)
"I have performed sacrifices for the sake of attaining residence in the same world as Urvaśī; therefore, O Pākaśāsana, separation from her would be unbearable for me. (81)
To him who had spoken thus, the thousand-eyed lord of Śacī said: "O best of kings, do not fear; I shall declare the release from the curse."
In the meritorious southern ocean, on Mount Gandhamādana, there is a most excellent holy site (tīrtha) known as Sādhyāmṛta.
It is served by all the gods, as well as by the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras; it is frequented by the hosts of great yogis and sages, such as Sanaka and others.
O King, there exists a sacred ford (tīrtha) that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men and grants release from all curses; go there with haste.
Since the nectar of all [beings] is to be attained here through bathing, it is therefore renowned in all the worlds as "Sādhyāmṛta" (the attainable nectar). || 86 ||
By bathing there, you will again attain union with Urvaśī and you will dwell in my world; of this there is no doubt. (87)
Thus instructed, the king, with a joyful heart, set out in an instant toward the great holy ford known as Sādhyāmṛta.
O Brahmins, he bathed there in that Sādhyāmṛta, which destroys great sins; by bathing there, the king was immediately released from the curse.
Immediately after his bath, he united with Urvaśī; seated in a celestial chariot together with her, he departed for Amarāvatī.
He sported again with her in the celestial palace like a god; such is the power of that sacred ford, which is the unsurpassed nectar of the Sādhyas.
Where Purūravas was united with Urvaśī through bathing, therefore one should bathe here at this holy site, which destroys even the greatest sins.
O Brahmins, one obtains all desired objects and shall go to the highest heaven; if a man bathes there free from desire, he attains liberation.
The man who recites or hears this purifying chapter that destroys sin shall attain a dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, O Brahmins, I have described to you with faith in detail the sin-destroying majesty of the Sādhyāmṛta Tīrtha. 95.
That which the four-faced Brahmā formerly proclaimed to Sanaka and the others.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Purūravas’s Liberation from the Curse," within the Praise of the Sādhyāmṛta Tīrtha, in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: Having bathed in the Sādhyāmṛta Tīrtha, which grants liberation from the king’s curse, a man endowed with self-restraint should then proceed to Sarvatīrtha.
This Sarvatīrtha is of great merit and the destroyer of great sins; whether one is burdened by a single great sin or burdened by all sins, [one is purified].
O you of excellent vows, all sins remain within the body for only so long as one does not bathe in the Savartī Tīrtha; by bathing there, one becomes pure at that very moment.
Until that sinful man has immersed himself in all the holy fords of this place. || 1 ||
O twice-born ones, seeing a man going to this all-encompassing holy ford for the purpose of bathing, [they spoke].
All sins tremble, thinking, "Our destruction will come about"; meanwhile, a person on earth undergoes the sufferings of dwelling in the womb and so forth. || 5 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should not bathe in this [ordinary] sacred ford until one has performed great sacrifices and likewise resorted to true sacred fords.
By means of the recitation of great mantras such as the Gāyatrī according to the prescribed rules, and by repeating each of the four Vedas one hundred times; (7)

Whatever fruit a mortal obtains by worshipping the gods such as Śiva and Viṣṇu with devotion, and likewise by fasting on lunar days such as Ekādaśī, he shall obtain that very same fruit by bathing here.
The sages said: O Sūta, how did this place acquire the renown as "Sarvatīrtha"? O Sage, tell us this meritorious account in detail as we listen.
Śrī Sūta said: Formerly, there was a sage named Sucarita who was bound by his religious observances.
Born of the lineage of Bhṛgu, he was blind from birth and afflicted by old age; O twice-born ones, due to the absence of eyes, he was incapable of undertaking pilgrimages.
Desiring to bathe in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), the great sage went to the meritorious Gandhamādana mountain by the southern ocean.
Having gone there, he performed a most difficult penance directed toward Śaṅkara; fasting and with his senses subdued, he worshipped Śambhu three times a day.
Likewise, he bathed three times a day, honored guests in that same manner, stood in the midst of water during the cold season, and remained in the midst of five fires during the summer. (14)
During the rainy season, he endured the downpours; subsisting on water or feeding on air, he constantly bore the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
In accordance with the Jābālopaniṣad, the twice-born one likewise wore rudrākṣa beads; thus he performed severe penance for ten years.
O twice-born ones, Śaṅkara, the moon-crested Lord, being well-pleased by his ascetic penance, appeared before that sage Sucarita.
Having mounted a great bull, attended by a multitude of spirits, bearing the body of half-Girijā, holding a trident, and possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns; || 18 ||
Then, illuminating all directions with his own radiance and dispelling all darkness, he appeared with his entire body white as ashes, adorned with a circle of matted locks.
Then Śambhu, adorned with the ornaments of the infinite Diśā-mahānāgas, manifested and bestowed two eyes upon him.
Then, O Brahmins, for the purpose of beholding his own self, Śaṅkara, the lord of Girijā, granted a pair of eyes to Sucarita. Having beheld the Supreme Lord, he, with a tranquil mind, offered praise.
Sucarita said: Victory, O God, O Maheśāna! Victory, O Śaṅkara, O Dhūrjaṭi! 22.
Victory to you, who are worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods; O destroyer of Tripura, O ender of Yama! Victory, O Lord of Umā, O Mahādeva, O ender of Kāma, O stainless one! 23.
Victory to you, the physician of saṃsāra! You are the protector of beings, known as Śiva. O Three-eyed One, salutations to you, who are consecrated to the protection of your devotees. 24.
O Vyomakeśa, salutations to you; victory to you, the embodiment of compassion! O Nīlakaṇṭha, salutations to you; victory to you, the liberator from saṃsāra! 25.
O Maheśvara, salutations to you, whose form is supreme bliss; O Gaṅgādhara, salutations to you, O Viśveśvara, O Mṛḍa, O Imperishable One.
Salutations to you, the Blessed One Vāsudeva, the source of auspiciousness; salutations to Śarva, Ugra, Garbha, and the Lord of Kailāsa.
Protect me, O ocean of compassion, by casting a glance of mercy; without considering my conduct, save me and deliver me out of grace. (28)
Śrī Sūta said: O Brahmins, having been thus praised, Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā and ocean of compassion, spoke these words to that sage Sucarita.

Mahādeva said: "O sage Sucarita, choose today the boon you desire. I have come to this auspicious and holy hermitage to grant you a boon. Thus addressed, the sage spoke to Mahādeva, the ocean of compassion. (30)
Sucarita said: "O Lord, O Moon-crested One, if you would be gracious to me," (31)
Therefore, I truly choose you as the boon desired by me; for my body is decayed by old age and grey hair, and I am unable to go anywhere.
"I have a desire to bathe in all the sacred fords (tīrthas). Therefore, tell me the means by which a person may obtain that fruit which one attains by bathing in all the sacred fords. (33)
Mahādeva said: "I shall invoke all the sacred fords (tīrthas) right here in their entirety."
"Since this mountain Gandhamādana has been purified by Rāma’s bridge," having spoken thus on Mount Gandhamādana, that Mahādeva—
The supreme one invoked the sacred fords (tīrthas) for the sake of pleasing the sage; then Śaṅkara, the ocean of compassion, spoke of his virtuous conduct.

O Sage, this [place] is indeed the destroyer of great sins due to its excellent conduct; because of the presence of all sacred fords (tīrthas), it is remembered by the name "All-Fords" (Sarvatīrtha). || 37 ||
Because I have mentally drawn all sacred fords (tīrthas) here, this place shall receive the name "Mānasa-tīrtha," which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Therefore, O lady of virtuous conduct, bathe here immediately for the sake of liberation, in this place which possesses a splendor like a forest fire to the masses of great sins. (39)
In destroying desire, delusion, fear, anger, greed, disease, and the like, and in being the cause of immediate liberation without the specialized knowledge of Vedānta—(40)
In crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, which is filled with the flood of crocodiles such as birth and death; and in destroying the fires of all the hells, such as Kumbhīpāka and others. || 41 ||
Thus addressed by Śambhu, the enemy of Madana, Sucarita bathed in all the sacred fords (tīrthas) in the presence of Mahādeva, O brahmins.
Having risen after bathing, Sucarita was beheld by all human beings as a youth, exceedingly handsome and free from old age and grey hair. (43)
Having beheld the beauty of his own body, the sage Sucarita then praised that sacred ford (tīrtha) in many ways, as did the other ascetics.
Immediately thereafter, Mahādeva spoke to Sucarita: "O twice-born Sucarita, you shall dwell on the bank of this sacred ford."
Perform your ablutions constantly while remembering me, the giver of liberation; O best of Brahmins, do not go to holy places in other lands.
"By the greatness of this sacred ford (tīrtha), you will certainly attain me at the end; and others also who bathe here, O twice-born one, shall likewise attain me. (47)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Īśa vanished right there; when Rudra had disappeared, the sage Sucarita then [proceeded].
Dwelling for many ages on the banks of all the sacred fords (tīrthas), he performed his ablutions at the Mānasa-tīrtha while remaining steadfast in his observances.
At the end of his body's life, being liberated from all bonds, he attained Śaṅkara and also achieved union (sāyujya) through the majesty of all the holy fords (tīrthas).
Thus, O brahmins, the majesty of all the sacred fords has been recounted to you; by reading or hearing this, one is liberated from all sins.

Comments on Koṭi/Dhanuṣkoṭi: Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of All Tīrthas," within the "Praise of All Tīrthas" section of the Setumāhātmya, in the third part (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 29.

The venerable Sūta said: Having performed his ablutions at all the most purifying holy fords (tīrthas), a mortal should then proceed to Dhanuṣkoṭi, which destroys sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
Merely by remembering her, a person on earth becomes liberated; so too for those who behold Dhanuṣkoṭi, bathe there, or speak of it. || 2 ||
They do not experience those twenty-eight varieties of hells: Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, and Raurava; || 3 ||
Kumbhīpāka, Kālasūtra, Asipatravana, as well as Kṛmibhakṣa, Andhakūpa, Sandaṃśa, and Śālmalī; || 4 ||
The Sūrmi, the Vaitaraṇī, the Prāṇarodha, and likewise the Viśasana; the Lālābhakṣa, the Avīci, and likewise the Sārameyādana. || 5 ||
Likewise, there was the piercing by diamond-tipped spears, the falling into caustic mud, the devouring by hosts of rākṣasas, impalement upon pikes, and being torn asunder.
O brahmins, there is also that known as Daṇḍaśūkāśana, that designated as Paryāvartana, that called Tirodhāna, and likewise that named Sūcīmukha.
And [there is] the consumption of pus and blood, and the torment by poison and fire; such is the collection of hells, numbering twenty-eight. (8)
O Brahmins, a man who has stolen the wealth, children, or wives of others does not go [to hell] by immersing himself at Dhanuṣkoṭi.
Bound by the noose of Time, he is cast for many years into the terrible Tāmisra hell by the fearsome messengers of Yama.
If he bathes at the tip of the bow, he is not cast down there; however, he who, having slain his master, enjoys his wealth and other possessions, [is cast down]. || 11 ||
He is cast into the Andhatāmisra hell, which is filled with great suffering; however, if he bathes at Dhanuṣkoṭi, he is not cast into that place.
That mortal who nourishes his own family by harming living beings will surely abandon them here and be cast down quickly into the Raurava hell. || 13 ||
If one bathes at the tip of the bow amidst that place crowded with great serpents full of virulent poison and with the servants of Yama, one is not cast down into it.
That mortal who nourishes only his own body, devoid of wife, sons, and the like, is cast into the terrible Mahāraurava hell to eat his own flesh.
If he bathes at the tip of the bow, he is not struck down by that [weapon], even though he indeed obstructs living beings, whether they be cattle or birds.
Those followers of Yama cast him, who is devoid of even a trace of compassion and is censured even by flesh-eating demons, into the boiling oil of the Kumbhīpāka hell.
If that lowest of men, who hates his mother, father, and Brahmins, bathes at the tip of the bow, he is cast down into it.
He fell into the Kālasūtra hell, which extends for ten thousand yojanas; it is heated by fire from below and by the rays of the sun from above. || 19 ||
O Brahmins, afflicted by hunger, he is thrown onto a threshing floor made of copper; yet if he bathes at Dhanuṣkoṭi, he is not cast down there.
The man who, transgressing the path of the Veda, proceeds upon a wicked path, is cast by the servants of Yama into the terrible forest of sword-leaves (Asipatravana). || 21 ||
If a king or a royal servant should inflict punishment upon one who does not deserve it, he is cast down from the tip of that very bow when he bathes there. (22)
O twice-born ones, he who inflicts corporal punishment upon a Brahmin is cast into a terrible hell, where he is crushed like sugarcane in a machine into the mouth of a boar.
If he bathes at the tip of the bow, he is not cast down into it; for he who would commit violence against living beings, whose very existence is dependent upon the Lord, [is spared].
Being tormented by those very creatures whom he himself had tormented, he is cast into a most terrifying blind well by the servants of Yama.
There, in that place thick with darkness, one should wander sleepless and at peace, provided that one is not struck down by the tip of the bow there.

O twice-born ones, that man who eats rice, soup, and other foods by breaking the order of the row, or who eats out of delusion without having performed the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña), [is a sinner]. (27)
He is cast down by the messengers of Yama into the Kṛmibhojana hell; being devoured by hundreds of worms, he himself devours the swarms of worms.
And he himself remains turned into a worm until his sins are exhausted; however, if he bathes at Dhanuṣkoṭi, he is not cast into that [hell].
Whether it be the king himself or his official, whoever should seize the wealth of Brahmins by theft or even by force, as well as the wealth of others— 30.
Greatly tormented by tongs in iron fire-pits, he is cast into the terrible Saṃdaṃśa hell by the servants of Yama.
If he bathes at the tip of the bow, he is not cast down into it; however, that lowest of men who would approach a woman who should not be approached [is cast down]. || 32 ||
O twice-born ones, if a woman should approach a man who is forbidden, they both [shall be made to enter] an iron woman and an iron man.
As long as the moon and sun endure, those two remain embracing a heated iron image; they are then cast into the terrible hell named Sūrmī, which is filled with many thorns.
If he bathes at the tip of the bow, he is not cast down there; yet he oppresses all living beings with various afflictions and calamities.
He is cast into the terrible Śālmalī hell, which is filled with many thorns; however, if he bathes at Dhanuṣkoṭi, he is not thrown into that place.
Whether a king or a royal servant, whoever follows heretical doctrines and destroys the bridges of dharma is cast into the Vaitaraṇī river.
If one who is defiled by association with a *vṛṣalī* and devoid of pure conduct such as ritual purification is struck at the tip of that bow, he falls down upon it. (38)
Having abandoned shame and abandoned the Vedas, and likewise being devoted to the conduct of beasts, he [is cast] into that [place] filled with pus, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, bile, and so forth.
He is cast into the Atibībhatsa hell by the servants of Yama; however, if he bathes at Dhanuṣkoṭi, he is not thrown into that place.
Just as a hunter might strike with stones or afflict deer with arrows, so too he, being pierced by floods of arrows, is struck in the next world by the servants of Yama.
One is cast into the hell named Prāṇarodha by the servants of Yama; however, if one bathes at Dhanuṣkoṭi, one is not cast into that place.
O twice-born ones, that hypocrite who sacrifices animals at a ritual while devoid of the performance of the prescribed injunctions slays them in the next world in the Vaiśasa hell.
Being cut by the servants of Yama, he is cast into a place crowded with suffering; yet if he bathes at the tip of the bow, he is not thrown into that [hell].
He who causes his own wife of equal caste to drink semen becomes a drinker of semen in the next world and is cast into the Pit of Semen.
If one who has taken to the path of bandits, who is a poisoner or a burner of villages, bathes at that tip of the bow, he is not cast down into it. (46)
And he who steals the goods of a merchant, O best of the twice-born, is cast for a long time into the hell known as Vajradaṃṣṭrāhika in the next world.
If he bathes at the tip of the bow, he is not cast into that [hell], nor indeed into any other hells that exist in the hereafter.
A person does not obtain those [other merits] by immersing oneself in Dhanuṣkoṭi; by bathing even once at Dhanuṣkoṭi, one obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
The knowledge of the Self becomes manifest, and liberation is likewise fourfold; the intellect finds no delight in sin, nor does suffering arise at all.
Great joy arises for the intellect from bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi; it is equal to the fruit obtained by men through the gift of their own weight in gold (tulāpuruṣa-dāna). || 51 ||
That fruit is obtained by men through immersion at Dhanuṣkoṭi, which is indeed the merit that would accrue to men from the gift of a thousand cows. || 52 ||
A mortal obtains that merit by immersing himself in Dhanaṣkā, whatever a person may desire among dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
By immersing oneself in Dhanuṣkoṭi, one immediately attains that very [fruit], whether one is burdened by great sins (mahāpātaka) or burdened by all possible sins.
O Brahmins, by immersing oneself in Dhanuṣkoṭi, one becomes instantly purified; [one attains] wisdom, fortune, fame, prosperity, knowledge, righteousness, and detachment.
The purification of the minds of men occurs by immersion at Dhanuṣkoṭi; even ten thousand killings of Brahmins, as well as ten thousand drinks of liquor, [are cleansed]. (56)

Ten thousand instances of approaching the teacher’s wife are a cause of sin; likewise, ten thousand acts of stealing gold and ten million instances of associating with such persons [are causes of sin]. (57)
By immersing oneself in Dhanuṣkoṭi, one quickly attains dissolution; [sins] equal to the killing of a Brahmin and equal to the drinking of liquor [are likewise destroyed]. 58.
O believers, those [sins] which are equal even to approaching the wife of a guru, as well as those equal to stealing gold and those equal to associating with such [sinners], [are enumerated]. (59)
All of those perish by immersing oneself at Dhanuṣkoṭi; no doubt should ever be entertained regarding these things that have been stated.
"I hold a heated axe upon the tip of my tongue; of this there is no doubt. One who speaks all of this as mere empty praise shall indeed become a denizen of hell. (61)
He should indeed be known as a *saṃkara* (of mixed caste), excluded from all ritual acts. Oh, what folly! Oh, what folly! Oh, what folly, O best of the twice-born! (62)
In the holy ford named Dhanuṣkoṭi, which destroys all sins, bestows non-dual knowledge upon men, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation; || 63 ||
Although it is eternally present as the bestower of desired objects and likewise the destroyer of ignorance, people indeed abandon it and take delight elsewhere.
Oh, the greatness of delusion! It is impossible for me to describe it; indeed, for one who has bathed at the tip of the bow, there is no fear of Death.
Those men who behold Dhanuṣkoṭi, bathe there, praise it, extol it, touch it, and bow down to it—O best of the twice-born, they shall never again drink the breast milk of their mothers.
The sages said: O Sūta, how did it come to be known by the name Dhanuṣkoṭi? (67)
"O bull among sages, tell all that in its true essence and in detail. Thus questioned by the inhabitants of Naimiṣa, Sūta spoke to them once again.
Śrī Sūta said: After Rāvaṇa, the thorn of the worlds, had been slain in battle by Rāma, and Bibhīṣaṇa was then established as the king in Laṅkā—|| 69 ||
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, accompanied by Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa, was surrounded by heroic monkeys headed by Sugrīva.
His own wondrous glory was constantly being praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, gods, Vidyādharas, and Ṛṣis, as well as by Apsarases.
Like Śiva, the destroyer of Tripura, who playfully wields his bow, Rāma, surrounded by all [his followers], followed Gandhamādana.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, who knew the dharma, with palms joined in reverence, made a request to the high-souled Rāghava, the destroyer of Rāvaṇa, as he stood there.
"O Rāma, by means of this bridge, all those kings, swelling with their armies, might come together and afflict my city. (74)
"Therefore, O scion of Raghu, pierce this bridge with the tip of your bow. Thus was that descendant of Raghu entreated by that descendant of Pulastya.
The joy of the Raghus pierced his own bridge with the tip of his bow; therefore, O twice-born ones, that holy site became renowned as Dhanuṣkoṭi.
He who beholds the line drawn by the tip of Śrī Rāma’s bow shall not experience dwelling in a womb, which is joined with manifold afflictions. || 77 ||
A line was drawn by Rāma upon the salt ocean at Dhanuṣkoṭi; liberation arises from the mere sight of it—I do not know the fruit born of bathing there.
Austerity performed on the banks of the Narmadā destroys even the greatest sins; however, death upon the banks of the Gaṅgā bestows the fruit of liberation.
O twice-born ones, charity performed at Kurukṣetra purifies even the sin of killing a Brahmin; likewise, austerity, death, or charity performed by men at Dhanuṣkoṭi [achieves the same]. (80)
O best of Brahmins, it shall be capable of destroying great sins, granting liberation, and accomplishing desired goals; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (81)
O Rāma, a living being is tormented by major and minor sins only so long as the Dhanuṣkoṭi, which bestows liberation, is not beheld. (82)
The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are severed, and sinful deeds are destroyed for one who beholds the tip of the bow. (83)
On the bridge over the southern ocean, that line which was indeed drawn by Rāmacandra with the tip of his bow for the benefit of Vibhīṣaṇa— 84.
That very path leads to the state of Kailāsa, as well as to Vaikuṇṭha and the world of Brahmā; it is the way to the heavenly realm—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (85)
Immersing oneself in Dhanuṣkoṭi is equal in merit to the fruits of sacrifices; it is a merit superior to all mantras and bestows the fruit of all desires at all times.
For those who behold the tip of the bow (Dhanuṣkoṭi), what is the use of austerities that afflict the bodies of men, what use are sacrifices, what use are the Vedas, or even the Śāstras? 87.
If men obtain a bath at the tip of Rāmacandra’s bow, what further need is there for the meritorious waters of the white and black rivers? (88)
If the vision of Rāmacandra’s Dhanuṣkoṭi can be obtained, why do men vainly pray for liberation through death at Kāśī? (89)
Without immersing oneself in Dhanuṣkoṭi, without fasting for three days, and without giving gold and a cow, one will undoubtedly become poor. (90)
The fruit that a man obtains by immersing himself in Dhanuṣkoṭi is not attained even by performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees. || 91 ||
One does not obtain that fruit; I speak the truth, the absolute truth. They know the holy ford named Dhanuṣkoṭi to be superior to all other holy fords.
O best of the twice-born, there are ten thousand crores of sacred fords on the surface of the earth; their presence is found here at Dhanuṣkoṭi.
The eight Vasus, the Ādityas, the Rudras, and likewise the Maruts; the Sādhyas along with the Gandharvas, as well as the Siddhas and Vidyādharas. || 94 ||
These and other gods always maintain their presence here at this sacred ford (tīrtha) at Dhanuṣkoṭi; likewise, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) is ever present. || 95 ||
Śiva, Viṣṇu, Umā, and Sarasvatī are present there; likewise, the gods and sages have performed penance at Dhanuṣkoṭi.
By the fruit of that [act], the lords of sages attained vast perfection; moreover, the man who bathes there and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods [attains the same]. (97)
Freed from all sins, that man who, filled with devotion, feeds even a single Brahmin here, is glorified in the world of Brahmā. || 98 ||
In this world and in the next as well, that man who does not subsist on vegetables, roots, and fruits enjoys infinite happiness. (99)
That man should bathe at the tip of the bow for the attainment of that fruit, he who does not possess the capacity to perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
O lords of sages, whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra, he who bathes at Dhanuṣkoṭi indeed attains the fruit thereof.

By immersing oneself in Dhanuṣkoṭi, one is not born into a censurable womb. Furthermore, that man who [immerses himself] at Dhanuṣkoṭi during the month of Māgha when the sun is situated in Capricorn (Makara), || 2 ||
O twice-born ones, I am not able to describe the merit of that man who bathes at Dhanuṣkoṭi during the month of Māgha.
O lords of sages, he who has bathed in all the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others, shall attain imperishable worlds and even obtain liberation.
Whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man since birth—all that shall go to destruction here through immersion in the month of Māgha.
