Just as the joy of the Raghus is the supreme among all the gods, so too is Dhanuṣkoṭi remembered as the best of all sacred fords (tīrthas).

In that place, bathing during the month of Māgha bestows all desired objects; even one who is self-restrained and has conquered his senses [attains this] by bathing for thirty days in the month of Māgha.
A man should bathe at Dhanuṣkoṭi for the sake of attaining the state of non-rebirth—any man who, having conquered anger and eating but one meal a day, does so here during the month of Māgha.
O best of Brahmins, that man who performs a bath at the tip of Śrī Rāma’s bow during the month of Māgha is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
At the conclusion of the bath on Śivarātri, fasting and with senses subdued, one should keep a vigil throughout the night, especially during each successive watch.
Having worshipped Mahādeva Rāmanātha according to the prescribed rites, and having bathed at Dhanuṣkoṭi on the following day when the sun had risen; || 11 ||
Having bathed in other sacred fords as well with a restrained mind, and having performed his obligatory rites and worshipped Rāmanātha; || 12 ||
O best of the twice-born, having fed the brahmins with food according to one's ability, and having given land, cows, sesame seeds, grain, and wealth according to one's means; || 13 ||
Having been authorized by the Brahmins, he himself eats while maintaining silence. For the man who has performed this, the Great Lord Rāmanātha [is pleased]. (14)
Having liberated one from all sins, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; therefore, O lords of sages, with every effort during the month of Māgha— || 15 ||
Indeed, men who desire liberation must bathe here at Dhanuṣkoṭi; for that man who bathes at Dhanuṣkoṭi on the Setu during the Ardhodaya [conjunction]... (16)
O twice-born ones, his sins perish in an instant; moreover, bathing here at Mahodaya bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whoever bathes at the tip of the bow on the day of Ardhodaya, the three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—become subject to his will.

O twice-born ones, bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi during the Ardhodaya and Mahodaya festivals is the cause for attaining Sāyujya liberation, even without the realization of non-duality (advaita-vijñāna). || 19 ||
In that regard, O twice-born ones, bathing during the Ardhodaya and Mahodaya [conjunctions] is prescribed by Manu and others for men; indeed, it is the true expiation for sinners. (120)
O Brahmins, if a man bathes here at this Setu, at Dhanuṣkoṭi, which is a great source of compassion where the ocean rises halfway, he truly performs a sacrifice even without a ritual.
A man who bathes here during lunar and solar eclipses obtains the complete fruit of sacrifices; of this there is no doubt. (22)
Even with the remainder of his life, it would be impossible to describe the fruit of the merit gained from bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi during lunar and solar eclipses.
The expiation for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin has been declared [to take place] at the tip of Śrī Rāma’s bow during lunar and solar eclipses.

Bathing is declared to bestow union [with the Divine] and grant the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), especially during lunar and solar eclipses, and at the occasions of Ardhodaya and Mahodaya. || 25 ||
"Men who desire the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation must bathe here; therefore, O best of sages, abandon everything else and proceed. (26)

Go there to Dhanuṣkoṭi, which is of great merit and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; and having gone there, perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for your ancestors.

By offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) here, there shall be satisfaction for the ancestors until the end of the kalpa; these three sites, which grant satisfaction to the ancestors, were established by Rāma.
By offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) here at the base of the bridge, at Dhanuṣkoṭi on Mount Gandhamādana, one shall be liberated from one's debts to the ancestors.
Setumūla, Dhanuṣkoṭi, and Gandhamādana—these three places created by the gods are known as Ṛṇamokṣa. || 130 ||
Therefore, with every effort, let Dhanuṣkoṭi be resorted to; having come here to Dhanuṣkoṭi and bathed according to the prescribed rules, [one attains the goal].
O lords of sages, the illustrious Aśvatthāman, son of Droṇācārya, was instantly liberated from the terrible sin of killing those who were asleep.
Thus, O Brahmins, has the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi been described to you; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men, and destroys all sins.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narration of the Majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi," within the Praise of Dhanuṣkoṭi, in the Setu-māhātmya of the Third Section, the Brahma-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 30 ||
The sages said: O Sūta, how did Aśvatthāman commit the slaughter of those who were asleep? And how was he liberated from that sin by immersing himself at Dhanuṣkoṭi?
O best of those who know the Purāṇas, speak this to us who are full of faith; for us, who drink the nectar of your words, no satiety arises. (2)

Thus questioned then by the residents of the Naimiṣa forest, Sūta bowed joyfully to his teacher Vyāsa and began to speak. Śrī Sūta said: O twice-born ones, formerly, when a great war joined by many akṣauhiṇīs had arisen between the Pāṇḍavas and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra for the sake of the kingdom— 4.
Having fought for ten days, Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu, was slain; Droṇa fought for five days, and likewise Karṇa for two days.
Likewise, O twice-born ones, after fighting for a single day and Śalya having met his death, Duryodhana [fell] there in that battle on the eighteenth day.
O Brahmins, when that best of kings had fallen with his thighs broken by Bhīma’s mace, all the monarchs made haste to take up their quarters.
Those kings who survived went away with joyful minds, as did Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, and all the Sṛñjayas indeed.
Then other rulers of the earth also departed for their own camps; thereafter, the great heroes, the sons of Pṛthā, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa and Sātyaki, [proceeded].
O twice-born ones, they entered Duryodhana’s deserted camp, where only elderly ministers, eunuchs, and female guards remained.
With palms joined in reverence and bowed low, clad in soiled saffron robes, those sons of Pṛthā were being saluted in the palace of the Kuru king.
Taking all the various kinds of goods found there, those mighty ones dwelt happily in the camp of Suyodhana.
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as if to please those sons of Pṛthā, said to them: "For the sake of auspiciousness, we must dwell outside the camp."
Having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva, the Pāṇḍavas replied, "So be it," and accompanied by Kṛṣṇa and Sātyaki, they departed from the camp.
Accompanied by Vāsudeva for the sake of auspiciousness, those best of men, the Pāṇḍavas, reached the bank of the river Oghavatī.
Having slain the hosts of their enemies, Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa spent that night there happily in the presence of Duryodhana.
Before the setting of the sun, they arrived in the afternoon; then, they beheld Suyodhana covered in the dust of the battlefield.
His thigh-staff was shattered by Bhīmasena’s terrible mace; with all his limbs drenched in blood, he writhed upon the surface of the earth.
Then Drona’s son and the other three did not grieve there; yet King Duryodhana, seeing them on the battlefield, himself began to grieve for them.
But seeing the king thus, his eyes clouded with tears, Aśvatthāman then blazed up with anger like a great fire.
Squeezing his hand in his own hand, his eyes wide with rage, he addressed Duryodhana in a voice faltering with tears: 21.
My father was struck down by base men through mere trickery on the field of battle; yet I do not grieve for him as much as I do for you, having been cast down.
Listen now to my words as I speak them truthfully, O King; I swear by my own good deeds, O high-minded Suyodhana. (23)
"Tonight, during the night, I shall slay the Pāṇḍavas along with the Sṛñjayas while Vāsudeva looks on; grant me your permission. (24)
Having heard those words of his, the king then said to the son of Droṇa, "So be it. O best of the twice-born, the king spoke again to Kṛpa.
"O Teacher, consecrate this son of Droṇa in the command of the army with water from the pitcher"; and then he (Aśvatthāman) did exactly so.
Then, having been consecrated, the son of Droṇa embraced that best of kings and departed swiftly, accompanied by Kṛtavarman and Kṛpa.
Then those three heroes set out facing the south and reached the vicinity of the camp before the setting of the sun.
Hearing that terrifying sound of the Pārthas, the three—Drauṇi and the others—desiring victory there, then pursued the frightened Pāṇḍavas. || 29 ||
Afflicted by exhaustion, they fled in fear facing the east for some distance; after traveling for a short while, they fell under the sway of anger and resentment.
Distressed by the slaughter of Duryodhana, they remained there for a moment; then they indeed beheld a forest covered with various trees and creepers.
It was crowded with many deer, teeming with flocks of cruel birds, and adorned by ponds filled with abundant water. || 32 ||
Having drunk the water there—which was crowded with hundreds of lotuses, blue lilies, and white water-lilies—and likewise having given water to the horses, they [proceeded].
Then, having reached that great tree, those three saw a banyan tree crowded with many branches.
Having descended from their chariots and unyoked the horses, they touched water there and performed the evening twilight devotions.
Then the sun reached the mountain of setting, its radiance departed; thereafter, a terrible night ensued, filled with thick darkness.
Nocturnal creatures wandered here and there, while diurnal creatures fell under the power of sleep.
At the time of nightfall, Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa, emaciated by grief, sat down near a banyan tree.
Then Kṛpa and Bhoja, who were accustomed to great luxury and undeserving of suffering, fell asleep; those who deserved comfort lay down upon the bare ground. (39)
But the son of Droṇa, his mind clouded by anger, O best of brahmins, could not find sleep, sighing like a serpent.
Then he gazed upon that terrifying forest; and then he saw a banyan tree crowded with many crows.
There, flocks of crows took up residence during the night; they slept comfortably and separately upon the various branches that had been broken apart.
While those crows were sleeping trustfully on all sides, the son of Droṇa then beheld the terrifying Bhāsa bird approaching.
Then Bhasa, uttering a fierce cry, vanished into a tree with his cruel body and tawny-brown limbs.
Leaping onto a branch of that banyan tree, that bird, the destroyer of crows, struck down many sleeping crows.
That bird tore out the wings of some crows, while for others he struck off their feet or their heads with his talons.
O twice-born ones, that powerful owl tore [them] apart in an instant; then, with many fragments of their bodies, he [overwhelmed] the crows.
Having destroyed those crows that had completely surrounded the entire Nyagrodha circle, the owl then rejoiced.
Having witnessed that deed performed by Bhāsa in this manner during the night, the son of Droṇa thought: "I too shall thus bring about the destruction of my enemies at night."
Thus he reflected alone, remembering this instruction: "The sons of Pṛthā cannot be conquered by one who fights according to the straightforward path. (50)
Therefore, under that very pretext, those who appear victorious must be slain by me; moreover, their death was vowed by me in the presence of Suyodhana.
"In a fair fight, my life will be lost; but for one who fights with deceit, there is victory and the destruction of the enemy. (52)
Whatever action may be censurable even by all people in the world, that very deed must indeed be performed by one who follows the dharma of a Kṣatriya. (53)
The sons of Pṛthā also performed this deed against Suyodhana through deception alone; regarding this matter, there are indeed verses spoken by those who know the past: [Verse 54]
When the enemy's force is exhausted, shattered, or engaged in eating; or during its departure or its entry—[the king] must strike, without a doubt. (55)
At midnight, against one afflicted by sleep, as well as against an army that has abandoned its weapons in battle, whose warriors are broken—all such forces may be attacked by enemies. (56)

Having thus made this resolve regarding the act of killing those who were asleep, that reckless son of Droṇa awakened the sleeping Bhoja and Kṛpa during the night; after meditating for a moment, he addressed them both.
Aśvatthāman said: "King Suyodhana, possessed of great strength and prowess, is dead. (58)
Though he was a man of pure deeds, he was slain by the Pārthas through many base acts; Bhīma, acting with extreme cruelty, struck off the king’s head with his foot.

"Therefore, having gathered at the cloth pavilion of the Pārthas tonight, we shall slay them with various kinds of weapons while they are sleeping soundly. O best of the twice-born, having heard this, Kṛpa spoke there as follows.
Kṛpa said: "In this world, the killing of those who are asleep is neither righteous nor is it honored."
"Likewise, for those who have laid down their weapons and abandoned their chariots and horses—listen to my words, my child; let this rashness of yours be relinquished. (62)
"But we shall inquire of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the devoted Gāndhārī, and Vidura as well; we shall do exactly as they say. Thus addressed, the son of Droṇa then spoke again to Kṛpa.
Aśvatthāman said: "In the past, my father was slain by the Pāṇḍavas through deceit in battle. (64)
O maternal uncle, those words of Dhṛṣṭadyumna—"I am the slayer of Droṇa"—truly cut through all my vital organs. (65)
How can I hear those words in the presence of the people, [words] by which those very Pāṇḍavas previously cast down the bridge of dharma?
Right before the eyes of all you kings, my father, having laid down his weapons, was struck down by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Likewise, Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, having cast aside his bow and being unarmed, was slain by Savyasācin with Śikhaṇḍin placed in front.
In this way, other kings as well have been slain by them through mere deception; likewise, I shall carry out the killing of those who sleep at night.
Having spoken thus, the son of Droṇa then mounted his chariot with its yoked horses and, blazing with rage, advanced toward his enemies.
Both Kṛtavarman and Kṛpa followed him as he went; they proceeded to their camp, where the people were then fast asleep.
Having reached the gate of the camp, the son of Droṇa remained there at night after propitiating Mahādeva, the storehouse of compassion.
He obtained a stainless sword from Mahādeva, the bestower of boons; then the son of Droṇa stationed both Kṛtavarman and Kṛpa.
At the gateway, the great hero Śibi entered the camp; once the son of Droṇa had entered the camp, both Kṛtavarman and Kṛpa [also entered]. (74)
Those two supreme archers stood alert at the gateway; then the son of Droṇa, highly incensed and as if blazing with splendor, [approached].
Taking up a stainless sword, he moved about in the camp at night; then he slowly approached the camp of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the others, exhausted there by the great battle, slept at night in trustfulness, surrounded by their respective armies.
Having entered the camp of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Droṇa, skilled in weapons, beheld from nearby that mighty warrior sleeping upon a radiant bed.
Out of anger, the son of Droṇa struck the sleeping one with his foot; having been awakened by that kick from his bed, he then rose up. (79)
Then the hero beheld the son of Droṇa standing before him; the powerful son of the preceptor Droṇa [beheld] him leaping up from his bed.
Having seized him by the hair, Dhṛṣṭadyumna crushed him against the surface of the earth with his two arms; thus crushed by him, he was then overcome with fear.
Blinded by sleep, he was unable to struggle after being struck by a kick; then the son of Droṇa, having stepped upon his chest and bound his neck with bowstrings, [strangled him]. (82)
He killed him as he was roaring and quivering like a sacrificial animal, and in that same manner, he likewise slew all of his troops.
[He struck] Yudhāmanyu of great heroism and likewise Amūrtarajas of supreme energy, as well as the sons of Draupadī and the remaining Somakas.
With his sword, he slew many others led by Śikhaṇḍin, as well as all the soldiers who had fled through the gates out of fear of him. (85)
Both Kṛtavarman and Kṛpa brought death [to their foes]; thus was that camp, its army destroyed, [overcome] by those of great strength. 86.
At that moment, the three worlds became empty as if at the time of universal dissolution; having thus slain them all, the three, headed by Droṇa’s son, [remained]. (87)
Terrified and overcome with fear of Pārtha, they all departed from that camp; moving swiftly, they fled each toward a different region. || 88 ||
Then, O Brahmins, the son of Droṇa went to the delightful bank of the Revā, where indeed thousands of sages, exponents of the Vedas, resided.
Engaging in conversation about meritorious matters, they performed unsurpassed austerities; then, the son of Droṇa proceeded there among the hermitages of the sages.
As soon as he had entered, the sages who discourse on Brahman, having learned of the son of Droṇa’s evil deed through the power of yoga, spoke to him.
O son of Droṇa, you are a sinful evoker of battle while asleep, the lowest of Brahmins; indeed, by the mere sight of you, our downfall becomes certain. (92)
"Merely by conversing with you, ten thousand murders of Brahmins would occur; therefore, O lowest of men, depart from our hermitages! (93)
Thus did the sages and twice-born ones present there speak to the son of Droṇa at that time; having been addressed in this way by the sages who discourse upon Brahman, the son of Droṇa then [acted].
Ashamed, he departed from that hermitage frequented by sages; in this manner, he proceeded to the holy pilgrimage sites such as Kāśī and others.
Reproached everywhere by all those high-souled twice-born ones, he sought refuge with Vyāsa, desiring to perform an act of atonement.
Then, having approached the great sage Dvaipāyana as he was seated in the Badarika forest, he bowed down with devotion.
Then the sage Vyāsa said to this son of Droṇācārya: "O son of Droṇa, depart from our hermitage with all haste. (98)

"By the sin of killing one who was asleep, you have become a perpetrator of a great crime (mahāpātakin). Therefore, from conversing with you, a great sin will accrue to me. Thus addressed, the sage Droṇaputra then spoke these words: [99]
Aśvatthāman said: "O Blessed One, censured by all, I have come to you for refuge. (100)
If even you speak thus, who else could be my refuge? O Brahman, show compassion toward me; the virtuous are affectionate toward the distressed.

"O Blessed One, please prescribe an expiation for me to pacify the sin of killing one who was asleep; for you are omniscient. Having been addressed thus by the son of Droṇa, Vyāsa meditated for a long time and then spoke to him.
Vyāsa said: For the pacification of this sin, there is indeed no expiation prescribed in the Smṛtis.
Nevertheless, I shall describe a means for the pacification of this fault of yours: at the meritorious Rāmasetu in the southern ocean, which bestows liberation.
O son of Droṇa, there is a most excellent sacred site known as Dhanuṣkoṭi; it is supremely meritorious and the destroyer of great sins.
It bestows heaven and liberation upon men, purifies even the sin of killing a Brahmin, is the most auspicious among all auspicious things, and grants all desired objects.
It is the purifier of purifiers and the most excellent among holy places; it is meritorious, destroying evil dreams and annihilating the sufferings of hell.
It pacifies untimely death for men, increases their victory, destroys the poverty of men, and is the cause of increasing their lifespan.
Having gone there to Dhanuṣkoṭi on Rāmasetu, which bestows purity of mind upon men, grants peace and self-restraint, and is the giver of liberation; (9)
"O son of Droṇa, perform an uninterrupted bath for one full month; you shall immediately be purified from the sin of killing one who was asleep. (110)
"O son of Droṇa, quickly carry out my word. Thus was the son of Droṇa addressed at that time by Vyāsa, the supreme ṛṣi.
Having reached Rāmasetu, the sanctifying Dhanuṣkoṭi, he bathed there continuously for one month according to the prescribed ritual resolve (saṃkalpa).
Day after day, he worshipped Rāmanātha at the three junctions of the day. Then, on the thirtieth day, due to bathing in water, the son of Droṇa [was cured].
Then, at Dhanuṣkoṭi, Droṇa’s son recited the five-syllabled mantra and observed a fast on that day.
He kept a vigil at night in the presence of Rāmanātha; on the following day, having bathed at Dhanuṣkoṭi according to the prescribed ritual resolve (saṃkalpa), || 15 ||
Having praised Rāmanātha with devotion, he served him; drenched in tears of joy, he danced before Śambhu.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, appeared before him; seeing Mahādeva there, he praised the Supreme Lord.
The son of Droṇa said: "Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Śaṅkara, the mine of compassion; whose lotus feet act as a boat for those submerged in the ocean of calamity."
O Mahādeva, embodiment of compassion, Dhūrjaṭi, Nīlalohita; O beloved of Umā, Virūpākṣa, Moon-crested One, salutations to you! || 19 ||
O Conqueror of Death, O Three-eyed One, protect me with your compassionate glance! To you, Śambhu, the Lord of Pārvatī and the Destroyer of Tripura; [salutations]. (12)
Salutations again and again to you, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the three-eyed one; O you who are adorned with the ornaments of great serpents such as Ananta serving as necklaces!

"O Trident-bearer, salutations to you! O Gaṅgādhara, O Mṛḍa, O Immutable One! Protect me, O Lord, by your grace from this cage of accumulated sins. Thus praised, Mahādeva, being delighted, spoke to the son of Droṇa.
Mahādeva said: "Your sin of killing one who was asleep is [removed] by immersion at Dhanuṣkoṭi."
"Aśvatthāman has perished; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows! When I am pleased, what could possibly be unattainable for men in the worlds? (24)
"Therefore, O son of Droṇa, choose now from me whatever you desire. Thus addressed by Śambhu, the son of Droṇa spoke to that Supreme Lord.
"O Maheśvara, by the sight of you today, I have attained my life's purpose; the vision of you is unattainable for those devoid of merit, even through ten million births. (26)
Therefore, let there be unwavering devotion toward your lotus feet; grant me this very boon, O Śambhu—salutations be unto you! (27)
Having said "So be it" to the son of Droṇa, Maheśvara, the God of gods, vanished right there while the son of Droṇa was looking on.
O best of Brahmins, even Aśvatthāman was instantly cleansed of sin and rendered stainless merely by bathing at Rāmacandra-dhanuṣkoṭi.
Then all the great seers accepted this son of Droṇa, who had shaken off his sins, as pure and stainless from that time forward.
Thus, O Brahmins, has been narrated to you the liberation of the son of Droṇa from sin, occurring solely through the power of bathing at Rāmacandra-dhanuṣkoṭi.
Whoever should read this chapter or listen to it with a concentrated mind, having shaken off their sins in this world, shall be glorified in the realm of Śiva.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Pacification of the Sin of Killing Aśvatthāman While He Was Asleep," within the Praise of Dhanuṣkoṭi, in the Setumāhātmya, in the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
The venerable Sūta said: O residents of the Naimiṣa forest, out of respect for you, I shall once again fully describe the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi.
A great king named Nanda, born of the Lunar dynasty, protected this earth as far as the oceans in accordance with righteousness.
He had a son known as Dharmagupta; having entrusted the burden of protecting the kingdom to his own son, Nanda [departed]. (3)
Having conquered his senses and subdued his appetite, he entered the penance grove; for when his father had gone to the penance grove, the king named Dharmagupta [ascended the throne]. (4)
Knowing the Dharma and devoted to statesmanship, he protected the earth; he worshipped the gods, led by Indra, with various kinds of sacrifices.
He gave wealth and many fields to the Brahmins; while that king ruled, all were devoted to their own duties.
No afflictions arising from thieves and the like occurred while he was there. Once, this Dharmagupta mounted an excellent horse.
O best of Brahmins, he entered the forest, eager for the pleasure of the hunt, while the quarters of the sky were filled with tamāla, tāla, hiṃtāla, and kurava trees.
He wandered in that forest, terrifying with lions and tigers, its quarters filled with the swelling resonance of swarms of intoxicated bees.
It was filled with ponds crowded with groves of lotuses, white lilies, night-blooming water-lilies, and blue lotuses, and it was graced by ascetics.
O Brahmins, as King Dharmagupta was wandering in that forest, night fell, its quarters shrouded in darkness.
The king also, having performed the evening twilight devotions while observing his religious vows, chanted the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, there in the forest.
While the prince was staying upon a certain tree out of fear of lions, tigers, and other beasts, a bear, tormented by the fear of a lion, then approached him.
A certain forest-dwelling lion pursued that bear; being chased by the lion, the bear climbed up a tree.
Having climbed that tree, the bear beheld the lord of the world, the high-souled one of great strength and prowess, stationed upon the tree. || 15 ||
Seeing the king, this forest-dwelling bear said: "O Indra among kings, do not fear; we two shall dwell here for the night."
The Great Being, possessing a massive body and bristling with great fangs, arrived at the foot of the tree like a most terrifying lion of Yama. (17)
"Enjoy half the night with sleep, being protected by me from the outset; then, O high-minded one, protect me while I am fast asleep for the remaining half of the night."
Having taken those words to heart while the son of Nanda was asleep, Hari said to the bear: "This king is asleep; let him be abandoned. (19)
O best of the twice-born, the bear, who knew the dharma, said to that lion: "O king of beasts, wanderer of the forest, you do not understand dharma. (20)
Indeed, for those who betray trust in this world, there are great sufferings; for the sin of those who harm their friends cannot be destroyed even by ten thousand sacrifices. (21)
Some atonement for sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa may somehow be found; however, the sin of those who betray the trusting shall not perish even in ten million births.
I do not consider Mount Meru to be a great burden on this earth; rather, I consider one who betrays trust to be a great burden in this world. (23)
When the bear had spoken thus, the lion then became silent; but once Dharmagupta had awakened, the bear went to sleep in the tree.
Then the lion said to the king, "Give this bear to me. When the lion had spoken thus, the king, without hesitation, [seized] the sleeping [bear].
He abandoned that bear, who had placed its head upon his own lap, onto the surface of the earth; then, as it was being cast down by the king, it clung to a tree with its claws.
By the power of his merit, the bear did not fall from the tree to the surface of the earth; that bear, approaching the king, spoke these words in anger: || 27 ||
O King, I am born of the lineage of Bhṛgu and am capable of assuming any form at will; known by the name Dhyānakāṣṭha, I have taken on the form of a bear.
"O King, because you have passed me by while I was sleeping and innocent, you shall therefore quickly wander about as a madman due to my curse, O lord of the earth. (29)
Having thus cursed the king, the sage then addressed the lion: "In former times, you were a great yakṣa named Nṛsiṃha, a minister of Kubera."
Once, having reached the Himavat mountain accompanied by your bride, you joyfully engaged in amorous play near the hermitage of Gautama out of ignorance.
Gautama also, having gone out from his hut by chance to gather sacrificial fuel, saw you naked and uttered a curse.
"Since you have stood naked today in my hermitage, therefore you shall become a lion this very day; of this there is no doubt. (33)
Thus, by the curse of Gautama, you who were formerly the Yakṣa named Bhadra, the minister of Kubera, attained the state of a lion in the past.
For Kubera is indeed virtuous in character, and his servants are likewise; therefore, for what reason do you kill me, a rishi who dwells in the forest? (35)
"O lord of beasts, I know all this here through meditation," said Dhyānakāṣṭha; and as soon as he had spoken, he quickly abandoned his lion-form.
Having assumed a divine yakṣa form as the attendant of Kubera, he approached the sage, who was like a wooden post in meditation, and spoke with palms joined in reverence and bowing low.
Today, O great sage, I have learned all that occurred previously; at the time of my cursing Gautama, he also spoke of the end of the curse.
"When you no longer have conversation with Dhyānakāṣṭha in the form of a bear, then, having shaken off your lion-nature, you will assume the form of a yakṣa. (39)
"Thus, O Brahmin, Gautama, the bull among sages, spoke to me: 'O great sage, today, through the destruction of my lion-nature, I recognize you. (40)
"O you who are called Dhyānakāṣṭha, pure and always assuming any form at will"—having spoken thus and bowed to him, that king of the Yakṣas [departed]. (41)
Having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he departed for the city of Alakā; but when that lord of the Yakṣas had gone, the great sage Dhyānakāṣṭha remained.

When that sage, who could assume any form at will, had ascended to the highest state of meditation, he proceeded across the earth according to his desire, moving with unimpeded progress wherever he wished.
Due to the sage’s curse regarding the protection of the Dharma, he went to the city as a madman; seeing that best of kings in the form of a madman, the ministers [acted]. (44)
They led him to his father’s presence on the delightful bank of the Revā river and informed him of his son's loss of mental composure.

Having learned the news concerning his son, Nanda, his father, then quickly took his son and went into the presence of Jaimini; he reported the account of his son's situation to him from the very beginning.
"O Blessed One Jaimini, my son has fallen into madness today. || 47 ||
"O Great Sage, tell me the means for the destruction of this madness. Thus questioned, Jaimini, the bull among sages, meditated for a long time.
Having meditated for a very long time, he then spoke to King Nanda: "Indeed, by the curse of Dhyānakāṣṭha, your son has become insane. (49)
I shall tell you the means for the release from that curse: at the Setu on the southern ocean, which is meritorious and the destroyer of sins.
There is a most excellent holy place known as Dhanuṣkoṭi; it is the purest of the pure and the most auspicious of the auspicious. (51)
O Lord of the Earth, having brought your son there today, bathe him in that place which is established by the Vedas, which yields great merit, and which purifies even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
"His madness shall perish at that very moment; of this there is no doubt. Having been addressed thus, he bowed down to Jaimini, the bull among sages. (53)
Then Nanda, taking his son with him, went to Dhanuṣkoṭi; and there he bathed his son according to the prescribed rules.
Then, immediately upon merely bathing there, the son was freed from his madness; Nanda himself also bathed with devotion at Dhanuṣkoṭi.
Having stayed there for one day, the father, together with his son, then worshipped Rāmanātha, who is the embodiment of compassion and accompanied by Ambā.
Having taken leave of his son, Nanda departed for the forest to practice asceticism; O twice-born ones, when the father had gone, the son Dharmagupta also became king.
He devotedly bestowed vast amounts of wealth upon Rāmanātha; at that time, he gave money, grain, and lands to the Brāhmaṇas. || 58 ||
Immediately thereafter, he departed for his own city together with his ministers; he then ruled the kingdom, its thorns removed, with righteousness.

O Brahmins, Dharmagupta was exceedingly righteous and inherited [his position] from his father and grandfather; he protected men who were afflicted by madness, epilepsy, and evil planetary influences.
O best of Brahmins, even those who have been seized by [sin] become liberated here through immersion at Dhanuṣkoṭi; I tell you the truth, the absolute truth.
He who, having abandoned Dhanuṣkoṭi, should go to another holy place, is like one who, having discarded the milk of the *snuhī* plant, begs for the milk of a cow that has already been milked.

"O twice-born ones, those men who, wherever there may be a body of water, recite three times, 'Dhanuṣkoṭi! Dhanuṣkoṭi! Dhanuṣkoṭi!'—[they obtain the same merit as if they had bathed at Dhanuṣkoṭi]. (63)
All those men indeed bathe who shall go to the abode of Brahmā; thus, O Brahmins, has this auspicious story of Dharmagupta been told to you.
By the mere hearing of which the murder of a Brahmin perishes, and other accumulations of sin, such as the theft of gold and so forth, shall likewise be destroyed. (65)

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Dharmagupta’s Liberation from Madness," within the Praise of Dhanuṣkoṭi, in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: Once again I shall proclaim the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi—most exceedingly wonderful, secret, and the sole purifier of all the worlds.

In ancient times, a Brahmin named Parāvasu, the most learned in the Vedas, killed his father through ignorance and incurred the sin of brahmin-slaughter (brahmahatyā). He too, having bathed at Dhanuṣkoṭi, was instantly liberated from that fault.
The sages said: "O Sūta, how did Parāvasu previously kill his father?"
Or how did his liberation from the tip of the bow come about, O Sage? You ought to explain this in detail to us who are full of faith. (4)
Śrī Sūta said: There was a king named Bṛhaddyumna, a universal monarch (cakravartin) of great strength, who protected the earth bounded by the oceans according to righteousness.
He performed a sacrificial session (sattra-yajña) for the gods, with Indra at their head; his officiating priest was the learned and most righteous Raibhya.
He had two sons, Arvāvasu and Parāvasu, both of whom were learned in the Vedas along with their six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga) and were experts in the rituals prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
He was a scholar in the systems of Kaṇāda and Jaimini, as well as in Sāṃkhya and the works of Vyāsa, in the treatise of Gautama and the science of Yoga, and in the grammar of Pāṇini.
Expert in the Smṛtis of Manu and others, and proficient in all the Śāstras, they were requested by Bṛhaddyumna to serve as assistants at the Sattra sacrifice.
Permitted by their father Raibhya, the two brothers went to the sacrificial session of Bṛhaddyumna, appearing like the two Aśvins in bodily form.
Raibhya remained in the hermitage together with his eldest daughter-in-law; those two brothers went there to the king’s unsurpassed sacrificial session.
The two brothers, Yāja and Yāmā, performed the sacrifice for the great king Bṛhaddyumna; there was no lapse by the brothers in the sacrificial rites along with their constituent parts.
While this sacrificial session of King Bṛhaddyumna was being continuously performed, all the sages, invited by the king, arrived to witness it.
Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Atri, Jābāli, and Kaśyapa; Kratu, Dakṣa, Pulastya, Pulaha, and the sage Nārada. (14)
Mārkaṇḍeya, Śatānanda, Viśvāmitra, Parāśara, Bhṛgu, Kutsa, Vālmīki, Vyāsa, Dhaumya, and others as well. (15)
Surrounded by many disciples and numerous grand-disciples beyond counting, King Bṛhaddyumna beheld them as they arrived.
He respectfully honored all the sages with offerings of water for the feet and other honors; they had arrived from various directions accompanied by fourfold armies.
The kings, accompanied by their attendants, arrived with great respect to witness the sacrifice; likewise, the Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and all four castes gathered together.
Then those in the stages of studentship, householders, forest-dwellers, and mendicants came to witness the sacrifice of that Bṛhaddyumna.
That best of kings honored them all according to their merit, and he gave food to everyone, including ghee, soups, and other such items. || 20 ||
And with garments, gold, and numerous necklaces and jewels, the king thus honored those who had assembled at the sacrifice.
Then, O brahmins, Raibhyaputra and the two, Arvāvasu and Parāvasu, performed the sacrificial rites and other rituals without any error.
Seeing that skill of the two sons of Raibhya, all the sages, headed by Vasiṣṭha, then praised it while nodding their heads.
Having performed certain rites there at the conclusion of the third libation, Parāvasu went to inspect the household duties.
O twice-born ones, at evening he departed for his own hermitage even without Arvāvasu; at that moment, Raibhya was seen covered in a black antelope skin.
Seeing his father wandering in the forest at night, in a dense and blinding darkness, he—clouded by sleep—mistook him for a deer.
Thinking, "This is a deer coming to kill me," that Parāvasu slew his own father in the great forest.
O Brahmins, desiring to protect his own body, he, having committed a great sin, unintentionally killed his father during the night.
Having approached him, he beheld him slain; recognizing his own father, he grieved at night with his senses deeply distressed.
Then, having performed all the funeral rites for his father, Parāvasu once again returned to the king’s sacrificial session.
He then related all his own deeds to his younger brother; upon hearing that his father was dead, he too became overwhelmed with grief. (31)
Then, O best of the twice-born, the elder brother spoke these words to his younger brother: "A great sacrificial session has been commenced by King Bṛhaddyumna. (32)
This child of yours lacks the capacity to carry out this task; moreover, his father was killed by me at night under the mistaken belief that he was a deer.
An expiation must be performed for the purification of the murder of a Brahmin; O dear youngest brother, perform the observance of a vow for my sake.
"I am capable of bearing the burden of the sacrificial rite alone," said Arvāvasu; thus addressed by his elder brother, he [the elder] assented to him.
"Let it be so; as the elder, I shall perform the supreme vow for the sake of purification from the slaughter of a Brahmin. You, however, take up the burden of the sacrificial session. (36)
Having spoken thus, the younger brother departed from that sacrificial session for his elder; once he had gone, the elder performed the ritual acts at that sacrifice.
O twice-born ones, even though he was the youngest, having performed the vow for the slaying of a Brahmin for twelve years, he returned again with joy to this sacrificial session.
Seeing his brother, the elder brother said to Bṛhaddyumna: "This Arvāvasu, a slayer of a Brahmin, has come to your sacrifice."
"O best of kings, drive him away quickly from this sacrificial session; otherwise, there will be a loss of the fruit of the satra sacrifice. (40)
Thus addressed by his own servants, he caused the king to be removed from the sacrifice. As he was being removed, Arvāvasu then spoke to the king: ||| 41 ||
"O sinless Bṛhaddyumna, this killing of a Brahmin was not committed by me; rather, O Lord, that killing of a Brahmin was indeed committed by my elder brother. (42)
"The vow for the slaying of a Brahmin has now been performed by me for that purpose. Even though addressed with these words by Parāvasu, the king— || 43 ||
Having been quickly expelled from his own sacrificial session by the Brahmins, who cried out "Fie upon him!", Arvāvasu then departed silently for the forest.
Having approached a penance grove crowded with throngs of sages, Arvāvasu performed austerities that are extremely difficult even for the gods to accomplish.
Performing penance, he thus worshipped the Sun with a concentrated mind; and by his great austerity, the Sun himself, whose intellect is pure, appeared before him in embodied form.
The Sun, the witness of actions, the eye of the world, and the leader of the gods, appeared with his own radiance, illuminating the surface of the earth. (47)
The gods appeared, placing the Lord of Śacī at their head; then, O twice-born ones, Indra and the other deities spoke to Arvāvasu.

O Arvāvasu, you are preeminent through austerity, through the practice of celibacy, through proper conduct, through sacred learning, and through instruction in the Vedas, Shastras, and other sciences. (49)
Although you have been greatly insulted by Parāvasu, you do not become angry because you are endowed with forgiveness. (50)

"O high-minded one, since it was Jyeṣṭha who killed our father, you have not committed the act of violence; therefore, you have performed the vow for the killing of a Brahmin for that very purpose. (51)
"Therefore, we accept you, but we reject Parāvasu. Having spoken thus, all the inhabitants of heaven, headed by Indra, [did so]. (52)
They chose him as their priest and dismissed Parāvasu; then Indra and the other gods again placed Divākara at their head.
They said this to Arvāvasu: "Choose a boon. And he, in turn, requested the restoration of Janaka to life.
"And let there be no remembrance among the gods of the slaying of yourself or of your father. "So be it," the gods replied, and then they spoke these words again: || 55 ||
"And we shall grant you another boon; choose it, O high-minded one. Being thus addressed by the gods, Arvāvasu spoke:
"O dwellers of the celestial abode, let my brother Arvāvasu be free from guilt. Having heard these words, the gods spoke again:
For Parāvasu, there was great sin due to the killing of his brahmin father; indeed, [the sin] of a crime committed by one person cannot be incurred by another who merely carried it out. (58)
Peace may be attained through expiation for the five great sins; however, there is absolutely no atonement for the father who has killed a Brāhmaṇa.
"Even by the vow performed by yourself, your evil deed is not removed; therefore, there is no atonement for your brother Parāvasu. (60)
Therefore, it is not possible for us to grant him freedom from fault; Arvāvasu, however, spoke again to the gods led by Indra. (61)
Nevertheless, O best of the gods, by virtue of your greatness and through your grace, [I shall tell you] concerning my father, the slayer of the brahmin, and my brother.
"Tell me how there may be atonement; speak thus, endowed with compassion. Having heard these words of Arvāvasu, the inhabitants of the celestial abode [replied].
Having meditated for a very long time and reached a firm conclusion, they said this: "We shall tell you a means that will ward off that sin."
In the meritorious southern ocean, at Rāmasetu which grants liberation, there is a holy place renowned as Dhanuṣkoṭi, which bestows emancipation.
It destroys the sins of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, violating the teacher’s bed, and even the fault of associating with those who have committed such acts.
Even one who bathes without desire [for reward] obtains that which bestows the fruit of liberation, destroys evil dreams, brings fortune, and eliminates the sufferings of hell. (67)
This [practice] grants the ultimate goal and is the cause for attaining states such as Kailāsa; it fulfills all desires for men and destroys debt and poverty. (68)
By the mere utterance of "Dhanuṣkoṭi, Dhanuṣkoṭi, Dhanuṣkoṭi," it bestows heaven and liberation upon men and grants the fruit of great merit. (69)
If your brother Parāvasu goes there and bathes, at that very moment your elder brother shall be liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
"This very great secret expiation has been proclaimed. Having spoken thus to Arvāvasu, the gods departed toward their own city.
Then Arvāvasu, taking his elder brother Parāvasu with him, went to Rāmacandradhanuṣkoṭi, which bestows liberation. 72.
Having made a solemn resolve at Setu according to the prescribed rules, Parāvasu bathed at Dhanuṣkoṭi together with his brother for the purification of his sin.
To him, who had arisen after bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi, an incorporeal voice spoke: "O Parāvasu, the sin born of your father's killing of a Brahmin has been destroyed."
"The murder of a Brahmin is most terrible, causing the suffering of hell"—having said this, that incorporeal voice then ceased.
Then, O Brahmins, Parāvasu, accompanied by his younger brother, bowed with devotion to Rāmacandradhanuṣkoṭi.
Having bowed with devotion before the great god Rāmanātha, O brahmins, he was freed from his sins and proceeded to his father’s hermitage.
Then Raibhya, having risen from death and seeing his two sons reunited, remained in his own hermitage with a heart full of contentment because of his two sons.
Then all the sages accepted this Parāvasu, whose sins had been destroyed by bathing at Rāmacandra-dhanuṣkoṭi.
Thus, O best of sages, the liberation of Parāvasu from the sin of killing a Brahmin was accomplished for you all merely by bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi.
O Brahmins, sins such as the drinking of liquor and the like are surely destroyed by immersion here; truly, truly, and again truly, I speak while raising my arm. (91)
And multitudes of great sins shall perish by bathing here for one who recites this chapter, which grants liberation from the murder of a Brahmin. (82)
The sin of killing a Brahmin would perish at that very moment; of this there is no doubt. Even the drinking of liquor and other such sins would quickly attain pacification for him.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Liberation of Parāvasu from the Sin of Brahmin-Slaughter," within the "Praise of Dhanuṣkoṭi" in the "Setu-māhātmya" of the third section, the Brahma-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: O best of beings, I shall again relate this history which extols Dhanuṣkoṭi, consisting of the dialogue between a jackal and a monkey.
In former times, there were two—a jackal and a monkey—both of whom remembered their past lives; even in their previous human existence, they had been friends.
Having entered other wombs—namely those of a jackal and a monkey—the two, O twice-born ones, both became friends, the jackal and the monkey. (3)
Once, having observed a jackal situated on the ground of Rudra in the middle of a cremation ground, the monkey spoke, recollecting his former birth.

The monkey said: "O jackal, what terrible sin did you commit in the past, that you eat corpses, putrid-smelling, and loathsome things in the cremation ground? Thus addressed by the monkey, the jackal spoke to him. (5)
The jackal said: "In a previous birth, I was indeed a Brāhmaṇa who had mastered the Vedas."
In that birth, I was a learned man named Vedaśarman, purified by the performance of all ritual acts; yet, having made a promise to a brahmin, I did not fulfill it.
"O monkey, that wealth was given [to me] at that time, and consequently I became a jackal; for that very reason, I eat such utterly contemptible food as this. (8)
Those evil-minded men who, having given their word, do not grant what was promised, O monkey, attain the most contemptible birth of a jackal.
He who, having given his promise, does not give—whether it be little or much—all his hopes perish, just as the procreation of a eunuch.
But if one promises to a Brāhmaṇa and does not give, O monkey, the merit accumulated over ten lifetimes perishes at that very moment. (11)
The sin that arises from failing to give after having made a promise is not purified even by a hundred horse-sacrifices.
"I do not know when this sin might perish; therefore, a wise person should always give the promised object. (13)
By failing to give after having made a promise, one certainly becomes a jackal; therefore, a wise and learned person must indeed give what has been promised. 14.
Having spoken thus, that jackal addressed the monkey again: "What sin was committed by you, by which you attained the state of a monkey? (15)
"O monkey, you have harmed innocent forest-dwelling birds; tell me now of that sin which has granted you this state of being a monkey. Thus addressed by the jackal, the monkey spoke to the jackal.
The monkey said: "In a former birth, I was a brahmin known as Vedanātha."
Viśvanātha is my father and Kamalālayā is my mother; indeed, even in our previous birth, there was a friendship between us like that of two jackals.
"You do not know all of that, but I know it through the weight of my merit; for in the past, having propitiated Giriśa through austerity, I obtained it by his grace. (19)
"Furthermore, past and future consciousness exists even in another birth; O jackal, in that very life, a vegetable was stolen by me from a Brāhmaṇa. (20)
Due to that sin, he was born as a monkey following his experience in hell; the wealth of a Brahmin must not be seized, for from such seizure, hell results.
Immediately thereafter, one will become a monkey; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, a wise person should never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa.
No sin exists that is greater than the seizure of a Brahmin’s property; poison kills only the one who has drunk it, but a Brahmin’s property consumes the entire family.
A sinner who seizes the property of a Brāhmaṇa is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells; afterwards, by the remainder of his karmic debt, he enters the womb of a female monkey.
The property of a Brahmin must not be seized; therefore, one should always be patient toward them. They may be children, poor, wretched, or devoid of knowledge of the Vedas and Shastras. (25)
Brahmins must not be disregarded, for if they are enraged, they are like fire; I possess knowledge of the past and the future, and I am aware of everything regarding the jackal.
"I do not possess that single knowledge which purifies this sin; for even though you are one who remembers past births, you do not perceive what is yet to come. (27)
Even regarding the past, you, being one who knows only a little, are subject to limitations; therefore, you do not know everything that has occurred or will occur.
For how long must we endure such calamity, devoured by this jackal? Who indeed shall be our deliverer from this sinful one? (29)
O twice-born ones, while the monkey and the jackal were thus conversing there, by chance, through the conjunction of destiny, and by the power of their former merit—
Then that sage named Sindhudvīpa, possessed of great luster, arrived; his entire body was smeared with ashes and his forehead was marked with the triple-line (tripuṇḍra).

The jackal and the monkey said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, O great sage Siṃhadvīpa! (33)
Protect us both with your compassionate gaze; look upon us repeatedly with joy, so that our state as a monkey and a jackal may perish. (34)
Tell us that means today, for you are the best among the meritorious, [to save] people who are helpless, miserable, ignorant, children, and afflicted by disease. (35)

"The virtuous always protect [others] out of compassion, remaining free from self-interest. Thus addressed by those two, the wise great sage Sindhudvīpa, having meditated for a long time within his mind, spoke to the monkey and the jackal.
Sindhudvīpa said: "I know you both well, O jackal and monkey! (37)
O jackal, in a previous birth you were indeed a twice-born man named Vedaśarman; having promised an āḍhaka of grain to a brāhmaṇa, you [failed to give it]. (38)
Because that wicked man did not give [the gift], he attained the womb of a jackal; and you, O monkey, were previously a twice-born named Vedanātha.
"Because you stole vegetables from the house of a Brahmin through theft, you have attained this birth as a female monkey, which strikes fear into all birds. (40)
I shall declare a means for the pacification of your sins: you two must go to Rāmadhanuṣkoṭi on the southern ocean.

"Go there and perform a bath; by that, you two shall be liberated from sin. In ancient times, the Brahmin Sumati, having drunk liquor due to association with a Kirāti woman, was liberated from that sin after bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi. (42)
The jackal and the monkey said: "Whose son was this Sumati, and how did he drink liquor? (43)
O great-minded one, how did you become attached to Kirātī in Siṃhadvīpa? Out of compassion, please tell us this in detail now.
Sindhudvīpa said: In the land known as Mahārāṣṭra, there was a certain devout Brāhmaṇa, renowned by the name Yajñadeva, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
That Yajñadeva indeed had a son named Sumati, who was compassionate, hospitable to guests, and a worshiper of Śiva and Nārāyaṇa.
Abandoning both his parents and even his devoted wife, he departed for the land of Utkala, intent upon the company of libertines.
A certain Kirāti woman, dwelling in that region, was enchanting to the young; she captivated all the possessions of the youths and seized them for a long time. (48)
That Sumati, the lowest of Brahmins, went to her house; however, that Kirāti woman did not accept the impoverished twice-born man.
Then, abandoned by her, Sumati, intent solely on union with her, continuously stole many goods here and there.
Having given it, he took pleasure with her for a long time and ate in her house; and with a single cup, he drank wine together with her.
Thus, sporting with her for a very long time, he, afflicted by sensual desires, did not remember his parents nor his own wife.
Once, he went with some Kirātas to commit a robbery; those Kirātas went to the territory of the Lāṭas to seize wealth. (53)
In the house of a certain brahmin, that daring man, wearing the guise of a hunter (kairāta) and holding a sword in his hand, went to steal wealth.
Having slain the brahmin who was the master of that house with his sword, the reckless man took much wealth and went to the abode of the Kirāta woman.
As he went, the terrifying Brahmahatyā followed him—wearing blue garments, fearsome, and with hair that was intensely red.
Roaring with a loud laugh and making heaven and earth tremble, he wandered over the surface of the earth, pursued by her.
Wandering thus over the entire earth, Sumati once returned to his own village out of fear, O jackal and monkey! (58)
Pursued by her, he fled in fear toward his own home; the Brahman-slaughter also pursued him and went with him to his house. (59)
"Protect my father! Protect him! cried Sumati as she sought refuge. "Do not fear," her father said to her, and prepared to protect him; at that moment, this Brahmahatyā addressed her father. (60)
Brahmahatyā said: "O Yajñadeva, best of the twice-born, do not accept him."
He was a drinker of liquor, a thief, a slayer of a Brahmin, and a perpetrator of heinous crimes; he was a traitor to his mother, a traitor to his father, an abandoner of his wife, and a doer of evil.
"O twice-born one, I will not release him, for he has been corrupted by association with a Kirāta woman; O Brahmin, if you take this son of yours, who is a great sinner. (63)
"O twice-born one, I shall devour your wife, his wife, you, this son of yours, and your entire lineage; therefore, release this son!"

"If you abandon this son, I shall release you all at once; O high-minded one, you ought not to destroy your entire family for the sake of a single individual. Thus addressed by her, Yajñadeva then spoke to her:
Yajñadeva said: "Affection for my son torments me; how can I abandon him? Hearing those words spoken by the twice-born, Brahmanicide then addressed him.
Brahmahatyā said: "For this man has become fallen, excluded from the castes and stages of life. (67)
"Do not feel affection for this corpse; its sight is censurable. Having spoken thus, while Yajñadeva was looking on, that Brahmahatyā [the personified sin of killing a Brahmin] departed. || 68 ||
He struck his son, named Sumati, with the palm of his hand; the boy wept, repeatedly crying out to his father, "O father! O father! (69)
Then Janaka, his mother, and the wife of Sumati all wept. In the meantime, Durvāsas, born from a portion of Śaṅkara, arrived there.

Then, by destiny, the yogi arrived, O jackal and monkey; having seen that sage, an incarnation of Rudra, and having heard of him, Yajñadeva bowed down and sought refuge for the sake of his son. || 71 ||
The father said: "O Durvāsas, you are a great yogi, truly born from a portion of Śaṅkara himself."
The sight of you shall never be for those devoid of merit; my son was a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, and a thief. (73)
The sin of killing a Brahmin, which came to strike him, is now turned away; may this son of mine be liberated from the great transgression. (74)
This slaughter of a Brahmin is terrible; tell me now the means by which it may quickly come to an end. Have compassion for my son. (79)
"O Sage, this alone is my son; I have no other offspring. If he dies, my lineage will be utterly destroyed, root and branch. (76)
Consequently, one would certainly not even be able to offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors. Therefore, O Blessed Sage, show us your grace. (77)
Thus addressed, Durvāsas, the partial incarnation of Śaṅkara, then spoke after meditating for a very long time upon Yajñadeva, the best of the twice-born.
Durvāsas said: O Yajñadeva, a most cruel sin has been committed by your son; there shall be no pacification of this sin even through ten thousand expiatory rites.
Nevertheless, O twice-born one, listen with an undistracted mind as I shall declare an expiation for the pacification of this sin of your son. (80)
If your son bathes at the tip of Śrī Rāma’s bow in the southern ocean, he will be liberated from his sin in an instant.
O best of the twice-born, by bathing there, a brahmin named Durvinīta was instantly liberated from the sins of violating his guru’s wife.
This very tip of the bow of Śrī Rāghava, who is Hari himself, shall destroy the flood of sins of your son by the mere act of bathing in it. 83.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Means for Sumati’s Liberation from Great Sins," within the Dialogue between the Jackal and the Monkey, in the Praise of Dhanuṣkoṭi, in the Setumāhātmya, in the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Yajñadeva said: O sage Durvāsas, O one of great wisdom, O discerning knower of the higher and the lower, who is this person named Durvinīta who approached the wife of his preceptor?

Whose son was that twice-born man who, by bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi, was instantly liberated from the sin arising from approaching the wife of his preceptor? You ought to relate this to me in detail, for I am full of faith.
Durvāsas said: In ancient times, there was a certain highly learned Brāhmaṇa in the Pāṇḍya country.
His wife was named Ruci, and he was known by the name Idhmavāha; their son was a twice-born man named Durvinīta.
In his childhood, the father of this son died.
Having performed the funeral rites for his father, that Durvinīta—
For some time he lived at home with his widowed mother; then a twelve-year famine occurred due to the lack of rain.
Then, O best of the twice-born, he went to another country together with his mother; having reached Gokarṇa, which was well-supplied with stores of grain, he settled there.
He lived for a very long time together with his widowed mother; then, after a great deal of time had passed, Durvinīta departed.
Alas, through the ripening of past evil karma, his intellect is deluded; with his body pierced by the arrows of the bodiless god of love, his mind is distorted by passion. (9)
O best of the twice-born, that sinner, his soul deluded by lust, forcibly dragged away his mother as she cried out "Do not! and enjoyed her through sexual union.
Exhausted and ill-behaved after the emission of semen, he contemplated a sin in his mind and wept, deeply afflicted by grief.
"Alas! I am an evildoer, the foremost among great sinners, because I, driven by the arrows of desire, approached my mother. (12)
Having reflected thus in his mind, he, feeling self-reproach in the presence of that sage, spoke these words to those sages: || 13 ||
O twice-born ones, you who know the true essence of the scriptures, please tell me out of mere compassion the expiation for the sin of approaching the wife of one's guru. (14)
If there were a remedy for death, I would die without a doubt; as for the expiation that you have now prescribed for me— (15)
"O twice-born ones, I shall do that truly, whether it be death or something else. Having heard those words of his, some of the lords of sages there [spoke].
Having firmly resolved that conversing with him would lead to evil, some sages adopted silence, while others remained intensely still.
"You are evil-minded, a violator of your mother, the foremost among the great sinners! Go, go!"—thus did those best of the twice-born speak these words many times. (18)
Having restrained them, the compassionate and omniscient Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, a treasury of mercy, spoke there to Durvinīta.
Go quickly, O Mother, to Dhanuṣkoṭi on Rāmasetu, remaining there continuously for one month during the month of Māgha when the sun is situated in Capricorn.
"With your senses conquered, your anger subdued, and free from malice toward others, perform a ritual bath along with your mother for one month while remaining without food."
"You shall truly become purified from the fault of having approached your teacher's wife; for there is no sin that would not be destroyed by bathing at the Setu. (22)
In the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, the praise of Dhanuṣkoṭi is recounted in many ways as the destroyer of the five great sins. (23)
Therefore, go quickly with your mother to Dhanuṣkoṭi; O twice-born one, make my word authoritative, just like the word of the Vedas.
O son of a twice-born, for one who has bathed at the tip of Śrī Rāma’s bow, even ten million great sins (mahāpātakas) are as if not even to be noticed. || 25 ||
Another expiation has been declared in the Smṛti by Manu and others; therefore, go to Dhanuṣkoṭi, which destroys even the most heinous sins.
O best of the twice-born, having been thus addressed by Vyāsa, Durvinīta, together with his mother, bowed to Dhanuṣkoṭi and to Vyāsa, and then departed.

When the sun is situated in Capricorn during the month of Māgha, for the duration of that entire month, he remained continuously without food together with his mother, having conquered anger and subdued his senses.
He bathed at the tip of Śrī Rāma’s bow according to his resolve, and thrice daily he paid obeisance to Rāmanātha with devotion.
At the end of the month, having performed the breaking of his fast together with his mother, the man of purified intellect went once more to the presence of Vyāsa to report what had occurred to him.
Having bowed again to Vyāsa, Durvinīta spoke these words: || 31 ||

Durvinīta said: O Blessed One, ocean of compassion, greatest of sages Dvaipāyana! By your grace, together with my mother, I shall remain without food for one month at Rāma-dhanuṣkoṭi during the month of Māgha, remaining vigilant. (32)
"But I performed my ablutions while offering salutations to Maheśvara. From this point forward, O Vyāsa, O Blessed One, you who are kind to your devotees—" (33)
"O Sage, instruct me truly regarding that which ought to be done. Having heard these words of Durvinīta, Vyāsa, who is a portion of Nārāyaṇa, spoke to that Durvinīta.
Vyāsa said: "O ill-behaved one, the sin born of union with your mother has departed from you today."
And the sin of your mother, born from the cause of her union with you, has been destroyed; no doubt should be entertained here, for I have spoken the truth to you. (36)
All your kinsmen and relatives, as well as all the other Brahmins, will seize you along with your wicked daughter-in-law. (37)
By my grace, through bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi, you have become purified; having taken a wife, practice the dharma of the householder's life.
Abandon the harming of living beings and practice the eternal Dharma; constantly serve the virtuous with a mind endowed with devotion. (39)
Do not abandon your obligatory duties, foremost among which is the twilight worship; restrain the collection of your senses and worship Hara and Hari.
Do not speak ill of others, and never indulge in envy; seeing the prosperity of another, do not feel groundless distress. (41)
Always look upon the wives of others as your own mother; never forget the entirety of the Vedas you have studied.
Do not disregard guests; perform the ancestral rites on the day of the ancestors. Never, even in a dream, speak words of malice toward others. (43)
Constantly study the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, as well as the Vedānta and the Vedāṅgas.
O Hariśaṅkara, casting aside all shame, recite [the names] and perform the application of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing with ashes using the mantras of the Jābāla Upaniṣad.
Always wear rudrākṣas and be devoted to purity and right conduct; with tulasī and bilva leaves, worship both Nārāyaṇa and Hara.
O sir, you worship [the Lord] once, twice, or thrice a day, with offerings mixed with Tulasī leaves and sprinkled with water from His feet.
Always eat the food offered as naivedya before Śambhu and Nārāyaṇa; perform the offering known as vaiśvadeva for the purification of the food. 48.
He gratified with food the lords of ascetics established in Brahman who had come to his house, as well as other elders, the helpless, the sick, and celibate students.
Perform service to your mother and be devoted to the domestic fire; [recite] the great five-syllabled mantra conjoined with the syllable Om. (50)
In the same way, O twice-born one, recite the eight-syllable mantra as well as other mantras, remaining self-restrained and meditating upon the presiding deities of those mantras.
In this way, always practice those other dharmas taught in the Smṛtis; for you who have thus observed your vows, there will surely be liberation at the end of the body.
Thus addressed by the sage Vyāsa, Durvinīta bowed to him, performed everything as he was instructed, and attained liberation at the end of his body.
His mother also, having died in due time through immersion at Dhanuṣkoṭi, attained supreme liberation that grants freedom from rebirth. || 54 ||
Durvāsas said: Thus, O Yajñadeva, I have described to you the liberation of that ill-behaved one and his mother through the ablution at Dhanuṣkoṭi.
O Brahmin, you too, taking this son with you for the sake of purification from the sin of killing a brahmin, go quickly to Dhanuṣkoṭi, which bestows liberation.
Sindhudvīpa said: Having been addressed thus by Durvāsas, O Rāma, Yajñadeva took his own son and went to Dhanuṣkoṭi, which bestows liberation.
Having gone there, O jackal and monkey, that twice-born man, being self-restrained, made his dwelling for six months together with his son.
That son indeed bathed at Dhanuṣkoṭi for six months; at the end of those six months, an incorporeal voice spoke to Yajñadeva.
The sin of Brahman-slaughter of Yajñadeva, your son, has been liberated from the theft of gold, the drinking of liquor, and likewise from sexual union with a Kirāti woman.
For this son of yours is liberated from other sins as well; do not entertain any doubt, O Yajñadeva, best of the twice-born.
Having spoken thus, that bodiless voice then ceased; and Yajñadeva, having heard those words from the bodiless one, [listened].
Contented and accompanied by his son, he worshipped Rāmanātha and, together with his son, then paid homage to Dhanuṣkoṭi.
He departed for his own country, for his own village, and likewise for his own home; accompanied by his sons and wife, he lived happily for a very long time, perfectly at peace.
Sindhudvīpa said: "O jackal and monkey, I have thus related to you both the liberation of this Sumati, the son of Yajñadeva. (65)

"From great sins as well, by immersing oneself in Dhanuṣkoṭi; therefore, both of you go to Dhanuṣkoṭi for the purification of sin. Otherwise, the purification of sin would not occur even through ten thousand atonements. (66)
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having heard these words of Sindhudvīpa, [the sages spoke].
The jackal and the monkey quickly crossed the great highway; having reached Dhanuṣkoṭi with effort, they bathed in its waters.
Liberated from all sins, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot, those two of great splendor were showered with a rain of flowers by the gods.

Adorned with necklaces, armlets, crowns, bracelets, and other ornaments, and graced by two chowries being waved by celestial women, they went to the beautiful city of the gods and took their seats upon half of Indra’s throne.
The venerable Sūta said: Thus has this been told to you concerning both the jackal and the monkey.
O Brahmins, liberation from sin comes from immersing oneself in Dhanuṣkoṭi; likewise for one who listens to or even recites this chapter with devotion.
That man obtains the fruit born of bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi, and he swiftly attains even liberation, which is difficult for hosts of yogis to reach.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Jackal and the Monkey," within the "Praise of Dhanuṣkoṭi" section of the Setumāhātmya, in the third part (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 35 ||
Śrī Sūta said: O twice-born ones, I shall once again proclaim the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi, where one named Durācāra was liberated after bathing.
The sages said: O Sūta, who is this one named Durācāra, you who are skilled in the knowledge of ultimate reality? And what sin, indeed, was committed by that Durācāra, O sage?
Or how is one liberated from sin by immersing oneself in Dhanuṣkoṭi? O Sage, tell this in detail to us who are desirous of hearing it.
The venerable Sūta said: O sages, listen to the sin of that Durācāra and how he was liberated from that sin by bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi.
O twice-born ones, there is a certain sinful brahmin named Durācāra who dwells on the bank of the Gautamī; he is always devoted to cruel deeds.
O twice-born ones, being defiled by association with them, he then lived together with those who were slayers of Brahmins, drinkers of liquor, thieves, and violators of the preceptor’s bed.
O best of the twice-born, through association with those who commit great sins, this twice-born man's entire Brahminhood has indeed been destroyed without remainder due to that fault.
If a twice-born man should dwell respectfully for even a single day with those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), that very moment his [status] as a twice-born man is indeed lost.
A Brahmin’s fourth part perishes without a doubt from serving, touching, seeing, or lying down with [such a person] for two days.
O twice-born ones, by eating together in the same row as those who have committed great sins, the second part of a Brāhmaṇa’s merit is destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Within three days, one-third indeed perishes; of this there is no doubt. Within four days, one-fourth certainly goes to destruction.
But from this point forward, by sharing with them their beds, seats, and meals, one becomes a sinner equal to them due to the occurrence of a great sin (mahāpātaka).
Therefore, O twice-born ones, this man named Durācāra, who was devoid of Brahminhood, was seized by a powerful and terrifying Vetāla.
O Brahmins, being under the control of another and excessively tormented by that Vetāla, he wandered from country to country and from forest to forest.
By the ripening of his past merit and through the turn of fate, that twice-born man [reached] Rāmacandra-dhanuṣkoṭi, which destroys great sins.
Pursued by that Piśāca and possessed by him, O twice-born ones, he went forth; that Vetāla then submerged him in the waters of Dhanuṣkoṭi.
Having been cast into the waters of Dhanuṣkoṭi by that Vetāla, he rose up in an instant, released by the Vetāla.
Then that twice-born man, O Brahmins, rose from the waters of Dhanuṣkoṭi; feeling restored, he reflected: "What land is this on the shore of the ocean? (18)
"How have I come here as a resident of the banks of the Gautamī?"—thus troubled by this thought, he [approached] the one dwelling at Dhanuṣkoṭi.
Having approached and prostrated before the high-souled Dattātreya, the most excellent among the foremost of yogis, that man of wicked conduct addressed him.
"O Blessed One, I do not know which region this is; please tell me now, for I am indeed named Durācāra and have my dwelling on the banks of the Gautamī. (21)
"O Brahmin, please tell me by what means I have come here. Thus was the sage of firm vows questioned by that man of wicked conduct.
Having meditated for a moment, that treasury of compassion spoke to Durācāra: "O Durācāra, because of your former association with great sinners... (23)
Your Brahminhood was lost, and a Vetāla seized you; possessed by him, you have arrived here helpless and bewildered in mind. (24)
But here, the Vetāla submerged you in the waters of Dhanuṣkoṭi; by that mere immersion, you were liberated from sin.
But those men who perform a bath at the meritorious Dhanuṣkoṭi—for them, indeed, the accumulation of the five great sins truly perishes. (26)
Merely by bathing here at Rāmacandra-dhanuṣkoṭi, your fault arising from association with great sinners has gone to destruction.
Upon its destruction alone, the Vetāla released you and vanished; that Vetāla who seized you previously was once a Brāhmaṇa. (28)
In the month of Bhādrapada, during the dark fortnight, he joyfully performed the Mahālaya rite for the ancestors according to the Pārvaṇa procedure.
Because of that, he was cursed by his own ancestors and became a Vetāla; yet even he [was liberated] merely by beholding the tip of his bow.
Having abandoned his state as a vetāla here, he attained the world of Viṣṇu; therefore, one should perform the Mahālaya rite during the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
But those who, out of excessive greed, do not perform [the rites] intended for their own ancestors, being possessed of great avarice, will truly become vetālas; of this there is no doubt. (32)
Therefore, in the month of Bhādrapada, during the dark fortnight, those who, for the sake of their ancestors, according to their ability [feed] Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas— || 33 ||
Those who feed [the ancestors] with abundant food do not encounter an evil rebirth; this applies to one who performs the Mahālaya rite in the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
According to his own capacity, he should feed one, two, or three Brahmins; even if he is destitute, he should do so, for never shall he fall into misfortune.
Because he failed to perform the ancestral rites in the month of Bhādrapada, this Brahmin—who seized you, O sinner—became a Vetāla.
The period for the Mahālaya rite is said by the sages who perceive the truth to begin from the month of Bhādrapada and extend until the end of Vṛścika.
The month is Bhādrapada; even within that time, it is further distinguished. O Durācāraka, the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) therein is indeed most excellent.
In that auspicious dark fortnight, on the first lunar day, the man who performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha with devotion [attains the highest reward]. (39)
The Blessed One, the Purifier who sanctifies all, is pleased with him; he attains the world of Fire and rejoices together with Agni.
And to that mortal who does not perform the Mahālaya rite on the first lunar day, even the god Jvalana bestows all sovereignty.
If a Veda-knowing Brāhmaṇa eats on the first day of the Mahālaya festival, fire shall burn his house, as well as his prosperity, fields, and other possessions. || 42 ||
The ancestors attain satisfaction for ten thousand kalpas by one who performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha with devotion on the second lunar day.
The Blessed Lord Īśvara, the husband of Bhavānī, is pleased with him; he attains Kailāsa and rejoices together with Śiva.
Maheśvara, being pleased, would bestow vast prosperity upon that mortal who does not perform the Mahālaya rite on the second lunar day.
If Śambhu becomes angry with him, he will destroy his spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) and cast him into the hells known as Raurava and Kālasūtra. || 46 ||
When a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas has eaten on the second day of the Mahālaya, the ancestors attain satisfaction for twenty thousand kalpas. || 47 ||
Through the grace of the ancestors, his progeny increases; on the third lunar day, a man should devotedly perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha.
The Blessed One, the world-protector and lord of wealth, is pleased with him; indeed, the great treasures such as Mahāpadma and others come under his control.
The three gods who follow him are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; on the third lunar day, whatever mortal does not perform the Mahālaya rite [is lost].
The Lord Dhanada seizes his prosperity in an instant and bestows upon him poverty, which is filled with manifold sufferings.
On the third lunar day, whatever mortal performs the Mahālaya rite, his ancestors remain satisfied for thirty thousand kalpas.
On the fourth day, however, a man should perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha with devotion; for him, the Lord Heraṃba, the son of Pārvatī, is pleased.
His obstacles perish through the grace of the Elephant-faced One; yet that mortal who does not perform the Mahālaya rite on the fourth lunar day [shall suffer].
Indeed, the Lord Vighneśa always creates obstacles for him, and he then falls into the hell known as Caṇḍakolāhala.
On the fourth lunar day, the ancestors of that mortal who performs the Mahālaya rite remain greatly delighted for forty thousand kalpas.
They will grant many sons continuously to the performer of the śrāddha; yet he who, out of devotion, does not perform the Mahālaya on the fifth lunar day— || 57 ||
The divine Lakṣmī abandons his residence, and Alakṣmī, the source of strife, appears in his home. (58)
On the fifth lunar day, however, the mortal who performs the Mahālaya rite—his ancestors remain satisfied for five thousand kalpas.
Being satisfied, they will grant him an uninterrupted lineage, and Pārvatī, the bestower of great sovereignty, will be pleased with him.
On the sixth lunar day, a man should devoutly perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha; the Blessed Lord Ṣaṇmukha, the son of Pārvatī, is pleased with him.
By the grace of Ṣaṇmukha, his sons and grandsons are never at any time afflicted by the planets or the sub-planets (upagrahas).
If a man does not perform the Mahālaya rite with devotion on the sixth lunar day, Skanda Mahāsena will undoubtedly turn his face away from him.
As soon as his offspring emerges from the womb, it perishes; furthermore, it is constantly afflicted by hosts of seizing spirits such as the Pūtanās.
He who, being faithful, performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha on the sixth lunar day, falls downward into the hell known as Vahnijvālāpraveśa.
