For sixty thousand kalpas, the ancestors shall remain satisfied; they will even grant sons as well as abundant prosperity.
If a mortal performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha on the seventh lunar day, the Lord Āditya, the golden-handed one, is pleased with him.
By the grace of the Sun-god, one shall be free from disease and possess firm limbs; the Lord Hiraṇyapāṇi himself [bestows] gold with his own hand.
With a joyful mind, he grants [the fruit] to the performer of the Mahālaya Śrāddha; however, on the seventh lunar day, he who does not perform the Mahālaya with devotion [is deprived of it]. (69)
He is afflicted day and night by diseases such as consumption and other ailments, and he falls downward into the hell known as Tīkṣṇadhārāstraśayya.
If a man performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha with devotion on the seventh lunar day, his ancestors indeed remain gratified for seventy thousand kalpas.
The hosts of ancestors shall always grant an uninterrupted lineage; therefore, on the eighth lunar day, a mortal should perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha.
Śaṅkara, the wearer of the elephant hide who conquers death, is pleased with him; by the grace of Śaṅkara, liberation is held in his hand.
When the Three-eyed Lord himself is directly gratified by the Mahālaya Śrāddha, what could there be in the fourteen worlds that would be difficult for him to obtain? (74)
That fool-minded person who does not perform the Mahālaya rite on the eighth lunar day always sinks, suffering, into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra. || 75 ||
Never at any time on this earth does his desired object succeed; he falls into the hell named Vaitaraṇī until the moon and stars perish.
The man who, with faith, performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha on the eighth day—verily, his ancestors remain satisfied for eighty thousand kalpas.
They shall increase him with blessings, and his obstacles shall be dispelled; moreover, the hosts of ancestors shall always grant him an uninterrupted lineage.
On the ninth lunar day, if a mortal performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha, the divine Goddess Durgā, the consort of Śambhu, is pleased with him.
When satisfied, Durgā, the slayer of Mahiṣa, shall destroy consumption, epilepsy, leprosy, and others, as well as minor spirits such as pretas and piśācas.
On the ninth lunar day, however, the mortal who does not perform the Mahālaya rite shall be afflicted by epilepsy as well as by a Brahma-rākṣasa.
Furthermore, he would be incessantly oppressed by malevolent rites and spells; yet, on the ninth lunar day, that mortal who performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha— (82)
For ninety thousand kalpas, his ancestors indeed remain satisfied; moreover, the hosts of ancestors shall always grant him an uninterrupted lineage.
On the tenth lunar day, a mortal should perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha; on that day, the moon, possessing sixteen digits and filled with nectar, becomes propitious.
When this lord of herbs has been gratified by this śrāddha, the herbs shall always bestow grains such as rice and the like.
He who does not perform the unsurpassed Mahālaya rite on the tenth day—his medicinal herbs will be fruitless, and his agriculture as well will be fruitless.
If a mortal performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha on the tenth lunar day, his ancestors indeed remain satisfied for a hundred thousand kalpas.
The hosts of ancestors shall always grant him an uninterrupted lineage; on the eleventh day, a man should devotedly perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha.
Rudra, the destroyer of the entire world, becomes gracious toward him; through the grace of Rudra, the lord of the universe and the destroyer of all. (89)
This performer of the śrāddha rite continuously conquers his enemies; even ten thousand sins of killing a Brahmin perish for him at that very moment.
A man who, out of devotion, does not observe the Mahālaya vow on the Ekādaśī day, fails to obtain the full fruit of sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma.
Rudra indeed turns his face away from him and is never pleased; for his enemies, increasing on all sides, oppress him.
Sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, performed with abundant sacrificial fees, would indeed be fruitless for him, like oblations cast upon ashes.

Due to the fault of not performing the śrāddha, one becomes equal to a Brahmahatyā-vātaka (one who has committed the sin of killing a Brahmin). However, he who performs the Mahālaya-śrāddha on the lunar day of Ekādaśī [is freed from that]. || 94 ||
Indeed, his ancestors remain satisfied for two hundred thousand kalpas, and the hosts of ancestors shall always grant him an uninterrupted lineage.
If a mortal performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), Janārdana, the Lord of Lakṣmī himself, becomes pleased with him.
When Janārdana, the Lord of gods and God of gods, is pleased, the entire world of moving and unmoving beings is undoubtedly pleased as well. 97.
The earth, beloved of Hari, causes his crops to flourish; and Lakṣmī, the consort of Hari, increases in his residence.
The mace named Kaumodakī, which rests in the hand of Nārāyaṇa, always destroys spirits such as those causing epilepsy and other ailments. (99)
Likewise, his sharp-edged discus burns his enemies, while his conch shell drives away the Yātudhānas, Piśācas, and other such beings. (100)
In this way, Keśava wards off all suffering for him; O virtuous man, he who does not perform the Mahālaya rite on the twelfth day [is deprived of this].
His fields and his prosperity will undoubtedly perish; likewise, afflictions such as epilepsy and other spirits, as well as enemies of great strength, shall prevail. (2)
Yātudhānas indeed afflict him who is averse to Viṣṇu, and he is cast even into the hell named Asthibhedana.
He who, endowed with devotion, performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha on the twelfth lunar day, his ancestors indeed remain gratified for six hundred thousand kalpas.
The ancestors also grant him an uninterrupted lineage; therefore, on the thirteenth lunar day, a man should devotedly perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha.
The Blessed Lord Kandarpa, the leader of Rati, is pleased with him; as are garlands, sandalwood, and other enjoyments, as well as charming women.
By the grace of Kāmadeva, all his goals are always accomplished; from birth until the end of death, he experiences only happiness.
He who does not perform [the rites] on the thirteenth day, nor the Mahālaya Śrāddha—Kāmadeva turns his face away from him and shall destroy his women and enjoyments.
He who performs the Mahālaya rite on the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) for the sake of his ancestors causes that person to fall into the hell known as Aṅgāraśayyābhramaṇa.
For a thousand times a thousand kalpas, his ancestors indeed remain gratified; then the hosts of ancestors shall grant him an unbroken lineage.
On the fourteenth day, a person should perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha with devotion; for the granting of his desires, the Blessed Lord Śiva remains awake.
Having imparted the knowledge of Śiva, he even grants union with him; [he destroys] even ten thousand acts of drinking liquor, as well as ten thousand acts of stealing gold.
They perish at that very moment from the Mahālaya on the fourteenth day; even the fault of association with Caṇḍālas, Vṛṣalas, and women is destroyed.
Through the Mahālaya rite on the fourteenth day, there shall be the abundant attainment of the fruits of a thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices and ten thousand Pauṇḍarīka sacrifices.
He who does not perform this Mahālaya Śrāddha on the fourteenth day shall [suffer] for a thousand crores of kalpas as well as a hundred crores of kalpas.
He would fall into the great blind well of saṃsāra from which there is no deliverance, even without having stolen gold or drunk liquor. (16)
That person of deluded intellect is tainted by faults such as the drinking of liquor; likewise, even sacrifices performed according to the prescribed rules become fruitless.
Whoever performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha on the fourteenth lunar day (Caturdaśī) gains [the merit of] thousands of lakṣas and koṭis, and hundreds of lakṣas and koṭis.
His ancestors remain satisfied for kalpas; of this there is no doubt. Even those ancestors dwelling in hell go to heaven, filled with great joy.
Then the hosts of ancestors shall grant him an uninterrupted lineage; therefore, on the new moon day (Amāvāsyā), a man should devotedly perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha.
The satisfaction of his ancestors shall be infinite; there is no doubt about this. It will indeed be like the satisfaction that the gods experience in heaven upon tasting the nectar of immortality.
Such infinite satisfaction arises from the Mahālaya rite on the new moon day (amāvāsyā). The new moon day is immensely meritorious and is saluted by the ancestors and the gods.
For she is peaceful and the supreme, most beloved consort of Śiva; during the Mahālaya Śrāddha, one should feed those who are most learned in the Vedas at her [shrine].
By that, the ancestors shall attain infinite satisfaction, and Śiva is pleased; the five great sins, such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, shall meet their destruction. || 24 ||
All sacrifices would have been performed according to the injunctions with their proper sacrificial fees, and all eternal duties would have been practiced in accordance with the prescribed rules.
He who performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha on the day of the new moon, having realized his identity with the inward-facing Brahman, attains union (sāyujya) without a doubt. || 26 ||
If an unintelligent person does not perform the Mahālaya rite on the new moon day, his ancestors, even if they have reached the world of Brahmā, fall into hell.
The continuity of this deluded person would indeed be severed at that very moment; for that alone is a great calamity when men [die] on an inauspicious lunar day (amāyā-tithi).
O best of Brahmins, if those entitled to the Mahālaya rite are not fed according to the rules when the month of Bhādrapada has arrived, the ancestors and deities dance [in anger]. (29)
"Let my sons feed the best of the twice-born on our behalf; by that, the terrible suffering of hell shall not befall us. (130)
And there shall be residence in the heavenly world as long as the moon and stars endure; when the month of Bhādrapada arrives, it bestows satisfaction upon the ancestors.
One should feed a single Brahmin every day with devotion; thus, the ancestors born of the families of one's father and mother shall attain satisfaction.
Especially during the dark fortnight, the wise man should feed Brahmins with grains, ghee, soups, and other foods, preceded by an oil massage.
Beginning from the seventh day of the dark fortnight, men who perform this every day will cause their ancestors to drink nectar with great joy for an entire kalpa.
On the new moon day, one should honor and feed three Brahmins at each meal; beginning from the twelfth lunar day, however, one must certainly feed three Brahmins every day.

Otherwise, there would be a loss of sovereignty and one would become subject to great poverty; therefore, abandoning greed for wealth, one should honor the Brahmins with soup, clarified butter, and other offerings.
With milk, with milk-rice, with curds, cakes, and the like, as well as with various kinds of drinks, things to be licked, things to be sucked, and things to be chewed; (37)
One should feed the foremost among those learned in the Vedas so that they may be satisfied; by that, Brahmā, Hari, and Śambhu will be satisfied—of this there is no doubt. (38)
The ancestors, such as the Agniṣvātta-s, as well as the deities, such as Indra—what need is there to say more? By him, the three worlds were satisfied.
One should perform the Mahālaya śrāddha according to the Pārvaṇa rite; in the Mahālaya śrāddha, a man [honors] the ancestors of his paternal lineage just like the [immediate] Pitṛs.

One should joyfully feed the paternal ancestors as well as those belonging to the maternal lineage for their spiritual welfare; and one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability and in accordance with one's wealth.
In that Mahālaya Śrāddha, one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is indeed said to be the leader of all sacrifices.
Just as a cart on a road fails when deprived of its lead oxen, so too this ancestral sacrifice perishes when it is devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 43 ||

Therefore, even a small sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given by one who knows this during sacrifices; likewise, the Mahālaya rite should be performed even by widows and women without sons. || 44 ||
It should be performed by means of a feast with abundant food intended for one's husbands; otherwise, there would be a loss of dharma and a great hell would ensue. (45)
When the month of Bhādrapada has arrived, he who does not perform the Mahālaya rite causes his lineage to perish and incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin. || 46 ||
Those endowed with faith who perform the Mahālaya rite for their ancestors shall never suffer the extinction of their lineage, and their prosperity shall remain imperishable. (47)
For "ālaya" is declared to be an abode, and "mahaḥ" is said to mean auspiciousness; because it is the abode of all that is auspicious, it is proclaimed as Mahālaya. (48)
Therefore, a mortal should perform the Mahālaya rite for the attainment of auspiciousness; if he does not perform the Mahālaya, misfortune shall befall him.
Even if one does not perform the śrāddha on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father, a wise person should nevertheless perform the Mahālaya-śrāddha without failing to remember them.
If one does not have the capacity to perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha, a man should nevertheless perform that Mahālaya for his ancestors even by begging [for the necessary means].
One should request wealth and grain from distinguished Brahmins; one should never accept wealth and grain from those who have fallen [from their status]. (52)
If grain, wealth, or other such things cannot be obtained from the Brahmins, one desiring to perform the Mahālaya rite should beg from the best of Kṣatriyas.
If the kings do not become givers, one should beg even from the Vaiśyas; for indeed, if there are no givers among the Vaiśyas in this world, [then one must beg from others].
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should give a mouthful of grass to a cow for the satisfaction of the ancestors; or else, having gone outside into the forest, one should weep.
Beating his own belly with both hands and shedding tears, a man would speak thus loudly in those forest regions: (56)
"May all the ancestors of my lineage hear my words: I am poor, wretched, shameless, and a doer of cruel deeds. (57)
The month of Bhādrapada has arrived, which increases the delight of the ancestors; yet I truly lack the power to perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha.
"Even though I have wandered over the entire earth, nothing at all has been obtained by me; therefore, I shall not perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha for you. (59)
"Forgive me for that, for you are indeed compassionate; a poor man such as I would surely weep thus in the forest lands. (160)
Hearing his weeping, the ancestors born of his lineage become joyful and attain satisfaction, just as the gods do upon drinking nectar.

Just as satisfaction arises when a multitude of Brahmins has eaten for the sake of the Mahālaya rite, so too does the satisfaction of the ancestors arise through the offering of a mouthful of grass to a cow or by weeping in a forest. || 62 ||

If an obstacle should arise in the month of Bhādrapada due to birth-impurity (sūtaka) or similar causes, one should perform the rite after the days of impurity have passed, up until the month of Āśvina.
For the sake of Mahālaya, the wise man should choose nine Brahmins; he should choose one for the sake of the father, and likewise one for the sake of the grandfather.
A twice-born man should likewise choose one Brahmin for the sake of his great-grandfather, and similarly, he should indeed choose one Brahmin for the sake of his maternal grandfather.
One should choose a single twice-born man for the sake of one's maternal grandfather, and one should choose another, designating him for one's maternal great-grandfather.

In the same manner, he should choose two most excellent brahmins for the sake of the Viśvedevas; however, for the sake of Viṣṇu, he should choose one brahmin who is the best among those who know the Vedas.
Thus, in the Mahālaya Śrāddha, one should invite nine Brāhmaṇas; or else, for the sake of the group of ancestors, one may invite a single learned Brahmin.
Having designated his maternal grandfather and others, he should invite one Brahmin; another for the sake of the Viśvedevas, and likewise another for the sake of Viṣṇu. (69)
In this manner, O Brahmins, one should indeed invite four [priests] at the Mahālaya; the wise man should invite Brāhmaṇas who are perfected in the Vedas and possessed of good character. (170)
He who chooses those of immoral conduct is indeed a destroyer of the śrāddha, especially when the month of Bhādrapada has arrived during its dark fortnight.
O Durācāra of great intellect, that man who performs the Mahālaya Śrāddha with faith has bathed in all the sacred fords.
Even a hundred sacrifices, such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, were performed by him; indeed, gifts such as the Tulāpuruṣa and other principal offerings were also bestowed.

There is no doubt that the Cāndrāyaṇa and other ascetic penances (kṛcchras) have indeed been performed; one shall obtain the fruit of reciting the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (sāṅga). || 74 ||
Likewise, one shall obtain the merit of reciting great mantras such as the Gāyatrī, and one shall obtain the fruit of reciting the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
There is no religious merit on the surface of the earth equal to that of the Mahālaya; from the Mahālaya, one attains the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
The Śrāddha ceremony, such as the Mahālaya and others, is considered both obligatory and optional; therefore, by its non-performance, a great transgression occurs. (77)
By performing the Mahālaya rite, there will undoubtedly be the attainment of one's desired goals; through its performance, spirits, vetālas, and other such beings [will be subdued]. (78)
Furthermore, there are those seized by epilepsy-demons, as well as hosts of Śākinīs and Ḍākinīs, Yātudhānas, Piśācas, and terrifying Vetālas. (79)
Likewise, other malevolent spirits perish at that very moment; by performing the Mahālaya rite, one enjoys abundant prosperity.
Formerly, King Daśaratha, following the instruction of Vasiṣṭha, performed the Mahālaya Śrāddha when the month of Bhādrapada had arrived.
He obtained four sons, Rāma and the others, who were esteemed by the world; he attained a supreme fame and a splendor that surpassed the entire universe. (82)
By performing the Mahālaya rite, Yayāti, the best of kings, obtained great sons who were the leaders of the Yadu clan and the increasers of his lineage.
Duṣyanta attained heaven, difficult for others to reach, through the merit of the *śrāddha* rite; he obtained Bharata by performing the *mahālaya* ceremony.
By means of the Mahālaya ritual, Nala, the husband of Damayantī, having crossed over a most grievous hardship, regained this earth once more. (85)
He subdued the terrible Kali and also his enemy Puṣkara; and he obtained a most righteous son named Indrasena.
The great king Hariścandra, the best among the truthful, was liberated from the suffering caused by Viśvāmitra through the performance of the Mahālaya rite.
By means of the Mahālaya rite, the powerful son of Kṛtavīrya again obtained his wife Candravatī and his son Lohitāśva.
Rāma also attained sovereignty over the eighteen islands by means of the Mahālaya ritual performed in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Having slain Rāvaṇa in battle, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, regained Sītā by performing the Mahālaya rite.
Having crossed the ocean of suffering, he slew the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; and by performing the Mahālaya rite, Vasiṣṭha became the best of sages.
Atri, Bhṛgu, Kutsa, Gautama, Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, and the Jar-born (Agastya). || 92 ||
Parāśara, Mṛkaṇḍa, and those other best of sages, having performed the unsurpassed Mahālaya Śrāddha according to the prescribed rules, [attained their goals]. || 93 ||

They have become the abodes of the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*, as well as of religious observances and austerities; likewise, they have become those who transcend the entire universe.
All those best of sages indeed became liberated while living; therefore, one who desires prosperity should perform the Mahālaya Śrāddha.
Therefore, O man of evil conduct, even today one who does not perform the Mahālaya rite shall face great terror from spirits, vetālas, and the like. (96)
By failing to perform the Mahālaya rite, one may attain the state of a Vetāla; this being was possessed by you because you were a Brahmin in a previous birth. 97.
The noble-minded one, known by the name Vedanidhi, was meritorious and descended from Bharadvāja; he resided in a village called Kuśasthalī.
Because he did not perform this Mahālaya Śrāddha according to the prescribed rules, he has consequently attained the state of a Vetāla due to the curse of his ancestors. || 99 ||
Therefore, O Durācāra, in the month of Bhādrapada, feed the Brāhmaṇas with food of six flavors and with devotion for the sake of the ancestors.
By this, poverty shall not be yours and you shall indeed become happy; from now on, do not associate with great sinners.
"The suffering you experienced arising from the possession by the vetāla has been endured; go now, I give you leave, back to your own country—do not delay. (2)
Thus addressed by the yogi sage Dattātreya, he bowed to him and departed for his own country with a heart that felt its purpose fulfilled.
And having returned to his own home, O best of the twice-born, that brahmin of evil conduct was freed from the fear of the vetāla and cast off the cloak of his sin.
With a delighted mind, following this path taught by Dattātreya, he abandoned the company of sinners and became intent upon the conduct prescribed for his own stage of life.
Then, due to the merit of bathing at the Rāmacandra-dhanuṣkoṭi tīrtha, that man of evil conduct attained supreme liberation at the end of his body.
The venerable Sūta said: Thus has been narrated to you this meritorious account of liberation from wicked conduct; this is that holy Dhanuṣkoṭi, the destroyer of great sins.
For by merely bathing there, even one of wicked conduct was liberated; or rather, what indeed could be the measure of the tip of that bow? (8)
That which destroys even those sins for which no atonement exists—indeed, whatever sins there may be that lack a prescribed expiation.
Even those [sins] perish here by immersion at Dhanuṣkoṭi; likewise for a twice-born man who bows down to a Liṅga or Viṣṇu that has been worshipped by a Śūdra.
No expiation for that has been declared by the supreme sages in the Smṛtis; yet even his sin shall perish by immersion in Dhanuṣkoṭi.
For those men who have committed slander against Brahmins, no expiation exists; and for betrayers of trust and ungrateful persons, there is no atonement.
There is no expiation for those who take pleasure in their brother's wife, nor for those who are habituated to the food of Śūdras, nor for those whose souls delight in censuring the Vedas.
[The sin] of Brahmins who sell their daughters, as well as those who sell horses, those who sell [images of] gods, and those whose souls are devoted to the selling of the Vedas; || 14 ||
For men who sell the Dharma, likewise for those who sell their vows, and for men who sell sacred pilgrimage sites, no expiation exists.
The sins of those who have committed offenses against their mother, their father, or their preceptor, as well as those whose souls are devoted to theft, are destroyed by immersion at Dhanuṣkoṭi.
And for those intent on reviling their gurus, whose souls delight in reviling Śiva, who are devoted to reviling Viṣṇu, and whose souls delight in reviling ascetics; || 17 ||
And for those who defile sacred discourses, no expiation exists; however, their purification shall come about through bathing here at Dhanuṣkoṭi. || 18 ||
Thus, O Brahmins, has the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi been recounted to you; by hearing which, a human being on earth is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pacification of the Fault Arising from Association with the Wicked," within the Praise of Dhanuṣkoṭi, in the Setu-māhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: O all you ascetics, residents of the Naimiṣa forest, [I shall describe] to you the holy sites beginning with Rāmadhanuṣkoṭi and Cakratīrtha.
I have now described to you the twenty-four sacred sites (tīrthas). What else, other than this wonder, do you wish to hear further? || 2 ||
The sages said: O sage, we wish to hear the majesty of Kṣīrakuṇḍa, near which you previously mentioned the Cakratīrtha.
And where is that Kṣīrakuṇḍa, and what is its majesty? How did it come to be known by the name Kṣīrakuṇḍa? (4)
"You ought to tell this in detail to us who are full of faith. Śrī Sūta said: "I shall speak, O all you sages; listen with well-composed minds. (5)
Not far to the west of the highly meritorious Devīpura, there is a most magnificent place known as Phullagrāma.
From the place where Rāma began the construction of the bridge across the great ocean, there is indeed that most meritorious sacred field, the city named Phullagrāma.
The Kṣīrakuṇḍa is located right there; it destroys great sins and bestows liberation through sight, touch, meditation, and even glorification.
I shall respectfully relate to you the renown of that meritorious holy site as "Kṣīrakuṇḍa"; listen with faith.
For in ancient times, there was a sage named Mudgala who followed the path prescribed by the Vedas, on the shore of the southern ocean in the most sacred village called Phullagrāma.
He performed an excellent sacrifice that was pleasing to Nārāyaṇa; Viṣṇu, his soul being gracious, was thoroughly satisfied by that sacrifice.
O best of the twice-born, he appeared before him in the sacrificial enclosure; seeing Viṣṇu, whose form was graced by Lakṣmī, Mudgala [was filled with joy].
His body was like a dark rain-cloud, resplendent with yellow garments, mounted upon the son of Vinatā, and his chest adorned with the Kaustubha gem.

Beholding with devotion his four arms shining with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, Mudgala—overwhelmed by that sight and adorned with the sprouts of horripilation—praised him with words pleasing to the ear.
Mudgala said: First to the creator of the world, and thereafter to its protector. (15)
And thereafter, salutations to You, Nārāyaṇa, the Withdrawer; salutations to the one in the form of a fish, to the tortoise, the conscious Self. (16)
Salutations to the one with the form of a boar; salutations to the one with the form of a lion; salutations to you, Vāmana; salutations to you, the son of Jamadagni.
Salutations to you, O Rāghava; salutations to you, O Balabhadra; salutations to you, O Kṛṣṇa and Kalki; salutations to you whose form is supreme knowledge.
Protect me, O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the Universe, Ocean of Compassion—me who am shameless, wretched, cruel, backbiting, hypocritical, and emaciated. (19)
O Hari, out of compassion, protect me, whose mind is possessed by envy and who is solely intent upon the wives, wealth, and fields of others. 20.
O best of the twice-born, Hari himself, being thus praised by Mudgala, spoke to the sage Mudgala with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Śrī Hari said: "I am pleased with this hymn and with your sacrifice, O Mudgala. I have come to your sacrifice to personally partake of the oblation."
Thus addressed by Hari, the brahmin Mudgala, his mind delighted and filled with supreme devotion, spoke to Adhokṣaja.
Mudgala said: "I have achieved my purpose, O Hṛṣīkeśa; my wife has attained blessedness. Today my birth is fruitful, and today my ascetic penance is truly successful. (24)
Today my lineage has indeed become fruitful; today my sons have become fruitful; today my hermitage has become fruitful; today everything of mine has become fruitful. (25)
Since you have come here to my sacrificial enclosure to partake of the oblation—that which yogis, devoted to yoga, seek within their hearts. (26)
"Having seen you face-to-face today, this sacrifice of mine has become fruitful. Having spoken thus, he worshipped Viṣṇu with a seat and other offerings.
Having offered arghya with sandalwood, flowers, and other items to Viṣṇu, he affectionately presented the sacrificial oblation, such as the puroḍāśa cake, before Viṣṇu.
Taking it himself with his own hand, Viṣṇu, the creator of the world, consumed that oblation offered by Mudgala.
O twice-born ones, when that oblation had been consumed by the all-powerful Viṣṇu, all the gods, together with their fires, became fully satiated.
The officiating priests, the sacrificer, and the Brahmins present there, as well as whatever exists in this world of living beings—whether moving or unmoving. (31)
When Viṣṇu had consumed the entire oblation, the whole world was satisfied; thereupon Hari, with a gracious soul, addressed Mudgala.
"I am pleased and ready to grant a boon; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows. When Keśava had spoken thus, the great ṛṣi then addressed him.
Mudgala said: "Since you have consumed my sacrificial offering in person at this sacrifice, by this alone I am fulfilled; what boon could be greater than this?"
Nevertheless, O Lord Viṣṇu, may my devotion toward you always remain steadfast and sincere; this is my first boon. (35)
"O Hari, every day at dawn and dusk, I offer oblations here to Agni in your form for your pleasure, O Surabhi, with your milk. (36)
"O Giver of Boons, I wish to perform the oblation; grant me another boon for that purpose. For the daily oblation with milk twice a day is indeed enjoined by the Vedas. (37)
"I have no fragrant flowers, being an ascetic and without wealth," said Mudgala; thereupon the Lord Nārāyaṇa Hari [replied].
Having summoned Viśvakarman, the immortal Tvaṣṭṛ, he had that craftsman construct a single, beautiful lake.

With various kinds of stones such as crystal and others, Viśvakarman made it perfectly level once again, and adorned it with ramparts and other structures. Then the Blessed One summoned Surabhi and spoke these words: ||| 40 ||
Śrī Hari said: "O Surabhi, this Mudgala is my devotee; he [serves me] daily with joy."
She now desires to perform an oblation of milk for my pleasure; therefore, O Goddess, being impelled by me, you must go from here for my sake. 42.
"O auspicious Surabhī, coming here every day at evening and morning, fill this lake with the milk produced from you. (43)
With that milk, he shall offer oblations daily, both evening and morning; having been thus addressed by Nārāyaṇa, Surabhi replied, "Om."
Then the god Nārāyaṇa addressed Mudgala: "By means of Surabhi’s milk, which remains constantly in this lake... (45)
"O highly fortunate one, offer oblations here to Agni every day at dawn and dusk for my pleasure; by that, I shall be pleased with you. (46)
"O Mudgala, by my grace, you shall attain all perfections; and this place shall become famous as the sacred ford named Kṣīrasaras."
For those who have bathed at this sacred ford of the Milk Lake, the five great sins as well as other sins shall perish in that very instant.
"O Mudgala, you too shall come to me at the end of your body, freed from all bonds. Having spoken thus, the Lord Viṣṇu embraced that Mudgala.
Having been saluted by him, Viṣṇu vanished right there; and Mudgala, after Viṣṇu had departed, [remained] for many hundreds of years.

Offering oblations to Agni with the milk of a Surabhi cow for the satisfaction of Hari, he lived constantly, self-restrained, in Phullagrāma, which bestows liberation; at the end of his body, he attained liberation in the form of union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu.
The venerable Sūta said: "O best of the twice-born, thus has this been narrated by me to you."
Just as there was formerly a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) named Kṣīrasaras for this site, so too is this meritorious Kṣīrasaras renowned throughout all the worlds. (53)
O best of the twice-born, it was there that Kadrū, the wife of the sage Kāśyapa, having bathed at the command of her husband, remained observant of her religious vows.
By this artifice, he was immediately released from the fault of having conquered his co-wife; therefore, those men who bathe here in this holy place with pure minds [attain liberation]. || 55 ||
For those whose bonds have been severed, who are liberated, and who have performed meritorious deeds—what need have they for sacrifices, or for the Vedas, or for frequenting sacred pilgrimage sites?
O twice-born ones, by means of recitations or even by religious observances, a man whose body is touched by the wind from the Kṣīrakuṇḍa becomes one who beholds the Kṣīrakuṇḍa.
Having reached the world of Brahmā, one is liberated right there; those submerged in this pool of milk do so even while disregarding the son of the Sun (Yama). 58.
Upon their heads may there stand blazing fires like the sacrificial fire, while for those submerged in this pool of milk, the river Vaitaraṇī is cool.
Indeed, all the hells truly become useless, even while that milk-pot, equal to the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), remains present—oh!
O best of Brahmins, that man wanders elsewhere to bathe even when cow's milk is available; he goes instead for the sake of camel's milk. || 61 ||
For those who have bathed in this pool of milk, there is indeed nothing that cannot be attained; liberation shall be as if already held in the palm of one's hand—what is the use of further words?

Raising my arms, I declare to you the truth, the absolute truth: whoever shall read this chapter or listen to it with a concentrated mind, he obtains the supreme fruit of bathing in the Kṣīrakuṇḍa lake.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Kṣīrakuṇḍa," within the "Praise of Setu" in the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O Sūta, how was Kadru liberated by immersion in the Kṣīrakuṇḍa? How did she, fixed in her sinful resolve, practice deception toward her co-wife?

Whose daughter was that Kadrū, and whose wife was her co-wife? For what purpose did Kadrū deceitfully cause her co-wife to be defeated? O Sūta, ocean of mercy, tell this to us who are full of faith. (2)
The venerable Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to this history of great fruit. Formerly, O brahmins, in the Kṛta age, there were two daughters of Prajāpati.
Kadru and Vinata were born as sisters; they both became the wives of Kaśyapa—namely, Kadru and Vinata.
Vinatā gave birth to two sons, Aruṇa and Garuḍa; and from her husband, Kadrū obtained many sons who were serpents.
Once, those two sisters, Kadrū and Vinatā, [beheld] Ananta, Vāsuki, and the others, who were filled with the pride of their poison.
Not seeing [the horse] approaching from afar, Kadrū, upon beholding the steed Uccaiḥśravas, spoke thus to Vinatā: || 7 ||

"O Vinatā, tell me truly: is the horse's tail white or black? Having spoken thus, O Brahmins, Vinatā said this to Kadrū: "O slender-waisted one, the horse appears to me to have a white tail; what do you think, Kadrū? Vinatā asked her. (9)
Having thus questioned Vinatā, Kadrū expressed her own opinion: "O blameless one, I consider this horse to have a black tail."
Then, O best of the twice-born, having mutually made the state of slavery the wager for defeat, those two illustrious co-wives remained [as they had agreed].
Then Kadrū said to her own sons, the snakes headed by Vāsuki, "O dear sons, act in such a way that I am no longer her slave."
For the sake of accomplishing her desired goal, she spoke with great urgency: "Let the young Uccaiḥśravas be concealed by you. (13)
Then the Nāgas did not accept her proposal; enraged by Kadrū, she, blazing with fury and overwhelmed by anger, cursed her sons.
"O sons of Pārīkṣita, you shall all truly die during a sacrificial session"—when this curse was uttered by his mother, Karkoṭaka was then terrified.
Bowing at her feet, Kadru, dejected, spoke these words: "I shall turn the hair of Uccaiḥśravas into the color of collyrium."
Then the serpent Karkoṭaka, distressed by the curse, said, "O mother, you must not be afraid," and he turned the white tail of Uccaiḥśravas upward.
Having covered them with her own body, she displayed the luster of collyrium; then those two, Vinatā and Kadrū, both entered into a wager regarding servitude.
She approached them with great haste to behold the horse of the king of gods, which was the very cause of the moon, the conch, rubies, pearls, and Airāvata.
Having passed beyond the ocean, the lord of rivers, where Hari lies down in his yogic sleep at the time of the end of the age, Kadrū and Vinatā reached the sea.
Having gone there, they saw the horse, the mount of the king of the gods; seeing that horse with its black tail, Vinatā became sorrowful.
While Vinatā was thus suffering, Kadrū appointed her to the state of a slave; in the meantime, Tārkṣya also emerged from his egg like a blazing fire.
O best of Brahmins, he appeared with a body as large as a mountain; seeing the majesty of that form, the three worlds became terrified.
Then the gods praised Garuḍa, the best of birds, seeing the majesty of his body, by which even the three worlds would be struck with terror.
Having reflected thus and withdrawn his exceedingly terrifying body, he placed Aruṇa upon his back and approached his mother.
Then Kadrū said to Vinatā, who was bowed down and deeply distressed: "O servant, I am making preparations to go to the abode of the Nāgas."
"Let your son Garuḍa carry me and my sons. Then Vinatā addressed her son Garuḍa.
"I shall carry this Kadrū; you, however, must carry her sons. "So be it," O twice-born ones, Garuḍa accepted his mother's words.
Vinatā carried Kadrū, and Garuḍa carried all of them; then the serpents, having come near the sun, were struck by his rays.
Kadrū praised the wielder of the thunderbolt for the sake of pacifying the suffering of her sons; the king of the gods, too, allayed every affliction with showers of water.
Then, being carried away by the powerful Garuḍa, the serpents quickly reached that place and spoke to the son of Vinatā. (31)
"We are all in a hurry to go and see another continent; therefore, O Garuḍa, son of a servant-woman, carry us there in an instant."
Then, O twice-born ones, Garuḍa questioned his mother Vinatā: "Why do I carry these [serpents], while you always carry her? (33)
"Why do these reptiles call me 'the son of a slave-girl'? O Mother, tell me all of this in truth as I ask you. (34)
Thus questioned by her son, the mother spoke to her son Garuḍa: "O son, I have been defeated through a stratagem by my cruel sister."
Today I am her slave and you are the son of a servant; therefore, you carry the snakes while I always carry her. (36)
He reported all these events to him from the beginning; then Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā, spoke to his mother.
"What must now be done by me for you in order to secure release from this slavery? Thus questioned by her son, Vinatā then spoke to him.
"O Garuḍa, ask the serpents regarding the liberation of my mother; tell them now: 'What service can I perform for your mother? (39)
Thus addressed by his mother, Garuḍa went toward the serpents and questioned them, O best of the twice-born; they then spoke to him.
O Vainateya, when you swiftly carry away the nectar from the abode of the immortals, your mother shall indeed be liberated from slavery this very day.
Then, approaching his mother with prostration, Garuḍa said: "O Mother, give me food as I go to fetch the nectar."
Thus addressed, the mother Vinatā spoke to her son: "O son, some Śabaras are dwelling in the midst of the ocean."
"Having devoured those Śabaras, bring the nectar back here. There was a certain twice-born man there who was lustful and eager for union with a Śabarī."
Abandon that Brahmin who burns your throat with his brahmanic luster; may the gods, headed by the Maruts, protect your wings and other limbs. (45)
Thus, strengthened by the blessings of his own mother, Garuḍa departed; having reached the abode of the Śabara, he opened his mouth to devour him.
They entered the enclosure like hunters entering a mountain cave; then, O best of sages, that Brāhmaṇa also arrived at its entrance.
To that Brahmin who was burning his throat, the son of Vinatā said: "O Brahmin, even though you are a sinner, you are not to be killed; therefore, depart from here."
Thus addressed, the brahmin then replied to Garuḍa: "My wife, the Kirātī, must also go forth with me."
"So be it," the Lord of Birds said to that Brahmin; then Garuḍa disgorged the Brahmin along with his wife.
The Brahmin also set out for his desired lands together with Niṣādī; meanwhile, Garuḍa, the best of birds, having devoured the Śabaras, [departed].
Having approached his father Kaśyapa with speed, Garuḍa was asked by him, "Where are you going? and he spoke to him.
I came here to bring the nectar in order to liberate my mother from her state of servitude; yet, even after devouring many Kirātas, no satisfaction has arisen within me. (53)
"O Brahmin, endless hunger torments me day and night; O you whose wealth is asceticism, grant me some food that will bring it to an end. (54)
"By what means, O father, might I be able to fetch the nectar by my own power? Thus addressed, Kaśyapa spoke to his son born of Vinatā.
Kaśyapa said: Formerly there was a sage named Vibhāvasu, who had a younger brother; his brother was named Supratīka, and those two were enemies of their own lineage.
O brahmins, filled with great wrath, they cursed one another; Supratīka became an elephant and Vibhāvasu became a tortoise.
Thus, having quarreled over their wealth, the two remaining brothers cursed each other: "May Gaja be six *yojanas* in height and twice that in length. (58)
The tortoise is three yojanas in height and ten yojanas in breadth; both of these have harbored a deep-seated enmity toward one another in this lake, O bird. (59)
Remembering their former enmity, they both fight with the desire to conquer; having devoured them both, you shall bring back the nectar and be fully satisfied.
Thus urged by his father, the bird went and lifted up those two—elephant and tortoise—who were massive in body and possessed of great strength and prowess.
Crossing by means of his two claws, he reached the ford named Viḷambā; O twice-born ones, having beheld the king of birds arrived there, [the sages said]: 62.
On its bank stood a great, towering tree named Rohiṇa, which spoke thus to Vainateya, who is possessed of great strength and prowess: || 63 ||
"Ascend this branch of mine, which extends for a hundred yojanas; staying here, O best of birds, you may devour the elephant and the tortoise. (64)
Thus addressed by the young man, that bird, swift as thought, remained there; O best of the twice-born, under its weight, the branch of the tree broke.
Seeing the Vālakhilya sages hanging there with their faces turned downwards, Garuḍa, fearing that they might fall, seized that branch.
Then Gaja and Kūrma, holding that branch, went through the sky; there, his father spoke to Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā.
"O son of Vinatā, abandon this branch on a desolate mountain. Thus addressed, he went accordingly to that tree devoid of people and [cut] the branch.
Having placed them there, the bird then devoured that elephant and tortoise; at that moment, a portent occurred in the sky.
Having seen the portent, the enemy of Bala (Indra) repeatedly asked his own priest, "O Jīva, what is the cause of this portent here? Then, O best of the twice-born, Bṛhaspati spoke to Śakra.
Bṛhaspati said: "O Hari, in former times the sage Kāśyapa indeed performed a sacrifice with a ritual."
O twice-born ones, he dispatched all the ṛṣis, gods, siddhas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras for the purpose of procuring the materials for the sacrifice.
Seeing the Vālakhilyas—small as a thumb, yet carrying their sacrificial requisites—sinking in the water of a cow’s footprint, you laughed. (73)
O Hari, then the Vālakhilyas, insulted by you and filled with rage, their faces aflame with anger, offered oblations into the sacrificial fire.
"May there be a son of Kaśyapa who is an enemy who strikes fear into the lord of the gods. Today, his son Garuḍa is eager for the task of seizing the nectar.
"Because he has come here, this portent has arisen. Thus addressed, Indra spoke to the gods, headed by Agni: || 76 ||
"The bird is coming to seize the nectar; let it be guarded!"—thus urged by Indra, the gods, equipped with weapons, protected the nectar.
Then the king of birds approached the gods who were bearing weapons; seeing that immensely powerful Garuḍa, the deities indeed trembled.
Then a great battle took place between Garuḍa and the gods; Bhaumana, the protector of the nectar, was struck down by the beak of the bird.
Then the gods struck Garuḍa with various weapons many times; Garuḍa was exceedingly oppressed by the gods who held weapons in their hands.
With its two wings it cast the gods, led by Agni, far away; then the gods, struck by those wings, became exceedingly enraged.
Shattering iron arrows and hurling various weapons, Garuḍa then, with great speed, [discharged] that which obscures the vision of the gods.
The son of Vinatā raised up dust with his two wings; the best of the gods quelled that dust with the wind.
O twice-born ones, Garuḍa afflicted the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Maruts, and other gods with his wings and beak.
When the gods had fled, he beheld a blazing fire before him; seeing the fire burning on all sides, he strove to extinguish it.
Having become thousand-faced and drinking hundreds of rivers with them, he, acting with haste, extinguished that fire with those waters.
Seeing a white-edged, whirling discus nearby that was protecting the nectar, he entered through a hole in its enemy with his body drawn together.
Then he saw two serpents with manifest mouths and terrifying forms; even at the sight of them one would be reduced to ashes, yet Garuḍa then [confronted] those two serpents.
Having torn [the vessel] apart with his wings and beak and seized the nectar, Garuḍa rose up; then Mādhava spoke to Garuḍa as he was departing after having uprooted the machine.
"I am pleased with you, O Lord of Birds; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows. Then the bird spoke to Hari, the leader of the lotuses: [90]
"May my abode be upon you, and may old age and death not come to pass. "So be it," Hari said, adding, "Choose a boon from me."
Thus addressed, Hari said to him: "O son of Vinatā, you shall become my vehicle, and you shall be my banner atop my chariot."
"So be it," the bird also said to Acyuta, the Lord of Kamalā. Then, hearing that the bird had carried away the nectar, Ākhaṇḍala quickly [set out].
Having swiftly approached, the bird hurled the thunderbolt at his wing; then Garuḍa, laughing, spoke to the subduer of Pāka (Indra).
O Hara, no pain at all has been caused to me by the falling of the thunderbolt; O leader of the gods, may your strike with the vajra be fruitful for you. (95)
Uttering thus, he then cast off a single feather from his wing; because its leaf was beautiful (*śobhana*), he became known as Suparṇa.
O best of the twice-born, all were filled with wonder at that golden-hued Suparṇa; then Garuḍa spoke to Śakra.
O Lord of the Gods, I possess an unfailing power to constantly bear this entire world, including all things moving and unmoving, together with you. (98)
"O Hari, even a thousand Indras shall not be obtainable by me in battle," said Garuḍa; to him who was speaking thus, Pākaśāsana replied: || 99 ||
"What use would you have for the nectar? Let the nectar be given to me. O son of Vinatā, you should give this ambrosia to those [whom I intend]."
Now, by drinking the nectar, they will become free from old age and death; possessing even greater prowess than us, they would likewise harass the gods. (1)
O twice-born ones, as the lord of the gods was speaking thus, Garuḍa also said to him: "Wherever I shall establish this, you should come there."
When told, "Seize [him] instantly," the slayer of Vṛtra said to Garuḍa: "I am pleased with you; I shall grant you a boon. Choose one, O high-minded one! (3)
To the one who had spoken thus, Garuḍa said to the subduer of Pāka: "The reptiles, who employ deceitful means, shall become the slaves of my mother."
"O Pākaśāsana, O slayer of Vṛtra, let them be my food forever! Thus addressed by him, Śakra said to him, "So be it."
Then, O Brahmins, this Garuḍa departed carrying the nectar; as he went, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, followed after that Garuḍa.
O best of the twice-born, that king of birds, eager to carry away the nectar, approached his mother with speed and spoke to the serpents.
"O serpents, in this manner I have now placed nectar upon the kusha grass; having bathed, being pure and well-composed, eat that ambrosia."
"O serpents, my mother shall also be liberated from her state of servitude," said Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā; the snakes replied, "So be it."
O best of the twice-born, at that very moment Vinatā was liberated from her state of servitude; then all those serpents went to bathe for the sake of consuming the nectar.
At that moment, Śakra took that nectar and departed; having bathed and returned, those serpents did not see the nectar there.

Thinking, "This is indeed excellent nectar placed upon the darbha grass," they licked it with their tongues; from that time forward, the tongues of serpents have been split by the tips of darbha grass.
O best of sages, because they became two-fold, they are remembered as "dvijihva" (two-tongued); furthermore, through contact with nectar, the darbha grasses attained purity.
And having liberated his mother from the state of slavery, Garuḍa, enraged, cursed Kadrū, who had defeated her by means of deceit.
"Since you have deceitfully defeated my mother, Kadrū, you shall therefore no longer be worthy of serving your husband. (15)
Having thus cursed Kadrū, Garuḍa departed as he pleased; and both Kadrū and Vinatā went into the presence of their husband.
Then Kaśyapa, turning away from her, spoke to Kadrū in anger: "Since you have defeated Vinatā through deceit... (17)
Therefore, O evil-minded one, you are not fit for my service; whether it be a woman or a man, a female or even a male. (18)
He who wins by means of fraud becomes a perpetrator of a great sin; by conversing with one who has won through fraud, one becomes a slayer of a Brahmin. || 19 ||
He should be known as a thief, a drinker of liquor, and one who takes pleasure in the wife of his guru; he is proclaimed by the sages to be defiled by the fault of association. 120.
"O Kadrū, O cruel one, because of conversing with you, a fault would accrue to me that leads to hell; therefore, depart from my presence."
If a man on earth eats in a row with one who has been defeated by the six vices, he shall immediately fall into the ocean of hell merely by conversing with him.
Having observed the one who has conquered through deceit, for the sake of pacifying that sin, he should look toward the sun, or water, or fire.
Wherever a person who has conquered the six internal enemies may reside—whether in a hermitage or even in a house—others must certainly not dwell there; for one who lives there partakes in hell.
Therefore, depart, depart from my path of vision; you have surpassed this humble woman, who is upright in her own station. || 25 ||
Having thus suddenly rebuked Kadrū, the high-minded Kaśyapa then accepted Vinatā, who was of pure character. 26.
Thus addressed harshly by Kaśyapa, Kadrū, weeping and afflicted by intense grief, fell at his feet.
Seeing Kadrū fallen at his feet, Kaśyapa, the bull among sages, did not accept her at all, remembering the evil deed she had committed.
Then, having bowed down to Kaśyapa, Vinatā spoke these words: "O Blessed One, O treasure-house of compassion, please accept this sister of mine. (29)
"Whatever sin has now been committed by the deluded Kadrū out of ignorance, you ought to forgive all of that; for the virtuous are indeed compassionate by nature. (130)
The sage Kaśyapa, who had been told by Jananī just as Garuḍa was, said to Vinatā: "O Vinatā, there is no atonement for this sin except through her."
"I shall seize you, you of evil conduct; I swear this to you thrice! Having heard the words of Kaśyapa, Vinatā spoke again:
"O Brahmin, tell me the atonement for my sinful sister, so that she may become worthy of serving you. (33)
O Brahmins, having been thus addressed by her, Kaśyapa Mārīca then meditated for a moment in his mind and subsequently spoke as follows.
On the shore of the southern ocean, in the village of Phullagrāma which bestows liberation, there is a sacred ford named Kṣīrasaras that destroys all sins.
By merely bathing at that sacred ford (tīrtha), her fault is destroyed; even by ten thousand penances (prāyaścitta), it cannot be removed without immersion in that tīrtha.
"This fault of hers will not perish; therefore, let her go to that lake. When the husband had spoken thus, Kadrū bowed to that best of the twice-born.
At that very moment, Kadrū, accompanied by her sons, set out for the lake of milk; having gone there with her sons, after a few days had passed, she arrived.
Having reached the holy Kṣīrasaras, purified and with her senses subdued, she bathed according to the prescribed rules after making a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) at the Kṣīrakuṇḍa.

Having fasted for three days, she bathed in the waters of that Milk Lake; on the fourth day, while she was performing her bath with devotion, O best of the twice-born, a bodiless voice arose from the sky.
The incorporeal voice said: "O Kadrū, because of your deceitful victory here through immersion, you shall suffer for that fault. (41)
"You are liberated and fit for service to your husband; of this there is no doubt. Even the curse uttered by Garuḍa has come to an end here through immersion."
"Go to your husband; he too will accept you. Having spoken thus, the bodiless voice from the sky then ceased.
Having offered salutations to that Speech, Kadrū, her mind filled with joy, circumambulated the sacred ford and bowed down together with her sons.
Out of a desire to serve her husband, she went into his presence; and he, beholding her who had arrived having bathed in the waters of the Milk Lake, [was filled with wonder]. (45)
Having known through meditative absorption that she was cleansed of sin, Kaśyapa accepted her as his wife, for she was now fit to serve him.
Thus, O Brahmins, has been narrated to you the liberation of Kadrū from her curse; by bathing in the holy waters of the Milk Lake, it grants liberation to men.
The person who hears this chapter or even reads it obtains the supreme fruit of bathing in the Kṣīrakuṇḍa.
He enjoys the complete fruit of sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha; he certainly becomes one who has bathed in all the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā. (49)
Whoever recites this chapter in praise of Kṣīrakuṇḍa obtains the complete fruit of those who bestow a thousand cows.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Narrative on the Pacification of the Fault Arising from Kadrū’s Deceit," within the Praise of Kṣīrakuṇḍa, in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the majesty of Kapitīrtha; that sacred site was formerly located on the entirety of the Gandhamādana mountain.
O twice-born ones, it was constructed by the monkeys for the benefit of all, immediately after Rāvaṇa and the other Rākṣasas had been slain.
Having created a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) right there, the monkeys joyfully bathed; and the monkeys, who could assume any form at will, granted a boon to that tīrtha.
Those whose minds are inclined toward devotion who have immersed themselves in this sacred ford—all of them shall partake in liberation, being freed from even the greatest of sins.
For those submerged in this sacred bathing place (tīrtha), there shall be no fear born of hell; indeed, all men who bathe here do not encounter poverty.
"For those submerged in this sacred ford, there shall be no affliction even from Yama; I shall go to Kapitīrtha," thus saying constantly— || 6 ||
O Brahmins, he who walks a hundred steps [toward it] shall go to the supreme station; there has never been, nor will there ever be, a holy place equal to this tīrtha.
Having thus granted this boon to that sacred ford, all the lords of the monkeys bowed to Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, and then made their request.
"O Lord, let a wonderful boon be granted to this sacred ford by you. O Brahmins, thus requested by the monkeys, Rāmacandra was exceedingly delighted.
He granted a boon to that sacred ford for the sake of pleasing the monkeys: "Those who immerse themselves in this holy place shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. (10)
May there be the merit born from bathing at Prayāga, as well as the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), and the unsurpassed fruit of sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma.
The merit of chanting great mantras such as the Gāyatrī shall likewise accrue; those who give a thousand cows obtain the full and unimpaired fruit.
One shall obtain the fruit of reciting all four Vedas in their entirety; one shall obtain the fruit of worshipping the gods beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. || 13 ||
O twice-born ones, Rāma thus granted this boon to Kapitīrtha; and when the boon had been granted by Rāma there, out of curiosity—
Brahmā with six faces and three eyes, the thousand-eyed Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Agni, Vāyu, Kubera, and even the Moon; || 15 ||
Āditya and Nirṛti, the Sādhyas and the Vasus, as well as all the other gods, such as the Viśvedevas and so forth. || 16 ||
Atri, Bhṛgu, as well as Kutsa, Gautama, Parāśara, Kaṇva, Agastya, Sutīkṣṇa, Viśvāmitra, and others. || 17 ||
Then the yogis, Sanaka and the others, as well as the celestial sages such as Nārada, praised in many ways that sacred ford where Rāma had bestowed his boon.
And they bathed there at that sacred ford which grants all desired objects, since this unsurpassed tīrtha was constructed by the monkeys.
"It shall become renowned in the world as Kapitīrtha," so said all those gods and sages.
Therefore, those seeking liberation must certainly go to Kapitīrtha. O twice-born ones, in ancient times Rambhā became a stone due to the curse of Kauśika.
Having bathed there, he regained his own form and went to heaven; the majesty of this sacred site cannot be described by me.

The sages said: O son of a Sūta, for what reason did Kauśika curse Rambhā? How did that celestial nymph, having turned into stone, come to Kapitīrtha? O best of sages, tell us all of this in detail. (23)
The venerable Sūta said: In former times, there was a king named Viśvāmitra in the lineage of Kuśika.
Once, that mighty great king, surrounded by his army and eager to inspect his kingdom, traversed the earth.
Having wandered through many countries, he went to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha; there, he was chosen by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha to receive hospitality.
"So be it," said that king, bowing down like a staff before Viśvāmitra, the lord of the earth, through the power of Kāmadhenu. (27)
O Brahmins, Vasiṣṭha, the joy of the sages, offered hospitality; for the son of Kuśika had indeed come to know the power of Kāmadhenu.
He requested Vasiṣṭha for the wish-fulfilling cow who grants all desires; having been refused by Vasiṣṭha, he dragged her away by force.
He was defeated by the Mlecchas and others released by Kāmadhenu; however, having propitiated Mahādeva and obtained weapons from him, he [conquered them].
Having gone to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, that best of kings discharged multitudes of arrows; he released all his weapons and even the Brahmāstra.
And Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, destroyed all those weapons with a single Brahmadaṇḍa through the power of his own asceticism.
Then, O Brahmins, having been defeated and deeply ashamed, Viśvāmitra went to the forest to perform austerities for the sake of attaining the status of a Brāhmaṇa. || 33 ||
He performed penance in the three directions—east, west, and north—and in each of those directions, Kauśika encountered great obstacles that had arisen.
Having reached the northern direction on the pure Himalaya mountain, on the auspicious bank of the river Kauśikī, which destroys all sins.
For a thousand divine years, he remained without food, with his senses conquered; devoid of light, his breath controlled, his anger subdued, and perfectly steady.
In summer he stood amidst five fires, in winter he remained in water, and during the rains he constantly stayed in the open air with his arms raised high, without any shelter.

For the sake of attaining the status of a Brahmin, he performed most severe and great penance. The gods dwelling in the third heaven, their minds filled with anxiety, together with Indra, spoke these words to Rambhā: 39. "He performs most fierce and very great austerity for the sake of attaining Brahminhood; the gods residing in the celestial realm, their minds agitated, along with the Slayer of Jambha, addressed Rambhā with these words."
The gods said: "O Rambhā, you [should go] to the sage dwelling on the bank of the Kauśikī on the Himavat mountain. (39)
"Entice Viśvāmitra as he performs austerities with your wiles; act in such a way that an obstacle to his penance will arise. (40)
Thus addressed then by the gods led by Indra, Rambhā, bowing with palms joined in reverence, replied to all the deities.
Rambhā said: "The great sage Viśvāmitra is exceedingly cruel and possessed of great wrath; he will curse me in his anger, O gods, and I am afraid of him."
"Protect me, your servant, out of compassion! Thus addressed by Rambhā, Jambhāri spoke to her there: ||| 43 ||
Indra said: "O Rambhā, you need have no fear of Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is his asceticism; I too shall come as your companion, accompanied by Manmatha."
Spring, sweet with the warbling of cuckoos, will also arrive; you, being of most beautiful form, must entice the great sage.
Thus addressed by Indra, Rambhā went to the hermitage of Viśvāmitra; standing within the range of his vision, she assumed a charming form.
She attempted to entice the sage with captivating gestures; at that very moment, even the cuckoo sang, gladdening the mind.

Having heard the song of the cuckoo and having seen Rambhā, that bull among sages, his heart filled with doubt and recognizing that as the work of Śakra, Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is asceticism, cursed Rambhā in anger.
Viśvāmitra said: "O Rambhā, since you provoke me, who am seeking to conquer anger... (49)
"Therefore, O Rambhā, you shall become a stone here for ten thousand years; within that interval, protected by a Brāhmaṇa, you will attain liberation. (50)
O twice-born ones, by the curse of Viśvāmitra, she then became a stone; having become a stone, she remained for a long time in his hermitage.
The righteous Viśvāmitra, having again performed great penance at the word of Vasiṣṭha, obtained the status of a Brāhmaṇa, which is difficult for kings to attain.
For a long time, Rambhā remained as a stone in that hermitage; in that very same sacred hermitage, there was a highly esteemed disciple of Agastya.
A sage named Śveta, desiring liberation, performed supreme austerity; while that great sage was performing penance for a long time, [the following occurred].
A certain exceedingly cruel Rākṣasī, known as Aṅgārakā, arrived there, her voice as loud as the roar of clouds. || 55 ||
The terrifying woman defiled him with urine, blood, feces, and other such things, and likewise afflicted that sage with various other calamities.
Then the enraged sage Śveta, employing the Vāyavya weapon, hurled a stone at the Rākṣasī who had been cursed by the son of Kuśika.
That Rākṣasī fled, pursued by the Vāyavya weapon; she was driven away by that discharged Vāyavya weapon as if by a falling rock.
Afflicted by fear, she fled toward the shore of the southern ocean; and as she ran, he pursued her, employing his stone-missile.
As the Rākṣasī was sinking into Kapitīrtha, she fell upon a precipice; there, by the falling of a rock upon her own head, that Rākṣasī died.
Cursed by Viśvāmitra, she abandoned her form as a stone through immersion at Kapitīrtha and assumed the form of Rambhā.
Showers of flowers rained down by the gods upon that delightful woman, who had ascended a celestial chariot and was resplendent in divine garments.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and nose-ornaments, she was surrounded by her companions, the Apsarases such as Urvaśī and others.
Praising again and again the greatness of Kapitīrtha, she worshipped Rāmanātha, Śaṅkara, who is adorned by the moon.
By the curse of the highly powerful son born from a jar (Agastya), that Rākṣasī also went to the beautiful Amarāvatī, the city of Ākhaṇḍala (Indra).
For Ghṛtācī, a celestial nymph of the gods, had assumed the form of a Rākṣasī; she too regained her own form by bathing here in the waters of Kapitīrtha.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, Rambhā and Ghṛtācī attained [their state] by bathing at Kapitīrtha through the grace of Śveta, the disciple of Agastya.
Having abandoned their state as rākṣasīs and their state as stones and returned to their own forms, therefore one should bathe with every effort at Kapitīrthaka. 68.
The person who hears this chapter or even reads it obtains the supreme fruit born of bathing at Kapitīrtha. || 69 ||

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Rambhā and Ghṛtācī from their Curse," within the Praise of Kapitīrtha, in the Setumāhātmya of the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 39 ||
Śrī Sūta said: Now, therefore, O sages, I shall fully proclaim the greatness of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī, which purifies the world and bestows liberation upon men.
It destroys the great sins of those who hear it and those who recite it; it bestows great merit upon men and eliminates the sufferings of hell. || 2 ||
Those men who joyfully bathe in the Gāyatrī and the Sarasvatī shall not dwell in a womb again; rather, their liberation will certainly be attained.
And because of the presence of Sarasvatī and Gāyatrī on Mount Gandhamādana, as well as the two wives of Brahmā, these two [tīrthas] are named after them.
The sages said: "O Sūta, tell us why there was indeed the presence of both Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī on Mount Gandhamādana."
Sūta said: O brahmins, in ancient times, the deluding Prajāpati, having become lustful, joyfully desired his own daughter named Vāk.
Then, seeing his desire directed toward her own self, the daughter of Prajāpati became ashamed and assumed the form of a female deer (rohit).
Then Brahmā, having become a deer and desiring to sport with her, followed her as she went along, assuming the form of a female deer.
Seeing him, all the deities thought: "This Brahmā, out of respect for approaching his daughter, is committing an improper act characterized by incest."
Thus the Brahmins censured him, the creator and lord of the worlds, upon seeing that Parameṣṭhin intent on performing prohibited acts.
The Lord Hara, assuming the form of a hunter, took up his Pināka bow and drew an arrow from it until it reached his ear.
Having joined it with that [weapon], he pierced the Creator with that sharpened arrow of Tripurāntaka; struck by it, he fell to the earth.
Then, rising from his body, a great light of immense radiance became the constellation known as Mṛgaśīrṣa in the sky. || 13 ||
Taking the form of the constellation Ārdrā, Hara also followed him, afflicting the constellation named Mṛgaśīrṣa which was in the form of Brahmā.
Even now, O twice-born ones, the Destroyer of Tripura is clearly seen in the sky in the form of a hunter, near the constellation Mṛgaśīrṣa.
When the Supreme Lord had thus slain him, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī were immediately overcome with grief.
"O best of sages, being bereft of our husband and longing for his life, what indeed shall we two do?"—thus did they deliberate with one another. (17)
For the sake of attaining the life-force of her husband, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī went to Mount Gandhamādana, the most excellent abode of Śiva.
When [the king] prepared to perform a penance that grants all desired objects to men, [his two wives] went toward Śiva to perform penance endowed with religious observances (niyama). || 19 ||
O Brahmins, for the purpose of their own ablution, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī indeed created two holy bathing places (tīrthas) in their own names that destroy all sins.
There, for a long time, they joyfully performed their ablutions three times every day, abstaining from food and free from desire, anger, and other such passions.
The auspicious woman, who had passed away while devoted to meditation on Śiva and strictly bound by the singular discipline of reciting the great five-syllabled mantra, [attained her goal]. || 22 ||
Indeed, for the sake of their husband’s life, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī performed penance directed toward Mahādeva. || 23 ||
Then, gratified by their ascetic penance, Mahādeva Maheśvara, assuming his great form, manifested himself before them with the desire to grant the fruit of their austerities.
Then [he beheld] Śiva, the beloved of Pārvatī, who was present there, attended on both sides by Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya.
Having seen him, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī, their hearts filled with contentment, praised Mahādeva, the storehouse of compassion, who is worthy of praise, with hymns of laudation.

Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī said: "Salutations to the sole cause for the destruction of the darkness of the insurmountable saṃsāra; salutations to the one who consumed the Kālakūṭa poison, formidable with its rows of blazing flames. (27)
O Deluder of the World, sole cause for the destruction of the bodies of the five weapons; O cruel one who brings an end to the world, O Ender of Yama, salutations be unto you! 28.
Salutations to you, O Virūpākṣa, who wear a mass of matted locks joined with the waves of the Gaṅgā, and who bear the cool-rayed moon upon your head. || 29 ||
Salutations to you, who terrified the inhabitants of the three cities with the terrifying twang of the Pināka bow, and who severed the head of the creator of the world in its various forms. 30.
O son of Ṛkaṇḍu, you who are protected by the peaceful and stainless glance of compassion; salutations to you, O Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain; protect me, who has come to you for refuge. 31.
O Mahādeva, Lord of the World, Destroyer of Tripura, Śaṅkara! O Vāmadeva, Great God, protect me who has come to you for refuge.
Thus praised by those two, Śambhu, the God of gods, Maheśvara, being filled with affection, spoke to Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī.
Mahādeva said: O Sarasvatī, O Gāyatrī, I am pleased with you both. Choose a boon from me, whatever dwells in your hearts.
When this had been said by Hara, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī spoke to Mahādeva, the beloved of Pārvatī and the treasure-house of compassion.
Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī said: "O Lord, O God, O Sovereign of All, O Mine of Compassion, please restore our husband, the four-faced one, along with his vital breaths through your grace. (36)
O God, you are the father of us two, and we are both your daughters; therefore, O Destroyer of Tripura, protect us by granting us a husband.
O best of Brahmins, Śambhu, having been thus entreated by those two, said to Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī, "So be it."
Eager to join their heads to that very body of the Creator, those of excellent vows [offered] their heads there to the body of the Creator. (39)
Then Śaṅkara caused those many heads, along with the body, to be brought by the spirits headed by Nandin and Bhṛṅgin.
In an instant, he was sustained in the presence of Vāṇī and Gāyatrī; then, by Hara, that four-faced Lord of the World was restored.

O twice-born ones, at that very moment he rose up like one awakened from sleep. Then Prajāpati, beholding Śaṅkara adorned with the moon, together with his two wives, praised him with the most excellent words.
Brahmā said: Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Śaṅkara, the mine of compassion! 43.
Protect me from forbidden conduct, O Lord, ocean of compassion! By your grace, O Śambhu, may there never be any engagement in forbidden acts on my part.
"Let there be no further activity; protect me always in that manner. "So be it," the Lord of Girijā replied to Brahmā.
Henceforth, O Vidhi, do not commit negligence again; I am always the punisher of men who have set out upon the wrong path.
Having spoken thus to the four-faced one, O best of the twice-born, Mahādeva addressed Sarasvatī and Gāyatrī, pleasing them with his speech.
Mahādeva said: "O Gāyatrī, O Sarasvatī, by my grace, this husband of yours has returned, the four-faced one restored to life. (48)
"Let there be no delay; go with him to the world of Brahmā. Indeed, by your constant presence here at these two pools," (49)
Through bathing, there shall be for men liberation in the form of sāyujya; and by your names, there shall be this pair: Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī. (50)
This sacred ford shall attain eternal renown throughout all the worlds; indeed, among all sacred fords, these two fords shall always [be preeminent].
May it likewise bestow purity, destroy great sins, bring about great peace for men, and grant all desired objects. || 52 ||
This pair of holy fords, which generates grace in me and likewise brings pleasure to Viṣṇu, has never existed before, nor will there ever be another equal to them.
"Indeed, by bathing here, all desires of everyone shall be fulfilled. This great pair of pools has been created by you two in the world. (54)
And it shall become renowned by your name as a bestower of liberation; [even those] devoid of the worship of Gāyatrī and abandoned by the study of the Vedas [shall attain it]. || 55 ||

Those who are devoid of the domestic fire-ritual (aupāsana) and those who have abandoned the five great sacrifices shall obtain the respective fruits of those rites by bathing in your two sacrificial pits.
O best of the twice-born, others who are sinners and have abandoned their daily religious observances shall also become pure by bathing there in the two ponds.
"Sing to Sarasvatī and these three," having spoken thus, Maheśvara vanished in an instant while everyone was looking on.
Then, having obtained their husband, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī were filled with joy; O best of the twice-born, they went to the world of Brahmā along with him.
The venerable Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, has the presence of Sarasvatī and Gāyatrī on Mount Gandhamādana been described to you, along with its underlying cause.
Whoever listens to this chapter or reads it with devotion undoubtedly obtains the fruit of bathing in these two sacred fords.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Presence of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī on Gandhamādana," within the "Praise of the Gāyatrī-Sarasvatī Tīrtha" section of the Setumāhātmya, in the third part (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Sūta said: Now, therefore, O best of the twice-born, I shall fully relate a single purifying narrative concerning Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī.
Formerly, a twice-born man named Kaśyapa, having bathed in these two auspicious tirthas, was liberated from a very great sin that would have led him to hell.
The sages said: O sage, what sin indeed did this one named Kaśyapa commit, that by bathing here at both sacred fords he was instantly liberated?
O Sūta, by the power of your compassion, tell this to us who are full of faith; for those of us satiated by the nectar of your words, even thirst no longer exists.
The venerable Sūta said: I shall relate an ancient history (itihāsa) that establishes the majesty of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī, which destroys the sins of those who hear it.
The son of Abhimanyu, a king known by the name Parīkṣit, dwells in Hastināpura, protecting the earth according to dharma.
Once that king, devoted to the hunt, wandered in the forest; the monarch was sixty years of age and was tormented by hunger and thirst.
Searching with great care for that one lost deer in the forest, he saw a sage clad in bark garments absorbed in meditation and spoke to him.
"O Sage, I have just now pierced a deer with an arrow in the forest; O learned one, was it seen by you as it fled, terrified with fear? (9)
Established in meditative absorption, he said nothing at all because of his state of silence; then, that bow struck the shoulder of that great sage with its string.
Having placed the dead snake there, he departed for his own city in a state of anger. That sage indeed had a son named Śṛṅgin.
O best of the twice-born, Śṛṅgin had a friend named Kṛśa; then that friend named Kṛśa spoke to his friend Śṛṅgin.
"Your father now carries a dead snake upon his shoulder; O friend, let there be no pride in you, and do not indulge in vain arrogance. (13)
Enraged and wishing to cast a curse upon the king, Śṛṅgin said: "O fool-minded one, you who placed a dead snake upon my father! (14)
"Let him die within seven nights, bitten by the serpent Takṣaka! Thus did the son of the sage curse Parīkṣit, the grandson of Subhadrā.
Having heard that his son had cursed the king, the eminent sage named Śamīka spoke to his son Śṛṅgin.
Why have you cursed the king, the protector of all the worlds? How indeed shall we remain in a world without a ruler? (17)
Through anger, sin arises and you do not obtain happiness; for he who casts away the anger that has arisen by means of forgiveness alone [attains bliss]. 18.
In this world and in the next, such a person thrives in supreme happiness; for men endowed with forgiveness attain the highest good. (19)
Then Śamīka spoke to his own disciple named Gauramukha: "O Gauramukha, go and speak to King Parīkṣit."
"O high-minded one, having been bitten by the serpent Takṣaka as foretold by my son, come back to me quickly once again. (21)
Thus addressed by Śamīka, Gauramukha went to the king; having approached him, he spoke to the monarch regarding the son of Subhadrā, Parīkṣit.
Seeing a dead snake placed upon your father's shoulder by you, Śṛṅgin, the son of Śamīka, cursed you in a fit of rage. (23)
On the seventh day from this day, let the son of Abhimanyu be bitten by the great serpent Takṣaka and be consumed by the fire of his venom.
"O King, thus did Śṛṅgin, the son of that sage, curse you; it was to tell you this that his father sent me to your presence. (25)
Having thus addressed the king, Gauramukha departed quickly; after Gauramukha had gone, the king thereafter became devoted to grief.
Then that bull among kings constructed a vast pavilion in the middle of the Gaṅgā, which was sky-scraping, lofty, supported by a single pillar, and extremely wide.

Accompanied by those who know the mantras of the great Garuḍa, experts in medicinal herbs, and physicians, he applied himself with focused concentration to making an effort to destroy the poison of Takṣaka.
Accompanied by many eminent gods, brahman-sages, and royal sages, that king, a devotee of Viṣṇu, sat in that lofty pavilion.
At that moment, the brahmin Kāśyapa, the best of mantra-experts, set out to protect the king from the potent poison of Takṣaka.
