On the seventh day, the eminent brāhmaṇa, who was poor and desirous of wealth, [was present]; in the meantime, Takṣaka also arrived, disguised in the form of a brāhmaṇa.
Then, seeing Kaśyapa on the way, he addressed him: "O Brāhmaṇa, O great sage, tell me now, where are you going? (32)
Thus questioned, O twice-born ones, Kāśyapa then said to Takṣaka: "Today Takṣaka shall consume the great king Parīkṣit with the fire of his venom."
"I shall go near him to pacify that which will burn you. To the Brahmin who had spoken thus, Takṣaka replied again: || 34 ||
"I am Takṣaka, O best of the twice-born; once bitten by me, one cannot be cured even in a hundred years, nor even by ten thousand great mantras. (35)
"If you now have the power to cure what has been bitten by me, then [cure] this banyan tree, which is many yojanas in height."
"O Ten-headed one, revive him; you are capable of doing so. Having spoken thus, Takṣaka then bit that tree.
That tree, which was extremely dense, was reduced to ashes; however, a certain man had previously climbed up that tree. (38)
He too was then consumed by Takṣaka’s fiery poison-darts; neither Kāśyapa nor Takṣaka recognized that man.
Then Kāśyapa made his vow even as Takṣaka listened: "Let all these Brahmins now behold the power of my mantra. (40)
Having spoken thus, Kāśyapa, the best of mantra-experts, restored to life that tree which had been reduced to ashes by the fire of poison through the power of his mantras.
The man also was restored to life along with that tree. Then Takṣaka spoke to that Kāśyapa, who was skilled in mantras: || 42 ||
"O twice-born one, act in such a way that the word of the Sage does not prove false; I shall give you twice as much wealth as the king might grant you. (43)
"I give [this to you]; turn back at once, O best of the twice-born! Having spoken thus and having given him priceless jewels, that Takṣaka—
Having perceived with his vision of knowledge that the king was short-lived, that Kāśyapa turned back the Brahmin Maṃtraka.
Having obtained the jewel from Takṣaka, he returned silently to his own hermitage; at that very moment, Takṣaka summoned all the serpents and spoke to them.
Having approached that king while wearing the guise of sages, quickly present the offering-fruits to Parīkṣit.
Having said "So be it," all those serpents gave fruits to the king; and Takṣaka, at that time, [placed] within one of those jujube fruits— || 48 ||
Assuming the guise of a worm, he remained there intending to bite the king. Then the king was given [venom] by serpents disguised as brahmins. (49)
Parīkṣit, having given all the fruits to the elders learned in mantras, out of curiosity took a single large fruit in his hand.
At this moment, even the sun sank behind the western mountain; the people there [thought], "May the word of the sage not prove false. (51)
All the Brahmins and the kings spoke thus to one another; while they were all speaking in this way, that fruit became visible.
In the fruit was a red worm; King Parīkṣit also examined it all, and the king said, "Will this worm bite me today? (53)
O best of the twice-born, he placed that fruit, containing a worm, upon his ear; at that time, Takṣaka had previously been situated within that fruit in the form of a worm.
Emerging swiftly from that fruit, it coiled around the king’s palace; when the king was encircled by Takṣaka, those standing nearby fled in fear.
Immediately thereafter, O Brahmins, the king, along with his palace, was quickly reduced to ashes by the powerful poison-fire of Takṣaka.
Having performed the funeral rites for that king, the ministers, together with the family priest, installed his son named Janamejaya upon the throne.
They indeed consecrated the king with the desire to protect him from the elephant; then one named Kāśyapa arrived to save the monarch from Takṣaka.
O best of sages, that brahmin was censured by all people; reviled by everyone who was learned, he wandered through all the lands. (59)
He found no place to stay, whether in a village or even in a hermitage; wherever he went to various lands, he was driven away by the great folk there.

Driven away from those various regions, that descendant of Kaśyapa, censured by the people, sought refuge with Śākalya; having prostrated before the sage Śākalya, he made this representation to the high-souled Śākalya. (61)
Kāśyapa said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, Śākalya, beloved of Hari! (62)
Sages, Brahmins, and others, as well as my friends, censure me; I do not know the reason for this—why do these men revile me? (63)

Neither the killing of a Brahmin, nor the drinking of liquor, nor sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru, nor theft, nor the fault of social association has ever been committed by me at any time. (64)
O Sage, indeed no other sins have been committed by me; nevertheless, people, including my kinsmen and others, revile me in vain. (65)

"O Śākalya, if you know of any fault committed by me, speak it. Thus addressed by Kāśyapa, the great sage named Śākalya meditated for a moment and then spoke to that Kāśyapa, O best of the twice-born.
Śākalya said: "O you who are capable of protecting the great king Parīkṣit from Takṣaka..."
But on the way, he was stopped by Takṣaka, even though he was capable of treating those afflicted by poison, disease, and other ailments. || 68 ||
One who does not protect [the preceptor] out of greed, anger, desire, fear, avarice, or even delusion—him they call a slayer of a Brahmin. (69)
O best of Brahmins, he who does not protect a man afflicted by poison or disease is a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, and one who violates the teacher’s bed.
Furthermore, there is no atonement for one defiled by the fault of association with such people, nor for a seller of a maiden, nor likewise for a seller of horses.

For even in the case of an ungrateful person, an expiation is indeed prescribed in the scriptures; however, he who, though capable, does not protect one afflicted by poison or disease, [is beyond remedy].
No atonement for him has been declared, even by tens of thousands of penances; nor should a virtuous person eat in the same row as him. || 73 ||
One should not speak with him, nor should one ever look at that man; by merely conversing with him, one becomes a partaker in a great sin.
That great king Parīkṣit was virtuous and renowned for his merit; he was a devotee of Viṣṇu, a great yogi, and the protector of the four social orders.
Since you heard the story of Hari from the son of Vyāsa with devotion, yet failed to protect that king from the word of Takṣaka; 76.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, you are censured even by your kinsmen; for although that great king Parīkṣit lived but for a moment, he was [nevertheless] defiled by them.
Nevertheless, medical treatment should be administered by the wise until death, for as long as the life-breaths remain in the throat of a man who is about to die. (78)
"Medical treatment must be administered for that long; the course of time is crooked"—thus did physicians who have crossed the ocean of medical science proclaim this verse in ancient times. (79)

"Therefore, although you were capable of providing medical treatment, because you did not administer the remedy and turned back halfway, you have killed him. Thus addressed by Śākalya, Kāśyapa replied:
Kāśyapa said: "O observer of noble vows, tell me the means for the pacification of this fault of mine."
By means of which my kinsmen, along with my friends, might accept me. || 82 ||
"O Śākalya, beloved of Hari, show mercy toward me. Thus addressed by Kāśyapa, Śākalya, the lord of sages, meditated for a moment and then spoke thus to Kāśyapa out of compassion.
Śākalya said: I shall tell you the means for the expiation of this sin.
O twice-born one, you must perform that quickly; do not delay on the Gandhamādana mountain on the bridge by the southern ocean.
"O Brahmins, there are two sacred fords, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī; by merely bathing there, you shall become pure at that very moment. (86)
Men who touch the water and wind while reciting the Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī mantras shall shake off all sins and, becoming pure, go to heaven.
"Therefore, O Brahmin, go quickly to Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī. Thus was Kāśyapa addressed by that Śākalya, O best of the twice-born. (88)
Having bowed to the sage Śākalya and taken leave of that lord of sages, and being permitted by him, he departed for Gandhamādana.
Having gone there, Kāśyapa bowed with devotion to the two holy sites, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī, as well as to Daṇḍapāṇi and Bhairava.
Preceded by this resolve, he bathed in that sacred ford while observing the prescribed restraints; then, merely by bathing in those two sacred fords, Kāśyapa was liberated from sin.
He remained for some time on the banks of those two sacred fords (tīrtha). And at that time, O lords of sages, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī [were there]. (92)
The two goddesses appeared in embodied form, adorned with all ornaments; Kāśyapa, having bowed to them with devotion, paid his respects.

"Who are you two, endowed with such beauty and adorned with every ornament? asked Kāśyapa, his mind filled with joy upon seeing them. When he had thus questioned them, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī replied to him.
Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī said: "O son of Kaśyapa, we two are indeed Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī, who are dear to the Creator. (95)
Therefore, we two shall always abide here in the form of this sacred ford; by bathing in these two holy waters, we are now pleased with you.
"Choose a boon from me, O twice-born Kāśyapa, whatever is desired; we shall grant that which is sought by those who bathe here in these two sacred fords."
Having heard those words of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī, that Kāśyapa praised those two goddesses, the beloveds of Brahmā, with these foremost words: 98.
Kāśyapa said: I bow to the two auspicious goddesses, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī, who are the consorts of the four-faced one, the mothers of the world, and the very embodiment of knowledge. 99.

The two mothers of the Vedas, who bring about the creation, preservation, and end of the world, whose nature consists of the sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors (havya and kavya), and whose eyes are the moon and the sun.
I perpetually worship Vāṇī and Gāyatrī, the sovereigns of all the gods; and Girijā and Kamalā as well—you two alone exist for the welfare of the world. (1)
By the mere sight of you, the creation of the world and other such acts are conceived; by your closing of an eye, the constant dissolution of the worlds occurs. (2)
O Sarasvatī, from your opening [of the eyes] creation came into being for the sake of enjoyment; by the sight of you both today, I have indeed quickly become one who has fulfilled his purpose.
O best of sages, as well as O brahmins and kinsmen, please accept me today as one freed from sin by bathing here at these two sacred fords.
From now on, may my mind not incline toward sinful deeds; may it always incline toward righteousness—this alone is my supreme boon.
"O Great Goddesses, let it be granted; I desire no other boon," thus they were entreated by that Kāśyapa, O best of the twice-born.
Sarasvatī and Gāyatrī, the two goddesses dear to Brahmā, who are always the mothers of the worlds, spoke with affection to Kāśyapa.
"O Kāśyapa, all this that you have now requested as a boon shall indeed be yours before long through the grace of us both. (8)
Having spoken thus to him, O Brahmins, Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī then vanished in an instant from those two sacred fords.
Kāśyapa also, having accomplished his purpose, departed for his own country; all his kinsmen and the Brāhmaṇas [honored] Kāśyapa, whose sins had been removed.
And they accepted [the gift] by virtue of their immersion in the Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī. Thus, O Brahmins, has the liberation of Kāśyapa been narrated to you.
For by immersing oneself in the lake of the Gāyatrī, one is freed from sins; likewise, he who recites or listens to this chapter with a concentrated mind [is likewise purified]. || 12 ||
He who [worships] Sarasvatī in the Gāyatrī attains the fruit of bathing. || 113 ||

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Pacification of Kāśyapa’s Sins," within the "Praise of the Gāyatrī-Sarasvatī Tīrtha" section of the Setumāhātmya, in the third part (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The venerable Sūta said: Now, therefore, O lords of sages, I shall proclaim the majesty of all those holy fords situated within the Setu that have not yet been mentioned.
There is a sacred ford of great merit named Ṛṇamocana; by bathing here, the three debts of men are destroyed.
O best of the twice-born, as a twice-born man is being born, there are indeed three debts: those to the sages, to the gods, and to the ancestors.

By not practicing the life of celibate studentship (*brahmacarya*), one becomes a debtor to the sages (*ṛṣis*); and by not performing sacrifices and other rites, one becomes a debtor to the gods (*devas*). || 4 ||
Furthermore, by not procreating sons, one becomes indebted to the ancestors; even without celibacy, without sacrifice, and without a son [one remains in debt].
By merely bathing at the holy ford named Ṛṇamokṣa, human beings shall obtain liberation from their debts to the sages, the gods, and the ancestors.
Neither by celibacy, nor by sacrifice, nor even by the procreation of sons, are the sages, the gods, and the hosts of ancestors truly satisfied.

Just as people attain incomparable satisfaction upon being released from debt by means of a ritual bath, so too, what more need be said here of the poor and indigent debtors who bathe in this sacred ford?
There is no doubt that creditors will be freed from all debts by the liberation from debt that arises for men through bathing here.
Therefore, this sacred ford has been described by the name Ṛṇamocana (Liberation from Debt); hence, all those who are in debt should bathe here for the sake of being freed from that debt.
A holy place equal to this has never existed, nor will it ever exist; yet there is also another great holy place established here by the Pāṇḍavas.
This very sacred site, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is the one where the five Pāṇḍavas, headed by Dharmaputra, formerly performed their desired rites.
Indeed, ten thousand times ten million unsurpassed holy sites always maintain their presence here at this Pañcapāṇḍava-tīrtha.
Likewise, the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts are eternally present at the great sacred site of the Pāṇḍavas.
Whoever performs an ablution here and offers libations to the ancestors and the gods shall be liberated from all sins and honored in the world of Brahmā. || 15 ||
If one should feed even a single Brahmin on the pure bank of this sacred ford, by that deed he rejoices both in this world and in the next.
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even someone else entirely, having bathed in this best of holy fords, he certainly does not enter a degraded womb again.
That man who bathes at the great sacred ford of the Pāṇḍavas during auspicious conjunctions is the best of human beings; he shall never behold hell.
Whoever remembers this great sacred site of the Pāṇḍavas in the evening and in the morning has, without a doubt, bathed in all the holy waters, such as the Gaṅgā and others.
And where Indra and other deities performed sacrifices for the pacification of the Daityas—that other place known as Devatīrtha exists on Gandhamādana.
Having bathed at Devatīrtha, a man, liberated from all sins, shall attain imperishable worlds endowed with the fulfillment of all desires. || 21 ||
Whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man since birth, that is instantly destroyed by bathing in this Devakuṇḍa.
Just as Madhusūdana is indeed the foremost among all the gods, so too is the unsurpassed Devakuṇḍa the foremost among all sacred fords (tīrthas). 23.
He who might perform the Agnihotra sacrifice for a full hundred years, and he who might at any time perform a single bath in this Devakuṇḍa—[the latter is superior]. (24)
The merit of these two is exactly equal; there is no cause for doubt in this matter. In this divine sacred site (devatīrtha), both giving gifts and residing are difficult to attain.
Approaching a divine tīrtha and bathing there is exceedingly difficult to attain; having reached a divine tīrtha frequented by gods, sages, and ancestors, [one achieves great merit]. (26)
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu, whether staying for two days, three days, five, or even six.
Having dwelt on the bank of Devakuṇḍa, which destroys hell, one does not enter a mother's womb again and attains unsurpassed perfection.
Indeed, by bathing here for three nights, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice; by merely remembering Devatīrtha, a person is immediately liberated from sins. (29)
Having worshipped the ancestors and the gods on this bank of the holy ford, a person shall attain the fulfillment of all desires and obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a merit equal to this sacred ford; therefore, those seeking liberation must certainly bathe in the Devatīrtha.
O twice-born ones, the greatness of Devatīrtha has been recounted in brief for those humans who desire the attainment of fruits both in this world and the next.
I am not able to describe its greatness in detail; I shall now speak of Sugrīvatīrtha on Rāmasetu, which bestows liberation.
Having bathed here with devotion, a person attains the world of the Sun; by bathing at Sugrīvatīrtha, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Expiation for sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa also arises from going to Sugrīva-tīrtha; one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
By remembering it, one obtains the fruit of reciting the Vedas in their entirety; by merely fasting for a single day on the bank of that sacred ford (tīrtha), one gains that same merit.
O twice-born ones, there would be no destruction of great sins without expiation; however, one who performs an ablution there should also offer libations to the ancestors and the gods. (37)
By bathing at Sugrīva Tīrtha, one obtains eight times the fruit of the Āptoryāma sacrifice and attains the fruit of a human sacrifice (naramedha). || 39 ||
By bathing at Sugrīvatīrtha, a man becomes a rememberer of his past births; O brahmins, go to Sugrīvatīrtha for the attainment of your desired goals. (39)
O twice-born ones, thus has the majesty of Sugrīvatīrtha been recounted to you; now I shall proclaim to you the glory of Nalatīrtha.
By bathing at Nalatīrtha, a person attains the heavenly world; by bathing even once at Nalatīrtha, one is liberated from all sins.
Having stayed there for three nights and gratifying the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Agniṣṭoma, Atirātra, and other sacrifices.
O Brahmins, he shines like the sun and obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice. I shall now describe Nīlatīrtha, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
On the Setu, liberation was bestowed by Nīla, the son of Agni; by bathing at Nīlatīrtha, a man is released from all sins. || 44 ||
Having bathed at Nīlatīrtha, which bestows all desired objects, a man shall obtain a hundredfold the fruit of the Bahuvarṇya sacrifice.
One attains the world of Agni, endowed with the fulfillment of all desires. There is a sacred ford (tīrtha) created by Gavākṣa on the Gandhamādana mountain.
Merely by bathing there, he does not go to hell at all; there is a healing medicinal bath (agada-tīrtha) established at Setu, which bestows liberation.
By bathing here, a person attains the status of the Lord of the Gods (Indra). [One may also attain it] by means of an elephant, a gayal, or a highly powerful śarabha at this place.
The holy fords (tīrthas) that were established by Kumuda, Hara, and the powerful Panasa, as well as by all the other monkeys; || 49 ||
He who bathes in those holy fords at the highly meritorious Rāmasetu on Mount Gandhamādana attains immortality.
There is a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) established by Vibhīṣaṇa, which liberates one from sin, pacifies great suffering, and eradicates major diseases. || 51 ||
It is supreme, like fire for the masses of great sins, and the cause of destroying the sufferings of hells such as Kumbhīpāka.
It is auspicious, the destroyer of bad dreams, and the dispeller of great poverty; for whatever person bathes there, no sin remains in this world. (53)
He attains Vaikuṇṭha, from which there is no return; this is the group of four holy sites (tīrthas) established by the ministers of Vibhīṣaṇa.
O Brahmins, by bathing there at the Gandhamādana mountain, a person is liberated from all sins; and that river is the Sarayū.
He always remains there to serve Rāmanātha, the Great God; having bathed there, all men become freed from every sin. (56)
O best of the twice-born, they shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices, austerities, and the service of sacred fords; indeed, ten thousand crores of sacred fords [are present there].
All the rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, as well as the seven oceans, dwell upon this highly meritorious Gandhamādana mountain.
The holy hermitages of the sages, as well as sacred forests, and the unsurpassed sacred fields of Hira and Śaṅkara.
The Four-faced One (Brahmā) has declared that the Upavītāntara Tīrtha is always frequented by those who dwell on Mount Gandhamādana.
Thirty-three crores of gods, together with the hosts of ancestors, along with all the sages, yakṣas, siddhas, and kinnaras, dwell upon this bridge by the command of Lord Rāmacandra.
The venerable Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, thus has the majesty of the sacred fords been described by me.
By reading or hearing this, one is liberated from the mass of suffering and attains absolute liberation (kaivalya), which is free from rebirth.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Ṛṇamocana and Other Tīrthas," within the "Praise of All Tīrthas" section of the Setumāhātmya, in the third part (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 42 ||
Śrī Sūta said: Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the majesty of Rāmanātha, by hearing which a human being on earth is liberated from all sins.
The man who beholds even once the Liṅga installed by Rāma attains liberation in the form of union with Śiva.
Whatever merit is acquired by men in ten years during the Kṛta Yuga, that same merit is accomplished by them in a single year during the Tretā Yuga.
In the Dvāpara age, that same result is obtained in a month, and in the Kali age, it is attained in a single day; for men, that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold at every moment.
Without doubt, for those who behold Rāmanātha, all sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) are indeed present within the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara. || 5 ||
All the gods, sages, and ancestors are present there, whether once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or at all times.
O Brahmins, those who remember Mahādeva Rāmanātha, the giver of liberation, or who glorify him, are liberated from the cage of sins.
They indeed attain the non-dual Sāṃba Rudra, who is truth, consciousness, and bliss—the Liṅga known as Rāmeśvara, which was worshipped by Rāmacandra.
Merely by remembering it, even the torment of Yama shall not occur for those men who worship the great Liṅga Rāmeśvara even once.
They should not be known as mere humans, but rather as Rudras, without a doubt—those by whom the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara has not been worshipped with devotion.
Those men who behold the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara even once shall wander for a long time in the cycle of existence, which is crowded with suffering.
Of what use are gifts, of what use are vows, of what use are austerities, and of what use are sacrifices for those who do not contemplate the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara for even a moment? (12)
He shall be ignorant and sinful, as well as mute and deaf; he should be known as dull-witted and blind, and there shall always be a flaw in him.
O lords of sages, when the great Liṅga Rāmeśvara is seen even once, there shall likewise be the loss of his wealth, fields, sons, and so forth.
What is the use of Kāśī, or Gayā, or even Prayāga? What fruit is there for men on this earth who have obtained the rare human birth? (15)
Those who bow to and worship the great Liṅga Rāmanātha—their birth is indeed fruitful, and they alone have achieved their purpose, and no others. || 16 ||
When the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara is worshipped or even merely remembered, what need is there for Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śakra, or all the immortals?
Those men who are endowed with devotion toward the great Liṅga Rāmanātha, and those men who are engaged in bowing to it, remembering it, and worshipping it; || 18 ||
They do not behold sufferings, nor do they go to the abode of Yama, even if they have committed thousands of killings of Brahmins or tens of thousands of drinks of liquor. (19)
Upon seeing the god Rāmeśvara, all desires whatsoever completely dissolve; even those who always long for enjoyment and sovereignty in the abode of the gods [attain this]. (20)
Let them bow with joy even once to the supreme great liṅga at Rāma; whatever sins there may be, even those committed over ten million births. (21)
Upon seeing Rāmeśvara, those [sins] always go to destruction, whether one remembers him out of association, curiosity, greed, or even fear.
One who praises and worships the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara does not experience suffering either in this world or the next. (23)
One certainly attains a form identical to Rudra; there is no doubt in this matter. Just as a well-kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes in an instant, so too does he [reduce] [sins]. (24)
In the same way, all sins [are destroyed] by the sight of Rāmeśvara; devotion to the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara is said to be eightfold. || 25 ||
Affection for his devotees, satisfaction with their worship, personally worshipping him with devotion, and directing all bodily activity for his sake; (26)
Likewise, there is a devoted interest in hearing stories of his greatness, as well as the manifestation of physical transformations in one's voice, eyes, and body. (27)
Likewise, there is the constant remembrance of the great Liṅga Rāmeśvara, as well as making one's livelihood solely by depending upon the great Liṅga Rāmeśvara. (28)
Thus, even if such eightfold devotion exists in a barbarian, he alone is proclaimed to be an heir to the sacred fields of liberation.
Liberation is certain through non-dual devotion and the knowledge of Brahman, attained by ascetics of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) through the study of the Vedānta scriptures.
And that liberation occurs, O Brahmins, even without the arising of knowledge, vision, and hearing, as well as without a stage of life (āśrama) and likewise without detachment.
And for all castes and for those in every stage of life as well, it occurs simply through the sight of the great Liṅga Rāmeśvara alone.
Liberation, which grants freedom from rebirth, will occur without delay; for whether they be worms, insects, gods, or sages whose wealth is their austerity, [all shall attain it].
In the sacred field of Rāmeśvara, by the grace of Rāmanātha, [all sins] become equalized; therefore, do not harbor fear, thinking, "Many sins have been committed by me. (34)
No pride should be felt by people, nor the thought "I have performed a meritorious deed," once the great Liṅga Rāmeśvara has been beheld, which is Rudra himself accompanied by Ambā.
They shall neither be deficient nor excessive; rather, all people shall be equal, whoever beholds the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara with devotion. (36)
Even one who is learned in the four Vedas does not attain equality with that person on this earth who is a devotee of the great Liṅga Rāmeśvara, even if he be an outcaste. (37)
Gifts should be given to him and not to another, even if that other knows the three Vedas; for such is the destination of sages who are united with yoga and whose vital energy is drawn upward.
That is the destination for all living beings who behold Rāmeśvara; those men and twice-born ones who dwell in the sacred field of Śiva Rāmanātha [attain that same goal]. 39.
All of them should have five faces and their heads adorned with the moon; they are endowed with serpent ornaments and likewise possess the bull as their emblem.
Three-eyed, their limbs smeared with ashes, and adorned with crests in the form of skull-bowls, they become Mahādevas manifest with Ambā; of this there is no doubt.
Those men who go joyfully to the sacred field of Rāmanāthaśiva shall obtain at every step the merits of horse-sacrifices.
He who, having taken refuge at Rāmasetu for the propitiation of Rāmanātha, devoutly bestows a single village upon a Brāhmaṇa; || 43 ||
That man who offers a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water to Rāmanātha has given the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves.
With devotion one should give it; indeed, Rāmanātha shall protect it day and night within the great liṅga of Rāmanātha, the compassionate Śiva accompanied by Ambā. 45.
Devotion is extremely difficult to attain; even worship of Him is exceedingly difficult to attain. Hymn of praise is said to be rare, and remembrance is most difficult to attain. (46)
Those who take refuge with a heart full of devotion in the Liṅga Rāmanātheśvara, the Great God Trilocana; || 47 ||
Blessed are they, and victorious are they, both in this world and in the next, whose intellect is directed toward the great Liṅga Rāmanātha. (48)
He who does not worship the auspicious Liṅga Rāmanātheśvara day and night is indeed the most unfortunate person on earth. (49)
He who worships the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara with devotion is not merely a recipient of worldly enjoyment, liberation, or even kingdoms. (50)
He is the supreme recipient of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as of kingdoms; indeed, there is no merit greater than the worship of Rāmanātha.
Whoever, established in delusion, hates the Rāmanātheśvara Liṅga, has committed ten thousand killings of Brahmins, which cause rebirth in hell.
By merely conversing with him, a human being goes to hell. The gods have Rāmanātha as their supreme goal; the sacrifices have Rāmanātha as their supreme goal. (53)
All are devoted to Rāmanātha; therefore, nothing else exists [for them]. Hence, having abandoned everything, one should take refuge in Rāmanātha. (54)
If a person goes for refuge to the great Liṅga Rāmanātha, he shall certainly be free from wickedness and will go to the world of Śiva. 55.
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and bathing at sacred fords—that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by the service of Rāmanātha.
Meditating upon the Rāmanātheśvara Liṅga for two ghaṭikās, one uplifts one's entire family lineage and is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 57 ||
He who beholds Rāmanātha Maheśvara for even a single day shall become wealthy in this very world and, at the end, shall be born as Rudra.
He who, having risen at dawn, remembers Rāmanātha, the Great Lord, dwells as Śiva himself upon this earth in that very body. 59.
By the mere sight of one who beholds the great Liṅga Rāmanātha, the sin of other living beings is destroyed at that very moment.
Whoever beholds the Rāmanātheśvara Liṅga at midday, thousands of his acts of drinking liquor perish at that very moment.
Whoever beholds Rāmanātha with devotion in the evening, the sin arising from approaching the wife of one's guru is destroyed for him. (62)
Whoever praises Rāmeśvara with great hymns in the evening, thousands of his sins of stealing gold perish at that very moment.
If bathing at the tip of the bow and beholding Rāmanātha can indeed be obtained by men, what need is there for the service of the waters of the Gaṅgā?
That which cannot be obtained by serving the great Liṅga Rāmanātha could never be obtained by any other web of religious duties. (65)
He who never beholds the great Liṅga Rāmanātha should be known as a mere outcast (saṃkara), and not truly born from the seed of his father.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites the word "Rāmanātha" three times, the sin produced on the preceding day perishes in an instant. (67)
O you who are consecrated to the protection of devotees, at the great Liṅga Rāmanātha, even though food is available, why do you go about begging? (68)
When the great Liṅga Rāmanātha, the ocean of compassion, is pleased, all afflictions perish, just as frost vanishes at the rising of the sun.
If one should remember Rāmanātha at the moment of the departure of the vital breath, one will not be subject to rebirth and shall instead attain the state of Śaṅkara.
"O Rāmanātha Mahādeva, O ocean of compassion, protect me!"—he who constantly speaks thus is not afflicted by the Kali age. (71)
"O Rāmanātha, O Lord of the World, O Dhūrjaṭi, O Nīlalohita"—he who constantly speaks thus is not afflicted by Māyā. (72)
"O Blue-throated One! O Mahādeva! O Rāmeśvara Sadāśiva!"—by constantly speaking thus, a living being is never again tormented by desire. (73)
"O Rāmeśvara, O enemy of Yama, O swallower of the Kālakūṭa poison!"—by constantly uttering this, a person is not afflicted by anger. (74)
The man who constructs the temple of Rāmanātha with timber attains heaven, accompanied by thirty million members of his lineage.
He who constructs it with bricks shall attain Vaikuṇṭha; he who constructs it with stone slabs shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
By constructing a temple for this [deity] using various stones such as crystal and the like, a person attains the world of Śiva, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot. || 77 ||
By constructing the temple of Rāmanātha with copper out of devotion, one attains proximity to Śiva, seated upon half of His throne.
A man who joyfully constructs the temple of Rāmeśvara with silver attains the same form as Śiva and rejoices forever like Śiva himself. (79)
The man who devoutly constructs the temple of Rāmanātha with gold attains liberation in the form of union with Śiva.
A wealthy man constructs the temple of Rāmanātha with gold, while a poor man constructs it with clay; the merit of these two is remembered as equal.

O best of the twice-born, at the time of the bathing of the great Liṅga Rāmanātha, during the three junctions of the day, there shall be singing, dancing, and the playing of mouth-instruments and trumpets.
That man who plays other musical instruments with devotion is liberated from great sins and is glorified in the world of Rudra. || 83 ||
At the time of the consecration of Rāmanātha, the wielder of the trident, [he recited] the Rudrādhyāya, the Camaka, and likewise the Puruṣasūkta. || 84 ||
O Brahmins, one who recites the Trisuparṇa, the Pañcaśānti, the Pāvamānya hymns, and so forth, with devotion, does not experience hell.
Bathing the great Liṅga Rāmanātha with cow’s milk, curd, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and likewise with clarified butter, destroys the suffering of hell.
Whoever bathes the great Liṅga of Rāmanātha with ghee, the sin accumulated over births lasting an entire Kalpa perishes at that very moment. (87)
A person who bathes the great Liṅga of Rāmanātha with cow’s milk, having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
A person who bathes the great Liṅga of Rāmanātha with curd is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. || 89 ||
He who performs an oil massage with sesame oil for Śiva Rāmeśvara even once with devotion shall indeed dwell in the abode of Kubera.
Whoever performs even a single bath with sugarcane juice with devotion at the great Liṅga of Rāmanātha attains the world of the Moon.
A person who bathes the great Liṅga Rāmanātha with the essence produced from the juice of the *likuca* and mango attains the world of the ancestors.
Bathing Lord Rāmanātha Maheśvara with coconut water is proclaimed to be the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
By crushing ripe plantains against the great Liṅga of Rāmanātha, one destroys all sin and is honored in the world of Vāyu.
O best of the twice-born, by bathing the Great Lord Rāmanātha with water filtered through a cloth, one attains the world of Varuṇa.
O Brahmins, a person who bathes the Great Lord Rāmanātha with streams of sandalwood water shall attain the world of the Gandharvas.
By bathing Rāmeśvara with water scented with flowers, with water mixed with gold, and with water scented with lotuses—97.
Having ascended the throne of Mahendra, he rejoices together with him [Indra] amidst *pāṭala*, *utpala*, *kahlāra*, *puṇnāga*, and *karavīra* flowers.
O Brahmins, by consecrating the Great Lord Rāmeśvara with perfumed waters, one is liberated from even great sins. || 99 ||
And with whatever other fragrant and large flowers there were, having bathed that ocean of compassion with waters scented by their fragrance, [he worshipped him]. 100.
The great Liṅga Rāmeśvara is glorified in the world of Śiva with pure waters scented with cardamom, camphor, and lāmajjaka. || 1 ||
Having bathed the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara with a pure mind, one reaches the world of Agni and attains all desires.
He who provides earthen jars for the consecration of Rāmanātha shall live a hundred years in this world, possessing the fulfillment of all desires. || 3 ||
By the gift of a copper pitcher, one shall attain the status of Indra; by the gift of a silver pitcher, one enjoys the world of Brahmā.
By the gift of a golden pitcher, one is glorified in the world of Śiva; by the gift of a jeweled pitcher, one attains proximity to Śiva. || 5 ||
O twice-born ones, he who gives a milch cow for the sake of the consecration of Rāmanātha or even for the sake of the food offering shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
At the end of the body, he attains the form of Śiva and becomes a partaker of the world of Śiva—he who, at Rāmasetu and Dhanuṣkoṭi, utters the name "Rāmanātha. || 7 ||

Wherever one may perform a ritual bath, one shall obtain the fruit of bathing at the Setu; and whoever should cause the temple of Rāmanātha-Śiva to be plastered with lime, [attains that same fruit]. || 8 ||
I am not able to describe that merit, even in a hundred years, for that mortal who renovates the temple of Rāmanātha Śiva.

O twice-born ones, the fruit of merit for one who properly repairs what was broken or shattered in the temple of Śiva, the lord of the village, should be known to be a hundredfold greater than that of the original builder.
A person who joyfully offers lamps before Rāmanātha with devotion shall burn away even ten thousand sins of killing a Brahmin. (11)
Having pierced the veil of ignorance, one goes to the eternal Brahman. [One should offer] ghee, oil, as well as mung beans, sugar, rice, and molasses.
By bestowing [offerings] upon Rāmanātha, one attains the station of Indra; through the sight, worship, and remembrance of the great Liṅga of Rāmanātha, one attains that same state. || 13 ||
Even by touching it, sins go to destruction at that very moment; so too for one who gives a great bell and a mirror to Rāmanātha.

One shall dwell for a long time in the City of Śiva, enjoying the delights of hundreds of celestial chariots; [hearing] the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, war-drums, trumpets, clay drums, and so forth.
Offering bamboo and bell-metal instruments, as well as other musical instruments, with devotion to Rāmanātha, the Great God (Mahādeva). || 16 ||
He is honored in the world of Śiva for the duration of many yugas, traveling in celestial chariots of great splendor accompanied by the sound of musical instruments.
Whatever is given with devotion, even if it be very small, dedicated to Rāmanātha, that certainly yields infinite fruit for the donor in the hereafter. || 18 ||
Dwelling in the great sacred field of Rāmeśvara in the presence of Rāmanātha, one attains liberation from which there is no return. (19)
Life passes away swiftly; youth departs quickly; prosperity vanishes rapidly, as do wife, sons, and the rest. (120)
O Brahmins, wealth such as houses, fields, and so forth is subject to seizure by kings and others; likewise, everything including household utensils and the like is momentary.
Therefore, having completely abandoned all worldly indulgence, [one should resort to] the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara, which removes the suffering of afflicted men.
This should be heard, proclaimed, and remembered by the wise: he who indeed bestows villages upon the divine Lord Rāmeśvara. (23)
For at the end of the body commenced by him, he indeed becomes Śiva; Rāmanātha Maheśvara is the most excellent of all worthy recipients. 24.
By giving that to him, O twice-born ones, one enjoys true and infinite happiness; [one's] sin lasts only until the sight of the great Liṅga Rāmanātha. || 25 ||
By giving even a little to him, a person will certainly become a sovereign ruler of the earth; likewise, by giving a palm-leaf fan, a banner, an umbrella, sandalwood, and guggulu resin.
Those men who offer water-pots made of copper, bell-metal, silver, gold, or precious gems for the purpose of the consecration of Rāmanātha; || 27 ||
Those who produce flowers for the purpose of worshipping Rāmanātha are born as lords of the earth in their future existence.
They truly obtain the fruits of sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha when the great Liṅga Rāmeśvara is worshipped, bowed to, and remembered. (29)
O best of Brahmins, there is nothing whatsoever difficult to obtain regarding what has been heard or seen for that man who goes to serve the great Liṅga Rāmanātha. (130)
Upon seeing him, the flood of his sins quickly perishes; indeed, if Mahādeva Rāmanātha is beheld by men, [this occurs].
Of what use are the Vedas, or the Śāstras, or the frequenting of sacred pilgrimage sites? [One should offer] sandalwood, saffron, koṣṭha, musk, and likewise guggulu incense. || 32 ||
Whoever offers musk and sarala resin to Rāmeśvara shall be born here on earth as one wealthy and a master of the Vedas.
He who gives highly precious ornaments and garments made of pearls to the divine Lord Rāmanātha shall never encounter misfortune.
He who consecrates the great Liṅga of Rāmanātha with waters brought from the Gaṅgā is worthy of worship even by Śiva; of this there is no doubt.

O best of the twice-born, as long as death does not arrive, as long as old age does not overcome one, and as long as there is no impairment of the senses, for that very duration [one should act]. (36)
At that very time, Mahādeva Rāmanātha—Śiva—is to be constantly saluted, worshipped, meditated upon, and praised by those seeking liberation. || 37 ||
In all the Purāṇas and likewise in all the Śāstras, there exists no religious duty equal to the worship of the great Liṅga of Rāmeśvara. (38)
Those who constantly worship with devotion the Lord Rāmanātheśvara, the sovereign of great compassion, shall be endowed with happiness in this world of mortals. || 39 ||
Having enjoyed many pleasures together with their sons and wives, they shall, at the end of the fall of this body, attain eternal liberation.
Śrī Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, has the origin of Rāmanātha been narrated to you. Whoever should constantly hear this or read it with devotion—|| 41 ||
He shall obtain the unsurpassed fruit of service to Rāmanātha, and he shall attain the merit of bathing in the great sacred ford (tīrtha) of Dhanuṣkoṭi. || 42 ||

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Praise of Rāmanātha," in the Setumāhātmya of the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The sages said: O knower of the true essence of the meaning of all the Vedas, O you who have reached the further shore of the ocean of the Purāṇas, O you whose inauspiciousness has been removed by prostrating at the pair of lotus-feet of Vyāsa! (1)
O benefactor of all living beings through your instruction on the meaning of the Purāṇas, we have indeed been graced by you through this narration of the Purāṇa.
Now, O Sage, disciple of Vyāsa, O high-minded one, by this narration of the majesty of Setu, we have become exceedingly fulfilled. (3)
Just as Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, installed the liṅga, we desire to hear that; please tell it to us now.
The venerable Sūta said: O best of Brahmins, I shall now tell you for what purpose the Liṅga was installed on Mount Gandhamādana by Rāmacandra.

The wise and mighty Rāma, having been robbed of his wife by the powerful Rāvaṇa, was accompanied by an army of monkeys and joined by Sītā; thus, endowed with great strength, he went forth three times from the forest.
Having reached Mount Mahendra, he gazed upon the ocean; and having constructed a bridge across that shoreless sea, the scion of Raghu’s line [proceeded].
Having gone to the city of Laṅkā, which was protected by Rāvaṇa, at the onset of night on the full moon day when the thousand-rayed sun had set.
O brahmins, Rāma, together with his army, ascended Mount Suvela; then, at night, the powerful one beheld the Lord of Laṅkā situated upon his palace.
The son of the Sun struck his crown down to the ground; with his crown shattered, the Rākṣasa entered the interior of his house.
When the Lord of Laṅkā had entered his home, Rāma, accompanied by Sugrīva, descended from the mountain slope together with his younger brother and the army.
The heroic Rāma encamped his army near Laṅkā; then, as those monkeys were settling into camp, the followers of Rāvaṇa [attacked them].
Those of massive bodies, equipped with weapons and accompanied by their armies, approached: Parvaṇa, Pūtanā, Jṛmbha, Khara, Krodhavaśa, and Hari.
Prāruja, Aruja, and likewise Prahasta and the others—then, as those invisible and evil-minded ones were rushing forward, [the monkeys struck them]. 14.
There, Vibhīṣaṇa brought about their destruction by means of invisibility; they were being seen by the powerful monkeys who could leap great distances.
Slain on all sides, these [demons] fell down indeed, deprived of life; then Rāvaṇa, unable to endure this, went forth accompanied by his army.
Having arrayed all those monkeys, he warded them off with his arrows; then Raghava, emerging with his troops drawn up in battle formation, confronted the Ten-faced one.
Then, with great speed, he counter-attacked and a duel ensued; Indrajit, the son of Rāvaṇa, then fought with Lakṣmaṇa.
Sugrīva was [appointed] by Virūpākṣa, Kharvaṭa by Tāreya, Nala by Pauṇḍra, and Puṭeśa there by Panasa.
Other heroic monkeys as well, having engaged in single combat with the rākṣasas, waged a most tumultuous battle that increased the fear of cowards.
Then the rākṣasas, shattered by the monkeys of terrifying prowess, quickly fled from the battlefield toward Laṅkā, which was protected by Rāvaṇa.
When all the armies had been broken in battle by Indrajit, the son [of Rāvaṇa], who was indeed incited by Rāvaṇa, with exceedingly terrible serpent-missiles (nāgāstra), [the situation became dire].
O brahmins, both those sons of Daśaratha, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, having been pierced, were liberated by the high-souled Vainateya Garuḍa.
There, Prahasta, fierce in battle, having approached Vibhīṣaṇa with speed, roared and struck him with a mace.
Struck by that mace of terrifying velocity, the wise and mighty-armed one did not tremble, remaining as firm as the Himalayas.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, seizing his massive eight-bellied spear and consecrating it with mantras, hurled that great weapon toward his (Rāvaṇa’s) head.
As she fell with great force like a thunderbolt, the Rākṣasa was seen with his head severed, like a tree broken by the wind.
Seeing that night-stalker Prahasta slain in battle, Dhūmrākṣa rushed toward the monkeys with great speed.
Beholding the monkey army fleeing, the son of the Wind swiftly struck Dhūmrākṣa with an arrow at the forefront of the battle.
Seeing Dhūmrākṣa slain, the remaining night-stalkers reported everything exactly as it had happened to King Rāvaṇa.
Then the Lord of Laṅkā awakened Kumbhakarṇa as he lay sleeping, and once he was awake, Rāvaṇa dispatched him to the battle.
When Kumbhakarna had arrived, the enraged Lakṣmaṇa struck him in battle with the Brahmā weapon; he fell down, deprived of life.
There, Dūṣaṇa’s two younger brothers, Vajravega and Pramāthin, who were the equals of Rāvaṇa in battle, were slain by Hanumān and Nīla.
Nala, the son of Viśvakarman, struck Vajradaṃṣṭra, and Kumuda, the bull among monkeys, slew Akaṃpana.
On the sixth day, the defeated king then entered the city; likewise, Atikāya was slain by Lakṣmaṇa, as was Triśiras.
Devāntaka and Narāntaka were slain in battle by Sugrīva; both sons of Kumbhakarṇa were slain in battle by Hanumān.
Makarākṣa, the son of Khara, was slain by Vibhīṣaṇa; thereupon Rāvaṇa urged his son Indrajit forward.
Indrajit, having deluded those two brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with terrible arrows, stood in the sky while Aṅgada’s mount had been slain.
Accompanied by Kumuda, Aṅgada, Sugrīva, Nala, Jāmbavān, and others, all the monkeys fell down, slain by him.
Having thus struck down Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa along with their armies in battle, the exceedingly powerful Meghanāda then vanished into the sky.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, having bowed down again and again with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to Rāma, the ornament of the Ikṣvāku lineage. (41)
"O Rāma, subduer of enemies, having taken this water by the command of the king of kings, this Guhyaka has come into your presence."
"O Great King, O supreme ascetic, Kubera offers this water to you for the purpose of seeing beings who have become invisible. (43)
With your eyes touched by this, you shall see even invisible beings, or whoever else to whom you shall give this.
He too shall indeed behold beings who are hidden within the sky; saying "So be it," Rāma then accepted that water which had been offered with honor.
The mighty Lakṣmaṇa, as well as Sugrīva, Jāmbavān, Hanumān, and Aṅgada, performed the purification of their eyes.
Maiṇda, Dvivida, Nīla, and whatever other monkeys there were—all of them had their eyes purified by the water bestowed by Rāma.
Not seeing the heroic son of Rāvaṇa, who had vanished into the sky, the son of Sumitrā then rushed toward him as soon as he came within the range of his vision.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, whose auspicious marks were perfected and whose eyes had been purified by the waters sent by Kubera, struck out in great anger. || 49 ||
Then a great battle took place between Lakṣmaṇa and Indrajit, exceedingly wonderful and marvelous, like that between Śakra and Prahlāda.
Then, O twice-born ones, on the third day, with great effort, Indrajit was slain in battle by the more powerful Lakṣmaṇa.
Then the entire main force was destroyed by the wise Rāma; thereupon, Daśagrīva became enraged when his beloved son was struck down.
Mounting his chariot with a vast army, Rāvaṇa set out from the city intent on killing Jānakī, but he was stopped by Vindhya.
Then Mātali, the charioteer of Śakra, approached Rāma in battle with a chariot yoked to bay horses and radiant as the sun.
Having mounted the chariot of Indra, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma, slew the heads of the lord of the rākṣasas in battle with the Brahmā-weapon.
Then the gods, led by the sages, honored Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, who had slain the ten-necked one, with blessings joined with cries of victory.
The Siddhas and Vidyādharas, being thoroughly gratified, praised Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, and showered him with rains of flowers.
Rāma, accompanied by those hosts of gods and surrounded by his soldiers, and joined by Sītā and the son of Sumitrā, ascended the Puṣpaka chariot.
Having thus consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa as king in Laṅkā, Rāma, surrounded by the army of monkeys, followed Gandhamādana.
And having purified Vaidehī on Mount Gandhamādana, he remained there with the lotus-petal-eyed Rāma, surrounded by monkeys.
The hero, Lord of Laṅkā, together with his younger brothers and Vibhīṣaṇa, accompanied by his wife, and served by hosts of gods and the foremost of sages.
Sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest arrived to see him; placing Agastya at their head, they praised the Lord of Maithilī.
The sages said: Salutations to you, Rāmacandra, who bestows grace upon the worlds; salutations to him who descended to the surface of the earth to rid the world of Rāvaṇa.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of Tāṭakā’s body, the protector of Gādhi’s son’s sacrifice, the conqueror of Mārīca, and the one who took the life of Suvāhu. 64.
Salutations to you, whose lotus feet grant liberation to Ahalyā; salutations to you, who sportively broke the bow of Hara.
Salutations to you, who graced the festive occasion of the marriage with Maithilī; salutations to you, the one who brought about the defeat of Renukā’s son.
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, and due to the two boons granted by Kaikeyī, he has gone to the forest to make his father’s word true; salutations to him!
Salutations to you who gave the pair of sandals at the request of Bharata; salutations to you, the sole cause for Śarabhaṅga’s attainment of heaven.
Homage to you, the destroyer of Virādha, the friend of the king of vultures, who tore apart the limbs of the great and cruel illusory deer, Mārīca. || 69 ||
Having cremated Jaṭāyu, whose body was cast off in battle with the Lord of the World who had abducted Sītā, [he offered it] to the one who bestows absolute liberation.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of Kabandha, whose feet are worshipped by Śabarī, who attained friendship with Sugrīva, and who brought about the slaying of Vālin.
Salutations to the one who built the bridge across the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa; to the destroyer of all Rākṣasas and the taker of Rāvaṇa’s life.
Salutations to you, whose lotus feet are the boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra; salutations to the destroyer of the suffering of devotees, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Salutations to you, O auspicious Rāma, the cause of prosperity for the worlds; salutations to the remover of the sins of those who chant the holy names beginning with "Rāma. (74)
Salutations to you, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of all worlds; salutations to you, the embodiment of compassion, who are consecrated to the protection of devotees.
Salutations to you, O bestower of happiness upon Vibhīṣaṇa, together with Sītā; for by the slaying of the Lord of Laṅkā, O Rāma, the world has indeed been protected by you.
"Protect, protect us, O Lord of the World! Save us, O Lord of Jānakī! Having thus offered praise, all the sages, those best of the twice-born, remained silent.
Śrī Sūta said: He who recites with devotion this hymn of Rāmacandra, uttered by the sages, at the three junctions of the day, attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
For one who recites this at the time of departure, no fear arises; by the recitation of this hymn, spirits, vetālas, and the like [are overcome]. (79)
Diseases perish, they perish, and the accumulation of sins is destroyed; one desiring a son shall obtain a son, and a maiden finds a virtuous husband.
One who desires liberation shall obtain liberation; one who desires wealth shall obtain wealth; indeed, by reciting this hymn with devotion, one attains all desires. (81)
Then Rāma, having bowed down with palms joined in reverence, said to the sages: "I am to be attained for the sake of purification by all human beings. (82)
A living being within the range of my vision is always a vessel for liberation; nevertheless, the sages [should always regard them] with a mind endowed with devotion. (83)
I bow to those holy men who are satisfied with the attainment of their own true self, who are the greatest friends of all beings, free from egoism, peaceful, and whose vital energy is drawn upward.
Since I am a devotee of Brahman, I always honor the brahmins; therefore, I ask you something—please speak after due reflection. (85)

"O Brahmins, tell me the expiation for the sin that exists within me due to the killing of Rāvaṇa—the sin born from the slaughter of the descendant of Pulastya—by performing which, O best of sages, I shall not be released from that evil. (86)
The sages said: O Lord of vows, O Lord of the world, O bearer of the burden of protecting the universe! (87)
O Rāma, for the sake of benefiting the entire world, perform the worship of Śiva on this most meritorious peak of Gandhamādana, which bestows liberation.
O Rāma, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, perform the consecration of a Śiva-liṅga in order to remove the blemish arising from the slaughter of the ten-necked one.
Even the four-faced Brahmā is unable to describe the merit born from the installation of a Liṅga; how much less, then, can a lord of men do so? (9)
The sight of this liṅga which you are establishing on Mount Gandhamādana is equal for men to the sight of the Kāśī-liṅga. || 91 ||
It shall bear fruit multiplied ten million times more; of this there is no doubt. By your name, let this Liṅga attain renown in the world.
This Liṅga Rāmeśvara shall become famous in the world as the destroyer of the wood known as merit and sin, like a consuming fire. || 93 ||
O illustrious Rāmacandra, whose form is filled with compassion, do not delay in this matter of the installation of the Liṅga. (94)
Śrī Sūta said: O lords of sages, having heard these words of the sages, Rāma, the Lord of the Universe, then considered that auspicious time for two muhūrtas.
The scion of the Raghu dynasty dispatched Hanumān to Kailāsa, the abode of Śiva, in order to bring back a Śiva-liṅga for the purpose of its installation.
Rāma said: "O Hanumān, son of Añjanī, son of Vāyu, you of great strength! Go quickly to Kailāsa and bring the Liṅga; do not delay."
Having been thus commanded by Rāma, the heroic lord of monkeys slapped his arms and, having ascertained that the auspicious moment had arrived, waited for two muhūrtas.
While all the gods and the high-souled sages were looking on, he leapt up with great velocity, shaking Mount Gandhamādana.
Leaping through the path of the sky, he went to Mount Kailāsa; yet the monkey did not see Mahādeva, who was wearing the form of a liṅga.
On that holy mountain Kailāsa, protected by Śaṅkara, the son of Añjanā performed penance with devotion for the sake of attaining the Liṅga.
Seated upon kusha grass with its tips pointing eastward, O best of sages, he held his arms aloft, remained without support, held his breath, and had conquered his senses.
Propitiating Mahādeva, that son of the Wind-god obtained the Liṅga; meanwhile, O Brāhmaṇas, [it was attended to] by sages who perceive the ultimate truth.
Knowing that very little time remained until the future arrival of Hanumān, he spoke there to the high-minded Rāma.
O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, time is indeed passing away now; for that sand-liṅga which was fashioned playfully by Jānakī, O Lord— (5)
"Install today that great and unsurpassed Liṅga, the Talliṅga. Having heard these words, Rāma, together with Jānakī, acted with haste.

Accompanied by sages, having performed the auspicious rites of the marriage-thread with affection, [he did so] on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, under the conjunction of the weekday Wednesday and the lunar mansion Hasta.
On the day of Garānanda, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, when the Moon was in Virgo and the Sun in Taurus—on that most meritorious Daśa-yoga at Mount Gandhamādana.
In the middle of the bridge is Mahādeva, Hara, who assumes the form of a liṅga; he is Īśāna, clothed in animal skins, and bears the Gaṅgā and the crescent moon.
Rāma indeed installed an unsurpassed Śiva-liṅga; Rāghava worshipped the Lord together with Ambā (Umā) as residing within that liṅga.
Established within the liṅga, that Great God Śaṅkara, the Blessed One, together with Pārvatī, appeared visibly and granted an excellent boon.
O scion of Raghu, those who behold the Linga installed here by you for the sake of the high-souled Raghava, the refuge of all the worlds; ||| 12 ||
Even for those joined with great sins (mahāpātaka), their sin is destroyed; indeed, all sins whatsoever [are destroyed] by immersion at Dhanuṣkoṭi. 13.
O Indra among kings, O Rāmacandra, by the sight of the Rāma-liṅga, even great sins go to destruction; of this there is no doubt. (14)
Thus indeed did the Lord, the husband of Ambikā, grant the boon to Rāma; and in his presence, Rāghava installed Nandikeśa.
Then, O twice-born ones, for the sake of the consecration of the Lord, Rāghava pierced the earth with the tip of his bow and produced a well.
Therefore, taking up water, he bathed Śaṅkara; that most meritorious holy site is called Koṭitīrtha.

O best of sages, that majesty has been described by us previously: the gods, sages, nāgas, gandharvas, and hosts of apsarases—all these, as well as the monkeys, each fashioned a liṅga with devotion. (18)
Śrī Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, has it been narrated to you how [it was performed] by the wise Rāma.
Indeed, the Śiva-liṅga thus installed bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; whoever hears or reads this account of the installation of the liṅga [attains these]. (120)
He shall obtain the fruit of serving the Rāmeśvara Liṅga and attain union (sāyujya) through the majesty of Rāmanātha. || 121 ||

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Installation of the Rāmanātha Liṅga," in the Setumāhātmya of the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 44 ||
Śrī Sūta said: When the Liṅga had been thus installed by Rāma, the performer of effortless deeds, Hanumān arrived suddenly, taking the excellent Liṅga with him.
Having saluted the heroic Rāma, son of Daśaratha, that son of the Wind-god (Hanumān) subsequently bowed down to Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sugrīva.
Then, seeing the scion of the Raghus worshipping that Sītā-sand-liṅga along with the sages, the son of the Wind-god became enraged.
Exhausted by extreme fatigue and having exerted his efforts in vain, Hanumān, the son of Añjanā, spoke to Rāma, the knower of dharma.
Hanumān said: "O Rāma, I am ill-fated and born in vain, existing in this world solely for the sake of suffering. O Lord, I have been repeatedly tormented by Rākṣasas of cruel deeds. (5)
"May no woman with a parting in her hair ever give birth to a son like me, for because of such a one, infinite suffering is experienced in the ocean of worldly existence. (6)
"I was previously exhausted by service, and even more so by war; now there is endless suffering because you treat me with contempt. (7)
O scion of Raghu’s line, you were served by Sugrīva for the sake of his wife and kingdom, and by the Rākṣasa, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, for the sake of his own sovereignty.
"O high-minded Rāma, I have served you without any cause; indeed, today I have been commanded by you among many monkeys. (9)
In order to bring the Śiva-liṅga from Kailāsa, the best of mountains, I went quickly to Kailāsa, but I did not see the wielder of the Pināka bow there.
O Lord of the Raghus, having propitiated that bull-vehicled deity along with Sāmba through ascetic penance and having obtained his liṅga, he quickly returned.
O Lord, having now installed another linga made of sand, you worship it together with the sages, gods, and gandharvas.
"This Liṅga has been brought by me in vain from Mount Kailāsa; alas, my body becomes a burden to me, unfortunate as I am. (13)
O Great King, O Lord who delights Janaka’s daughter, O scion of Raghu, I am unable to endure this suffering of the earth.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? I have no refuge. Therefore, since I have been insulted by you, I shall cast off this body. (15)
Śrī Sūta said: O Brahmins, having thus lamented many times, the son of the Wind-god prostrated himself on the ground like a staff and became overwhelmed with anger and grief.
Seeing him, the Lord of the Raghus smiled and spoke these words, while all the gods, sages, monkeys, and rākṣasas looked on; he was consoling Māruti there and wiping away his sorrow.
Śrī Rāma said: "I know every matter, both my own and that of others."

O monkey, for one who has been born, for one currently being born, and even for one who has died, it is always the case that a single living being alone is born and dies by means of its own karma. (19)
Even the Supreme Self goes to hell; having thus ascertained the truth, do not grieve, O monkey. (20)
Constantly behold the Self, which is free from the three marks, the one stainless light, without support, and changeless.
Why do you indulge in grief, which is an obstacle to the knowledge of reality? O best of monkeys, always remain steadfast in the knowledge of reality. 22.
O monkey, constantly meditate upon the Self, which is self-luminous; abandon the sense of "mine-ness" regarding the body and so forth, for it is opposed to the knowledge of reality.
Constantly devote yourself to Dharma; abandon violence toward living beings; serve virtuous men, and subdue all your senses.
Constantly abandon the proclamation of the faults of others; O monkey, always perform the worship of the gods, such as Śiva and Viṣṇu. (25)
Speak the truth always and abandon your grief, O monkey; the knowledge of the oneness of the inner Self and Brahman has arisen from the substrate of delusion. (26)
In this [mind], the delusion of "beautiful" and "ugly," though imagined, presides over objects as if they were real, through the power of ignorance, as if they possessed true reality. (27)
O best of monkeys, disease arises for deluded men; bound by the power of passion and hatred, they fall under the sway of what is considered dharma and adharma. (28)
Gods, animals, humans, and other beings go to hell; even those who are most beautiful, such as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and the like. (29)
Since the body becomes impure through contact with it, how can it be happy? All objects, such as food and drink, are exceedingly beautiful [only when apart from it]. (30)
How can that body be pleasant, through contact with which excrement is produced; or how can fragrant, cool water become urine through contact with it? (31)
Therefore, tell me now, O monkey, how that alms-food could have become so excellent, since by contact with it these cloths have become exceedingly white and pure. (32)
They become soiled by perspiration; how then could they be beautiful? Listen to my ultimate truth, O Hanuman, son of the Wind. (33)
In this pit of saṃsāra, however, not even the slightest happiness is found. First, a living being undergoes birth, and after that, childhood. (34)
Afterwards he attains youth, and from that he experiences old age; afterwards he meets death, and then he undergoes rebirth. (35)
It is solely due to the power of ignorance that a human being experiences suffering; however, upon the cessation of that ignorance, one attains supreme happiness. (36)
The cessation of ignorance occurs through knowledge alone, not through action. Knowledge is indeed the Supreme Brahman; knowledge is that which is born from the statements of the Vedānta.
And that knowledge arises for one who is dispassionate, and not for anyone else; it arises for the primary qualified disciple through the grace of the teacher. (39)
When all desires that dwell within his heart are completely liberated, then the mortal becomes immortal even here and attains the Supreme Brahman.
Whether waking or sleeping, eating or standing, the cruel Kṛtānta (the God of Death) constantly drags this person away.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall; all unions end in separation, and life ends in death. (41)
Just as for ripe fruits there is no fear other than falling, so for men who are born there is no fear other than death. 42.
Just as a house with sturdy pillars perishes in time when it has grown old, so too do men perish, having fallen under the sway of old age and death.
As day and night pass, the lifespan of men perishes; grieve for yourself—why do you grieve for another? (44)
O Lord of Monkeys, life perishes even for one who stands still as well as for one who runs; death goes forth together with him, and death sits down together with him. (45)
Even after traveling to distant lands, death returns with him; wrinkles have appeared upon his body, and his hair has turned white. (46)
The body decays through old age as well as by means of asthma, cough, and other ailments, just as one piece of wood might meet another piece of wood in the great ocean. (47)
Having come together, O monkey, they depart again through the power of time; so it is with wife and son, as well as daughters-in-law, fields, and wealth. (48)
O monkey, they sometimes travel together and then again go elsewhere, just as some traveler standing on the road [joins] another traveler going along the path. (49)
"I too shall go along with you," he said; then, having stayed together for some time, the two of them went elsewhere once more.
Thus, O monkey, the union with wife, sons, and others is perishable; death certainly occurs together with the very birth of the body. (51)
For there is never any remedy against death, which is inevitable; yet, upon the fall of this body, the embodied soul follows the course of its karma. (52)
O child, having reached another body, it abandons the previous body; O monkey, for living beings there is never residence in one place alone. (53)
By the power of their respective karmas, all are separated from one another; just as the bodies of living beings perish and come into being. (54)
O best of monkeys, birth and death do not exist for the Self; therefore, O son of Añjanā, [realize] non-dual knowledge free from sorrow. (55)
Contemplate day and night the stainless Brahman, whose nature is existence; the action performed by you is performed by me, and likewise, the action performed by me is performed by you.
Therefore, O monkey, the installation of my own liṅga must take place before you install yours; for the auspicious moment has passed, and the sand-liṅga was made by Sītā.
Therefore, do not harbor anger or grief, for this has been established here by me. This Linga, which came from Kailāsa, has been installed on an auspicious day. (58)
By your name, let this Liṅga attain fame throughout the three worlds; having seen Hanūmadīśvara, Rāghaveśvara is to be visited. (59)
"O monkey, the hosts of Brahmarākṣasas have been slain by you; therefore, because of the installation of this Linga under your own name, you shall be liberated. (60)
Beholding the auspicious one named Hanumān, who was given by Hara himself, as well as Rāmanātha, a man shall have fulfilled his purpose.
Even from a distance of a thousand yojanas, by remembering the Liṅga of Hanumān and also by remembering Rāmanātheśvara, one shall attain liberation through union (sāyujya).
By him all sacrifices were performed and penance was practiced in its entirety, by which he beheld the two Great Gods, Hanumāneśvara and Rāghaveśvara.
The Linga established by Hanumat, the Linga which was made by me, the Linga of Janaki, and the Linga of Lakshmaneshvara—[these are the four]. (64)
That which was done by Sugrīva, and by Nala the builder of the bridge, and that which was done by Aṅgada, Nīla, and likewise by Jāmbavān.
Also, the jewel-liṅga which was installed by Vibhīṣaṇa, and the liṅga made by Indra and others which was installed by Śeṣa and the rest; || 66 ||
Thus, this Śiva shines forth directly in eleven forms; for Maheśvara is ever present within these liṅgas. (67)
Therefore, for the sake of purifying the flood of your own sins, install Maheśvara; otherwise, O highly fortunate one, if you should destroy the Liṅga, [the consequence will be great].
"O child, this sandbank was established here by me together with Sītā; thereafter, I shall install this linga fashioned by you. (69)
Having reached Pātāla, Sutala, Vitala, Rasātala, and Talātala, he stands having pierced through all of them.
"Whose power would there be to break this linga established by me? Arise, O monkey, and remove this linga which was installed by me! (71)
"Install the Liṅga brought by you quickly; do not grieve. Thus addressed, the monkey, whose true nature was unknown [to others], then bowed to him. (72)
I shall swiftly remove that excellent sand-liṅga and respectfully install the liṅga brought from Kailāsa.
"Upon my departure, what weight would this sandy mass become? Having reflected thus with his mind alone, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, [proceeded].
While all the gods, sages, monkeys, and rākṣasas were looking on, and while Rāmacandra and Lakṣmaṇa were also watching.
Even as Vaidehī was looking on, the powerful one forcibly seized that sandy image with his hand, using all his effort and speed.
Even though the son of the Wind-god exerted himself with great effort, he was not able to move that sand linga by his power. || 77 ||
Then, letting out a roar of triumph, that bull among monkeys raised his tail and, by his own power, cast it away with both hands.
Although the monkey, the son of the Wind, attempted to shake it in many such ways, he was not at all able to move it. (79)
Having wound his tail around that [pillar] and touching the earth with both hands, the monkey, son of the Wind, then leapt swiftly into the sky.
Shaking the entire earth with its seven continents and mountains, he fell unconscious within the distance of a *krośa* from the *liṅga*, vomiting blood.
O Brahmins, Hanumān fell to the surface of the earth with his limbs trembling; and from the mouth and the two eyes of the son of Vāyu as he was falling—
O best of the twice-born, a torrent of blood flowed from his nostrils, the openings of his ears, and his anus, and that became a pool of blood.
Then the entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, raised a cry of "Alas! as both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa rushed forward together with the monkeys.
Then those two heroes, accompanied by Sītā and the monkeys, were both exceedingly powerful; yet, O brahmins, they remained overwhelmed with grief along with Jānaki.
O Brahmins, they then shone upon Mount Gandhamādana like the moon and the sun accompanied by the host of stars at night. || 86 ||
They both beheld Hanumān with his body crushed, fallen unconscious upon the ground, vomiting blood from his mouth.
Seeing this, all the monkeys cried out "Alas! Alas! and fell to the ground; they tenderly took Sītā in their hands and placed her upon Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god.
"Father! Father! [he cried] as he touched him fallen upon the surface of the earth; Rāma too, seeing Hanumān, the lord of monkeys, fallen.
O twice-born ones, having placed him upon his lap and stroked his body with both hands, he shed tears from his eyes and spoke to Vāyujā.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction on the Knowledge of the Reality of Rāmacandra," in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śrī Rāma said: O bull among monkeys, in the Pampā forest we, who were miserable, were comforted by you after you had established friendship with the son of the Sun.
Having seen you, our father, our kinsmen, and even our mother Kausalyā, we do not remember them at all; indeed, you have done much for me.
For my sake, you crossed the ocean extending many yojanas; even Maināka, the best of mountains, was struck by the blow of your palm. (3)
Surasa, the mother of the nāgas, was conquered by you for my sake; and you slew the exceedingly cruel rākṣasī Chāyāgrahā.
Having reached Suvela in the evening and struck Lanka with your hand, you went to the house of Ravana for my sake, O great monkey! (5)
Having searched for Sītā in Laṅkā during the night, you became free from fear; yet, not finding Jānakī, you subsequently went to the Aśoka grove.
Having paid homage to Vaidehī and presented the token of recognition, he took from Jānakī’s hand the crest-jewel for my sake.
"O great monkey, you destroyed the trees of the Aśoka grove; therefore, [I shall send] eighty thousand Rākṣasas named Kiṃkaras."
For my sake, you indeed slew those who were equal to Rāvaṇa in battle, who swarmed with foot-soldiers, horses, elephants, and chariots, and who possessed great strength and prowess.
Then he slew Jambumālin, the son of Prahasta, who had arrived, as well as the seven sons of his ministers, who possessed the splendor of the seven-flamed fire.
Afterwards, you led the five generals to the abode of Yama; then, at the forefront of the battle, you slew Prince Akṣa.
Then Indrajit led him to the auspicious assembly hall of the lord of the rākṣasas; there, he treated the Lord of Laṅkā with contempt and insulted him with his speech.
O son of the Wind, you have shattered the city of Laṅkā for my sake; now you have returned once more to the great mountain Ṛṣyamūka.
You have thus undergone such great suffering for my sake; you lie here upon the earth, giving vent to your grief for me. (14)
"I shall give up my life if you are dead, O son of the Wind! What use have I for Sītā, or for my younger brother Lakṣmaṇa? (15)
What need have I of Bharata, or of Śatrughna, or even of royal fortune? I have no need for the kingdom either, O monkey, if you have departed. (16)
"Arise, dear Hanumān; why do you lie upon the ground today? O mighty-armed monkey, prepare a bed for me so that I may sleep. (17)
"Bring tubers, roots, and fruits for my food; I shall go to bathe today, so bring the water-jar quickly. (18)
"Bring forth deerskins, garments, and darbha grass; O Hari, bound by the Brahmāstra, I have been liberated by you. (19)
Indeed, by bringing the medicinal herb together with your brother Lakṣmaṇa, you became the giver of life to Lakṣmaṇa and the destroyer of the pride of Rāvaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya.
With you as my ally in battle, having slain the exceedingly powerful Rākṣasa heroes such as Rāvaṇa and others, I recovered Maithilī.
O Hanumān, son of Añjanā, destroyer of Sītā’s grief! How is it that you have thus abandoned Lakṣmaṇa, myself, and Jānakī?
"Why did you go without reaching Ayodhyā? Where have you gone, O great hero, thorn to the great rākṣasas? (23)
Seeing his face thus, the joy of the Raghus, rendered speechless, wept and drenched the son of the Wind with a torrent of tears.
Then, O twice-born ones, the son of Vāyu, having gradually recovered from his swoon, [beheld] him who had arrived for the sake of protecting the world terrified by the fear of Paulastya.
Having assumed a human form, he is the unborn and all-pervading Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by Jānakī and Lakṣmaṇa, and surrounded by monkeys.
Resembling a dark rain-cloud, sprinkled with the dust of battle, enriched by the beauty of his mass of matted locks, and possessing eyes as long as lotus petals.
And he beheld the joy of the Raghus, the slayer of enemies, exhausted from many battles and being praised by celestial sages, ancestors, and kinnaras.
Having seen Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, whose mind was overflowing with compassion, that monkey’s entire body was suffused by the touch of the Lord of the Raghus’ hand. (29)
Having prostrated himself on the ground like a staff with palms joined in reverence, O twice-born ones, he praised the Lord of Jānakī with hymns that were enchanting to the ear.
Hanumān said: Salutations to Rāma, to Hari, to Viṣṇu, the all-powerful; to the primordial god, the divine, the ancient, the wielder of the mace. (31)
To you, the Great Soul, who are eternally seated upon the Puṣpaka throne, and whose lotus feet are attended by the joyful host of monkeys.
