Salutations to the one who crushed the lord of the Rākṣasas, the ordainer of the world's welfare; salutations to the thousand-headed and thousand-footed one.
Salutations to you, the thousand-eyed, the pure, Rāghava, and Viṣṇu; salutations to you, the remover of the suffering of devotees, the husband of Sītā.
Salutations to you, Hari, in the form of Narasiṃha, the tearer of the king of the Daityas; salutations to you, Varāha, who lifted up the earth with your tusk.
Salutations to You, Trivikrama, the destroyer of Bali’s sacrifice; salutations to the one in the form of Vāmana, salutations to the upholder of Mount Mandara.
Salutations to you in the form of the Fish, the protector of the three Vedas; salutations to you as Paraśurāma, the ender of the Kṣatriyas.
Salutations to you, the slayer of Rākṣasas; salutations to you who take the form of Rāghava; O Mahādeva, O most formidable one, O piercer of the great bow! || 38 ||
Salutations to the one who brought an end to the Kṣatriyas, who caused terror to the cruel Bhārgava, who removed the torment of Ahalyā, and who wields the bow.
To the one who took the life of Tāṭakā, who possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants, and who shattered the broad chest of Vālin, which was as hard as a rock; 40.
Salutations to the one who destroyed Māyā and the deer [of lust], who removes ignorance, and who, in the form of Agastya, dried up the ocean of suffering consisting of ten chariots (ten directions).
To the sun of the solar dynasty, the witness of the world, who dispels the pride of the ocean tossed by many waves, and who captivates the mind of the princess of Mithilā.
Obeisance to you, O Lord of Kings; obeisance to you, Hari, the husband of Jānakī; obeisance to you, the Tāraka-Brahman, O lotus-eyed one.
Salutation to Rāma, to Rāmacandra, the most excellent one, whose nature is bliss, who is dear to Viśvāmitra, and the destroyer of Khara. 44.
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods, O bestower of fearlessness upon devotees! Protect me, O Rāmacandra, ocean of compassion; salutations be unto you. (45)
Protect me, O Raghava, who art beyond even the reach of the words of the Vedas! Save me with compassion, O Rama; I come to you for refuge. (46)
O Hero of the Raghus, now dispel my great delusion during bathing, sipping water, eating, and in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. (47)
In all circumstances and everywhere, protect me, O delight of the Raghus! Who in the three worlds is capable of praising your greatness? (48)
"O descendant of Raghu, you alone truly know your own greatness. Having thus praised Rāmacandra, the ocean of compassion, the son of Vāyu [spoke]. (49)
He also praised Sītā with a heart full of devotion: "O Jānakī, I bow to you, the destroyer of all sins. (50)
She who destroys the battle of poverty for her devotees, who bestows their desired objects, the daughter of the King of Videha, and the one who brings joy to Rāghava.

I bow to Sarasvatī, the daughter of the Earth, who is knowledge, the auspicious primordial nature (prakṛti), the destroyer of the sovereignty of Rāvaṇa, and the fulfiller of the desires of her devotees.
I bow to you, the daughter of Janaka, the foremost among women devoted to their husbands, the sinless one who is the supreme sovereign of grace, and the beloved of Hari.

I bow to the auspicious Lakṣmī, the daughter of the Ocean of Milk, who is the embodiment of the three Vedas, who is Umā herself, the knower of the Self, and who is inclined toward bestowing her grace. 54.
I bow to Sītā, the sister of the Moon, beautiful in every limb; I bow to her who is the abode of Dharma, compassion itself, and the mother of the Vedas.
I bow to Sītā, whose abode is the lotus, who holds a lotus in her hand, whose dwelling is the chest of Viṣṇu, who resides in the moon, and whose face resembles the moon. 56.

I bow to Sītā, whose form is joy, who is the perfected one, auspicious, the bringer of welfare, and the virtuous mother of the universe; she is the beloved of Rāmacandra and possesses limbs entirely beyond reproach—I worship her constantly with my heart. (57)
Śrī Sūta said: Having thus praised Sītā and Rāmacandra with devotion, Hanumān—
O best of the twice-born, his face drenched with tears of joy, he remained silent; for this [account] which destroys sin was narrated by the son of Vāyu.
The person who recites this hymn to Śrī Rāmacandra and Sītā every day attains great sovereignty and whatever he desires.
Numerous grains from many fields, milch cows yielding plenty of milk, longevity, knowledge, sons, and even a beautiful wife—(61)
O Brahmins, by reciting this hymn even once, one undoubtedly attains [this fruit]; by the recitation of this hymn, one shall never go to hell. (62)
Even the most grievous sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin, are destroyed; liberated from all sins, one attains liberation at the end of the body.
O Brahmins, having been thus praised by the son of Vāyu, Rāghava, the Lord of the World, together with Sītā, then spoke to Hanumān.
Śrī Rāma said: O best of men, this rash act was committed by you either out of ignorance, or even [by one like] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or the gods beginning with Śakra. (65)
"This linga established by me cannot be uprooted; due to an offense against Mahādeva, he has fallen down today in a swoon. (66)
Henceforth, let no offense be committed against the trident-bearing Lord Śiva along with Ambā. From this day forward, this pool shall be known throughout the three worlds by your name.
O best of monkeys, may you attain renown wherever you fall; by bathing here, there shall be the destruction of multitudes of great sins.
Born from the matted locks of Mahādeva, Gautamī is the best among rivers; she bestows the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices upon those men who bathe in her.
"O monkey, the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī are each a hundredfold more [meritorious] than that; at whatever place these three rivers flow together," (70)
O monkey, it is taught that bathing at the confluence there yields a thousandfold the fruit that men obtain from bathing in these rivers.
Having attained this rare human birth, one undoubtedly obtains that fruit by bathing in this Kuṇḍa of yours on the bank of the Hanumatkuṇḍa. (72)
O monkey, those whose ancestors depart disappointed and angry because he does not perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) with a mind endowed with devotion—[for them there is no peace]. (73)
Even the sages, as well as the gods along with Indra and the Cāraṇas, become angry with him by whom nothing has been given and no oblation offered on the bank of Hanumat-kuṇḍa.

That life is indeed lived in vain, bringing suffering both here and in the hereafter, by whom no water mixed with sesame seeds is offered near Hanumatkuṇḍa; yet his ancestors rejoice and drink from streams of clarified butter.
Śrī Sūta said: O Brahmins, having heard these words spoken by Rāma, that son of Vāyu [Hanumān]—
To the north of Rāmanātha, the son of Vāyu joyfully installed the Liṅga brought by himself, by the command of Rāmacandra. || 77 ||
It is directly perceived by all that even Hara bears three folds produced from its tail, which encircles the body of Kapila; and with joy, he establishes Gaurī in the northern direction.
Śrī Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, has been narrated to you that purpose for which the Liṅga was installed by Rāghava on the Setu, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
Whoever should read this chapter or listen to it with a concentrated mind, having shaken off their sins here, is glorified in the world of Śiva.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Cause for the Installation of the Rāmanātha Liṅga," in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O Sūta, O great sage, how did the high-souled Rāghava incur the sin of killing a Brahmin from the slaying of the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa?
O Sūta, from the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, the sin of Brahman-slaughter arises; yet the Ten-necked one was not a Brāhmaṇa—how is that so? Tell us, O Sage. (2)
The cruel sin of killing a Brahmin has befallen the wise Rāmacandra; out of compassion, tell this now to us who are full of faith.
Thus questioned by the residents of the Naimiṣa forest, the Sūta then began to speak the excellent answer to their question. (4)
Śrī Sūta said: O twice-born ones, there was a son of Brahmā of great splendor named Pulastya; his son was the renowned Viśravas. || 5 ||
The son of that Pulastya was Viśravas, a bull among sages; for a long time he performed a penance that was extremely difficult even for the gods to accomplish.
While he was performing those austerities, however, a Rākṣasa named Sumālī indeed roamed throughout the entire earthly realm from the subterranean world (Pātāla).
Wearing golden neck-ornaments and armlets, his complexion like that of a dark rain-cloud, he took his daughter, who was like the goddess Śrī deprived of her lotus.
While wandering upon the surface of the earth, he once beheld Kubera, the son of Viśravas and lord of wealth, seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot.
O best of Brahmins, that Rākṣasa Sumālī then reflected: "If we were to have a son equal to Kubera... (10)
"We all, the Rākṣasas, are indeed flourishing and free from fear from any quarter. Having reflected thus, the Lord of the Rākṣasas spoke to his own daughter.
"O beautiful Kaikasī, today is the time for your son's marriage; today you have reached the prime of youth, so you must indeed be given away to a suitor."
By not giving away their daughters, fathers experience suffering; moreover, O auspicious one, you are like the goddess Lakṣmī, preeminent in all virtues, in your daughter.
O auspicious one, you are not sought after by men for fear of being rejected; for the state of being a father of a daughter brings sorrow to all who desire honor. (14)
"I do not know which suitor might choose you, O maiden; therefore, choose the twice-born sage Viśravas, the son of Pulastya."
"Go yourself and choose one born of the grandfather's lineage; there is no doubt that your sons will become equal to Kubera. (16)
Having heard those words, that maiden Kaikasī, out of reverence for her father, accepted his speech with a pure smile, saying, "So be it. (17)
Having gone to the leaf-hut of the sage Viśravas, O best of sages, she stood near him, feeling ashamed with her face cast downwards.
At that moment, O Brahmins, the wise son of Pulastya was performing the Agnihotra sacrifice, resembling a blazing fire.
Disregarding the extremely cruel hour of twilight, the fair-browed Kaikasī approached that sage out of respect for her father's command.

Standing there, she scratched the ground with the tip of her big toe while keeping her face cast downward. Then, O Brahmins, having observed that slender-waisted Kaikasī, whose face resembled the full moon, Viśravas spoke to her with a smile.
Viśravas said: "O beautiful one, whose daughter are you, and from where have you come here?"
"O lady of pure smiles, for what purpose do you remain here? O blameless one, tell me everything today exactly as it is. (23)
O twice-born ones, having been addressed thus, that maiden Kaikasī, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the sage, bowing low and endowed with humility.
O Sage, illuminator of the lineage of Pulastya, by the power of your asceticism, you ought to understand my intention correctly this very day.
"I am indeed named Kaikasī, O Sage, the daughter of Sumālī; by my father's command, O Brahmin, I have come into your presence. (26)
"O Śeṣa, you ought to know this today through the vision of your knowledge, without any doubt. Having meditated for a moment, the sage Viśravas then spoke to Kaikasī.
"O fair-browed one, I know the desire that has arisen in your mind. You are longing for a son; do not go to me now, O auspicious lady. (28)
"Since you have now come to me at this cruel hour of evening, having become desirous of a son, therefore I speak to you. (29)
Listen attentively, O blameless Kaikeyī, to Rāma—[a man] who is cruel, of cruel appearance, and fond of a cruel lineage. (30)
"You shall give birth to sons who are Rākṣasas of cruel deeds. Having heard those words, Kaikasī bowed down to him.
With palms joined in reverence, O twice-born ones, she said to the son of Pulastya: "It is not fitting for me to obtain such sons as these from you, O Blessed One."
Thus addressed, the sage said to that slender-waisted Kaikasī: "Your last son shall be one who accords with my lineage."
"O Brahmins, he shall be righteous, learned in the scriptures, and peaceful, not one who acts like a Rākṣasa. Having spoken thus, Kaikasī, after some time had passed— || 34 ||
She gave birth to a cruel son in the form of a Rākṣasa, terrifying and fearsome, having five heads, twenty arms, and evil intent. || 35 ||
With copper-colored lips, a dark face, and red beard and hair, possessing great fangs and a massive body, he was always a source of terror to the worlds.
He became known as Daśagrīva and likewise bore the name Rāvaṇa; after Rāvaṇa was born a son named Kumbhakarṇa.
From her was born the cruel Rākṣasī named Śūrpaṇakhā; then, from Kaikeyī, there was born the one known as Vibhīṣaṇa.
The youngest son was the wise and righteous Dhīmat, who was learned in the Vedas and the Śāstras. O twice-born ones, these were the sons of Viśravas, beginning with Daśagrīva.
Therefore, from the slaying of Daśagrīva and even from the slaying of Kumbhakarṇa, the sin of killing a Brahmin accrued to Rāma, whose actions are effortless.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, for the sake of its pacification, Rāma installed the Liṅga named Rāmeśvara according to the Vedic ritual.
Thus, by the slaying of Rāvaṇa, the sin arising from the killing of a Brāhmaṇa accrued to the wise Rāmacandra, who is beloved by the world.
That sin arising from the murder of a Brahmin, which was declared by you to be accompanied by its causes, Rāma himself established this Liṅga for its pacification. || 43 ||
O twice-born ones, having thus installed the Liṅga, the exceedingly righteous Rāmacandra, along with Sītā and his younger brother, considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose.
Where the sin of Brahman-slaughter of King Rāmacandra departed, there arose a certain sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Brahmahatyāvimocana.
Bathing there is of great merit and destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin; indeed, Rāvaṇa is seen there even today in the form of a shadow.
In front of that is a very large cave belonging to the world of the Nāgas; [it is there that he deposited] the powerful sin of Brahmin-slaughter arising from the slaying of the Ten-necked one.
O twice-born ones, the beloved of Jānakī caused him to reach that cave; then, having constructed an excellent pavilion over that cave, he remained there.
Rāghava established Bhairava there for the sake of protection; the terrifying Brahmahatyā was then terrified by the command of Bhairava. (49)
O best of the twice-born, she was unable to emerge upward from that hole; the personification of Brahman-slaughter remained in that very hole, devoid of effort.
To the south of the great Liṅga Rāmanātha, Girijā dwells with joy, she who constitutes half the body of Śiva, the Supreme Bliss.
The Sun and the Moon revolve on either side of the wielder of the trident; the Fire-god stands before the Lord Rāmanātha.
Śatakratu dwells in the east, and likewise Anala in the southeast; Yama, the servant of Rāmanātha, dwells in the south. (53)
In the southwest, O brahmins, Nirṛti resides for the sake of Śaṅkara; and in the west, Varuṇa serves Rāghaveśvara with devotion.
In the northwestern quarter resides Vāyu, belonging to Śiva; and in the northern direction dwells Dhanada, belonging to Rāmanātha.
And in the northeastern quarter of this place, O twice-born ones, resides Maheśa, as well as both Vināyaka and Kumāra, the two sons of Mahādeva.
Now, Vīrabhadra and all the other lords of Maheśvara’s hosts abide in their respective places within the temple of Rāmanātha. (57)
In the temple of Rāmanātha, the sages, serpents, perfected beings (siddhas), and hosts of gandharvas and apsarases always dwell, each in their respective place.
With hearts full of contentment, they dwell as they please in the presence of Śiva, serving Rāmanātha with devotion. (59)
For the sake of worshipping Rāmanātha, the Lord of the Raghus established many learned Brāhmaṇas as priests at Rāmeśvara. (60)

One should worship the Brahmins installed by Rāma with offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya), and so forth; when they are satisfied, all the deities together with the ancestors are likewise gratified. (61)
O twice-born ones, the Lord of Jānakī also bestowed upon them villages with abundant wealth for the purpose of offering food (naivedya) to the Great God Rāmanātha.
The elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa bestowed many villages and great wealth, as well as ornaments such as necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and golden coins.
The son of Daśaratha gave many silk garments and various kinds of linen cloths to the god Rāmanātha.
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the holy Sarayū, and the Sarasvatī worship the god Rāmeśvara at the Setu for the pacification of their own sins.
By reading or even by hearing this chapter, a human being, liberated from all sins, attains union with Hari.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Cause of Rāma’s Arising of the Sin of Brahmin-Slaughter," in the Setumāhātmya of the Third Section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The venerable Sūta said: O best of sages, I shall narrate a sin-destroying story concerning Rāmanātha; listen with well-composed minds.
Formerly, there was a king named Śaṅkara, the sovereign of the Pāṇḍya country; he was devoted to Brahmanas, true to his word, a performer of sacrifices, and righteous.
He was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, a destroyer of enemy armies, and one who righteously protected all four stages of life and the social orders.
Devoted to Vedic conduct, he had mastered the Purāṇas and the Smṛtis; he was a constant worshiper of Śiva and Viṣṇu, yet also a worshiper of other deities.
Constantly bestowing great gifts upon the high-souled Brahmins, that wise king once went to a penance grove for the purpose of hunting.
It was terrifying with lions, tigers, elephants, and buffaloes—fierce creatures that struck fear; it was filled with the dreadful chirping of crickets and teeming with reptiles.
Then Śaṅkara, the crest-jewel of kings, entered a great forest filled with terrifying beasts of prey and fearsome with the danger of forest fires.
Accompanied by many soldiers and crowded with families of hunters, his feet were concealed by wooden sandals, he wore a red turban, and was clad in green garments.
With his finger-guards of iguana-skin bound on, holding a bow and arrows, with a great sword girded at his waist, he was mounted upon an excellent white horse.
Wearing fine attire, equipped with armor, and surrounded by a host of foot soldiers, he [searched] throughout all the forests, mountains, and caves.
Having crossed the great torrent, the youth, possessing the prowess of a lion, roamed through the caves with his forces, searching for deer.
"Let him be bound! Let him be slain! This deer is fleeing with speed through the forest!"—while the soldiers were speaking thus, Śaṅkara himself leapt up.
The great king, having entered the forest region, slays deer, as well as lions, boars, buffaloes, elephants, and śarabhas. || 13 ||
Slaying other wild animals here and there, King Śaṅkara reached a certain region of the forest where [he encountered] one dwelling in the midst of a cave.
He quickly struck with a straight-knotted arrow the peaceful sage, who was wearing a tiger skin and possessed a restrained mind, mistaking him for a tiger.
With great speed, O best of Brahmins, he struck his wife—who was devoted to her husband and seated near him—with an arrow, thereby taking away the life of her lord.
Seeing his parents slain in the forest, their son, afflicted by intense grief and overcome with despair, wept and lamented.
"O father, O mother, having abandoned me, where have you two gone now? Where shall I go, and who will be my refuge? (18)
"O father, who will teach me the Vedas or instruct me in the scriptures? O mother, who will give me food along with spiritual instruction? (19)
"Who now, O father, will teach me proper conduct once you have died? And who, O mother, will console me, a child filled with rage? (20)
"O blameless ones, by what sin have you two—who are devoted to asceticism, who are my very life-breaths, and who are my gurus—been slain today with arrows in the forest? (21)
Thus, O brahmins, their son wept aloud; then Śaṅkara, wandering in the forest, heard that lamentation.
Facing in the direction of that sound, he immediately went toward the mouth of the cave; the sages dwelling there also quickly arrived at that hermitage.
Seeing the sage slain by the arrow, O brahmins, as well as his wife who had been killed and the king holding his bow, all the sages were moved.
And seeing their son lamenting, they became deeply overwhelmed; they consoled their terrified son, saying, "Do not weep."
The sages said: Whether toward the wealthy or the poor, the foolish or even the learned, the fat or the thin—the King of the Departed (Yama) behaves with impartiality.
Whether in a forest, a city, a village, on a mountain, or in any other place, all living beings must indeed go under the sway of death. || 27 ||
O child, all beings—whether dwelling in the womb, already born, young, or old—must inevitably go to the city of Yama.
O son of a twice-born, when the time has come, this body must be abandoned by those in the student stage, by householders, by forest-dwellers, and by mendicants. (29)
O high-minded son of a twice-born, one must go to the abode of the departed by means of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, and even those of mixed castes. (30)
The gods, sages, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas, as well as all other beings, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the rest. || 31 ||
All shall go to dissolution; you ought not to grieve for that Brahman which is non-dual, consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss, as revealed in the Upanishads.
O best of beings, there is neither destruction nor birth for it, even though it resides within this nine-gated vessel of filth, a dwelling place of pus, blood, and gore. (33)
In this body, which is like a bubble, teeming with swarms of worms, and which gives rise to desire, anger, fear, malice, delusion, and envy; (34)
In one who is solely covetous of another's wife, another's field, and another's wealth; who is pervaded by violence, envy, and impurity; and who is a mere vessel for excrement and urine. (35)
He who would conceive a beautiful notion regarding this body—which is always impure and resembles a jar with many holes—is a fool and one of wicked mind. (36)
O twice-born one, how could there be a long-lasting stability for the wind known as prāṇa? Therefore, do not grieve for your mother and father.
Driven by their own karma, those two abandoned this home and went elsewhere; yet, driven by your own karma, you remain here upon this earth. (38)
When your karma is exhausted, then you too shall die; for a deceased spirit who is about to die laments for a deceased spirit who has already died. (39)
At the time when your mother and father were born, you were not yet born; therefore, your destinies are indeed distinct.
O Mahāmati, if your destiny were to be the same as theirs, then you too must go to that place where those two have gone upon death. (41)
Those kinsmen who shed tears on the ground for the deceased truly drink those very tears; indeed, the dead ones become ghosts (pretas) in the hereafter.
Therefore, casting aside grief and maintaining fortitude with a composed mind, perform for these two the Vedic funeral rites.
"Since these two have died from the strike of arrows, you must therefore take their bones in order to pacify the defilement caused by that. (44)
Establish likewise the Śrāddha, including the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa and other rites, at Rāmasetu, the field of Lord Śiva Rāmanātha, which bestows liberation.
O son of a Brahmin, perform [the rites] right there for the sake of their purification; by that, the evil of an untimely death will be pacified, and not otherwise. (46)
Śrī Sūta said: O twice-born ones, having been thus addressed by the sages, the son of Śākalya, named Jāṅgala, performed the entire Pitṛmedha rite for those two.
On another day, taking the bones, he set out for Hālāsya; from there, this Jāṅgala brāhmaṇa immediately went to Rāmeśvara.
In that place of Rāmeśvara, according to the method prescribed by the Sage (Vyāsa), he deposited the bones of his parents and performed the Śrāddha rites and other ceremonies accordingly.
He performed his duties there until the end of the first year; having stayed for one year, that son of the sage, known as Jāṅgala, remained alone.
On the day at the end of the year, the Brahmin beheld in a dream at night his own mother and father, bearing conches, discs, and maces.
Seated upon Garuḍa, adorned with garlands of lotuses, they were graced by wreaths of tulasī and wore shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings.
Having seen them thus—their chests adorned with the Kaustubha gem and resplendent in yellow garments—the son of the sage, Jāṅgala, became exceedingly serene in mind.
O twice-born ones, having returned to his own hermitage, Jāṅgala lived there in happiness; and he [related] that account of what was seen in the dream to his mother and father.
Extremely delighted, he reported everything to those Brāhmaṇas; having heard the account, those sages were filled with joy in their hearts. (55)
Then, beholding the king, all those great sages, the brahmins, became enraged and spoke while cursing King Śaṅkara.
O King of Pāṇḍya, you great fool, slayer of Brāhmaṇas through cruelty! Since you have now committed both the murder of a woman and the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. (57)
Therefore, abandon your body in the sacrificial fire; otherwise, there will be no purification for you even through hundreds of penances.
"By the mere act of conversing with you, ten thousand murders of Brahmins would be incurred. Depart from our presence, O defiler of the Pāṇḍya lineage! (59)
Thus addressed by the sages, O best of the twice-born, Śaṅkara, the Pāṇḍya king, said: "So be it; I shall cast off my body in the sacrificial fire."
"For the sake of purification from the murder of a Brahmin, I am here in your presence; may you, the best of sages, grant me your favor. (61)
"Likewise, by the abandonment of my body, may my sin go to its dissolution. Having spoken thus to all the sages, Śaṅkara, the Pāṇḍya king—
Having summoned his own ministers, he spoke these words: "O ministers, through lack of deliberation, I have committed the sin of killing a Brahmin."
And likewise, this cruel murder of a woman bestows a great hell; for the sake of purifying this sin, according to the words of the sages, I [have come]. (64)
"When the fire blazes with great flames, I shall cast off my body; bring wood quickly so that the fire may be kindled with it. (65)
"O ministers, do not grieve; establish my son Suruci in the kingdom without delay. Destiny is difficult to overcome."
Thus addressed by the king, the ministers then wept, saying, "O Great King, Lord of the Pāṇḍyas, you who are compassionate even toward your enemies! (67)
For we have always been nurtured by you like your own sons; without you, we shall not enter the city that resembles the city of the gods.
"We shall enter the fire, kindled with great logs of wood. Hearing their lamentation, King Śaṅkara Pāṇḍya spoke these words of consolation to all his ministers: || 69 ||
Śaṅkara said: "O ministers, what will you do with me, a great sinner?"
Alas, having ascended the lion-throne, it is not fitting to rule the earth bounded by the four oceans in a straightforward manner. (71)
"Therefore, quickly install my son Suruci upon the throne; bring wood at once so that he may enter the fire."
"You are my excellent ministers; abandon all delay now! Having been addressed thus, those ministers brought wood in an instant.
Then, having seen the fire kindled with wood, King Śaṅkara, having bathed and sipped water, became pure in soul in the presence of the sages.
Having circumambulated the fire and those sages with haste, and having paid homage to the fire and the sages, he meditated upon the Lord, the Consort of Umā.
Resuming his fortitude, the king began to throw himself into the fire while the brahmins and even the sages were listening. (76)
An incorporeal voice, sounding like Bhairava, arose: "O Śaṅkara, protector of the earth, do not enter the fire now! (77)
"O Great-minded One, let there be no fear in you on account of the murder of a Brahmin. I shall declare to you an instruction that is a secret, equal to the Vedas. (78)
Listen attentively, O King, and let that which I have spoken be carried out by you on Mount Gandhamādana, on the shore of the southern ocean.
At the highly meritorious Rāmasetu, which destroys great sins, is the Liṅga installed by Rāma, the Great Lord known as Rāmanātha. || 80 ||
Serve [the deity] for one year, three times a day, with devotion; indeed, perform circumambulation, walking around, and prostration.
"O King, let the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka) of Rāmanātha indeed be performed by you; and let various kinds of food offerings (naivedya) be presented day after day. (82)
Worship the Rāma-liṅga with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor; indeed, consecrate it with two bhāras of cow's products and clarified butter.
And every day, bathe that Linga of the Lord with the milk of two bhāras of cows and one droṇa of honey.
O King, perform the daily offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) every day, and carry out the daily worship with a lamp fed by sesame oil. 85.
By this, O Indra among kings, your sin of killing a woman and your sin of killing a Brahmin shall perish at that very moment for you, Rāmanātha, the wielder of the trident. || 86 ||
By the sight of Rāmanātha, hundreds of killings of embryos, ten thousand killings of Brahmins, and likewise ten thousand instances of drinking liquor [are purified]. (87)

O King, ten thousand instances of stealing gold, ten thousand instances of violating the teacher’s wife, and the faults arising from association with such persons—all these perish in an instant, O Lord. (88)
Whatever sins there may be that are equal to the great mortal sins (mahāpātaka), all of them indeed perish through service to Rāmanātha. (89)
If the great service of Rāmanātha can be obtained by men, what need is there for the Gaṅgā, Gayā, Prayāga, or even for sacrifice? 90.
Therefore, go to Rāmasetu and worship Rāmanātha incessantly; O Lord, do not delay, but make haste in your departure.
Having spoken thus, that incorporeal voice then ceased; and having heard it, all the sages urged the king to hasten.
"Go quickly, O Great King, to Rāmasetu, which bestows liberation. We spoke thus because we were unaware of the majesty of Rāmanātha. (93)
"Now, cast off your body into the blazing fire," thus was King Śaṅkara permitted by the excellent sages.
Having brought the fourfold army to the city with great haste, he bowed to all the sages with a joyful inner soul. || 95 ||
Accompanied by a few soldiers and taking with him much wealth, he went to Gandhamādana for the purpose of serving Rāmanātha.
He dwelt for one year at Rāmasetu, which bestows purity, eating but once a day, having conquered anger and subdued the entire collection of his senses.
Serving Rāmanātha with devotion at the three junctions of the day, he joyfully offered ten bhāras of wealth to Rāmanātha.
Every day he performed the great worship of Rāmanātha, and every day he also performed [the rites] at Dhanuṣkoṭi with devotion.
Every day he joyfully gave food to the Brahmins, as well as performed the entire ritual of worship as prescribed by the incorporeal voice.

O twice-born ones, when he had performed this for one year, at the end of that year, Śaṅkara became pure and, with a satisfied mind, praised Rāmanātha, the Supreme Lord and ocean of compassion. || 1 ||
Śaṅkara said: I bow to Rudra, the Lord, Rāmanātha, the consort of Umā. (2)
Protect me, O Lord, out of compassion; quickly burn away my sin of killing a Brahmin, O Mahādeva, destroyer of Tripura, consumer of the Kālakūṭa poison!
Protect me, O ocean of compassion; release me from this murder of a woman, O Gaṅgādhara, Virūpākṣa, Rāmanātha, Trilocana! || 4 ||
Protect me with your compassionate gaze and sever my sin, O Lord; O enemy of Kama, bestower of desires upon your devotees, Sovereign of the Raghus! 5.
Cast your side-glance upon me; O Dhūrjaṭi, make me pure. O Śiva, the conqueror of death, the immutable one who protected Mārkaṇḍeya from fear! 6.
Salutations to you, whose half is the Daughter of the Mountain; make me forever free from sin, O Śaṅkara, moon-crested one adorned with a garland of rudrākṣa beads.
Make me worthy of the right conduct prescribed in the Vedas; salutations to you, the destroyer of Sūrya’s teeth and the cutter of Bhāratī’s nose! 8.
Salutations to the divine Lord Rāmeśvara; may you grant me purity. [I bow to] Rāmanātha, the bull-bannered one, who is bliss, the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
"I bow down again and again; may my sin be destroyed. As he was thus praising Maheśvara Rāmanātha with devotion, [the Lord spoke].
From the mouth of the king emerged the most terrifying Brahmahatyā (the personification of Brahmin-slaughter), wearing blue garments, cruel, and with hair of deep red.
At the command of Rudra, Bhairava struck down that loathsome Brahman-slaughter as it emerged from the mouth of the king with his trident.
When the sin of Brahmin-slaughter had been destroyed by Bhairava at the command of Śiva, Rāmanātha, his mind pleased by the king's hymn of praise, spoke to the monarch.
Śrī Rāmanātha said: "O sinless Great King of the Pāṇḍyas, I am pleased with this hymn of yours; I shall grant you a boon—choose what you desire."
The fault that you had from the killing of a woman and the killing of a Brahmin has departed; you are pure, cleansed of sin—rule the kingdom as before.
Those men who serve me here with a mind endowed with devotion—I destroy even tens of thousands of their sins of killing a Brahmin.

O King, ten thousand acts of drinking liquor, ten thousand acts of approaching the wife of a guru, ten thousand acts of stealing gold, and likewise ten thousand acts of associating with such offenders [are thereby purified]. (17)
O King, I destroy all other sins as well, there is no doubt; those men who serve me do not wander through saṃsāra again.
However, those who praise me with this hymn preceded by devotion will undoubtedly attain liberation in the form of union (sāyujya) with me. (19)
O lord of men, being pleased by your devotion and by this hymn, I shall destroy the accumulation of these great sins.
"O King, ask from me, the giver of boons, whatever boon you desire. Thus addressed by Śiva, Śaṅkara, that bull among kings, then spoke to Rāmanātha, that Śaṅkara who is an ocean of compassion.
The king said: "O Maheśvara, by the mere sight of you, I have attained my life's purpose."
Beyond this, there is nothing further for me to pray for now than Your pair of feet, which remove the suffering of Mṛkaṇḍu’s son.
O Mahādeva, I have seen all that is to be seen; there is indeed nothing further to be sought from you, the Lord. May I possess unwavering devotion to the pair of your lotus feet.

"May there be no further birth for me in the impure womb of mothers for those men who recite this hymn composed by me to you, O Lord; may they be liberated from sin and obtain the fruit of your service. (25)
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, Rāmanātha, having favored him by saying "So be it," [departed].
Nīlakaṇṭha, the three-eyed one, was concealed within the form of the Liṅga; thereafter, the king too received the grace bestowed by Rāmanātha.
Having paid homage to Rāmanātha with a heart fulfilled within, he, surrounded by his army and filled with joy, departed for his own city.
They related this account to the forest-dwelling sages, and those sages, with delighted minds, consecrated the king in his kingdom.
O Brahmins, accompanied by his sons and wife, the king, having obtained a kingdom free from thorns, protected the earth for a long time together with his ministers.
Then, when the time of death arrived, meditating upon Śiva as Rāmeśvara, he attained the auspicious state of union (sāyujya) with Rāmanātha at the end of his body.
Thus, O Brahmins, has the majesty of Rāmanātha been recounted to you, as well as the meritorious life story and narrative of the king named Śaṅkara.
A person who listens to or reads this chapter with devotion, being completely liberated from all sins, attains Rāmanātha. (133)
Śrī Sūta said: Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the chapter of hymns (Stotrādhyāya) of the trident-bearing Rāmanātha, which is of great merit; listen with faith, O twice-born ones!
Once the Liṅga was firmly established, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā the daughter of Janaka, Sugrīva and the other lords of the monkeys, praised the Supreme Lord.
The gods, beginning with Brahmā, and the great sages, beginning with Agastya, each praised the Lord of Rāghava, filled with devotion. (3)
I shall declare that to you in due order; listen with great reverence, O twice-born ones! By the mere hearing of this, a human being shall become liberated. (4)
Śrī Rāma said: Salutations to you, the Great Soul, the wielder of the great illusion and the trident, who removes the suffering of those devoted to your lotus feet and who slays serpents.
Salutations to the God of gods, to Rāmanātha, the witness; salutations to him who is known through the Vedānta, the bestower of reality upon yogis.
Salutations to Śambhu, the Lord of the Universe, who is ever filled with bliss; salutations to the dust of his lotus feet, which are the cause for destroying the fear of his devotees.
Salutations to you, the Lord of all; salutations to the Supreme Self manifest before us. Salutations to you of wondrous valor, the destroyer of great sins.
Salutations to you, the Time of time, to Time itself, and to that which transcends time; salutations to you, the destroyer of ignorance, and salutations to the remover of sin.
Salutations to the sole cause for destroying the torment of those scorched by saṃsāra; salutations to the destroyer of my sin of Brahman-slaughter and the consumer of poison.
Salutations to you, O Lord of Pārvatī, eternal dweller of Kailāsa! O bearer of the Gaṅgā, O three-eyed one, protect me from all calamities.
Salutations to you who hold the Pināka bow in hand; salutations to the destroyer of Madana. Again and again, salutations to you at all times and in all circumstances. 12.
Lakṣmaṇa said: Salutations to you, O Rāmanātha, the destroyer of Tripura, Śambhu, the lord of Pārvatī’s life, and the father of Gaṇeśa and Skanda. || 13 ||
Salutations to you, whose eyes are the sun, moon, and fire; salutations to the one with matted hair. Salutations to Śiva, who is accompanied by Umā, and to Mārkaṇḍeya, the destroyer of fear.
Salutations to the cause of the creation, maintenance, and end of all phenomenal existence; salutations to the fierce one, to the formidable one, to Mahādeva, the witness. || 15 ||
Salutations to you, the omniscient, the most excellent, the giver of boons, the supreme; salutations to you, Śrīkaṇṭha, the destroyer of the five great sins.
Salutations be unto you, whose form is supreme bliss, truth, and pure consciousness; salutations to you, the destroyer of the disease of worldly existence; salutations to the Lord of the sinews. 17.
Salutations to you, the lord of thieves; salutations to you, the lord of forests; to you, the lord of hosts, the witness of all forms. || 18 ||
O Śambhu, wherever I may be born impelled by my karma, may I have devotion at Your pair of feet in each of those places. (19)
By your grace, may there be no delight for me in the path of the unreal; may there be delight in the path of Vedic conduct. Salutations to you! (20)

Sītā said: O Śaṅkara, supreme cause, O Dhūrjaṭi, adorned by the saffron from the breasts of the Daughter of the Mountain; grant my husband a mind that is always constant and never directed toward another man.
O Gaṅgādhara, Virūpākṣa, Nīlalohita, Śaṅkara, Rāmanātha; salutations to you, O mine of compassion, protect me! 22.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods; salutations to you, O abode of compassion. Salutations to you, the destroyer of the fear of worldly existence for those terrified by existence.

O Lord Śambhu, by meditating upon Your lotus feet, that son of Mṛkaṇḍu quickly cast off the fear of Yama, the son of the Sun, and swiftly attained immortality; O Supreme Lord, what indeed cannot be accomplished through taking refuge in You?
O Supreme Lord, O Supreme Bliss, O Protector of those who have sought refuge; grant me evermore devotion to my husband. Salutations, salutations unto You! || 25 ||
Hanumān said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Lord Rāma, ocean of compassion! May unwavering devotion toward your lotus feet be mine. (26)
Salutations to Śambhu, Rāmanātha, whose nature is true manifestation; without whom there would be neither the existence of the world nor its appearance.
Aṅgada said: "Salutations to that Śambhu, the Lord Rāma, by whose radiance the world shines, and without whose light the world does not manifest."
Jāmbuvān said: Since the bliss of all is, in the ultimate sense, radiant as bliss itself, salutations to this Rāmeśvara, whose form is supreme bliss. (29)
Nīla said: Salutation to this Rāmeśvara, whose nature is non-dual, who is always the undivided pair despite the distinctions of place, time, and direction. (30)
Nala said: Salutations to You, Rāmeśvara, who are free from ignorance, while Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are but manifestations of ignorance.
Kumuda said: To that Śambhu, Rāmanātha, who—due to the lack of full knowledge of his form—is conceived as the Pradhāna by virtue of being the cause; to him [I offer salutation]. || 32 ||
Panasa said: Salutations to Him who is the embodiment of knowledge, who is devoid of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth—all of which are the manifestations of ignorance. || 33 ||
The Elephant said: "Because of their failure to understand the true nature of things, the lowest of logicians have vainly imagined atoms to be the cause of all effects. (34)
I constantly worship that Maheśvara Rāmanātha, the witness of all, who is supreme bliss, as my very own self.
Gavākṣa said: I always go for refuge to the peaceful Śiva Rāmeśvara, the liberator from the bonds of those bound by the fetters of ignorance. (36)
The Gavaya said: I bow to Rāmanātha, Śiva, the moon-crested Lord of Umā, the support of this virtuous world and the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra. (37)
Śarabha said: I bow down to that Self, the Lord of Rāma, who is called the "inner organ" (antaḥkaraṇa) by those deluded through ignorance. || 38 ||
Gandhamādana said: For the sake of purifying all my sins, I worship Rāmanātha, Umānātha, Gaṇanātha, and Tryambaka—the Lord of the Universe. (39)

Sugrīva said: "In the midst of the ocean of worldly existence, which is terrifying with the waters of birth and death, and crowded with garlands of waves consisting of sons, wives, wealth, and fields; (40)"
And it has fallen into the fragment of the cosmic egg, unable to reach the further shore; wailing, helpless, miserable, and terrified by the serpent of the sense-objects. (41)
O Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, O Rāmanātha, salutations be unto you; protect me, who am terrified by the crocodiles of disease and afflicted by the pain of the three-fold torments. 42.
Vibhīṣaṇa said: In the midst of the forest of worldly existence, where my own path has been lost, where diseases are thieves, anger is a lion, birth is a tiger, and death is a serpent; (43)
In this great and terrifying blind well of childhood, youth, and old age; in the fire of anger, envy, and greed; and amidst the cruel mountain of sense-objects.
O Śambhu, O Rāmeśvara, lead Andhaka now along the auspicious path as he currently falters in this place abounding in the thorns of fear.
All the monkeys said: "O Lord, having been born in all kinds of censurable and non-censurable wombs everywhere, and having likewise fallen into the Kumbhīpāka and other hells," (46)
And having been born again in a loathsome womb due to the remainder of our karma, we have fallen into this cycle of existence; O Rāmanātha, O ocean of compassion! 47.
Protect us who are helpless, powerless, wretched, and crying out, O Śaṅkara! Salutations to you, O Ocean of Compassion, Rāmanātha, Maheśvara! 48.
Brahmā said: Salutations to you, the Lord of the worlds, the Lord Rāma, Śambhu! Be gracious to me, O Lord of all, and destroy my ignorance.
Indra said: I bow to that Śaṅkara, the Lord of Umā and Rāmanātha, whose power is the goddess Umā, the mother of the world, who consists of the three Vedas. || 50 ||
Yama said: I worship that very Rāmeśvara, whose two sons are Gaṇeśvara and Skanda, and whose vehicle is the bull, for the cessation of all ignorance.
Varuṇa said: "By the power of whose worship the son of Mṛkaṇḍu conquered death, that Rāmanātha, the conqueror of death (Mṛtyuñjaya), I worship within my heart. (52)
Kubera said: Salutations indeed to Rāmeśvara, the Lord, whose body is reddened by lac-dye and who is adorned with shimmering earrings. || 53 ||
The Sun said: Salutations to you, O Mahādeva, Rāmanātha, Tryambaka! Salutations to you who brought about the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice; protect me, O Śiva! 54.
Soma said: Salutations to you, who are smeared with ashes, who bear the trident, and who wear a garland of serpents; O Rāmanātha, ocean of compassion, refuge of the cremation ground! 55.
Agni said: O you whose lotus feet are served by all the guardians of the quarters beginning with Indra, salutations always to the pure Rāmanātha, who is clothed in the directions.
Vāyu said: O Rāmanātha, salutations to you, who possess the form of Hari, who wear a tiger-skin garment; be the granter of my desires. || 57 ||
Bṛhaspati said: O Rāmanātha, obeisance to You, the eternal witness of the ego, the innermost non-dual reality; quickly destroy my ignorance. 58.
Śukra said: Salutations to Śambhu, the Lord Rāma, who is unattainable by deceivers, who is the embodiment of the meaning of the great mantra, and who is free from duality. (59)
The Aśvins said: "O Lord of Rāghava, salutations to You, who eternally shine in the hearts of yogis as their very own self, and who are to be known through a realization that is non-dual. (60)
Agastya said: O primordial God, Great God, Lord of the Universe, immutable Śiva; O Lord of Rāmanātha and Ambikā, be gracious, O you whose banner is the bull! 61.
O Moon-crested Lord, forgive my thousand offenses; release me from this sense of "I" and "mine" regarding my sons and others.
Sutīkṣṇa said: "Fields, jewels, wealth, wives, friends, garments, cattle, horses, and sons—none of these are of any benefit to me, O Rāmanātha; therefore, grant me detachment. (63)
Viśvāmitra said: Even the study of the scriptures is fruitless, and the Vedas themselves are surely in vain, O Śiva, if there is no devotion toward you, the Lord Śrī Rāmanātha, for a mortal man. (64)

Gālava said: "Charities, sacrifices, observances, penances, and immersions in holy places such as the Gaṅgā—all these are in vain for those who do not bow to you, O Rāmeśvara; this is the certain conclusion in this matter. (65)

Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāmeśvara, even if a person has committed every kind of sin, if they approach you with devotion and bow down, those sins shall surely perish, just as darkness is utterly dispelled by the splendor of the sun.
Atri said: Having seen Rāmeśvara even once, and having touched and bowed to you, the Lord, that man shall not enter a womb again; rather, he attains your own twofold nature.

Aṅgiras said: If a person, having approached you, Rāmanātha, should remember his kinsmen while bowing, he would deliver them all from every sin; what wonder is there in his own attainment of purpose? (68)
Gautama said: O Śrī Rāmanātheśvara, this which is secret, mysterious, supreme, and free from sorrow belongs to those men who worship at the base of your feet; indeed, they too are blessed. (69)

Śatānanda said: "O Lord, O Master of the Heroes of the Raghus, this must indeed be understood by those seeking liberation who know the secrets of Vedāntic realization; for they abandon all scriptures to practice service unto you. (70)

Bhṛgu said: O Rāmanātha, one whose impurities have been shaken off by the practice of contemplating the pair of Your lotus feet proceeds fearlessly toward that non-dual, radiant, and truly blissful state which is the unfailing mass of consciousness. (71)

Kutsa said: O Rāmanātha, who that is a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor would not worship you—the service of whose feet always bestows the boons of worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men, and which destroys the Raurava and other hells?

Kāśyapa said: O Rāmanātha, for those who serve at your feet, what is the use of vows, or ascetic penances, or sacrifices? What is the use of the study and recitation of the Vedas and Śāstras, or even the water of the celestial river (the Gaṅgā)? What fruit [could there be]? (73)

O Śrī Rāmanātha, having arrived quickly at the time of my departure from this life, together with Bhavānī, lead me to Your own lotus feet—which are free from sorrow, free from delusion, blissful, and the very nature of consciousness.
The Gandharvas said: O Rāmanātha, for us who worship you in this shoreless ocean of worldly existence with its waves of suffering, there is indeed no other refuge but you. (75)
The Kinnaras said: O Rāmanātha, in this forest of worldly existence, which is terrifying with the tigers of disease, there would be no one other than you to show us the path. (76)
The Yakṣas said: "O Dhūrjaṭi, the affliction caused by the enemies that are our senses is always unbearable for us; O Lord Rāmanātha, become our ally in order to conquer them. (77)
The Nāgas said: O Rāmanātha, Lord of Ambikā, how shall we, of limited intellect, be able to praise you whose majesty is inconceivable? (78)
The Kiṃpuruṣas said: Birth and death in various wombs have occurred for us many times; destroy our ignorance as well, O Rāmanātha, salutations be to you! (79)
The Vidyādharas said: Salutations to you, the Lord of Ambikā, the unattached Great Soul; salutations to you, Rāmanātha; be gracious, O Bull-bannered One! (80)
The Vasus said: Obeisance to you, Rāmanātha Gaṇeśa, whose feet are worshipped by the hosts of Gaṇas; obeisance to the bearer of the Gaṅgā, the secret one; protect us always. (81)
The Viśvedevas said: "O Śaṅkara, protect us! Salutations to Rāmanātha with Ambā, who bestows liberation upon excellent yogins whose sole devotion is fixed on pure consciousness alone. (82)
The Maruts said: Salutations to you, Rāmanātha, the supreme reality among all realities, who in truth is the essence of all principles; salutations to Śambhu, whose light is self-manifest.
The Sādhyas said: Salutations to the divine Lord Rāmeśvara, who is devoid of anything other than Himself, who bestows existence upon the universe, and who destroys ignorance. (84)
All the gods said: "The Self that is Brahman is full of existence, consciousness, and bliss; it is devoid of any dualistic entity, self-luminous, and free from beginning, middle, and end. (85)
Unchanging, unattached, perfectly pure, and eternal; it is the supreme nectar, the witness of the manifold world beginning with space. (86)
Beyond all means of valid cognition, yet bestowing awakening even upon them; forever free from manifestation and disappearance, and devoid of contraction.
The witness of this phenomenal world superimposed upon Himself—untainted, supreme bliss, and devoid of all activity. (88)
We all [worship] Rāmanātha, the Great Soul, who is blissful existence, whose form is consciousness, and who is devoid of worldly enjoyment, for the purification of our own sins. (89)
Desiring to realize the bliss of our own self, we constantly contemplate it within our minds; O Rāma, ocean of compassion, protect us! O Lord, salutations unto you! (9)
Salutations to Rāmanātha, to Rudra, the remover of worldly existence, who appears divided in the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others through his own *māyā*.
The ministers of Vibhīṣaṇa said: "Salutations to you, Rāmanātha—the giver of boons, the most excellent, the three-eyed one, the wielder of the trident, the eternal object of meditation for yogis."
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having been thus praised by Rāma and all the others, Śiva, the Lord of Rāma (Rāmeśvara), summoned Rāma and the rest and spoke to them all.
"O Rāma, Rāma, O illustrious one, O Lord, delighter of Jānakī! O Saumitri, O auspicious Jānaki, and likewise you headed by Sugrīva! (94)
"O others who have Brahmā as your mouth, listen with well-composed minds; this meritorious chapter of praise has been composed by you with devotion. (95)
Those men who read, listen to, or cause others to hear this, shall obtain the fruit of my worship; of this there is no doubt.
One shall indeed obtain the merit of bathing at Rāmacandra-dhanuṣkoṭi, as well as the merit of residing at Rāmasetu for one year. (97)
Whatever merit arises from bathing in all the sacred fords situated in the midst of Gandhamādana, that shall be attained by him; there is no cause for doubt in this matter. (98)
Having spoken thus, Rāmanātha also vanished into his own self-liṅga. A man who constantly recites this meritorious chapter of hymns [attains the highest goal]. || 99 ||
Freed from old age and death, and devoid of the suffering of birth, he undoubtedly attains the liberation of union (sāyujya-mukti) with Rāmanātha. || 100 ||

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Hymn to Rāmanātha by Rāma and Others," in the Setumāhātmya of the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. 49.
Śrī Sūta said: Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the majesty of Setumādhava; listen with devotion, O sages, to this supreme merit that destroys all sins.
In ancient times, a king named Puṇyanidhi, born of the lunar dynasty, ruled over Madhurā, which was adorned by the Lord of Hālāsya.
Once, that protector of the earth, accompanied by his fourfold army and surrounded by the retinue of his inner apartments, [went] to his own son in Madhurā.
Having halted at Rāmasetu, he proceeded, eager for a bath; having gone there to Dhanuṣkoṭi, he bathed according to the prescribed ritual of formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
And at other sacred sites as well that were located there, the best of kings bathed and worshipped the god Rāmeśvara with devotion.
Thus he dwelt happily for a long time right there on the meritorious Gandhamādana mountain at Rāmasetu.
Once, the king performed a sacrifice that brought pleasure to Viṣṇu; at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the king was joyfully eager for the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
O twice-born ones, having bathed at Rāmadhanuṣkoṭi along with his wife and attendants, and having paid homage to Rāmanātha, he departed for his own home.
While that king, a treasury of merit, was thus dwelling there, once Lakṣmī was agitated by a playful quarrel with Hari.
Having made an agreement with Hari in order to test the king's devotion, Lakṣmī, whose abode is the lotus, was sent from Vaikuṇṭha by Viṣṇu.
Possessing the form and age of an eight-year-old girl, she went to Gandhamādana; having arrived there at Dhanuṣkoṭi, that Kamalālayā remained.
O brahmins, at that moment, King Guṇanidhi went to Rāmadhanuṣkoṭi with his wife and his army to bathe.
Having gone there, that king bathed according to the prescribed rules and performed all the foremost gifts, beginning with the Tulāpuruṣa.
Desiring to go to his own abode, he beheld a certain maiden, eight years of age, endowed with extraordinary beauty and possessing a pure smile. (14)
Having seen her, the king questioned that girl of beautiful eyes—she who possessed a lovely smile, beautiful teeth, lips like the bimba fruit, and a slender waist. (15)
Puṇyanidhi said: "Who are you, O girl? Whose daughter are you, or from where have you come here? What is the purpose of your arrival here, my child, O girl of pure smiles? (16)
In this manner, the king questioned that lotus-eyed maiden; thus questioned, O brahmins, the maiden then spoke to the king.
"I have no mother, no father, and likewise no kinsmen; O Great King, I shall be without a protector and yet your daughter. (18)
"O father, I shall dwell in your house, seeing you constantly; and whoever by force drags me away or attempts to seize me by the hand, him I shall [punish]. (19)
O King, if you will grant me this instruction, then, O father, O treasure-house of virtues, I shall dwell in your palace for a long time, having become your daughter.
Thus addressed, the king, a treasury of virtues, then said to the maiden: "O auspicious maiden, I shall do everything as you have spoken."
I too have no daughter; I have only one son who upholds our lineage. O auspicious lady, if you take pleasure in him, I shall give you to him.
"Come to my house, O maiden; dwell in my inner apartments, becoming the daughter of my wife, O blameless one, according to your desire. (23)
Thus addressed by the king, that lotus-eyed maiden said to the king, "So be it," and went home with him.
The king gave that auspicious maiden into the hand of his own wife; then the king spoke to his wife, Vindhyāvalī.
"O Queen Vindhyāvalī, auspicious and beloved one, this is our daughter; you must protect her in every way from other men. (26)
Thus addressed by the king, that wife Vindhyāvalī then said "Om," and took her daughter, the maiden, by the hand.
Nourished and protected by the king like a daughter, she lived very happily in the royal palace, always cherished.
Then, O twice-born ones, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, having mounted Garuḍa (the son of Vinatā), set out from Vaikuṇṭha with great care to search for Lakṣmī.
Having departed from Vaikuṇṭha and traversed the path of the sky, he wandered through many lands, yet he did not see Lakṣmī there.
Then he went to Rāmasetu on Mount Gandhamādana; having searched for Rāmasetu everywhere, O Indra, he wandered about.
At that very time, out of curiosity for gathering flowers, she went with her friends to the trees in the palace garden.
She was gathering flowers with her companions in the forest; then, O twice-born ones, Viṣṇu arrived there, assuming the form of a brahmin.
Placing the water of the Gaṅgā upon his shoulder and holding an umbrella with his hand, he fashioned for himself an appearance like that of a twice-born man who bathes in the Gaṅgā.

Holding in his right hand a purifier made of a knot of kusha grass tips, with all his limbs smeared with ashes and adorned with the marks of the triple horizontal lines (tripuṇḍra), [he should perform the rite]. || 35 ||
Chanting the names of Śiva, wearing a garland of rudrākṣa beads, and dressed in an upper garment, Janārdana arrived, O brahmins, appearing pure and radiant.
Seeing that brahmin who had arrived, the maiden stood there motionless; he beheld his beloved, eight years of age, gathering flowers. (37)
Seeing the sweet-spoken maiden, that brāhmaṇa Garuḍadhvaja quickly seized her by force with his hand.
Then that maiden, along with her friends, cried out in the forest; hearing that cry, the king arrived there. (39)
Surrounded by a few soldiers, the king proceeded to the palace garden; having arrived there, the monarch questioned that maiden and her female companions as well. (40)
"O maiden, for what reason have you now been crying out with your friends in the palace garden? Let the cause of it be told. (41)

"By whom have you been insulted, my daughter, that you were dragged away by force? Thus questioned, the maiden—with a face filled with tears, distressed, enraged, and deeply terrified—related the matter to the king, who was a treasure-house of virtues. (42)
The maiden said: "O Lord of the Pāṇḍyas, this brahmin forcibly seized me. (43)
"Father, he stays here at the foot of this tree, free from fear from any quarter. Having heard those words of hers, the wise King Guṇanidhi—
The ignorant man then seized the Brahmin with force, and having restrained him by sheer violence, he took him to the temple of Rāmanātha.
Having bound him with fetters and nooses and led him to that pavilion, the king consoled his daughter and brought her to the inner apartments.
The bull among kings himself proceeded to his beautiful palace; then, while sleeping at night, the king beheld that brahmin in a dream.
[He saw] Hari, adorned with a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, and a forest garland; his chest embellished by the Kaustubha gem, and wearing yellow garments.
He has the complexion of a dark cloud, is lovely, and is seated upon Garuḍa; he possesses a beautiful smile and beautiful teeth, and his crocodile-shaped earrings are shining.
He is served by attendants such as Viṣvaksena and others, reclines upon the couch of Śeṣa, and is praised by sages such as Nārada and others.
And he beheld his own daughter seated upon a blooming lotus, holding a lotus in her hand, with dark, curly hair. (51)
She whose dwelling is the chest of Viṣṇu, whose breasts are uplifted, whose limbs are consecrated by the elephants of the quarters, who is dark-complexioned and clothed in yellow garments.
Her hair was adorned with a garland fashioned from golden lotuses; she was richly endowed with the splendor of divine ornaments and graced by a beautiful necklace.
Adorned with a nose-ornament fashioned from priceless gems, decorated with ornaments of refined gold coins, and resplendent with a girdle and anklets; 54.
That king beheld his own daughter, Mahālakṣmī, at night; having thus seen both that brahmin and his own daughter in a dream, the monarch [was amazed].
Suddenly rising from his bed, he reached the maiden’s chamber; there he beheld the maiden exactly as he had seen her in his dream.
Then, when the sun had risen, the king, taking his daughter, reached the temple of Rāmanātha and stationed the Brāhmaṇa elsewhere.

In that excellent pavilion, the king beheld the Brahmin in the form of Hari, marked with the forest garland and other signs just as he had seen him in his dream; recognizing him as Viṣṇu, the sovereign Lord Hari, the king offered praise.
Puṇyanidhi said: "Salutations to you, O beloved of Kamalā; be gracious, O you whose banner is Garuḍa. (59)
O wielder of the Śārṅga bow, salutations to you; forgive my transgression. Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, wielder of the discus, Lord of Śrī. (60)
Salutations to the one whose chest is adorned with the Kaustubha gem, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark; salutations to you, the son of Brahmā, the destroyer of the hosts of Daityas.
Salutations to you, who possess the lotus that is the abode of all worlds without exception, the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and the bringer of the end to Rāvaṇa.
Salutations to you, the protector of Prahlāda and the lord of the earth; salutations to Viṣṇu, who is devoid of qualities, immeasurable, and the witness of the intellect.
Salutations to you, Śrīnivāsa, the sustainer of the world, the Supreme Self, the divine Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, the enemy of Madhu.
Salutations to the one whose navel is a lotus; salutations to the one whose eyes are lotuses; salutations to the lord who has lotuses in his hands and lotuses for his feet.
Again and again, O Lord of the World, salutations to you who wear a garland of lotuses; O embodiment of compassion, salutations to you, forgive my transgression.
O Madhusūdana, O Lord, that misconduct which was committed by me with fetters and snares was done because I did not recognize your true nature.
"Therefore, O Madhusūdana, this transgression of mine must be forgiven. Having thus praised Mahāviṣṇu, O twice-born ones, King Puṇyanidhi—
With joy, he praised Lakṣmī, the mother of all living beings: "Obeisance, O Goddess, sustainer of the world, whose abode is the chest of Viṣṇu! (69)
Salutations to you, O Mahālakṣmī, born from the ocean, beloved of Hari; constant salutations to Siddhi, Puṣṭi, Svadhā, and Svāhā.
Salutations again and again to Saṃdhyā, Prabhā, Dhātrī, and Bhūtī; salutations again and again to Śraddhā, Medhā, and Sarasvatī.
O Goddess of gods, you are the science of sacrifice, the great science, the beautiful secret science, and the science of the self, which grants liberation to all embodied beings. (72)

O Mother of the World, whose form is the triple Veda, who ordains the protection of the universe; O You who cause the creation, maintenance, and end of all things, protect me with Your compassionate gaze.
"Again and again, salutations to you, O Maheśvarī, who are the very essence of Brahman. Having thus praised Mahālakṣmī, he entreated Mādhava.
O Viṣṇu, whatever offense I have now committed against you out of ignorance—this act of hostility, namely binding your feet with shackles—may it be forgiven by you. (76)
All these worlds are your children, O Hari; you are the father of the worlds. O Madhusūdana, the offense of a son must be forgiven by his fathers.
You have even granted the true forms to the offending Daityas; O Viṣṇu, you must indeed forgive this offense of mine as well. (77)

O Blessed One, in the past, even when Pūtanā approached with the intent to kill me, my misfortune was turned toward Your lotus feet; therefore, O Treasure of Compassion, protect me! O Keśava, Beloved of Lakṣmī, cast Your merciful glance upon me. (78)
Śrī Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, having been thus entreated by that king, Viṣṇu then spoke with a profound voice to the monarch, Puṇyanidhi.
Viṣṇu said: "O King, you should not feel fear arising from the cause of my binding."
Now, by your performance of this sacrifice here, which brings me great pleasure, my subjection to your devotion has been accomplished by me.
Therefore, O King, treasure-house of merit, you are now my devotee; for that reason, I am subject to your will, bound by the fetter of your devotion.
O subduer of enemies, I always forgive the offenses of my devotees; she was indeed sent forth by me, desiring to test your devotion.
"O King, my beloved Lakṣmī has now been protected by you; therefore, I am pleased with you, for she is always of my own nature. (84)
He who possesses devotion toward her in this world is called my devotee; he who is averse to her, O King, is always considered a hater of me.
Since you have worshipped this [image] endowed with devotion, my own worship has thereby been performed; for this [image] is non-different from me. (86)
Therefore, O lord of men, no offense has been committed by you against me; rather, by honoring it, you have performed an act of worship toward me.
Since you previously made an appointment with my wife, it was for the purpose of going to that rendezvous that you bound me. (88)
Therefore, O King, I am pleased with you; Lakṣmī has now been well protected by you. That Lakṣmī is my own form, the mother of the world, consisting of the three Vedas.
O King, O Indra among monarchs, that which you have done in binding me while protecting me is pleasing to me; let no fear be felt by you.
"This Lakṣmī is truly your daughter; there is no doubt about this. When Hari had spoken thus, Lakṣmī then addressed the king.
Lakṣmī said: "O King, I am pleased with you because you have protected me in your home; or rather, both Viṣṇu and I were here for the purpose of testing your devotion."
O King, O scorcher of foes, we have come here under the pretext of sport and quarrel; we are satisfied by your yoga and your devotion.
O King, by our grace may you always possess happiness; may the sovereignty over all the realms of the earth be yours forever and evermore.
May you possess steadfast devotion to our pair of feet; at the end of your body, may there be for you union with me, free from rebirth. (95)
O King, may you always be thus; may your mind never be inclined toward evil. May your intellect always be devoted to dharma and endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu.
Having spoken thus to the king, Lakṣmī went to the chest of Viṣṇu; then, O best of the twice-born, Viṣṇu spoke this to the monarch.
O best of kings, just as I have been bound here by you with this chain, I shall dwell in that very form, known by the name Setumādhava.
O King, this bridge was built by me alone for its protection; I am here for the sake of pacifying fears from the hosts of spirits and rākṣasas. (99)
Brahmā also dwells here day and night for the sake of protecting the bridge; furthermore, Śaṅkara, known as Rāmanātha, dwells eternally upon the bridge.
Indra and the other guardians of the world dwell here filled with joy; therefore, I shall reside here under the name Setumādhava.
Indeed, for the sake of protecting the bridge, for the pacification of all calamities, for the attainment of the desired goals of all, and for the subsiding of all sins; || 2 ||
O King, those men here who serve me while I am bound in chains by you shall attain union with me (sāyujya) as well as all their desired objects.
Those who indeed read this account of my and Lakṣmī’s conduct shall not fall into poverty; rather, they attain sovereignty. || 4 ||
O lord of the people, those who—filled with joy—recite, hear, or write this hymn composed by you for my sake, [attain prosperity]. || 5 ||
"There shall never again be a return for them from my world," having said this to King Puṇyanidhi there at that time, Hari [departed].
O Brahmins, King Puṇyanidhi always maintained [the deity] in his complete form as Setumādhava right there.
Having bowed to Viṣṇu with devotion and performed a great worship, and having served Rāmanātha, he went to his own abode.
He resided there at that supreme bridge for as long as he lived, and he installed his own son, Pālaka, in Madhurā.

Dwelling right there, the king attained liberation at the end of his body; and his wife Vindhyāvalī, devoted to her husband and whose life was her husband, followed him in death and likewise went to the supreme goal.
Śrī Sūta said: Those who, endowed with devotion, constantly serve Setumādhava here—
Those men who do not perform service here to Setumādhava shall never again experience a return from Kailāsa.
The service rendered to Rāmanātha will not bear fruit for them, even if they take sand from the Setu and cast it into the Gaṅgā. || 13 ||
O Brahmins, that man who desires to go to the Gaṅgā should dwell in Vaikuṇṭha at Mādhavapura in the vicinity of Setumādhava.
Having resolved to go to the Gaṅgā, one should depart; that pilgrimage shall become fruitful. Having brought the water of the Gaṅgā and having consecrated Rāmeśa with it, || 15 ||
"By casting that burden upon the Setu, one attains Brahman without a doubt; thus, O Brahmins, has the majesty of Setumādhava been recounted to you. (16)
By reading or hearing this, one attains the destination of Vaikuṇṭha. || 117 ||

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Story of Puṇyanidhi," within the "Praise of Setumādhava" section of the Setumāhātmya, in the third part (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 50 ||
Sūta said: Now, therefore, O twice-born ones, I shall fully describe the procedure for the pilgrimage to Setu, by hearing which a human being is instantly liberated from all sins.
Having bathed and sipped water, the wise one, with a purified soul and having performed his daily rites, [did so] for the sake of pleasing Rāmanātha and for the sake of delighting Rāghava.

Having fed the Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas according to his capacity, with all his limbs smeared with holy ashes and his forehead marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra), [he should proceed].
Or, having smeared himself with gopīcandana on his forehead and bearing the ūrdhvapuṇḍraka mark, adorned with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, pure and holding the pavitra grass in his hand; || 4 ||
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) with devotion, "I shall perform the pilgrimage to Setu," he should depart from his own home observing silence while muttering the eight-syllabled mantra.
With a restrained mind, one who has conquered anger and subdued the senses, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), should recite the five-syllabled name-mantra once.
Devoid of sandals and an umbrella, abstaining from betel-leaf, free from the anointing of oil, and avoiding contact with women and the like; || 7 ||

Endowed with purity and other virtuous conducts, devoted to the twilight prayers (sandhyopāsana), performing the worship of Gāyatrī at the three junctions of the day, he was a constant meditator upon Rāma.
Constantly reciting with devotion the *Setumāhātmya* along the way, or else reciting the *Rāmāyaṇa* or another Purāṇa; || 9 ||
Abandoning useless speech, one should go to the Setu for purification; one should not accept gifts and should not neglect proper conduct.
One should perform the worship of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others on the path according to one's ability; likewise, one should carry out the Vaiśvadeva and other rites according to one's ability.
One should perform the duties beginning with the Brahma-yajña and the worship of the sacred fire; one should also bestow food, drink, and other necessities upon guests according to one's ability.
One should give alms even to ascetics, abandoning all stinginess regarding one's wealth; and on the road, one should recite the names of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others, as well as hymns of praise.
One should always practice righteousness and abandon forbidden acts; endowed with such rules as these, one should then proceed to the base of the Setu.
Having gone there with a concentrated mind, one should first offer a stone; then, having invoked the ocean there, one should thereafter prostrate before it.
One should offer the *arghya* to the ocean and thereafter offer prayers; then one should seek permission and subsequently bathe in the great ocean.
Then, O Brahmins, one should perform the libation for the sages, the gods, the monkeys, and likewise the ancestors, while mentally recollecting Hari. (17)
Regarding the number of stones: O best of Brahmins, one should give seven stones or even just one; through the gift of stones, the bath becomes fruitful, and not otherwise. (18)
The mantra for the offering of stone: "O you who were born from Pippalāda, O performer of rites who causes terror to the world! This stone is given by me to you; let it be prepared as your food. (19)

The mantra for requesting the presence [of the deity]: "O you of universal radiance, O you who shine with clarified butter, O you whose vehicle is the universe, O Lord of the people! O God, grant your presence here in the salt-water ocean. (20)

The mantra of salutation: "Salutations to you, the protector of the universe; salutations indeed to Viṣṇu, the lord of the waters. Salutations to the one with golden horns; salutations to the lord of rivers. Having thus uttered [the name] of the ocean, the wind, one should likewise bow down. (21)
The Arghya Mantra: O glorious one, composed of all jewels, source of the mine of all jewels! You who are preeminent among all jewels, O great ocean, accept this arghya offering. (22)
The mantra for requesting permission: O support of the entire world, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace; O Lord, grant me permission to resort to your sacred ford. (23)
The mantra of supplication: One should remember Sugrīva in the eastern direction and Nala in the southern direction. (24)
In the west he saw one named Mainda, and likewise Dvivida in the north; as well as Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and the illustrious Sītā.
One should remember Aṅgada, the son of Vāyu, and Vibhīṣaṇa in the center; [and one should say]: "O Great Ocean, whatever holy places exist upon the earth have entered into you. (26)
"Grant me the fruit of my bath; protect me from all sin. With these two verses beginning with "hiraṇyaśṛṅga," one should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa at the navel.
Meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa during rituals such as ritual bathing and other rites, one attains the world of Brahmā and is certainly not born here again. || 28 ||
From that, there shall be atonement for all sins. With a one-pointed mind, one should meditate upon Prahlāda, Nārada, Vyāsa, Ambarīṣa, and Śuka, as well as other devotees of the Lord. (29)

The Bath Mantra: He who is the beginning of the Vedas, whose source is the Veda and Vasiṣṭha, the lord of rivers, the ocean, and the source of jewels; he who is fire and brilliance, the earth and splendor, the bestower of seed, Viṣṇu, and the navel of immortality. (30)

This water of yours is unequalled by any other waters, whatever streams enter the Sindhu; having approached it with my head, I cast off evil from my body, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin. (31)
O twice-born ones, one should again pay homage to the ocean, the lord of rivers, which is pure and composed of all sacred fords (tīrthas), and which is the source of the winds.
Having again recited, "The two oceans," one should perform the bath [with the mantra]: "O Ravi, the holy fords within the belly of the cosmic egg have been touched by your hand. (33)
"By that truth, O Sun, grant me a holy ford at the Setu; and in the eastern direction, [grant one] for Sugrīva," and so forth, according to the sequence of the ritual.
Having remembered this again, O twice-born ones, one should perform a third bath at the Setu; if a person should proceed forth starting from Devīpattana.
Then, at that bridge which grants liberation, one should perform a bath in the ocean amidst the fresh stones for the removal of the multitude of one's own sins.
If one should go to the Setu that bestows liberation by way of the path of the Darbha-bed, then one should perform a bath right there in the ocean for the sake of liberation.
The Procedure for Tarpaṇa: [One should offer libations to] Pippalāda, Kavi, Kaṇva, Kṛtānta, Jīviteśvara, Manyu, Kālarātri, Vidyā, and Ahargaṇeśvara. (38)
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Parāśara, Umāpati, Vālmīki, Nārada, and likewise the Vālakhilya sages.
Nala, Nīla, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Gandhamādana, Mainda, Dvivida, Śarabha, and likewise Ṛṣabha. || 40 ||
And Sugrīva, Hanumān, and Vegadarśana; and Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and the highly fortunate and illustrious Sītā. || 41 ||
O twice-born ones, having recited these mantras in their proper order, one should offer libations three times, using the names of the All-pervading Lord in the dative case.
O twice-born ones, having uttered the names of the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors in the dative case, one should satisfy them according to the rules with water and sesame seeds.
Standing in water with a pure mind and holding a pavitra-grass ring, one should perform the libation; through this libation, one obtains the fruit of bathing at all sacred pilgrimage sites.
Having thus gratified these [deities] and paid homage, one should emerge from the water; casting off the wet garment, one should be clothed in dry clothing.

Having sipped water (ācamana) while holding the pavitra grass, one should perform the śrāddha according to the rules; likewise, one should offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) to the ancestors with sesame seeds and rice grains.

O best of the twice-born, this Śrāddha has been described by me for one who is incapable [of performing the full rite]. One who is wealthy should indeed perform the Śrāddha with food possessing the six flavors. (47)
