One who possesses wealth should perform the gift of cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth; one should act in this very same manner at Rāmacandra-dhanuṣkoṭi. || 48 ||
O twice-born ones, beginning with the gift of stones and ending with the libations, he indeed performed these rites according to the rules at the base of the Setu.
Then, having gone to Cakratīrtha, one should perform a bath there as well, and behold the Lord Nārāyaṇa Hari, the master of the Setu.
Proceeding by the western path, one should bathe at the Cakratīrtha located there and behold the god Darbhaśaya with devotion.
Then, having reached Kapitīrtha, one should perform a bath there as well; then, having reached Sītākuṇḍa, one should perform a bath there as well. || 52 ||
Then, having reached the highly meritorious Ṛṇamocana Tīrtha and having bathed there, one should bow down to Rāma, the Lord and beloved of Jānakī.
One should go to Lakṣmaṇatīrtha; having shaved one's head above the throat, one should bathe there as well, even while reflecting upon one's evil deeds.
Then, having bathed at Rāmatīrtha, one should proceed to the temple; likewise, having bathed at Pāpavināśana and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.

O best of the twice-born, having bathed in the Sāvitrī, the Sarasvatī, and the Gāyatrī, one should then bathe in the Hanumatkuṇḍa for great fruit; thereafter, reaching the Brahmakuṇḍa, one should bathe according to the prescribed rites.

Then, having reached Nāgakuṇḍa, which destroys all sins, a man should perform a bath, O Brahmins, which eliminates the sufferings of hell; for all rivers such as the Gaṅgā and all holy places (tīrthas) without exception [are present there].
For the sake of pacifying their own sins, they always dwell at Nāgakuṇḍa; this most excellent place [is guarded] by the eight great nāgas, beginning with Ananta.
Having reached Agastyakuṇḍa on Rāmasetu—a sacred ford fashioned by the gods that bestows liberation and grants auspiciousness—one should then bathe in that unsurpassed place.
Then, having reached Agnitīrtha, which destroys all evil deeds, one should bathe, offer libations according to the rules, and perform the śrāddha ceremony while remembering the ancestors.
Having given cows, land, gold, grain, and so forth to Brahmins according to one's capacity on the bank of the Agnitīrtha, one is liberated from all sins.
Alternatively, O best of brahmins, those holy places beginning with Cakratīrtha which have been enumerated are indeed removers of all sins.
One should bathe according to that sequence, or one may bathe according to one's own preference; having thus bathed in all the sacred fords, one should perform the śrāddha and other rites.
Afterwards, having reached Rāmeśvara and worshipped the Supreme Lord, he arrived at Setumādhava as well as at Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rules in all the holy bathing places (tīrthas) located there, [he visited] Sītā, the son of the Wind-god (Hanumān), and other foremost among the monkeys.
Having bowed to Rāmanātha and likewise to Rāmacandra and others, and having paid homage to Dhanuṣkoṭi, a person should then proceed to bathe there.
There, one should observe the previously mentioned rules regarding the offering of stones and other items; and at Dhanuṣkoṭi, one should give gifts according to one's wealth.
One should respectfully give kṣatriyas, cows, and likewise other garments to Brahmins learned in the Vedas, according to one's wealth.
Then, having reached Koṭitīrtha, one should bathe according to the prescribed rules; thereafter, one should bow down to the god Rāmeśvara, whose emblem is the bull.
When wealth is available, one should give a golden sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins, as well as sesame seeds, grain, a cow, a field, garments, and other items such as rice.
Free from greed for wealth, one should give incense, lamps, food offerings, and other articles of worship according to one's means. (71)
Having praised the god Rāmeśvara and having bowed down with devotion, one should give [an offering] to the god Rāmeśvara according to one's wealth. || 72 ||
Then, having taken leave, he should go to the presence of Setumādhava; and having offered incense and other offerings to Him, he should take leave of Mādhava.
Endowed with the previously mentioned observances, he should return again to his own home and feed the Brāhmaṇas with foods replete with the six flavors.
By that very [act], Rāmanātha, being pleased, grants him his desired object; there is no hell for him at all, and his poverty perishes. (75)
O best of the twice-born, the lineage of that man increases; having quickly shaken off saṃsāra, he shall even attain union [with the Divine]. (76)

If one is unable to come here, then whatever collection of texts exists within the Śruti, Smṛti, and Āgamas that is highly meritorious and indicative of the greatness of Setu— [one should listen to that]. (77)
O Brahmins, one should cause that text, which destroys great sins, to be recited; or else, one should recite this *Setumāhātmya* with devotion. (78)
By that [act], one obtains the meritorious fruit of bathing at Setu; of this there is no doubt. This has been declared by the wise to refer specifically to those who are blind, lame, and so forth.
Śrī Sūta said: Thus, O Brahmins, O twice-born ones, the sequence of the pilgrimage to Setu has been narrated to you. By reading or hearing this, one is liberated from all suffering.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Sequence of the Pilgrimage," in the Setu-māhātmya of the third section, the Brahma-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The venerable Sūta said: O best of sages, out of respect for you, I shall speak once more concerning the majesty of the Setu; listen with attention.
Of all sacred places, this place is the most exalted; whatever is chanted, offered in sacrifice, performed as austerity, or given as a gift here is declared to be inexhaustible.
By immersing oneself in this very great place, Dhanuṣkoṭi, one obtains the merit equivalent to residing in Vārāṇasī for ten years. || 3 ||
O twice-born ones, having bathed at that place, Dhanuṣkoṭi, and having beheld Lord Śiva as Rāmeśvara with devotion, a person should reside there for three days.
O best of Brahmins, the merit arising from residing there in Puṇḍarīkapura for ten years destroys even great sins.
By reciting the original six-syllable mantra one thousand and eight times here with devotion, a person shall attain union with Śiva.
In Madhyārjuna, Kumbhakoṇa, Māyūra, Śvetakānana, Hālāsya, Gajāraṇya, Vedāraṇya, and Naimiṣa; || 7 ||
At Śrīparvata, at Śrīraṅga, and likewise at the illustrious Vṛddhagiri; at Cidambaram, at Valmīka, at Śeṣādri, and at Aruṇācala.
In glorious Dakṣiṇakailāsa, on the Veṅkaṭa mountain at Haristhala, as well as in Kāñcīpura, Brahmapura, and Vaidyeśvarapura; || 9 ||
O best of beings, at Dhanuṣkoṭi, a man joyfully obtains the merit arising from a year's residence even in other abodes of Śiva and Viṣṇu.
If one should bathe in the month of Māgha while aiming for this bridge, known as "The Two Oceans," according to the Śruti, he attains [the goal] without a doubt. (11)
O best of brahmins, O bulls among sages, there exists that eternal Mother, who is other than this which is called "the wife" (dāru), wherein [all else] resides.
There is a Vedic scripture that beholds the deeds of Viṣṇu and proclaims the majesty of the Setu; likewise, there is another [scripture] beginning with "That Viṣṇu... (Tad Viṣṇoḥ).
O you whose wealth is penance, the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Smṛtis indeed proclaim the greatness of the Setu with one voice.
By performing an immersion in the Setu during lunar or solar eclipses, one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā for ten years at Avimukta.
The sin committed over ten million lifetimes perishes in that very instant; one obtains the unsurpassed fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
On the equinoxes, the solstices, the transits of the sun, on Mondays, and on festival days, by the mere sight of the Setu, the inauspiciousness accumulated over seven births is destroyed. (17)
O best of the twice-born, they attain the heavenly realm; this occurs when the sun is situated in Capricorn during the month of Māgha, at sunrise.
Having bathed for three days at Dhanuṣkoṭi, a mortal becomes free from sin and obtains the merit of bathing in all the holy places, such as the Gaṅgā and others. || 19 ||
O best of Brahmins, the man who performs a ritual bath at Dhanuṣkoṭi during these five days shall obtain the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and other such rites.
One shall obtain the fruit of performing penances such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, as well as the fruit of reciting all four Vedas in their entirety. || 21 ||
By bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi during the ten days of the month of Māgha, ten thousand sins of killing a Brahmin are destroyed; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
That person who performs the ritual bath at Dhanuṣkoṭi for fifteen days in the month of Māgha shall attain Vaikuṇṭha.
Performing the bath at Rāmasaitu in the month of Māgha for twenty days, one attains proximity to Śiva and rejoices together with Śiva.
Performing the ritual bath for twenty-five days, one attains sārūpya (conformity in form); performing the bath for thirty days, one certainly attains sāyujya (union).
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, a wise man must certainly perform his ritual bath at Rāmasetu during the month of Māgha when the sun has slightly risen. (26)
O twice-born ones, O best of the twice-born, performing a ritual bath at Rāmasetu during an eclipse of the moon or sun, as well as during an Ardhodaya or Mahodaya, [yields great merit]. (27)
One does not behold the dwelling in a womb, which is joined with manifold afflictions; it is proclaimed as the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. (28)
It is proclaimed as the subduer of all hells, and it is proclaimed as the source of all prosperities. (29)

Likewise, O twice-born ones, it bestows the state of residing in the same world (sālokya) and other such realms for all the worlds beginning with Indra, during lunar and solar eclipses as well as during the Ardhodaya festival.
Bathing at Mahodaya Dhanuṣkoṭi is most certainly ordained; it was established in ancient times by Rāma for the purpose of destroying Rāvaṇa. (31)
It was frequented by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Uragas, and served by hosts of Brahmanical seers, celestial rishis, royal rishis, and ancestors.
O twice-born ones, that man who, while recollecting the meritorious Rāmasetu—which is served with devotion by the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā—[attains the highest goal]. (33)
And one may bathe anywhere in a reservoir such as a pond or the like; never shall any evil deed of his ever come to pass.
By giving even a mere handful [of alms] at the holy fords situated in the middle of the Setu, all diseases as well as the sin of foeticide and others are destroyed.
Whoever beholds the holy line drawn by Rāma upon his bow shall never again return from Vaikuṇṭha.
Known in the world as Dhanuṣkoṭi, which destroys all sins, it was established by the wise Rāma at the request of Vibhīṣaṇa.
Dhanuṣkoṭi is of great merit; having bathed there with devotion, one should give gifts of wealth, lands, and likewise cows.
Of sesame seeds, rice grains, and other cereals, as well as of milk, garments, ornaments, mung beans, and cooked rice. || 39 ||
Of curds, clarified butter, waters, vegetables, and whey; of pure sugars, grains, and likewise of honey. (40)
O twice-born ones, it is said that at Rāmasetu, the giving of modakas, apūpas, and other such offerings bestows all desired objects. (41)

Therefore, free from greed for wealth, one should give at Rāmasetu; for whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, performed as austerity, recited as mantra, or observed as a vow and so forth [becomes inexhaustible]. 42.
The forest at the tip of Śrī Rāma’s bow bestows infinite fruit; by that, the Vedas are satisfied, and likewise the ancestors are satisfied. (43)
All the sages are pleased, as are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; the nāgas, kimpuruṣas, and yakṣas—all are certainly pleased. 44.
By beholding Dhanuṣkoṭi, one becomes purified oneself, and one purifies all the men born of one's own lineage as well as one's ancestors.
And by beholding Dhanuṣkoṭi, one shall deliver one's entire lineage, through the immersion in the Revā performed at the tip of Rāma’s bow. || 46 ||
The destruction of ten million great sins (pañcapātaka) shall certainly occur at that very moment for whoever beholds the line drawn by the tip of Śrī Rāma’s bow.
By immersing himself in that sacrificial pit where Sītā had encountered the fire, he did not behold the dwelling in a womb, which is filled with manifold afflictions.
O Brahmins, even a hundred instances of foeticide perish in a mere moment. As is Rāma, so is the Setu; as is the Gaṅgā, so is Hari. (49)
If a person, chanting "O Gaṅgā! O Hari! O Rāmasetu! bathes anywhere outside [the sacred precinct], he attains the supreme goal by that act. (50)
Having bathed at Setārdhodaya on Mount Gandhamādana, he who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍas) even the size of mustard seeds for the sake of his ancestors, [attains great merit].
The ancestors attain satisfaction for as long as the moon and sun endure, even if [an offering] the size of a śamī leaf is given with devotion for the sake of the ancestors.
If a piṇḍa is offered by a twice-born man, one is liberated from all sins; even if situated in heaven, such a person attains liberation, and if situated in hell, he goes to the celestial realm.
At Setu, Padmanābha, Gokarṇa, and Puruṣottama, bathing in the waters of the ocean is desired at all times.
One who desires progeny should never bathe in the salt water on the days of Venus, Mars, or Saturn, except at the Tīrtha.

A wise man who has not yet performed the funeral rites for his deceased kin, or one who is the husband of a pregnant woman, should never bathe in the ocean at any time other than at a sacred ford (setu).
O twice-born ones, for the Setu, constant bathing is praised without regard for time; indeed, restrictions regarding days of the week, lunar dates, and asterisms apply elsewhere than at the Setu.
One should bathe on behalf of those who are living, but one should not bathe on behalf of the deceased; having fashioned an image with kuśa grass, one should bathe it with the waters of sacred fords.
Having recited this mantra with a serene sense organ and mind: "Thou art Kuśa; thou art pure; thou wast held by Viṣṇu in ancient times. (59)
When you have bathed, he for whom this is the binding of the knot has also bathed; everywhere the ocean is meritorious, always on every sacred festival day.
Indeed, daily bathing is prescribed at Setu where the Sindhu meets the ocean, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the sea, at Gokarṇa, and at Puruṣottama.
One should never touch the Lord of Rivers (the Ocean) except on a festival day, while the ancestors, all the gods, and even the sages are listening.
Accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma made this vow: "Indeed, those men who perform their ablutions here once this bridge has been built by me," (63)
By my grace, they shall all attain rebirth; all their sins shall perish by the mere sight of my bridge.
I am not able to describe the majesty of Rāmanātha nor the glory of Matsetu, even in hundreds of millions of years.
Having heard these words of Rāma, the gods and great seers, being well-pleased, praised those words, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! (66).
In the middle of the bridge, Caturvaktra, accompanied by all the gods, always dwells there for the sake of protecting it by the command of the Lord.
Indeed, for the sake of protection, Mahāviṣṇu dwells upon the Rāma-setu under the name Setumādhava, bound by fetters.
And the great seers, the ancestors, and the promulgators of the Dharmaśāstras; as well as the gods together with the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Mahoragas. (69)
Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, and Kimpuruṣas, as well as all other beings, dwell here day and night. (70)
O best of the twice-born, whether seen, heard, remembered, touched, or entered into, this Rāmasetu protects one from all evil.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter in the Setumāhātmya of the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 52 ||

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. I bow to that Supreme Lord Śrī Rāmacandra, who is self-luminous and stainless; He is the boat by which the three worlds may cross the ocean of dissolution; He by whom all this universe shines, is born, persists, and evolves; He who is the embodiment of pure consciousness, beyond all means of proof, and known through the Upanishads. Wife, sons, wealth, kinsmen along with their retinues, beloved ones, mother, brother, father, the family of one's father-in-law, servants, power, riches, learning, beauty, a splendid home, youth, or even a circle of young women—all these are useless at the time of death; Dharma alone is the companion. In the Naimiṣa forest, the field of Nimi, the sages headed by Śaunaka performed a sacrificial session lasting a thousand years for the sake of attaining the heavenly world. 1. In the Naimiṣa forest, the field of Nimi, the sages headed by Śaunaka performed a sacrificial session lasting a thousand years for the sake of attaining the heavenly world.

Once, seeing Sūta approaching, Śaunaka and the others were filled with supreme joy; with clear minds, they drank him in with their eyes, and those ascetics gathered around there, eager to hear his wonderful stories.

"O dear one, in former times your father studied the entire Purāṇa; O Lomaharṣaṇa, have you also studied all of it?"
O Sūta, tell us the meritorious story that destroys sin; by hearing which, the sin accumulated over hundreds of births goes to its dissolution.
Sūta said: Having bowed down to the pair of feet of Śrī Bhāratī and the pair of feet of Gaṇanātha, as well as to all the gods, I shall speak.
Having paid homage to the Śaktis, the Vasus, the planets, the deities of sacrifice and so forth, as well as to the auspicious Brahmins and the foremost of poets in every respect; || 8 ||
Having prostrated before his chosen deity and the most excellent of gurus, and having paid homage to the auspicious gods, and especially to Rāma and the others; || 9 ||

By remembering whom one is liberated from various sins—of them there is no doubt—I shall, through their grace, declare the supreme fruit of the sacred fords (tīrthas), after first bowing down to the righteous-souled Lord who is the controller of all.

May that Lord Dharmeśvara—who is the lord of the forest of Dharma, the lord of heaven, and the eternal lord of Bhavānī; who is easily attained through the yoga of steady enjoyment; who, having pervaded the hearts of all with a portion of his own life-force, remains forever there; and meditating upon whom men do not enter again the prison-house of saṃsāra—protect you from evil. (11)
Sūta said: Once that Dharma indeed went to the assembly of Brahmā; having beheld that assembly, he then became established in knowledge.
Beholding the assembly hall frequented by gods, the best of sages, as well as by gods, yakṣas, nāgas, pannagas, and asuras, he was filled with wonder.
O Brahman, that assembly hall, its appropriate seats occupied by ṛṣis, Siddhas, and Gandharvas, was full of comfort—neither cold nor heat-giving.
Furthermore, they experience neither hunger, nor thirst, nor exhaustion; that assembly hall was constructed as if from various kinds of excellent jewels.
Supported by pillars, it is eternal and inexhaustible; with various divine forms shining with immeasurable splendor, it possesses boundless radiance.
Shining with her own radiance, she surpasses the moon, the sun, and Agni; stationed upon the vault of heaven, she seems to outshine even the sun itself.
In that city, the Blessed One Brahmā himself—the sole grandfather of all the worlds—teaches incessantly various gods and humans. (18)
Moreover, the Lords of Creatures wait upon that Lord: Dakṣa, Pracetas, Pulaha, Marīci, and the lord Kaśyapa. (19)
Bhṛgu, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and likewise Aṅgiras; Pulastya, Kratu, Prahlāda, and Kardama as well. (20)
The Atharvāṅgirases, the Vālakhilyas, and the Marīcipās; mind, the intermediate space, the sciences, wind, fire, water, and earth. (21)
Sound and touch, as well as form, taste, and likewise smell; nature and its transformations, and likewise the cause that is both existent and non-existent. || 22 ||
And Agastya of great splendor, the heroic Mārkaṇḍeya, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Saṃvarta, and likewise Cyavana. (23)
And Durvāsas, O illustrious one, and the righteous Ṛṣyaśṛṅga; and the blessed Sanatkumāra, a teacher of yoga and a man of great austerity. || 24 ||
Asita Devala, Jaigīṣavya who knows the truth, the eightfold Āyurveda, and Gāndharva [science] were indeed present there.
The moon together with the constellations, the sun with its rays, the winds, the threads [of the cosmic web], as well as volition and the vital breath. (26)
These and many others—embodied great souls devoted to their lofty vows—worshipped Brahmā.
Wealth, righteousness, and pleasure; joy, hatred, darkness, and self-restraint—all these come together in her, as do the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases. (28)
Venus and the other planets, as well as those others who were near him, the *Rathaṃtara* mantra, and also Harimān and Vasumān [were there]. (29)

Whatever is seen in the three worlds, whether stationary or moving—knowing that all of it was seated within her, that knower of dharma [reflected]. (38)

Having heard that extensive discourse concerning the origin of the universe, his eyes blossomed with joy, and having obtained Brahmā’s permission, [he departed].

Permitted by him at that time, he departed for the abode of Yama; and having heard [the account] which bestows merit through the grace of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Having [delivered] the divine, purifying, and sin-destroying discourse on the Dharmāraṇya, he then departed for Saṃyaminī together with his attendants.
Yama entered his own city together with his ministers and attendants; in the meantime, the highly effulgent Nārada, the best among sages, arrived there.

Difficult to behold, yet endowed with compassion, he was a seer of equality and a treasure-house of austerity; though his body was consumed by penance, he remained solely devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
Nārada, who is all-pervading, all-knowing, and ever pure, and who is habituated to the study of the Vedas, arrived there at that assembly.

Today my birth has become fruitful; today my lineage has become fruitful; today my dharma has become fruitful, now that you, O rich in asceticism, have arrived. (51)

Having performed worship according to the prescribed rules with the rites for the water of honor and the water for the feet, and having prostrated before him like a staff, he was then seated according to the ritual injunctions.
Upon their own great, divine seats, adorned with jewels and gold, the entire assembly appeared like figures depicted in a painting, as steady as lamps sheltered from the wind.
Having inquired after his welfare and greeted him with a welcome, he experienced incomparable joy while recollecting the story of Dharmāraṇya.
Having honored Nārada with a joyful inner soul, and seeing Yama thus delighted, Nārada’s face was filled with wonder.
He reflected in his mind, "Why is Hari so joyful? And seeing that great joy in him who had the form of King Yama, Nārada, with a mind full of wonder, then questioned him.
Nārada said: "What wonder have you seen, or what great state have you attained? You are wicked, a performer of evil deeds, evil-minded, and one who assumes a form of anger. (57)
The restraint of sinners is of such a form, yet this [form] is even greater; how has it become so gentle in appearance? This is my doubt, O Lord. (58)
Today you appear filled with joy; for what reason is this? O large-bodied one, tell me the very cause of your gladness. (59)
The King of Dharma said: "Listen, O son of Brahmā; I shall tell you this without any doubt. Formerly, I went to the abode of Brahmā to pay my respects."
Seated there in the midst of the assembly, he was the sole object of worship for all the worlds.
There, various discourses endowed with the categories of Dharma were heard.
These meritorious, delightful discourses, endowed with righteousness and joined with virtue, desire, and wealth, were heard from the mouth of Vyāsa; they destroy the entire flood of all sins.
O Sage, by hearing which one is liberated from all sins, including the murder of a Brahmin, and one delivers one hundred and one generations of one's paternal ancestors.
Nārada said: O Yama, O mighty-armed one, what kind of story is that which has been praised by you? I am desirous of hearing that story.
Yama said: Once, for the purpose of deliberating upon what ought and ought not to be done, I went to that region in the world of Brahmā in order to pay homage to the Grandfather.
O best of sages, I have seen and heard there a marvel—the divine narrative of Dharmāraṇya as proclaimed by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
O Brahmin, having heard this highly meritorious, auspicious narrative concerning the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), which is full of virtues and endowed with truth, he was thrilled with joy.
Furthermore, O best of sages, the reason for your arrival is indeed for the sake of auspiciousness, happiness, well-being, and victory. (68)
"O Sage, today I am one who has accomplished his purpose; today I am a man of merit. By the sight of your pair of feet, I have today truly become the Dharma itself. (69)
O Nārada, today I am worthy of worship, I have achieved my purpose, and I am blessed; and by the grace of your feet, I am honored throughout the three worlds. (70)
Sūta said: Thus gratified by such words, the best of sages, with supreme devotion, inquired about the auspicious narrative of Dharmāraṇya.

Yama said:

Nevertheless, association with the virtuous indeed leads to righteousness; it brings security and happiness both in this world and in the next. (74)
Whatever was heard in the presence of Brahmā as uttered by Vyāsa, all that I shall relate for the benefit of mankind.

Between the ages of Kali and Dvāpara, that Nārada went to the mortal world to see Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, and indeed the kingdom of the son of Dharma.

Accomplished by the assembly of great sages, learned, and a knower of the Gāndharva-veda, that Brahmin was skilled in the playful arts of enmity, like another Kali born of Brahmā.

Then that imperishable brahmin-sage Nārada, who wanders through the world of Brahmā, arrived with joy at the city protected by Dharmarāja.

Having presented him with a cow, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and half [of his possessions], that knower of dharma honored him with jewels and all objects of desire.
Having received worship in the proper manner, the knower of dharma was satisfied; "Are you well, O highly fortunate one? Is all well with your asceticism? (90)

"O Sage, no wicked Daitya indeed oppresses the Lord of Heaven; for you are auspicious in form, saluted by gods and asuras alike, all-pervading, omniscient, the son of Brahmā, and a treasure-house of compassion. (91)
Nārada said: "By the constant grace of Brahmā, all is well with me today. O illustrious Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, you too are well."
O Indra among kings, his mind delights in righteous duties along with his brothers, as well as with his wives, sons, servants, and his skillful elephants and horses.
O son of Dharma, you protect your subjects according to dharma as if they were your own legitimate sons; what wonder is there in this? For indeed, those subjects are blessed by you.
"Because of protecting and nourishing men, dharma certainly arises; you are indeed the enjoyer of that respective dharma"—thus Manu declared. (99)
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "By the touch of your feet and by the sight of you, O illustrious one, my kingdom and I are well; I have become cleansed of all sin. (96)
"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, and I am fortunate upon this earth; today I have become a man of merit because my son has come home. (97)
"O Brahmin, O best of sages, from where have you come today? Is it for the sake of favoring the virtuous, or for what purpose? (98)
Nārada said: O best of kings, I have come from the presence of Śamana with this auspicious ancient narrative told by Vyāsa in the presence of Brahmā. (99)
This divine [narrative], which takes refuge in the forest of Dharma and removes all afflictions—he who hears it is liberated from all sins, even the killing of a Brahmin. (100)
It pacifies ten thousand killings and destroys the threefold suffering; indeed, upon hearing it with supreme devotion, even a hard-hearted person attains softness.
Having heard that [account] which had been reported to him by Dharmarāja in my presence, the Lord of immeasurable soul questioned him about that story which delights the mind with its righteousness.

And the dharmas of the Purāṇas, as well as numerous vows, various types of sacred fords (tīrthas), and all places of pilgrimage (āyatanas). || 17 ||

I wish to hear in truth about the sacred fords situated in the Dharma-forest; by whom was this place established, and for what reason was it created? (19)
By whom was it protected and guarded, and at what time was it created? What exactly occurred there in the past? Tell me this as I ask you. (120)
Tell me today everything that has been, that is, and that will be in that place, as well as the current state of the sacred fords (tīrthas). || 121 ||

"Excellent, O King, you have asked most excellently concerning Vārāṇasī. O best of kings, listen very attentively to [the account of] Dharmāraṇya."
All sacred fords (tīrthas) are located right there; therefore it is called Ūṣara. It is frequented by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, as well as by Indra and the rest.
It was served by the world-protectors, the guardians of the directions, the Mothers, the powers of Śiva, as well as by Gandharvas and Apsarases, through the performance of sacrificial rites.
It was being attended by spirits, vetālas, śākinīs, planetary grahas, gods, and supreme deities, as well as by the seasons, months, fortnights, and by the gods and asuras.
And that was the primary royal seat, bestowing all happiness, and likewise served by many sacrifices and the most excellent sages.
With lions, tigers, and elephants, as well as various birds; with cows, buffaloes, and the like, and with cranes, deer, and boars.
O tiger among kings, it was frequented by various beasts of prey as well; there, birds, insects, and other creatures met their death.
Domestic animals and wild beasts, those that move in water and on land, those that fly in the sky and those that roam upon the earth, as well as ḍākinīs and rākṣasas—[all these were present]. || 9 ||
Together with one hundred and one [others], their liberation is indeed eternal; they all go to the worlds of Viṣṇu, without a doubt. || 10 ||
He causes ten ancestors and ten descendants to cross over by means of barley, rice, sesame seeds, ghee, bilva leaves, and dūrvā grass.

It is joined with many kinds of trees and beautifully adorned with creepers and shrubs; it is always bestowing merit and is ever endowed with fruit. (13)
O King, in that forest of Dharma, which is free from enmity and fear, cows and tigers play together, as do cats and mice. (11)
The frogs play with snakes, and humans dwell together with rākṣasas; they live there on the surface of the earth in Dharmāraṇya without fear.
In that divine realm consisting of great bliss, the supreme purifier of all purifiers, the sweet-voiced cuckoo dwelling in the groves warbles with longing melodies.

One established in meditation will then hear [the sound] as "pārāvatyeti" (it is being warded off); the male ruddy goose (*keka*), having abandoned his mate (*kokī*), remains silent out of fear of that. || 17 ||
The cakora bird, a consumer of moonlight, remains as if observing a vow of fasting at night; the sarika birds recite the essence, and oh, the parrot awakens them!
Śiva bestows the further shore upon the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra; he who, even through laziness, should depart from his home toward the forest of Dharma.
At every step, his merit shall exceed that of the horse-sacrifice; for indeed, there reside Brahmins endowed with the power of both cursing and blessing.
Eighteen thousand were appointed to meritorious tasks, while thirty-six thousand were the servants of those merchants on earth.

Endowed with devotion to the twice-born, devoted to Brahman, and not born from a womb, they are knowers of the Purāṇas, of virtuous conduct, righteous, and pure in intellect; the gods in heaven praise those who dwell in Dharmāraṇya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When was it that the gods established this place as Dharmāraṇya? Why did it become a purifier on the surface of the earth, and by whom was it created? (23)
Tell me, for what reason is it indeed a sacred ford (tīrtha)? How many Brāhmaṇas are there, and by whom were they established in ancient times? (24)
For what purpose were the eighteen thousand established? In which portion did those Brahmins, the best of the knowers of Brahman, arise? (25)
They were proficient in all branches of learning and had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; they were experts in the Ṛgveda and had exerted themselves in the study of the Yajurveda.

They were masters of the Sāmaveda and its auxiliary sciences, possessors of the three Vedas, and most knowledgeable in dharma; they were devoted to austerity, of auspicious conduct, and dedicated to the vow of truth.

"O best among speakers, tell me all of that from the beginning in its entirety: how is it that these people—who have been emaciated by month-long fasts as well as by the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances, who are of virtuous conduct, devoted to Brahman, and always subsisting on water—have come to be so? (28)
How is it that the Dānavas, the Daityas born of Bhūtas and Vetālas, as well as the Rākṣasas and Piśācas, do not cause them distress there? (29)

Vyāsa said: Listen, O tiger among kings, to this auspicious ancient tale; having heard it, one is liberated from all sins—of this there is no doubt.
Once, indeed, Dharmarāja performed a most difficult penance, enduring showers of water, heat from the sun, and other hardships, even against the efforts of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others.
O King, in the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, for thirty thousand years, he performed penance in the middle of a forest at the foot of an Aśoka tree.
A heap of bones bound together by dried tendons, motionless in appearance, its every drop of blood sucked dry by millions of ants from anthills.
It was a heap of bone without flesh, as motionless as a crystal stone, possessing a splendor like that of a conch shell, a tusk, the moon, snow, or a great white shell.

His life-breath was sustained by clinging to his being, preserved by the remainder of his lifespan, and the fact of his living was indicated only by the movement of the winds of inhalation and exhalation.
It reduced all living beings to the state of beasts by the movement of its opening and closing, and it illuminated the quarters of the sky with eyes of shimmering rays reddened by the sun.
The forest, withered by the forest fire of the flames of that [worldly] heat, was revived as all its trees were drenched by the rain of the nectar-water of his tranquility.
Having assumed a human form as if performing penance before one's very eyes, he rendered [the world] formless and spaceless, and made devotion golden.
It was surrounded by herds of wandering young deer and protected by forest-born beasts with mouths terrifying from their roars.
Seeing him thus, most formidable, the gods together with Indra meditated upon Mahādeva, the bestower of fearlessness upon all.
All the deities, beginning with Brahmā, went toward Kailāsa, where [Śiva] was seated together with Umā in the shade of a Pārijāta tree.
Nadirbhrṅgi, Mahākāla, and other great hosts, as well as the lordly Skandasvāmin and Gaṇapa, and the gods led by Brahmā, all remained there in their respective places.
Brahmā said: Salutations to you of infinite forms; O Nīla, salutations be to you! Salutations to the one whose true nature is unknown, to the absolute liberation, and to the immortal.
Even the gods do not know the end of him; salutations again and again to him! Salutations to that Self of Consciousness whom words do not praise.
Salutations to that glorious Brahman, whom yogis, remaining motionless through their resolve, perceive as a form of light within the casket of the heart.
Salutations to the one who transcends time, to Time itself, to the Person by His own will, to Him whose nature consists of the three qualities, and to Him whose form is primordial nature (prakṛti).
Salutations to Viṣṇu, who is the form of *sattva*; to Vedhas, who is the form of *rajas*; and to Rudra, who is the form of *tamas*, the agent of preservation, creation, and destruction. || 18 ||

Salutations to the one whose nature is intellect, who takes the form of the threefold ego, who is the form of the five subtle elements, and salutations to the one whose form is primordial nature (prakṛti). || 19 ||

Salutations again and again to you whose essential nature is the five faculties of cognition; salutations to you who consist of the five forms beginning with earth, and who are the self of the sense-objects. 20.
Salutations to You who are the form of the cosmic egg and who abide within it; salutations to You whose universal form encompasses both the near and the far.

Salutations to the one whose form is both impermanent and eternal, the Lord of existence and non-existence; salutations to You, who manifest Your body by Your own will out of compassion for Your devotees.
The Vedas are Your breath; the entire universe is Your Veda. All beings are Your feet; the sky has evolved as Your head. (23)
From Your navel arose the intermediate space, and from Your body hair the forest trees; O Lord, the moon was born from Your mind, and the sun from Your eye. 24.

You alone are everything; O God, everything is in you. You alone are the one to be praised here by all hymns of praise. O Lord, indeed this entire universe is pervaded by you. Homage be to you, again and again; salutations, salutations unto you!
Having thus praised Mahādeva, they fell upon the ground like a staff; then Śambhu replied, "I am the giver of boons; what do you desire?"
Mahādeva said: "O Brahman, why are all the gods, led by Bṛhaspati, so distressed? Tell me that cause of your suffering. (27)
Brahmā said: O Nīlakaṇṭha, Mahādeva, bestower of fearlessness and destroyer of suffering, listen to our misery which I shall describe to you. (28)
The righteous King Dharmarāja also performed most difficult penance; I do not know what he desires—the supreme station of the gods? || 29 ||
Terrified by that ascetic power, all the gods, led by Indra, for a long time directed their minds toward your feet. O Lord of Gods, raise him up; what does that King of Dharma desire?
Īśvara said: "Indeed, you have no fear of dharma; I tell you the truth. (31)
Then all those gods, together with the inhabitants of heaven, having risen, circumambulated Rudra and bowed down to him again and again.
Accompanied by Indra, they all returned from Kailāsa; then all the inhabitants of heaven quickly departed to their respective abodes.
Even Indra, the lord and sovereign, having gone to the Sudharmā assembly hall, found neither sleep there, nor pleasure, nor peace.
He reflected in his mind, "An obstacle has arisen for me"; then the god, the lord of Śacī, fell into great anxiety.
In order to seize my position, he performed extremely difficult penance; having summoned all the gods, he spoke these words: || 36 ||

Indra said: "Let all the deities hear the cause of my sorrow; what indeed could Yama desire that has been obtained by me through this suffering? Then Bṛhaspati, having looked upon all the gods, spoke thus. (37)
Bṛhaspati said: "O dwellers of heaven, you have no power to create obstacles to his asceticism; rather, let Urvashi and the others be summoned and sent there."
He set out for each door in order to bring them back; having gone there and gathered them, he quickly returned to the assembly hall. || 39 ||
When they had arrived, Hari said: "A great task has arisen; all of you go quickly and proceed swiftly toward Dharmāraṇya."
It was there indeed that Dharmarāja performed most difficult penance, [disturbed] by smiles, side-long glances, songs, dances, and the like. || 41 ||
"Entice that self-controlled one so that he may fall from his state of asceticism. Having heard the words of the god, the hosts of Apsarases did accordingly.
Having deliberated with one another, they resolved to act together; then Urvaśī, that celestial nymph, set out for Dharmāraṇya.
They praised him and showered flowers upon his head; then he was being lauded from all sides by the gods and the brahmins.
With supreme joy, he departed for the most sacred forest, which was thick with *bilva*, *arka*, and *khadira* trees, and crowded with *kapittha* and *dhava* trees.
There, even the sun does not shine; it is enveloped in great darkness, desolate, devoid of people, and extends for many yojanas. 46.
It was surrounded by fierce deer, lions, and other forest-dwelling creatures; it was strewn with flowering trees and possessed most enchanting meadows.
It was vast, made resonant by the sweet songs of birds, enriched by the warbling of male cuckoos, and filled with the humming of swarms of crickets.
It was covered with large, thick trees providing pleasant shade; its ground was concealed by trees and it was endowed with supreme beauty.
In this forest, there was no tree that lacked flowers, none that lacked fruit, nor any that was thorny; indeed, there was nothing that was not swarming with bees.
It was indeed exceedingly resonant with the songs of birds and adorned with flowers; it was completely covered by trees bearing blossoms of every season and providing pleasant shade.
There, the trees with flowering branches, stirred by the wind, released a wonderful rain of blossoms from their trunks.
Then, reaching toward the sky and well-nourished by birds with sweet songs, the trees there shone, covered with fragrant blossoms.
And the bees, desiring honey and uttering sweet sounds, settle upon the coral branches that are bent down by the weight of flowers and hum there.
There, he saw many regions adorned with sprouts of fragrant flowers, surrounded by bowers of creepers, which increased the delight of the mind.
Beholding this, she of great splendor then became joyful, seeing the trees covered with blossoms and their branches intertwined with one another.
That forest shone with trees resembling the banners of Mahendra; and the breeze, carrying the pollen of flowers, was pleasant, cool, and fragrant.
Then she beheld that forest endowed with such qualities, where the pure and radiant daughter of the Sun was shining.
And there he beheld a most excellent and delightful hermitage, surrounded by the Vālakhilyas and filled with hosts of sages.

It was filled with many fire-sanctuaries from which tree branches hung down, and likewise with ascetics clad only in the directions (naked) who were scattering drops of pungent-smelling drinking-water.
There, the wild animals became even more gentle; likewise, cats lived there with mice, and mongooses with snakes. (61)
Likewise, lions became like fawns in their disposition, and they played with one another just as if they were brothers. Then, seeing the forest from afar, the god spoke at that time: || 62 ||
Indra said: "Indeed, this Dharmarāja stands engaged in intense austerity; he desires my kingdom. Therefore, let an effort be made here for his sake."
"Let them create obstacles to my penance; by my command, go there. Having heard Indra's words, both Urvaśī and Tilottamā [prepared to depart]. (64)
Sukeśī, Mañjughoṣā, Ghṛtācī, Menakā, Viśvācī, Rambhā, and the sweet-voiced Pramlocā; || 65 ||
Pūrvacitti, Surūpā, Anumlocā, and Yaśasvinī—these and many others who were present there deliberated.
Indeed, looking at one another and fearing out of dread, both Yama and Śakra said, "This is surely your abode."
Having reflected thus in many ways, O Bhārata, the one named Vardhanī—the most excellent of all Apsarases and adorned with every ornament—[approached]. (68)

Urvaśī spoke there: "O fair-faced one, why do you grieve? O subduer of Pāka, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, I shall act by means of the power of my illusory form so that the duty of my caste may be fulfilled. (69)
Indra said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! You are named Vardhanī and are firm in your vows. Go yourself quickly, O auspicious one; perform the task, O slender-waisted lady. (70)
"O fair-browed one, there is no other capable of protecting the wise besides you. Having said, "So be it," Vardhanī went to where that King of Dharma was.
Having fashioned a beautiful form with magnificent ornaments, she was adorned with saffron, collyrium, garments, and jewelry.
She was adorned with flowers and garments, her hips resplendent with small bells, and her two feet decorated with tinkling ornaments.
Richly adorned with various ornaments, anointed with various types of sandalwood paste, graced with various flower garlands, and covered in auspicious silk garments.
Holding a perfectly pure lute in her hand, she who was beautiful in all her limbs performed there a threefold dance that delighted the world.
In a loud voice, it was blended with the sweet sound of the flute. || 76 ||

Accompanied by melodies (*mūrcchanā*) and rhythmic cycles (*tāla*), and endowed with the resonance of stringed instruments (*tantrī-laya*), the god Dharmarāja, who had conquered his own self, suddenly became despondent in an instant, O prince. || 77 ||
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O Brahman, O best of the Brahmins, a supreme wonder has arisen in me: how was it that the cutting off of his asceticism occurred for one who was so endowed with Brahman? (78)
In Dharma are both the earth and heaven; in Dharma is Pātāla itself. In Dharma are the moon, the sun, and the waters; in Dharma are the wind and fire. || 79 ||
And since the entire universe rests in Dharma alone, O Lord of noble vows, how has that Dharma fallen into such agitation? Tell me the truth regarding that distraction.
Vyāsa said: This Yonikuṇḍa was created on earth as the cause for the downfall of those who commit rash acts, and it is equal to the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Having bound them firmly with the rope of the eyes, they overpower even the wise; while the mindless one is being beaten by great clubs in the form of their breasts.
O best of kings, having indeed created her, they quickly cast her into hell; for thus was the woman fashioned as a deluder of all living beings.
Alas, let the mind maintain its steadiness and its unagitated, truthful learning only so long as it does not fall, like a snare, before the face of an intoxicated woman.
So long indeed does there increase of asceticism, so long charity, compassion, and self-restraint; so long the practice of Vedic study, so long purity, and so long the observance of vows. (85)
As long as one does not behold that fickle glance of a frightened doe, so long is there a mother, so long a father, so long a protector, and so long a circle of friends. (86)

So long indeed does shame persist, so long does fear, and so long does one's own proper conduct; so long indeed do knowledge, magnanimity, and sovereignty shine forth—until one is cast down by the nooses of intoxicated women, those very bonds. (87)
Vyāsa said: Hereafter I shall proclaim the deeds of Dharmarāja, hearing which no fear of the messengers of Yama exists anywhere.
She was seen by Dharmarāja, that excellent Apsarā named Vardhanī; for who is this woman of beautiful limbs, so exceedingly beautiful, in this great forest? (2)
Realizing that this forest was devoid of humans and terrifying with lions and tigers—a supreme marvel—the King of Dharma spoke these words.
The King of Dharma said: "O proud lady, why do you wander alone in this desolate forest? From what place have you come, and whose wife are you, O beautiful one? (4)
"Whose daughter are you, O lady of beautiful thighs? You are exceedingly beautiful and auspicious; are you a human, or a Gandharva woman, or an immortal goddess, or a Kinnarī? (5)
Is she an Apsaras, or a bird, or perhaps a forest deity? Is she a Rākṣasī or a Khecarī? Tell me, whose wife is she?
"Speak the truth to me, O fair-browed one," the son of the Sun then said. "What do you desire, O blessed lady? Or what task must be done by you here? Speak indeed. (7)
"O lady of beautiful thighs, whatever you desire, I shall grant it to you."
Varddhanī said: "O Lord, everything indeed—both the stationary and the moving—rests upon Dharma. O sinless one, why do you perform such a difficult task?"
Yama said: "O beautiful lady, I desire to see the form of Īśāna; therefore, joined with Śivā through this austerity, I shall behold Śaṅkara."
"I shall attain fame, I shall attain happiness, and I perform what is most difficult to do; may my renown endure through age after age—such is my thought. (11)
"May my fame increase further in every age and in every great aeon (mahākalpa); for this reason, O fair-browed one, she performs supreme austerity. (12)
"O blessed lady, why have you come? Tell me exactly as it is. What is your purpose and for what reason? You ought to tell me the truth. (13)
Varddhanī said: "O Dharma, it was through your very asceticism that the Lord of Heaven became terrified; therefore, I have been impelled here by him out of a desire to destroy your penance. (14)
"O illustrious one, terrified by fear of Indra’s throne, I have been sent here by Hari into the presence of Hari; indeed, I speak the truth. (15)
Sūta said: Then the son of the Sun, being gratified by her truthful words, spoke to her: "O highly fortunate lady, I am a granter of boons; choose one from me."
I am Yama for all wicked beings who perform evil deeds; indeed, I am Dharma in form for all men of self-restraint. (17)
"O lady of excellent hips, I am that Dharma; I shall grant you what is difficult to obtain. O best among Apsarases, ask of me all that you desire immediately. (18)
Varddhanī said: "O Lord, best among the upholders of dharma, grant me a state of eternal stability in the ever-delightful abode of Indra, indeed for the welfare of the worlds. (19)
Yama said: "So be it," he said to her, "choose another boon quickly; I shall grant you an excellent boon, for I am pleased by your singing."
Varddhanī said: "O high-minded one, let there be a holy site (tīrtha) of mine in this great field (mahākṣetra), which shall destroy all sins and become renowned by my name. (21)
Whatever is given as a gift, offered in sacrifice, performed as austerity, or recited there becomes inexhaustible. One should resort to the Vardhamāna lake for five nights.

"May his ancestors be satisfied as they are gratified day after day. Having said "So be it," Dharma remained there and observed a vow of silence. After circumambulating Dharma three times and bowing to him, she departed for heaven.
Varddhanī said: "O Lord of Gods, do not fear Yama, the son of the Sun; this Dharma, intent on his own self-interest, would practice [virtue] merely for the sake of fame. (24)
Vyāsa said: The auspicious-faced Vardhanī was honored by that Śakra: "Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! You have performed the work of the gods."
O lady of auspicious countenance, you shall always possess fearlessness in the house of your husband, a happy dwelling, fame, happiness, and beautiful prosperity. (26)
"So be it," the gods replied to her with hearts full of fearless joy; and having paid homage to Śakra, she departed for her own auspicious abode.

Sūta said: O king of kings, when the Apsaras had departed, Dharma remained there according to the prescribed rule; he performed a most terrible penance that caused agitation to the entire universe. || 28 ||
O King, when the month of Śukra was scorched by the sun, Pañcāgni performed a penance that was exceedingly difficult to endure and unassailable even by the gods.
Then, when a hundred years had passed, Antaka adopted silence; covered by hundreds of anthills, he remained as motionless as a log of wood.
O King, because various flocks of birds had built their nests there, that Lord of Dharma, while seated in his vow, could not be seen at all anywhere.

Then, remembering the blameless Lord of Devas, the husband of Umā, the gods, along with the Gandharvas and Yakṣas, their minds filled with anxiety, once again went to the peak of Kailāsa into the presence of Śiva.

The gods said: "Save us, save us, O Mahādeva! O Śrīkaṇṭha, Lord of the universe! Save us, O Lord of the past and the future! Save us, O you whose banner is the bull! You are compassionate, O Lord of mercy; O Śaṃkara, make us free from obstacles!"
Īśvara said: By whom have the gods been offended, or by whom has their honor been crushed? Is it among mortals, in heaven, or among the nāgas? Tell me this quickly, without delay. (34)
"With this very trident, or else with the khaṭvāṅga, or indeed with the Pāśupata weapon, I shall slay him in battle. Speak quickly, indeed, the reason for your arrival here! (35)
The gods said: "O Ocean of Compassion, O Lord of Gods, O Bringer of Joy to the World! Today we have no fear of humans, nor of Nagas, nor of gods or Danavas. (36)
In the world of mortals, O Mahādeva, the Lord of the Pretas, possessing a massive form, will surely cause great distress for his own purpose; this is certain. (37)

"O Sadāśiva, by means of fierce austerity, we have caused ourselves to suffer through our own efforts; because of that, all of us gods are distressed here. We have come to you for refuge; do whatever you desire. (38)

Sūta said: Having heard the words of the gods, the bull-bannered Lord, mounted upon his bull, took up his weapons and his most beautiful armor, and then went to that place where Dharma was stationed. (39)
Īśvara said: "O Dharma, my mind is well-pleased by this austerity. Choose a boon, choose a boon, choose a boon! he said.
"O blessed one, whatever desires you wish for, exactly as they reside in your mind—whatever you pray for, I shall grant it to you right now. (41)
Sūta said: O King, seeing the god Maheśvara thus conversing, he rose from the anthill, joined his palms in reverence, and praised the Lord of the World with pure words, O subduer of enemies.
Dharma said: Salutations to you, O Lord; salutations to you who possess the form of yoga; salutations to you whose form is splendor; O Blue-throated One, let there be salutations to you. (43)
Salutations to You, who are accessible through devotion according to the disposition of meditators; salutations to You whose form is Brahman, and salutations be to You whose form is Viṣṇu. 44.

Salutations to the gross, to the subtle, and indeed salutations to the one whose form is atomic; salutations to you who can assume any form at will, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction. || 45 ||
Homage to the eternal, gentle, and compassionate Hari; homage to you, the heat-giver, and homage to the moon, the maker of cold.
Salutations to you whose form is creation; salutations be to you, O Guardian of the World. Salutations to the fierce one, to the formidable one, and salutations to you of peaceful form.

Salutations to you whose form is infinite, salutations to you whose form is the universe; salutations to him whose limbs are smeared with ashes, salutations to you, O Moon-crested One; salutations be to the five-faced one, salutations be to you, the three-eyed one.

Salutations to you who are adorned with serpents and who wear a loincloth; salutations to the destroyer of Andhaka and the remover of Dakṣa’s sins. O enemy of Tripura, salutations be to you, the consumer of Kāma. || 49 ||
Whoever should recite these forty names that have been spoken by me—whether having become pure, they recite them at the three times of day, or even merely listen to them.
A cow-killer, an ungrateful person, a drinker of liquor, one who violates the teacher's bed, a slayer of a Brahmin, a stealer of gold, or indeed the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī). || 51 ||

A killer of women and children, a sinner who speaks falsehoods, one of improper conduct, a thief, one who violates another's wife, a doer of forbidden acts, a destroyer of what ought to be done, a hater of Brahmins, and the lowest of Brahmins—[these are those who must be avoided]. (53)
Sūta said: Although thus repeatedly praised with many words by Dharmarāja with great devotion, he himself bowed his head in salutation.
Then Śambhu, being pleased, spoke these auspicious words to him: "O highly fortunate one, choose a boon—whatever resides in your heart. (55)
Yama said: "If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, having shown compassion toward me, then grant that, O illustrious one, throughout the three worlds with all things mobile and immobile. (56)
"Indeed, this place shall become famous in the world by the name of Manu; it is indestructible, indivisible, meritorious, and the destroyer of sins. (57)

"O Mahādeva, O Bhava, if you are pleased with me, grant me a place. Then, O King, Śiva granted him a site equal to Kāśī. Having given that, he spoke again: "O best of beings, choose another boon. (58)

Dharma said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased and have shown compassion toward me, O illustrious one, then grant this: that in every age I may attain renown throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, by means of this very boon. (59)
Īśvara said: "Speak, O Kīnāśa, all that; I shall accomplish your desire. Indeed, being gratified by your penance, I grant you the boon you seek. (60)
Yama said: "O Lord Śaṅkara, if you grant my desire, then always bear my name in this place, this great sacred field."
O God, O Maheśvara, act in such a way that the fame of this place as "Dharmāraṇya" arises throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.

Īśvara said: "O God, may this place known as Dharmāraṇya remain famous forever in age after age; established under your name, it shall attain renown. Furthermore, tell me whatever else I may do for you. (63)
Yama said: "This supreme holy site (tīrtha), two yojanas in extent, is named after me; it is the eternal abode of liberation and a purifier for all embodied beings. (64)
Flies and insects, as well as beasts, birds, and wild animals; moths, spirits, vetālas, piśācas, serpents, and rākṣasas. || 65 ||
Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever gives up their dear life-breaths here in my field known as Dharmāraṇya, let there be eternal liberation for them. || 66 ||
"So be it," said all the gods, including Brahmā and the others; showering flowers, they attained supreme joy. || 67 ||
The celestial drums resounded, the lords of the Gandharvas sang, holy winds blew, and throngs of Apsarases danced.
Sūta said: Sadāśiva, being truly gratified by Yama’s austerity and devotion, spoke these words to the god—charming, excellent, and pleasing to the mind.
"Grant me your permission, O Father, so that I may go quickly to Kailāsa, the best of mountains, out of a desire for the welfare of the gods. (70)
Yama said: "O Maheśvara, it is not fitting for you to abandon my abode; O Lord, by your word this place shall become even greater than Kailāsa. (71)
Śiva said: "Well spoken by you; it is fitting that my presence here exists in one part. O virtuous one, this exceedingly pure place of yours has not been abandoned by me."
"The Great Liṅga Viśveśvara shall exist here under my name. Having spoken thus, Mahādeva vanished right there.
Then, by the word of Śiva, that wonderful Liṅga appeared there; and having seen it, the gods there proclaimed its name according to tradition.
Then, each of their respective lingas was created in Dharmāraṇya by the best of the gods; whichever deity’s linga it was, it was proclaimed by that deity's name.
Sūta said: The Liṅga established by Dharma, Dharmeśvara, has arrived; by remembering it or worshipping it, one is liberated from all sins. || 76 ||
That Brahman which is accessible to yogins and resides in the hearts of all—its self-manifested *liṅga* remains established as such. || 77 ||
Having fully worshipped the Lord of Beings (Bhūtanātha), people are liberated from diseases; thereafter, he also constructed a beautiful Dharmavāpī there.
Having taken water from ten million sacred fords (tīrthas), he released it into the pond; and having performed a delightful bath in the form of the Yamatīrtha, he remained there. (79)
It is for the bathing of the deities and the sages of purified souls; having bathed and drunk there, one is liberated from all sins.
Having bathed in the Dharmavāpī and beheld the auspicious Dharmeśvara Śiva, a man is liberated from all sins and shall not enter a mother’s womb again.

Having bathed there, the man who performs the libation (tarpaṇa) to Yama for the sake of destroying the defects of disease and for the pacification of the defects of suffering—offering it to Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, Antaka, Vaivasvata, Kāla, Dadhna, and Parameṣṭhin—[attains his goal]. || 82 ||
Salutation to you, Vṛkodara, to Vṛka, to the Lord of the South; salutation to you, Nīla, to Citragupta, O Citra, O Vaicitra! || 83 ||
Whoever shall perform a libation at the Dharmavāpī with these names accompanied by unbroken grains of rice—for that person no misfortune shall occur. (84)
The tertian fever occurs every other day, as does the quartan fever; likewise, that fever which arises at a specific time is known as the cold-fever (śītajvara). || 85 ||
Neither the planets such as Revatī, nor the defects, nor the ḍākinīs and śākinīs can afflict one whose mind is of this nature. (66)
There shall be an abundance of wealth and grain, and one's progeny will always increase; having bathed well and subdued the senses, one should worship Bhūteśvara.

By performing the recitation of the Rudra-mantra along with its ancillaries (sāṅga), one is liberated from the affliction of disease. On the new moon day, on a Monday, during the Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti yogas, at the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), and during an eclipse—on these occasions, the performance of Śrāddha for men is traditionally prescribed.
By that man who is renowned as a human being, a *śrāddha* is performed for a thousand years; having cast this aside, the ancestors eat even water mixed with sesame seeds which he offers. (89)
By offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā twenty-one times, that which is given even once at Dharmeśvara becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors.
To the west of Dharmeśa, or even within Viśveśvara, there is the famous Dharmavāpī, which bestows the stairs to heaven.
Formerly, it was created by Dharmabuddhi for the sake of auspiciousness through righteous means; having bathed there and drunk [the water], the ancestors and deities were gratified.
Furthermore, the man who offers a funeral ball (piṇḍa) even the size of a śamī leaf at the highly meritorious Dharmavāpī shall not undergo residence in a womb again.
O King, one is liberated from the most terrible Kumbhīpāka hell, and again from the Raurava and Andhatāmisra hells; of this there is no doubt.
Sūta said: O best of men, at Dharmavāpī, one should offer libations for a single year; however, regarding the season, month, and fortnight, the opposite may occur.
The Barhiṣads, the Agniṣvāttas, the Ājyapas, and likewise the Somapas, attain supreme satisfaction through libations at the step-well. || 96 ||
Sacred fields such as Kurukṣetra, cities such as Ayodhyā, and all places beginning with Puṣkara are indeed known by the name "liberation. (97)
All those are equal, but the Dharma-well is superior; so too are mantras, the Vedas, sacrifices, gifts, and vows.
O Lord of Men, by giving and by reciting [these mantras], inexhaustible results are produced; as are the rites of sorcery (abhicāra) and others well-established in the Atharvaveda. || 99 ||
O best of kings, all those who have performed rites at that place attain perfection; it is the primordial holy site (āditīrtha) frequented by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.

The abode of Siddhi is exceedingly serene and is frequented even by Brahmā and the other gods; it remains [active] until the end of the Kṛta Yuga, and for five hundred thousand years during the Tretā Yuga.

In the Dvāpara age, however, the fruit is obtained in one hundred thousand [years], whereas in the Kali age, it is attained in a single day. O Brahmā, this description of Dharmāraṇya has been told by me; indeed, the entire fruit thereof was spoken by Dvaipāyana.
Sūta said: Hereafter I shall proclaim the delightful discourse on dharma, which he spoke after giving his command for the benefit and welfare of the gods.
Dharma said: In this sacred field, those deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu commit adultery, which is a great evil, as well as the theft of gold and other such acts.
Furthermore, one who performs any improper act whatsoever shall go to hell; however, sin committed in another field is destroyed in Dharmāraṇya. (5)
A sin committed in the forest of Dharma will become as indelible as diamond; for as merit is, so too is sin—whatever is auspicious or inauspicious.
All that increases constantly for a hundred years; it is meritorious, granting the desires of those who possess desire and bestowing liberation upon yogis. || 7 ||
Dharmāraṇya is always proclaimed as the bestower of perfection upon the perfected ones; one without a son obtains sons, and one who is destitute becomes wealthy.

This meritorious narrative was told by Dharma in ancient times. Whatever man listens to it with devotion, or whatever woman causes it to be heard, he or she shall obtain the fruit of a thousand cows and, at the end, go to the city of Hari.
Vyāsa said: Hereafter, I shall declare what must be performed here by a man dwelling in Dharmāraṇya who is observing the householder stage of life.
Those born in the forests of Dharma, Brāhmaṇas of pure lineage, numbering eighteen thousand, were created by the lords of Ka and Aja.
The Brāhmaṇas who are of virtuous conduct, pure, and most proficient in the knowledge of Brahman—by the mere sight of them, one is liberated from great sins. (3)

Yudhiṣṭhira said: O son of Parāśara, O Lord, tell me of right conduct (sadācāra). Through conduct one attains dharma; through conduct one obtains the fruit [of one's actions]; through conduct one attains prosperity—therefore, tell me that conduct.
Vyāsa said: Stationary beings, worms, aquatic creatures, birds, animals, and humans—these become increasingly righteous in this sequence; more righteous than these are the gods.
In the first [kalpa] there were a thousand parts, and likewise in the sequence of the second; all these highly fortunate ones found refuge in liberation from sin.
Among all four types of beings, those with life-breath are indeed most excellent; and among those with life-breath, O best of sages, all who subsist by means of intelligence are superior.

Men are superior to those who possess intellect; among them, the Vāḍavas (brahmins) are superior. Among brahmins, the learned are superior, and among the learned, those whose minds are perfected [in wisdom] are superior. (8)

O Bhārata, those who perform actions for the sake of those whose intellects are perfected, and those who are devoted to Brahman among the performers of action—there is no one superior to them in the three worlds.
They indeed honor one another on account of their excellence in austerity and knowledge; for the Brāhmaṇa was created by Brahmā as the lord of all beings.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa alone, and no other, deserves everything that exists in the world; for one who possesses good conduct is worthy of all, whereas one who has fallen away from good conduct is not.
Therefore, O Sage, a Brahmin should always be characterized by good conduct; he should practice that which is free from hatred and passion.
The wise know that this practice of good conduct is the root of Dharma; even one who is devoid of auspicious marks, if he is devoted to right conduct, [is esteemed]. (13)
A man who is faithful and free from malice shall live for a hundred years, following that which is declared by the Śruti and Smṛti in regard to his respective duties.
One should, unwearied, practice good conduct, which is the root of dharma; for a man who delights in misconduct becomes an object of reproach in the world. (15)

One would be overcome by diseases, always short-lived, and a partaker of great suffering. Action dependent on others should be abandoned; one should always perform action that is under one's own control.
For one who is dependent on others is always miserable, whereas one who is self-dependent is happy; that action in which the inner self rejoices while it is being performed [should be done]. (17)
That very action should be performed, and never its opposite; for it has been declared that the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) constitute the primary essence of dharma. (16)
Therefore, one who desires righteousness must indeed exert effort toward these very qualities: truthfulness, forgiveness, seasonal conduct, meditation, benevolence, and non-violence.
Self-restraint, serenity, gentleness, and mildness—these are the ten *yamas*. Purity, bathing, austerity, charity, silence, sacrifice, study, and vows [are the *niyamas*]. (20)
Fasting, [celibacy], and the staff—these ten are recorded as the restraints (niyamas): desire, anger, self-control, delusion, envy, and greed. (21)
Having conquered these six enemies, one shall be victorious everywhere; one should gradually accumulate merit, just as a horned insect builds up an anthill.
For one who does not cause suffering to others, dharma alone shall be his companion in the next world, protecting him as he travels there.
A living being is born with parents, children, brothers, wives, and kinsmen as superiors; yet it is born alone, and likewise, it dies alone.

Alone one experiences the fruit of good deeds, and alone one experiences the fruit of evil deeds; when the body has reached its dissolution into the five elements, [the self] abandons it like a piece of wood or a clod of earth.
Relatives turn their faces away [at death], but dharma follows one who departs; therefore, one should accumulate dharma as a companion for both this world and the next.
Having obtained Dharma as a companion, one should cross over the darkness that is difficult to traverse; the wise man should always associate with the most excellent among the excellent.

Having abandoned those who are base and more base, one should lead one’s family to excellence; one should approach only the highest of the high and avoid those who are inferior. A Brāhmaṇa attains preeminence through this, but through transgression he reaches the state of a Śūdra. (28)
Death afflicts that Brahmin who is habitually neglectful of Vedic study, who transgresses the rules of good conduct, who is indolent, and who eats forbidden food.
Therefore, a twice-born man should always practice good conduct with diligence; even sacred fords long for the company of those who possess good conduct.
The half-yāma at the end of the night is called the Brāhma period; having risen during that time, a wise person should always contemplate his own welfare. (31)
First, one should meditate upon the Elephant-faced One (Gaṇeśa), then on the Lord (Śiva) together with his Mother, then on Śrīraṅga accompanied by Śrī, and then on Brahmā, who is born from the lotus.
[He saw] all the gods beginning with Indra, the sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha, all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, and all the mountains beginning with Śrīśaila.
The oceans beginning with the Ocean of Milk, the lakes beginning with Lake Mānasa, the forests beginning with Nandana, and the cows beginning with the wish-fulfilling Kāmadhenu; || 34 ||
He also saw wish-fulfilling trees and other trees, minerals primarily consisting of gold, celestial women headed by Urvaśī, and the beloved attendants of Hari, beginning with Prahlāda.

Having remembered his mother’s feet, which are the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas), and having meditated upon his father and his teachers within his heart with a tranquil mind, [he spoke].
Then, in order to perform the necessary rite, one should go toward the southwest direction; one should travel one hundred bows from a village, and four times that distance from a city.
Having covered the ground with grass and veiled his head with a cloth, with his sacred thread over his ear, he should face north during the day as well as at the two twilights.
In the night, one should void excrement and urine while maintaining silence, facing the south; O Brahmin, one should not do so while standing, nor too quickly, nor facing cows, fire, or the wind.
One should not look at a ploughed area of ground, nor at a road or a surface frequented by people; nor should one look at the quarters of the horizon, the orb of light, the sky, or impurity.
Holding his penis with his left hand, he should rise up with effort; then he should take up earth that is free from insects and gravel.
Having discarded the earth dug up by mice, which is leftover and strewn with hair, one should apply a single application of clay to the private parts and then wash it with water.
Again, with the left hand, one should wash the anus five times; likewise, one should apply one portion of clay to each foot and three portions to the two hands.

In this manner, a householder should perform purification until the odor and the smear are removed; for the other three stages, beginning with the student (brahmacarya), he should perform it with double the effort in successive order.
One should perform half of the purification prescribed for the day during the night; half of that again in another village, and half of even that while on a road.

Half of that [measurement] should be used for those who are ill, and one should not make it less even when healthy; this applies even with the waters of all rivers and with heaps of earth resembling mountains.

One who is defiled in heart does not partake of purity even if he performs the ritual cleansing at the outset. For the purpose of purification, it is prescribed that the amount of clay should be equal in measure to a fresh *dhātrī* fruit. (47)
All oblations and even the morsels in the Cāndrāyaṇa penance should be offered in this same manner; one should sit comfortably on pure ground, facing either the east or the north.
One should perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) with water that is free from husks, charcoal, bones, and ashes; it should be perfectly clear and reach as far as the heart, doing so without haste.

A Brāhmaṇa should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with water purified by his sight using the Brahma-tīrtha; a king (Kṣatriya) becomes pure when it reaches the throat, and one of the Vaiśya class when it reaches the palate. || 50 ||
A woman or a Śūdra are purified by mere touch; or one may recite the word "Śiras" along with the neck-mantra (the Śikhā) in the water, even if the topknot is untied.
One whose feet have not been washed is considered impure even if he has sipped water; for the sake of purification, one should sip water three times and then cleanse the bodily apertures.
One should wipe the lower lip with the base of the thumb; having touched the heart with water, one should touch the head with all the fingers.
Likewise, one should touch both shoulders with the tips of the fingers; having sipped water (ācamana), one should sip water again after walking upon a road.
After bathing, eating, drinking water, or beginning auspicious rites; after sleeping, putting on a garment, or likewise seeing something inauspicious—(one should perform the purification). || 55 ||

If one becomes impure through negligence, one shall become pure by sipping water twice after remembering [the transgression]. One should perform the cleansing of the teeth according to the rules prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras; for even one who has sipped water remains impure if he has not cleansed his teeth.

On the first, sixth, and ninth lunar days, as well as on the ninth day of the fortnight and on Sundays, the contact of a wooden stick with the teeth shall burn one's family unto the seventh generation.
If tooth-sticks are unavailable, or if the day is prohibited for their use, twelve mouthfuls of water should be taken for the purification of the mouth.
The tooth-stick for cleansing the teeth should be the size of the tip of the little finger, with its bark intact, free from wounds or blemishes, twelve finger-breadths in length, and fresh.
One should chew that tooth-stick, measuring one finger-breadth in length; having performed the morning bath, especially at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), for the sake of purification.
Since this body is always impure, it must be purified by bathing at dawn and other rites; for its filth flows out indeed day and night through the nine apertures.
They say that it increases enthusiasm, intellect, good fortune, and the perfection of physical form; it is equal to the Prājāpatya penance and brings about the destruction of great sins.
The morning bath removes sin, misfortune, and exhaustion; it also bestows contentment, nourishment, and freedom from impurity and bad dreams. (63)
Indeed, the wicked never approach one who bathes in the morning; therefore, one should perform the morning bath, for it yields both seen and unseen fruits.

In this connection, O best of kings, I shall describe the procedure for bathing; for they say that a bath performed according to the prescribed rite is a hundred times superior to other forms of bathing. (65)
Having taken pure clay, sacrificial grass, sesame seeds, and cow dung, and having placed them in a clean spot, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and then proceed with the bath.

Having taken hold [of the water] with his topknot tied, he should enter into the midst of the water; he should perform the bath according to the rules prescribed in his own Vedic school (śākhā) and in accordance with the ritual injunctions.

Having bathed in this manner and wrung out his garment, he should put on two washed cloths; then, having sipped water (ācamana), he should perform the morning twilight devotion (prātaḥsaṃdhyā) while holding kuśa grass.
A Brahmin practicing breath control while firmly restraining the mind is instantly liberated from the sins committed during a day and night. (69)
If ten or twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are performed while restraining the mind, then great austerity has been practiced by that person.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava, performed daily, purify even the slayer of a fetus within a month.
Just as the impurities of the earthly elements are burned away by smelting, so too the defects produced by the senses are consumed by the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma). 72.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity; and there is nothing superior to the Gāyatrī as a purifier, O best of kings. (73)
Whatever sin one commits by deed, thought, or word during the night, one should purify it by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) upon rising at the morning twilight.
