Whatever sin one commits during the day through the actions of mind, speech, and body, one dispels it by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) while seated at the evening twilight; indeed, sitting for the evening twilight, one destroys the impurity created during the day.
He who does not attend upon the morning [prayer] and he who does not worship at the evening [prayer] should be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra. (76)
Having approached the vicinity of water, one should perform the daily rites; then one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules and in the proper sequence.

Then one should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," [placing the water] on the ground, on the head, and in the air; and in the air, on the ground, and on the head.

One should likewise cast [the water] nine times upon the head and upon the ground; by the word "ground" (bhūmi) the feet are meant, and "space" (ākāśa) is traditionally understood as the heart. The word "head" (śiras) refers specifically to the crown of the head; purification is said to be performed with these [mantras].

This supreme Brāhma-bath is superior even to the baths dedicated to Varuṇa, Agni, Vāyu, and Indra, and even superior to the bath performed with mantras. He who has bathed with the Brāhma-bath is pure both externally and internally.
And yet, he is honored everywhere by the Arhats in rites such as worship of the gods; are fishermen, who immerse themselves in water day and night, truly purifying? (81)

Even if they have bathed in that manner hundreds of times, those whose internal dispositions are corrupted are not purified; however, the sacred ash shall sanctify those whose inner faculties are pure.
Why are donkeys, grey with ash, proclaimed as purifiers? He who is free from all impurities has bathed in all sacred fords.
He whose mind here is stainless has performed hundreds of sacrifices; O Sage, listen now to how that very mind may become stainless. (84)
If Viśveśa should be gracious, then [liberation] would occur, and never otherwise; therefore, for the sake of purifying the mind, one should take refuge in the Lord of Kāśī. || 85 ||
Having cast off this body, he attains the Supreme Brahman; then, having recited the Drupadā verse to its end and taking water in his hand.
One who knows the ritual procedure should perform the Aghamarṣaṇa with the mantra with due respect; and the wise man, having immersed himself in the waters, should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa three times.
Whether in water or on land, whoever performs the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, their mass of sins shall perish, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Standing, one should cast three handfuls of water with joined palms, reciting the Gāyatrī preceded by the Mahāvyāhṛtis and beginning with the Praṇava, while omitting its head (the Śiras).
By that adamantine water, the rākṣasas named Maṃdehas quickly cause the splendor of the sun to perish, like mountains [obscuring] the light of the sun.
And that twice-born man who does not offer three handfuls of water for the sake of assisting the Sun shall himself become a *mandahe* (a ghost) for the destruction of his own body. || 91 ||
In the morning, one should remain standing while reciting [the mantra] until the sun is seen; in the evening, one should recite while seated until the stars become visible.
A twice-born man desiring his own welfare must not neglect the proper time; therefore, at the moment of half-rise or sunset, he should cast vajra-water [into the fire].

Even if performed according to the rules, the twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) becomes fruitless if it is past its time; for this is indeed the illustration, just like sexual intercourse with a barren woman. || 94 ||
That twilight prayer which is performed by twice-born men while keeping the left hand in the water should be known as a *vṛṣalī* (a low-caste woman), which brings joy to the hosts of Rākṣasas. (95)

Then, one should perform the ritual attendance according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedic branch (śākhā), reciting the Gāyatrī mantra either a thousand times or, alternatively, a hundred times.
Then, one should perform the ritual attendance upon the Goddess ten times; [reciting] the Goddess who has a thousand as the maximum, a hundred as the middle, and ten as the minimum.
The Brahmin who recites the Gāyatrī is not defiled by sins, [using] water mixed with red sandalwood, flowers, and Kuśa grass. || 98 ||
One should cause the arghya offering to be presented with mantras spoken in the Vedas or the Āgamas; by him by whom Savitṛ is thus worshipped, the three worlds are worshipped. (99)
When worshipped, Savitṛ bestows sons, cattle, and wealth; he removes diseases, grants long life, and fulfills even one's desires.
For this Rudra is the Āditya, he is the golden-hued maker of day; he is Ravi, he is the one of golden form, and he is Aryaman, whose form is the triple Veda.

Then one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic school (śākhā), [offering it] to all the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as to the sages beginning with Marīci.
One should satisfy [the deity] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, fragrant flowers, and pure waters, while reciting: "May they be satisfied. (3)

Wearing the sacred thread around his neck (nivītī), the twice-born should offer libations with barley to Sanaka and the others, as well as to human beings, placing straight darbha grasses between his two thumbs.

One should satisfy the divine ancestors, beginning with Kavyavāḍ and Anala, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin) and using double-folded darbha grass mixed with sesame seeds.
On Sunday, on the thirteenth lunar day, on the seventh, at night, or during the two twilights, a Brahmin seeking spiritual welfare should never perform the libation with sesame seeds.
If he should perform it, then the skillful man should do so with white sesame seeds; afterwards, he should satisfy the fourteen Yamas, uttering their names.

Then, having uttered his own lineage, he should joyfully offer libations to his ancestors with the left knee pressed down, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors), while remaining silent.
The gods desire one handful [of water] each, while Sanaka and the others desire two each; the ancestors desire three, and women desire one handful each.

The divine [tīrtha] is indeed at the tip of the finger; that of the sages (ārṣa) is at the base of the fingers; that of Brahmā is at the base of the thumb; and that of Prajāpati is in the middle of the palm.
The space between the thumb and the forefinger is declared to be the ancestral (pitrya) tīrtha; [through it] reach all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—gods, sages, ancestors, and humans.
"May all the ancestors—the mothers, maternal grandfathers, and others—be satisfied. These and other mantras, whether proclaimed in the Vedas or originating from the Purāṇas, have been declared. (12)

One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) along with its ancillaries, which bestows happiness upon the ancestors; then, having performed the fire-ritual (agnikārya), one should thereafter engage in the study of the Vedas.
The practice of the sacred revelation (śruti) is fivefold: its acceptance, reflection upon its meaning, repeated recitation, austerity, and instruction to disciples. (14)
O best of kings, this morning duty has been prescribed for the twice-born for the sake of preserving what has been gained and acquiring what has not yet been gained. (15)

Alternatively, having risen in the morning and performed the necessary duties, and having taken up purification and ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should use a tooth-stick for cleansing the teeth.
Having purified all his limbs, he should perform the morning twilight devotion (prātaḥsaṃdhyā); indeed, he should master the meanings of the Vedas as well as various other scriptures.
One should teach pure disciples who are well-disposed toward me and endowed with intelligence; one should also approach the Lord for the sake of attaining security, prosperity, and other such goals.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the midday rites, one should perform the previously mentioned bath; having bathed, the wise person should perform the midday *saṃdhyā* worship.
Having fully worshipped the deity, one should then perform the occasional rite; having kindled the fire of the wind, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
One should avoid flat beans, split pulses, cooked mung beans, and chickpeas; one should also avoid all food fried in oil, as well as uncooked food and anything mixed with salt.

One should avoid, in the Vaiśvadeva rite, food made of *āḍhakī* beans, food made of lentils (*masūra*), food derived from round grains, as well as the remnants of what has already been eaten or food that is stale. || 22 ||
Holding darbha grass in his hand, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), he should then perform the sprinkling (paryukṣaṇa) with the mantra "pṛṣodivī. || 23 ||
Having sprinkled water clockwise around the fire and having spread *kuśa* grass twice around it, one should place the fire in front of oneself with the *rāporddha-deva* mantra.

Having worshipped Vaiśvānara with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), the wise man should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the procedure prescribed in his own Vedic branch (śākhā).
The traveler, the one whose livelihood is exhausted, the seeker of knowledge, the one who supports his teacher, the ascetic, and the student—these six are beggars for the sake of dharma. (26)
A guest should be known as a traveler who is learned in the Vedas and has mastered the scriptures; these two are to be honored by householders who desire to attain the world of Brahmā.
Even for an outcaste or a dog, food shall never be fruitless; when a petitioner has arrived here, one should not consider whether they are worthy or unworthy.
One should scatter food on the ground outside for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers (candālas), those afflicted with foul diseases, crows, and insects.
May those who belong to Indra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu, as well as those who belong to Soma and Nirṛti—may these crows accept this ball of rice offered by me upon the ground. (130)
Having thus performed the *bali* offering and waited for the duration of a cow’s milking, he should then enter the dining hall once a guest has arrived.

Without having offered the *vāyasa-bali* (the offering to crows), one should perform the daily ancestral rite (*nitya-śrāddha*). In the daily ancestral rite, according to one's own capacity, one may feed three, two, or even one [person].

One should feed [the guests] for the sake of the ancestral sacrifice (pitr-yajña) and offer water after drawing it up; the daily śrāddha (nitya-śrāddha) is devoid of rites for the gods and is free from restrictive observances (niyama).

Having thus performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), which—even though devoid of ritual fees (dakṣiṇā)—brings complete satisfaction to both the giver and the recipient, one whose mind is established in itself and who is free from affliction [should proceed]. (34)
Having occupied a seat that is not defective, he should eat together with children; being fragrant, cheerful, wearing a garland, and clothed in two clean garments. (35)
Facing either the east or the north, one should eat what has been consumed by the ancestors; having made that food "not naked" (covered) both above and below.
Having performed the ritual of *āpośāna*, the wise twice-born man should eat; he should offer three oblations (*bali*) on the ground and then pour water over them. (37)
Having touched water once, with darbha grass in hand and a tranquil mind, he should offer the five oblations beginning with prāṇa into the fire of the stomach-pit.
But for one who eats with darbha grass in hand, no fault is found; he may eat that which has become contaminated by hair, insects, and the like, provided he holds the darbha. (39)
Then one should eat in silence and must not make any grinding of the teeth; the hand should be washed at the base of the right thumb.

May the water from the remnants [of this offering] remain inexhaustible for those dwelling in the lower worlds, in the hell of Raurava, that abode of the unrighteous, who long for such water. || 41 ||
Having sipped water again, the wise man, having become pure through diligent effort, should then perform the purification of the mouth by means of listening to the Purāṇas and other such activities.

Having passed the remainder of the day, one should then perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā). It is recorded that the twilight devotion performed at home is ordinary, while that performed in a cow-pen is ten times more meritorious.

In the presence of Śiva, the number of rivers becomes infinite; even the Sandhyā performed outside purifies falsehood, the scent of liquor, daytime sexual intercourse, and the dwelling place of a Śūdra.
Thus has this rule for the eternal one been declared in brief; a Brahmin who practices in this manner never comes to grief. (145)
Vyāsa said: I shall describe to you exactly how dharma is practiced for the benefit of virtuous householders living in the stage of the householder.
O child, by establishing himself in the householder’s life, a man nourishes this entire world; through that, he conquers the worlds he desires.
The ancestors, sages, gods, living beings, and likewise humans; as well as worms, insects, moths, birds, ancestral spirits, and asuras. || 3 ||
They depend upon the householder, and from him they attain satisfaction; they gaze at his face, thinking, "Will he give us water? || 4 ||
O child, those cows consisting of the three Vedas are the support of everything; upon them the entire universe is established, and they are considered the cause of the universe.

She has the Ṛgveda as her back, the Yajurveda as her joints, and the Sāmaveda as her belly and breasts; she has sacrifices and charitable works as her horns, and the hymns of the virtuous as her body hair.
She is peace, nourishment, feces, and urine; she is established upon the feet of the [four] castes; she is the means of subsistence for all worlds through her padas, kramas, jaṭās, and ghanas.
O son, the utterances Svāhā, Svadhā, Vaṣaṭ, and Hanta constitute her four breasts.

The gods and the ancestors have the utterance of "svāhā" as their breast full of the *svadhā* offering; and the sages, the gods, the spirits, and the lords of the immortals have the utterance of "vaṣaṭ" as their breast.
Just as humans constantly consume food with the utterance of "hantakāra" and drink from the breast, so too should one cause the three Vedas to be studied every day.
That man who commits endless sins and brings about their destruction sinks indeed into the hell of Andhatāmisra.
But that man who worships this cow at the proper time with her own offspring—the gods and others—is destined for heaven.
Therefore, my son, a human being must nourish daily the gods, sages, ancestors, men, and all living beings, just as one's own body.

Therefore, having bathed and become pure, one should, at the conclusion of a sacrifice and likewise at the proper time, perform the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors with water while remaining composed.
Having worshipped the gods with *sumana* flowers and fragrant blossoms, the person should then perform the libation for the fire and likewise offer the ritual oblations (*bali*).
One should offer the bali-oblation to the nocturnal spirits from the air; then, facing south, one should likewise present it to the ancestors.
The householder, becoming intent upon that with a concentrated mind, then takes water and performs the rite of respectful offering by pouring it upon those very [images].
The wise man should place [the offerings] in their respective places, designating the deities by name; having thus given the bali offering in the house, the master of the house becomes pure. (18)
Having sipped water for purification, the wise man should then look toward the door; he should wait for a guest during the eighth part of the hour.
To a guest who has arrived there, hungry, weary, and destitute, having come as a suppliant, one should offer water for the Arghya and Pādya rites. (20)
The wise have declared that a Brahmin is a guest; having honored him according to one's ability, a learned man should not inquire about his conduct or his Vedic study. (21)
One should consider that Prajāpati possesses both beautiful and unbeautiful forms; because he abides as impermanent, he is therefore called a guest (atithi). || 22 ||
The man who eats after having given to him eats nectar; however, he from whose house a guest returns with his hopes frustrated [eats nothing but sin]. (23)

Having given his misdeed to him, he departs taking away the merit; or else, by the gift of vegetables or by the offering of water, a man should worship him with devotion, and by that very act he is liberated.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "The forms of marriage are the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and the eighth is called Paiśāca. (25)
Tell me their ritual procedure and how it should be performed according to reality; likewise, tell me specifically the duties of householders.
Parāśara said: When a maiden, well-adorned, is given after having summoned a Brāhma bridegroom, the son born of that union shall sanctify twenty-one generations.

The Daiva marriage is that which is given to a priest officiating at a sacrifice; its offspring sanctifies fourteen generations. The Ārṣa marriage consists of taking a pair of cattle as a gift from a bridegroom; its offspring sanctifies six generations. (28)

When both together practice their duty, that is declared to be the Prājāpatya rite; the Gāndharva rite occurs by the mutual consent of the bridegroom and the bride through their own desire; and the Rākṣasa rite, consisting of the forcible abduction of the maiden, is censured by the virtuous. (29)
The eighth, the Paiśāca form, consisting of the abduction of a maiden by force, is despised. Generally, the Gāndharva, Āsura, and Rākṣasa forms are prescribed for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
But this eighth is the most wicked, the very source of the most wicked; the hand must be grasped by one of the same caste, and the arrow must be held by a Kṣatriya woman.

A goad should be held by the Vaiśya wife, and likewise the hem of the garment by the Śūdra wife; this is the rule for wives of a different caste when their husband is engaged in the act of intercourse, as seen in the Smṛti.
The hand should be taken by all [wives] who are of the same caste; this is the rule. In a lawful marriage, righteous sons who live for a hundred years are born.
Those devoid of dharma, lacking merit, wealth, and long life, [suffer]; this is the supreme duty of a householder regarding approaching his wife at the appointed time.
Or, having reflected upon the best of women, it may be according to one's desire; however, approaching them during the day is considered most detrimental to the lifespan of men. (35)
One worthy of ancestral rites (śrāddha) should not visit all festive occasions (parva) if he is wise; by going there out of delusion to a woman, he falls away from the supreme dharma.

He who approaches his wife only during her fertile period and is devoted solely to his own wife should always be known as a celibate practitioner (brahmacārī), even while living in the householder stage of life (gṛhāśramī). || 37 ||
In the Ārṣa form of marriage, the pair of cattle that is prescribed there is commended; however, even the slightest bride-price for a girl brings about the sin of selling a daughter. (38)
For selling one's offspring, one shall dwell for a kalpa in the hell known as Viṭkṛmibhojana; therefore, men must not derive even the slightest wealth from a daughter.
There, Mahālakṣmī, being pleased, shall dwell with the enemy of the Dānavas; likewise, trade, service to the low-born, and the non-study of the Vedas [shall be absent].
An improper marriage and the neglect of sacred rites are the causes of a family's downfall. A householder should perform the domestic rituals daily in the nuptial fire.
Furthermore, the householder in the stage of life must perform the five great sacrifices and the daily cooking, as well as the work of the five slaughter-houses day after day.

The mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-pot, and the broom—these are the causes for the removal of those five slaughter-houses; five sacrifices have been prescribed as the means to increase the welfare of the householder.

Recitation is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), libation is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛkratu); fire-offering is the sacrifice to the gods (daiva), the bali offering is the sacrifice to beings (bhautika), and hospitality is the sacrifice to men (nṛkratu), in that order.
One who arrives during the Vaiśvadeva rite is known as a *sūryoḍha* guest; these guests should be fed even before others—of this there is no doubt. (45)
Having given to the ancestors, the gods, and human beings, the householder eats nectar; but he who eats food without having given is merely one who fills his own belly. (46)
Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and excluded from hospitality—whether they have acquired the Vedas or not—all such twice-born men are to be known as Śūdras. (47)
Those lowest of the twice-born who eat without having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite shall be destitute of food in this world and thereafter enter the womb of a crow.
One should perform the obligatory rites prescribed in the Vedas without laziness; if one performs them according to one's ability, one shall attain the supreme state.
Sin resides in oil on the sixth and eighth lunar days; it always resides in meat, as well as in shaving and sexual intercourse on the fourteenth and fifteenth lunar days.
One should not look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting, nor when it is at the zenith; one should not look at the sun when it is eclipsed by Rāhu, nor when it is within its disc.
One should not look at one's own reflection in water, nor run in mud; one should not look at a naked woman, nor enter the water naked. (52)
A temple, a Brahmin, a cow, honey, and likewise clay; as well as one advanced by birth, one advanced in age, and one advanced in learning. (53)
While walking, one should perform a circumambulation of the aśvattha tree, a sacred shrine tree, one's teacher, a water-filled jar, prepared food, curd, and white mustard seeds.
One should not have intercourse with a woman during her menses, nor eat together with one's wife; one should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor eat while seated on a high seat.
A twice-born man desiring spiritual luster should not look upon an impure woman; nor should he ever eat food without first having gratified the ancestors and the gods.
One who desires to live for a long time should not eat cooked food containing meat, nor should one urinate in a cow-pen, on an anthill, or in ashes.
Neither while standing nor while walking, nor when his limbs are covered with living creatures, should he look at a Brāhmaṇa, the sun, fire, the moon, the stars, or his teachers.
One should not discharge feces or urine while looking [at them]; one should not blow on a fire with the mouth, nor should one look at a naked woman. (59)
One should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor cast any impure substance into it; one should not commit violence against living beings, nor eat during the two twilights.
A wise man should never go to sleep during either the morning or evening twilight; he should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor should he display a rainbow.
One should never sleep alone in a deserted place, nor should one wake someone who is sleeping. One should not travel alone on a road, nor should one drink water from the hollow of one's joined palms.
One should not eat curd from which the cream has been removed during the day, nor at night; one should not address a woman in her menses, nor should one eat until full satisfaction during the nights.

One should not be fond of the threefold arts (dancing, singing, and instrumental music), nor should one wash one's feet in a vessel of bell-metal. That ignorant man who, having performed a śrāddha, eats at another’s śrāddha [is censured]. 64.
There is no fruit of the *śrāddha* for the giver; indeed, the eater shall partake of sin. One should not wear clothing or even sandals that have been used by another.
One should not eat from a broken vessel, nor sit on ground defiled by fire and the like; one should mount the backs of cows, and [sit upon] the smoke from a funeral pyre or a riverbank.
One who desires to live long should avoid the morning sun and sleeping during the day; after bathing, one should not wipe the body, nor should one loosen the topknot while on the road.
One should not shake one's hands or head, nor should one drag the seat with the foot; nor should one wipe the body with the hand or again with the bathing garment.
If the body becomes defiled by the leavings of a dog, it is purified by bathing again; one should never ever pluck out hair or nails with the teeth.

For the sake of auspiciousness, one should avoid cutting one's nails with one's own fingernails; since that would have to be abandoned in the future, one should diligently refrain from performing such an act.
One should never go even to one's own house by a way other than the door; one should not play with the ignorant, nor sit with those who destroy dharma, nor with those afflicted by disease.
One should never sleep naked, nor should one ever eat with food held in the hand; he who eats while his feet, hands, and face are still wet does not live for long.
A twice-born man should not go to sleep with wet feet, nor should he go anywhere while still impure from food; nor should he eat or drink water while remaining on his bed.
One should not sit down wearing shoes, nor should one drink water while standing; one who desires health should not consume anything that is entirely sour.
One should not look at feces or urine, nor, while impure from eating, should one touch the head; one should not stand upon husks, embers, ashes, hair, or potsherds.
Dwelling together with those who have fallen leads only to one's own fall; one should never give a seat or a couch to a Śūdra. (76)
A Brahmin falls from his status as a Brahmin, and a Śūdra falls from dharma; teaching the dharma to Śūdras would destroy their own welfare. (77)
Service to the twice-born is indeed considered the supreme duty for Śūdras; for scratching the head with one's hands is not regarded as auspicious. (78)
One should never instruct a Vedic mantra to a Śūdra; if a Brāhmaṇa gives it to a Brāhmaṇī, he falls from his dharma. || 79 ||
Beating with the hands, crying out, and plucking out the hair; furthermore, acting contrary to the scriptures and accepting gifts from a greedy person. (80)
And that brahmin indeed goes to twenty-one hells: when there is unseasonable thundering of clouds, during the rainy season, and when there is a rain of dust. || 81 ||

The following are proclaimed as times for the suspension of study (anadhyāya): during the roar of a great storm at night, upon the fall of a meteor, during an earthquake, when the quarters of the sky appear to be ablaze, and at midnight.

On the two middle days, at the end of the period of impurity for a Śūdra, during the death-impurity (sūtaka), on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, on the new moon day, on the day of a Śrāddha ceremony, and also on the first lunar day (pratipad).

On the full moon day, as well as on the eighth day, during the conjunction of the moon with the asterism Viśākhā, during national upheavals, at the commencement and conclusion of Vedic study, and on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Kalpas and Yugas. || 84 ||
Even after studying the Āraṇyaka, one should never study it at the sound of arrows or Sāmans, nor during these periods of non-study (anadhyāya).

On the eighth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight, as well as on the fifteenth, one should always remain a celibate student. Approaching another man’s wife in this world shortens one's lifespan; therefore, that should be avoided from afar, as should the service of enemies.
One should not despise oneself for being deprived of former prosperity; for those who are always diligent, neither fortune nor knowledge is difficult to attain. (87)
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant, nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the dharma prescribed.
One should avoid the impulse of speech, the impulse of mind, and the impulse of the tongue; even the hairs born in the private parts become impure through contact with them. 89.
One should cast far away, indeed very far, the water used for washing the feet, urine, food remnants, other waters, spittle, and phlegm.
By reciting the Veda day and night, by practicing purity and proper conduct, and by maintaining a mind free from malice, a twice-born man shall remember his previous birth.
One should respectfully salute the elders and offer them one's own seat; moreover, one should follow behind them with a bowed neck.
One should never, under any circumstances, utter censure against the Vedas, Brahmins, gods, kings, virtuous people, ascetics, or women devoted to their husbands.
Having taken up five lumps of earth, one should bathe in another person's reservoir; whatever wealth is given with faith after having obtained a worthy recipient, [that is meritorious].

Given in the proper place, at the proper time, and according to the prescribed rite, that gift leads to infinity; the giver of land becomes a sovereign of a realm, and the giver of food is happy everywhere. (95)
The giver of water shall be handsome; the giver of food shall be well-nourished; the giver of a lamp shall have clear eyes; and the giver of a cow shall attain the world of Aryaman.

The giver of gold shall be long-lived; the giver of sesame seeds shall have excellent offspring; the giver of a house shall become the lord of lofty mansions; and the giver of clothing shall dwell in the world of the Moon.

The giver of a horse attains a divine body; the giver of a bull becomes possessed of prosperity; the giver of a good wife obtains an excellent spouse; and the giver of a palanquin as well as a fine couch likewise [attains these rewards].
He who receives with faith and he who gives with faith—both of them shall go to heaven; but those lacking faith fall downward.
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride; fame perishes without generosity; and life perishes from insulting a Brahmin. 100.
Fragrance, flowers, kusha grass, cows, vegetables, meat, milk, curd, gems, fish, a house, and grain—these, when offered, may be accepted. (101)
Honey, water, fruit, roots, medicinal herbs, and the gift of fearlessness—these, even when offered by a person of low status, should be accepted as they are presented. (102)

Among the Śūdra class, these are those whose food may be eaten: the slave, the carpenter, the cowherd, the family friend, and the partner in a ploughshare; likewise, one who has dedicated himself to the teacher. (103)
Thus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, has this duty of conduct for those dwelling in Dharmāraṇya been declared; this is the dharma prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti.
Vyāsa said: Having reached Dharmavāpī, he who performs the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) causes his ancestors to attain satisfaction for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
And here the ancestors are to be honored, as well as those forefathers who have gone to heaven; one should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to them upon reaching this place which bestows liberation.

O Brahmins, he who offers the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) with single-minded devotion in the Kali age [obtains the same merit] that is gained in five days during the Tretā age, or in three days during the Dvāpara age.
In this world, when the Kali age has arrived, human beings are greedy; people take pleasure in the wives of others, and women, moreover, are exceedingly fickle.
All men, women, and eunuchs were devoted to harming others; they were constantly intent on censuring others and looking for their faults. || 5 ||
"Quarrels that cause distress to others and lead to the breach of friendships—all these indeed attain purity; so the Lords of Kāśī themselves have declared. (6)
O highly fortunate one, this description of Dharmāraṇya and all its fruit has indeed been told here as it was spoken by the Trident-bearer.
Pure in speech, mind, and body, they turned their backs on the wives of others; free from malice, impartial even when provoked to anger, they were devoted to their mother and father.
Those who are free from greed, devoid of avarice, devoted to the duty of giving, possessed of faith, knowers of the Dharma, and dedicated to devotion toward their master; || 9 ||
But those women who are devoted to their husbands, who take pleasure in serving their husbands, who are non-violent, hospitable, and always intent on their own duty; (10)
Śaunaka said: Listen, O illustrious Sūta, best among those who know all dharmas; I have heard from your mouth the virtuous conduct of householders.
O son of Sūta, tell me today that one thing which is desired by my mind; tell me, what is the characteristic of all those women who are devoted to their husbands?
Sūta said: The life of that man in whose house there dwells a devoted wife is fruitful; she is like the very shadow of his body, and her story brings merit.
[They were] devoted wives: Arundhatī, Sāvitrī, Anasūyā, Śāṇḍilī, Satī, Lakṣmī, and Śatarūpā. || 14 ||
She was equal to Menā, Sunīti, Saṃjñā, and Svāhā; for such indeed are the duties of devoted wives proclaimed by the Sage. (15)
She eats when her husband has eaten, she remains standing when he stands, she sits when he sits, she sleeps when he has fallen asleep, and she wakes up before him. (16)
While her husband was present in the country, she did not adorn herself; when he had gone abroad somewhere for the sake of business, she was devoid of all ornaments.
She does not utter her husband’s name, for the sake of increasing his lifespan; nor does she ever utter the name of another man.
Even when dragged away, she does not speak abusively; even when struck, she remains serene. And she says, "O Master, please consider this done" whenever she is told, "Do this. (19)
"Called, she goes quickly, abandoning her household duties. For what reason has she been summoned, O Lord? Let favor be shown. (20)
He does not linger at the door, nor does he frequent the gateway; he never takes anything that should not be given, nor does he ever give anything away on his own initiative.
One should personally prepare all the articles for worship that have not been mentioned, including the ritual water, sacrificial grass, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth. (22)
And while awaiting whatever boon is appropriate for the occasion, she should present all of it without agitation and with great joy. (23)
She partakes of the remnants of her husband’s food, whether it be desired rice, fruits, or other such things; she avoids from afar the sight of social gatherings and festivals. (24)
One should not go to places such as pilgrimages or to witness weddings and the like, nor to where someone is sleeping comfortably, sitting at ease, or enjoying themselves according to their own whim.
Even in matters of urgent necessity, she should never wake her husband; moreover, while experiencing the menses, she must not show her face for three nights.

She should not even utter her own words until she has become pure by bathing; having bathed well, she should look at the face of her husband and never that of another. Or else, meditating on her husband in her mind, she should gaze upon the sun.
Turmeric, saffron, vermilion, and collyrium, as well as a bodice, betel-leaf, and auspicious, beautiful ornaments. (28)
Desiring long life for her husband, a devoted wife should not discard items that groom the hair or ornaments such as bracelets and earrings. (29)
She never converses with a woman who hates her husband; she is never left alone anywhere, nor does she ever bathe naked. (30)
A virtuous woman should never sit upon a mortar, nor on a pestle, nor on a broom, nor even on a grinding stone; nor on a water-wheel, nor on the threshold. (31)
Except during the time for sexual union, she should never display boldness; wherever her husband finds pleasure, there she should always be full of affection.
This alone is the vow for women, this alone is the supreme excellence: this indeed is their worship—that they do not transgress the word of their husband.
Whether her husband be impotent, in a difficult situation, diseased, or even aged; whether he be well-established or poorly situated—she must never disregard her one husband.
Even when ghee, salt, asafoetida, and other provisions are exhausted, a devoted wife should not say "there is no husband"; nor should she feed [strangers] in iron vessels.
Even one desiring to bathe at sacred pilgrimage sites should drink the water used for washing her husband’s feet; for to a woman, her husband alone is superior even to Śaṅkara or Viṣṇu.
She who performs vows, fasts, and religious observances in defiance of her husband takes away his longevity; upon death, she goes to hell. (37)
A woman who, being intent on anger, gives a retort when spoken to, is born as a dog in a village or as a jackal in a lonely forest. (38)
For women, indeed, one supreme rule has been declared: having honored the feet of her husband, she should eat with firm resolve. (39)
One should not use a high seat, nor should one go to the houses of others; there, one must never utter harsh words. (40)
Nor should one speak loudly or cause a commotion in the presence of gurus.
That evil-minded woman who, having abandoned her husband, wanders about in secret, is born as a cruel female owl dwelling in the hollow of a tree.
If she strikes back one who has struck her, she is a tigress or a female jackal; and she who casts a sidelong glance at another indeed becomes squint-eyed.
She who abandons her husband and eats sweet food alone shall become a sow in a village, or else a bat, or a vulture.

She who speaks unpleasantly after having committed a harmful act is indeed born mute; she who envies her co-wife is born unfortunate again and again; and she who, casting aside the gaze of her husband, looks toward another man [is likewise reborn in such states]. (45)

She may even be born one-eyed, averse [to her husband], or ugly. However, seeing him approaching from outside, she should quickly attend to him with water, seats, betel leaves, fans, and by massaging his feet and so forth. || 46 ||

In that very way, she who, being herself delighted, gladdens her beloved with charming words and supreme efforts to dispel his perspiration, has thereby gladdened the three worlds. For a father gives but little, a brother gives but little, and a son gives but little. (47)

Who would not honor her husband, the giver of the immeasurable? The husband is the god, the husband is the guru; he is dharma, the sacred ford, and the vows. Therefore, setting aside everything else, she should worship her husband alone. (48)
Just as a body devoid of life becomes impure in an instant, so too a woman deprived of her husband is always impure, even if she has bathed well. 49.
Among all inauspicious things, a widow is the most inauspicious; from the sight of a widow, success never arises anywhere at any time.
A wise man should abandon all women who are devoid of auspiciousness, even his own mother, and likewise renounce their blessings, which are like venomous serpents.
At the time of the maiden’s marriage, the twice-born should cause [the bride] to recite: "May I become the companion of my husband, whether he be living or even deceased. (52)
Following her husband from the home to the cremation ground with joy, she undoubtedly obtains at every step the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. || 53 ||
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole, so too does a virtuous wife, having transcended her messengers, go to heaven with her husband.
Upon seeing that devoted wife, the messengers of Yama flee; indeed, the sun grows hot and even the fire burns fiercely.
All splendors trembled upon seeing the great majesty of her devotion to her husband; for as many hairs as she possesses, so many tens of millions of crores [of other lights] were shaken.
Enjoying heavenly bliss with her husband, that devoted wife is blessed; blessed indeed is her mother in this world, and blessed as well is her father. (57)

Blessed is that illustrious husband in whose house dwells a devoted wife; by the merit of that faithful wife, three ancestors on each side—on the father’s line, the mother’s line, and the husband’s line—enjoy the pleasures of heaven.
Those of evil conduct who break their vows of morality cause the downfall of three lineages—of their father, mother, and husband—and remain miserable both in this world and the next. (59)
Wherever the foot of a devoted wife touches the earth, that ground becomes a sacred site (tīrtha) worthy of honor; there is no purifying power greater than this. 60.
Even the sun fears to touch a devoted wife; even Soma and the Gandharvas do so for the sake of their own purification, and not otherwise.
The waters always long for the touch of a devoted wife; Gāyatrī destroys sin through her mantra, but she removes it through her devotion to her husband.
In every house, there are women proud of their beauty and charm; however, it is only through devotion to the Lord of the Universe that a woman devoted to her husband is obtained.
The wife is the root of the householder; the wife is the root of happiness. The wife exists for the very fruit of dharma; the wife is for the increase of progeny. (64)

This world and the next world are both won through a wife; through a wife there is satisfaction for the gods, the ancestors, and guests in the home. He alone should be known as a true householder in whose home dwells a devoted wife.
Just as the body becomes purified by bathing in the Ganges, so too does a household become purified by the sight of a devoted wife.
A widow who sleeps on a bed causes her husband to fall; therefore, she should sleep on the ground out of a desire for her husband's welfare.
A widow must never perform the rubbing of unguents on her limbs, nor should she ever enjoy the use of fragrant substances. (68)

Every day, a libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed for the husband with water containing kusha grass and sesame seeds, preceded by the mention of his name, lineage (gotra), and so forth; and likewise for his father and his grandfather.
The worship of Viṣṇu should be performed with the thought that he is her husband, and not otherwise; she should always meditate upon Hari, who bears the form of Viṣṇu, as her very husband. (70)
Whatever is most beloved in the world, whatever is desired by her husband—that very thing should be given to one who possesses virtuous qualities, out of a desire to please her husband. (71)
In the months of Vaiśākha and Kārttika, one should observe special vows: bathing, giving gifts, pilgrimage to sacred fords, and listening to the Purāṇas repeatedly. (72)
In Vaiśākha, water-pots; in Kārttika, ghee-lamps; and in Māgha, the offering of grain and sesame seeds—these are especially distinguished in the heavenly world.

A water-stall should be constructed in the month of Vaiśākha, and a water-dripping vessel should be offered to the Lord; likewise, uśīra root, a fan, an umbrella, fine garments, and sandalwood paste [should be given]. (74)
Betel-leaf with camphor, as well as offerings of flowers, numerous water-vessels, and likewise flower-houses.
Various drinks and grapes and plantain fruits should be given to the foremost of the twice-born with the thought, "May my husband be pleased. (76)
For the sake of vigor, one should eat barley food or else the food of a single person; however, one should avoid eggplant, the suraṇa tuber, and the śūkaśiṃbī bean.
In the month of Kārttika, one should avoid oil and also avoid using bell-metal; in the observance of silence during Kārttika, one should offer a beautiful bell.
One who eats from leaves should give a bell-metal vessel filled with ghee; for one observing the vow of sleeping on the ground, a smooth bed provided with a cotton mattress should be given.

Upon the renunciation of fruit, the fruit itself should be given; upon the renunciation of juice, that juice; and upon the renunciation of grain, that grain—or it is traditionally taught that rice may be given. One should diligently give a cow, adorned with ornaments and accompanied by gold.
On one side are all gifts whatsoever, and on the other side is the gift of a lamp; the former do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of giving a lamp during the month of Kārttika. (51)
O King, these rules have been proclaimed for widows and others of this kind; their fruit is this, and never that of anyone else. (82)
Having reached Dharmavāpī, a wise person should give a gift; it increases ten-millionfold eternally, according to the word of Brahmā. (83)
And he who, standing before Dharmeśvara, should give a sesame-cow, is honored in the heavenly world for as many years as there are sesame seeds.
Having reached the field of Dharma, one should perform the Śrāddha rite with vigilance; for that person, the ancestors will certainly remain satisfied for the duration of a year.
And those other ancestors in heaven, and those others dwelling in hell, and those who have fallen into the state of animals, and those situated among the spirits and so forth—|| 86 ||

One should indeed perform the Śrāddha for all of them at the Dharmakūpa according to the prescribed rule. As for that scattering [of food] which is performed here on the ground by men, by that those who have attained the state of Piśācas obtain satisfaction. (87)
But for those, O son, whose bathing-cloths fall upon the ground, satisfaction is produced for those who have attained the state of trees by means of that [cloth]. (88)
Indeed, those grains of barley that fall upon the surface of the earth provide nourishment for those who have attained the state of divinity.
When the rice-balls have been offered, whatever grains of rice remain on the ground, by those there is nourishment for those [ancestors] who have gone to the netherworld (pātāla).
Indeed, those who have neglected the duties of their caste and stage of life, and who remain unrefined, become ruined in this world if they subsist on the water used for sweeping.
The water that falls upon the ground after the Brahmins have eaten, as well as the water used for sipping (ācamana), indeed brings satisfaction to other beings as well.
Thus, whatever the sacrificer does, and whatever those twice-born ones do—such as the scattering of water and food—it must be pure and entirely untouched by impurity. (93)
And those others who have been born in hell, having entered other wombs there, O child, attain nourishment through the proper performance of śrāddha rites.
The śrāddha that is performed by men with wealth acquired through unjust means causes [the ancestors] to find satisfaction in the wombs of outcasts such as Caṇḍālas and Pulkasas. (95)
O child, in this way, many kinsmen are nourished by that; for even if one is unable to perform the śrāddha rite with [meat], it is indeed accomplished even with vegetables.
Therefore, a man who performs a śrāddha with devotion, even if only with vegetables, according to the prescribed rule, his lineage never perishes. || 97 ||
If all evil has been committed, that evil certainly increases; one who acts thus is cooked in a terrible hell—of this there is no doubt. (98)
O best of kings, just as merit, so too does sin—whatever action has been performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious—all of that surely increases in Dharmāraṇya. 99.
Dharmāraṇya is always proclaimed as the one that fulfills desires, the god who grants all wishes, the bestower of liberation upon yogins, and the giver of perfection to the perfected ones. 100.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Righteous Conduct," in the *Dharmāraṇya-kṣetra-māhātmya* of the first part of the third section (*Brahmakhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Lord, having heard this meritorious narrative of Dharmāraṇya, I am not yet satiated. Whenever you speak, my mind becomes more eager to hear. What happened after this? For my curiosity is indeed great. || 1 ||
Vyāsa said: Listen, O Pārtha, to this highly meritorious and auspicious narrative originating from the Skanda Purāṇa, concerning Dharmāraṇya, which was told by Sthāṇu to Skanda.

[She praised] the one who bestows the fruit of all sacred fords, the destroyer of all calamities—the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, five-faced, ten-armed, three-eyed, and holding a trident in his hand. || 3 ||
There he saw him holding a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, surrounded by his attendants, and saluted by gods and demons.
Having prostrated before Mahādeva, who was seated there—served by Gandharvas and Apsarases, accompanied by Nārada and others singing songs of manifold forms and qualities—the son spoke.

Skanda said: "O Lord, Indra and the other gods, as well as Brahmā and all the rest, have arrived at your gate, longing solely for the sight of you. What do you command, O God? What shall I do before you?"
Vyāsa said: Having heard the words of Skanda, Hara rose from his seat; though he did not mount his bull, he then became desirous of departing.
Seeing Śiva desiring to go, Skanda then spoke these words: || 8 ||
Skanda said: "O God of gods, what task is there for the deities that you are being summoned so urgently? O ocean of compassion, if you have pity for me, tell me, setting aside your bull."
Or is there a battle between gods and demons, or some other matter of even greater importance? (10)
Śiva said: Listen with a one-pointed mind to that by which my heart has become distracted; there is a place of great merit on the surface of the earth called Dharmāraṇya. || 11 ||
Even there, O Six-faced One, I desire to go along with the gods.
Skanda said: "O Mahādeva, having gone there, what will you do now? Tell me that, O Lord of the World, and all that must be done, without omission. (13)
Śiva said: "Listen, my son, to these words which cause delight to the mind, the great [account] that from the beginning effects the creation and maintenance of all occurrences. (14)
But when the dissolution had occurred and everything was enveloped in darkness, there then existed the one Brahman—the attributeless, imperishable seed.
Indeed, that which is first fashioned by means of the qualities is declared to be a "great substance" (mahaddravya). || 16 ||
And when the great aeon had arrived and the world of moving and non-moving beings had gone to its destruction, the Lord of the World, assuming the form of water, sported there in divine play.
After a long time had passed, he too, by means of the true principles (tattvas) such as earth and the rest, produced a tree beautiful with ten thousand branches.
Covered with large fruits and beautified by its trunk and branches, the great banyan tree possessed massive spreading limbs, rich with an abundance of fruit and entwined with matted roots.
Then, assuming the state of a child, that Vāsudeva Janārdana lies upon the leaves of the banyan tree, eager to create the universe.
Indeed, Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, was born from the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu; beholding everything as consisting of water, appearing in various forms yet devoid of material substance.
Seeing him, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, was suddenly seized with agitation and then spoke these words: "O son, what shall I do? he asked decisively.
Then, from the sky, an incorporeal voice arose from the God, saying: "O Creator, O Ordainer, perform penance so that I may grant you my vision. (23)
Having heard those words there, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, performed a most terrible, supreme, and great penance that was difficult to accomplish.
Then, laughing while in the form of a child, the compassionate Lord of Kamalā spoke sweet words with the playful charm of a boy.

The illustrious Viṣṇu said: "O son, today, according to the prescribed rite, fashion within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍagolaka) the netherworld (pātāla), the surface of the earth (bhūtala), as well as the rivers, oceans, and forests."
Trees, mountains, bipeds, and likewise beasts; birds, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas. || 27 ||
And those living beings such as beasts of prey, belonging to the eighty-four classes of birth—whether born from sprouts, born from sweat, born from a womb, or born from an egg. (28)

"Perform quickly everything in its entirety—twenty-one lakhs of births for each [being]—and having spoken thus, he vanished. The entire Brahmāṇḍa was created by Brahmā exactly as it had been described. (29)
In whom was born the Grandfather, the sole Lord, Prajāpati; Sthāṇu, the preceptor of the gods, Bhānu, Pracetas, and Parameṣṭhin.
Just as Dakṣa and the sons of Dakṣa were, so too were the Seven Sages; from them, twenty-one Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) came into being.
The Puruṣa is immeasurable; thus the ancestral sages know him, as do the Viśvedevas, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins.
The Yakṣas, Piśācas, Sādhyas, Pitṛs, and Guhyakas [were born]; from them were then produced the eight stainless and wise Brahmarṣis.
And many royal sages, all endowed with every virtue, as well as heaven, the waters, the earth, the wind, the intermediate space, and the directions [were present]. (34)
The years, seasons, months, fortnights, days and nights in succession, as well as the units of time such as kalā, kāṣṭhā, muhūrta, nimeṣa, and lava [all proceed from Him]. (35)
The circle of planets along with the constellations, the Yugas, the Manvantaras, and whatever else there may be—all that has come into being with the world as its witness. (36)
Whatever wheel is seen here, whether stationary or moving, O son, it is withdrawn once again when the dissolution of the eon arrives for the world.
Just as the characteristic signs of the seasons appear again and again in their cycle according to their names and forms, O child, so too do the ages and other such phenomena.
Śiva said: Hereafter, O son, I shall proclaim an auspicious Puranic narrative, as well as the genealogy of Brahmā’s lineage.
The six great sages known as the mind-born sons of Brahmā are Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Kaśyapa was the son of Marīci, and from Kaśyapa were born the last of all creatures—the thirteen highly fortunate daughters of Dakṣa.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Danāyu, Siṃhikā, as well as Krodhā, Provā, Vasiṣṭhā, Vinatā, and Kapilā. || 42 ||
Kaṇḍū and Sunetrā then gave [their sons] to Kaśyapa; indeed, twelve Ādityas of auspicious countenance were born from Aditi.

From Sūrya indeed Dharmarāj was born; this was not created in the past by him. Seeing that the unsurpassed Dharmāraṇya was created by Dharma, O Skanda, it was called "Dharmāraṇya" by me, bestowing merit. 44.
Skanda said: "O Maheśvara, I desire to hear the supreme and most purifying narrative of Dharmāraṇya; tell me all of that."
Ishvara said: "All the gods, headed by Indra, have gone there along with Brahma; I too shall indeed go to that sacred field which destroys all sins."
Skanda said: "O moon-crested one, O lord of the sky, I too shall come to see him."
Sūta said: Then Skanda, as well as Rudra, Sūrya, Anila, and Anala, along with the Siddhas together with the Gandharvas, and likewise the auspicious Apsarases, [departed].
The Piśācas and all the Guhyakas, Indra and Varuṇa as well, all the Nāgas, Śukra, and Vācaspati likewise, all assembled together.
All the planets together with the constellations, the eight Vasus headed by Dhruva, all those who move through the intermediate space, and others who dwell in the mountains; || 50 ||
Then all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, went to Vaikuṇṭha with supreme joy; at that time, Brahmā approached Viṣṇu of immeasurable luster for the purpose of consultation.
Having gone to that Vaikuṇṭha, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, meditated for a moment and spoke to Viṣṇu with great joy.
Brahmā said: O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, O compassionate Supreme Lord! You alone are the creator and you alone are the destroyer; you indeed are the father of the universe. || 53 ||
Salutations to you, O gentle Viṣṇu; salutations to you, whose banner is Garuḍa. Salutations to you, O beloved of Kamalā; salutations to you, whose form is Brahman.

Salutations to you who have the form of a fish; salutations indeed to you whose form is the universe. Salutations to you, the destroyer of the Daityas, and the grantor of fearlessness to your devotees.
"Salutations to the slayer of Kaṃsa; salutations to the conqueror of the Daitya Bala. Thus praised by Brahmā, Janārdana became manifest before his eyes.
Clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, having the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa) as his vehicle, four-armed and of great splendor, he holds the conch, the discus, and the mace.
That god of immeasurable prowess was praised by all the gods, as well as by the Vidyādharas and Nāgas, being lauded from every side.
Then that god, possessing the immeasurable radiance of the sun, rose up, adorned with a crown and other ornaments resplendent with the light of ten million jewels.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O tiger among kings, to this most excellent and meritorious narrative; while being praised, the Lord of the World spoke these words. || 1 ||
Viṣṇu said: For what purpose have you all come, O best of gods, beginning with Brahmā? Is all well on earth, and from whence has fear come upon you?
Then, being delighted, Brahmā spoke these words to Keśava: "No fear exists for us in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile."
I have come into your presence for the purpose of making a single request; therefore, I shall explain it fully—listen now to these words of mine. || 4 ||
But, O Lord Janārdana, by your grace, I desire to behold that supreme sacred site (tīrtha) which was formerly established by Dharma. (5)
Therefore, O Lord of the gods, set your mind upon going there, so that this unsurpassed Dharmāraṇya may attain the status of a sacred pilgrimage site.
Viṣṇu said: "Excellent, excellent, O illustrious one! Haste there; do not delay. My mind, too, is intensely longing for that very sight."
Vyāsa said: Having mounted Tārkṣya, Govinda indeed arrived there with great speed; then those gods, together with Indra and the hosts of sages, were joined by Dharma.
Having seen Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others from afar, he rejoiced; and Dharmarāja too, having seen those gods headed by Viṣṇu, [rejoiced].

Having arrived there from his own hermitage and received their worship, he rose quickly from his seat before them; and taking up the articles of honor, he then performed worship for each one individually and separately.
There, the son of the Sun performed worship for them according to the prescribed rites; having seated them upon thrones, he then offered them most venerable worship.

Yama said: O son of Devakī, by your grace, by the performance of your satisfaction, and through the compassion of Śiva, this sacred field has today assumed the form of a holy pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my ascetic penance has become fruitful; today my station has become fruitful through the meeting with the lords of the Kāji lineage.
Vyāsa said: Thus praised at that time, Viṣṇu spoke these sweet words: "O King of Dharma, O Lord, I am pleased with this hymn of yours."
Ask a boon from me; I shall fulfill your desire. Whatever you wish for, I will grant it to you without a doubt. (15)
Yama said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if you will grant my desire, then establish hermitages for the sages in the highly meritorious Dharmāraṇya."
Where Brahmins dwell and sacrificers perform their rites, that supreme sacred site shines forth, resounded by the chanting of the Vedas. || 17 ||

"O Śauri, living beings will defile this holy ford (tīrtha) which is not fit for non-Brāhmaṇas; therefore, bring many Vāḍava sages so that Dharmāraṇya may shine throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile. (18)

Then Viṣṇu, the thousand-eyed, the thousand-headed, and the thousand-footed one, who is devoted to righteousness, assumed a form with a thousand [features]. And in whatever place there were Brahmins of virtuous conduct and auspicious vows— || 19 ||

Skilled in all dharmas without exception and proficient in all treatises, renowned for their austerity and knowledge, and devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman—all eighteen thousand sages were thus established.
Having brought them from various countries, those gods established many hermitages there, which had been constructed by Brahmā and Śiva as well.
Through the instruction of the Dharma by Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā, and Śiva, Keśava established them each in their own appropriate place.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: In which lineage were those Brāhmaṇas born who have mastered the Vedas, who were established together with their retinues and surrounded by sons and grandsons, who are joined by many disciples and devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice? Tell me their places and their names exactly as they are. (23)
Vyāsa said: Listen, O tiger among kings, [to the account] of those who dwell in Dharmāraṇya.
I shall now declare the names of those great-souled Brāhmaṇas, the sages of perpetual celibacy, as well as the names of their sons and grandsons.
O bull among the Pāṇḍavas, there are twenty-four lineages (gotras) of the twice-born; they have branches and sub-branches, as well as sons, grandsons, and so forth.
Many sons were born by the hundreds and thousands; I shall proclaim to you the names of the twenty-four principal ones. These twice-born are declared to be Ṛṣis; likewise, hear their pravaras.
Bhāradvāja, as well as Vatsa, Kauśika, and Kuśa; Śāṇḍilya, Kāśyapa, Gautama, and likewise Chāndhana. || 28 ||
Jātūkarṇya, as well as Vatsa, Vasiṣṭha, Dhāraṇa, Ātreya, and Bhāṇḍila; and from here onwards, the Laukikas.
Kṛṣṇāyana, Upamanyu, Gārgya, Mudgala, Auṣaka, Puṇyāsana, Parāśara, and thereafter Kauṇḍinya. || 30 ||
Likewise, there are the Gārgya and Āsana lineages, with twenty-four pravaras; however, for the Jāmadagnya gotra, there are indeed only five pravaras.
Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, and Jamadagni—these five, O King, are the renowned and world-famous Pravaras.
Thus, those born of the Vāḍava lineage were masters of the Vedas, devoted to the rites of honoring the twice-born, and dedicated to various sacrificial acts. (33)
Those twice-born ones from various lands who were endowed with virtue, devoted to the six duties, and possessed of such great fortune, [were present]. (34)
The third pravara consists of Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, and Jāmadagnya; and for the Ātreyas, the third [set] is Ātreya, Arcanānasa, and Śyāvāśva.
In this lineage there are Brahmins who are wicked and crooked in their ways, yet they are wealthy, devoted to dharma, and masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. || 36 ||
All of them are devoted to charity and enjoyment, esteemed for their adherence to the Śruti and Smṛti; they are to be known as belonging to the Māṇḍavya gotra and endowed with five pravaras.
Bhārgava, Cyavana, Atri, Āpnuvāna, and likewise Aurva—those Brahmins born in this lineage are devoted to the Śruti and Smṛti.

O best of the Kurus, all the Māṇḍavyas were diseased, greedy, and wicked; though devoted to performing sacrifices for themselves and officiating at sacrifices for others, they were entirely intent upon Vedic rituals.
For those born in the lineage of Gārgya, there are three pravaras: Aṅgiras, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva as the third.
Born in this lineage, they are of virtuous conduct and speakers of truth; though they are peaceful, they are of diverse complexions, impoverished, and clad in tattered garments.
O King, the twice-born of the Vatsa lineage are indeed endowed with affection for their offspring and are steadfast in the Vedas and Shastras; there are exactly five pravaras among them.
Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, and Jamadagnika—by these five, the twice-born are renowned as being of the very nature of Brahman.
They were peaceful, self-controlled, and of excellent character, well-endowed with sons who followed the Dharma; though devoid of Vedic study, they were skilled in all ritual activities.
They were handsome, possessed of virtuous conduct, and firmly established in all dharmas; all those twice-born ones were devoted to the duty of giving, bestowing both food and water.
O King, the Brāhmaṇas of the Kāśyapa lineage are compassionate, virtuous, devoted to the welfare of all beings, and endowed with three pravaras.
Kāśyapa, Apavatsāra, and Naidhruva as the third—these were knowers of the Vedas, fair-complexioned, lifelong celibates, and performers of sacrifices. || 47 ||
They were fond of dwelling [in sacred places], highly capable, always devoted to their gurus, possessed of stability and honor, and dedicated to the welfare of all beings.
And the twice-born descendants of Kaśyapa perform great sacrifices; they belong to the Dhāraṇa gotra and are endowed with three pravaras.
Agasti, Darvi, Śvetāśva, and Dadhyavāhana—those born in this lineage are devoted to righteous deeds. (50)
They were all cruel in their actions and likewise possessed large bellies; they had long ears and large tusks, and though appearing as Brahmins, they were solely devoted to wealth.
Those born of Laugākṣa who are indeed Vāḍavas, abiding in truth, though they may be wrathful and hateful, are the bringers of fear to all beings. || 52 ||
And their three eminent lineages (pravara) consist of the nature of the knowledge of reality: Kaśyapa, Vatsa, and Vasiṣṭha as the third. || 53 ||
The Vaiṣṇavas are renowned for their virtuous conduct and possess many livelihoods; the Vāḍavas, however, are covered with many hairs and are dark in complexion.
They were peaceful, generous, and virtuous, always devoted to their own wives; they were born in the lineage of Kuśika and endowed with three ancestral sages (pravara).
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and Audala—these three who are born in this lineage are weak and low-spirited. (56)
The Brahmins were speakers of truth, and the best of kings were handsome; the Brāhmaṇas were skilled in all branches of knowledge and were the most excellent among those devoted to Brahman. || 57 ||
Those belonging to the Upamanyu gotra are endowed with three pravaras: Vasiṣṭha, Bharadvāja, and Indrapramada. || 58 ||
But those Brahmins in this lineage who are cruel, crooked in their ways, corrupters, hateful, base, and intent on amassing everything—59.
They are skilled at inciting quarrels, wealthy, and likewise proud; they are always utterly corrupt and devoted to the company of the wicked. (60)
The Brāhmaṇas born in the Vātsya lineage, endowed with five Pravaras, are sickly, weak, and deprived of the means for their livelihood. || 61 ||
The Bhārgavas, Cyāvanas, Āpnuvānas, Aurvas, and Jamadagnikas—the Brahmins born in this lineage are robust and possessed of great intelligence. (62)

They were devoted to all ritual actions and remained steadfast in all dharmas; they were skilled in the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras, and took delight in performing sacrifices for themselves and officiating at those performed by others.
They were of virtuous conduct, handsome in form, and far-sighted in intellect; they belonged to the Vātsyāyana lineage and were endowed with five pravaras.
Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, and Jamadagni—these previously mentioned Pravaras have been declared to you, O Bhārata. || 65 ||
But those born in this lineage who are always devoted to *pākayajña* sacrifices are born greedy and prone to anger, yet they produce many offspring. (66)

They were always devoted to bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts, with their senses fully subdued; they were the builders of thousands of step-wells, wells, and tanks. They observed vows and possessed good character, yet they were ignorant fools who had abandoned the Vedas.
Those born in the Kauśika lineage are endowed with three ancestral sages (pravara): Viśvāmitra, Aghamarṣaṇa, and Kauśika as the third.
And those Brahmins born in this lineage who know the Veda—peaceful, self-controlled, of excellent character, and devoted to all duties. (69)
Likewise, those best of the twice-born who were childless, harsh, and devoid of luster belonged to the Bhāradvāja gotra and were endowed with five pravaras.
The Aṅgirasas, the Bārhaspatyas, the Bhāradvājas, the Sainyās, and the Gārgyas—these are to be known as the five pravaras. (71)
And those who were born in this lineage—the Vāḍavas—were wealthy, auspicious, endowed with garments and ornaments, and devoted to the service of the twice-born. || 72 ||
All were devoted to the food of Brahman and dedicated to all dharmas; they were born in the lineage of Kāśyapa, endowed with three pravaras. || 73 ||
Kāśyapa, Apavatsāra, and Raibhya—these three are renowned; the Brahmins born in this lineage have red eyes and cruel gazes. (74)
All those who are devoted to the greed of the tongue seek the ultimate truth; yet these same people are impoverished, diseased, thieves, and speakers of falsehood. (75)
All those who do not understand the meaning of the scriptures and are devoid of the Vedas and Smṛtis, even if born among Śunakas, are Brahmins devoted to meditation.
Ascetics and yogis who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), as well as virtuous men of righteous conduct devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu. || 77 ||

The best of the twice-born there are short in stature, of variegated complexions, and possess many wives; they are compassionate, straightforward, peaceful, and devoted to the consumption of food offered to Brahman.
Those born among the Śaunakaseṣas are endowed with three pravaras: Bhārgava, Śaunahotra, and Gārtsyapramada—these three. || 79 ||
O King, the Vāḍava Brahmins born in this land are difficult to endure; they are exceedingly fierce, large-bodied, tall, and arrogant with pride. (80)
Having the form of afflictions, they are black in color and proficient in all scriptures; they have many arms, are proud, skillful, and free from passion and hatred. || 81 ||
Indeed, those Brāhmaṇas who discourse upon the Veda, who are born in the lineage of Vasiṣṭha and endowed with three Pravaras, possess forms adorned with fine garments and ornaments. || 82 ||
Vasiṣṭha, Bhāradvāja, and Indrapramada—these are the Brahmins belonging to this lineage who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
They were performers of sacrifices, devoted to ritual, possessed of beautiful voices, and likewise happy; they were free from hatred, wealthy, blessed with sons, and endowed with virtues. || 84 ||
O King, those born in the Gautama lineage are broad-chested, heroic, and destroyers of their enemies; indeed, there are exactly five principal branches (pravaras).
The Kautsas, Gārgyas, and Umavāhas, as well as Asita and Devala—those Brahmins born in this lineage are supremely purifying. (86)
All were benefactors of others, devoted to the Śruti and Smṛti; yet they were also deceitful like herons, crooked, and intent on fraudulent conduct.
They are skilled in the meaning of various scriptures, adorned with diverse ornaments, expert in tasks such as tree-planting, long-suffering in their anger, and prone to disease.
Those born in the lineage of Aṅgiras are endowed with three pravaras: Āṅgirasa, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva as the third.
And those born in this lineage are speakers of truth, likewise masters of their senses, handsome, moderate in diet, and fair-faced. (90)
They were observers of the great vows, knowers of the ancient lore, devoted to great acts of charity, free from hatred yet possessed of greed, and intent upon the study of the Vedas.

They were far-sighted and possessed great splendor, yet they were utterly deluded by a great illusion; they belonged to the Śāṇḍila lineage and were endowed with the three ancestral lineages (pravara). || 92 ||
Asita, Devala, and Śāṇḍila as the third—these highly fortunate ones belong to this lineage, as do the Kubjas, O best of the twice-born. (93)
They suffer from eye diseases, are extremely wicked, lack great renunciation, and are short-lived; they are skilled at inciting quarrels and intent on amassing everything for themselves. (94)
They were impure and arrogant, yet experts in the science of astrology; they were born in the lineage of Atri and possessed five pravaras. || 95 ||
Ātreya, Arcanānasa, Śyāvāśva, Āṅgirasa, and Atri—those twice-born who were born in this lineage possessed the splendor of the sun. (96)
All were as cool as the moon, established in the forest of Dharma; they were of virtuous conduct, highly proficient, and devoted to the Vedas and the Śāstras.
And the performers of sacrifices were of auspicious conduct, devoted to truth and purity, knowers of dharma, charitable by nature, stainless, and full of great zeal. || 98 ||
They were devoted to austerity and the study of sacred texts, and were dedicated to justice and righteousness. || 99 ||
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O mighty-armed one, tell me the nectar-like story of Dharmāraṇya, by hearing which one is liberated even from the terrible sin of killing a Brahmin.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, I shall relate this story which is very difficult to obtain.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others used to terrify the brāhmaṇas; there was a yakṣa named Jṛmbhaka in the vicinity of Dharmāraṇya.
He constantly causes distress to those dwelling in the forest of Dharma; therefore, it was reported by those foremost of the twice-born to the gods. (3)
O gods, we have been humiliated by yakṣas, rākṣasas, and others; out of fear of them, we shall abandon this excellent abode today—of this there is no doubt. || 4 ||
Then the Siddhas and the excellent Yoginīs, headed by the Śrīmātṛs, were established there on the ground by the gods together with the Gandharvas.
Indeed, for the sake of protecting the brahmins and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, one Yoginī was then established for each of the lineages (gotras).
Whichever clan possessed whatever power capable of protection and preservation, that very power became manifest there as its family deity (kuladevī).
Śrīmātā, Tāraṇī Devī, Āśāpūrī, Gotrapā, Icchā, Artināśinī, Pippalī, and Vikāravaśā. (8)
Jaganmātā, Mahāmātā, Siddhā, Bhaṭṭārikā, as well as Kadaṃbā, Vikarā, Mīṭhā, Suparṇā, and Vasujā. || 9 ||
Mātaṅgī and Mahādevī, Vāṇī and Mukuṭeśvarī, Bhadrī the great Śakti, and Saṃhārī the very powerful one. || 110 ||
Cāmuṇḍā and Mahādevī—these are the clan-mothers (gotramātaraḥ) established there for protection by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others. || 11 ||
The best of Brahmins, always devoted to their own duty, worship them; from that time forward, the Yoginīs have been well-guarded at their respective times.

The Vāḍavas, surrounded by their sons and grandsons, attained a state of well-being. Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, their minds overflowing with joy, mounted excellent celestial chariots and went to heaven, those consumers of nectar.
O King, when a hundred years had passed, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, remembering Dharmāraṇya, came out of curiosity to behold it. 14.
Then at dawn, O King, when the sun had risen, they arrived, having ascended an excellent celestial chariot and being attended by throngs of Apsarases.
O King, while being sung to by Gandharvas and praised by bards, those twice-born ones remained in that place with many sacrificial fuels, flowers, and kusha grass.
Having abandoned those hermitages, they all departed in the ten directions; and seeing that hermitage site empty, Maheśvara [reflected].
The knower of dharma spoke these words: "O Lord, the Brahmins are suffering; it is my opinion that one should provide for them in order to fulfill their service. (18)
Having heard the words of Śambhu, Janārdana, the god of gods, said "Truly, truly! and spoke this to Brahmā.

"O Brahman, arrange for the service of the twice-born; for today the creation shall be eternal, and let the assembly of the twice-born also be happy. Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [acted accordingly].
As he was indeed remembering Kāmadhenu, by that very act of remembrance, at that very moment, the cow arrived there in the sacred Dharmāraṇya.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, to that auspicious account as it occurred in Dharmāraṇya, which I shall relate to you in its entirety; it is the destroyer of the multitude of all sins. || 1 ||
Then, O King, Kāmadhenu was summoned by the Self-born One, who had been impelled by Aja; she spoke to him.
"O Mother, grant attendants to the Brahmins—one to each twice-born—and likewise two pure-souled ones to each; be gracious to me. (3)
Having said "So be it," the great cow moistened the earth with her milk; from his *huṃkāra* sound, men emerged wearing topknots and sacred threads.
And thirty-six thousand merchants of great strength, wearing sacred threads, highly skillful, and proficient in all the scriptures [followed]. (5)
They were endowed with devotion to the twice-born, devoted to Brahman, possessed of ascetic power, knowers of the Purāṇas, of virtuous conduct, righteous, and providers of food for Brahmins.
In heaven, the gods praise those who dwell in Dharmāraṇya, for they are beyond the reach of the senses at all times in their penance, study, and charity.
O lord of the earth, two *caras* were given to each individual twice-born man; and whatever was the lineage (*gotra*) of the *vāḍava*, it was proclaimed of old.
Having thus established the rule that their lineage and that of his attendant were mutually [interconnected], they dwelt there upon those lands.
Then the gods granted him discipleship on earth, and Brahmā explained everything to them for the sake of his instruction.
"Follow their word and grant them whatever they desire; bring firewood, flowers, kuśa grass, and other such items day after day. (11)
Act according to their permission; do not show contempt for them at any time. [Perform] the birth rite, the naming ceremony, and likewise the auspicious first feeding of solid food.
Shaving the head, the initiation ceremony (upanayana), as well as the Mahānāmnī and other rites, whatever ritual acts there may be, vows, giving of gifts, and fasting—[all these are performed]. (13)
"O lords of the world, this must be done with their permission," they said. "If anyone should undertake a task without their permission... (14)
Whether it be a new-moon sacrifice, a funeral rite, or anything auspicious or inauspicious, [it brings] poverty, grief for a son, and likewise the destruction of one's reputation. (15)
"They are constantly oppressed by diseases and do not obtain happiness anywhere. To this, the gods, the best of the immortals, headed by Śakra, replied, "So be it. || 16 ||
Standing before the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), all those gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—then offered praise, having achieved their purpose.
