You are the mother of all the gods, and you are the cause of sacrifice; you are the sacred ford of all sacred fords; salutations be to you, O eternally sinless one! 18.
Upon her forehead are the moon, the sun, and Aruṇa; the bull-bannered Śiva is on the *huṃ* syllable; and all the *nāgas* are upon the *kaṃbala*.
On the back of the razor [of his tongue] are the Gandharvas and the four Vedas; on the tip of his mouth are all the sacred fords, both stationary and moving.
Pleased by such words spoken many times, the cow, being very well-disposed, then said, "What shall I do? (21)
The gods said: "O Mother, O Goddess, all these auspicious attendants have been created by you. By your grace, O highly fortunate one, the Brahmins have become happy. (22)
Then, O King, that illustrious Surabhi departed for heaven; thereupon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others vanished right then and there.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Brahmin, those immensely radiant ones were born from cows and had no wives; how was it that they were married, and when did their sons come to be?
Vyāsa said: For the sake of their marriage, Gandharva maidens were brought by Rudra and Yama and provided there as their wives.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who is this king of the Gandharvas? What is his name? Where does he dwell? How many daughters does he have, and what is their conduct? Tell me. (26)
Vyāsa said: O King, there is a lord of the Gandharvas known as Viśvāvasu; sixty thousand maidens reside in his palace.
In the intermediate space, his house was a beautiful city of the Gandharvas; there were auspicious maidens born of the Gandharvas, endowed with youth and great beauty.
O King, Nandin and Bhṛṅgin, the two auspicious-faced attendants of Rudra, spoke of Śiva to those maidens whom they had seen before.
O Mahādeva, O All-pervading Lord, in the past I beheld innumerable thousands of maidens in the house of Viśvāvasu within the city of the Gandharvas.
"O Lord, bring them here and hand them over by force to the Gobhuja kings. Having heard this, the god Sadāśiva, the destroyer of Tripura, [acted accordingly].
O descendant of Bharata, he dispatched a messenger named Vijaya; having gone there, he reached the place where Viśvāvasu, the subduer of enemies, was staying.
And he spoke these words, which were beneficial and uttered by Śiva: "O highly fortunate one, [these temples] were constructed by the Lord of Kāñcī in Dharmāraṇya. (33)
Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas were established there; and for the sake of their service, the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) was requested.
Those merchants, who practiced auspicious conduct under her guidance, were not born from a womb; they were thirty-six thousand youths of great strength. (35)
"Sent indeed by Śiva, I have come into your presence; for the sake of the maiden, O illustrious one, say 'Give her! Give her! he said. (36)
The Gandharva said: "O high-minded one, having abandoned all the gods and Gandharvas, how indeed can I give [myself] to humans in this world? (37)
Having heard his words, Vijaya then turned back and related all of that great account of the Gandharva's conduct.
Vyāsa said: Then the Blessed One, the benefactor of the world, Sadāśiva, overcome with anger, mounted his bull with trident in hand.
The Lord was surrounded by thousands of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and others; then likewise the gods, nāgas, bhūtas, vetālas, and sky-dwellers [approached].
Overcome by great wrath, they arrived by the thousands; as that army surged forward, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
The goddess Earth trembled, the guardians of the quarters were overcome with fear, terrible winds blew unceasingly, and the elephants of the directions let out a roar.
Vyāsa said: Seeing that great army approaching, trembling with fear, they all fled from the city of the Gandharvas in the ten directions.
O King, the king of the Gandharvas abandoned his city and went to Mount Meru; those maidens were endowed with youth and possessed of beauty and nobility.
Then, O King, he took all of them and gave them to the merchants in the presence of the deity, according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
Then, having offered a portion of clarified butter to the Gandharva, the sons of the cow likewise [offered it] to the gods who were born before them, as well as to the Sun and the Moon.
Then they offered a portion of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) to Yama and Mṛtyu; having offered the portions of clarified butter according to the rule, those of auspicious vows made their request.
From that time forth, whenever a Gāndharva marriage was at hand, they have taken up the portion of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) even today, everywhere in abundance.
And thirty-six thousand youths presented themselves; their sons and grandsons were by the hundreds and thousands. For this very reason, all of them were indeed reduced to servitude. (3)
And the great heroic kṣatriyas were indeed fashioned for the state of servants. || 50 ||
Then, O King, all the gods departed as they had come; once the god had gone, all those twice-born ones continued to dwell in this place.
O King, accompanied by their sons and grandsons, they dwell free from fear on all sides; those who know the Vedas recite them, while at times they expound the meaning of the scriptures.

Some here chant the name of Viṣṇu, and some indeed chant that of Śiva; some chant the name of Brahmā, while others chant the Yama-sūkta. O observer of noble vows, the officiating priests perform sacrifices and attend to the Agnihotra with the utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ.
The entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, were filled with sounds; and the merchants, being highly skillful, were eager to serve the twice-born.
They dwell, perfectly established, in that auspicious and divine forest of Dharma; there they find all things such as food and drink, as well as sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, fruits, and the like.
Those merchants, whose offspring were cows, filled [the world] with the twice-born. || 57 ||
The collection of flower offerings, the washing of bathing garments and other items, the fashioning of stones and such, and auspicious activities such as sweeping; || 58 ||
The merchant women perform tasks such as husking and grinding, and they indeed serve those Brahmins at the command of Kājeśa.
Then all the twice-born became healthy and devoted to joy; indeed, they worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others day and night, as well as at the two twilights.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Merchant’s Acceptance," in the *Dharmāraṇya-māhātmya* of the first part of the third section, the *Brahmakhaṇḍa*, within the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O best of the twice-born, tell me what happened after this; O Lord, having drunk the nectar of your words, I am not yet satiated."
Vyāsa said: Then, after some time had passed and at the conclusion of the Yuga, at the beginning of the Tretā age, Lolajihvākṣa became the lord of the Rākṣasas.
By him, the entire triple world, including all that is mobile and immobile, was put to flight; having conquered all the worlds, he arrived at Dharmāraṇya. || 3 ||
Having seen that entire auspicious and beautiful city inhabited by the twice-born, he, out of hatred for Brahmanas, set that splendid city on fire.
Seeing the city burning, those best of the twice-born who dwelt in Dharmāraṇya perished and departed by the same way they had come. || 5 ||
Then the goddesses, Śrīmātā and the others, being provoked by the Rākṣasa, indeed began to strike him with shouts after threatening the Rākṣasa.
Then hundreds and thousands of goddesses rose up, bearing excellent tridents and holding conchs, discs, and maces.
Some carried water-pots (kamaṇḍalu), others held staffs and swords; one bore a noose and a goad, while another carried a sword and a shield.
One held an axe in her hand, while another bore divine weapons; she was enriched with various ornaments and adorned with diverse jewels.
For the destruction of the Rākṣasas and for the welfare of the Brāhmaṇas, they came to that place where the Rākṣasa Lolajihva resided.
Having large fangs, a massive body, and a tongue like lightning, the terrifying Rākṣasa let out a fierce lion’s roar upon seeing them. || 11 ||
By that great roar, the three worlds were terrified; all the directions were filled, and many oceans were agitated.
O King, a great clamor arose then in Dharmāraṇya; hearing that, Vāsava then dispatched Nalakūbara.
"What is this? Go and see; having seen it, report it to me. Having heard those words of his, Nalakūbara indeed departed. (14)
Having witnessed that great battle between Śrīmātā and Lolajihva right there, he reported it exactly as it had been seen and exactly as it had occurred before Śakra.
"Having departed from here for the forest of Dharma, he terrifies the three worlds. Having heard this, Vāsava informed Viṣṇu and returned to the earth.
That beautiful city, difficult even for the gods to attain, was set ablaze; the Vāḍavas were not seen there, as they had all fled to the ten directions.
There, the illustrious mother Yoginī engaged in a supreme battle; all the subjects, crying out "Alas! Alas!", fled hither and thither. (18)
Having heard that, O King, Vāsudeva took up the Sudarśana and descended from Satyaloka to the surface of the earth.
Then, having gone to the Forest of Dharma (Dharmāraṇya), he released that discus; thereupon the Rakṣasa, his tongue lolling, fell down unconscious.
Then, pierced by the trident and struck by the spears, the Rākṣasa, overwhelmed with rage while being slaughtered, abandoned his life-breaths and went to heaven. || 21 ||
Then the gods, together with the gandharvas, their minds overflowing with joy, arrived from Satyaloka and praised that Lord of the World.
Beholding that desolate place, Viṣṇu spoke these words: "Where are all those brahmins in the hermitage of the sages? (23)
Then, O King, having swiftly searched for the gods and Gandharvas who had fled here and there, the Brāhmaṇas spoke as follows: || 24 ||
"O Brahmins, hear our words: that lowest of Rākṣasas has been slain; he was cut down by the god Vāsudeva with his discus. (25)
Having heard that, O King, all the Brahmins, their eyes wide with joy, assembled together and took their seats in their respective places.

Then, O King, these pleasing words were spoken to the Lord of Śrī: "Since you, the Lord of the Universe, have come from Satyaloka, this city has been established for the welfare of those whose nature is that of the twice-born. (27)
In that time, it shall become renowned in the world as Satyamandira; in the Kṛta Yuga it is Dharmāraṇya, and in the Tretā Yuga it is Satyamandira.
Having heard that and having agreed, saying "So be it," Vāsudeva, all those Brāhmaṇas, together with their sons and grandsons, [departed]. || 29 ||
Accompanied by their wives and followers, they dwelt as before, engaged in austerities, sacrificial rites, and the study of the Vedas.
Thus has all this been declared to you regarding Dharma in the Temple of Truth.
Vyāsa said: Then, O best of kings, for the sake of protection, that city was established by the gods as Satyamandira; indeed, from that very day, it became known by the name Satyā.
In the east is the god Dharmeśvara; in the south, Gaṇādhipa; in the west is stationed Bhānu; and in the north is Svayaṃbhuva. || 2 ||
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By whom was Gaṇeśa established, and for what reason did he establish him? O illustrious one, tell me his name; do not delay. (3)
Vyāsa said: Now I shall proclaim the cause of Gaṇeśa’s birth.
O Great King, at that time all the deities and Mothers assembled together; and in Dharmāraṇya, the son of Caṇḍikā was established.
O best of kings, at the beginning, the gods indeed constructed a wall for the virtuous women on that ground, adorned with banners and flags.
There, within the circular enclosure of the Brāhmaṇa’s hermitage, a very beautiful pedestal was constructed in its center out of bricks.
There are indeed four main gates, pure and adorned with archways; at the eastern gate is the deity Dharmeśvara, and at the southern is Gaṇanāyaka.
The Sun was established in the west and the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) in the north; thus has the account of the origin of Dharmeśvara been narrated before you.
Now I shall proclaim the cause of Gaṇeśa’s birth. Once, Pārvatī performed the rubbing of her body with unguents. (10)
Seeing the impurity produced by that [act] on his own body, he took it in his hand; then, having fashioned an image, he beheld a beautiful form.
Having transferred his life-force into her, he stood up before her; he then said to his mother, "What shall I do at your command?"
Pārvatī said: "Until I have finished my bath, you must remain at my door, along with all my weapons, such as the axe and the rest. (13)
"While you remain at my door, let no one create an obstacle. Thus addressed by the Great Goddess, he stood at the gate, armed with his weapons.
In the meantime, the god Mahādeva arrived; Maheśvara set his mind upon entering the inner sanctum.
Gaṇeśa, standing at the gate, did not grant him entrance; thereupon, the enraged Mahādeva fought with him.
Then, having fought and each desiring the other's death, O Lord, he struck a most auspicious mark upon the forehead with his axe.
Then the god Mahādeva, raising his trident, struck him; he severed the head with the trident, and it fell upon the earth.
Seeing her son fallen, Pārvatī wept aloud; when he had been struck down, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there at that time.
Seeing Pārvatī distressed, Maheśvara, the God of gods, reflected: "What have I done so fruitlessly?"
In the meantime, he beheld Gajāsura there; and having seen that great Daitya, he who is uniquely honored by all the worlds [acted].
Having struck it and seized that head—which had been made into a child by Pārvatī—he rose up there with his attendants in the presence of Mahādeva.
Then they clearly gave him the name Gajānana; all the gods were gathered there, as were the joyful sages.
They constantly praise with hymns him who brings welfare to his family, yet he sells his family for the sake of a sweetmeat to one who worships [him].
And at the southern gate, the self-existent one himself worshipped that single-tusked Mahādeva, who is stout and honored by the gods.
He had matted hair and was short of stature; he wore a serpent as his sacred thread, possessed three eyes and a massive body, and held a banner and an axe in his hands.
Holding a lotus in his hand that destroys all wicked brahmins, he resided to the south of the city for the protection of the worlds.
To the exceedingly gracious leader of the Gaṇas, who is saluted by Siddhi and Buddhi, who has the luster of vermilion, the best of gods, the auspicious one holding a sharp goad; || 28 ||
Having worshipped him with auspicious *śatapuṣpa* flowers, the lord of the immortals and the gods then bowed down with great devotion and praised him. (29)
The gods said: Salutations to you, the Lord of the gods; salutations to the Lord of the Gaṇas. O Elephant-faced one, salutations to you, the presiding deity of Mahādeva. (30)

"Obeisance to you, O Lord of the Gaṇas, the God who is dear to his devotees! Being praised with these auspicious hymns, the Lord of the Gaṇas, the Chief of the Gaṇas, being well-pleased, then spoke these words.
The leader of the Gaṇas said: "O gods, I am pleased with you; speak what you desire and I shall grant it to you."
The gods said: "O illustrious lord, remaining here, perform for us the task concerning the brahmins and the merchant residents in Dharmāraṇya. (33)

O Lord of the Gaṇas, always be the protector of those who are righteous and devoted to the practice of celibacy and other virtues, as well as of those belonging to the various castes and stages of life, and others.
O highly fortunate one, by your grace may all the twice-born be constantly endowed with wealth and happiness, and may the merchants be possessed of great strength. (35)
"O Lord, you must protect [this] as long as the moon, the sun, and the earth endure. "So be it," replied Maheśvara, the Lord of Gaṇas.
And the gods, having attained joy, worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas; then the gods, filled with delight, [honored him] with offerings of flowers, incense, and other libations.
And whatever other men in the world worship [it] for the sake of being free from obstacles; || 38 ||
May you be worshipped first at marriages, festivals, and sacrifices; and may you always remain gracious toward those born in Dharmāraṇya. 39.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Installation of Gaṇeśa," in the first part of the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: To the western part of Śambhu, the son of Kaśyapa was established; there, O highly fortunate one, is that sacred field of the Sun (Ravikṣetra), so it is called.
There, two great divine beings were born, endowed with beauty and youth—the gods Nāsatya and Aśvin, renowned as the destroyers of disease.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O illustrious grandfather, please graciously tell me how the two Aśvins were born and how they came to be in the world of mortals.
How was the Sun brought down from the world of the gods to the earth? Please explain all of this to me with care and favor.
For by hearing this, O illustrious one, one is indeed liberated from all sins.

Vyāsa said: O King, you have asked well regarding the narrative of the higher worlds; by hearing which, O tiger among men, one is liberated from all diseases. Saṃjñā, the daughter of Viśvakarman, was chosen by Aṃśumat, the radiant Sun.
Having seen Sūrya, Saṃjñā always practiced the restraint of her eyes; because of that, the Sun, filled with wrath, spoke these words to Saṃjñā.
Sūrya said: "O foolish woman, because you always close your eyes whenever you see me, therefore Yama, the restrainer of living beings, shall be born."
Then the goddess saw her trembling and overwhelmed with fear; seeing her eyes rolling, Ravi spoke to her again.
"Since your gaze has now become agitated upon seeing me, therefore, O lady of agitated mind, you shall give birth to a daughter. (10)
Vyāsa said: Then, indeed, by that curse of her husband, there were born to her Yama and this Yamunā, who is celebrated as a very great river.
And that beautiful woman, unable to endure the great heat of the sun's splendor, then reflected thus in her mind.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? And where, having gone, will there be peace for me? How might the anger of my husband, who is like the sun, be extinguished? (13)
Having reflected thus in many ways, the highly fortunate daughter of Prajāpati then considered taking refuge with her father to be the best course.
Then, having resolved to go to her father’s house, that illustrious goddess, the beloved of the Sun, summoned her own shadow.
And she said to her: "You must remain here just as I am with Bāṇa; likewise, you must conduct yourself properly toward his children and toward Ravi."
"O sinless one, you must not speak even what is unpleasant to me as if it were highly esteemed; rather, you should say to me, 'I am that very same Saṃjñā. (17)
Chāyāsaṃjñā said: "From the seizing of my hair until the utterance of the curse, I shall do exactly as you say; I will carry it out as long as my hair is being pulled."
Having been addressed thus, the goddess then went to her father’s abode; there she beheld Tvaṣṭṛ, whose sins had been shaken off by ascetic penance.
And out of great respect, she was honored by Viśvakarman as well; thus, that blameless woman remained in her father’s house for some time.
Then that knower of dharma, Viśvakarman, her father, spoke with love and great respect to his daughter, who had not been away for very long.
O child, for me as I behold you, even very many days would be equal to a single moment; however, dharma is being violated.
For women, a long-term residence with their kinsmen does not bring glory; it is the desire of relatives that a wife remain in her father's house. (23)
"O daughter, you have been united with your husband Sūrya, the lord of the three worlds; you ought not to remain in your father's house for a long time. (24)
Therefore, go now to your husband’s house; you have seen me and have been honored by me. O lady of auspicious eyes, you must come again for a further visit. (25)
Vyāsa said: Having been addressed thus, O sage, she then quickly replied, "So be it," and after honoring her father, she departed for the Northern Kurus.
Not desiring the heat of the sun and fearing its brilliance, she performed penance there as well, having assumed the form of a mare.
Thinking that it was indeed Saṃjñā, the Lord of Heaven begot two sons and one beautiful daughter on the second day.

Just as Chāyā’s affection was focused exclusively upon her own sons, so too it was not directed toward the daughter Saṃjñā or her two sons; and day by day, there was a distinction made regarding their fondling and their meals. (29)
Manu forgave her, but Yama did not tolerate it; then, out of anger, he raised his foot to strike her, yet, with a mind inclined toward forgiveness, he did not let it fall upon her body.
Then, O King, Chāyāsaṃjñā, her lips slightly quivering and her sprout-like hands trembling, cursed Yama out of anger. (31)
"If you forcibly raise your foot against me, who am my father's wife, then this foot of yours shall sink into the earth this very day. (32)
Having heard this curse, Yama became deeply apprehensive toward his mother; approaching his father, he spoke to him with a prostration.
"O father, this is a great wonder never seen before," saying this, the mother, out of maternal affection, pronounces a curse upon her son. (34)
Just as my mother told me, "She is not my mother," so it is for me; even toward sons who are devoid of virtue, a mother does not become devoid of virtue. || 35 ||
Having heard these words of Yama, the Blessed One, the dispeller of darkness, summoned Chāyāsaṃjñā and asked, "Where has she gone? (36)
And she said: "O Vibhāvasu, I am Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ; I am your wife, and these offspring were begotten by you upon me."
When she did not speak even though Vivasvat questioned her thus many times, the radiant one became enraged and prepared to curse her. (38)
Then she related everything exactly as it had happened to Vivasvat; and the Blessed One, having understood the matter, went to the abode of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ worshipped him, who is honored by the three worlds, saying: "O Radiant One, why have you returned to your own home devoid of your Śakti? (40)
He questioned Saṃjñā, and she, who knew the truth, said to him: "O Ravi, she has come here to my house, sent by you."
Then Divākara, established in meditative absorption, beheld her performing penance in the form of a mare among the Northern Kurus.
Unable to endure the splendor of the sun and excessively tormented by it, she abandoned her shadow-form, which was like the appearance of fire.
O King, having arrived at Dharmāraṇya, he performed extremely difficult penance; there he beheld Chāyāputra Śani, Yama, and others.
At that very moment, the Sun-god was struck with wonder upon seeing his two wicked sons; he meditated for a moment to understand, and having reflected, he realized the cause of it all.
Burning her body with the heat of her loathing, that devoted wife performed penance so that she was unable to even look upon me with my splendor.
When fifty years had passed, Pradyotana, having reflected thus, went quickly with the speed of thought and performed penance in Kāu.
In that excellent and meritorious Dharmāraṇya, where Saṃjñā was established in asceticism, she became a mare upon seeing the Sun who had arrived there. (48)
The sun’s wife was always Saṃjñā, and from her the horse was born; he then entered into union with them both, having placed his organ in her nostril.
Then the twin Aśvins were born upon the earth, and water appeared there from his right hoof.
When that portion of the ground was split open, a second pool appeared there, arising from the rear half of his foot.
The sage has declared that here in this pool, the fruit is equal to that of Gaṅgāpurī, as well as the northern-flowing Kāśī, Kurukṣetra, and other such places.
One obtains that fruit at Taptakuṇḍa without a doubt; by performing a bath right there, one is liberated from all sins.
Furthermore, a body afflicted by diseases such as leprosy shall not be born again. O King, this cause of the birth of the two Aśvins has been told to you.
Then, O King, the gods beginning with Brahmā arrived there, having granted them a brilliant boon of consciousness that indeed exceeded their expectations.
Having installed there Ravi, the lord of the forest named Bakula, they then worshipped him; at that time, Saṃjñā returned to her former form.
At that time, the queen and the twin princes were established there. O high-minded king, listen as I describe the fruit of this sacred site.
O best of the Kurus, this is the primordial site, difficult even for the gods to attain; having bathed in Ravikuṇḍa, a man endowed with faith and self-controlled [attains it]. (58)
He who drinks the water with faith, having first offered libations to the ancestors and the deities, shall deliver all his ancestors, even those who have gone to the great hells.
Whether it be very little or even much, everything shall become multiplied ten millionfold on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, or during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
And those who have bathed in the Ravikuṇḍa do not enter a womb again, especially during the transits of the sun, the Vyatīpāta yoga, the Vaidhṛti yoga, and on the sacred festival days (parvan).
Whoever bathes in the Ravikuṇḍa on the full moon, the new moon, or the fourteenth day of either the bright or dark fortnight, shall obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
A person who worships Bakula and Arka with single-minded devotion goes to the supreme abode for as long as the sun shines. (63)
His fortune shall surely be stable, he shall obtain progeny and happiness, and the host of his enemies shall go to ruin through the grace of the Lord of Heaven. (64)
For him there shall be no fear of fire, nor of tigers, nor of elephants; nor shall there be fear of serpents anywhere, nor any dread of spirits, ghosts, and the like.
May all the Bālagrahas, as well as Revatī and Vṛddharevatī, all go to their destruction; O Bakulārka, salutations to you! (66)
His cattle increase, as do his wealth and grain; and his lineage shall remain unbroken when Bakulārka is saluted.
The woman who bears only one child like a crow, she who is childless, she whose offspring have died, the barren woman, the deformed woman, and those women who are poison-maidens; || 68 ||
O King, by bathing in this pool, people are thus liberated from their faults; they obtain good fortune, wives, sons, and beauty in every respect. (69)
Even a mortal man seized by disease, if he bathes well in Ravikuṇḍa for six months, is liberated from all ailments.
Whoever indeed performs the rite of releasing a dark-colored bull in the field of the Sun, the ancestors attain satisfaction until the dissolution of all beings.
And he who performs the gift of a daughter in marriage in this sacred field, O son, being purified in soul by the wedding rite, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
The gift of a cow, a bed, coral, and likewise a horse; a female slave, a buffalo, and bells, along with sesame seeds combined with gold. (73)
O Bhārata, one should give a cow made of sesame seeds in this sacred field, as well as sandals, an umbrella, and likewise protection against the cold and other such necessities.
Likewise, one who performs the Lakṣahoma, as well as the Rudra and the Atirudra rites, and whatever else one gives at that place endowed with faith—[all that becomes inexhaustible]. (75)
O dear one, I shall tell you the fruit of each one; listen to it according to the truth. Through giving, one obtains enjoyments both in this world and in the next. (76)
A mortal man obtains a kingdom by performing marriage; through a wife, dharma, kāma, and artha are attained—of this there is no doubt. (77)
One obtains happiness through worship in birth after birth; whoever should remember the Bakula-Arka on the seventh lunar day conjoined with the Sun [Sunday], [attains this]. (78)
For him, there is no fear of fever and the like, nor of enemies, nor of disease. (79)
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Sage, how did the name Bakulārka come to belong to the Sun? O best among speakers, you ought to explain this truth to me. (80)
Vyāsa said: O Indra among kings, when Saṃjñā, with single-minded intent, performed penance beneath a Bakula tree for the sake of the Sun, in order to pacify her husband’s splendor. (81)
Seeing the appearance of the sun, the mare was born; meanwhile, the bull remained exceedingly calm in the vicinity of the Bakula tree.
And then the queen gave birth to two divine and charming sons; because of them, the name of that Sun became celebrated as Bakulārka.
Whoever performs a ritual bath there shall not be afflicted by disease; they obtain dharma, artha, and kāma—of this there is no doubt. (84)
Within six months, a man attains perfection and obtains liberation. Thus, O Great King, has been described the majesty of Bakulārka. 85.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Bakulārka," in the Dharmāraṇya episode, within the first part of the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 13.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O ocean of compassion, O illustrious one, O all-pervading Lord of the gods! When indeed was penance performed here by Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor? || 1 ||
It was indeed told to Skanda by the high-souled Śarva; you yourself must relate it all in its proper sequence.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O child, O best of kings; I shall tell you how once in Dharmāraṇya, Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor performed penance.
Skanda said: How did the lake named Devasaras, as well as Paṃpā, Campā, and Gayā, come to be? And how is it that Vārāṇasī became even more preeminent, and how did Hari become horse-faced?
Īśvara said: Here the god Nārāyaṇa performed a most difficult penance for three hundred divine years; he became one with a perfectly beautiful countenance. || 5 ||
O dear son, O one of great luster, the great Viṣṇu, Hari, performed penance at that place of the Siddhas for the sake of obtaining a beautiful form, assuming the face of a horse.
Skanda said: Tell me the reason why Hari, the horse-faced one, is not here today; he who is the slayer of the great enemy, the god of gods, and the lord of the universe.
O illustrious one, by whose name even many sins dissolve with great force, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
His wondrous deeds are indeed heard to be truly marvelous; the Supreme Lord is the cause of all living beings.
How can the Lord, who exists in the form of the vital breath, assume the form of a horse? He is proclaimed to be the single form of all the tantras.
Accessible through devotion for those who partake in dharma, he is the embodiment of bliss, eternally pure; though beyond qualities, he is eternal, all-pervading, and likewise devoid of attributes.
He is the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of all embodied beings; he is unmanifest, highly resplendent, and well-disposed—why then did he become horse-faced? (12)
From whose body-hair the gods, trees and other plants, serpents, and mountains arise; from whose body the entire universe is born in every kalpa.
He alone is the source of the universe; He alone is the ultimate cause, by whom the sciences and sacrifices that had reached dissolution were brought back again.
That wicked Daitya, who had exerted himself for the sake of the Vedic meaning, has been slain; thus was Mahāviṣṇu [described], so how did he become horse-faced? (15)
By him, the jewel-wombed earth is held playfully upon his back; by him, the entire world, both stationary and moving, is maintained in its proper order.
How did that god, who is indeed omniform, come to have the face of a horse—he who, having assumed the form of a boar, was the slayer of Hiraṇyākṣa? (17)
The one of great splendor, having entered the waters of the ocean, which were exceedingly pure, lifted up the entire earth along with its oceans and mountains.
And surely the earth was lifted up by him with ease upon the tip of his tusk, after he had assumed the form of a tawny boar that destroys all sorrow. (19)
How did that Lord Īśāna come to assume the form of Hayagrīva? And for the sake of Prahlāda, how did that Īśāna manifest a terrifying form?
The Great God in the form of Narasiṃha, the warder-off of all evil, protected that most excellent devotee who was situated upon the mountain, amidst fire, and by the ocean.
At the onset of night, he slew the wicked Hiraṇyakaśipu and established Prahlāda upon Indra’s throne, bestowing happiness upon him.
And indeed, for the sake of Prahlāda, he assumed the form of Nṛsiṃha; at that time, he became a petitioner before the son of Virocana.
And he who was worshipped by Bali during the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha)—by him the earth was taken away, having made heaven and earth his three steps.
By whom, indeed, in his universal form, Bali was cast down into the netherworld; and by whom alone, twenty-one times over, the Kṣatriyas were subdued upon the surface of the earth.
Having slain [the king], he of great majesty gave the earth to the Brahmins; by him alone was the Haihaya king killed, by whom his own mother had been slain.
By him indeed, on this earth, the wicked-natured Rākṣasī named Tāḍakā was slain by the grace of Kauśika while he was still a child. (27)
In Viśvāmitra’s sacrifice, by him who had assumed a human body as a mere sport, fourteen thousand Rākṣasas were slain by force.
By him Śūrpaṇakhā was struck down and Triśiras was felled; having slain Vālin, he made Sugrīva his ally with the help of Sugrīva. (29)
Having built a bridge across the ocean and slain the ten-headed Rāvaṇa in battle, he reached Dharmāraṇya and honored the Brāhmaṇas.
Having bestowed many villages upon the best of the twice-born as a religious endowment, and having bathed in the Dharmavāpī, he gave excellent gifts of cows.
Having protected the virtuous and for the sake of restraining the wicked, he likewise performed other deeds as they are heard of upon the surface of the earth.
How did that Lord, having acted out of divine play, become horse-faced; he who was born in the Yādava lineage and [performed such deeds as] the destruction of Pūtanā and Śakaṭa?
The Daitya Ariṣṭa, Keśin, Vṛkāsura, Bakāsura, the great Asura Śakaṭāsura, Tṛṇāvarta, and Dhenuka; || 34 ||

How indeed did he become horse-faced? [He was] Malla, as well as Kaṃsa, and likewise Jarāsaṃdha; and the slayer of Kālayavana, having conquered the Asura Tāraka in battle, as well as the sixty thousand cities.
And he who married sixteen thousand maidens, having made them non-human in this way—how did he come to have the face of a horse? (36)
He who is the protector of all devotees, the slayer of all the wicked, and the establisher of dharma—that Kalki also resides in the station of Viṣṇu.
This which has been revealed by you is indeed a great marvel; O Destroyer of Tripura, tell me the entire reason for this.
Śrī Rudra said: "Well asked, O mighty-armed one! I shall tell you the cause of that; listen with a one-pointed mind to [the account] of Hayagrīva Kṛṣṇa. (39)
Vyāsa said: Formerly, a sacrifice was indeed commenced by the gods upon the surface of the earth; all of them, led by Rudra, sought to invoke [the deity] with Vedic mantras.
They all went to Vaikuṇṭha and to their own abode in the Ocean of Milk; yet even after returning to Pātāla once more, they did not behold Kṛṣṇa.
Then, overcome by delusion, they all ran hither and thither; yet at that time, Janārdana in the form of Brahmā was not seen by them at all.
All those gods, led by Indra, deliberated: "Where has that Great Viṣṇu gone, and by what means can he be seen? (43)
Having bowed their heads to the god Vāgīśa, they spoke with reverence: "O God of gods, Mahāviṣṇu, please tell us out of your grace."
Bṛhaspati said: I do not know for what purpose the high-souled Viṣṇu, the Lord of Yoga, Hari, the infallible one, having ascended to yoga, became the very form of yoga. 45.
Having meditated for a moment upon his own self, Hari was made known by Dhiṣaṇa; then all the gods went to that place where the god, the Lord of the World, was present.
Then Mahāviṣṇu, that Janārdana, was seen absorbed in meditation; having meditated upon the slayer of Daityas, who bore the form of his task and held an arrow, [he arose].

Then, having observed their position, he set about a means for awakening; and at that time, the ants said to them with effort, "If they cut the bowstring, Hari himself will be awakened by that sound. (48)
The gods said: "O ants, consume the sacrificial offerings so that this Hari may awaken; we, who are intent on the sacrifice, inform our Lord."

The ants said: "One who causes the interruption of sleep, the breaking off of conversation, the estrangement of a couple's friendship, or the separation of a child from its mother, shall go to hell. (50)
The Lord of the World has ascended to yoga; the mighty one is established in samādhi. We shall certainly not create any obstacle for that glorious Jagadīśa.

Brahmā said: "If you would perform the work of the gods, you must all become omnivorous; furthermore, O ants, you must act in such a way that the success of the sacrifice may be achieved. Then, O child, that queen of the ants spoke thus once more.
The female bee said: "O Brahmin, how can the Lord of the World—who is as difficult to approach as the Malaya breeze and is worshipped by the gods—be awakened by us?"
"I have no need for sacrifice, nor likewise for the gods; yet, O gods, grant me a share in all sacrificial rites. (54)
The gods said: "We shall always grant a share to Vamrī in the sacrifices; do exactly as we say, for this has been offered by us for the sake of the sacrifice. (55)
"So be it," said the Ant even as she was being commanded; O King, she performed every task, such as eating the [enemy's] virtues and so forth.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O Brahmin-sage, son of Satyavatī, this is truly a marvel—that the gods [are concerned] with his awakening, with the destruction of his qualities, and with his meditative absorptions. (57)

Vyāsa said: All the gods were distracted in mind; they did not perceive that Hari’s bow had been drawn, being utterly deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, as if wondering for what purpose this was done.
Joyfully they released those anthills before Hari; then that mountain-like anthill was led to the side of Koṭi.
And as soon as that bowstring was consumed and rendered defective, his head, along with the ends of the bowstring, was severed and went to heaven.
When their head had departed, those gods became deeply distressed in mind; they all ran in every direction to look for the head. || 61 ||
Vyāsa said: At that time, the gods, beginning with Brahmā, did not see his head; exclaiming "Alas! What shall we do?", those wise ones reflected.
Then Brahmā, accompanied by the gods, spoke to Viśvakarman.
Brahmā said: "O All-pervading Lord, you alone are Viśvakarman, the eternal maker of all works. Do you indeed quickly fashion a dense face for the archer."
Having then paid homage to him and being praised, that divine architect spoke with supreme devotion to Brahmā, who was born from the lotus.
Having quickly completed the sacrificial rites, the various gods spoke.
What more can I say before you, O God, since I have been deprived of my share of the sacrifice? May I likewise receive a share of the sacrifice along with the gods.
Brahmā said: "O increaser of the gods, I shall grant you a share in all sacrifices. O hero, you are worshipped first among those learned in the Vedas at the Soma sacrifice."
"O architect of the immortals, join that head of Viṣṇu. Viśvakarman said to the gods, "Bring the head here."
"O best of kings, all the gods say that he does not exist; yet at midday, the Sun-god appears in his chariot in the sky. (8)
Then, O protector of the earth, all the gods saw that they led the horse away from the chariot, having severed the head from the neck of Hari’s steed.
The highly skillful Viśvakarman joined it to the headless trunk; seeing that Lord of the gods of gods, the deities offered hymns of praise.
The gods said: "Salutations to you, O seed of the universe; salutations to you, O Lord of Kamalā. Salutations to you, O Sovereign of the gods; salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one. (11)
You are the sustenance of all beings; you alone are the refuge of the virtuous; you are the slayer of all the wicked—O Hayagrīva, homage be to you! 12.
You are the syllable Om, the Vaṣaṭ-call, and the fourfold Svāhā and Svadhā; you are the primordial one, O Lord of the Gods, and you alone are my eternal refuge.
The sacrifice, the lord of sacrifice, the sacrificer, the sacrificial material, the priest, and the oblation—O God, all these are offered for your sake; you alone are my refuge and my friend. (14)
You are Time of terrible form; you are the sun and the moon; you are Agni and Varuṇa; and you are the one who brings about the destruction of time.
You alone are the three qualities here, yet you are indeed devoid of qualities; you are the abode of all qualities and the protector of all living beings.
You exist as both female and male, and you are the fourfold family (kula) consisting of beasts, birds, and other human beings, characterized by eighty-four lakhs of species. || 17 ||
O Hari, you are indeed the end of days, the end of fortnights, the end of months, the year, the yuga, the end of the kalpa, the great ends, and the end of time itself.
O King, being thus praised by the gods with such great divine hymns, the Lord, being well-pleased, spoke in the presence of all the deities.
The Blessed Lord said: "For what purpose have all you hosts of gods arrived here on earth? O gods, what is the cause of this; are you perhaps oppressed by the Daityas?"
The gods said: "No fear has arisen from the Daitya; we are intent upon the sacrificial rites. All of us, devoted to beholding you, are indeed surveying the ten directions."
All of us, deluded by your māyā, were distracted in mind and overcome with fear; yet we have beheld your supreme form as one established in yoga.
And the female termite was urged by us, O Lord, for the purpose of waking you; and then there occurred that unprecedented event: your head was severed.
Having brought the head of Sūrya’s horse, the exceedingly skillful Viśvakarman joined it to the head of Viṣṇu; therefore, O Lord, he is known as Hayagrīva.
Viṣṇu said: "I am pleased, O all you inhabitants of heaven; I grant you the desired boon. I, the God of gods and Lord of the universe, have been born as Hayagrīva. (25)
Neither fierce nor deformed, yet served even by the gods; O gods, I have been born as a bestower of boons, having been propitiated as Hayānana. (26)
Vyāsa said: Then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the wise Creator, with a satisfied mind, gave a portion of the sacrificial offering to the ants and to Viśvakarman.
And at the conclusion of the sacrifice, having paid homage to the best of the gods, he went to heaven; know this to be the reason why Hari became horse-faced.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By whom, in truth, has the entire earth been traversed by a single stride, such that it exists separately in every single pore? (29)
O one of great splendor, thousands of cosmic eggs are seen; since even the Veda does not know their limit, how indeed could there be a blow to the head? (30)
Vyāsa said: Listen, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, to this auspicious ancient narrative; indeed, neither among the moving nor the unmoving beings does anyone truly know the deeds of the Lord.
Once, the gods together with Indra went to the assembly of Brahmā, as did all those belonging to the world of earth and the rest, including both the stationary and the moving beings.
All the gods and the celestial sages (brahmarṣis) came to pay homage to the Grandfather (Brahmā); Viṣṇu also arrived there in the assembly for the purpose of consultation.
Then Brahmā, free from pride, spoke these words: "O gods, listen! Who among the three is the great cause?"
"O gods, let them speak the truth from amidst Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu. Having heard those words, the gods were filled with wonder.
Then the gods said, "O Suras, we do not know. Thereupon, the wife of Brahmā spoke to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods: "Tell me who among the three gods is the greatest. (36)
Viṣṇu said: "The three worlds have been deluded by the power of Viṣṇu’s māyā. Then Brahmā said this: "O Lord, you do not understand this. (37)
Neither is he deluded by the power of your illusion, nor is it otherwise; for the Lord, the sustainer of the world and the master of the universe, is beyond pride and intent on non-violence. (38)
"Enveloped by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, all these wretched ones do not know you as the eldest. Thereupon, Brahmā became enraged with fury, his face quivering.
He spoke these words in anger: "O Viṣṇu, listen to my words, [the consequences] of that mouth with which such speech was uttered in the assembly. (40)
"May that head fall quickly, indeed within a short time! Then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from everyone, including Indra and those led by the sages.
The best of the gods asked Brahmā for forgiveness regarding Viṣṇu; and Viṣṇu, having heard those words, said, "It shall be true, truly so."

Then Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods, possessed of great splendor, performed penance there in Dharmāraṇya by means of creating a sacred ford; Janārdana, having seen the horse-headed face, became Hayagrīva.
O highly fortunate one, O descendant of Bharata, he performed penance according to the prescribed rite; it was not possible for anyone else to do so, yet by his own self, he alone was satisfied.
Brahmā also, endowed with ascetic fervor, performed penance for three hundred years, remaining standing before Viṣṇu, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu.

The God of gods, the Lord of the universe, being pleased, has consumed [the sacrifice] for the sake of the ritual; O Brahmā, you possess liberation from the very beginning, yet my Māyā is difficult even for you to endure.
Then Brahmā, having obtained the boon, with a joyful heart, O Janārdana, spoke sweet words for the sake of the welfare of all.
Here there was a great field of merit that destroys sin; let this place consist of Brahmā and Viṣṇu—of this there is no doubt. (48)
O King, such is the majesty of that sacred ford; at that time, Hari, whose head was like a horse, indeed became possessed of an auspicious face through that very eastern countenance.
O King, at that time Kṛṣṇa was born with the beauty of ten million Kandarpas; even Brahmā, engaged in penance for three hundred divine years, [was moved].
In that place where Sāvitrī performed her rites, Viṣṇu’s Māyā could not prevail; yet by means of her own Māyā, she fashioned a fifth head for the tiger.
In the past, Viṣṇu granted a boon to Hara for the beautiful grove he had created in the Forest of Dharma, which had been cut down; having given him that boon, Viṣṇu then vanished from sight.
O subduer of enemies, having established the ritual there, he likewise established the holy ford named Mukteśa, the Tīrtha of Liberation belonging to the God Trilocana.
That best of gods also departed for his own abode, which is served by the gods; there, the deceased ancestors go to heaven when they have been fully satiated by the libations.

Bathing there yields the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, and drinking [the water] yields the fruit of gifting a cow; likewise, all sacred sites such as Puṣkara and all rivers such as the Gaṅgā are present there.

The deities and the ancestors likewise come here for the purpose of bathing; he who worships Mukteśa on the full moon day of Kārttika during the conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation [attains great merit].
Having bathed in the beautiful Devasaras and having bowed to the god Janārdana, the man who performs [this rite] with devotion is liberated from all sins.

Having enjoyed pleasures according to his desire, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu; [so too does] a woman without sons, one whose children are like crows, one whose offspring die at birth, or one whose progeny has perished.
When both husband and wife, having bathed well while wearing only a single garment, perform this according to the rules, it will surely destroy that fault which obstructs the birth of offspring. (59)
By the grace of Mokṣeśvara, one shall increase one's sons, grandsons, and progeny; with a single-minded heart, one should offer fruits accompanied by the Truth.
By placing [the offering] even in a bamboo vessel, a woman is liberated from her fault; and the gods, O King, obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Vidhātṛ, Hari, and Hara likewise perform supreme penance in Dharmāraṇya, having bathed in the Devasaras lake at the three junctions of the day.
There, Śambhu, the Lord of Liberation, was indeed installed by the gods; having performed the recitation (japa) along with its ancillaries there, one shall not become a suckling again.
Thus, O Great King, this sacred field is renowned throughout the three worlds; whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony there for the ancestors, endowed with faith, [attains great merit].

One may uplift seven lineages and a hundred and one members of one's family. The divine lake is exceedingly beautiful, endowed with various flowers, dark-hued with full-blown white lilies, and filled with diverse aquatic creatures. (65)
It is served by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, as well as by gods and humans; it is auspicious on all sides and frequented by Siddhas, Yakṣas, and sages.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O best of the twice-born, what is that famous lake like in that place? Describe its form and its nature exactly as they are.
Vyāsa said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly wise Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma! By the mere recitation of which one is surely liberated from all sins. (68)
O best of kings, its water was exceedingly clear, cool, and possessed a luster like the waters of the Gaṅgā; it was pure, sweet, and delicious.
It was vast and expansive, deep, a divine excavation, and enchanting; it was profound with its waves and the like, and filled with foam and whirlpools.
It was crowded with large fish, frogs, tortoises, and crocodiles; it was filled with conch shells, pearl oysters, and the like, and was beautifully adorned by royal swans.
It was filled with banyan and plakṣa trees and surrounded by aśvattha and āmra trees; it was frequented by ruddy geese, cranes, and ṭiṭṭibha birds.
It was beautifully adorned with lovely, fragrant, and pure lotus petals, served by all the twice-born, and graced by cranes and other birds.
O protector of the earth, it is frequented by gods, sages, brahmins, and mortals alike; it destroys suffering and annihilates all sins. (74)
O best of kings, that lake, which is without beginning or end and frequented by circles of perfected beings (siddhas), is always to be served through ritual bathing and other rites.
He who performs the *nīlotsarga* rite according to the prescribed rules on its bank shall have no ghosts (*preta*) in his family for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
And those who perform the gift of a maiden there according to the prescribed rite, O King, they shall dwell in the world of Brahmā until the dissolution of all beings.
A buffalo, a female domestic slave, a cow together with its calf, gold, knowledge, as well as land, chariots, elephants, and garments. (78)
He who gives there with faith enjoys an imperishable heaven; and he who recites the majesty of Devakhāta in the presence of Śiva obtains long life as well as happiness—of this there is no doubt. (79)
O Yudhiṣṭhira, whether it be a man or a woman who hears this wonder with devotion, there shall be welfare for their lineage even until the end of the kalpa.
All this has been narrated by me regarding the origin of Hayagrīva and the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha) for the removal of all sins. 81.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: For the destruction of the fear of the Rākṣasas, Daityas, Yakṣas, and birds, [the Lord] was worshipped by the lords of the quarters for the sake of the inhabitants of Dharmāraṇya. || 1 ||
Indeed, various powers have been established for men in many ways; tell me their locations, names, and forms according to their respective appearances.

Vyāsa said: Listen, O Pārtha, O mighty-armed one, O embodiment of dharma, O best of kings! The Śakti has indeed been established in her proper place by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva as the protectress of the lineage.
Śrīmātā is at Madārikā, and Śāntā is in the excellent city of Nandāpura; they stand in the four directions for the protection of the foremost brahmins.
O best of kings, they were joined by all the gods in their respective places; indeed, they all remained in the middle of the forest for the protection of the twice-born.
O great king, she became known by the auspicious name Sāvitrī; born of knowledge, she was established by the gods for the purpose of slaying the asuras.
The goddess Gātrāyī, Pakṣiṇī, Chatrajā, Dvāravāsinī, Śīhorī, she who is known as Cūṭā, as well as Pippalāśāpurī, and many others indeed have been established for protection from fear.
Indeed, she was established by the gods in the west, north, and south; she bore various weapons and was adorned with various ornaments.
Mounted upon various vehicles, she assumes diverse forms; she is endowed with manifold wrath and is the destroyer of manifold fears.
She should be established in her mother’s proper place, according to what is appropriate for each respective direction; she is mounted upon Garuḍa and holds a trident and a boon-granting gesture.
Mounted upon a lion, possessing a pure form and intoxicated by the drinking of wine, she of auspicious countenance shines with hands endowed with a sword, a shield, and arrows.
Clad in red garments, with full and elevated breasts, she possessed the luster of the rising sun’s orb, her eyes rolling with intoxication.
Thus, this great divine [image] was then established by the lords of Brahmā and Śiva for the protection of all living beings who dwell in the Temple of Truth. 13.
O tiger among kings, that goddess, when praised and worshipped together with [her consort], grants all desired objects of longing, O best of monarchs. (14)
To the west of Dharmāraṇya stands the auspicious Chatrajā; stationed there, endowed with some measure of power, she protects the brahmins. (15)
Assuming a terrifying form for the sake of slaying the Rākṣasas, they thus wielded weapons for the protection of the Brahmins from fear.
He created before him an excellent lake filled with water; O highly fortunate one, having performed his bath and the libation of water in this lake, [he proceeded].

All offerings, such as the giving of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and so forth, become truly inexhaustible; likewise, divine handfuls of water cast upon the ground, as well as incense, lamps, and other offerings, are always [inexhaustible]. || 18 ||
For us, neither disease nor the destruction of enemies causes affliction; one should further perform offerings of oblations and other rites there according to one's own ability. (19)
Enemies shall go to their destruction, wealth and grain shall increase, and joy shall be established, O King; such is the delightful portion of Śakti.
O Lord of the Earth, hear the majesty [of this] for the sake of protecting the twice-born: she is divine, wearing white garments and adorned with golden ornaments. (21)
Mounted upon a lion, possessing four hands, with the moon as her crest-ornament, adorned with strings of pearls, and having full, elevated breasts that are yellowish-white.
She has a rosary and a lion in her hands, and she holds a bowstring and a javelin; she bears an excellent stream of divine fragrance and is adorned with a celestial garland.
O King, the sattvic power, consisting of bliss, was established in that city from of old; one should indeed worship her with camphor, saffron, and sandalwood.
O King, for the pleasure of Bhavānī, one should feed [the goddess] with pure milk-rice (pāyasa) together with honey, clarified butter, and sugar, and likewise perform the worship of young maidens.
O best of kings, whatever is chanted, offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, or meditated upon there—all that becomes inexhaustible; of this there is no doubt.

O best of kings, in that place where there are three qualities, there will surely be a threefold increase for the practitioner, resulting in the attainment of wealth, wives, and other such things. (27)
For him there is no loss, nor disease, nor enemy, nor evil deed; his cows increase, and he becomes filled with wealth, grain, and other riches. (28)
He shall have no fear of a Śākinī, nor of a king or an enemy; he shall have no fear of disease either, and he shall be victorious everywhere. (29)
The fourteen branches of knowledge shine for him as if they were recited; like the sun, that man shines upon the earth, resting in bliss.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Establishment of Ānanda," in the Dharmāraṇya-māhātmya of the first half of the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 16.
Vyāsa said: O King, the goddess Śāntā, who possesses great power, was established in the south; she wears various garments and is adorned with a forest garland.
O great king, that [form] which destroys Madhu and Kaiṭabha is tāmasī; O best of kings, the consort of Śiva was indeed placed there by Viṣṇu.
And she herself is eight-armed, beautiful, dark as a rain cloud, and enchanting; the goddess wears black garments and is seated upon a tiger mount.
Clad in a leopard skin and adorned with divine ornaments, she is auspicious, bearing a bell, a trident, a rosary, and a water-pot.
The goddess, whose arms are adorned and who is saluted by all the gods, bestows wealth, grain, sons, and enjoyments upon her devotees. || 5 ||
One should worship with divine lotuses, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood; for that purpose, one should likewise honor the most excellent of the twice-born right there.
One should feed young maidens with various kinds of food with a spirit of devotion, and one should worship them with incense, lamps, beautiful fruits, and offerings such as wine.
With various divine meats, or else with those made from ground grains, and with other various grains, as well as with milk-rice (pāyasa) and meat-balls (vaṭaka).
With great concentration, one should worship with rice, kṛśara, and cakes, and right there with the recitation of hymns and charming praises of Śakti.
His enemies perish and he becomes victorious everywhere; in battle, in the royal court, and in gambling, he obtains the auspiciousness of victory. || 10 ||
O great king, that auspicious and peaceful Kulamātṛkā has been established; she is renowned as Śrīmātā—listen, O lord of the earth, to her majesty. (11)
O best of kings, the Great Power, the Mother of the Family, resides there; she is the Virgin Daughter of Brahmā, appointed by the Creator for the sake of protection.
That goddess is Sthānamātā, known by the name Śrīmātā; she is threefold in form and was created for the protection of the twice-born.
O King, that auspicious goddess, possessing a beautiful form, held a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), was adorned with ornaments of bells, and was endowed with a rosary of beads. 14.
She is the Virgin, the Primordial Mother, and the protector of one's station; she is the slayer of the Daityas, the bestower of desires, and the destroyer of great delusion. || 15 ||
And that goddess Kumārī, the daughter of Brahmā, is accessible through devotion; she wears red garments and is anointed with red sandalwood paste.
Adorned with red garlands, ten-armed, and five-faced, she is the sovereign of the gods; wearing the moon as her crest-jewel, she is the Mother, saluted by both gods and demons. (17)
Manifest in the form of Sarasvatī herself, she was created by Brahmā for the sake of protection; that highly meritorious Oṃkāra was fashioned by the Lord of Kāma.
Having been saluted by the ṛṣis, Siddhas, Yakṣas, gods, Pannagas, and humans, she grants them whatever they desire in their minds from her pair of feet.
And she indeed protected the established order for the welfare of the twice-born, just as a mother protects her own biological sons here with virtuous qualities.
Then the goddess Śrīmātā, the family deity, while protecting [the practitioner], shall constantly destroy all calamities when she is praised. (21)

Indeed, by the mere remembrance of the illustrious Mother, all obstacles are pacified; [she is to be invoked] at a wedding, at the investiture of the sacred thread, at the parting of the hair, and in every auspicious rite. (22)
In all ritual activities involving food offerings, Śrīmātā is always worshipped; just as one should begin [any rite] after having worshipped the god Laṃbodara. (23)
O King, for every auspicious rite, one should likewise worship Śrīmātā; furthermore, whatever food one offers there to the Brāhmaṇas, [it becomes inexhaustible]. (24)
Alternatively, O King, whatever is performed in mutual consultation should be reported; by failing to report it, one will encounter obstacles.

Therefore, having first offered it to her, one should then commence the ritual; for by her grace, every rite is indeed accomplished without obstacle. When the seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira have arrived, one should worship the daughter of Dharma.
O King, having had it inscribed on a golden plate or else having it fashioned out of silver, one should present an excellent sandal to Śrīmātā.
Having bathed and become pure with water mixed with sesame seeds and *āmalaka* fruits, [he should worship] with garments, flowers, and beautiful, charming silk cloths. || 28 ||
And one should smear [the image] with pure sandalwood, saffron, and vermilion, as well as with pastes mixed with camphor, agallochum, and musk.
With *karṇikāra*, *kahlāra*, and white and red *karavīra* flowers; with *campaka*, *ketakī*, and likewise with *japā* blossoms.

One should satisfy [the deity] with yakṣakardama paste, unbroken bilva leaves, palāśa and jasmine flowers, cakes made of black gram (māṣa), flour-cakes, boiled rice, dālī, and various collections of vegetables.

One should worship the Mother of the World preceded by incense, lamps, and other offerings; with that same intention, one should feed young maidens and Brahmins as well, O King, with milk-rice mixed with ghee and sugar.

One should satisfy them with cooked foods such as modakas and other delicacies with a spirit of devotion; when even a single twice-born man is thus satisfied, one enjoys the fruit of satisfying a thousand.
One should recite the hymn that slays the Daityas again and again; he who, with a one-pointed mind, praises the illustrious Mother [shall attain his goal]. (34)
When she has been bathed, worshipped, and praised, the Daughter of Dharma, being pleased, shall grant a boon and destroy all undesirable things. (35)
One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth becomes wealthy; one desiring a kingdom obtains a kingdom, and one desiring knowledge obtains that [knowledge]. (36)
One seeking prosperity obtains fortune, and one seeking a wife obtains her; through the grace of Sarasvatī, this happens—of this there is no doubt. (37)
And by the grace of Sarasvatī, a person eternally attains that supreme state which is difficult even for the gods to reach. (38)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Śrīmātā," in the Dharmāraṇya-māhātmya, within the first part of the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Rudra said: Listen, O Skanda of great wisdom, to this wonder that was performed by me. In Dharmāraṇya, there was a most wicked Daitya named Karṇāṭaka. || 1 ||
Having approached secretly, he created obstacles for the couple; seeing him, the people fled continuously out of fear of him.
O son, having abandoned their place, all the merchants, the Vāḍavas, and the others departed; this illustrious lady here has assumed the form of Mātaṅgī.
The Rākṣasa named Karṇāṭaka, the slayer of Brahmins, was killed; then all the Brahmins were indeed delighted by that deed.
Devoted merchants praised and worshipped her; every year they performed the auspicious worship of Śrīmātā. || 5 ||
O son, in all auspicious undertakings, one should first worship her; from that moment on, he shall encounter no obstacle.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who was that wicked great Daitya, and in which lineage was he born? What did he do, O dear one? Tell me everything, O observer of noble vows. (7)
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, I shall describe the exploits of Karṇāṭaka, who was difficult for even the gods and dānavas to withstand, being arrogant in his prowess.
Evil in deed and wicked in conduct, the mighty-armed Mahārāṣṭra conquered all the worlds and traveled back and forth throughout the three realms.
O King, having gone to where the gods and sages dwell, that great asura creates obstacles there, either through deceit or by force.
Out of fear of him, the gods in this world would not study the Vedas, nor would the Brahmins perform the worship of the twilight prayers and other rites. (11)
Neither ritual sacrifice nor the worship of the gods prevails there—not everywhere in every land, in every village, and in every city.
At every sacred ford (tīrtha) everywhere, the asura creates obstacles; however, he is simply unable to enter Dharmāraṇya.
Then, out of fear and due to his lack of power before the illustrious Mother, the Dānava became despondent, reflecting: "By what means can I go back to that very place? || 14 ||
"How indeed shall I create an obstacle for these great-souled Brahmins, who are engaged in the study of the Vedas and presiding over the ritual acts of the sacrifice? (15)
O King, upon hearing from afar that sound produced by the study of the Vedas, that Dānava trembled like an elephant struck by a thunderbolt. || 16 ||
He released his breaths out of rage, grinding his teeth against each other; biting his own lips, he crushed both his hands together.
O noble one, he wanders here and there like a madman, just as a human being does when afflicted by the disorder of a deranged humoral combination.
In that very same way, the terrible Dānava, having approached the vicinity of Dharmāraṇya, wandered about and scorched [the area], filled with fear even from afar. || 19 ||
Having assumed the form of a twice-born Brahmin at the time of their wedding, the invincible one arrived there and carried off that excellent couple.
That lowest of asuras leapt from the surface of the earth into the sky; that wicked one took delight himself in his malice, due to the inherent nature of his species.
And thus, having repeatedly taken the couple from Dharmāraṇya, he committed a sin that was unbearable even for the gods. || 22 ||
That wicked one constantly creates obstacles for couples on earth, performing most terrible deeds in that excellent city.
Thereupon, all the twice-born, being agitated, fled in the ten directions; all those gods of the earth departed, abandoning that charming place.
O best of kings, at that time, wherever there was a great sacred ford (tīrtha), the twice-born went there; consequently, that city became deserted.
There, neither the study of the Vedas nor the performance of sacrifice proceeds; men dwell there, afflicted by the fear of the Karṇāṭas. || 26 ||
Then, O King, all the twice-born and the highly illustrious merchants gathered together in one place to deliberate on what was appropriate.
The best of the twice-born were deliberating upon the means for the slaying of Karṇāṭa; while they were thus reflecting, by divine providence, an incorporeal voice arose.
Worship the illustrious Mother, who removes all suffering, who brings about the destruction of all demons, and who annihilates all calamities.
Having heard that, all the Vāḍavas, their eyes agitated with joy, approached Śrīmātā and took an excellent offering.
Honey, milk, curd, ghee, and sugar—these five streams—as well as incense, a lamp, sandalwood, and flowers. (31)
O King, having taken various fruits, the brahmins also took diverse kinds of grain, O monarch, along with cooked rice and cakes soaked in ghee.
Cooked barley, fried cakes, milk-rice mixed with ghee, sohalikās, dīpikās, and likewise moist fried cakes. || 33 ||
There, cakes resembling the orb of the moon were prepared, smeared with mustard seeds and provided with nine holes.
Having performed the ceremonial bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and scented water, they gratified the Goddess with incense, lamps, and food offerings.
O King, Śrīmātā, the destroyer of all calamities, was propitiated with lustration rites accompanied by camphor, flowers, lamps, and excellent sandalwood.
Śrīmātā, the Mother of the World, Brāhmī, the gentle one, the bestower of boons—assuming these three forms, she protects the three worlds. (37)

O you whose nature is dharma, they protect the temple of truth in the form of the three Vedas; those best of the twice-born have assembled here, having conquered their senses and mastered their selves. (38)

Having honored their mother with all those offerings, such as sandalwood paste and other gifts, they satisfied her; then, standing before the daughter of Brahmā with single-minded devotion, they began to offer praise through the actions of speech, mind, and body. (39)

The Brahmins said: Salutations to you, O daughter of Brahmā; salutations to you, O observer of celibacy. Salutations to you, O Mother of the worlds; salutations to you, O omnipresent one, forever. (40)
You are hunger and sleep, you are thirst, as well as anger, lethargy, and the rest; you are peace and you are passion, and you are likewise Jaya and Vijaya.
O Sovereign of the Gods, you have been sought for refuge by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others; you are established as Sāvitrī, Śrī, and Umā, and you are the Mother.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lords of the gods are established upon your support; salutations to you, O Mother of the World, whose very nature is fortitude and nourishment.

O Goddess, you are Rati, Krodhā, Mahāmāyā, Chāyā, and she whose nature is light; you are the one who effects creation, preservation, and destruction, and you are always the bestower of cause and effect.
Earth, fire, air, water, and space—salutations to you, O Mahāvidyā, who are composed of supreme knowledge, O sinless one! 45.
O you who are the syllable Hrīṃ, you are the form of the gods; O you of great splendor, you are the syllable Klīṃ! You are the beginning, the middle, and the end; protect us from this great fear.
For this wicked-souled Daitya, a great sinner, is now harassing us; you alone are our family deity, appearing as our protection. 47.
Save us, save us, O Great Goddess! Protect us, protect us, O Maheśvarī! Slay, slay the wicked Dānava who creates obstacles for the twice-born! 48.
Thus praised then by the twice-born, the goddess Mahāmāyā, for the sake of slaying Karṇāṭa and for the welfare of the twice-born, became manifest there and said, "Choose a boon."
Śrīmātā said: "By whom indeed have the brahmins been terrified, and by whom have they been further agitated? Enraged by that, I shall lead those brahmins to the abode of Yama."
"Know that the man whose life has been exhausted is he by whom you have been oppressed; I shall give him to the twice-born—please tell me what you desire. (51)
O Brahmins, out of devotion to you, I shall indeed do so; there is no doubt in this matter. || 52 ||
The twice-born said: "A most fierce Dānava named Karṇāṭa, arrogant with pride, constantly creates obstacles for those who dwell in Satyamandira. (53)

O high-minded one, that hateful man constantly hates those brahmins who are devoted to truth and character and are intent on the study of the Vedas; O one of great splendor, slay this wicked hater of the Vedas!
Vyāsa said: Having said "So be it," that goddess, the family deity, laughed and reflected upon a means for his destruction in order to protect her devotees.
Then, O best of kings, Śrīmātā became overcome with anger; knitting her brows in rage, she made her eyes red at the corners.
Possessed by great rage, O Bhārata, she was like a blazing fire, emitting great flames from her mouth, eyes, nose, and ears.
Born from that splendor was Mātaṅgī, who can assume any form at will; she is Kālī, with handsome arms and a beautiful face, radiant with a countenance difficult to behold. (58)
Wearing red garlands and garments, her eyes rolling with intoxication, Śrīmātā then took refuge near a banyan tree.
That auspicious and most beautiful Mother has eighteen arms; the Goddess holds a bow and arrows, and she bears a sword and a shield.
He bore an axe, a razor, a trident, a drinking vessel, a mace, a serpent, an iron club, a Pināka bow, and a noose.
O King, she held a rosary and carried a jar of liquor; likewise, she bore a fierce spear, a pestle, a knife, and a skull-bowl.
Carrying a thorn-laden jujube tree, the large-faced one arrived; there occurred a great, tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end.
O best of kings, [this occurred] with Mātaṅgī together with the Dānava Karṇāṭa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O knower of dharma, O noble one, tell me how that battle took place and how it concluded; who indeed was victorious? Tell me this."
Vyāsa said: Listen, O Indra among kings, to what once occurred in the battle with the Daityas; I shall relate all of that exactly as it happened in the past.
O best of kings, O Bhārata, those Brahmins and merchants who had lost their wives arrived at Dharmāraṇya when the month of Caitra had arrived.
Those brahmins of firm vows married Gaurī, having recognized that place as their own auspicious abode and likewise as the most excellent king of holy fords (tīrtharāja).

O highly wise one, those best of the twice-born gathered there to perform the wedding; at that great festival, ten million maidens were assembled in one place in Dharmāraṇya—I tell you the truth, the absolute truth. (69)
On the fourth night, during the latter part of the night, they established the fire within; having offered a seat to the Brahman priest and having circumambulated the fire from left to right.
Then, having prepared the *sthālīpāka* offering and having constructed auspicious altars (*vedī*), each four cubits in size, complete with water-jars and provided with serpent-nooses (*nāgapāśa*).
Then the twice-born ones consecrated them with auspicious Vedic mantras, having served the wandering couple as was appropriate.
Accompanied by Brahmā, those Vāḍavas there were greatly delighted and produced the resonance of the Vedas, made to ring out with loud voices.
By that great sound, the entire sky was filled. Hearing that Vedic resonance uttered by the twice-born, the terrible Dānava [was moved].
Deprived of his senses, he quickly leapt from his seat along with his army; as all his servants and others ran after him, he spoke to them. (75)
"Listen, from where has this sound of the Vāḍavas arisen? Hearing those words of his, the Daityas went there with great haste.
With their minds utterly bewildered, they all ran hither and thither; some went to Dharmāraṇya, where they saw certain twice-born brahmins.
O King, at the time of the wedding, reciting the Vedic hymns, they reported everything to the wicked-souled Karṇāṭa.
Hearing that, O noble King, the hater of brahmins, his eyes copper-red with rage and filled with fury, rushed toward where that couple was.
Then, O King, relying on the earth and employing his demonic illusion, that Rākṣasa carried off the royal couple, who were adorned with all their ornaments.
Then all those Brāhmaṇas, having gathered together, raised a tumultuous roar and cried out, "Save us! Save us! to the Mistress of the World.
Having heard that, Mātaṅgī, the mother of all beings and sovereign of the world, bearing her excellent trident, let out a lion’s roar.
Then a battle commenced between the Goddess and Karṇāṭa, while the sages, the merchants, and the twice-born looked on.
As they watched that tumultuous and hair-raising battle for non-existence, Mātaṅgī cut down her enemy, who was overwhelmed by intoxication, with her weapons.
Then that Daitya struck her in the chest with a single arrow, and she too, struck by his trident, fell into a swoon.
That Asura also struck the Goddess with his fists, but he was then quickly bound by the Goddess with the serpent-noose.
Then that very Daitya took up the Garuḍa weapon; he, however, discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon to bring down the arrow.
Thus, drawing each other toward one another and fighting with a desire for victory, the preeminent Daitya then took up an iron club.
Enraged at Mātaṅgī, the slayer of enemy heroes struck her; the goddess, filled with wrath, crushed the Dānava with blows from her fists.
By that blow of the fist, he fell down unconscious; then, rising suddenly and joyfully grasping a spear in his hand, [he stood up]. (90)
The Dānava hurled a śataghnī at her, but that auspicious-faced goddess Mātaṅgī cut the spear asunder. || 91 ||
Thus that fair-complexioned woman laughed loudly as she hurled a *śataghnī* weapon resembling a thunderbolt; in this manner, they tormented one another with floods of various weapons.
Then, struck in the heart by the trident, he fell down; however, that Daitya, regaining consciousness, employed his Rākṣasa illusion.
While they were looking on, the great asura became invisible; then the goddess drank the beverage and laughed with her eyes reddened.
That goddess pervades all that exists in the three worlds, including both the moving and the unmoving.
"Where is Pāśyastī? she asked. "Tell me now," he replied. "O wicked Karṇāṭaka, come quickly and fight! (96)
Then there occurred a great battle, fierce and terrifying; the exceedingly powerful goddess drank the *maireya* liquor for the sake of slaughter.
Then Mātaṅgī, enraged, cast the Dānava into her mouth; yet even from there, the fierce Dānava emerged through the cavity of her nostril.
That Daitya Karṇāṭa, filled with intoxication, fought once more; then the goddess Mātaṅgī, herself filled with intoxication, became enraged.
Having ground it with my teeth and chewed it again and again, I have properly devoured a human corpse—a skeleton filled with marrow, flesh, and other such things. (100)
Having placed the asura, whose hair was bristling with claws, into his belly, he blocked the mouth with one hand and the nose with the other.
Then the mighty Daitya emerged through the opening of the ear; thereupon, that Great Goddess bestowed upon him a name on this earth.
The wise know that he who was born from the cavity of Karna's ear is Karṇāṭa; indeed, this Daitya, arrogant in his strength, has returned for the sake of battle once again.
The Asura stood there in battle, roaring and equipped with weapons; seeing that Daitya who was difficult to withstand, he reflected upon him again and again.
O descendant of Bharata, Mātaṅgī indeed reflected upon the means of his destruction; while the goddess Mātaṅgī, filled with passion, was thus reflecting, (verse 5).
Assuming a form created by illusion, the flower-armed god of love became a fair-complexioned Karṇāṭaka youth, sixteen years of age, with eyes like lotus petals.
Approaching the goddess, he said, "O beautiful one, choose me as your husband."
