The illustrious one said: "O King of the Daityas, what you have spoken is excellent and well-ascertained; there is no other equal to you in beauty within the three worlds. (8)
O best of Asuras, have you heard the vow I made previously? My younger sister, the auspicious Śyāmā, desires to be married, O Brāhmaṇa.
O Daitya, she was indeed established by my father for the protection of the twice-born; she alone, with her dark-limbed form, brings benefit to all the worlds. (110)
"Having said, 'No one shall choose a maiden,' she was thus established [in her vow]. Tell me quickly how there may be welfare for you; having heard it, I shall explain the auspicious means. (11)
"O Lord of Daityas, I have a sister named Śyāmalā who is unmarried; she has been protected for your sake, O hero, so marry her according to the ancient custom."
O Mahāvīra, that father will surely give this beautiful woman to you; go, for Śyāmalā, filled with anger, must indeed be won over.
Then the wicked-souled Karṇāṭaka, filled with rage, seized a powerful spear and rushed forward, desiring the death of Śyāmalā.
Seeing the Asura arrived, the high-minded Śyāmalā understood the supreme intention of that evil-minded one regarding her marriage. || 15 ||
O King, a great battle then took place there between Śyāmalā and the chief of the Asuras; it was tumultuous on the earth for three months.
O King, on the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, at the time of midday in the great forest of Dharmāraṇya, the one named Karṇāṭa was struck down.
Kārṇāṭi fell there where he had been struck down by the Goddess; his excellent head, resembling a mountain peak, fell.
The entire earth, along with its oceans, islands, and mountains, trembled; then those brahmins, filled with joy, cried out, "Victory to the Mother!"
The lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced, performing songs and auspicious dances while celebrating that festival.
With milk-rice, fried cakes, and likewise with offerings of sweetmeats, they praised him with auspicious words in that excellent place, Moṭeraka.
That illustrious goddess, when worshipped, bestows sons, happiness, and wealth; and when a great festival has arrived, the worship of Mātaṅgī is beneficial.
Those who, having installed [the image], worship it for the sake of attaining wealth, sons, and their goals, shall obtain happiness, fame, long life, glory, and merit. || 23 ||
Diseases go to destruction, and the planets, beginning with the Sun, become auspicious; ghosts, vetālas, śākinīs, jambhas, and others do not cause affliction.
In that manner, no affliction from ghosts or other such beings arose anywhere; consequently, the brahmins were overjoyed and prepared to offer praise. (25)
Then, filled with great joy, he praised Śrīmātā, the Śaktis, Mātaṅgī, and the Great Goddess Śyāmalā.
The Brahmins said: "O Mother, remain thus as our protector in this place for the sake of the welfare of married couples, so that the twice-born may not be agitated. (27)
Mātaṅgī said: "O highly fortunate ones, O twice-born, I am pleased with you by this hymn of praise; choose a boon that is desired by your hearts. (28)
The Brāhmaṇas said: "O Goddess, we shall offer whatever oblation is in your mind; for the sake of protecting us, husband and wife, remain steadfast. (29)

The Goddess said: "Let all the twice-born be at ease, and no affliction shall come upon them; while I am present, the Daityas and other Rākṣasas, however difficult they may be to overcome, [shall have no power]. (130)
Śākinīs, bhūtas, pretas, and likewise the grahas such as Jambha; indeed, the grahas beginning with Śākinī, as well as serpents, tigers, and the like. (131)
While I remain established in my teaching, they shall not cause affliction anywhere; for whoever performs a great festival when a marriage has arrived, [there shall be no harm]. (32)
Indeed, for the sake of the welfare of husband and wife, a man should always worship me; I shall undoubtedly destroy all his afflictions. (33)

Neither mental anxieties nor physical ailments, neither afflictions nor agitation shall exist; one always attains supreme happiness, fame, merit, and wealth. For such a person there is no untimely death, nor any disorders of wind, bile, and so forth. (34)
The Brahmins said: "By what rite is worship performed? What should the food offering (naivedya) be like? And what kind of incense (dhūpa), O Mother? How should one arrange the worship? (35)
The Goddess said: "O Brahmins, listen to my words: whoever, having written [this] upon a golden leaf, should worship it, shall become a long-lived couple. (36)
Alternatively, on a silver plate or again on a bronze plate, one should draw the eighteen-armed goddess, anointed with sandalwood paste.
In his hand, he should cause him to hold a winnowing basket with arrows, a dog, and again a supreme lotus; as well as a single pair of shears, a quiver, and bows.
A shield, a noose, a mallet, a bell-metal gong, and likewise a javelin; a conch, a discus, a bright mace, a pestle, and a splendid iron club.
The Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśvarī) is endowed with these eighteen weapons: the khaṭvāṅga, the jujube fruit, and the beautiful goad.
One should draw the goddess adorned with earrings, her arms decorated with anklets, and endowed with armlets, pearl ornaments, lotuses, and garlands of severed heads.
Having drawn Bhuvaneśvarī, encircled by the letters of the alphabet, adorned with a ring, and enriched with the splendor of various ornaments; 42.
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of consecration, one should worship her who is renowned as Mātaṅgī with delightful sandalwood paste and flowers. (43)
Having brought yakṣakardama, the wise one should worship Mātaṅgī; he should kindle an auspicious lamp with seven wicks using ghee.
Then one should incense [the deity] with fragrant guggulu mixed with clarified butter; and the couple should offer the arghya water using a bright coconut.
One should perform four very beautiful circumambulations, having covered [the image] with a fine cloth and having placed the couple in front.
Having performed the sprinkling ritual and having consumed the excellent honey-wine (mādhvīka) of Mātaṅgī, the wise man should worship Mātaṅgī with the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
Likewise, auspicious women born of the Mātaṅgī lineage should dance before the couple for the sake of pacifying all calamities. (48)
The auspicious food offering consists of eighteen varieties of diverse foods: white fried cakes (vaṭakas), flour cakes (apūpikas), and milk mixed with sugar. (49)
Ballākara, vara, yūpā, kṣiptakulmāṣaka, sohālikā, bhinnavaṭā, lāpsikā, and padmacūrṇaka. || 150 ||
In that [month], one should prepare pure and delightful *parpaṭas*, *śālakas*, and so forth, along with *śaiveyas* and *vimalas*, as a filling for that month. (51)
The husband and wife should prepare well-prepared rājamāṣa beans there, and they should also make delightful pheṇikās and ropikās.
One should prepare these other eighteen cooked foods, combined with clarified butter and sugar, and accompanied by various collections of vegetables.
One should keep a vigil at night and worship a married woman; furthermore, the husband and wife should both gaze upon their own faces reflected in clarified butter (ājya).
Indeed, one should perform this for one another to pacify calamities. Thus has this auspicious worship of Mātaṅgī been described by me. (55)
For that fool who does not worship her, she brings about the death of the couple, as well as the loss of wealth and great terror. (56)
One perceives affliction, disease, and likewise the outbreak of fire; for this reason, O Brahmins, the wise man should worship Mātaṅgī. (57)
And for all married couples, for the twice-born, and for merchants, the Great Goddess always ensures that they remain free from obstacles.
When they had replied, "So be it," he spoke these words again: "O Brahmins, all of you, listen to the great festival beginning with the marriage."
Having heard my words, perform the rite accordingly when the time for marriage has arrived, for the sake of the happiness of the couple. (160)
To ensure freedom from obstacles, one should apply collyrium to the eyes along with one's own servants and kinsmen in every respect.
O Brahmins, one should fashion from the middle of the eyebrows a shape resembling a half-moon, and above that, one should place a beautiful bindu.
When this is done, O Brahmins, peace is attained and not otherwise. This tilaka in the shape of a half-moon increases one's progeny; it removes all obstacles and destroys all misfortune and disease.
Vyāsa said: Then, O lord of men, all the subjects became peaceful in Dharmāraṇya through the grace of the goddess Mātaṅgī in Satyamandira.
Then, with joyful hearts, those brahmins worshipped the daughter of Vidhi; and they established that the worship of Mātaṅgī should be performed year after year.
On the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, through offerings of various kinds of food and edibles, the birth of Karṇāṭa occurred once again upon the earth.
Out of fear, he then abandoned that place and went toward the south; as he was departing, the Daitya, appearing in the form of consumption (yakṣman), spoke.
"Listen, O all you twice-born ones dwelling in Dharmāraṇya, and you merchants as well; let this great word of mine be observed. (68)
Indeed, in the month of Māgha, for my pleasure and for the sake of constant freedom from obstacles on earth, [one should worship] with three-petaled grains and especially with radishes. || 69 ||
Or a man of restrained vows may perform [this rite] with sesame oil; indeed, he should eat but one meal daily without interruption for the propitiation of Yakṣman. (170)
In this world, whether one is a child, a youth, or even an old man, this supreme vow for the cure of consumption (yakṣman) should always be performed year after year. (71)
In whatever house there are [images] having the form of human beings, they should always be devoted to a single meal and perform the invocation for that [house]. 72.
For the sake of a child, the mother performs an excellent vow; or likewise, the father or even a brother may perform the vow for that purpose. (73)
She shall have no fear anywhere, nor disease, nor bondage; for the sake of her husband, a woman may act even when she is incapable, and likewise by other means.
Having thus instructed him and abandoned Satyamandira, that Daitya went toward the southern direction to the excellent shore of the ocean.
Having obtained a vast territory, that king Karṇāṭa established that excellent land under his own name.
O King, that Karṇāṭa country, in which all things—wealth, grain, and many other riches—are found in abundance, has long remained surrounding him. (77)
O best of men, those who listen to or cause others to hear this meritorious discourse on the Dharmāraṇya and the majesty of Śrīmātā—[they attain the highest state]. (78)

In their families, misfortune never arises at any time; the childless obtain sons, and those lacking wealth obtain prosperity, as well as long life, health, and sovereignty, through the grace of the Mother Śrī. (179)
Vyāsa said: Having bathed in Indrasaras and beheld the auspicious Indreśvara Śiva, a person is liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By whom was that Tīrtha, the most excellent of all the excellent, first created? O Blessed One, best of the twice-born, describe it to me exactly as it is.
Vyāsa said: O great king, Indra himself performed a most difficult penance there for a hundred years in the northern direction of the village.
O Bhārata, with his arm raised and his great splendor blazing, he stood facing the sun, performing the most terrible *śivoddeśa* rite with only one thumb.
For the removal of whatever sin was incurred from the slaying of Vṛtra, he became one-pointed and self-restrained, devoted to the worship of Śiva. || 5 ||
Then Śambhu, the moon-crested Lord, was gratified by that asceticism; he arrived there, matted-haired, with ashes on his body, and having the bull as his emblem.
He carries a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), has five faces, ten arms, and three eyes; he bears the Gaṅgā, is mounted upon a bull, and is surrounded by spirits, ghosts, and other beings.
Then the Lord, the best of gods—highly pleased, compassionate, and the bestower of boons—spoke these words to Indra with a joyful mind: || 8 ||
Hara said: "O God, whatever you request, that I shall grant to you."
Indra said: "If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, O Maheśvara, ocean of compassion; for the sin of killing a Brahmin, O God, constantly torments me. (10)
O Supreme among Gods, O All-pervading Lord, destroy that sin born from the slaying of the demon Vṛtra, which constantly brings me suffering. (11)
Hara said: "O Lord of the Gods, in Dharmāraṇya, the sin of killing a Brahmin shall not afflict one; nor the slaughter of cows, of the twice-born, or even of children and women. (12)
"O Lord of the Gods, by my word, and by the words of Brahmā, Keśava, and Yama, O Jiṣṇu, this slaughter shall certainly not remain here. Having entered, O Great King, perform your ablutions here. (13)
Indra said: "O Maheśvara, ocean of compassion, if you are pleased with me, O Śaṅkara, Mahādeva, then remain established here under my name. (14)
Having said "So be it," the Great God Hara, being well-pleased, then revealed right there the linga that destroys all sins.
Having raised [him] from the back of the tortoise by means of his own yoga, Śambhu remained right there as Śrīkaṇṭha; so know those who understand the three periods of time.
O King, at that time in the forest, Indreśvara remained there in the presence of the king of the gods, who was terrified by the slaying of Vṛtra. || 17 ||
O Indra among kings, for the sake of purifying all sins and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, one should always worship Indreśvara with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
And a person who worships with devotion on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, especially in the month of Māgha, is liberated from all sins.
For the sake of purifying all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva; and that mortal who performs the release of a dark bull in front of it [the image], [attains the same]. || 20 ||
He who indeed performs the recitation of the Sāṅga Rudra on the fourteenth day rescues seven lineages and one hundred and one members of his family.
One whose self is purified of all evil attains the supreme state. || 22 ||
Having fashioned a golden eye, adorned in the center with jewels, he who gives it to the twice-born at the excellent Indratīrtha likewise [attains great merit].
Blindness shall not befall him for sixty births; perpetual clarity arises in his eyes. Furthermore, other great diseases likewise depart upon bathing before that [deity]. (24)
Even with a single act of worship, one is not liberated from all diseases; however, that man who bathes in the pool and offers libations to the ancestors [attains such liberation].
O King, his ancestors and grandfathers are always satisfied—even those embodied beings who have been seized by great diseases such as leprosy and the like. (26)
Merely by bathing, those men who have fallen into the distress of fever and other ailments become completely purified and attain divine bodies for their own welfare. (27)
By merely bathing, they become completely purified and attain divine bodies; having bathed, one should worship the God and is thereby released from the bondage of fever.
Fever that recurs every day, every two days, every four days, or every third day; the affliction of irregular fever, and fever occurring after a month or a fortnight. (29)
And by the grace of Indreśvara, [the fever] is destroyed; there is no doubt in this matter. One truly becomes free from fever, O King; this is the truth, the absolute truth. (30)

A barren woman, an unfortunate woman, one who has borne only a single child, one whose offspring have died, one whose children die at birth, or one who is greatly wicked—by bathing in the pool before Śiva and worshipping with a single-minded focus, she becomes pure by that very act of bathing alone. || 31 ||
Having thus granted many such boons, O Pārtha, the wielder of the Pināka bow departed for his own city, being attended by gods and asuras.
Then Śakra, endowed with great splendor, departed indeed toward his own city; by Jayanta as well, an excellent liṅga was installed right there.
Hara, the Lord of the Gods, being pleased with Jayanta and constantly praised at that liṅga, would come there thrice daily accompanied by his son for the purpose of worship.
O mighty-armed one, he indeed comes, having abandoned his own abode; all this has been fully explained, which bestows all happiness. (35)
O King of kings, by worshipping Jayaṃteśa, one obtains that very same merit which comes from Indreśvara; this is the truth, the absolute truth, there is no doubt.
O great king, having bathed in the pool and worshipped with a one-pointed mind, one whose soul is purified of all sins is glorified in the world of Indra. (37)
The man who hears this with devotion is liberated from all sins; through the grace of Jayanteśa, he attains all his desires.
Vyāsa said: Hereafter I shall describe the unsurpassed Śivatīrtha, where that Lord Śaṅkara took on birth once again.
O illustrious one, Śaṅkara, the three-eyed lord of the gods, was pinned down by Girijā and cast upon the surface of the earth.
Staggering and becoming deluded, he did not distinguish between day and night; the three-eyed one became as if paralyzed, [confused] regarding males, females, and neuters.
When he was thus pinned down by Pārvatī, it was as if the end of the eon had arrived; she then suddenly performed that act of pinning him.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This speech which you have uttered is truly incomparable and wonderful, for he who is always the preceptor of all the gods and of the yogins as well— (5)
Why was Śiva pinned down by Pārvatī, and how did he lose his composure? Tell me the reason for that, for my curiosity is indeed great.
Vyāsa said: O King, various multitudes of mantras born from the Atharvaṇa Upaveda were revealed by Śaṅkara in the presence of Pārvatī, O great king.
Śākinī, Ḍākinī, Kākinī, Hākinī, as well as Ekinī and Lākinī—these six varieties are proclaimed therein.
O best of kings, having extracted the seeds from those [plants], a single-stringed garland was made; and this was indeed described by Śambhu in the presence of Pārvatī.
O sinless one, when that extraction of the mantra has been performed by those very [eight], that extremely wicked Śākinī will bring about the ruin of women.

Śrī Pārvatī said: O Lord, these six divisions have indeed been revealed by you. O Lord, the sixfold powers are the Agamyā and Yogamālinī; tell me how all this that has been described as sixfold was made into a single peak-syllable (kūṭa) by you alone.
Śrī Mahādeva said: O Great Goddess, it is unmanifest to gods, asuras, and humans.
Pārvatī said: Salutations to you who possess all forms; salutations to you whose banner is the bull. O Lord of matted hair, salutations to you; O Blue-throated One, salutations be to you. (13)
"O ocean of mercy, salutations to you; salutations to you who take the form of Time! With these many gentle words, [they addressed] the treasure-house of compassion. (14)
Having propitiated her and prostrated like a staff, the daughter of the mountain grasped her pair of feet; he, being supremely compassionate, spoke to her.
"For what purpose are you being praised, O blessed lady? Let that which is desired in your mind be requested. (16)
Pārvatī said: If I am dear to you, then explain in full detail the practice of withdrawal (samāhāra) along with meditation (samyāna), entirely and without any doubt.
Śrī Rudra said: "O Goddess, you must not reveal the fruit arising from this collection. I shall declare the entire truth, beginning indeed with the peak of mantras."

O fair-faced one, the seed-syllable of Māyā is indeed common to all the peak-syllables (kūṭas); it consists of the middle letter of all [the syllables], adorned with the Bindu and the letter Ā. || 19 ||

The seed-syllable of fire (ra) together with wind (ya), combined with the seed-syllable of the tortoise (la); this is the seed-syllable born of the Sun (sūrya), which always arises from the seed-syllable of Śakti (hrīṃ). || 20 ||

This is considered the peak-syllable (kūṭa) and the first seed-syllable; the second belongs to the All-pervading Lord (Vibhu), and the third is the seed-syllable of Fire conjoined with the Bindu and the Moon.
The fourth is joined with the remainder; likewise, the fifth is the seed-syllable of Brahmā and the sage, while the sixth is the seed-syllable of Kāla and the seed-syllable of Earth.
In the seventh and eighth [sections], the external [mantra] is combined with Nṛsiṃha; in the ninth, the second and first [mantras]; and in the tenth, the eight-fold peak (aṣṭakūṭaka).
O excellent wanderer, the seed-mantra of those two is reversed in the Rudrākṣa; it is joined with the earth-seed (la) for the sake of the dative case in the fourteenth [syllable]. || 24 ||
O King, when some of the remaining syllables were protected by Menakā’s daughter, Śiva’s wife then fell to the earth.
There, the destroyer of Tripura, smiling, comforted her: "O blessed lady, because you have fallen [in love] with Rāma, you shall possess the power of a Jambū tree."
In killing, bewildering, subjugating, attracting, and agitating—whatever one truly desires, that very thing shall certainly be accomplished. (27)
Having heard this, the goddess, evil-minded yet possessing a pure smile, [was addressed]; then Śambhu spoke to those heroes who remained as a deceptive remnant.
And the ocean of compassion said: "Accomplish it according to the prescribed rites; for Hara has gone from Kailāsa to Dharmāraṇya with great haste. (29)
Having learned this, O best of kings, the goddess went to that place where the bull-bannered god was; at that very moment, he fell to the ground in Dharmāraṇya.
Matted locks, the moon, serpents, the trident, the bull, and other weapons.
A garland of shaven heads, a loincloth, and indeed a skull-bowl belong to Brahmā.
The hosts of bhūtas and pretas fled everywhere in the ten directions; and the Lord Maheśvara, perceiving himself to be unconscious, [reflected]. || 32 ||
Furthermore, the groups born from sweat, such as the Kūṭas and others, having produced the five Kūṭas, [bestowed them] upon that Ādhamūlin.
O Great King, those practitioners were devoted to recitation and burnt offerings; they all sat upon the corpses of the deceased, stationed atop the Kālakūṭa poison.
They spoke of themselves as that by which liberation from the wielder of the Pināka bow [Śiva] might be attained; thereupon Gaurī was overcome with distress, distressed by the fear of the fire.
Śiva was honored by them, while Gaurī, feeling bashful, cast her face downward; remaining there, she performed penance, carrying out the command of Śaṅkara.

Having practiced the austerity of the five fires and performed the inhalation of smoke while facing downwards, she praised him with cryptic syllables; by those means, the Bull-bannered Lord was gratified.
O King, this sacred field on earth destroys sins and grants all desires; the auspicious Devamajjanaka shines resplendent in this very place. (38)
O King, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, by bathing and drinking [the water] there, one is liberated from all sins.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods and observed a fast according to the prescribed rules, Śākinīs, Ḍākinīs, Vetālas, Pitṛs, and Grahas [are propitiated]. (40)

The planets and the sacred hearths are not afflicted; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one! By performing the recitation of the Rudra-mantra there along with its ancillaries, one is liberated from sins.
The three kinds of diseases perish—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O King! All this has been declared by me; now hear about the bathing of the deity.
By performing thousands of horse-sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, a man who hears this or causes it to be heard obtains that same fruit. (43)
One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth shall obtain wealth; he obtains long life, health, and sovereignty—of this there is no doubt. (44)
O King, whatever threefold sin has been produced by mind, speech, and body—all that goes to destruction through remembrance and recitation.
O child, one who hears this greatness—which brings merit, fame, and long life, and bestows a succession of happiness—shall be endowed with all forms of well-being.
O King, whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, whatever fruit results from all acts of charity, and whatever merit arises from all sacrifices—that is obtained by hearing this.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of Dharākṣetra," in the Dharmāraṇya-māhātmya of the first part of the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: And by her, O King, the family deities were produced from her own body.
Bhaṭṭārikī, Tathāchatrā, Ovikā, and likewise Jñānajā. || 1 ||
Bhadrakālī (5), Māheśī (6), Siṃhorī (7), and Dhanamardanī (8).
Gātrā (9), Śāntā (10), Śeṣadevī (11), Vārāhī (12), and Bhadrayoginī (13). || 2 ||
Yogeśvarī (14), Mohalajjā (15), Kuleśī (16), and Śakulācitā (17).
Tāraṇī (18), Vanakānaṃdā (19), Cāmuṇḍā (20), and Sureśvarī (21). || 3 ||

Beginning with Dārabhaṭṭārikā and so forth, there are one hundred individual [deities]; furthermore, auspicious Śaktis endowed with various forms have arisen therein. Hereafter, I shall proclaim the most excellent deities.

Aupamanyava-gotra, Pravara 3; Gotra-devī Gātrā, Vasiṣṭha 1, Bharadvāja 2, Indrapramadaka Vyāsaga. Śaga-gotra, Gotra-devī Jñānajā 2, Pravara 3: Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, Raibhya. Māṇḍavya-sagotra 3, Gotra-born Dārabhadārikā 3, Pravara 5: Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, Jamadagni. Kuśika-sagotra, Born-Araṇī 6, Mahābalā, Pravara 3: Viśvāmitra, Devarāja, Uddālaka. Śaunaka-sagotra 7, Gotra-devī Śāntā, Pravara 3: Bhārgava, Vaitahotra, Gārtsamada. Kṛṣṇātreyasagotra-vī, Gotra-devī Abhadrayoginī 8, Pravara 3: Ātreya, Arcanānas, Śyāvāśva. Gārgyāyaṇasagotra, Gotra-born Śāntā, Pravara 5: Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, Jamadagni. Gārgāyaṇagotra, Gotra-born Jñānajā, Pravara 5: Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, Śāṇḍila, Asita, Devala. Gāṅgeyasagotra-devā Śāntā Dvāravāsinī, Pravara 3: Gārgya, Gārgi, Śaṅkha-Likhita. Paiṅgyasagotra-born Jñānajā Śeṣalaudha, Pravara: Āṅgirasa, Āmbarīṣa, Yauvanāśva. Vatsasagotra, Gotra-born Jñānajā, Pravara 5: Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, Purodhasa. Vātsasagotra, Gotra-born Jñānajā, Pravara 5: Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, Purodhasa. Vātsyasagotra, Gotra-born Śīharī, Pravara 5: Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, Purodhasa. Śyāmāyanasagotra, Gotra-born Śīharī, Pravara: Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, Jamadagni. Dhāraṇasagotra, Gotra-born Chatrajā, Pravara 3: Agastya, Dārvacyuta, Dadhyavāhana. Kāśyapagotra, Gotra-born Cāmuṇḍā, Pravara 3: Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, Naidhruva. Bharadvājagotra, Gotra-born Pakṣiṇī, Pravara 3.

Of the lineage of Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja (22); of the Vatsa, Vātsya, and Vātsyāyana lineages of the Māṇḍavya *gotra* (4); of the common Laugākṣa *gotra*, the *gotra*-born Bhadrayoginī has three *pravaras*: Kāśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and Avatsāra (20). Of the Kauśika *gotra*, the *gotra*-born Pakṣiṇī has three *pravaras*: Viśvāmitra, Atharvan, and Bhāradvāja (21). [The following have] common *pravaras*: Paimagya and Bharadvāja (2) have two common *pravaras*; Laugākṣa, Gārgyāyana, Kāśyapa, and Kaśyapa (4) have three common *pravaras*; Kauśika and Kuśika (2) have four common *pravaras*; Aupamanyu and Laugākṣa (2) have common *pravaras*. (5)

Among as many individuals as there may be who follow even a single one of the prominent [lineages], such as Viśvāmitra, there should be no mutual marriage among them due to their sharing the same *gotra*.

One should avoid a girl who has the same *pravara* as one's own, one who belongs to the same *gotra*, one who is a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother, one afflicted with an incurable disease, one whose pubic hair has not yet grown, one who has previously belonged to another, the daughter of a sonless man, and one who is excessively dark-complexioned.
Wherever a single seer alone recurs among the *pravara* ancestors, there is the state of having a common *gotra*, except for the groups of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases.

Marriage is prohibited between those who share five, three, or two common elements due to general similarity; this applies likewise to the Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras clans, while among the remaining groups, even a single common element should prevent it.
Having married and approached a maiden of the same lineage and *pravara*, and having procreated a *caṇḍāla* upon her, one falls from the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
Kātyāyana says: Having married a woman of the same gotra or likewise one with the same pravara, a twice-born man shall abandon her and then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having abandoned that wife, he should then protect her like a mother.

Yājñavalkya: [One should marry] a woman who is free from disease, has brothers, and is not born of the same Ṛṣi-lineage or Gotra; she should be beyond the fifth degree on the mother’s side and the seventh degree on the father’s side. 12.

Gautama states that marriage is with those who do not share the same *pravara*. If even one *pravara* is identical, or if it matches the *pravara* of the mother’s lineage, marriage must not be performed there; such a girl would be as a sister. (13)
He who enters into marriage and the consecration of the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*.

A girl who is destined for rebirth must always be avoided as the lowest of her lineage—whether she has been given by word, given in thought, or for whom the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony has already been performed. (15)
She who has been touched by water, she who has been taken by the hand, she who has circumambulated the fire, she who is a remarried woman (punarbhū), and she who is a child of such a union; || 16 ||
These, as spoken by Kāśyapa, burn the family like fire. || 17 ||

Now the Avaṭaṅkas are being described: Gotra 1, Pātra 2, Dātra 3, Trāśayatra 4, Laḍakātra 5, Maṇḍakīyātra 6, Viḍalātra 7, Rahilā 8, Bhādila 9, Vālūā 10, Pokīyā 11, Vākīyā 12, Makālyā 13, Lāḍaā 14, Māṇavedā 15, Kālīyā 16, Tālī 17, Velīyā 18, Pāṃvalaṇḍīyā 19, Mūḍā 20, Pītūlā 21, Dhigamagha 22, Bhūtapādavādī 23, Hophoyā 24, Śevārdata 25, Vapāra 26, Vathāra 27, Sādhakā 28, Bahudhiyā 29. || 18 ||
Having married the daughter of a maternal uncle, or likewise one of the mother's lineage, or even one of the same *pravara*, one shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance after abandoning her.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The Yoginīs who dwell in fixed locations were created by Kāmeśa; tell me, in which place are which goddesses, and what are they like?
Vyāsa said: "O sinless Yudhiṣṭhira, you are all-knowing and well-born; you have asked a virtuous question. I shall relate everything to you in its entirety."
Richly adorned with various ornaments, embellished with diverse gems, clothed in various garments, and endowed with various youthful qualities. || 3 ||
Equipped with various vehicles and resounding with diverse sounds, these were created by the Lord of Kāñcī for the destruction of the fear of the Brahmins.
For they were established in the east, the south, the north, and the west, as well as in the regions of the southeast, the southwest, the northwest, and the northeast.
Āśāpurī, Gātrā, Chatrā, Jñānajā, as well as Pippalāmbā, Śāntā, Siddhā, and Bhaṭṭārikā. || 6 ||
Kadambā, Vikaṭā, Mīṭhā, Suparṇā, and likewise Vasujā; Mātaṅgī, the Great Goddess Mahādevī, Vārāhī, and Mukuṭeśvarī. || 7 ||
Bhadrā, Mahāśakti, Siṃhārā, and Mahābalā—these and many others cannot even be fully described. || 8 ||
The goddesses, assuming various forms and resorting to diverse attire, are situated in the northern direction from this place, near Āśāpūrṇa.
To the east, however, resides the goddess Ānandā, the bestower of bliss; and to the north dwell the goddesses, joyfully assuming various forms.
Satisfied by the offering of water, these [deities] bestow desired objects; situated in the southwestern direction, Śāntā is the bestower of peace.
Seated upon a lion, four-armed, and bestowing boons, Bhaṭṭārī, the Great Śakti, likewise stands right there.
Praised and worshipped with devotion, she is the destroyer of the fear of her devotees; she is established at Kṣemalābhā, seven krośas from this place.

She, consisting of food-offerings, is worthy of worship; when meditated upon, she bestows success. In the eastern direction, she is gratified by people with the offering of bali-oblations. Accompanied by her retinue, she grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
With inconceivable form and conduct, she is the destroyer of all enemies; indeed, she is seen as visibly present during the three periods of the twilight.
Seven krośas from that place to the south dwells Vindhyavāsinī; she is armed, endowed with beauty, and the remover of fear for her devotees.
In the west is the goddess born of the neem tree, who rests upon that ground; she is possessed of great power, and even when seen, she bestows delight upon the eyes. (17)
To the north of that place, situated on the ground at the same distance, is the Śakti Bahusuvarṇākṣā; when worshipped, she bestows much gold.
Situated at a distance of one krośa in the north-western corner from that place, the great goddess Kṣetradharā resides, holding a goat during the appointed time.
At a distance of one krośa to the north of the city is Karṇikā, who is devoted to the welfare of all and the destroyer of calamities affecting the locality. (20)
In the region of the southwest from that place, there exist the goddesses known as the Jalamātṛs, headed by Brahmāṇī, who assume various forms. || 21 ||
Vyāsa said: Hereafter I shall proclaim that which was performed by Brahmā in the past; I shall relate all of that today, so listen with a one-pointed mind.
A war arose between the gods and the dānavas due to their enmity; in that most wicked battle, the minds of the gods became distressed.
They became agitated there and went to Brahmā for refuge.
The gods said: "O Brahmā, by what means shall I now bring about the slaughter of the Daityas? Tell me the remedy quickly."
Brahmā said: Indeed, in ancient times, Dharmāraṇya was created by me, by Śaṅkara himself, and likewise by Viṣṇu, being gratified by the penance of Yama.
Whatever gift, sacrifice, or supreme austerity is performed there, all that shall become multiplied ten millionfold; of this there is no doubt.
Whether it be sin or merit, everything becomes ten millionfold; therefore, O gods, he has never been overcome by the Daityas.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, all the gods, filled with wonder, placed Brahmā at their head and proceeded to Dharmāraṇya.
Having selected Aṅgiras and likewise Mārkaṇḍeya as their preceptors, they commenced there an unsurpassed sacrificial session lasting for a thousand years.
Having appointed Atri and Kaśyapa as the Hotṛ priests, the high-minded one assigned Jamadagni and Gautama to the office of Adhvaryu.
He then appointed Bharadvāja and Vasiṣṭha to the office of Adhvaryu, and he exhorted Nārada and Vālmīki at that time.
And they respectfully established Brahmā upon the Brahmāsana; then, having constructed an altar measuring four krośas, by the gods.
All the twice-born were summoned for the sake of the sacrifice—those chanters who indeed recite the Vedas, namely the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva.
Likewise, [he praised] Gaṇanātha, Śambhu’s son Kārttikeya, Indra the wielder of the thunderbolt, and Jayanta, the son of the Moon.
And four brave gods were manifested as gatekeepers; then the bearer of oblations was invoked with the Rakshoghna mantra.
Then, O lord of men, those gods offered oblations of sesame seeds mixed with barley and combined with honey and clarified butter, using Vedic mantras.
Having offered the two Āghāra libations and the two Ājyabhāga portions, and thereafter [offering] grapes, sugarcane, betel nut, orange, citron, and pomegranate; || 17 ||
To the north, one should place a coconut and a pomegranate in due order, along with honey and clarified butter mixed with milk, and rice cooked with sesame (kṛśara) combined with sugar.
Restraining their speech during the sacrifice, those highly fortunate ones performed the rite with rice grains and lotuses, having offered the prescribed sacrificial fees.
Having performed the most excellent and auspicious hymn of praise, they attained great joy; they distributed food without restraint even to the wretched, the blind, and the miserable.
To the Brahmins, food was given especially according to their desire: milk-rice mixed with sugar, accompanied by ghee and vegetables. (21)
Maṇḍakas, vaṭakas, pūpas, as well as auspicious veṣṭikas, a thousand modakas, pheṇikās, ghurghuras, and so forth. || 22 ||
Likewise, there was boiled rice and auspicious dal made from *āḍhakī* beans, as well as mung bean dal, *parpaṭa* pancakes, and meat balls. (23)
Various kinds of foods to be licked, prepared with a collection of the three pungent spices (tryūṣaṇa), along with boiled grains (kulmāṣa), vellaka, and tender, auspicious vālaka stalks.
Karkaṭikā fruits combined with fresh ginger and endowed with black pepper—such foods and various kinds of vegetables as these [should be offered]. (25)
O King, he then fed all eighteen thousand twice-born residents of Dharmāraṇya, together with their sons.
Then the gods fed the Brahmins every day; thus the immortals performed that sacrifice for a thousand years.
O King, having accomplished the slaughter of the Daityas, all those gods and hosts of Maruts attained fearlessness and immediately went to heaven. (28)
In that same way, all the Apsarases, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, went to the beautiful peak of Kailāsa and to Vaikuṇṭha, the beloved abode of Viṣṇu.
Having reached the highly meritorious world of Brahmā, all the inhabitants of heaven attained supreme joy, as if having reached the most excellent Nandana grove.
Having become firm in their respective places, they all indeed remained there free from fear. || 31 ||
Then, after a long time, at the transition of the age known as Kṛtayuga, the demon Lohāsura, who was always intoxicated with pride and dressed in the garb of a Brahmin, [appeared].
Having arrived, he shall assault all the brahmins who are most knowledgeable in dharma, and he shall strike the śūdras and merchants with blows of the staff.
He shall destroy sacrifices and other rites, and consume the substances for the fire-oblation; seeing the altar and the oblong pond, he shall defile them with impurity.
O King, he defiles sacred lands with his urine, excrement, and secretions; likewise, he indeed corrupts women through his lustful passion.
Then all those Vāḍavas, afflicted by the fear of Lohāsura, perished along with their families and fled indeed in the ten directions.
O King, those merchants, agitated by fear and terrified by a great danger, followed the Brahmins; having gone a long distance and reflected upon their situation, [they spoke]. (37)
Then, having all become one with the Śūdras and the twice-born, they went to Muktāraṇya, the most meritorious and indeed uninhabited forest, and they entered it.
O Lord of Men, they established their residence not far away; indeed, they settled that village under the name Vajrin. (39)
O King, because it was established by the merchant Śambhu out of fear of the demon Lohāsura, it was created under the name "Vipra"; therefore, it bears that name.
It became renowned in the world as Śambhugrāma and attained great fame; meanwhile, at that time, some merchants first fled out of fear. (41)
Having gone not very far, they indeed formed an excellent mandala; desiring the arrival of the Brahmins, they established their residence there.
Having established a village by the name of Maṇḍala, they settled there; meanwhile, some merchants who had become separated from their caravan of Brahmins were also present at that time.
Those who had indeed gone by another path, afflicted by the fear of Lohāsura, went not very far from Dharmāraṇya and fell into deep anxiety.
"Which path have we reached? Where have the twice-born arrived?"—filled with such great anxiety, they nevertheless made their dwelling there. (45)
Because they had gone by another path, they settled on the earth a village named after that origin, called Aḍālañja.
O Lord of the Earth, whatever name a merchant residing in a village might have, that indeed became the name of that village. 47.
And likewise the merchants and the Brahmins, overcome by delusion and afflicted by fear, all spoke thus to the king: "O King, let them be known by the name 'Delusion' (Moha). (48)
Thus utterly ruined and destroyed, they fled in every direction; neither the Brahmins nor the merchants remained in Dharmāraṇya.
For at that time, Dharmāraṇya became desolate and difficult to reach; yet that ornament of all sacred fords was established by Lohāsura.
Having rendered that place devoid of twice-born brahmins and devoid of sacred fords, the Dānava attained supreme joy and then departed for his own abode.
Vyāsa said: O lord of the earth, I have thus declared before you the majesty of this sacred ford (tīrtha), which destroys the sins arising from many previous births.
The supreme among all places, the great and ultimate source of well-being, was proclaimed of old by the wise Mahārudra in the presence of Skanda.
"O Pārtha, by bathing there, you shall indeed be liberated from all sin. Having heard those words of Vyāsa, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira [acted accordingly].
Then, O dear one, the son of Dharma entered Dharmāraṇya, intent upon protecting the virtuous and for the destruction of great sins.
Having bathed there at the sacred fords and in the temples of the deities, he performed all acts of sacrifice and charitable works as desired.
Then, liberated from sin, O Mahāsena, he returned to his own city of Indraprastha and ruled over the surface of the earth.
For those best of men who, having reached this place, listen [to this], for them there will be both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having enjoyed earthly pleasures, those twice-born ones who recite this when the time for the śrāddha has arrived shall attain supreme nirvāṇa.
By them, the ancestors have been uplifted as long as the moon, sun, and earth endure; this was spoken by the high-souled Vyāsa when he appeared in the Dvāpara age.

In the Dharmavāpī, which contains nothing but water, one obtains the fruit of performing a śrāddha at Gayā. For the mortal who has come here, whatever sin was situated in the realm of Yama [is removed]. (10)
This was spoken by the Son of Dharma out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds: "Even without food, without *darbha* grass, or even without a seat... (11)

The sin committed over ten million lifetimes is destroyed by water alone; and the merit gained by giving a thousand cows with large horns in Kurujāṅgala during a solar eclipse is equaled by the libation performed at Dharmavāpī.
All this activity of Dharmāraṇya has been told to you; by hearing which, even a slayer of a Brahmin or a killer of a cow is liberated from all sins.
By performing the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā twenty-one times, one obtains that same fruit by merely hearing this [account] once.
Sūta said: Now I shall further proclaim another supreme majesty of a sacred ford (tīrtha), concerning how the Sarasvatī was brought from Satyaloka to Dharmāraṇya.
To Mārkaṇḍeya, who was sitting comfortably, attended by great sages, resembling the rising sun, and proficient in all the scriptures.
He was composed of all sacred fords, divine, the most excellent of sages and twice-born, seated upon his throne, disciplined, blessed, worthy of worship, and firm in his vows.
The pervasive Lord, whose self is yoga, supremely peaceful, holding a water-pot, bearing a rosary, tranquil, and likewise clothed in garments of the cosmic age (kalpa). || 4 ||
Having thus seen Akṣobhya—the wise one, established in his own state, possessing the splendor of the Grandfather (Brahmā), and absorbed in samādhi with eyes blossoming with great joy—(he spoke).
Having bowed down with appropriate hymns of praise, the sages spoke to Mārkaṇḍeya: "O Blessed One, in the Naimiṣa forest, during a twelve-year sacrificial session..."
O Brahman, that river which is the daughter of Brahmā was brought down by you; thus was the descent of the Gaṅgā onto the earth accomplished right there.
While it was being sung before the sage Śaunaka, the lord of the lineage, it was proclaimed by the sage Sūta for the hearing of others as well.
Having heard that great narrative, it remains established in our hearts; it destroys the sins and generates merit for living beings even by its mere sight.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O brahmins, I have brought the Sarasvatī from Satyaloka to Dharmāraṇya, upon the Surekha mountain, as a refuge for those seeking protection.
On the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, which is endowed with great merit, [one should go] there to the holy site of Dvārāvatī, frequented by sages and Gandharvas.

And on that day, one should cause the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and other rites to be performed at that sacred ford; one obtains the full fruit thereof, and what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
This entire narrative of the Great One (Mahābhārata) destroys all sins and bestows merit; it is the most sacred of sacred things and the destroyer of great calamities.
The water of the Sarasvatī is the most auspicious of all auspicious things and is meritorious; what other merit exists above in heaven that is established at the end of Prabhāsa?

The water of the Sarasvatī removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin from men. Having bathed in the Sarasvatī and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, those who subsequently offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) shall no longer be sucklings at the breast [in future births]. 15.
Just as cows that yield all desires become the bestowers of desired fruits, so too is Sarasvatī the sole cause for both heaven and liberation.
Vyāsa said: The gate of heaven, which had been opened by Mārkaṇḍeya, stands wide open; those who cast off their bodies there out of a desire for rewards [attain it]. || 1 ||
They indeed obtain that fruit and ultimately attain union with Viṣṇu; therefore, what is the use of saying more? Men should always [reside] in Dvāravatī.

Those best of men who, desiring to conquer the world of Viṣṇu, perform the abandonment of the body through fasting, by water, or by fire, are forever liberated from all sins and go to the city of Viṣṇu. || 3 ||
Furthermore, any man who, being free from disease, undergoes fasting unto death, shall be liberated from all sins and go to the city of Viṣṇu.
At the end of a hundred thousand years, the twice-born shall dwell in heaven; on this earth, there is nothing more purifying or sanctifying than the Brāhmaṇas.
There is no act of austerity found equal to fasting; there is no scripture superior to the Veda, and no teacher equal to a mother.

In this world, there is no austerity higher than the Dharma, and none superior to fasting; likewise, he who bathes here and performs the Śrāddha, the offering of rice-balls, and the water-libation [attains the highest goal].
The ancestors of that man who, having bathed in that sacred ford, worships Keśava, remain satisfied for as long as day and night endure in the realm of Brahmā.
He shall attain the world of Viṣṇu, freed from all sins; for that is the most excellent of holy places where Hari is ever present.

For one stationed at that sacred ford (tīrtha), it removes all sin; it bestows liberation upon those desiring liberation, wealth upon those seeking wealth, longevity and happiness, and indeed grants the fruit of every desire. || 10 ||
What need is there for any other sacred ford here, since Lord Janārdana himself dwells eternally out of compassion for all? (11)
Whatever gift is given there, endowed with faith, all that becomes inexhaustible both in this world and in the next.
Whatever fruit is obtained by the wise through sacrifices, gifts, and austerities, that is attained here merely by bathing, even by Śūdras who are good servants.
In that regard, whoever, having fasted on the eleventh day, performs a śrāddha ceremony, shall deliver all his ancestors from the hells; of this there is no doubt. (14)
The Supreme Self, Janārdana, attains inexhaustible satisfaction; whatever is given here with him in view is declared to be imperishable.
Sūta said: There, situated near him, was the holy site named Govatsa, which had been observed by Mārkaṇḍeya and was renowned everywhere on earth. || 1 ||
Having descended there, the Lord of Ambikā, the Master of the worlds, remained in the form of a calf and in the form of a self-manifested liṅga.
There was a king named Balāhaka, a devotee of Rudra and possessed of great strength; he was a conqueror of enemy cities who was devoted to the sport of hunting.
Seeing a calf standing within a herd of deer, I, who was walking on foot, said to the king: "O best of kings, I have seen a marvel. (4)
I saw a calf standing in the midst of a herd of deer; though deprived of its mother, it was devoted to them alone. || 5 ||
Out of curiosity to see him standing before him on foot, the king said, "Show me," and he entered [the chariot] along with the cow-calf.
Having gone to the forest, he was then shown to the king by the foot-soldier; when the herd of deer was terrified and fled, the foot-soldiers pursued them.
When the calf had gone toward the *pīlu* bush, the king, desiring to seize it, then entered the thicket with great haste.
While standing there, the king himself did not see the calf; as soon as he reached out to seize it, it became a brilliantly radiant linga.
Seeing him, the king was struck with wonder and thought, "What is this? Even as he was reflecting thus, [the man] abandoned his body and ascended to heaven.

In the meantime, the thunderous roar of the gods' cries of victory was heard everywhere in the sky; a rain of flowers fell from the heavens, and at that very moment, the king departed for the abode of Śiva.
Then he beheld that calf standing at his navel like a young boy; "Surely this is Mahādeva, the Great Lord Maheśvara, in the form of a calf. (12)
The king endeavored to bring it forth and indeed lifted it up; however, O Lord, that divine Liṅga did not rise up by any means whatsoever. Then the gods, together with him, entreated the Lord.
The gods said: "O Blessed One, Lord of all gods, O All-pervading One, you who desire the welfare of all worlds, you must remain here in the form of a white linga."
Śrī Mahādeva said: "O deities, I shall always remain here in the form of a liṅga; because on the new-moon day (kuhū) in the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada," || 15 ||
Likewise, those who perform their bath there according to the prescribed rite on that day and worship the Liṅga—for them no fear exists. || 16 ||
And without the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), those ancestors who have gone for eternal years to the terrible Raurava hell and to Kumbhīpāka [suffer]. || 17 ||
And for those dwelling in many hells and those who have entered the wombs of animals, by the offering of a single ball of rice, their destiny shall become inexhaustible.
Then King Balāhaka, accompanied by all the gods, installed that liṅga in the presence of all the gods. || 19 ||
Out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, he made many gifts; even as he was thus performing worship, Rudra himself arrived.
Rudra said: "O Lord of Gods, those men who, endowed with faith and devotion, worship you this night, their merit shall be infinite."
Those mortals who shall perform the vigil preceded by songs and sacred scriptures will deliver one hundred and one generations of their lineage.
So long do the sacred fords—Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Gayā, Prayāga, Prabhāsa, Dvārakā, Mathurā, and Arbuda—proclaim their greatness.
As long as the most wonderful mark of the calf is not seen, he indeed maintains his intention regarding the departure of the calf.
Then all those born of their own lineage certainly danced with joy. || 25 ||
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, hear now another wonderful account that occurred there, by the mere hearing of which the destruction of all sins shall come to pass.
When indeed that ancient Liṅga was established by all the gods, it was due to the merit of Viṣṇu’s installation and that of all the inhabitants of heaven.
He grew day by day by the measure of an atom; then those gods and men, being afraid, went to him for refuge.
The gods said: "O Lord of Gods, withdraw this increase; may there be well-being for the worlds. When this was said, an unembodied voice then spoke from the Liṅga.
The voice of Śiva said: "O people, let there be no fear for you; listen to this remedy. Let someone certainly bring a Caṇḍāla and place him before me."
They brought together some Caṇḍālas and placed them before the god; nevertheless, his growth did not cease at all. || 31 ||
The voice said: "O people, let that man who is a Caṇḍāla by his actions be placed before me. Hearing that, they were struck with great wonder and fixed their gaze upon him.
While searching through villages and cities at that time, they saw a certain wicked man who called himself a Brahmin, devoted to his work.
At midday, that man of cruel mind drove out bulls yoked to heavy loads, which were weak and overcome by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion.
Even without bathing, the twice-born there indeed consumed stale food; taking that Lord of Devas with them, they went to where the Teacher of the World resided.
Respectfully, they placed him on the ground in front of the temple; however, as soon as he was positioned before the calf of the cow, he suddenly turned to ashes.
This place became famous on earth as Caṇḍālasthala; even today, that temple is not seen by those residing there. (37)
From that time forward, that Liṅga attained a state of equality; the twice-born Dhautapāpman went to the holy ford because he had beheld the Liṅga.
Having been freed from sin, he worshipped the calf every day, especially on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight when it arrived.
This is that wonder of the trident-bearing God; the man who hears it with devotion is liberated from all sins.
The Bhūta said: This [place] known as Govatsa, which bestows supreme merit upon men and destroys the sins of many births, was described by Mārkaṇḍeya. (41)
A single bath at that sacred ford bestows the world of Rudra upon men whose souls have been afflicted by sin, for the sake of purifying their sinful bodies.
In the Kali age, satisfaction is attained through libations and ancestral rites at the well, especially at the end of the fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada.
If libations are performed twenty-one times at Gayā, the ancestors attain supreme satisfaction; however, that same satisfaction is attained once at Gaṅgākūpaka.
Near that Govatsa stands the Gaṅgākūpaka; by offering libations of water with sesame seeds at that place, those who are satisfied attain a virtuous state.
The ancestors, even from hell, are praised by that highly meritorious and wise one; at that sacred site, the lords of sages commend the gift of a cow.
The gift of gold to a Brahmin leads a man to the world of Rudra; likewise, [the gift of land] at Sarasvatī, Śivakṣetra, Gaṅgā, and Gaṅgakūpaka [does so]. (47)
These three, when united in one place, are the cause of heaven and liberation; this sacred site (tīrtha), frequented by seers and perfected beings, is renowned everywhere.
A pair of *pīlu* trees stands there at that sacred ford (*tīrtha*) frequented by sages; it bestows heaven through bathing and grants purification from sin through drinking [its water]. (49)
From its glorification arises merit, and from its service comes supreme liberation; even a slayer of a Brahmin or a slayer of his mother, if they behold it with devotion, [is purified].
Those who kill children, those who kill cows, and those who kill women or Śūdras; those who administer poison, those who set fires, and those who are intent on betraying their teachers.
Those who revile ascetics, those who give false testimony, those who speak of the faults of others, and those who suppress the virtues of others; || 52 ||
Even one consisting of all sins is liberated here by the sight of the Liṅga. || 53 ||

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Balāhaka," in the *Dharmāraṇya-māhātmya* of the Pātālakhaṇḍa, within the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Vyāsa said: To the southwest of Govatsa, an iron pillar is seen; there Rudra himself resides in the form of a self-manifested *liṅga*. Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: At the Mokṣatīrtha on the Sarasvatī, during the month of Nabhasya when the moon has waned, one should worship the Brahmins according to the rules and give them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Whatever fruit is obtained by men at Gayā through twenty-one offerings of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with devotion, that is certainly attained here through this libation (tarpaṇa).
When a Śrāddha is performed with an iron staff on the new moon day of the month of Nabhasya, the ancestors, liberated from the state of being a ghost (preta), sport in heaven.

May he who indeed offers sesame-water, or even a funeral cake (piṇḍa), or water during the fortnight of the deceased at the rising of the moon, be present for us even in the midst of a tumultuous battle.
O sages, if the ancestors are dear to them, people should perform the Śrāddha rite on the new moon day of the month of Bhādrapada at the Lohayaṣṭi; so the sages have declared.
But he who bathes in the waters of the Sarasvatī with milk and white sesame seeds and offers libations to the ancestors, his ancestors certainly become satisfied.
There, those desiring liberation for their ancestors should perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) with barley meal and milk, having reached the day of the new moon.
Then, at Rudratīrtha, one should give a cow adorned with garments and other ornaments; and at Viṣṇutīrtha, one who desires liberation should also bestow gold.
At Gayā, Janārdana himself exists in the form of the ancestors; by meditating upon that lotus-eyed one, one is liberated from the three debts.

Having gone there, one should pray to that Janārdana, the God of gods: "O Lord, I have come to Gayā with the desire to offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to my ancestors; O Janārdana, this cake is offered by me into your hand."
"You shall indeed become the giver for those who have gone to the other world; and with this very mantra, you should give [the offering] there into the hand of Hari. (11)

When the moon has waned on the fourteenth day of the month of Nabhasya, one should offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa); there will be inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors, of this there is no doubt.
By offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with devotion at Gayā twenty-one times, and by performing libations for the ancestors at Lohayaṣṭi, one attains satisfaction.
The giver of water attains satisfaction here; indeed, he obtains imperishable happiness. The giver of fruit obtains devoted sons, and the giver of fearlessness obtains health. (14)
Even a small gift of wealth acquired through righteous means given there yields great fruit; indeed, by merely bathing at that sacred ford, one becomes an attendant of Rudra.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "A Brief Description of the Greatness of the Tīrthas," in the Dharmāraṇya-māhātmya, within the first part of the Brahma-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 28 ||
Sūta said: Listen now to the deeds of Lohāsura; I shall also relate the famous account of the hundred sons of Bali.
From that time forth, the Daitya Lohāsura conceived a sense of detachment, seeing how those two aged brothers had attained the highest state.
What shall I do? Where shall I go to find an excellent place for asceticism, the further shore of which neither gods, sages, nor men know? (3)
"Which deity should be propitiated by me, whom he contemplates so intensely in his heart?"—as that high-souled one was reflecting thus, an idea arose in his mind.
He placed Gaṅgā upon his head, Puṣpavantau (the Sun and Moon) in his two eyes, the god Nārāyaṇa in his heart, and Brahmā upon the region of his hips.
All the deities, beginning with Indra, who are reflected within his body, perceive him as their own self, just as the sun is seen in water.

"I, being stainless, shall worship Him alone who is untainted. Having thus resolved his mind, the Daitya performed a most difficult penance—one that is hard even for great souls to perform—out of fear of the terrible cycle of birth.

Subsisting on water, subsisting on air, and likewise eating only withered leaves, he performed great penance for more than a hundred divine years; then the Blessed One, the bearer of the excellent trident, was pleased.
Īśvara said: "Choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever is desired by your mind. O Lohāsura, there is nothing that cannot be granted to you by me through the power of your asceticism."
Thus addressed there in the presence of Śaṅkara, the Dānava spoke these words: || 10 ||
Lohāsura said: "If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, I choose one boon: may there be no aging for my body, nor any fear of death for me. (11)
"O Lord, may you remain in my heart in this birth. "So be it," Śiva replied there to that lord of the Dānavas.
Having obtained boons from Śarva by divine fortune, he again performed great penance on the beautiful bank of the Sarasvatī in order to cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
For thousands, millions, and billions of years, the venerable Indra remained fearful, trembling at the power of his asceticism.
"O Daitya, may I never suffer a fall from my station due to you, the Asura Loha; for Maghavan, having approached this hermitage forest in a disguised form," (15)
Causing the great asura to tremble, they brought about the destruction of his ascetic power and struck him on the body with fists that were sharp and harsh.
Then that Daitya, abandoning his meditation, looked on; Indra performed all those acts intended to destroy the power of his asceticism.
Then a fierce battle took place between him and those harsh ones, Indra and the others; he, being alone, fought together with many gods in that encounter.
Their bodies drenched in blood and shattered by blows, they sought refuge in Keśava, crying out, "Save us! Save us! (19)
Sūta said: Having heard the words of the gods, Vāsudeva Janārdana, Keśava, indeed fought with him in battle for a hundred years.
Then he, exalted by his excellent boon, defeated Nārāyaṇa there; thus the god Nārāyaṇa was conquered by Lohāsura.
He consulted again and again with Rudra and Brahmā; having deliberated, the three gods once more prepared for battle.
Upon seeing the body of the Daitya Lohāsura restored to its former state, a great battle then ensued once more between the Daitya and Keśava.
When the Daitya did not die despite being struck by the powerful Viṣṇu, Keśava also violently cast him down upon the earth.
Seeing him fallen face upwards, the Supreme Lord, the wielder of the Pināka bow, who is himself devoid of form, held his own form within his heart.
Then Brahmā stood upon the throat of that Lohāsura, while Puruṣottama pressed down his two feet with his own presence.
Then the Daitya rose up forcefully upon the ground even though he was firmly bound; seeing the Daitya thus risen and striking down the foremost of the gods, [the gods were terrified].
Virañci, whose seat is the lotus, spoke with a divine voice.
Brahmā said: O Lohāsura, always protect the dharma of speech constantly; that which was requested by you from Rudra has now come to pass.
"I, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—these three best of gods—shall occupy your body until the dissolution of all beings. (30)
O Lord of the Dānavas, the attainment of Śiva occurs only through devotion born of inner feeling; how then can the thought of moving Śiva arise in you? (31)
He who causes the immovable temples, Brahmins, and cities to tremble will be tainted by sin in no time at all.
One who is excluded from truth and dharma should be abandoned like a cremation ground. You are a speaker of truth; may it be well with you; do not cause the deities to waver.
One should travel by that path by which one's fathers have gone and by which one's grandfathers have gone; the way of the virtuous must not be transgressed.
O Lord of the Dānavas, your father indeed gave the three worlds to Hari; bound by the noose of his word, that lord of the earth ruled his kingdom in Pātāla.
Likewise, you are endowed with devotion to Śiva; O Lord of Daityas, remain upon the earth and do not suffer any impairment of speech. (36)
We shall grant you boons; for the gods must not be made to waver.
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of Brahmā, the lord of the Dānavas was satisfied and spoke with a gracious voice to Brahmā, Keśava, and Hara. (38)
Lohāsura said: "I stand bound by the noose of your words, and not by the strength of you all. These three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—are the best among the gods. (39)
"If they remain within my body, what then have I not gained? For this body of mine has indeed been ascended by the three gods."
O best of gods, by my power, let it become renowned upon the earth. || 41 ||
Delighted by the words of the demon Lohāsura, the three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—gave him this reply.
Since the Daitya has not wavered from the truth because of the bond of his truthful word, we are satisfied by that truth and shall grant you your heart's desire. (43)
Brahmā said: O Daitya, just as bathing at Gayātala constitutes the knowledge of Brahman and the abandonment of the body, so it is likewise at Dharmāraṇya, situated before Dharmeśvara. || 44 ||
The ancestors in heaven praise the libation and Śrāddha performed at the well, just as they are satisfied by the offering of rice-balls at Gayā. (45)
In Dharmāraṇya, they desire libations at the well for the sake of purification; O Lord of Dānavas, your body shall indeed become a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
O Lord of the Dānavas, when the libation (tarpaṇa) is performed twenty-one times at Gayā, that supreme satisfaction which arises for the ancestors occurs.
O Lord of Dharma, that satisfaction which occurs once before the libation to the ancestors shall indeed be tenfold; this is the truth, there is no doubt. (48)
"By the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to the ancestors, may there be inexhaustible satisfaction here on this earth in Dharmāraṇya, within the interior of Śiva’s form. (49)

Indeed, the rites of the śrāddha, the piṇḍas, and the water-libations must be performed with faith alone; likewise, especially so for us during this interval, the śrāddha and the piṇḍa must be offered.

Likewise, O observer of noble vows, you are truly such that even in the body, that thought [of yours] is present; truth, which is difficult to attain in the three worlds, resides within you in heaven.
O best of asuras, by virtue of these true words of mine, that sacred site on the surface of the earth has become even greater than Gayā.
Our stay within your body is unwavering, of this there is no doubt; O sinless one, we are bound to you very firmly by the tether of truth. (53)
Viṣṇu said: The fruit of offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Lohayaṣṭi on the fourteenth or the new moon day is remembered by some as being even greater than that of Gayā or Prayāga. || 54 ||
"By the truth of Bali’s son, there is indeed great satisfaction here; do not entertain any doubt regarding this, for I myself am present within your body. (55)
Furthermore, Sarasvatī, whose waters are meritorious, proceeds from the world of Brahmā; well-united with me, she shall flood the limbs of my body.
Just as Dvārakā is indeed the abode of the god Maheśvara, so too is Virañci; these three are the sacred fords (tīrthas) upon the surface of the earth.
And it shall exist in Pātāla, in the heavenly world, and in the abode of Yama, O best of Asuras, renowned for the sake of providing satisfaction to the ancestors. (58)
Now I shall proclaim another supreme verse composed by the ancestors; it is indeed in the form of an injunction for sons. Listen to it from me, O sinless one. (59)
The Pitṛs said: "The place situated before Śaṅkara bestows the world of Rudra upon men for the sake of purifying their sinful bodies, whose souls have been struck down by sin. (60)
By that [offering], even with water mixed with sesame seeds, the ancestors, being satiated by a wise and excellent son, attain a good rebirth or are released from hell.
They praise the gift of a cow there for the sake of the liberation of one's ancestors; having beheld Rudra and Keśava, one should dedicate it specifically to one's father and the rest.
On the fourteenth day and likewise on the new moon day, we shall attain supreme satisfaction by offering a lump of sesame oil-cake as libation to the ancestors.
One should offer funeral cakes to those whose lineage and birth are unknown; they too all go to heaven—such is the sacred revelation (śruti) regarding those to whom [the offering] is given. (64)

Having renounced all worldly duties, men desiring merit should go to Lohayiṣṭakā when the month of Bhādrapada has arrived; even for one whose lineage and name are unknown, hear this mantra for the funeral cake (piṇḍa). || 65 ||
May this pinda reach those who have died in the paternal lineage, as well as those in the maternal lineage, and all those born of the family who have passed away.
Viṣṇu said: O best of gods, with this very mantra in my presence, one should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) on the fourteenth day of the waning moon in the month of Nabhasya.
There will be inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors, of this there is no doubt; by means of a funeral cake made of sesame and oil-cake, the ancestors shall attain liberation.
There is no doubt that on the surface of the earth, human beings will be liberated from the three moments [of existence] by means of a copper staff and the libation of sesame seeds.
Whoever bathes here and performs the rites of offering rice-balls and water to the ancestors, his ancestors remain satisfied for as long as the day and night of Brahmā endure.
Having reached the new moon day in the month of Bhādrapada, whoever performs the libation for the ancestors at the Brahma-staff pillar by the lake [attains great merit]. || 71 ||
His ancestors shall remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings; toward them, the Blessed One, the primordial god Maheśvara, is well-pleased.
Those whose minds shall be set upon the pilgrimage to this sacred ford, having bathed in the waters of the Sarasvatī with cow’s milk and white sesame seeds, [shall attain their goal]. (73)
For him, an inexhaustible satisfaction arises for the ancestors; he should indeed perform the śrāddha with groats together with milk. (74)
Having reached the day of the new moon (amāvāsyā), one desiring the joy of the ancestors should then give a cow at Rudratīrtha and garments at Yamatīrtha.

One who desires liberation for the ancestors should give gold at Viṣṇutīrtha; even without unbroken rice (akṣatas), without Darbha grass, and without a seat, one obtains the fruit of a Śrāddha performed at Gayā by means of water alone from an iron rod.
Sūta said: O Brahmins, this deed of Lohāsura has been narrated to you; by hearing which, even a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa or a killer of a cow is liberated from all sins.
By hearing this once, one obtains that same fruit which is gained by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at Gayā twenty-one times. 78.
Four crores, two hundred thousand, one thousand, and one hundred cows would be considered given by him; now hear the greatness of that which he attains. (79)
Vyāsa said: Formerly, when the Tretā Yuga had arrived, the lotus-eyed Rāma, a portion of Viṣṇu and the upholder of the Raghu lineage, was born in the Solar dynasty.
Both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, still wearing the side-locks of youth, followed Viśvāmitra in obedience to their father’s command.
For the sake of protecting the sacrifice, the two heroic princes were given by the king; bearing bows and arrows, they were the executors of their father’s word.
While he was traveling on the road, a rākṣasī named Tāḍakā approached and stood before him for the purpose of creating an obstacle.
With the permission of the sage, Rāma struck down Tāḍakā; and the son of Gādhi imparted the science of archery to Rāma.
By the touch of his foot, through the power of Indra’s yoga, Ahalyā, the wife of Gautama, was restored to her own form once again.
When Viśvāmitra’s sacrifice had duly commenced, that best of the Raghus slew Mārīca and Subāhu with his supreme arrows.
The bow of Ishvara, which had been broken and remained in the house of Janaka, [Rama broke]; and in his fifteenth year, Rama [took] Maithili, who was six years of age.
Then, O King, he married the lovely Sītā, who was not born from a womb; having obtained Sītā, Rāghava then felt his purpose was fulfilled.
On the way to Ayodhyā, having encountered the son of Jamadagni, a battle then took place, O King, which was unbearable even for the gods.
Then, having defeated Rāma, he returned home with Sītā; thereafter, Rāma enjoyed himself with her for twelve years.
Then, in his twenty-first year, Kaikeyī requested two boons from the king, who was about to bestow upon him the status of crown prince.
Of those two, Rāma, wearing matted hair and accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, shall go into exile here for fourteen years.
But Bharata, out of delusion due to Manthara’s words, requested this boon by means of the second [formula]: "Let him be my heir-apparent. (14)
The king sent Rāma, accompanied by Jānakī and Lakṣmaṇa, into exile; for three nights he subsisted on water, and on the fourth day he ate fruit.
In the fifth [chapter], Rāma established his residence at Citrakūṭa; at that time, Daśaratha went to heaven, proclaiming, "Rāma! (16).
Having made the curse of Brahmā fruitful, did he go to heaven? Thereafter, Bharata and Śatrughna arrived at Citrakūṭa. (17)
O King, having informed Rāma that his father had gone to heaven, and having offered words of consolation to Bharata regarding his return, [he departed].
Then Bharata and Śatrughna arrived at Nandigrāma; both remained there, devoted to the worship of the sandals while governing the kingdom.
Having seen the high-souled Atri, he went to the Daṇḍaka forest at the commencement of the slaughter of the hosts of Rākṣasas, once Virādha had been struck down.
In the thirteenth year, he indeed dwelt at Pañcavaṭī; there, as he was wandering in the forest together with Jānaki, he disfigured the night-stalker Śūrpaṇakhā.
That terrible Rākṣasa came for the abduction of Sītā; then, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, at the moment known as Vṛnda.
The Ten-necked one abducted Sītā in the absence of the two Rāghavas; having gone to Mārīca’s hermitage, he did so by means of that [demon] who had assumed the form of a deer.
Having led Rāghava, who was accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, far away, Rāma then swiftly slew Mārīca in the form of a deer.
Upon returning to the hermitage, Rāma beheld it indeed empty of Sītā; while being carried away right there, she wailed like a female osprey.
"Rāma, Rāma! Protect me, protect me, for I am being carried away by a demon, just as a hungry hawk might carry off a quail that is crying out. (26)
Thus, having come under the power of passion, this Rākṣasa was carrying off the daughter of Janaka; hearing that, the king of birds then [acted].
He fought with Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, and was struck down; he fell while dwelling in Rāvaṇa’s abode on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha.
Then those two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, were searching for him.
Upon seeing Jaṭāyus and realizing that Sītā had been carried off by the Rākṣasa, the bird was then consecrated with funeral rites by him out of devotion.
Rāma went on ahead, with Lakṣmaṇa following in his footsteps; having reached the vicinity of Pampā and having shown grace toward Śabarī.
Having touched that water, he beheld Hanumān; then Rāma indeed formed a friendship with Hanumān.
Then, having approached Sugrīva, he slew the monkey Vālin; and by the command of Lord Rāma, those led by Hanumān were dispatched to find his beloved.
Taking the ring, Sampāti, the son of Vāyu, arrived at the end of the tenth month and reported that matter to the monkey.
Then, at his word, Hanumān leaped across the ocean for a hundred yojanas; that very night, he searched all around Laṅkā.
During the remainder of that night, Hanumān beheld Sītā; on the twelfth day, Hanumān remained stationed at the Śiṃśapā tree.
On that night, he spoke this conversation to inspire confidence in Jānakī; then, on the thirteenth day, the battle commenced with Akṣa and the others.
On the thirteenth day, the monkey was bound by Śakrajit with the Brahmāstra; meanwhile, he addressed harsh and cruel words to the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Bound by the Brahmā-weapon and joined with fire at its tail, the son of Vāyu said to him: "The burning of Laṅkā has been accomplished. (39)
On the full moon day, the monkey returned to Mount Mahendra; he spent five days on the road from the first day of Mārgaśīrṣa.
It is said that on the day of the full moon, Madhuvana was destroyed; on the seventh lunar day, there is the bestowing of recognition and the offering of everything.
On the eighth lunar day under the constellation Uttaraphālgunī, during the hour named Vijaya, he reported everything regarding the presentation of the jewel to Sītā to Rāma.
When the thousand-rayed sun had reached the meridian, Rāghava made his departure; for Rāma had indeed made a vow to travel toward the southern direction.
"Even having crossed the ocean, I shall slay the Lord of the Rākṣasas; Sugrīva became my companion as I set out for the southern quarter. (44)

Within seven days, the encampment of the army took place on the shore of the ocean; from the first day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa until the third, Rāghava remained stationed by the sea together with his host.
On the fourth day, Vibhīṣaṇa joined with Rāma; on the fifth, a council was convened for the purpose of crossing the ocean.
Rāma undertook a fast unto death for four days; meanwhile, he obtained a boon from the ocean along with the revelation of a means [to cross].
The commencement was on the tenth day and the conclusion on the thirteenth; on the fourteenth, Rāma encamped his army on Mount Suvela.
On the second day after the full moon, within three days, Rāma, accompanied by his army of heroic monkeys, crossed the ocean.
And he of auspicious marks besieged the city of Laṅkā for the sake of Sītā; his encampment lasted for eight days, from the third day until the tenth.
The arrival of Śuka and Sāraṇa there took place on the eleventh day; and on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa, the numbering of the army was carried out.
Śārdūla’s description of the strengths and weaknesses of the monkey leaders took place in Laṅkā over three days, beginning on the thirteenth day and ending on the new moon.
