Then Rāvaṇa made a count of his army and displayed his zeal for battle; on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, Aṅgada set out on a mission as an envoy.
And then, on the second day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, after seven days—on the eighth day—Sītā beheld her husband’s illusory head and other [limbs].
On the night of the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, there occurred a tumultuous battle between the Rākṣasas and the Vānaras in the conflict with Indrajit.
It is said that Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were bound by the noose of the Nāga, while the lords of the monkeys were utterly distressed and all their hopes were destroyed on every side.
Then, upon the instruction of Vāyu, Rāghava remembered Garuḍa; for the sake of liberation from the serpent-noose, Garuḍa arrived on the tenth day.
The withdrawal took place on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha for two days; on the twelfth day, the son of Añjanā slew Dhūmrākṣa.
On the thirteenth day, however, the Ten-necked one, having displayed an illusory Sītā to Rāma, had Akampana slain by him in battle.
And he terrified everyone present in the army from the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha until the first day of the dark fortnight.
The slaying of Prahasta was carried out by Nīla within three days, from the second day of the dark fortnight of Māgha until the fourth day—thus in three days.
In that tumultuous battle, Rāvaṇa was put to flight from the field by Rāma; however, from the fifth day until the eighth, he was rallied back by Rāvaṇa.
Then Kumbhakarṇa took his meals for four days; Kumbhakarṇa engaged in battle from the ninth day for four days.
On the day of the new moon, Rāma slew in battle the one who devoured many monkeys; indeed, there was a cessation of eating due to grief.
During the four days beginning with the first day of the month of Phālguna and ending on the fourth, five Rākṣasas, headed by Narāntaka, were slain.
From the fifth day until the seventh, the slaying of Atikāya occurred within three days; from the eighth until the twelfth, he was slain within five days.
These two, Nikumbha and Kumbha, as well as Makarākṣa, were conquered by the slayer of Śakra in four days; indeed, on the second day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, he was truly victorious.
From the third day onwards, for five days ending with the seventh, there was indeed a cessation of activity due to the distraction caused by the procurement of medicinal herbs.
On the eighth day, the evil-minded Rāvaṇa killed the illusory Maithilī; then, overcome by a surge of grief, Rāma halted the army.
Then, on the thirteenth day, after five days had passed, Indrajit—renowned for his strength and prowess—was slain in battle by Lakṣmaṇa.
On the fourteenth day, Daśagrīva undertook the initiatory rite (dīkṣā) for the purpose of carrying away [Sītā]; on the new moon day, the ten-necked one set out toward the east for battle.
During the five days from the first to the fifth of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Rāvaṇa was engaged in battle, and there was a great slaughter of the Rākṣasas.

Until the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, [he performed] the slaying of Syandana, Aśva, and the others; and on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, he performed the piercing of Saumitri’s spear.
Overcome with anger, Rāma put the Ten-necked one to flight, aided by the counsel of Vibhīṣaṇa and by Hanumān in the battle.
Having come from Mount Droṇa to fetch the herb for the sake of Lakṣmaṇa, he took the Viśalyā and made Lakṣmaṇa drink it.

On the tenth day, there was a cessation of hostilities, but at night there was fighting among the Rākṣasas; on the eleventh day, however, a chariot with Mātali as its charioteer was provided for Rāma.
Having set out for battle on the twelfth day until the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, Rāma slew Rāvaṇa in a duel of chariots on the eighteenth day.
The magical powers of Rāvaṇa and the others failed on the new moon day; when a tumultuous battle ensued, Rāma achieved victory. (78)
From the second day of the bright fortnight of Māgha until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, there are thus eighty-seven days, with fifteen days in the middle.

The suspension of hostilities and the battle lasted for seventy-two days. On the first lunar day (tithi) of the month of Vaiśākha, Rāma stayed upon the fields of battle; on the second day, Vibhīṣaṇa was consecrated in the kingdom of Laṅkā.
On the third day, there was the purification of Sītā and the obtaining of boons from the gods; then came the arrival of Daśaratha and his approval. || 81 ||
Having swiftly slain the Lord of Laṅkā, the powerful elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa took hold of the virtuous Jānakī, who had been made miserable by the Rākṣasa.
Taking Jānakī with supreme joy, Rāma returned, having mounted the Puṣpaka chariot on the fourth day of the month of Vaiśākha.
Having returned through the air toward the city of Ayodhyā, he arrived when the fourteenth year was complete, on the fifth day of the month of Mādhava.
Rāma, together with his retinue, entered the hermitage of Bhāradvāja; however, on the sixth day, he arrived at Nandigrāma by means of the Puṣpaka chariot.
On the seventh [day], that scion of Raghu was consecrated once again in Ayodhyā; indeed, Maithilī had been with him for fourteen months and ten days. (85)
She dwelt in the residence of Rāvaṇa, separated from Rāma; it was in the forty-second year that Rāma ruled his kingdom. || 87 ||
At that time, thirty-three years had passed for Sītā; then, at the end of fourteen years, the Lord entered his own city.
Joyful, having destroyed the pride of Rāvaṇa, Rāma, together with his brothers, ruled the kingdom there in the city named Ayodhyā. (89)
Having protected the kingdom for ten thousand and ten hundred years, Rāma departed for the abode of the three heavens.
At that time, in Rāma’s kingdom, the people became filled with hearts overflowing with joy; they were men enriched with wealth and grain, and endowed with sons and grandsons. (91)
The rain-cloud pours down according to one's desires, the crops are full of excellence, cows yield pots full of milk when milked, and trees always bear fruit. (92)
O lord of men, in Rāma’s kingdom there were neither mental anxieties nor physical ailments; the women were devoted to their husbands, and the men were intent on devotion to their fathers.
The twice-born are eternally devoted to the Vedas, the Kṣatriyas serve the twice-born, and those of the Vaiśya caste always practice devotion toward the twice-born and the cows. (94)
There was no confusion of castes there, nor any confusion of conduct; there were no barren women, no unfortunate women, no women who gave birth only to daughters, and none whose children died.
There was no widow at all, nor did any woman with her husband living lament; likewise, no one showed disrespect toward their mother, father, or teacher. (96)
The merit-accumulating king did not transgress the words of the elders; he did not seize land there, and he turned his face away from the wives of others. 97.
The world was not intent on slander, nor was there any who was poor or afflicted by disease; there were no thieves or gamblers, and no women addicted to liquor, nor were there any evildoers. 98.
He was neither a stealer of gold nor a slayer of a Brahmin, nor one who violated the teacher’s bed; he was neither a killer of women nor a killer of children, nor was he a speaker of falsehoods. (99)
There was no one who interrupted the performance of duties, nor indeed any false witness; no rogue, no ungrateful person, and no one impure was ever seen. 100.

O King, in the highly renowned kingdom of Rāma, Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas were always honored everywhere; there was no one there, O King, who was not a Vaiṣṇava or who failed to observe vows.
While he was ruling the kingdom, his family priest Vasiṣṭha, the best among eloquent men, having visited numerous sacred fords together with other sages, [arrived]. || 2 ||
The highly fortunate son of Brahmā, a treasury of asceticism, arrived; Rāma honored that preceptor together with the sages.

Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages, having honored Rāma with rising to meet him, the offering of water for the feet (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and other rites of worship, inquired after his welfare.
When the sage was then asked, "O Rāma, is all well with the kingdom, the horses, the elephants, the treasury, the country, and your good brothers and servants? [he replied: 5.
Rāma said: "By your constant grace, all is well with me today. Rāma then inquired after the welfare of Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages.
"Are you indeed well in every respect, together with your wife and sons? He then related everything concerning the holy fords (tīrthas) in their entirety, exactly as they occurred.
Having visited sacred fields and shrines upon the surface of the earth, he then reported that all was well everywhere to Rāma.
Then Rāma, the lotus-eyed one, filled with wonder, inquired about the greatness of that sacred ford (tīrtha), which is the most excellent among all sacred fords.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, you have visited many sacred fords (tīrthas); tell me, O Giver of Honor, which among them is the supreme tīrtha.
But during the abduction of Sītā, I killed several Brahmarākṣasas; tell me of the most excellent of all holy places (tīrthas) for the sake of purifying that sin.
Vasiṣṭha said: The Gaṅgā, Narmadā, Tāpī, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Gaṇḍakī, Gomatī, and Pūrṇā—these rivers are exceedingly purifying.
Among these, O Rāghava, the Narmadā is the most excellent, while the Gaṅgā flows through the three paths; both burn away every sin merely by being seen.

Having seen [her], she destroys the sins of a hundred births; having gone [to her], she destroys those of three hundred births; and having bathed [in her], O Revā, she destroys those of a thousand births in the Kali age.

Having spoken thus, Rāma, with a delighted inner soul, [beheld] the ponds of the gods and their most beautiful ramparts.
He constructed wide main streets equipped with defensive fortifications, as well as sacrificial pits, lakes, and ponds.
And having expanded all these—reservoirs of dharma, wells, and other structures fashioned by the gods—in the delightful Dharmāraṇya; || 50 ||
Furthermore, with supreme faith, he bestowed upon the foremost of those learned in the three Vedas this edict of Rāma inscribed on a copper plate; and whoever should violate it— || 51 ||
His ancestors fall into hell first, not his progeny; then Rāma, having summoned the son of Vāyu, spoke these words. (52)
"O great hero, son of Vāyu, worship shall be yours; for the protection of this field, establish your residence here. (53)
Āñjaneya, having bowed his head to those words, accepted them; then, having performed the restoration of the ancient [shrine], he became one who had accomplished his purpose.
Then, having worshipped Śrīmātā with a serene inner soul and having paid homage to Śrīmātā, Rāghava [visited] other sacred fords (tīrthas).
Those gods also, with Brahmā at their head, went to their own abodes.
Having bestowed a blessing upon Rāma, he said: "Your desire shall be fulfilled; O Rāma, you have performed a noble deed by establishing these brāhmaṇas and so forth. (57)
"Even for us, affection has been shown by you, who are meritorious"; praising him thus, those gods returned to their own abodes.
Vyāsa said: O knower of dharma, in this manner the restoration of the ancient [shrine] was formerly performed by Rāma for the benefit of the twice-born and at the word of his venerable mother. (1)
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Brahmin, what kind of edict was written by Rāma in the past? Please tell me out of grace, for it was during the Tretā age, the abode of truth. || 2 ||
Vyāsa said: O best of Brahmins, while the lord Nārāyaṇa remained present in the excellent and divine Dharmāraṇya at Bakulārka, he stood there as the master of the empty abode.
In that realm where the Lord is the Protector, the Omniscient One, the Leader of Virtues, there the Yoginī is the savior for those submerged in the ocean of existence.
Therein lies the teaching of Rāma, known by the name of Rāghava; hear now that which is inscribed there concerning Tāmra, as derived from the Dharmaśāstra.
That [state] is indeed most wonderful and persists for many eons; for while every other element goes to destruction, gold alone does not perish.
O son, the indestructible ordinance of the twice-born is seen directly before our eyes; for there exists therein the cause for the non-destruction of copper.
O Bhārata, for it is Viṣṇu alone who is described as everything declared in the Vedas, as well as in the Purāṇas, the Vedas, and the Dharmaśāstras.
Everywhere Viṣṇu is praised as the refuge of various dispositions, by those who practice diverse duties in diverse lands and according to diverse religious systems.
In all various forms, it is Viṣṇu alone who is meditated upon; he is indeed the ancient Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) who has manifested in person.
For the destruction of the enemies of the gods and for the protection of the Dharma, O son, he has bestowed this teaching which is imperishable by nature.
By whose prowess the mountain was cast from the midst of the waters, Laṅkā was surrounded by monkeys with ease, and the Rākṣasas were slain. (12)
Rāma brought back to life the son of the sage who had died; he by whom Dundubhi was slain and likewise Kabandha was struck down.
Tāḍakā was slain, the seven palm trees were split asunder, and Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and the great asura Triśiras were likewise destroyed.
Fourteen thousand [demons] were slain in battle by his speed; how could this edict bestowed by him not be imperishable? (15)
Having himself written a description of his own lineage there, he recorded everything—including the place, time, and other details—in accordance with the prescribed rules.
There, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, at the age of forty-four, bestowed [the kingdom] marked with his own seal upon those learned in the three Vedas.
At that time, O Bhārata, a great wonder indeed occurred there; it was like gold and also like silver.
He carried water at the sacred ford to satisfy the gods, sages, and ancestors; that very act had already been performed by the Sun-god in the presence of the leader of his own lineage.
Having witnessed that great marvel and having worshipped Viṣṇu, Rāma [established] a charter of righteousness inscribed with various wonderful lines of Rāma.
Since all the twice-born, upon seeing it, no longer perform that which binds one with the fear of saṃsāra, it is therefore the protector of all.
In former times, he brought about his renown for the purpose of awakening those who are most wicked, of evil conduct, and devoted to betraying their friends.
O Nārada, these words are indeed heard in the royal edict upon a variegated copper plate, adorned with various inscriptions.
The ancestors clap their hands and the grandfathers say: "A giver of land has been born in our lineage; he shall deliver us. (24)
This earth has been enjoyed by many kings in many ways; for whoever possesses the land at any given time, his is the fruit thereof. 25.
The giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years; the one who seizes it, or even consents to its seizure, shall go to hell for that same duration. (26)
Being tormented with tongs, struck down with mallets, and tightly bound with nooses, he cries out with a great sound.
Being beaten on the head with clubs, he embraces the Fire-god; being cut by a razor-edged blade, he cries out with a great roar.
Those who violate the conduct of Brahmins are thus tormented by extremely terrible messengers of Yama and by such great hosts of highly wicked beings.
Thereafter, one attains the state of an animal, or the womb of a rakshasi, a female dog, a female serpent, a female jackal, or a female pisacha—forms that are terrifying to all great beings. (30)
For how could one who takes even a finger’s breadth of land commit sin? And how could one who gives even a finger’s breadth of land perform merit? || 31 ||
The giver of land obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices, and the gift of a hundred maidens. (32)
Longevity, fame, happiness, wisdom, righteousness, grain, wealth, victory, and progeny—these always increase for the giver of land; he enjoys eternal happiness. (33)
Those wicked men who seize even a single inch of land are born as black serpents dwelling in dry hollows within waterless, barren forests; for they have stolen what was given to them as a grant.
A usurper of land is purified by [the merit of] building a thousand tanks, or by performing a hundred horse-sacrifices, or by the gift of ten million cows. (35)
Who indeed, being virtuous, would take back again those riches given here as gifts for the sake of Dharma, profit, and fame, which were offered with magnanimity and announced to the Brahmins? (36)

In this world of living beings, which is as flickering and unstable as a trembling leaf, and wherein all worldly pleasures have a substance as light as a blade of grass—a man of evil desires, longing to fall into the whirlpools of the deep pit of hell, seizes the teaching of the Brahmins. (37)

Those kings who shall behold this earth and enjoy it in its entirety will all pass away; yet the earth has never gone with anyone, nor does it go, nor will it ever go with anyone. Whatever exists on earth is entirely perishable, but fame alone is enduring. Thus, even though the earth itself must eventually be abandoned by those who have benefited it, their noble fame should never be lost.
In this world, the earth given by a Brahmin is but one sister to all kings; it is neither to be enjoyed nor to have taxes levied upon it. (39)
Having granted the land, Rāmacandra entreats the future lords of the earth again and again: "This bridge of dharma is common to all kings; it must be maintained by you each in your own time. (40)
"If there shall be any king on earth in this lineage, I am at his service, provided that what has been granted by me is upheld. (41)
Having written the edict, the wise Rāma honored the best of the twice-born, who were masters of the four Vedas, and presented it in the presence of Vasiṣṭha.
At the command of Rāma, those Vāḍavas took that auspicious copper plate, inscribed with golden letters, which was righteous and adorned by dharma. (43)
Desiring devotion for the sake of worship, they performed its protection with divine sandalwood and fragrant flowers. || 44 ||
Likewise, the Brahmins perform auspicious worship for you day after day with golden flowers or silver flowers. (45)
O King, before that [liṅga], the twice-born offer a lamp with pure ghee provided with seven wicks, as well as the arghya offering. (46)
O best of the twice-born, they constantly offer food oblations with devotion, and indeed they chant the mantra: "Rāma, Rāma, Rāma. (47)
While eating, sleeping, drinking, walking, or sitting; whether in happiness or in sorrow, one should recite the Rāma-mantra. (48)
For him there shall be no suffering or misfortune, nor any fear of mental anguish or physical disease; his lifespan, prosperity, and strength increase day by day. (49)
By the name "Rāma," one is indeed liberated even from terrible sin; one shall not go to hell, but attains the eternal state. (50)
Vyāsa said: Having done this, Rāma then considered his purpose accomplished; he then circumambulated and bowed down to many twice-born brahmins.
Having given away an abundance of gifts—cows, horses, buffaloes, and chariots—he then spoke these words to all his own people and to them as well.
Let all of you remain right here as long as the moon and the sun endure, as long as Mount Meru remains upon the surface of the earth, and as long as the seven oceans exist.
"You must remain right here, there is no doubt; for when the kings on earth do not respect the teaching, O Brahmins," (54)
Or perhaps those merchants are brave men, deluded by intoxication and deceit; they do not carry out my command, or else they simply disregard it. (55)
Then indeed, O twice-born ones, let the son of Vāyu be remembered; as soon as he is remembered, Hanumān will surely arrive and act.
"Truly, by my word, there is no doubt that those kings who shall uphold this delightful edict will instantly be reduced to ashes. (57)
The Son of Vāyu will always bestow upon him happiness and supernatural power; he grants sons, grandsons, a virtuous wife, fame, and victory.
Having spoken thus and having consoled Hanumān, Lord Rāma turned back along with his army and his retinue.

With the auspicious arrival being proclaimed in all directions by the sounds of musical instruments, he—attended by a white parasol and fanned by men with chowries—reached the city of Ayodhyā and ruled the kingdom for a long time.
Nārada said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, cause of creation and destruction, you who transcend the qualities (guṇas) yet are endowed with them, the supreme means for attaining liberation.
Having duly established the temple of the Vedas for the best of the twice-born, what did Raghunātha do next when he returned to Ayodhyā? || 2 ||
What rites did the Brāhmaṇas perform there in their own abode? Brahmā said: They were devoted to sacrifices and works of public utility, peaceful, and averse to accepting gifts. (3)
The preceptor, the best of the twice-born, governed this forest; he spoke of the supreme majesty of the sacred fords (tīrtha) in the presence of Rāma.
The majesty of Prayāga, the supreme fruit of Triveṇī, the greatness of the Prayāga-tīrtha, and indeed that of Śuklatīrtha as well.
O Nārada, Vasiṣṭha then recounted the greatness of the Siddhakṣetra, of Kāśī, and likewise of the Gaṅgā, as well as other sacred fords (tīrthas).
All acts such as bathing and giving gifts performed at Dharmāraṇya, Suvarṇā, and that Harikṣetra are even greater than those performed at Vārāṇasī.
Having heard this, Rāmadeva, his mind filled with wonder, set out once again, desiring to undertake a pilgrimage to Dharmāraṇya.
Accompanied by Sītā, the knower of dharma was preceded by a great army; he was with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and had Bharata as his companion.
Surrounded by Śatrughna, he went to the city of Moheraka; having arrived there, that high-minded one questioned Vasiṣṭha.
Rāma said: O best of the twice-born, what should be performed in the great sacred field of Dharmāraṇya—is it charity, or a religious observance, or bathing, or supreme austerity? (11)
Whether it be meditation, or a sacrifice, or an oblation, or the highest recitation; or charity, or a religious observance, or ritual bathing, or the highest austerity—12.
O best of the twice-born, tell me that which, when performed at this sacred site, liberates one from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O highly fortunate one, perform an excellent sacrifice in Dharmāraṇya for as long as a hundred years, so that it may yield a crore-fold merit day by day."
Having heard that from his preceptor, he commenced the sacrifice; at that moment, Sītā joyfully addressed Rāma.
"O Lord, those Brahmins who were previously chosen by you—those twice-born ones created of old by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa—" (16)
"In the Kṛta and Tretā Yugas, those Brāhmaṇas residing in Dharmāraṇya—choose them indeed; by them alone shall the sacrifice be accomplished. (17)
Having heard that, the Brahmins were then summoned by Rāmadeva and established as before in this wretched city of Mōha.
With those eighteen Trivedyas, who were like great sacrificial fires and possessed expansive intellects, he performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rules.
Kuśika, Kauśika, Vatsa, Upamanyu Kāśyapa, Kṛṣṇātreyo Bharadvāja, Dhāriṇa, and the excellent Śaunaka. || 20 ||
Māṇḍavya, Bhārgava, Paiṅgya, Vātsya, and Laugākṣi; Gāṅgāyana, Gāṅgeya, Śunaka, and likewise Śaunaka. || 21 ||
Brahmā said: O King, having completed the sacrifice according to the rules with these brahmins, Rāma performed the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) after honoring the brahmins with devotion.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, Rāma was addressed by the well-mannered Sītā: "O you of noble vows, grant a sacrificial fee for the successful completion of this ritual. (23)
"And let a city be established there immediately under the name of Manu. Having heard Sītā’s words, the best of kings did exactly so. (24)
And for those Brāhmaṇas, a single place entirely free from fear was granted by King Rāma for the satisfaction of Sītā.
At that time, it is said, he gave it the name Sītāpura; Śāntā and Sumaṅgalā are its two presiding goddesses.
Rising up with great joy, he gave twelve villages situated before Moheraka to the learned Brāhmaṇa.
The knower of dharma quickly went to another sacred ford on the bank of the river Kāśyapī; those certain Vāḍavas were led there along with Rāma.
He immediately went to Dharmālaya, where formerly the garland and water-pot were kept, and where, O sage, Dharma performed great penance.
From that time onwards, it became renowned as Dharmālaya; so it is heard. There, the son of Daśaratha bestowed sixteen great gifts (mahādānas).
Then, fifty villages together with Sītāpura, as far as Satyamandira, were indeed [granted] by the descendant of Raghu at that time.
At the word of Sītā and indeed by the command of his preceptor, that best of the Raghus gave [the land] to the twice-born for the sake of increasing his own lineage.
There was a family of eighteen thousand twice-born men: Vātsyāyana, Upamanyu, Jātūkarṇya, and Piṅgala.
Bhāradvāja, as well as Vatsa, Kauśika, and Kuśa; Śāṇḍilya, Kaśyapa, Gautama, and likewise Chāndhana. || 34 ||
Kṛṣṇātreyas, as well as Vatsa, Vasiṣṭha, Dhāraṇa, and Bhāṇḍila should be known; after him comes Yauvanāśva. (35)
Kṛṣṇāyana, Upamanyu, Gārgya, Udgala, Maukhaka, Puṣi, Parāśara, and after him Kauṇḍinya. || 36 ||
The names of the fifty-five villages are as follows, in their proper order: Sītāpura, Śrīkṣetra, Muśalī, and likewise Mudgalī. (37)
Jyeṣṭhalā is the abode of excellence, as are Dantālī and Vaṭapatrakā; Rājñaḥpura, Kṛṣṇavāṭa, Deha, Loha, and Canasthana [are likewise].
Koheca, Candanakṣetra, Thala, Hastināpura, Karpaṭa, Kañcanajahnavī, and the forest of Uḍaphanaphāvalī.

The Vaṭamālikā [praise] is for Govinda, who has abandoned the state of being born, who is the destroyer of delusion and pride, and who is attained by the Cāraṇas and Siddhas through the offering of the Udgītha.
Godharā, Māraṇajā, Mātrāmadhyā, and Mātṛkā; Balavatī, Gandhavatī, Īrāmlī, and Rājyajā. (41)
Rūpāvalī, Bahudhana, Chatrīṭa, Vaṃśaja, Jāyāsaṃraṇa, Gotikī, and likewise Citralekha. (42)
Dugdhāvalī, Haṃsāvalī, Vaihola, Caillaja, as well as Nālāvalī, Āsāvalī, and Suhālī, following after Kāma. (43)
Rāma himself constructed fifty-five villages for their residence and bestowed them upon those very brahmins.
For the sake of serving them, Rāma assigned thirty-six thousand Vaiśyas, and four times as many Śūdras to them. (45)
To them were given gifts of cows, horses, and garments, as well as gold, silver, and copper, with supreme faith and joy. (46)

Nārada said: "O observer of excellent vows, those eighteen thousand Brāhmaṇas were masters of the Vedas; how did they divide the villages, as well as the wealth produced in the village, the clothing, the ornaments, and so forth? Tell me that. (47)

Brahmā said: "O son, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, as soon as the sacrificial fees were accepted by the officiating priests, everything including the great gifts and so forth was entrusted to them alone. (48)
At that time, villages were granted as common property and great sites were indeed bestowed, with the intention: "Let these belong to those who dwell right there. (49)
At the word of Vasiṣṭha, those villages there were made over to the Brahmins by the steadfast descendant of Raghu, so that the twice-born would not suffer distress.
Indeed, immeasurable wealth and grain were bestowed upon those brahmins; then Rāma, with palms joined in reverence, spoke this to the brahmins.
Just as it was in the Kṛta age and formerly in the Tretā age, O Brahmins, so indeed must it be conducted today in my kingdom; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever wealth or grain, vehicles or garments, jewels, gold and the like, as well as other riches there may be—53.
"Now request copper and the like, as well as silver and so forth from me; whether now or in the future, whatever is appropriate should be requested. (54)
"O best of the twice-born, my verbal message is always to be dispatched: 'O Lord, whatever desire you may pray for, that very thing I shall grant. (55)
Then Rāma respectfully replied to his servants and others: "The command of a Brahmin must not be transgressed; it should be carried out with diligent effort."
"Whatever desire they may pray for, grant it to them from that very source. Having bowed thus, whoever performs service to the Brahmins— || 57 ||
That Śūdra attains heaven and shall become possessed of wealth and sons; otherwise, he certainly incurs poverty—of this there is no doubt. (58)
Whether it be a Yavana, one of the Mleccha tribes, a Daitya, or even a Rākṣasa—whoever here creates an obstacle, he is reduced to ashes at that very moment. || 59 ||
Brahmā said: Then, having circumambulated the twice-born ones, Rāma, filled with great joy and greeted by the brahmins with blessings, set his face toward his departure.
Having followed him as far as the boundary, their eyes agitated with affection, all the twice-born returned from Dharmāraṇya, bewildered.
Having done this, Rāma then set out toward his own city; and the Kāśyapas and Gargas, firm in their vows, having accomplished their purpose, [departed]. 62.
Seated upon a grand vehicle, accompanied by his wife, friends, and sons, Rāma then reached the virtuous capital city of Ayodhyā.
Seeing the illustrious descendant of Raghu, all the people were filled with joy; then the righteous Rāma, who was devoted to the protection of his subjects, [reigned].
Then that righteous and wise king, ruling the kingdom together with Sītā, caused Jānakī to conceive for the sake of one born of the solar dynasty.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Restoration of the Ancient Sacred Site and Field of Dharmāraṇya by Śrī Rāmarudra," in the *Dharmāraṇya-māhātmya* of the first part of the third section (*Brahmakhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 35 ||
Nārada said: O observer of noble vows, tell me what happened after that; and first, O best among speakers, describe it to me in its entirety.
Tell me, for how long will that place remain stable? By whom is it being protected, and whose command prevails there, O Lord? (2)
Brahmā said: From the end of the Tretā age until the arrival of the Kali age, Hanumān, the son of the Wind, alone shall be the protector.
O son, no one else is capable in any other way except Hanumān, by whom Laṅkā was destroyed and the powerful Rākṣasas were slain.
O dear son, he himself protects that place by the command of Rāma; likewise, the command of the twice-born and of Śrīmātā is put into effect there.
Day after day, great joy arose among the people residing there; the twice-born ones recited there the hymns characterized as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman.
There they recited the Atharvaveda day and night; the sound produced by the resonance of the Vedas pervaded the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
Festivals are held there in every village and in every city; various sacrifices are performed, based upon diverse religious duties.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Has there ever been a destruction of that place, or not? Has the place ever been conquered by the Daityas or by wicked Rākṣasas?"
Vyāsa said: O King, you have asked well; you are always pure and a knower of dharma. Listen now, O sir, to what is given when the Kali age has first arrived.
For the welfare, the desire, and the happiness of the worlds, I shall describe the sacrifice; listen to all of that, O lord of the earth. (11)
Now, when the Kali age had arrived, there was a certain king named Āma, the illustrious lord of Kānyakubja, who was a knower of dharma and devoted to statesmanship.
Peaceful, self-controlled, virtuous, and devoted to truth and righteousness—O best of kings, he appeared at the end of the Dvāpara age, before the arrival of the Kali Yuga.
Out of fear—specifically the fear of the Kali age and the fear of unrighteousness—all the gods abandoned the earth and took refuge in the Naimiṣa forest.
O King, Rāma also went to the construction of the bridge accompanied by his allies.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "What kind of insurmountable fear indeed exists in the world when the Kali age has arrived, in which the Earth, the womb of jewels, has been abandoned by the gods? (16)
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, to how the characteristics of the Kali age will come to be; people will be speakers of untruth and devoted to censuring the virtuous. (17)
All were devoted to the deeds of bandits and devoid of devotion to their ancestors; they took pleasure only in the wives of their own kin and were intent on thoughts of greed. || 18 ||
In the Kali age, all will be haters of Brahmanas, mutually antagonistic, and slayers of those who have come for refuge. (19)
When the Kali age has arrived, Brahmins will be devoted to the conduct of Vaiśyas, fallen from the Vedas, and conceited; these twice-born ones will neglect the twilight prayers.

They were brave in times of peace but cowardly in fear; they were devoid of ancestral rites and libations; they were devoted to the conduct of asuras and were utterly lacking in devotion to Viṣṇu. || 21 ||
Brahmins will covet the wealth of others and take delight in accepting bribes; they will eat without having bathed, and Kshatriyas will avoid battle.
When the Kali age has arrived, all will become impure and of wicked conduct; indeed, everyone will be devoted to drinking liquor and will act as priests for those unworthy of sacrifice.
In the Kali age, women will become haters of their husbands, sons will become haters of their fathers, and base men will become haters of their brothers. (24)
Those Brāhmaṇas who are intent on wealth are indeed sellers of cows; for when the Kali age has arrived, cows no longer yield milk.
O Bhārata, trees never bear fruit at any time for those who sell their daughters or who sell cows and goats.
In the Kali age, there will be sellers of poison, sellers of mercury, and sellers of the Vedas.
A woman indeed conceives a child after eleven years; thus, people have desisted from fasting on the eleventh lunar day in every respect. (28)
The Brahmins will not be devoted to visiting sacred fords; they will consume much food and be overwhelmed by excessive sleep.
All were devoted to crooked conduct and intent upon reviling the Vedas; they were likewise intent upon reviling ascetics and practiced deception toward one another.
In the Kali age, there will be no fear of the defects of touch; Kṣatriyas will be deprived of their kingdoms, and a Mleccha will become king. (31)
O King, all those who betray trust, as well as those intent on harming their gurus, those devoted to betraying friends, and those solely devoted to their genitals and bellies [fall there]. 32.
O Great King, when the Kali age has arrived, even the four castes will become of a single color; my word shall not be otherwise.
Having heard this from his preceptor, the powerful lord of Kānyakubja, known on earth by the name Āma, established his kingdom there.
Having attained universal sovereignty and being intent on protecting his subjects, the minds of the people there became inclined toward sin through the influence of Kali.
Having abandoned the Vaiṣṇava dharma, they adopted the Buddhist dharma; the subjects, following his lead, were awakened by the Kṣapaṇas.
That king had a chief queen, renowned by the name Māmā; she, endowed with all auspicious marks, conceived a child from the king. (37)
When the tenth month was complete, at the proper time, a beautiful daughter was born to the queen, her face resembling the full moon.
Known by the name Ratnagaṅgā, she was adorned with jewels and rubies; once, by the turn of fate, a man arrived from another land. (39)
In this land of Kānyakubja, there was indeed a man named Indrasūri; that princess was sixteen years old, yet she had not been initiated.
O descendant of Bharata, having met with another female servant, Indrasūri Jīvika taught him the mantra-lore of the Śabaras.
But she, deluded by the karma of her own actions, became single-minded; then, having fallen into a state of infatuation, she devoted herself entirely to those words.
O child, awakened by the Kṣapaṇas and devoted to the Jaina dharma, she [was given] to the wise Kumbhīpāla, the lord of Brahmāvarta.
Thus the valorous one gave that great queen Ratnagaṅgā; deluded by fate, he gave him a single mohara at the wedding.
Having arrived at Dharmāraṇya, he then established it as his capital; and he installed deities ordained by the Jaina Dharma. (45)
All castes likewise became such [as they were], having taken refuge in the Jaina Dharma; Brahmins were no longer honored, nor were rites for peace or prosperity performed.
At such a time, no one ever gives a gift; thus does time proceed. The Brahmins, though possessing royal edicts, have their ownership lost day and night.
With their minds deeply agitated, they approached the king at Āmā, the hero residing in Kānyakubja who was surrounded by heretics.
O King, having reached the city of Kānyakubja after some days, those exhausted Moḍha Brāhmaṇas took up residence on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Those who had been informed by the spies arrived before the king; the Brahmins, summoned in the morning, came into the royal assembly.
The king did not respectfully rise or offer salutations to the brahmins; instead, he merely questioned all of them as they stood there. (51)
"For what purpose have you Brahmins come? Tell me, what is the business at hand?"
The Brahmins said: "O lord of men, we have come here from Dharmāraṇya into your presence. O King, Kumārapālaka shall be the husband of your daughter. (53)
By him, acting according to the Jaina dharma and impelled by Indrasūri, the great and wonderful teaching of the Brahmins was utterly destroyed. (54)
The king said: "By whom indeed were you established in this city of Moheraka? O Brahmins, tell me all this account exactly as it happened."
The Brahmins said: "In former times, it was established by Brahmā, Īśa, and the wise Dharmarāja; and thereafter, the city was built here in this auspicious place by Rāma."
O best of kings, having seen this edict of Rāmacandra, it has indeed been protected according to dharma by other kings as well. (57)
"Now your son-in-law does not protect the brahmins at all. Having heard those words of the brahmin, the king then spoke to the brahmins.
"O Brahmins, go quickly indeed; by my command, let them say: 'O King Kumārapāla, you must give the Brāhmaṇa settlement. (59)
Having heard those words, the brahmins then attained supreme joy; exceedingly delighted, they departed from there after the message had been delivered.
Having heard his father-in-law's words, King Kumārapāla spoke these words: "O Brahmins, I shall certainly not uphold the command of Rāma. (61)
I renounce the Brahmins at the sacrifice who are intent upon the injury of animals; therefore, O twice-born ones, let there be no devotion for me toward those who are violent.
The Brāhmaṇas said: O best of kings, how is it that you, whose royal authority has been subverted by heretical doctrines, continue to rule? Do not set your mind upon such sin!
The king said: Non-violence is the supreme dharma; non-violence is the supreme austerity; non-violence is the supreme knowledge; non-violence is the supreme fruit. (64)
In grasses and indeed in trees, in winged insects and in men, in worms such as bedbugs and the like, and in goats, horses, and elephants—|| 65 ||
O Brahmins, among spiders, serpents, buffaloes, and the like, as well as among creatures both minute and large, they are indeed similar.
"How is it that you proceed, O Brahmins, being devoted to violence? Having heard those words, which were like a thunderbolt, the best of the twice-born [replied].
All the Brahmins replied, their eyes red with anger, as they glared at him.
The Brāhmaṇas said: "Non-violence is the supreme dharma; this which has been spoken by you is true. Nevertheless, there is another dharma as well—listen with a one-pointed mind. (69)

The conclusion is that violence ordained by the Vedas is not truly violence; for even when one is struck with a weapon, the suffering that arises in living beings [is not the same as that caused by Vedic rites]. (70)
O best among those who know the dharma, that very thing is indeed unrighteousness in this world: that living beings are slain by Vedic mantras without the use of weapons. (71)
Indeed, that which causes pain to living beings is never a source of happiness; helping others leads to merit, while harming others leads to sin. (72)
"Even after performing violence prescribed by the Vedas, one is not tainted by sins. Having heard the words of the Brahmins, he spoke these words again: || 73 ||
The King said: Dharmāraṇya is the supreme and unsurpassed field of Brahmā and the other gods; yet now those [deities] such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the rest are not present here. (74)
No dharma exists here, nor is Rāma said to be human; where indeed is that long-tailed one who was released for your protection? (75)
"If you have not seen the teaching, then I shall certainly not protect it. Then the twice-born, overcome with anger, gave this reply. (76)
The twice-born said: "O fool, how do you know this? You speak thus because you are intoxicated by pride; he [was born] for the destruction of the Daityas and for the protection of dharma. (77)

Rāma, the four-armed one, has personally descended to the earth in human form; he is the giver of refuge to those who have no refuge, devoted to righteousness, compassionate, merciful, and the protector of all living beings.
The king said: "Where is Rāma today? Where indeed is the son of Vāyu? All of them have vanished like clouds; where are Rāma and Hanumān? (79)
But if Rāma and Hanumān were present everywhere, my mind would think that assistance from the Brahmins would come now. (80)
"Show us Hanumān, or Rāma, or likewise Lakṣmaṇa; O Brahmins, if there is any proof whatsoever, let it be shown to us. (81)
It was said by Rāmadeva, having made the son of Añjanī his messenger: "O King, one hundred and forty-four villages have been granted. (62)
Having returned, thirteen villages were granted at this site; and at Kāśyapī and on the Gaṅgā, sixteen great gifts (mahādānas) were bestowed.
O hero, very beautiful villages were given to the foremost of Brahmins; furthermore, fifty-six [villages] were resolved upon once again.
And thirty-six thousand excellent Gobhujas were born; one hundred and twenty-five thousand merchants were given the title of Māṇḍalika.
He said: "O all you brahmins, show me indeed the son of the Wind (Hanumān), by the mere recognition of whom I shall grant him his former status. (86)
If proof is shown, I shall perform the word of the Brahmins; then all will become devoted to the dharma of the Vedas. || 87 ||
"Otherwise, conduct yourselves in every way according to the Jaina dharma. Having heard the king's words, they returned to their respective places. (88)
The Vāḍavas, their minds distressed and blinded by anger, stood upon the earth sighing and crying out, "Alas! Alas! (89).
Rubbing all their teeth together and squeezing hand against hand, they spoke to one another, "What shall we do from here? (90)
Having assembled, all the Vāḍavas held an excellent consultation, meditating upon the words of Rāma in their hearts and likewise upon the son of Añjanā.
The children, and even those who were the eldest, held a gathering of the twice-born; then the eldest brahmin among them spoke these auspicious words.
Of our sixty-four clans, there are seventy-two; each clan has its own insignia and speaks only of its own village. (93)
Let one wise brahmin from each respective group proceed to Rāmeśvara on the Setubandha; Hanumān resides there. (94)
May they all go there, to the side of Rāma, free from ailment, abstaining from food, having conquered anger, and furthermore, devoid of illusion.
With one-pointed minds, let everyone praise, meditate upon, and recite that [mantra]. Then, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, having shown compassion toward the twice-born, [will grant their desires]. 96.
And he will bestow an unshakeable teaching in age after age; being pleased by great austerity, he will grant whatever is desired.
Whichever member of a group does not go where the Brahmin goes, he should undoubtedly be expelled from that group, for he has violated the dharma of his station. 98.
They have no connection in the conduct of trade, nor ever in marriage; they have no connection in the affairs of the village; they are excluded from every station.
Having heard those words of the assembly, the pure Vāḍava, eloquent, skillful, and well-versed in grammar, caused the twice-born to hear [his speech] three times with distinct sounds.

Standing there, clapping his hands at every sentence, he spoke these words: "Whatever sin belongs to those who speak untruth, to those who revile others, to the man who approaches another's wife, and to the man intent on harming others; [may that sin be mine]. (1)

Whatever sin exists among those who drink liquor, and whatever sin exists among those who steal gold—that same sin shall belong to him who turns his face away from going [to her]. Now, what is the use of much speaking? O best of the twice-born, let them go to Satya.
Having heard those harsh words, he set his mind on departing. Hearing that those twice-born ones were leaving, King Kumārapālaka [acted].
"Having summoned [them], I shall undoubtedly cause the fruits of my labor—whether from agriculture or from wandering for alms—to reach Brāhmaṇas of various lineages."
Hearing that, they were all distressed, wondering what would happen thereafter; thus, three thousand of them then formed a league.
"We shall all go toward Rāma, there is no doubt; indeed, the Brahmins have already exchanged hand-written signatures with one another. (6)
Then the Brahmins, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words: "The knowledge of the three Vedas perishes here, and the Embodiment of the Three Vedas becomes enraged. (7)
Therefore, eighteen thousand [people] must go to that very place; then he summoned all those cowherd merchants.
The best of kings spoke these words: "Restrain the twice-born! || 9 ||
Vyāsa said: Those best of merchants, the Gobhujas, were not stained by the Jaina dharma; out of fear of the loss of their livelihood, they maintained a strict silence regarding it.
"O King, how can we ward off the brahmins who are like fire? By the fire of their curse, the twice-born will be intent on death. (11)
The king summoned those Śūdras who were born in the Āḍāla villages and said to the Brāhmaṇas who were preparing to depart, "Let them be excluded. (12)
Among them, a few who had taken refuge in the Jaina faith went to the groups of Brahmins at the king's command to prevent [the slaughter].
Some Śūdras said: "Where is Rāma accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, and where is the mighty son of Vāyu? O best of the twice-born, this must be told according to the present time. (14)
In a forest infested with tigers and lions, a wilderness inhabited by wild elephants, they abandoned their dear lives, sons, wives, and homes. (15)
"For what purpose, O brahmins, do you go to that kingdom indeed ruled by a wicked sovereign? Having heard that, some of the brāhmaṇas reflected upon those words in their minds.
Those fifteen thousand Vāḍavas [received it] from that best of kings; out of fear, greed, and the desire for gifts, he said, "Let all this be yours. (17)
"By means of preparing our livelihood alone, we shall at some time perform agricultural work, or perhaps go about begging for alms. (18)
Then those fifteen thousand best of the twice-born spoke these harsh words to them: "Let the others go as is appropriate. (19)
"May the teaching granted by Rāma be yours, without a doubt; all of you shall be renowned as the foremost among the Vāḍavas, masters of the three Vedas. (120)
And there were certainly three thousand who were masters of the three Vedas. || 21 ||
The king said: "The kingdom and a portion of the earth were given with a fourth part; therefore, it is known as 'fourfold' (caturvidha), and beyond that is the bond of kinsmen."
"Cyavana will give away his daughter; you all shall obtain a daughter. Neither livelihood nor kinship shall ever belong to you. (23)
Having heard these words of his, all the brāhmaṇas learned in the three Vedas departed for their respective places, without returning from their agreement.
Then fifteen thousand of those bulls among the twice-born, all of them excellent brahmins learned in the four Vedas, departed by the same way they had come. (25)
Having passed that day with a mind filled with anxiety, they were restrained by their sons and by their wives who were full of humility.
With their minds one-pointed, they all found no sleep; having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, they indeed abandoned worldly illusion.
Having abandoned their beloved sons, wives, and even their dwellings, all those eminent brāhmaṇas gathered together at the outskirts of the village.
Then, having performed the daily rites three thousand times, he gave sacrificial fees to the Brahmins and worshipped the Mother of the Family.
Stationed at the southern gate for the destruction of the assembly of Brahmins, the Leader of the Gaṇas was worshipped with vermilion and flower garlands. || 130 ||
Bakulasvāmī, the accomplisher of all goals through the sun, was worshipped; likewise, the Great Power, Śrīmātā, was worshipped with reverence.
Having paid homage to Śāntā, who was born of knowledge and the mother of their lineage, they attained supreme joy as they prepared for their departure.
The twice-born masters of the four Vedas, having addressed them once more, repeatedly asked them the entire reason for their arrival.
The Brahmins said: "You must certainly not go; or, having gone, return with all speed. (34)
"Just as you have prepared that which was indeed given by Rāma, so shall it be accomplished without delay. Having heard this, those best of the twice-born, masters of the four Vedas, spoke again.
Neither by reason of our station, nor by our being twice-born, nor in any way because of our livelihood shall we come again; this must certainly not be told to others once more.
"O best of the twice-born, a livelihood has indeed been granted to you by the scion of Raghu; we shall attend to that livelihood through prayers, burnt offerings, worship, and other such rites. (37)
Those fifteen thousand spoke again with respect: "We must remain here, devoted to the service of the fire. (38)
"You all must go there for the accomplishment of everyone's purpose; we shall provide mutual assistance to one another, of this there is no doubt. (39)
"You will abandon your own words and become devoid of livelihood. Then, from among them, a certain scholar of the four Vedas said: ||| 140 ||
Cāturvidya said: "O twice-born ones, Rāma indeed previously granted us our livelihood—those of us who are masters of the four Vedas, possessed of great courage, and upholders of our own duty."
"Engaged in officiating at sacrifices and teaching, you were created by the Lord of Kāśī; yet, after giving you a gift, Rāma indeed spoke to you again: 42.
"One must not depart from one's place; such indeed was the rule established. However, in times of calamity, the mighty son of Vāyu should be remembered. (43)
"Since they were previously established by Rāma in their own positions, how could they now go back on that word of Rāma and act otherwise? (44)
Therefore, we say to you: "Go for the accomplishment of your task; for the sake of accomplishing your purpose, we shall perform oblations, worship, and other rites. (45)
"Success in the task shall be achieved instantly; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. Having heard these words, those twice-born ones then set out on their journey.
Having first made their preparations for the journey, those best of the twice-born then set out from there; three thousand in number, they directed their minds toward departure.

Having traveled from country to country and from forest to forest, performing śrāddha ceremonies at every sacred ford (tīrtha), those virtuous ones, devoted to the vow of truth, traveled a long distance seeking a vision of Hanumān. (150)
They constantly performed their twilight devotions at the three times of day with single-minded concentration; as they proceeded in this manner, auspicious omens appeared to them.
As they were traveling in this manner, their provisions for the journey were then exhausted; all became weary and overcome with fatigue, yet they remained fixed upon the supreme goal.
Having traversed some distance, they were no longer able to take another step; yet, having made a firm resolve in their minds and steadied their hearts, they continued on. (53)
"Without having seen the mantra, we shall not go home; let the three Vedas go to that place where Rāmeśvara Hari resides. (54)
Firm in their vows and devoted to truth, subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits, they meditated upon "Rāma, Rāma" and again upon "Hanumān."
Having undertaken their vow and likewise renounced both food and water, they, devoted to their religious observance, departed though afflicted by thirst and hunger.
While the twice-born were thus being afflicted, Rāma, who was a vessel of devotion and whose mind was deeply distressed, then spoke to Hanumān.
"Go quickly for the sake of the twice-born, O son of the Wind, you who know the dharma; all the Brahmins dwelling in Dharmāraṇya are suffering. (58)
My mind is burning today; there is no peace for me otherwise. One who causes suffering to Brahmins must be punished; of this there is no doubt. (59)
"O monkey, I am indeed distressed because those brahmins are distressed. (160)
Having heard Rāma’s words and having paid homage to the descendant of Raghu, the Lord of Monkeys appeared, filled with supreme compassion.
In the form of an old Brahmin, for the purpose of testing the twice-born, he spoke with supreme devotion to the Brahmins who were weakened by fatigue.
Having joined his palms in reverence and set down his water-pot from his hand, he then saluted them all in return and spoke these words: || 63 ||
From what place have you arrived here, and where indeed do you wish to go? For what purpose are you all traveling to this dreadful forest? (64)
The brahmins said: "O twice-born ones, we have come from Dharmāraṇya to report our own suffering; indeed, we desire to go for the sake of seeing Rāma."
At Setubandha, the great holy ford that grants all desires, those established in their vows, with emaciated bodies, were eager to behold Rāma. (66)
"Where the god Rāmeśvara resides, there is the monkey, the son of Vāyu himself. Having heard that, the twice-born man said: "Where is Rāma, and where is the son of Vāyu? (67)

"O twice-born ones, where is Rāmeśa at Setubandha? It is far, far away, O brahmins! There is a vast, most terrible, and fierce forest, teeming with tigers and lions; once one has gone there, those who depend on it do not return. Turn back, O illustrious ones, if indeed my word is to be heeded. (69)
"Or rather, you may go, O Brahmins; live long and be happy. Having heard those words of the elder, the Vāḍavas became of one mind.
"O Brahmin, let us all go without doubt to the side of Rāma; even if one should die on this path, they would attain the world of Rāma. (71)
O Lord Rāma, one attains a means of livelihood; of this there is no doubt. Otherwise, there is no refuge for us except for Rāghava. (72)
Having spoken thus, they all departed, intent on seeing Rāma; then, after the end of the day had passed, at the clear dawn, [they returned].
Hanumān, assuming the form of a Brahmin, was an elderly man endowed with former virtues; the wise one carried a water-pot and was intent upon offering salutations.
"O Brahmins, from what place have you all come here? Where is this great gain, or perhaps a wedding festival? (75)
Having heard these words of his, the Brahmins were filled with wonder; with great respect, they made a formal representation preceded by prostrations. (76)
But listen, O god of the earth, to our great and wondrous past account, since you appear to us as one who is compassionate. (77)
At the beginning, at the commencement of creation, we were established by Keśava; indeed, we were established as the triad of forms (trimūrti) by Śiva and Brahmā as well. (78)
Thereafter, they were re-established by Śrī Rāma through the restoration of the ruins; and Harirāja respectfully granted a salary for the villages.
Four hundred and forty-four villages, including Sītāpura, were granted for the purpose of worship. || 180 ||
And thirty-six thousand merchants for the protection of the twice-born; those Śūdras known as Gobhūjas numbered one hundred and twenty-five thousand from them. (81)
And they, O dear one, were born in three ways: those born from cows, those born from the earth, and likewise those born from Jāḍālas; these three types are indeed beautiful.
For the sake of their livelihood, he indeed gave them millions of priceless jewels; at that time, those Moḍhas numbered eighteen thousand, as did the Gobhujas.
There are 125,000 Māṇḍalikas and 18,000 Aḍālajas. || 83 ||
Now, O best of Brahmins, a wicked-minded king named Āmōn does not honor the command of Rāmacandra. (84)
His son-in-law was indeed wicked, named Kumārapālaka; he was constantly surrounded by heretics and was devoted to the ways of the Kali age.
Urged by the Jaina Indrasūtra, who was a follower of the Buddhist faith, he indeed destroyed the teaching bestowed by Rāma; of this there is no doubt. (86)
Certain merchants became so intent upon him that they sought to dissuade Rāma and the highly intelligent Hanumān.
"O Brahmins, I am determined that I will not give [the gift] without a guarantee. Knowing this, these Brahmins sought refuge with Rāma. (88)
Therefore, O high-minded one, let us all go toward Rāma, to the great hero Hanumān, the executor of Rāma’s command.
"If Añjaneya does not grant us our desired object, we shall abandon our lives by means of a vow of fasting. (190)
We have explained this to you in detail because you asked; considering our affection for you, quickly reveal your own conduct.
Hanūmān said: "O Brahmins, when the Kali age has arrived, where can there be a vision of the gods? O best of Brahmins, turn back if you desire great happiness. (92)
In a forest teeming with tigers and lions, desolate and inhabited by wild elephants, and pervaded by many forest fires, it is simply impossible to enter.
The Brahmins said: "O Brahmin, on the day before yesterday, one Brahmin spoke this; today you have arrived and speak in exactly the same way. (94)
"Who are you in the form of a Vāḍava? Are you Rāma or perhaps the son of the Wind? O great twice-born one, having shown compassion toward us, tell us the truth. (95)
Hanumān spoke that which had been concealed before the foremost of the twice-born: "O Brahmins, know for certain that I am indeed Hanumān. (96)
Having manifested his true form, he displayed his great tail.
Hanūmān said: "This is the ocean itself, the delightful Setubandha; this is the Lord Rāmeśvara, who brings about the destruction of dwelling in the womb. (98)
This excellent city, renowned by the name of Laṅkā, is where Sītā—who removes the grief of Rāma—was found by me. (99)
O best of the twice-born, at the tip of my forefinger shines that golden city, which is inaccessible to others except for me, and within which Vibhīṣaṇa rules his kingdom.
This great city of Laṅkā was established by Lord Rāma, and it has been visited by groups of holy men observing vows on the occasion of their pilgrimage.
Having brought the waters of the Gaṅgā and having consecrated Rāmeśa, these great burdens were cast away and are now seen within the ocean.
By that [act], they became sinless, virtuous, and firm in their vows; indeed, when merit arises, increase occurs, and when there is sin, loss occurs.

In former times, the twice-born masters of the four Vedas were deprived of their positions; however, by Rāma, through the restoration of what was decayed, they were indeed established once again. O Brahmins, in a previous birth, worship of Hari was performed by me. (204)
Now, indeed, unwavering devotion is seen in your service to me; therefore, gratified by the power of that merit, I shall grant you a boon.
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, and I am fortunate upon this earth; today my birth has become fruitful and my life well-lived. (206)
That I have come into the presence of the feet of the Brahmins. || 207 ||
Vyāsa said: As soon as they beheld Hanumān, their bodies bristling with horripilation, those masters of speech spoke these words with voices choked with emotion. (208)

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Meeting with Hanumān," in the *Dharmāraṇya-māhātmya* of the third section, the *Brahmakhaṇḍa*, within the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 36 ||
Vyāsa said: Then all those brahmins replied to the son of the Wind-god: "Now our birth has become fruitful and our life well-lived. (1)
Today, for us people of Moḍha, our dharma and our homes are indeed blessed; and the entire earth is blessed, for there are many sacrificial rites and religious duties. || 2 ||
Salutations to the devotee of Śrī Rāma and to the destroyer of Akṣa; salutations to the one who set the city of the Rākṣasas ablaze and who wields the thunderbolt.
To the one who protects the heart of Jānakī, whose very nature is compassion, and who is dear to Śrī Rāma, who was tormented by separation from Sītā; (4)
Homage be to you, O Great Hero; protect us as we sink into the earth! Homage to the god of the Brahmins; homage to you, the son of Vāyu. || 5 ||

Salutations be to you, O Rāma, who are devoted to your devotees and who work for the welfare of cows and Brahmins; salutations to you, whose form is that of Rudra and whose face is dark as the darkness.
Salutations always to the son of Añjanī, the remover of all diseases, who wears a serpent as a sacred thread; salutations be to you, the powerful one.
To him who crossed the ocean himself and caused the construction of the bridge.
Vyāsa said: Pleased by this very hymn of praise, the son of Vāyu spoke these words: "Listen, O Brahmins, to the boon that is pleasing to your hearts. (9)
The Brahmins said: "O Lord of gods, O Master who obeys the command of Rāma, if you are pleased, show us your true form today; O Hari, reveal what has been done in Laṅkā."
In that same way, you shall today utterly destroy the sinful king Kumārapāla, who is wicked, as well as Āma himself; of this there is no doubt. (11)
"Act accordingly so that you may immediately incur the fruit of losing your livelihood; O mighty-armed one, tell us why you delay, even for the sake of our conviction. (12)
"O Hero, by giving with a sincere heart, that king shall partake in merit; once the proof is shown, he will uphold the teaching. (13)
"The triple Vedic dharma shall indeed attain expansion upon the earth; O steadfast in dharma, O great hero, reveal your true form to us. (14)
Hanumān said: "O Brāhmaṇas, know that my own form, which is of great body, divine, and consisting of a mass of splendor, is not within the range of sight in the Kali age. (15)
Nevertheless, being pleased by your supreme devotion and your hymns of praise, I shall reveal my form veiled by a garment; behold! (16)
Thus addressed, the brahmins, eager to accomplish all their tasks, [beheld] one of great form, great body, and possessed of a massive tail.
Seeing Hanumān in his divine form, they rejoiced; then, somehow summoning their courage, the brahmins spoke slowly and softly. (18)
Indeed, exactly as it is stated in the Purāṇas, so it is seen there; for he spoke to all of them as they stood with their eyes covered.
"O lords of sages, take these fruits for the purpose of eating; for when these have been consumed, O brahmins, there will indeed be complete satisfaction."
Without the forest of Dharma, your hunger will surely be appeased by this [food] today. || 21 ||
Vyāsa said: Then, overcome by hunger, those brahmins indeed consumed fruits; it was like the tasting of nectar, and they attained satisfaction.
O King, the brahmins, their minds afflicted by thirst and hunger, suddenly became possessed by wonder, their hearts filled with amazement.
Then, O twice-born ones, when the Kali age had arrived, the son of Añjanī said: "I shall not go there, leaving behind Śiva Rāmeśvara."
"I have given you this token; taking it, go there. There is no doubt that the truth of this will be recognized by that king. (25)
Having spoken thus, he raised both his arms and, gathering the hairs from each one separately, formed them into two small bundles.

She granted the fulfillment of desires to the devotee of Rāma while causing the destruction of others; and when the king said, "Let a sign be given," she spoke.
Then let the packet produced from the left armpit be given quickly; or else, throw the packet at the gate of that king.
It will set that army ablaze, as well as the palace and the treasury; the queens, the sons, and everything else shall become consumed by fire.
But when the Brāhmaṇas shall grant the means of subsistence, the villages, the taxes of the merchants, and whatever else was previously established. (31)
Having written it down and made a firm resolve, he should then give it as before; and when the king has joined his palms in reverence, he should prostrate himself.
O best of the twice-born, having previously obtained the means of subsistence granted by Rāma, this small packet of hair from his right armpit was then [given].
"Then let the army be cast [into the fire], and it shall become as it was before; likewise the houses, the treasury, and the sons, grandsons, and so forth. (34)
"They are seen to be released from the fire at that very moment. Having heard these supreme words, full of nectar, spoken by Hanumān, [they were filled with joy]. (35)
The Brahmins attained joy; they danced and sang loudly. Some shouted cries of victory, while others laughed at one another. (36)
With their entire bodies covered in horripilation, they praised him again and again; some, filled with longing, took hold of his tail and kissed it.
One says, "My task must certainly be accomplished with effort," while another says, "O illustrious one, this has already been done by me. (68)
Then Hanumān said: "O Brahmins, stay here for three nights so that you may obtain the fruit of Rāmatīrtha."
Having said, "So be it," those Brahmins then performed the Brahma-yajña; by that great sound of Vedic recitation, the forest was rendered deaf.
Having stayed for three nights, those brahmins, having resolved to depart, spoke these words with great devotion before Hanumān during the night: || 41 ||
The Brāhmaṇas said: "We shall go tomorrow morning to the perfectly pure Dharmāraṇya; we must not be forgotten by you, O dear one—forgive us, forgive us! (42)
Then, O King, the son of Vāyu [Hanumān] took from the mountain a great rock and a massive four-winged palace, ten yojanas in length.
Having spread [the grass] upon a stone slab, O best of the twice-born, he said to those brahmins: "O brahmins, being protected by me, sleep here free from all anxiety. (44)
Having heard this, they all then attained a blissful sleep; thus, having accomplished their purpose, they slept at the onset of night. (45)
And that compassionate one, whose nature is Rudra and who is the protector of Rāma’s command, remained upon the surface of the earth for the sake of protecting the brahmins. (46)
Vyāsa said: When midnight had arrived, everyone had fallen asleep; he then made a request to his father, saying, "May you be gracious to me. (47)

Cacāī was of the Vatsa lineage, and Śāntā was born of the Kutsa lineage; by these three and five [others], the twice-born were of the nature of Brahman.
They were peaceful, self-controlled, and of excellent character, endowed with wealth and sons; though devoid of Vedic study, they were skilled in all activities. (70)
Handsome, of virtuous conduct, and established in all dharmas, all the twice-born born here are givers of water and devoted to the duty of charity. (71)
Thus ends the fifth point. 5.
Those born in the Śerathā villages are indeed endowed with two *pravara*s: Kuśa and Bhāradvāja, as well as the two goddesses.
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and the third, Dala; likewise Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja. (73)
Kamalā is Mahālakṣmī, and likewise the second is Yakṣiṇī; those wise ones born in this lineage are devoted to the Śrauta and Smārta rites. (74)

Those who are habituated to the study of the Vedas, ascetics who subdue their enemies, yet are wrathful, greedy, wicked, and devoted to performing sacrifices for themselves or for others—all such Brāhmaṇas are described by me as belonging to the sixth station. Thus ends the sixth station.
The Dantālīyas, as well as the Bhāradvājas, Kutsas, and Śāyās; likewise, the Āṅgirasas, Bārhaspatyas, and Bhāradvājas. (76)
The goddess is called Yakṣiṇī, and the second is Karmalā; those born in this lineage are Brāhmaṇas who are wealthy and auspicious.
Adorned with garments and ornaments, they were all devoted to the service of the twice-born; all were intent on feeding the Brahmins and all were dedicated to righteousness.
Thus ends the seventh station. || 7 ||
In the lineage of Vaḍodrīya, four pravaras are recorded: Kuśa, Kutsa, Vatsa, and likewise Bhāradvāja. (79)
I shall declare their pravaras as well as their lineages (gotras) in due order: Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and thirdly Audala. (80)
Āṅgirasa, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva as the third; Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and likewise Jamadagni. (81)
Likewise, there were Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja; as well as Karmalā, Kṣemalā, and Dhārabhaṭṭārikā. || 82 ||
The fourth is declared to be Kṣemalā, the mother of the lineage in due order; those born in this lineage are always devoted to the five great sacrifices.
Those who are greedy and wrathful give birth to many offspring; they are constantly devoted to bathing, giving gifts, and other such rites, with their senses always fully subdued. (84)
There were thousands of makers of step-wells, wells, and tanks; they observed vows and possessed good character, yet they were ignorant and devoid of Vedic knowledge. (85)
Thus ends the eighth section. 8.
In the village named Godaṇīya, two families belonging to the Gotra lineages resided there: the first was of the Vatsa Gotra, and the second was of the Bhāradvāja Gotra. (86)
Bhṛgu, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Purodhasa—these are to be known as the first Śīharīs; likewise, Yakṣiṇī is the second. || 87 ||
The Brahmins born in this lineage will be endowed with wealth and grain, yet they will be full of resentment, devoid of greed, and likewise hateful and crooked.
O King, those who are violent and greedy for wealth have been described by me. (89)
Thus ends the ninth station. 9.
In the village of Kaṇṭavāḍīā, there are Brāhmaṇas of the Kuśa gotra, born of the Śuklaśuś clan. O best of kings, I shall state their pravara; listen to it. (90)
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and Uddālaka are remembered as the three; that goddess is called Cācāī—listen to this, O best of kings. (91)
There, the Brāhmaṇas—skilled in all branches of knowledge, speakers of truth, and possessed of joyful hearts and single-minded focus—perform sacrifices with various rites. (92)
Thus ends the tenth station. 10.
O best of kings, listen as I describe the Vekhaloyas, who were born in the lineage of Kutsa and are endowed with three *pravara*s. (93)
Viśvāmitra, Devarāja, and Audala—these three are remembered; Cacāī Devī is indeed remembered as the protectress of their lineage. (94)
And there were high-souled Brāhmaṇas, endowed with courage and possessed of virtues, as well as ascetics and yogis who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
The virtuous, who follow right conduct and are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, are constantly intent on ritual bathing and the twilight prayers, and are dedicated to feeding the Brahmins.
I have described this lineage; now listen to what follows from here.
Thus ends the eleventh section. 11.
Those who are declared to be Dehaloḍīyas are endowed with the Kutsa Pravara; [the three pravaras are] Āṅgirasa, Āmbarīṣa, and Yuvanāśva as the third. || 98 ||
I have declared that the family deity (gotradevī) is Śrī Śeṣadurbalā; and those born in the Kutsa lineage who are of good conduct and speakers of truth, [should worship her]. || 99 ||
They are habituated to the study of the Vedas, yet they look only for the faults of others; full of resentment, lacking in self-control due to greed, they are likewise hateful and crooked. (100)
Those who are violent, greedy for wealth, and those born of the Kutsa lineage; || 1 ||
Thus ends the twelfth station. 12.
And the Brāhmaṇas of the Koṣṭha lineage are said to be endowed with three gotras: Bhāradvāja, Vatsa, and the third is Kuśa. || 2 ||
I shall likewise declare the most eminent [lineages] according to the order of their *gotras*: Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Jamadagni. (3)
The third pravara is Kuśa-pravara, and there are indeed three pravaras: Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and the third is Audala.
The first yakṣiṇī is proclaimed [as such], and the second is likewise Śīhurī; the third is proclaimed as Cacāī, born of their respective lineages in due order.
The Brahmins born in this lineage are wise, devoted to the Śrauta and Smārta rites, habituated to the study of the Vedas, ascetics, and subduers of enemies.

Angry, greedy, and wicked, yet devoted to performing sacrifices for themselves and for others—all these have been declared by me to be the best of the twice-born who are intent upon the duties of Brahmins. (7)
Thus ends the thirteenth station. 13.
Those born in Cāndanakheda are descended from Bhāradvāja; their gotras are Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and thirdly, Bhāradvāja.
And the wise Vyāsa has declared that his goddess is indeed Yakṣiṇī; as for those twice-born ones born of Bhāradvāja, they are of the very nature of Brahman.
In Dharmāraṇya there were excellent brahmins, peaceful, self-controlled, virtuous, endowed with wealth and sons, and skilled in the performance of sacrificial rites.
All those devoted to devotion for the guru illuminate their own lineage.
Thus ends the fourteenth topic. 14.
And those born in Thalagrāma are descended from Bhāradvāja; Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja as the third. || 12 ||
And those who are born in this lineage are Vāḍavas, wealthy and auspicious, endowed with garments and ornaments, and devoted to the service of the twice-born. || 13 ||
All were devoted to the food of Brahman, and all were dedicated to righteousness; the family deity I have proclaimed is the Yakṣiṇī named Rakṣiṇī.
Thus ends the fifteenth station. 15.
And those who were born of Moūtrī have two lineages (gotras) proclaimed therein: Bhāradvāja and Kaśyapa; likewise, there are two goddesses. || 15 ||
Cāmuṇḍā and Yakṣiṇī are proclaimed here as the goddesses; Kaśyapa, Avatsāra, and Naidhruva is the third.
The first was Āṅgirasa, the second Bārhaspatya, and the third Bhāradvāja; they were pleasant in speech, greatly capable, and always devoted to their preceptor. || 17 ||
Those twice-born Kāśyapas who are always established [in virtue] and devoted to the welfare of all beings perform the great sacrifices.
Those who perform sacrifices for all people are remembered as the most excellent among officiating priests.
Thus ends the sixteenth station. 16.
Those born in the Hastijaṇa [gotra], as well as the Vatsas and Bhāradvājas, and Jñānajā and Yakṣiṇī—these are proclaimed as the two family deities (gotradevīs). 120.
And those born in this lineage who are always devoted to the five sacrifices—though they may be greedy and prone to anger—are possessed of many offspring and are deeply learned. || 21 ||

They were devoted to bathing, giving gifts, and other such rites, and were entirely dedicated to devotion to Viṣṇu; they observed vows and possessed virtuous conduct, yet they were ignorant of the knowledge of qualities and devoid of Vedic learning.
Thus ends the seventeenth station. 17.
The Brāhmaṇas born in Kapaḍvāṇa are the Bhāradvājas and the Kuśas; the goddess is said to be Yakṣiṇī, and the second is Cacāī. || 23 ||
Āṅgirasa and Bārhaspatya, Bhāradvāja as the third; Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and Audala as the third. || 24 ||
And those born in this lineage are speakers of truth, victorious in their vows, masters of their senses, handsome, moderate in diet, and fair of countenance. (25)
They were ever-vigilant, knowers of the Purāṇas, devoted to great acts of charity, free from hatred yet possessed of desire, and intent upon the study of the Vedas. || 26 ||
They were far-sighted, possessed of great splendor, and deluded by the Great Māyā. || 27 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth point. 18.
The Janhorī Vāḍavas are said to be endowed with the Kuśa pravara; Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and the third is Audala. (28)
Tāraṇī, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), is proclaimed as the family deity; O King, in this lineage were born the Vāḍavas, who were difficult to withstand.
Extremely fierce, large-bodied, long-limbed, and highly arrogant, they have the form of afflictions (*kleśa*), are black in color, and are experts in all the scriptures.
The Brāhmaṇas, who were exponents of the Veda, were eaters of much food, wealthy, skillful, and free from hatred and sin; though possessing beautiful garments and ornaments, they appeared deformed.
This is the nineteenth point. || 19 ||
And those who were born of Vanoḍī have exactly three lineages (gotras): Kuśa and Kutsa are the two pravaras, and Bhāradvāja is the third.
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and the third, Audala; Āṅgirasa, Āmbarīṣa, and the third, Yuvanāśva. || 33 ||
Likewise, there are the Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja [gotras]. Śeṣalā is declared to be the first, and Śāntā is the second.
The third is Dhāraśānti, and then the lineage goddesses (gotradevīs) in due order. Those born in this lineage who are weak and dejected in mind— || 35 ||

O best of kings, those Brahmins who speak untruths and are greedy, though they may be skilled in all branches of knowledge and most eminent among the knowers of the Veda, [are not true Brahmins]. (36)
Thus ends the twentieth point. || 20 ||
The place called Kīṇāvācanaka consists of twenty-one [villages]; the eminent Brahmins there are the Bhāradvājas, who are declared to be auspicious Brāhmaṇas. || 37 ||
Āṅgirasa, Vārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja, as well as the goddess Yakṣiṇī, are proclaimed to be the family deities (gotradevīs). || 38 ||
And those born in this lineage who are Brahmins—wealthy, auspicious, endowed with garments and ornaments, and devoted to the service of the twice-born; || 39 ||
All were devoted to the feeding of Brahmins, and all were dedicated to righteousness.
This is the twenty-first point. || 21 ||
And those best of Brahmins who were born in their own place as Govindanas, their lineage is declared to be Kuśa, with three pravaras. || 41 ||
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and Audala are the pravaras; and Cacaī is proclaimed as the great goddess, the deity of the lineage (gotradevī). || 42 ||
