And those Brāhmaṇas born in this lineage, who know the Veda, perform sacrifices there with joyful hearts and single-minded devotion. || 43 ||
They were skilled in all branches of knowledge, devoted to Brahman, and the foremost among those who know Brahman. || 44 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second point. 22.
For the best of Brahmins born in Thalati reside in two lineages; indeed, there are these two lineages: Dhāraṇa and Saṃkuśa.
Agastya, Dārḍhyacyuta, and Rathyavāhana; Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and the third, Audala. || 46 ||
The goddess Chatrajā is said to be the first, and Thala-jā is the second; those born in the Dhāraṇa lineage are devoted to Brahman and are the best among the knowers of Brahman.
They were renowned as belonging to three lineages (tripravaras), full of courage, and endowed with virtues; and those born in their lineage were devoted to righteous deeds. || 48 ||
The wealthy and those devoted to knowledge, engaged in austerities, sacrifices, ritual acts, and so forth—this is declared as the twenty-third station for those of the Moḍhaka caste.
Thus ends the twenty-third topic. 23.

And those Brāhmaṇas who are declared to be perfected in self-restraint, who possess the highest knowledge and wealth of wisdom; and those learned men in this lineage who are speakers of truth and conquerors through their vows. (150)
They have conquered their senses, possess beautiful forms, eat little, and have auspicious countenances; they are ever-striving, knowers of the Purāṇas, and devoted to great acts of charity.
Free from hatred and devoid of greed, they were devoted to the study of the Vedas; they were far-sighted, possessed of great splendor, yet deluded by the great illusion (mahāmāyā). || 52 ||
The twenty-fourth is declared to be the supreme Svasthāna.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section. 24.
And here, indeed, the Brāhmaṇas born from the forehead are said to be speakers of truth. || 54 ||
I shall declare the five and three pravaras respectively for those two lineages, Vatsagotra and Kuśagotra: Bhṛgu, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Jamadagni.
Āṅgirasa, Auṃbarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva as the third; and here also are the two goddesses, Śāntā and Śeṣalā.
Born in this lineage were those of virtuous conduct and truthful speech; though they were peaceful, they were of mixed castes, impoverished, and clad in tattered rags. (57)
Proud, possessed of greed, yet firm in the Vedas and Shastras; this is declared as the twenty-fifth station for the Moḍha lineage. 58.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth position. || 25 ||
And those Brāhmaṇas who reside in Mahovīā, the most excellent knowers of Brahman, have but a single, pure lineage known as Kuśa.
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and the third, Audala, as well as the goddess Cāvāī, are stationed here in the form of protectors. || 160 ||
And those born in this lineage who are truthful, have conquered their senses, are devoted to the vow of truth, handsome, moderate in diet, and auspicious in appearance—[they shall dwell here]. (61)
Compassionate, merciful, and devoted to the welfare of all beings—this is declared to be the twenty-sixth abode of those who discourse upon Brahman.
And they were likewise praised by Rāma, as well as by his younger brother.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth station. 26.
Now, following the Tiyāśrīya, I shall describe the twenty-seventh station; and those Brāhmaṇas who are born in this station are masters of the Vedas.
And here the Śāṇḍilya gotra has been declared by the best of Vedic scholars; furthermore, five pravaras have been proclaimed, and Jñānajā is the deity here. 65.
Kāśyapa, Āvatsāra, Śāṇḍila, Uśanas, and Devala as the fifth—these are the ancestral lineages (pravara) respectively; and the goddess Jñānajā is declared to be the presiding deity of the site.
And those twice-born ones who were born in this lineage were all radiant like the sun, cool like the moon, and established in Dharmāraṇya.
O Great King, they were always of virtuous conduct, devoted to the Vedas and Shastras, performers of sacrifices, of auspicious behavior, and dedicated to truth and purity.

Those who know the Dharma, who are generous and virtuous, who are indeed stainless yet free from the intoxication of pride, who are devoted to austerity and sacred study, and who are dedicated to justice and righteousness—this is described by the best among the knowers of Brahman as the twenty-seventh station. (69)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh point. 27.
I shall now describe, in due order, those born of the Godharī lineage who were Brahmins most excellent in knowledge, as well as the three lineages.
The first is Dhāraṇasa, the second is Jātūkarṇa, and the third is Kauśika, according to their proper sequence.
Those born in the Dhāraṇa gotra are endowed with three pravaras: Agasti, Dārḍhacyuta, and the one named Idhmavāhana.
Vasiṣṭha, likewise Atri, and Jātūkarṇa as the third; Viśvāmitra, Mādhucchandasa, and Aghamarṣaṇa as the third. || 73 ||
Mahābalā, Māleyā, and the second Yakṣiṇī, and the third Mahāyogī—these are proclaimed as the deities of the Gotra. || 74 ||
And those Brahmins born in this lineage are speakers of truth, free from greed, performers of great sacrifices, and upholders of the Vedic injunctions. (75)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth topic. 28.
Those born at Vāṭastrahāla belong to three lineages (gotras). The first is to be known as Dhāraṇa, and the second is named Vatsa. || 76 ||
The third is named Kutsa, and likewise the lineage goddesses; first is Dhāraṇa of the same lineage, together with the three *pravara*s. (77)
Agasti, Dārḍhacyuta, and Idhmavāhana; these are indeed the five pravaras for the second group known as Vatsa.
Bhṛgu, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Jamadagni; likewise, the third is known as Kutsa—these indeed constitute the three *pravara* lineages. (79)
Āṅgirasa, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva as the third; and Devī Cacchatrajā, while Śeṣalā was the second. (180)
Jñānajā, Caiva, Devī, and Gotradevī follow in sequence; and those Brahmins in this lineage who are truthful in speech and have conquered their senses— || 81 ||
They were handsome and moderate in diet, devoted to great acts of charity; free from hatred yet possessed of greed, they were intent upon the study of the Vedas. || 82 ||
They were far-sighted, possessed of great splendor, like great meteors, and speakers of truth. || 83 ||
This is the twenty-ninth point. 29.
Māṇaja and Mahāsthāna, as well as the two lineages of Śāṇḍilya and Kuśa—these are declared to be the two [other] lineages. (84)
Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, Śāṇḍilya, Asita, and Devala as the fifth—these are proclaimed to belong to a single gotra. || 85 ||
And likewise, that very goddess Jñānajā is mentioned here; furthermore, there is the second lineage, Kuśa, with its three pravaras.
Viśvāmitra, Devarāja, and Tṛtīyodala; and here the goddess Jñānadā is proclaimed as the second. (87)
But those born in this lineage, O best of kings, are weak, dejected in mind, speakers of untruth, and greedy, O Brahmins. (88)
The Brahmins, most excellent among those devoted to Brahmā, are skilled in all branches of knowledge.
Thus ends the thirtieth point. 30.
And Sāṇadā is considered the supreme, most sacred place; the Brahmins dwelling there, born of the foremost lineage of Kuśas, are remembered as purifiers. (190)
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and Tṛtīyoda are [the sages]; and Jñānadā, the Great Goddess, is proclaimed as the family deity (gotradevī). || 91 ||
But those born in this lineage, O best of kings, are weak, dejected in mind, speakers of untruth, and greedy, O Brahmins. (92)
The Brahmins were skilled in all branches of knowledge and were the foremost among those who know Brahman.
This is the thirty-first point. 31.
Ānandīya is their *saṃsthāna*, and they possess two *gotras*: one named Bhāradvāja and the second Śāṇḍilya. || 94 ||
The lineage is Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja as the third; and the goddess Cacāī is proclaimed here as the deity of the clan (gotradevī). || 95 ||
Kāśyapa, Āvatsāra, Śāṇḍilya, Asita, and Devala as the fifth—these are the pravaras in their proper order.
And likewise, the goddess Jñānajā is declared to be the deity of the lineage (gotradevatā). Those born into this lineage are free from greed and possess pure minds. || 97 ||
The Brāhmaṇas, the foremost knowers of Brahman, were content with whatever they obtained by chance.
Thus ends the thirty-second point. 32.
Pāṭaḍīyā is proclaimed as the supreme and sacred place; here the lineage shall be Kuśa, endowed with three pravaras. || 99 ||
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and indeed Audala as the third; those born in this lineage are devoted to the Vedas and the Śāstras. (200)
And those brahmins, though arrogant with pride, were promoters of the path of justice. || 1 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third point. 33.
Ṭīkoliya is the supreme station, and likewise Kuśagotra; Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and thirdly Audala. (2)
Cacāī is indeed the goddess here, proclaimed as the deity of the lineage; the Brahmins born in this lineage are devoted to the Śruti and Smṛti.

Those who are diseased, greedy, and wicked, yet devoted to performing sacrifices for themselves or for others—all such people have been declared by me here to be "moḍhas," though they are intent on Vedic rites. || 4 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fourth point. 34.
The supreme station called Gamīdhāṇīya is indeed declared to be the thirty-fifth; herein lies Dhāraṇasa, and here also resides the goddess Mahābalā.
Agasti, Dārḍhacyuta, and those known as Idhmavāhana—these are the Brāhmaṇas born in this lineage who are devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
Free from greed and possessed of great wisdom, they were observers of the injunctions of the Vedas.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth section. 35.
The Mātrā is the supreme station, the purifier for all embodied beings; the Kuśa lineage is indeed pure, and it is established here as the highest.
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and Dala as the third; and Jñānadā, the Great Goddess, the sole protector of all the worlds. || 9 ||
Born in this lineage were Brahmins devoted to the gods, who performed the *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ* invocations and were propagators of the Vedas and the Shastras. (210)
Thus ends the thirty-sixth point. 36.
There is no place higher than Nātamora, which is pure, supreme, and auspicious; and there exists the Kuśa lineage, endowed with three pravaras.
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and the third, Audala; and here the goddess Jñānajā is proclaimed as the family deity (gotradevī). 12.

In this lineage, those who have been born—those Brahmins who are the foremost knowers of Brahman, who understand dharma, who speak the truth, and who are devoted to vows and charity—[have flourished]. (13)
Thus ends the thirty-seventh point. 37.
Balolā is a great site, pure and most wonderful; it is declared to belong to the Kuśa lineage and possesses three eminent branches.
The previously mentioned lineage and the goddess Mānadā are declared here to be the supreme ones in this dynasty, created by Kājeśa. (15)

O best of kings, those Brahmins who speak untruths and are greedy, though they may be proficient in all branches of knowledge and be the most excellent among the Brahmins, [are not true Brahmins]. (16)
Thus ends the thirty-eighth point. 38.
The Rājyajā lineage has Mahāsthāna as its *pravara*, while the Laugākṣa lineage likewise has three *pravara*s: Kāśyapa, Āvatsāra, and Vāsiṣṭha.
Bhadrā and Yoginī are proclaimed as the family deities (gotradevī); the Brāhmaṇas born in this lineage are devoted to the Vedas. 18.
They were devoted to daily bathing, daily fire-sacrifices, and daily giving; they delighted constantly in dharma and were intent upon regular and occasional rites.
This is the thirty-ninth point. || 39 ||
Rūpolā is the supreme abode, pure and bestowing great merit; and within these three lineages, there is indeed a triad of goddesses.
The first two were named Kutsa and Vatsa; the third was Bhāradvāja. Then there was Āṅgirasa and Ambarīṣa; the third was Yauvanāśva. (21)
Bhṛgu, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, Jagadagni, as well as Āṅgirasa, Vārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja. || 22 ||
Kṣemalā is indeed the goddess, and likewise Dhārabhaṭṭārikā; the third is called Kṣemalā, who is the lineage-mother in due order.
And those born in this lineage who are always devoted to the five sacrifices, though they may be greedy and prone to anger, are born with many offspring. (24)
They were always devoted to bathing, giving gifts, and other such rites, with their senses perpetually conquered; they were the makers of thousands of step-wells, wells, and tanks.
Thus ends the fortieth point. 40.
Bodhaṇī is the supreme place, pure and the destroyer of sins; there are also two lineages, namely Kuśa and Kauśika. (26)
Viśvāmitra, Prathama, Devarāta, Udalaka, as well as Viśvāmitra, Aghamarṣaṇa, and Kauśika. || 27 ||
The first is Yakṣiṇī, and the second is Tāraṇī; those born in this lineage are indeed weak and dejected in spirit. (28)

O best of kings, those Brahmins who speak untruths and are greedy, though they may be proficient in all branches of knowledge and be the most excellent among the Brahmins, [are not true Brahmins]. (29)
This is the forty-first point.
And Chatroṭā is the supreme station, uniquely honored by the entire world; it is declared to be of the Kuśa lineage, indeed possessing three *pravara*s. (230)
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and the third is Dalama; and here the goddess Cacā is indeed proclaimed as the family deity (gotradevī). || 31 ||
In this lineage, you shall indeed be devoted to the Vedas and the Shastras; those Brahmins will be highly prosperous and promoters of the path of justice.
Thus ends the forty-second point. 42.
In this place, Khala is the settlement; there are indeed forty-three [families]. These Brāhmaṇas, born of the Vatsa lineage, are engaged in the occupation of agriculture. || 33 ||
The goddesses born of the lineage and born of knowledge are indeed five prominent ones: Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Jāmadagnya.
The Brahmins born in this lineage are devoted to the maintenance of the Vedic fires, habituated to the study of the Vedas, ascetics, and subduers of enemies. (35)

They were prone to anger and greed, yet joyful; they delighted in performing sacrifices for themselves and for others, were permeated with compassion for all beings, and were likewise benefactors of others.
Thus ends the forty-third point. 43.
And for the Vāsantaḍyas among the Brahmins, the Kuśa gotra is declared; Viśvāmitra is the Ṛṣi, Devārāta is the second, and Audala is indeed the third.
Cacāī is indeed the goddess here, proclaimed as the family deity (gotradevī); and those born in this lineage who were previously mentioned are devoted to Brahman.
They are indeed benefactors of others, conforming to the minds of others, averse to the property of others, and promoters of the supreme path. || 39 ||
Thus ends the forty-fourth point. 44.

Beyond this, the lineage (saṃsthāna) is declared to be Jākhāsaṇa; the family name (gotra) is indeed Vātsya, and the one born of that lineage is Śīhurī. Thus, the five pravaras have been revealed by me to you. (240)

Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Purodhas are remembered [as the ancestors]. And those Brāhmaṇas born in this lineage are known as Vāḍavas who dwell happily; they are large-bodied, wise, and indeed devoted to all ritual duties. || 41 ||

They all placed their sole trust in the Dharma, were uniquely honored by the entire world, were experts in the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, and were devoted to performing sacrifices for themselves and for others.
They are of virtuous conduct, handsome, pot-bellied, and far-sighted; and here, indeed, the goddess Śīhurī is celebrated as the family deity (kuladevī). || 43 ||
Thus ends the forty-fifth point. 45.
The forty-sixth station of the Moṭas has been revealed; the name of the Gotīās is indeed the Kuśa-gotra here. (44)
Viśvāmitra is the first, Devarātaka is the second, and Audala is the third; this indeed is the triad of pravaras. (45)
And here indeed dwells the Yakṣiṇī goddess, the destroyer of Rākṣasas; and those Brāhmaṇas born in this lineage who are devoted to Brahman—|| 46 ||
Their intellects were directed toward the Dharma, and they were firmly established in the treatises on righteousness. || 47 ||
Thus ends the forty-sixth point. 46.
The forty-seventh configuration has been fully proclaimed; the configuration known as Varalīya is considered supremely sacred. (48)
Likewise, the lineage is Bhāradvāja, and the pravaras are the same; furthermore, the goddess Yakṣiṇī is proclaimed here as the family deity (kuladevī). || 49 ||
The Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, and Bhāradvāja [gotras] constitute the third; and those Brāhmaṇas of purified form who were born in this lineage [are likewise honored]. || 250 ||
By the water of whose words alone sinful men are purified.
Thus ends the forty-seventh section. 47.
The supreme station named Dudhīya, as well as the two lineages (gotras), namely Dhāraṇasa and likewise Āṅgirakasama; || 52 ||
Agasti, Dārḍhacyuta, and the one named Idhmavāhana; and Chatra is the Mahādevī. Now hear the second Pravara.
Āṅgirasa, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva as the third; Jñānadā and Śeṣalā—she is indeed the giver of knowledge to all embodied beings. (54)
O King, born in this lineage are the Vāḍavas, who are unbearable, intoxicated with pride, massive in body, capable of seizing, and arrogant with rut. (55)
Having the form of afflictions, they are black in color and skilled in all weapons; they are gluttonous, wealthy, and clever, yet free from hatred and sin. || 56 ||
Thus ends the forty-eighth section.
I shall describe Hāsolāsa, whose own location is well-known here; it belongs to the Śāṇḍilya gotra and is endowed with five pravaras.
Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Jāmadagnyaka; and here also is the goddess Yakṣiṇī, who is pure and the destroyer of sins.
And those Brāhmaṇas with gross bodies who were born in this lineage were large-bellied, long-eared, long-handed, and great twice-born ones. || 59 ||
The gods are always free from disease, being devoted to the vow of truth.
This is the forty-ninth point. || 49 ||
The fifty-first sacred site is indeed named Vaihāla; its lineage is Kuśa, and the goddess here is Mahābalā.
In this lineage there are brahmins who are wicked and crooked in their ways; yet there are also those who are wealthy, devoted to righteousness, and masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
All were devoted to giving and enjoyment, and their intellects were firmly established in the revealed scriptures (śruti). || 63 ||
Thus ends the fiftieth point. 50.
Asālā is indeed the supreme place, consisting of two lineages: Kuśa and Dhāraṇa are the lineages in their respective order. (64)
Viśvāmitra, Devarāta, and Devala as the third; and Jñānajā is likewise the goddess proclaimed as the family deity (gotradevī). || 65 ||
This is the fifty-first point. || 51 ||
The fifty-second [tīrtha] is indeed Nālolā, the supreme station; likewise, the second is renowned as Vatsagotra, and Dhāraṇasa as well.
The lineages previously mentioned were indeed spoken of by the Goddess long ago; those born in this lineage are considered pure and supreme.
O Brahmins, what is the use of speaking at length? All of these here are the most excellent beings; all are pure, high-souled, and all possess a noble lineage.
Thus ends the fifty-second point. 52.

Dehola is the supreme abode of the Brāhmaṇas, O scorcher of foes! There, O best of men, were born the Brāhmaṇas born of the lineage of Kuśa; their pravaras are exactly as previously mentioned, and the goddess was also described by me earlier. (69)
In that lineage were born twice-born men endowed with the qualities previously described. || 270 ||
Thus ends the fifty-third point. 53.
The place is indeed Sohāsīyāpura, and there are three lineages: the renowned Bhāradvāja, as well as the Vatsa lineage. (71)
Yakṣiṇī, Jñānajā, and Siholī, in their respective order; this examination of their lineages has been previously described, O best of kings. (72)
Thus ends the fifty-fourth point. || 54 ||
I shall now describe to you the fifty-five-fold sacred site; formerly, this place named Saṃhāliyā was indeed bestowed by Rāma.
There indeed were Brāhmaṇas belonging to the Kutsa lineage, possessing the splendor of Brahman; they were constantly devoted to their own duties and ever intent upon their own specific tasks.
Then follow those of Āṅgirasa, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva; and here indeed is the goddess Śāntā, who bestows peace in rites for pacification.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth section. || 55 ||
Thus have I described those lineages and their respective locations, as well as the most eminent among them here, O scorcher of foes, for the sake of the Brahmins.

Henceforth, O scorcher of foes, I shall proclaim the supreme status of those who possess the threefold knowledge (traividyas), according to their respective positions in due order as they have been declared by me. (77)
Śīlā is the first station, Maṇḍorā is the second; Evaḍī is indeed the third, and Guṃdarāṇā is the fourth. (78)
The fifth is Kalyāṇīyā Degāmā, the sixth is likewise; the seventh is Nāyakapurā, and the eighth is Ḍalīā. || 79 ||
Kaḍovyā is the ninth, and likewise Kohāṭoyā is the tenth; Haraḍīyā is the eleventh, and likewise Bhadukīyā is the twelfth. || 280 ||
Saṃprāṇāvā is likewise proclaimed here, as well as Kaṃdarāvā; Vāsarovā is the thirteenth, and Śaraṇḍāvā is the fourteenth. || 81 ||
Lolāsana is the fifteenth, Vārolā is the sixteenth, and Nāgalapura has likewise been mentioned by me here as the seventeenth.
Brahmā said: Those Brahmins learned in the four Vedas who had not yet arrived returned once more; those best of the twice-born established their residence there in that delightful place.
Numbering twenty-four, they went toward Hanumān out of a desire for Rāma’s command, but having turned back, they returned once more.
Due to their fault, they all fell from their positions; after some time had passed, a conflict arose among them. (85)

With different customs and different languages, they have fallen into a state of uncertainty regarding their dress; fifteen thousand of them, along with whatever other Brāhmaṇas were in the middle [of the land], [were thus transformed]. 86.
Some were devoted to agricultural work, some were dedicated to performing sacrifices; some became wrestlers, and others indeed became reciters of the Vedas.
Some were devoted to Āyurveda, some were washermen and priests; some were intent on the twilight prayers and ritual bathing, while others were dyers and those who employed dyers. || 88 ||
When the Kali age has arrived, those twice-born who are devoted to begging for thread from weavers and other such artisans will undoubtedly become fallen; of this there is no doubt. (89)

O lord of men, when the Kali age has arrived, there will be distinctions of caste even among Śūdras; they will be corrupted in conduct, yet they will consider themselves superior and be tormented by the bonds of kinship.

O King, abandoned by their own people for lack of food and clothing, no one would ever marry a girl due to the [social] stigma. Therefore, O King, those merchants became oil-pressers in the Kali age. (91)

Some were makers of charcoal, some were preparers of rice; some were dependent on princes, and others were dependent on various castes. When the Kali age arrived, some merchants on the face of the earth fell from their status.
Their practices were indeed distinct and their lineages were made separate; some came to reside in Sītāpura. || 93 ||
Some were settled here and there on the banks of the Sābhramatī; they were those who had previously come from Sītāpura, fleeing in fear. || 94 ||
Those who are established in Śrīkṣetra on the northern bank of the Sābhramatī—when their station and place were indeed granted as a dwelling of happiness. (95)
They immediately departed for that city of Sītāpura themselves; furthermore, fifty-five villages were granted for their future return.
Rāma established dwellings for those Modha Brāhmaṇas among them; however, those Brāhmaṇas who were excluded from the means of subsistence remained within Dharmāraṇya.
"O best of Brahmins, we have no concern whatsoever with the livelihood of merchants or the affairs of the village; indeed, our dwelling here is what pleases us. (98)
When this was said, those best of the twice-born, learned in the three Vedas, gave their permission; and in those villages, those excellent brahmins became masters of the four Vedas.
Devoted to their own duties, peaceful, and dedicated to agricultural work, they graze their cows not far from Dharmāraṇya.

There were many cowherd boys who were twice-born children; these youths, learned in the four Vedas, tended the cows for them. For their meal, there was an abundance of food, drink, and other excellent provisions. || 1 ||
Indeed, even young women, widows, and children were bringing [the offerings]. || 2 ||
After some time, O King, mutual affection arose among them; out of love, the cowherd girls enjoyed themselves with the daughters of the twice-born.
All those women were seen by those best of the twice-born to have conceived; they were expelled from their homes and reviled by that man of sinful deeds.
O best of the twice-born, those Kārtībhās and Golakas who were born from them, as well as those born of Dhenu, attained renown in the world of mortals.
O Brahmins, their livelihood is indeed external, for they constantly beg for alms; furthermore, O King, hear this regarding the twice-born Traividyas.
Whether he be a leper, or likewise a cripple, a fool, or even deaf; or perhaps one-eyed, or hunchbacked, or again, mute.
For these boys, O King, were unmarried and had taken refuge with those learned in the four Vedas; by means of great wealth, they obtained daughters from them.
O King, those who were married at that time and the children born from them became known thereafter as the Tridalajas throughout the world of mortals.
Those Brāhmaṇas, born from mutual intermixture, established their means of livelihood; hear now another matter, O King, concerning the twice-born Traividyas.
For the purpose of collecting taxes, the entire village headed by Rāmadatta united with all the twice-born and presented that village as an offering.
Those twice-born ones, partaking in greed, offered half [of the food] and kept half concealed, thinking, "This much has been obtained. (12)
And those who had gone to that great place were filled with amazement; then, a certain brahmin among them, being provoked, spoke these words to them.
The Brahmin said: "Overcome by great greed, they speak untruths; being excessively covetous of the property of Brahmins, they bring about the destruction of their sons and grandsons. (14)

They say that poison is not truly poison; it is the property of a Brahmin that is called poison. Poison kills only a single person, but the property of a Brahmin destroys even one's sons and grandsons.
When sons, wives, houses, and so forth are consumed by the property of a Brahmin, they do not remain even for them, being destroyed by that Brahmin's property. (16)
Then, that person who constantly seizes the property of a Brahmin does not attain heaven; this is true even for those who steal as little as a single cowrie shell from a Brahmin.
Then, for three births, the one who steals it shall go to hell; his ancestors shall never enjoy the water offered by him at any time.
On the anniversary of his death, they do not partake of his offerings of rice-balls and water; he does not obtain progeny at all, and even if obtained, it does not survive. (19)
If she should live by chance, it is possible that she might fall away from right conduct. || 320 ||
The eleven brahmins said: "O brahmins, you have not spoken untruth; why indeed do you revile us? For to whom is harsh speech appropriate, unless there has been an offense? (21)
O Pārtha, having heard that, the merchant who had caused the village to be seized was questioned by those twice-born men, and he explained the entire reason for it.
O best of the twice-born, the tribute was indeed given to me by the merchants; all of that has been told to you brahmins with a pure heart. (23)
Then, realizing that he had taken only half a share, those sons of brahmins became enraged; consequently, those eleven brahmins were indeed excluded from their livelihood.
The kinship extends for eleven generations and is renowned throughout the three worlds; no matrimonial alliance or marriage occurs among them.

Those who reside outside the village for eleven years—thus arose these various divisions among the Moḍha twice-born, according to the times, following the course of the Yugas, and due to the [conduct] of their kinsmen or their virtue. (326)
Nārada said: O Brahman, when that division among the kinsmen had arisen in that city of Moheraka, what did the Traividyas do? Tell me that as I ask you.
Brahmā said: All the Vāḍavas remained in their own places with minds overflowing with joy; some were devoted to the Agnihotra fire-sacrifice, and others were intent upon the performance of Yajñas.

Some were constantly engaged in maintaining the sacred fires, some were followers of the Smṛtis, some were knowers of the Purāṇas and Nyāya, and others were exponents of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas).
Performing their own traditional practices with ease, those exponents of the Veda who are virtuous in soul thus carry out the proper observance of dharma.

The local customs, family traditions, and the teachings of the presiding deities, as well as everything established in the Dharmaśāstras and proclaimed by the lords of the quarters (Lokapālas), [he should observe].
Those best of the Vāḍavas spoke of the Dharma handed down through tradition.
The Brahmins said: "O Vāḍavas, he who honors that which is inscribed with red feet is to be known as the best among kinsmen; after that, a tribute (bali) should be given."

Then, having consecrated red sandalwood and likewise established one's own lineage, [one should worship] with those [deities] whose feet are reddened by saffron and who are anointed with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
That which is written collectively is called Raktapāda; let all of you, with concentrated minds, honor this writing of Rāma.
Let the twice-born always worship the hand-seal of Rāma; even for those who may have faults such as deviance from right conduct and the like.
The punishment prescribed for them by the twice-born according to the rules must be carried out, provided they do not bear the seal of Rāma as a mark until the penalty has been paid.
Without being granted a staff, one does not wear the insignia of the *mudrā*; O best of kings, those Brahmins who bear the *mudrā* on their hands should be recognized as such. (12)
When a son is born, the father should always offer an oblation to Śrī-mātā: twenty palas of clarified butter and five palas of jaggery.
Having worshipped with saffron and other offerings, O King, as soon as the son was born, she always worshipped the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī on the sixth day.
There, one should offer an oblation with clarified butter and perform the fivefold bali-offering; one should give five measures of oblations together with garments and bilva fruits.
Having worshipped Śrīmātā with saffron and other offerings with devotion, one should not practice deceit, so that the lineage may increase in prosperity. (16)
For when that wealth has been offered and the prosperity has been restored, the birth-rite (jātakarman) must again be performed according to the rules immediately after birth.
The livelihoods proclaimed by the Brahmins are also divided; furthermore, whatever livelihood is actually obtained is considered the first. (18)
Let half of that income be assigned to the family deity (gotradevī); and when a son is born, let there be twice as much for the merchant. || 19 ||

And for those Śūdras who belong to the circle (of the community), this tax is as follows: it is threefold for those born of illicit unions (aḍālajas) and fourfold for those who enjoy the cattle (gobhuja).
All this has been told regarding the Śūdra castes, as well as other matters concerning him in whom the fault of killing has arisen by the power of fate.
Punishment must be duly inflicted upon him by those learned in the Vedas; for he who speaks of justice while practicing injustice is one who attributes fault to the innocent.

It is recorded that one who causes a breach in the ranks is considered equal to the slayer of a thousand cows; likewise, the distribution of shares of livelihood and the deliberation of justice must be carried out in the presence of Śrī Rāma’s messenger—this is the settled rule. (23)
One should perform its worship at that time or always; indeed, one should smear its body with oil for the pacification of obstacles.
One should indeed offer incense, a lamp, fruit, and various kinds of flowers; when Hanumān is thus worshipped, he grants that person's desire.
One should perform the *pratiputra* rite before him and nowhere else; however, the portion for the venerable Mātābakuḷasvāmin should be placed in the east. (26)
It was thus determined that the acceptance of gifts by Brahmins should take place during assemblies of Brahmins for the purpose of deciding what is just and what is unjust. (27)
Having held the final decision in his heart, he should announce it to the twice-born present there; he should do so solely with a sense of dharma and must avoid partiality. (28)
A task approved by all is indeed free from fault; therefore, if a Brahmin summoned to the assembly feels fear, [it is a sign of his own guilt]. (29)
The word of one against whom an exclusion is carried out by all the Brāhmaṇas acting in concert must not be heard when there is an attempt to overturn a settled matter.
One should avoid all dealings with him, such as providing food, drink, and so forth; one should not give a daughter to him, nor associate with one who associates with him. (31)
Then, all the best of the twice-born should indeed impose a fine; according to the opinion of the son of Daśaratha, this consists of a meal and the giving of a maiden in marriage.
Whatever sin one commits in order to obtain land or even food—whether that food be dry or moist—one should therefore renounce such food.
By doing so, he would partake in that sin and deserve punishment according to the law, since he always fails to see justice when he has the power to do so.
"He should be known as a partaker of sin; this is the truth, there is no doubt. He who accepts a bribe from evildoers of wicked deeds shall incur all their sin; of this there is no doubt. (35)
The food of that man is never accepted, nor is his daughter ever taken in marriage, even if he acts for the welfare of his own sons. (36)
"He shall observe all these rules; of this there is no doubt. Having thus written the document, those Brahmins were filled with joy.
Knowing that they would not commit sin even when the terrible Kali age had arrived, they all established the practice of justice and righteousness.
Vyāsa said: When the Kali age has arrived, all the twice-born will be displaced from their positions here and there; they will adopt the faction of Utkala and thus become partisans.
It is said that in the Kali age, those Brahmins who have fallen away from the Vedas will devour the villages of the Mlecchas with the destruction of all [dharma], like boars.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Those Brahmins and merchants will travel from region to region; O noble one, by what sign indeed can they all be recognized?"
In whichever lineage those Vāḍavas of great power were born. || 42 ||
Vyāsa said:
Then, the designation of lineage is known through their prowess; for each individual, there is a mark corresponding to his specific deed. (43)
For they are recognized by their insignia (avaṭaṅka), and not otherwise recognized anywhere; by their lineages (gotra) and ancestral sages (pravara), and indeed by their insignia, O Prince. (44)
For it is known, O King, that the Moḍha Brāhmaṇas are the best among the twice-born.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O Grandfather, these [lineages] have been heard by me from your mouth according to their *gotras* and *pravaras*; tell me, however, which branch of the Veda they study. (16)
Vyāsa said: Wherever the mighty followers of the Mādhyandina school are known to reside, some Brahmins endowed with virtues have likewise taken refuge in the Kauthuma tradition.
O Great-minded One, the branches born of the Ṛg and Atharva Vedas have perished; such indeed are those Vāḍavas who have arisen from dharma as they exist today. (48)
In Dharmāraṇya, the highly fortunate Śūdras became endowed with sons and grandsons; all those illustrious ones were surrounded by their children and descendants. || 49 ||
In the great sacred ford of Dharmāraṇya, they all became servants of the twice-born, devotees of Rāma, and they carried out the command of Rāma. || 50 ||
If even the heroic Hanumān were to protect this place with diligence at the command of his minister, he might do so now, even though the Kali age has indeed arrived.
Invisible in form, Hanumān wanders there constantly, where the Traividyas, Vāḍavas, and likewise the Cāturvidyas reside.
Those who, seated in the assembly, commit an injustice, [shall suffer defeat]; for victory belongs to those who act with justice, while defeat belongs to those who act unjustly.
But toward one who shows partiality toward a son, a father, or even a brother when they have committed an offense, the Son of the Wind becomes angry.
This Hanūmat, when enraged, truly brings about the destruction of wealth; he likewise brings about the destruction of sons and the destruction of one's very abode. || 55 ||
If a Śūdra created for the purpose of service does not serve the Brahmins, or if he does not provide them with their livelihood, Hanumān becomes angry with him. || 56 ||
Remembering the words of Rāma, the son of the Wind-god indeed brought about the destruction of wealth, the destruction of sons, the destruction of his position, and great fear. (57)
O best of kings, wherever they may reside—whether Brahmins or Śūdras—may they never be destitute through the grace of Rāghava. (58)
That fool who is unrighteous by nature and has resorted to sinful heresies, having abandoned his own Brahmins, considers those of other lineages to be superior. (59)
The merit previously performed by him is reduced to ashes; it cannot be otherwise. To others, a gift may be given, whether it be small or great. (60)

Just as it was formerly performed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, so too the gods do not accept his *havya* (offerings to the gods), nor do the ancestors accept his *kavya* (offerings to the manes). || 61 ||
If one deceives his own Brahmins and bestows [the gift] upon others, the merit accumulated by him throughout his life is reduced to ashes at that very moment.
Those best of the twice-born who are honored by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—those Śūdras who are averse to them dwell in the Raurava hell.
He who, out of greed, should cause the destruction of family custom or clan custom, and who, being utterly deluded, never performs his own proper conduct; || 64 ||
His total destruction occurs and he is reduced to ashes at that very moment; therefore, all family traditions as well as local customs [must be observed]. 65.
The conduct of one's lineage should be maintained according to one's means; thus, O King, has this ancient Dharmāraṇya been described to you. 66.

Established by the gods of gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, Dharmāraṇya was known as Satyamandira in the Kṛta Yuga, Vedabhavana in the Tretā Yuga, and in the Kali age, it is remembered as Moheraka.
Brahmā said: O son, whoever shall listen with supreme faith to this majesty of Dharmāraṇya, which destroys all sins, [shall attain the highest goal]. (68)
Whatever threefold sin has been produced by mind, speech, and body—all that goes to destruction through hearing and reciting this meritorious [work]. (69)
O child, a person who desires to attain all happiness should listen to this greatness, which is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, and bestows a continuous succession of joys. (70)
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords (tīrthas) and whatever fruit is found in all holy fields (kṣetras), one attains that very fruit by resorting to Dharmāraṇya.
Nārada said: I have heard from the lotus of your mouth the greatness of Dharmāraṇya, where Dharma performed most difficult penance at Dharmavāpī.
I have ascertained from you the greatness of that sacred field; may it be well with you, for I shall depart with a desire to behold Dharmāraṇya.
There, O Four-faced One, I was purified by the flood of the waters of his speech.
Vyāsa said: O son of Pāṇḍu, this entire narrative has been told; by hearing which, a human being obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
One without a son obtains sons; one who is destitute becomes wealthy; the sick shall be liberated from disease, and the bound shall be released from bondage.
A seeker of knowledge obtains supreme knowledge that accomplishes all rites; he gains the fruit of a pilgrimage to sacred fords and the merit of giving ten million maidens in marriage.
O best of men, whether it be a man or a woman who listens with devotion, they shall not see hell, accompanied by one hundred and one [members of their lineage].

Then, O King, having placed the ancient manuscript in an auspicious location, covered with linen cloth and other materials, one who is self-restrained and esteemed by the learned [should proceed]. (79)
And one should worship them individually with perfumes and garlands according to the rule; O King, at the conclusion of the book, there should be the worship of the reciter.
For the sake of attaining the complete fruit according to the prescribed rule through acts such as giving, [he should offer] a signet ring, earrings, and a golden sacred thread (brahmasūtra).
Having performed worship like that of a deity with various garments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments, one should also give a milch cow.
Having thus heard this narrative of Dharmāraṇya according to the prescribed rule, one undoubtedly attains the fruit of residing in Dharmāraṇya. (83)

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Hearing the Purāṇa of Dharmāraṇya, preceded by the Description of the Regulations for the Residents of Dharmāraṇya," in the *Dharmāraṇyamāhātmya*, within the first part of the third section (Brahmakhaṇḍa) of the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.

Salutations to the venerable Gurus. Now begins the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa. Om, salutations to Śiva! Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful, the Brahman in the form of the Liṅga, whose nature is pure light alone and whose eye is stainless knowledge. || 1 ||
The sages said: O Sūta, you have narrated the supreme majesty of Viṣṇu; we have heard it from you in brief, for it is meritorious and removes all sins.
Now we wish to hear the greatness of the Enemy of Tripura, as well as the supreme greatness of his devotees, which removes all sins without exception.
O best of the twice-born, likewise describe the majesty of those mantras, as well as the power of the narrative concerning them and of devotion to them.
Sūta said: This alone is the supreme, eternal welfare for mortals: that unconditioned devotion indeed arises toward the discourse of the Lord.
Therefore, I shall describe the majesty of even a small fraction of devotion to Him; one with a lifespan of an entire kalpa would not be able to describe it in full detail anywhere.
Of all merits, of all forms of excellence, and of all sacrifices, the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is remembered as the supreme.
In that regard, first of all, the fruit of the sacrifice of recitation is a great means of securing well-being; the great sages have declared the divine six-syllabled mantra of Śiva to be such. (8)
Just as the Destroyer of Tripura is indeed the supreme god among the gods, so too the six-syllabled mantra of Śiva is the supreme mantra among mantras.
This five-syllabled mantra bestows liberation upon those who recite it; it is practiced by all the foremost sages who desire spiritual perfection. (10)
Even the four-faced Brahmā is not capable of fully describing the greatness of this very syllable, wherein the Vedas have reached their final conclusion and attained supreme peace.
He who is omniscient, perfect, and characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss—that Śiva rejoices in the auspicious five-syllabled Śaiva mantra.
By means of this king of mantras, which is the soul of all the Upaniṣads, all the sages attained the supreme Brahman, free from all affliction.
Through the act of salutation (namaskāra), one attains life within Śiva, the Supreme Self; having attained oneness with Him, this mantra is indeed composed of the Supreme Brahman.
Out of a desire for the welfare of embodied beings bound by the noose of worldly existence, Śiva himself [bestowed] the primordial mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya."
What need has he for many mantras, what need for sacred fords, or what need for austerities and sacrifices, for whom the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya" has entered the range of his heart? (16)
Embodied beings wander in this dreadful saṃsāra, crowded with suffering, for as long as they do not recite this mantra even once. (17)
This king of the sovereign mantras is the crest-jewel of all Vedāntas; it is the treasury of all knowledge, and it is indeed this six-syllabled mantra.
This six-syllabled mantra is the lamp on the path to liberation, the submarine fire for the ocean of ignorance, and the forest fire for great sins. (19)
Therefore, this five-syllabled mantra is remembered as the giver of everything; it is worn by women, Śūdras, and those of mixed caste who desire liberation.

For this mantra, there is no initiation, no fire-oblation, no purificatory rite, and no libation; there is no restriction of time and no formal instruction required, for this mantra is eternally pure.
The two syllables "Śi-va," joined with the act of salutation, are sufficient for the destruction of great sins and lead to liberation. (22)
When taught by a true guru and recited in a sacred field, it bestows the desired accomplishment immediately; what wonder is there in this? (23)
Therefore, having taken refuge in a true guru, this leader of mantras should be received; when recited in sacred fields, it bestows immediate accomplishment.
The gurus are stainless, peaceful, virtuous, and moderate in speech; they are completely free from desire and anger, possessed of noble conduct, and have their senses subdued.
A mantra given by these out of compassion is swiftly successful. I shall now briefly describe the places suitable for recitation. (26)
Prayāga, Puṣkara, the beautiful Kedāra, Setubandhana, Gokarṇa, and Naimiṣāraṇya grant immediate perfection to men.
In this regard, the virtuous recount an ancient history which bestows auspiciousness upon those who hear it, whether repeatedly or even once. (28)
In Mathurā, there was a wise king of great energy and great strength, the best of the Yadus, renowned as Dāśārha. || 29 ||
He was learned in the scriptures, heroic in his conduct and speech, steadfast, and possessed of immeasurable luster; he was invincible, profoundly deep, and never retreated in battles.
A great chariot-warrior and a mighty archer, skilled in the meaning of various scriptures, generous, endowed with beauty, youthful, and possessed of auspicious marks. || 31 ||
He married the daughter of the King of Kāśī, the lovely Kalāvatī by name, who was endowed with beauty, virtuous conduct, and excellent qualities.
Having performed the marriage ceremony and reached his own palace, that lord of kings summoned her, who had ascended to her bed at night, for union.
Though summoned by her husband and entreated many times, she did not fix her mind upon him, nor did she go near him.
When his beloved did not come when summoned for their union, the lord of the earth rose up, desiring to seize her by force. (35)
The queen said: "Do not touch me, O Great King; I am established in a vow and know its purpose. You understand righteousness and unrighteousness; do not commit an act of violence against me. (36)
In some cases, that which is enjoyed by the beloved is pleasing to the wise; through the union of the couple in love, their meeting increases their affection. (37)
Only when pleasure arises for me will there be attachment to you. What joy or what happiness is there for men from the forced enjoyment of women? (38)
A man should not forcibly desire a woman who is displeased, ill, pregnant, observing a vow, menstruating, or unwilling. || 39 ||

Having provided delight, fondling, nourishment, pleasing, gentleness, and compassion, a husband full of love should approach his young wife; for one who desires happiness, these same qualities must be applied toward a young woman and a flower alike. (40)
Although addressed thus by that virtuous woman, the king, overwhelmed by passion, forcibly drew her by the hand and embraced her with a desire for sexual union.
As soon as he touched her, who was like a red-hot iron ball and seemed to burn him to the very soul, he abandoned her, overwhelmed by fear.
The king said: "O my beloved, what a truly great wonder this that has been seen by me! How has your body, tender as a young sprout, become like fire? (43)
Thus greatly amazed and terrified, the king and that beloved queen replied to him with a smile, speaking with modesty and a pure radiance. (44)
The queen said: "O King, in my childhood long ago, the eminent sage Durvāsas compassionately instructed me in the five-syllabled Śiva-vidyā. (45)
By the power of that mantra, my body has become free from impurity; it cannot be touched by men possessed of sin, nor even by gods who have been forsaken [by merit].
O King, being by nature thus, you always consort with women such as unchaste wives and courtesans who are devoted to the tasting of wine.
"You do not bathe daily, nor do you recite the pure mantras; you do not propitiate the Lord Īśāna—how can you be worthy of touching me? (48)
The king said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, tell me that auspicious five-syllabled mantra of Śiva; with my sins destroyed by this knowledge, O beloved, I desire union with you. (49)
The queen said: "I shall certainly not give you instruction; you are my guru. O King, attend upon the guru Garga, the best among those who know the mantras."
Sūta said: Thus conversing, the couple approached the presence of Garga and, with palms joined in reverence, bowed their heads at his feet.
Then the king, with a humble soul, having repeatedly honored his gratified preceptor, disclosed his own secret desire.

The king said: O Guru, you whose mind is moist with compassion, make me one who has attained his purpose; it behoves you to instruct me in the five-syllabled lore of Śiva, which I have now approached.
O Guru, grant me that mantra by which whatever sin has been committed through royal affairs—whether unknown or known—may be purified.
Thus entreated by the king, Garga, the bull among brahmins, led the two of them to the most meritorious and excellent bank of the Kālindī.
Then the Guru himself sat down there at the foot of that most meritorious tree, facing the king, who had bathed in the waters of a sacred ford and observed a fast.
Then, having seated him facing east and bowed to the lotus feet of Śiva, he placed his hand upon the disciple's head and imparted the mantra whose essence is Śiva.
Merely by the retention of that mantra and through the touch of his guru’s hand, hundreds of millions of crows emerged from his body.
With their wings burnt, crying out as they fell upon the surface of the earth, they were all seen by the thousands reduced to ashes.
Seeing that flock of crows being consumed by fire, the king and the queen were greatly astonished and questioned their preceptor.
"O Blessed One, how has this marvel arisen from the body? A flock of crows was seen; what is this? Please explain it well. (61)
The venerable Guru said: "O King, as you have wandered through thousands of births, many insurmountable sins have been accumulated by you."
Whatever merits exist from those thousands of births, by virtue of their preponderance, one is born somewhere among meritorious wombs.
Likewise, he may at times enter an evil womb due to sin; yet, when there is an equality of merit and demerit for both, he attains a human womb.
When the five-syllabled Śaiva mantra entered your heart, millions of sins departed from you in the form of crows.

Tens of millions of killings of Brahmins, tens of millions of instances of forbidden sexual intercourse, tens of millions of thefts of gold, drinking of liquor, and abortions, as well as whatever other heaps of sins exist throughout thousands of millions of births—[all these are destroyed]. (66)
When the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva is held, [sins] are indeed reduced to ashes in an instant; O Indra among kings, today millions of your sins have been burnt away by this recitation.
"O pure-souled one, sport with her as you please. Having spoken thus and having imparted that mantra to him, the best of sages— || 68 ||
Accompanied by those two, whose minds were filled with wonder, he went to his own home; and having taken leave of the excellent preceptor, that joyful couple departed as well. (69)
Then, having reached their own abode, those two of great splendor shone forth.
The king, firmly embracing his wife who was cool as sandalwood, attained supreme satisfaction, just as a pauper does upon acquiring wealth.

This supreme and great power of the five-syllabled mantra alone—which is the crest-jewel of all the Vedas, Upaniṣads, Purāṇas, and Śāstras, and which brings an end to sin—has been recounted by me in brief. (71)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Five-Syllabled Mantra," in the Brahmottara Section of the third part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Now I shall speak of another majesty of the Enemy of Tripura, by the mere hearing of which all doubts are swiftly severed.
There is nothing superior to this for the purification of sins; it brings joy to all, is glorious, and accomplishes every desire and purpose.
The supreme worship of Maheśa, performed with undivided devotion, bestows the fruits of long life, victory, health, worldly enjoyment, and liberation. (3)
Whether they are fresh or dry, small or large, this alone is prescribed as the supreme expiation.
It is the cause for the destruction of sins that are otherwise indestructible at all times, through the supreme expiations prescribed by the Great Sage.
This alone is the supreme good, as determined by all the scriptures: that which is the worship of the Supreme Lord with devotion and supreme compassion. (6)
Whether knowingly or unknowingly, for whatever reason, any action whatsoever performed for the sake of the God bestows liberation.
Fasting on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha is extremely difficult to achieve; even more difficult than that, I consider, for men, is the keeping of a vigil at night.
I consider the sight of Śiva’s liṅga to be exceedingly rare; I consider the worship of the Supreme Lord to be even more difficult to attain.
Furthermore, through the ripening of the mass of merit produced over hundreds of millions of existences, one may obtain there the worship of the Lord with bilva leaves.
A man obtains that same fruit by worshipping with a single bilva leaf which would otherwise be gained by bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā river for ten thousand years.
Whatever meritorious deeds have been performed here in every age, they all remain in their entirety on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
In this world, the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, praise this very fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha.
Fasting performed here by anyone is superior to hundreds of sacrifices; keeping a vigil at night is meritorious, exceeding the penance of ten million kalpas.
If the worship of a Śiva-liṅga is performed with even a single bilva leaf, who in the three worlds would desire to equal its merit? (15)
In this regard, a meritorious and most beautiful verse is described here; though it ought to be kept secret, it has been revealed by Gautama out of compassion. (16)
Born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, there was a glorious and supremely righteous king named Mitrasaha, the best among all wielders of the bow. (17)
That king was knowledgeable in all weapons and the scriptures, a master of sacred learning, a hero of extreme strength and energy, ever-diligent, and a treasury of compassion.
His form shines forth like a collection of merits, like a cage of splendors, and like a field of wonders. (19)
His heart was overcome with compassion, his body was graced by splendor, and his feet were touched by the rays from the crest-jewels of neighboring kings.
Once, that lord of the earth, eager for the sport of hunting, entered a formidable cave surrounded by a great army.
There he pierced with his arrows śārdūlas, gavayas, and deer; he also struck ruru deer, boars, buffaloes, and even lions in great numbers.
That charioteer, devoted to hunting, while moving through the dense forest clad in armor, struck down a certain night-stalker who resembled a blazing fire.
His younger brother, overcome with grief upon seeing his brother slain and having watched him vanish from afar, reflected thus in his mind: ||| 24 ||
"Indeed, this king is invincible even to the gods and the Rākṣasas; my enemy must be conquered through guile alone, and not otherwise. (25)
Having thus resolved, the wicked Rākṣasa in human form approached the best of kings like a personified omen of calamity.
Seeing him with a humble appearance, having come to serve as a servant, that lord of the earth, out of ignorance, appointed him as the superintendent of the kitchen.
Then, having sported for some time in that forest, the king desisted from the hunt and returned once more to his own city.
To that preeminent lord of kings, known by the name Madayanti, there was a beloved and virtuous wife named Damayanti, just as she was to Nala.
At that time, when the day of the ancestors had arrived, the king invited Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages, and brought him to his home.
Seeing that the vegetable and meat had been mixed with human flesh by the Rākṣasa disguised as a cook and placed before him, the Guru then spoke: || 31 ||
"Fie, fie upon this human flesh, O King! Since it has been offered to me today by you, a wicked man acting under a disguise, therefore you shall become a Rākṣasa."
Not realizing that this had been done by a Rākṣasa, the preceptor then uttered a curse; but reflecting upon it again, he made that curse last for twelve years.
The king, becoming enraged, said: "Since this was not my doing and was not known to me, you have cursed me in vain; I shall likewise curse my preceptor. (34)
Having thus taken up water with his joined palms, he prepared to curse the Guru; Madayantī, however, fell at his feet and restrained him.
Then, having desisted from that [act] due to the curse and out of respect for her words, he released the water from his feet; his two feet had become stained with impurity.
From that time forth, the king became known as Kalmaṣāṅghri; by the curse of his preceptor, he became a Rākṣasa who roamed the forests.
Assuming a terrible Rākṣasa form resembling the Destroyer (Kāla) at the end of time, that forest-dweller devoured various creatures, including humans and others.
Once, in a certain forest, he saw a young sage couple, appearing like two young elephants in rut, enjoying themselves together after their recent marriage.
A Rākṣasa who subsisted on human flesh, afflicted by a curse, seized the young son of the sage in order to devour him, just as a tiger seizes a fawn.
Then, seeing her husband seized by a Rākṣasa, his beloved wife became terrified; the young woman spoke piteously, weeping and trembling violently. || 41 ||
"O Māma! Do not commit this sin, O upholder of the glory of the Solar dynasty! For you are the husband of Madayantī, a lord of kings, and certainly not a Rākṣasa. (42)
"Do not devour my husband, O Lord, who is dearer to me than life itself; for you alone are the refuge and the goal for those who are distressed and seeking protection. (43)
What use have I for these wicked, dull-witted breaths of life, like a mere collection of evils, or for this body which is now a heavy burden without my high-souled lord?
What happiness can there be in this body composed of the five elements, which is defiled by sin? This boy is a knower of the Vedas, peaceful, an ascetic, and learned in many scriptures. (45)
Therefore, by granting him his life, you have protected the world; O Great King, show mercy toward this young Brahmin woman. (46)
"Truly, the virtuous are compassionate toward the helpless, the wretched, and the afflicted. Thus entreated, even that pitiless man-eater [replied]: || 47 ||
Having cut off the head of the brahmin’s son, the evil-minded one devoured it; then the virtuous woman, emaciated and miserable, lamented, being deeply afflicted by grief.
Having gathered her husband's bones, she prepared a formidable funeral pyre; following after her husband, she was about to enter the fire.
She struck that king, who had the form of a rākṣasa, with the weapon of a curse: "O sinful-souled king! By you my husband has been devoured! (50)

"Therefore, you must suffer the curse of this devoted wife in its full severity. Having said, "From this day forward, whenever you have union with women, that shall be your death," the virtuous woman entered the blazing fire.
That king also, having experienced the guru’s curse for its fixed duration, resumed his own form and went to his home rejoicing.
Having learned of the curse from the virtuous Brahmin woman, his wife, fearing the extreme misery of widowhood, restrained her husband who was longing for sexual pleasure.
Childless and despondent regarding the enjoyments of sovereignty, that king renounced all his royal fortune and went once more into the forest.
For the sake of establishing the Solar dynasty, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, begot an excellent son upon her, Madayantī.
Having renounced his kingdom, the king, while wandering over the entire earth, beheld a Piśācī of terrifying form following behind him.
For she was indeed terrible embodied Brahman-slaughter, difficult to overcome; since he, fallen by that curse, devoured the sage’s son. (57)
By means of that very act of his own, the king realized through the instruction of the best of sages that he was being pursued from behind by the sin of Brahman-slaughter.
Seeking an atonement for that [act], the king, with a despondent mind, wandered through various sacred fields and pilgrimage sites for many years. (59)

When, despite bathing repeatedly at all the sacred fords, the sin of killing a Brahmin was not removed, she then went to Mithilā; there, as she stood in the outer garden, she was tormented by intense anxiety.
He beheld the sage Gautama approaching, pure in intention, like the sacrificial fire attended by all the hosts of ascetics.
Like the sun, he utterly dispelled the darkness of the fault of density; like the moon, he fearlessly manifested the arising of pure qualities.
Like Maheśvara, he was glorious, bearing the digits of the king of the twice-born (the moon); he was peaceful, accompanied by a host of disciples, and the sole vessel of austerities.
Approaching him, that lord of kings prostrated himself again and again; and Gautama, the best of sages, likewise [honored] the king born of the solar dynasty.
Having greeted him with affection, the sage spoke with a gentle smile.
Gautama said: O King, is all well with you? Is your state immutable?
Are the subjects virtuous, or is even the people of the inner apartments so? For what purpose have you come here, having abandoned all your royal splendor?
Moreover, O King, what are you meditating upon as you sigh so long and hot? (68)
The king said: "O Brahmin, by your grace we are all well."
For the prosperity of kings born of the highest lineages is indeed dependent upon Brahmins; why then does this ghastly-looking ogress torment me? (69)

"Alas, what an insurmountable deed has been committed by me, consumed as I am by a curse—scolding her at every step while unnoticed by those others intoxicated with passion! No peace arises for that act even through thousands of expiatory rites. (70)

Various sacrifices were performed by me, with my entire treasury given away as sacrificial fees; I bathed in all the rivers and lakes that are worthy of veneration on this earth; and I wandered through and visited every sacred field (kṣetra).
All mantras have been recited, all deities have been meditated upon, and the great vows have been observed by me while subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits.
All of them have never once made me well; today, it seems as though the fruitfulness of my birth has finally been attained. (73)
For by the mere sight of you, my soul has become a partaker of bliss; whereas one who seeks it elsewhere may find his heart's desire only after many series of years. (74)
Thus, even this popular rumor has come to be true in my case, due to the rising tide of merits accumulated since birth. (75)
Since you, the protector of those afraid of worldly existence, have come within the range of our vision, from which region have you come here, O dispeller of the fear of saṃsāra? (76)
I suspect you have come here, weary from wandering afar; seeing you like a great marvel, you are filled with joy, as evidenced by the splendor of your face. (77)

You gladden my heart with your affection, as if through a personal conversation. O illustrious one, grant peace today to me, a sinner who has now taken refuge at your lotus feet, so that I may attain happiness. (78)
Thus instructed by him, Gautama, the treasury of compassion, duly prescribed the atonement for those terrible sins. (79)
Gautama said: "Excellent, O Indra among kings! You are blessed; cast off your fear of great sins."
O Śiva, the protector of devotees, where is there fear for those seeking refuge? Listen, O highly fortunate King; another sacred field has been established. (81)
The delightful place named Gokarṇa destroys even the great sins; there, no sins—neither small nor even those greater than the great—can remain.
For it is remembered that Śiva, who destroys all sins without exception, is ever-present there, just as he is on the peak of Kailāsa or upon the summit of Mandāra.
The residence of Śambhu was thus determined within the region of Gokarṇa; it is not [measured] by fire, nor by the moon, nor by the leaders of the stars and planets.
Just as darkness is completely dispelled by the sight of the sun, so too is it not dispelled by other sacred fords (tīrthas) nor by beautiful holy fields (kṣetras). || 85 ||
There shall be immediate purification from sin, just as by the sight of Gokarṇa; even after committing a hundred sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin, a human being [is purified].
Having entered Gokarṇa even once, one indeed never fears sin anywhere; for all the great-souled ones there have attained peace through austerity. (87)
It is served by Indra, Upendra, Viriñci, and others who desire spiritual perfection; for even that supreme vow which is performed there for a single day [yields great fruit]. (88)
That which was performed elsewhere for a hundred thousand years becomes equal to that [merit] where [this is done], out of a desire for the welfare of Indra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods. (89)
The god Mahābala himself is present there; he was obtained by the Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa through formidable ascetic penance.
The leader of the Gaṇas established that great Liṅga at Gokarṇa; so too did Indra, Brahmā, Mukunda, the Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the two Dasras, the Moon, and the Sun—these gods, together with their retinues, travel in celestial chariots.
They attend upon the eastern gate of the trident-bearing God of gods; there dwell Yoni, Mṛtyu himself in person, Citragupta, and Pāvaka.
Varuṇa, the lord of rivers, together with the Pitṛs and the Rudras, took his place at the southern gate, accompanied by hosts of rivers such as the Gaṅgā.
Resorting to the western gate, one should worship Mahādeva; likewise Vāyu, Kubera, Deveśī, and Bhadrakarṇikā. (95)
And the Mothers, Caṇḍikā and the others, have taken refuge at the northern gate; likewise Viśvāvasu, Citraratha, and the mighty Citrasena.
Together with the hosts of Gandharvas, Rambhā, Ghṛtācī, Menā, Pūrvacitti, and Tilottamā worshiped the one of great strength.
Urvaśī and other celestial women dance before Śambhu; so too do Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Kaṇva, and Viśvāmitra of great asceticism.
Jaimini, Bharadvāja, Jābāli, Kratu, and Aṅgiras—O Indra among kings, all these as well as we ourselves are stainless Brahman-sages.
Together with Marīci, Atri, Dakṣa, and other lords of sages, we worship the God of great power with devotion from all sides.
The high-souled Sanaka and others were seated there worshipping him, as were the sages and the Sādhyas, clad in deerskins.
Staff-bearers with shaven heads, bath-graduates, and celibate students, whose limbs consisted of nothing but skin and bone, had their sins burnt away by austerity.
The gods, along with the Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas, worship the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, with supreme devotion. || 3 ||
Vidyādharas, Kiṃpuruṣas, Kinnaras, Guhyakas, birds, Nāgas, Piśācas, Vetālas, and the exceedingly powerful Daityas. || 4 ||
Endowed with various riches, possessing diverse ornaments and vehicles, they traveled in celestial chariots resembling the sun, glowing like fire, and radiant as the moon.
Surrounded on all sides by others resembling masses of lightning, they praised him, sang his praises, recited hymns, and prostrated before him.
O Lord of the Earth, they dance and rejoice at Gokarṇa; they obtain their desired objects and sport according to their pleasure.
Within the sphere of the cosmic egg, there is no sacred field equal to Gokarṇa; it was there that the high-souled Agastya performed severe penance.
Likewise, O King, [it was performed] by Sanatkumāra, by the sons of Priyavrata, by Agni, the best of gods, and by Kandarpa.
Likewise, [he was accompanied] by the goddess Bhadrakālī, by the wise Śiśumāra, by Durmukha, and by the lord of serpents named Maṇināga.
By the nāgas beginning with Ilāvarta, by the powerful Garuḍa, and also by the rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa.
The high-souled Vibhīṣaṇa performed meritorious penance; so too did these and other gods, Siddhas, Dānavas, and humans. || 12 ||
Having worshipped Śiva, the Lord of the gods of gods, with devotion at Gokarṇa, he installed thousands of Liṅgas inscribed with his own name.
They attained supreme perfection and likewise established sacred fords; O King, here exist the abodes of all the gods.
And of Viṣṇu, the god of gods; of Brahmā, the supreme lord; of the heroic Kārttikeya; and of the elephant-faced one, O sinless one. (15)
O high-minded one, there exist tens of millions upon tens of millions of Śiva-liṅgas at Gokarṇa belonging to Dharma, Kṣetrapāla, and Durgā.
Innumerable sacred fords exist at every step; O King, what is the use of saying more regarding those situated at Gokarṇa? (17)
All stones are lingas, and all waters everywhere are sacred fords; at Gokarṇa, there are likewise numerous Shiva-lingas and sacred fords.
O King, the greatness [of this place] is sung by the great seers in the Purāṇas; and at Gokarṇa, Koṭitīrtha has attained preeminence among all sacred fords.
Among all the Śiva-liṅgas, Mahābala is the sovereign; in the Kṛta age he is Mahābala, and in the Tretā age he is Atilohita (the very red).
In the Dvāpara age he will be yellow in color, and in the Kali age he will become dark-complexioned; though possessing great strength, he will traverse even the seven netherworlds.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, the supreme sacred field of Gokarṇa, situated on the shore of the western ocean, will attain gentleness.
What wonder is there that it burns away sins such as the killing of a Brahmin? For here are those who have killed Brahmins, those who harm living beings, and the deceitful. (23)
Those who are devoid of all virtues, those who are devoted to the wives of others, those who are ill-behaved, of wicked conduct, of bad character, and those who are miserly; || 24 ||
Those who are greedy, cruel, wicked, foolish, thieves, and excessively lustful—all of them, having reached Gokarṇa and bathed in the waters of the sacred fords (tīrtha), [are purified]. || 125 ||
Having beheld the god of great power, they departed for the abode of Śaṅkara; there, on auspicious lunar days, under auspicious constellations, and on auspicious days.
Those who worship Maheśāna shall undoubtedly become Rudras; whether at any time whatsoever, and whoever that man may be, [if he goes] to Gokarṇa.
Having entered, he should worship the Lord; he shall go to the abode of Brahmā. When the new moon (darśa) occurs on the days of the Sun, Moon, or Mercury, [he should act]. || 28 ||
Then, bathing in the ocean, giving gifts, libations to the ancestors, worship of Śiva, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, observance of vows, and honoring the twice-born [are performed]. (29)
Whatever action whatsoever is performed during the Vyatīpāta and other such yogas, as well as during the sun's transits (saṃkrāntis), yields infinite fruit. || 130 ||
At times of great transgression, the worship of Śiva grants liberation. Now, O King, I shall describe to you one lunar day that bestows liberation. (31)
That most meritorious Kṛṣṇa-caturdaśī in the month of Māgha, on which it is said that the great hunter attained the supreme state of Śambhu, [is celebrated]. 32.
The Śiva-liṅga, the bilva leaf, and [the auspicious day]—these four are indeed difficult to obtain. Oh, how powerful is Māyā, by which even the great festival of Śiva [is obscured]! 33.
The Triple Veda is not honored by foolish people, who are like the utterly mute; [they neglect] fasting, keeping vigil, and the presence of the Supreme Lord. (34)
Gokarṇa is a flight of stairs for men leading to the world of Śiva; listen, O King, for I too have now come from Gokarṇa. (135)
Having worshipped this auspicious lunar day and observed the great festival, on this day of Śiva all were eager to behold the grand celebration.
Great crowds of people belonging to all four castes have arrived from all countries—women, the elderly, and children, as well as those residing in the four stages of life. || 37 ||
Having arrived and beheld the Lord of Gods, they attained the fulfillment of their purpose; then I too, as well as these disciples, the sages, and others likewise [did so].
O Indra among kings, the royal sages and the celestial sages, beginning with Sanaka and others, having bathed in all the holy fords, worshipped Mahābala.
Having attained the fulfillment of their birth, they have departed in every direction today by this king Janaka, who is desirous of performing a sacrifice.

Having been invited, I arrived from Gokarṇa, the abode of Śiva; O dear one, O lord of the earth, having seen some marvel on the way, I have returned with a mind full of great joy, feeling that my life’s purpose has been fulfilled. (141)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Gokarṇa," in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa of the third section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The king said: "O Brahmin, what wonder have you seen on the road, or where? Tell me that, so that I may attain the fulfillment of my purpose. (1)
Gautama said: O lord of the people, while returning from Gokarṇa, at some place when midday had arrived, I found a pure lake.
Having sipped water there and dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he took refuge under a banyan tree that offered very pleasant and cool shade.
Then, not far away, [he saw] an old Caṇḍāla woman who was blind, emaciated in form, with a parched face, deprived of food, and afflicted by many diseases.
Her limbs were covered with leprosy sores, teeming with swarms of emerging worms; her hips were draped in a tattered rag soaked in pus and blood.
Afflicted by a great consumption residing in her throat, she was distressed by the constriction of her windpipe; her teeth were decayed, her speech indistinct, and she rolled about repeatedly.
She was drenched in dust, harsh and hot from contact with the rays of the fierce sun; her limbs were smeared with feces, urine, and pus, and she was difficult to approach due to the stench of blood.
I saw her on the verge of death, afflicted by many phlegmatic diseases, labored breathing, and extreme pain; her hair and limbs were wasted away.
Beholding such agony, I was overwhelmed with compassion; awaiting her death, I remained right there for a moment.
Then I beheld a divine celestial chariot brought by the servants of Śiva, which seemed to drench the path of the atmosphere with its rays.
In that celestial chariot, which was like a cage of light from the sun, moon, and fire, I beheld the attendants of Śiva, who were as radiant as the sun.
They indeed held tridents, khaṭvāṅgas, axes, shields, and swords in their hands; they were adorned with crescent moons and possessed a great luster like that of the full moon and the kunda flower.
I beheld four auspicious followers of Śiva, radiant with crowns, earrings, and great serpent-bracelets. (13)
Seeing them approaching while stationed in their celestial chariots, I was greatly amazed; drawing near to them as they remained in the sky, I questioned them with urgency.

Homage, repeated homage, to the most excellent among the thirty deities, who follow at the feet of the glorious Three-eyed Lord; to those who carry out the rite for the protection of the three worlds, and who bear the trident, shield, sword, and mace. || 15 ||
For I have recognized you as followers of the state of Maheśvara; is this your way of acting for the sake of protecting the world, or is it born of mere sport?
Moreover, tell me out of compassion why you have come here, for you are all making an effort to conquer the flood of sins of all people. (17)
The messengers of Śiva said: "This old Caṇḍāla woman, on the verge of death, is seen here before us. We have been commanded by our Lord and have come to fetch her. (18)
When this had been said by those messengers of Śiva, I, my mind filled with wonder, stood before them with palms joined in reverence and questioned them once again. (19)
"Aha! How can this most wicked and terrible Cāṇḍālī deserve to ascend a celestial chariot, like a female dog entering the sacrificial arena? (20)
"From birth she has been full of impurity, sinful, and followed by evil; how can you wish to lead this woman of wicked conduct to the world of Śiva? (21)
She possesses no knowledge of Śiva, nor does she perform the most formidable penance; she has neither truth nor compassion—how can you wish to lead her away? 22.
How can you wish to lead her—who constantly takes food made of animal flesh, whose belly is filled with wine, and who delights eternally in the slaughter of living beings? (23)
"The five-syllable mantra has not been recited, nor has the worship of Śiva been performed; the Lord Śambhu has not been meditated upon—how then do you wish to lead her away? (24)
