The auspicious lunar day was not observed as a fast, nor was worship of Śiva performed; he knows nothing of kindness toward living beings, nor does he offer bilva fruits to Śiva; nor has he performed sacrifices or works of public utility—how then do you wish to lead him away? (25)
No sacred fords have been visited, no gifts have been given, and no vows have been observed; how then do you wish to lead her away? (26)
She must be avoided even at a mere glance, how much more so in conversation and other interactions? How can you wish to lead this fierce woman, who is devoid of association with the virtuous?
Does she possess some merit acquired in another birth? For how else could she be overcome by this leprosy and its worms? (28)
Oh, how inconceivable is this conduct of the Lord toward embodied beings! Even those of sinful nature are led to the supreme state through His compassion. (29)
Having been addressed thus by me, those messengers of the trident-bearing God of gods then replied to me with affection, dispelling all my doubts.
The messengers of Śiva said: "O Brāhmaṇa, listen to this very great marvel if you have curiosity regarding what has just been said by you concerning this Caṇḍālī."
In a previous birth, she was a certain Brahmin girl named Sumitrā, whose face resembled the full orb of the moon.
She was a virtuous daughter of a certain eminent brahmin of Kaikeya, her limbs possessing the delicate beauty of a garland of full-blown jasmine flowers.
Seeing her, endowed with every auspicious mark like another embodiment of Rati, growing up in her father’s house, the people were filled with wonder.
Growing day by day and cherished exceedingly by her kinsmen, she gradually attained youth, like the great bow of Smara.
Then that maiden, together with her assembled circle of kinsmen, was given by her father according to the prescribed rites to a certain son of a brahmin.
Having obtained her husband, she, endowed with fresh youth and virtuous in conduct, enjoyed herself for some time surrounded by her kinsmen.
Then, O Sage, by the power of time, her husband—who was handsome, youthful, and beloved—fell victim to a severe illness and passed away.
When her husband had died, that virtuous woman, her heart consumed by grief, lived for some months with excellent conduct and her senses subdued.
Then, as the burden of her youth constantly expanded, her heart became tremulous with the god of love.
Though guarded by her circle of kinsmen and instructed by the most excellent elders, that woman was unable to restrain her mind, which was drawn away by passion.
Overcome by intense passion, she, endowed with beauty and youth—especially as a widow—became devoted to the pursuit of lovers. (42)
The wise woman, though most wicked, did not reveal herself as a paramour to anyone; for a certain time, she concealed her own misconduct. (43)
In time, even her circle of kinsmen perceived that she, overcome by pregnancy-longings and possessing breasts with dark blue nipples, had been defiled by a paramour.
Thus, terrified by great affliction, he fell into an insurmountable anxiety: "Women are ruined by lust, and Brahmins by service to the lowly. (45)
Kings [fall] by the Brahmin’s curse, and ascetics by their accumulation of enjoyments; likewise, food licked by a dog, or milk mixed with liquor, [is unfit]. (46)
"Physical deformity brings leprosy, and a wicked wife destroys the family. Having reflected thus, all the brothers gathered together. (47)
Taking her by the hair, they cast her far away from their kin; that woman was abandoned by all her relatives along with the ritual pitcher.
Wandering about and sporting with a Śūdra, that woman, who was fond of pleasure, went outside the village and was seen by a certain Śūdra.

Seeing that woman of beautiful hips with full and elevated breasts, the leader of the Śūdras brought that widow to his home with gentle words; having become his queen, she spent her days and nights with him.
Delighting herself in a certain place, that beloved of the house dwelt there; there she constantly subsisted on flesh and drank wine.
Delighting in pleasure, she obtained a son from the Śūdra while sporting with him; once, when her husband had gone somewhere, she drank wine.
Intoxicated by wine, she desired a meal of flesh; then, while the sheep were tied up outside in the pen along with the cows, (she set out).
Taking up her sword, she went forth at the onset of night; driven by the onset of intoxication and being fond of meat, she did not reflect, perceiving him as a ram.
One night, an unfortunate woman killed a lowing calf; having brought the slain calf home, the woman realized it was indeed a calf.
Terrified, she cried out "Śiva, Śiva! due to some meritorious deed; having meditated thus for a moment, she became once more eager for flesh and blood.
Having cut that very calf, she made it her desired food; then, having taken her meal with half the body of the calf, she [proceeded] once more.
Leaving half of its body outside, he cried out in feigned distress: "Alas! This calf in the cow-pen has been mangled and devoured by a tiger! (58)
Thus her cry was heard throughout all the houses; then all the Śūdra people gathered together and stood nearby. (59)
Seeing the calf killed by the tiger, they were overcome with grief; and when they had all departed, the night then dawned.
Her husband, having returned home, saw the ruin of the household. Thus, after much time had passed, that beloved of the Śūdra—
Having fallen under the power of Time, she went to the abode of Yama; and Yama too, having observed her dharma and her past actions, [acted accordingly].
Having extinguished the dwellings of hell, he created a womb of the Caṇḍāla caste; she too, fallen from the city of Yama, entered the womb of a Caṇḍāla woman.
Then she became blind from birth, her limbs as dark as extinguished embers; her father was a certain Caṇḍāla residing in a certain region.
Out of compassion, he nourished that daughter even though she was such [a girl]: with inedible, wretched food, licked by a dog, and putrid.
Nourished day by day with unwholesome juices, she became blind from birth and was afflicted by the disease of leprosy in her childhood.
She was extremely unfortunate and had not been married by anyone, not even by a Cāṇḍāla; in the time following her childhood, she was left with her father and mother destroyed.
Abandoned by her kinsmen and brothers as one of ill fortune, she was then afflicted by hunger, wretched, lamenting, and deprived of sight.
Holding a staff and carrying a clod of earth, she moved about with great difficulty, begging day after day even in all the cities. (69)
He satisfied the fire of his stomach with morsels of food left over by a Cāṇḍāla; in this manner, he spent a very great portion of his life through immense hardship.
With all her limbs seized by old age, she experienced insurmountable suffering; once, being destitute of food, drink, and clothing, she [beheld] great crowds of people.
On that auspicious lunar day (Śivatithi), as people were arriving, he perceived travelers departing for that festival of the gods from various regions and distant lands.
Of the high-souled Brahmins who maintain the sacred fire along with their wives, and of the kings together with their harems, elephants, chariots, and horses; 73.
Of those accompanied by their retinues, adorned with vehicles, parasols, and the like, as well as others consisting of thousands of Vaiśyas and Śūdras mixed together; || 74 ||
Of those laughing, singing, dancing somewhere, or running; of those smelling, drinking, moving about out of desire, or shouting back in response. (75)
A very great commotion arose among the people during their departure, as they all proceeded toward Gokarṇa, the abode of Śiva. || 76 ||
All the gods, stationed in their celestial chariots, watched with curiosity; and then this Cāṇḍālī woman also, out of hunger and thirst for food and clothing, [beheld them].

She moved forward very slowly to beg from the great multitude of people, supported by the hand of another due to the karma she had accumulated in a previous birth; after traveling for several days, she arrived at the sacred field of Gokarṇa.
Then, seated by the side of the road at some distance, with her palms outstretched, she spoke these piteous words repeatedly, entreating the travelers. (79)
O people, show compassion by giving me merely food, for I have long been tormented by the multitude of sins accumulated in previous births. (80)
Saviors of those in extreme distress, givers of the highest blessings, performers of many meritorious deeds—O people, show compassion! (Ra) 1.
O people, show compassion toward her who is destitute of clothing and food, sleeping upon the bare ground, and buried deep in the great dust! 82.
O people, show compassion toward me, who am afflicted by great heat and cold, tormented by severe illness, blind, and old. (83)
O people, show compassion toward her, whose every limb is being consumed by the fires of digestion kindled through long fasting! (84)
O people, show compassion toward this sinful and unfortunate woman, who has failed to accumulate merit even throughout hundreds of previous births. (85)
As the Caṇḍāla woman was thus entreating with her palms outstretched in reverence, a single most meritorious traveler cast a cluster of bilva blossoms into them.
Having repeatedly examined it as it lay fallen on the hem of her garment, she, concluding that it was indeed unfit for consumption, cast it away at a distance in distress.
Released from her hand at night, that cluster of bilva blossoms fell, by some stroke of fortune, upon the top of a certain Śiva-liṅga.

Thus, on the night of the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight dedicated to Śiva, although she repeatedly begged from the travelers for something, by the turn of fate she obtained nothing at all. (89)
She spent that night there, behind Bhadrakālī, in a place slightly to the north, not very far away, at half that distance.
Then at dawn, her hopes shattered and overwhelmed by great sorrow, she returned slowly and dejectedly all alone toward her own country.
Exhausted by long fasting, stumbling at every step, crying out, afflicted by many diseases, trembling and extremely distressed. || 92 ||
Scorched by the heat of the sun, her body naked and clutching a staff, she fell unconscious after having traversed this much ground.
Then Śambhu, the Lord of the Universe and an ocean of the nectar of compassion, commanded us, along with our celestial chariots, saying, "Bring her here."

This conduct of the Cāṇḍālī has been proclaimed here to you, as well as Śambhu’s compassion toward the wretched. Behold, O high-minded one, the destiny arising from the ripening of karma: even the lowest woman ascends to the supreme, painless state.
Because she did not perform acts such as the giving of food in her previous existence, she is therefore tormented here by the afflictions of hunger, thirst, and the like. (97)
Because she, blinded by the force of intoxication, committed such a terrible sin, she became blind from birth in this very life due to that action.
Moreover, because she previously ate her own calf even after recognizing it, by that deed she became a despised Caṇḍālī in this world. (99)
Because she formerly abandoned the path of the noble ones and delighted in the way of paramours, by some such evil karma she has become ill-behaved or even unfortunate.
In the past, when that widow, overcome by passion, embraced her paramour, she became possessed of many leprosy sores due to that great sin. (101)
Since this woman, afflicted by desire, formerly took her pleasure at will with a Śūdra, she is now tormented by that sin with great quantities of blood, pus, and worms.
She did not observe sacred vows, nor did she perform sacrifices, purificatory rites, or other meritorious acts; deprived of all enjoyments, she suffers because of that sin. (3)
Because she drank liquor in a previous existence while deluded, she is now tormented by that evil deed with the afflictions of a great consumption and pains in her heart.
O tiger among sages, all the signs of sin among all mortals here are perceived in their entirety by high-souled ones possessed of discernment.
In this regard, those who are afflicted by many diseases, and those who are destitute of sons and wealth; || 6 ||
And those beggars who are afflicted by ill-omened marks and devoid of shame, [he satisfies] with clothing, food, drink, bedding, ornaments, ointments, and so forth.
Those who are lowly, deformed, despondent, deficient in limbs, or deprived of good food; those who are unfortunate, censured, and others who are servants of others. || 8 ||
"All these were performers of very great evil in their previous lives"; having thus reflected with effort and observed the condition of worldly beings, [he spoke].
The wise man commits no evil; were he to do so, he would be a destroyer of his own self. This human body of a living being is the sole vessel for manifold karma.
One should always practice virtuous deeds and constantly abandon evil deeds; one who seeks happiness should perform merit, while one who seeks suffering may commit sin.
When one of these two has been chosen in the world by a wise person, having relied upon this human body which is most difficult to obtain— (12)
If any person who seeks his own welfare should take refuge in the One God, then that man, even while constantly committing all manner of sins, [is saved]. (13)
One who meditates with a one-pointed mind on Śiva crosses over sin; for when she died in a previous birth and reached the abode of Yama, [she was saved]. 14.
Then a very great doubt arose among the members of Yama’s assembly: "Even though this woman is a Brahmin, she has defiled the conduct of a noble family. (15)
Therefore, she has been brought here by us, whether she goes to hell or not; for perhaps even a slight fragment of merit was acquired by her in her childhood. (16)

Nevertheless, having reflected well in this manner, the punishment should be meted out here and not otherwise; for it results from the ripening of merit accumulated over many thousands of births. (17)
Indeed, birth in the family of Brahmā is obtained by men only with great difficulty; therefore, she has committed no sin in her successive previous births. (18)
Otherwise, how could she have obtained birth in a noble family? In this very life, she must have committed an inescapable sin. (19)
Nevertheless, she does not deserve to go to the abode of hell; however, having killed the calf, her fear has arisen upon reflection. (120)
By virtue of karma accumulated in previous births, she utters "Śiva, Śiva"; for even once, this brings about great auspiciousness for the destruction of her sins. (21)
If one should utter the name of Śiva with devotion, then one shall go to the supreme state; such is the fruit of even this terrible act committed in a single birth.
Having experienced these in succession and having become one born of the Cāṇḍāla caste, what other hell could there be for men here than this? (23)
That which is the constant torment by the multitude of manifold afflictions; birth in a low family, poverty, great disease, and delusion. (24)
Was it each hell individually, or all of them together, that she—rendered helpless by the weight of merit from her previous birth—spoke? (25)
By that [act], she will perform abundant merit in another birth; by that great merit, having crossed over the multitude of her sins, she will be liberated.
Led by his servants at the end, she shall go to the supreme state. We are never the judges of such mortals; having reflected for himself, let the Lord do whatever is appropriate. (27)
Thus, after deliberating in the city of Vaivasvata with all those led by Yama, including Citragupta and others, she was released and fell to the earth.

Because this woman, though not virtuous, had at first uttered the name of Śiva even through negligence, she obtained here once again the merit of worshipping Śambhu with bilva sprouts by virtue of that good deed. (29)
Having fasted at the auspicious Gokarṇa on the lunar day sacred to Śiva, she indeed kept a vigil at the head of Śiva and offered *bilva* leaves at night.
The fruit of this very merit performed unintentionally, she shall enjoy this very day; behold, it is not false.
Gautama said: Having spoken thus, those messengers of Śiva drew out the fragment of her life-force from her cāṇḍāla womb and united it with divine splendor.
Those joyful servants of Śiva placed her, whose divine body was manifest and who blazed like a mass of splendor, upon a celestial chariot.
Then she, endowed with most noble beauty and charm, her limbs radiant with divine ornaments and wearing celestial garments, [appeared].
Moving in her celestial chariot, she shone with a body possessing divine fragrance, radiant with divine splendor, and adorned with divine garlands and ear-ornaments.
Amidst the sounds of songs and musical instruments, and with jeweled parasols, banners, and other ornaments, that beautiful-faced woman rejoiced in the midst of the messengers of Śiva.
Having remembered again and again the births she had experienced, she was struck with fear and trembling; yet, seeing this firm wonder, she was as if awakened from a dream. (37)
"Who am I? Who are these great Siddhas? What is this enchanting world? Where has my body gone—alas, that body born of the fierce Caṇḍāla lineage? (38)
"Oh, what a truly great marvel has been seen, born from the play of Māyā, which I have wandered through again and again throughout thousands of births! (39)
Oh, how wonderful is the greatness of the worship of the Lord! He who is satisfied with a mere leaf bestows his own abode. (140)
Thus, having placed her—who had conceived world-weariness and was remembering the station of the Blessed One—upon a divine celestial chariot, those servants of Maheśvara [departed]. (41)
While all the Lords of the World gazed on with wonder, they addressed her and led her into the presence of the Supreme Lord.
O King, you have related this most wonderful account of the majesty of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain; even a mere fragment of devotion to him destroys the entire mass of sins.
The king said: "O Blessed One, what is the nature of the supreme world of the Supreme Lord? If you have compassion for me, tell me its characteristics. (44)
Gautama said: That world where bliss is eternal, which is extremely difficult to attain even in the worlds of the lords of the gods beginning with Brahmā—that is the world of the Supreme Lord.
That world of the Supreme Lord is where there is the transcending of all things, where light is firmly established, and where there is no contact with darkness anywhere.
Having completely transcended the functioning of the qualities (guṇas), that world where all yogins have arrived is the realm of the Supreme Lord, from which none shall fall again. (47)
That world belongs to the Supreme Lord, wherein anger, greed, pride, and the like find no dwelling, and wherein states such as birth and so forth do not exist.
That which is called the single field of all the Vedas, than which there is no higher wealth—that is the state of the Supreme Lord. (49)

It is that which yogis always strive to attain through the paths of yoga, such as withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), postures (āsana), meditation (dhyāna), and the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyamana). || 150 ||
That world of the Supreme Lord is where the God sports together with the Goddess, whose form is eternal bliss and stainless knowledge.
There, men and women who have ascended by means of the masses of merit accumulated over many thousands of births sport together in union.
Completely merged within that beautiful mass of light which is difficult to perceive, they never again experience the distinction of day and night or other such temporal states.
That realm of the Supreme Lord is indeed difficult for a false yogin to attain; it is reached only by those who are completely full of devotion to Him. 54.

Those who experience joy from hearing and reciting his stories, who are friends to all beings and solely devoted to tranquility, having transcended the wheel of saṃsāra and cast off delusion, attain the state of Śaṅkara and rejoice in bliss.
In the same way, O Indra among kings, you too, having gone to Gokarṇa, the abode of Giriśa, shall have the flood of your sins pacified and attain the state of one who has fulfilled his purpose.
There, having bathed at all times and worshipped Mahābala, one should, with a concentrated mind, observe a fast on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight dedicated to Śiva.
Having kept a vigil at night and worshipped Śaṅkara with bilva fruits, you shall be liberated from all sins and attain the world of Śiva.
O King, this pure instruction has been given to you by me; may it be well with you, for I shall now depart for the city of the Lord of Mithilā.
Having thus addressed him with affection, the sage Gautama departed for Mithilā; the king, too, with a joyful heart, proceeded toward Gokarṇa.
Having seen Mahādeva there, bathed, and worshipped the Greatly Powerful One, he was cleansed of the entire flood of his sins and attained the supreme state of Śambhu.
Whoever should constantly listen to this captivating story of Śiva, or should cause others to hear it with devotion, that person attains the supreme goal.
Even one who listens to this story with faith, even if only once, shall attain the world of Śiva together with twenty-one generations of his kin.

Thus has been told in its entirety the noble life-story of the Enemy of Manmatha—the seed of all blessings, the destroyer of the evils of hundreds of births, and the dispeller of the darkness of delusion; it is fit to be sung by the gods and should be constantly cultivated by those who desire well-being. 164.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Gokarṇa on Śiva-Caturdaśī," in the Brahmottara Section of the Third Part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Once again I shall proclaim the most wonderful majesty of Śiva, which destroys all sins for those who hear it and grants liberation from the bonds of worldly existence. 1.

For those whose minds are attached to sense-objects and who are sinking in the ocean of misfortunes that is difficult to cross, no raft whatsoever has been determined to exist except for the worship of Śiva.
A wise person in this world should always perform the worship of Śiva; if he is unable to do so, he should, with a mind bowed by devotion, behold the worship that has been performed.
Even one who performs the worship of Śiva, which grants liberation, with a lack of faith, or even one who merely beholds it, shall in due course of time attain the supreme state.
In the lands of the Kirātas, there was a king named Vimardana; he was a hero, exceedingly invincible, a conqueror of enemies, and possessed of great majesty.
Always addicted to hunting, miserable, pitiless, and powerful, he was a consumer of all kinds of meat, cruel, and surrounded by women of every caste.
Nevertheless, he constantly performed the worship of Śambhu without weariness, especially on the fourteenth day of both the bright and dark fortnights.
Having performed a worship endowed with great wealth, he rejoices; overcome with great joy, he dances, praises, and sings. (8)
As that king, who devoured everything and was of wicked conduct, lived in this manner, his queen was deeply distressed by his behavior.
That queen, named Kumudvatī, endowed with virtuous character and qualities, once approached her husband in private and asked him this.
O King, this conduct of yours is a cause of great wonder: where was your former great misconduct, and where now is this devotion to the Supreme Lord? (11)
"You are always a consumer of all things, lustful for all women, and cruelly intent on harming all beings; how can there be devotion to the Lord in you? (12)
Thus questioned, that king, who knew the three periods of time, reflected for a very long while; then, smiling with great curiosity, he spoke to her.
The king said: "O fair-faced one, in a previous birth I was a certain dog; having taken refuge in the city of Paṃpā, I used to roam about everywhere. (14)
As time passed in this manner, I once arrived at that very same excellent city, at a beautiful and auspicious temple.
While the worship was being performed on the great lunar day of the fourteenth, I, stationed at the outer gate, beheld the festival from afar.
Then, pursued by those who were extremely enraged and carrying staffs in their hands, I fled from that place, intent solely on saving my life.
Then, having circumambulated the beautiful temple of Śiva and reached the gateway once more, he was again turned back.
Having circumambulated that very temple of Śiva once more, he returned to the door again out of greed for the sacrificial offerings and morsels of food.
Having thus repeatedly performed circumambulations there, they struck him with sharp arrows as he sat at the gateway.
With his body pierced, he suddenly lost his life at the gateway of Śiva; by the power of Śiva’s presence, I have been born into a family of kings. (21)
"Having witnessed the worship on the fourteenth day and observed the garlands of lamps, by that great merit, O beautiful lady, I have become a knower of the three periods of time."
Due to the latent impressions of my previous births, I am merciless and a consumer of all things; for the nature consisting of latent impressions is difficult to overcome even for the wise. (23)
Therefore, I worship the Lord, the Teacher of the World, on the fourteenth day; you too, O blessed lady, should worship the god who wields the Pināka bow with faith.

The queen said: "O Indra among kings, by the grace of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, you are a knower of the three periods of time; you ought to relate my previous birth's history according to the truth. (25)
The king said: "In a previous birth, you were a certain female pigeon wandering through the sky; by chance, she found me somewhere together with my bones. (26)
Then, seeing that some powerful vulture had seized the meat you were holding, another terrifying vulture, himself devoid of meat, rushed toward him with great speed. (27)
Then, O lady of beautiful countenance, seeing him, you fled in terror, pursued by that terrible being who desired to seize you as a lump of flesh.
By good fortune, having reached Śrī Giri, she became weary there and, after performing a circumambulation of the temple of Śiva, she came to stand at the tip of the flagpole. (29)
Then, having suddenly pursued you, that sharp-beaked bird struck you down, cast you below, and departed taking your flesh.
"Because you performed circumambulation of the trident-bearing God of gods and because of your death in his presence, you have been born here as the wife of a king. (31)

The queen said: "I have heard in its entirety all that was done in my previous birth. A great wonder has arisen, and devotion has taken root in my heart. Now, O high-minded one who knows the three periods of time, I desire to hear something else: after casting off this body, what destination shall we two go to? (32)
The king said: "Therefore, I shall be born in this second existence as the Sindhu king."
"For you are the daughter of Sṛñjayīśa, and you shall indeed obtain me as your husband; moreover, in my third birth, I shall become a king in Saurāṣṭra."
"You, the daughter of the King of Kaliṅga, shall become my wife; and in the fourth birth, I shall be the sovereign of the land of Gāndhāra. (35)
There, you shall be the daughter of the King of Magadha and my wife; in the fifth birth, I shall become the Lord of Avanti in another life.
"You alone, daughter of the King of the Dāśārhas, are my beloved. In this very birth, in my sixth incarnation, I shall become a king in Ānarta. (37)
"Having been born as a maiden in the lineage of Yayāti, you shall come to me alone; for I shall become the prince of the Pāṇḍyas in my seventh birth. (38)
In that regard, there is no one else like me in terms of physical beauty, nobility, virtues, and so forth; I am a knower of the true meaning of all scriptures, powerful, and firm in my prowess. (39)
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, delightful to all the world, he was renowned as Padmavarṇa, possessing a splendor equal to that of Padmamitra.
And you, O daughter of Vidarbha, shall become peerless on earth in beauty; renowned by the name Vasumatī, you will be radiant with the splendor of your form and limbs. (41)
Delighting the minds and eyes of all the princes, you, having bypassed all those sons of kings at your svayaṃvara—
"You shall obtain me as your boon, just as Damayantī obtained the King of Niṣadha; for I, having conquered all kings, have now won you, O woman of excellent complexion. (43)
"Remaining in my own kingdom, I shall enjoy all pleasures for many years, having performed various auspicious sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) and others. (44)
Having satisfied the ancestors, gods, and sages with gifts, and having worshipped Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Gods of gods and the benefactor of the world, O best of the twice-born; (45)
Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to my son, I shall go to the forest for asceticism; and there, having obtained the knowledge of Brahman from Agastya, the best of sages.
I shall go with you to the supreme abode of Śiva, having thus worshipped Śaṅkara on every fourteenth lunar day.
"O fair-faced one, you shall become a king for seven births; this merit has been obtained merely by the sight of the worship. Where is that wicked-souled dog, and where is such a meeting? Alas! (48)
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by her own lord, that queen of auspicious marks [departed].
Filled with supreme wonder, she joyfully honored him; and that king, together with her, enjoyed pleasures as he desired. (50)
At the end of seven births, he went to that supreme abode of Śambhu. Whoever hears or even recites this most wonderful majesty of the worship of Śiva shall go to the supreme abode. || 51 ||

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Fourteenth Day," in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa, the third section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Śiva is the Guru, Śiva is the God, Śiva is the kinsman of all embodied beings; Śiva is the Self, Śiva is the individual soul—there is nothing whatsoever other than Śiva.
Whatever is given, recited, offered in sacrifice, or performed with Śiva in mind is declared to yield infinite fruit; this is certain according to all the Āgamas.
A leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, even if it be very small or extremely meager, when offered with devotion to Śambhu, leads to infinite merit.
Having abandoned all dharmas determined by all the scriptures, he who worships Śiva alone is liberated from all bonds.
If that same affection which one has for one's own son, for one's wife, or even for wealth, were directed toward the worship of Śiva, what wonder is there that it would grant protection? (5)
Therefore, some great-souled ones renounce all the intoxicating draughts of sense-objects, and for the sake of worshipping Śiva, they even abandon their own bodies, which are so difficult to give up.
That is a true tongue which praises Śiva; that is a true mind which meditates upon Śiva; those are true ears which long for his stories; and those are true hands which worship him.
Those two eyes behold worship; that head bows before Śiva; and those two feet are the field of Śiva, which they always traverse with devotion.
He whose senses all engage in auspicious deeds crosses over saṃsāra and attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 9 ||
A mortal endowed with devotion to Śiva—whether a Cāṇḍāla or a Pulkasa, a woman, a man, or even a eunuch—is instantly liberated from the cycle of worldly existence.
Of what avail is lineage, of what avail are conduct, character, or virtue? He who possesses even a fraction of devotion to Śambhu is worthy of being saluted by all embodied beings. (11)
In Ujjayinī there was a king named Candrasena, born in human form like a second Indra. (12)
In that city, Candrasena, the best of kings, worships with devotion the Supreme Lord Mahākāla who dwells there.
Maṇibhadra, the foremost of Śiva’s attendants, who had conquered all misfortune and was honored by all the worlds, became a friend to that king.
Once, the high-minded Maṇibhadra, a follower of Śaṅkara who was pleased with that lord of the earth, gave him a divine cintāmaṇi jewel.
That jewel, shining like the Kaustubha gem and resembling the sun, bestows whatever is desired upon men when it is seen, heard, or meditated upon. || 16 ||
Touched by even a mere fragment of its luster, bell-metal, copper, iron, tin, stone, or any other material immediately becomes gold. (17)
Wearing that wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) around his neck, the king ascended the royal throne; he shone like the sun itself in the midst of the gods.
Having heard that the best of kings always wore a wish-fulfilling gem around his neck, all the other kings became agitated at heart, their longing increasing even further.
Out of affection some begged, while others, intoxicated by pride, asked out of sheer audacity; these envious kings did not realize that the jewel had been obtained through destiny.
When his entreaties to all the kings were rendered futile by him, the rulers of all lands then gave way to great agitation.
The Saurāṣṭras, Kaikayas, Śālvas, Kaliṅgas, Śakas, Madrakas, Pāñcālas, Avantis, Sauvīras, Māgadhas, Matsyas, and Sṛñjayas. || 22 ||
These and other kings, together with their horses, chariots, and elephants, made a vigorous effort to conquer Candrasena in battle.
All of them, highly enraged and causing the earth to tremble, besieged the four gates of Ujjayinī with their vast armies.
Being besieged by arrogant kings upon seeing his own city [under attack], Candrasena went for refuge to that very Mahākāla.
Free from conceptual construction and abstaining from food, that king of firm resolve worshipped the Lord of Gaurī day and night with undivided mind.
In the meantime, there was a certain cowherd woman living in that city who had been there for a long time; she was childless, having only one son, and was bereft of her husband.
Carrying a five-year-old child, she, whose husband had departed, beheld the great worship performed for the Lord of Girijā by the king.
Having witnessed that entire wondrous and magnificent festival of Śiva’s worship, she prostrated herself and returned once more to her own camp.
Having seen all of this in its entirety, that son of the cowherd woman, out of curiosity, performed the worship of Śiva which bestows detachment.
Having brought a pleasing stone to that empty and most excellent camp of Śibi, he fashioned a Śiva-liṅga not far from his own camp.
Having brought whatever flowers were available for his own hands, he bathed that liṅga and worshipped it with devotion.
Having prepared perfumes, ornaments, garments, incense, lamps, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth, he also offered an oblation of food (naivedya) made of divine artificial materials.
Having worshipped him again and again with leaves and beautiful flowers, and having performed various dances, he bowed down repeatedly.
While he was thus performing the worship of Śiva with undistracted mind, the cowherd woman affectionately called her son to take his meal.
Although called many times by his mother, he—his mind intent on worship—did not desire food even though he was a child; then the mother went there herself.
Seeing him seated before Śiva with his eyes closed, she seized his hand, pulled it away, and struck him in anger.
When his own son did not come even when summoned or beaten, he destroyed that worship by casting the linga far away.
Then, rebuking her son who was crying out "Alas! Alas!", the gopī, filled with rage, re-entered her own home.
Seeing the worship of the trident-bearing God destroyed by his mother, that boy cried out, "O God of gods! and fell down. (40)
Suddenly losing consciousness and overwhelmed by a flood of tears, he regained his senses after a moment and opened his eyes.
Then that very camp became a sanctuary of auspiciousness, resplendent with pillars of jewels, with golden door-panels and archways, and featuring a dais of precious, pure blue diamonds.

That boy beheld that beautiful city of Śiva, delightful with crystal palace floors illuminated by many diverse jars of molten gold, and in the center of the excellent pedestal, he saw the Liṅga together with jewels.
Upon seeing him, he rose up suddenly, his mind filled with fear and wonder, as if submerged in an ocean of supreme bliss born of contentment.
Having realized the greatness of the worship of Śiva through its power, he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff in order to pacify the sins of his mother.
O Lord, O Consort of Umā, forgive the transgression of my mother; be gracious, O Śaṅkara, for she was deluded and did not know you.
O Śiva, if there exists in me any merit whatsoever arising from devotion to you, by that alone may my mother obtain your compassion. (47)
Having thus propitiated Giriśa and bowed down to him again and again, the boy departed from the temple of Śiva when the sun had set.
Then he beheld his own camp, resembling the city of Indra, suddenly turned into gold and resplendent with manifold splendors. (49)
Entering the palace at the onset of night, he rejoiced within that place which was strewn with clusters of great jewels and resplendent with heaps of gold.
There he saw his own mother, free from fear and remembering [him], reclining upon a white bed on a couch of precious gems.
Her limbs were radiant with jewel ornaments, she shone in divine garments, and endowed with divine marks, she was like a celestial nymph in person.
With eyes wide open in agitation, he raised her up with speed and said, "O Mother, wake up! May it be well with you; behold this great marvel! (53)
Thus awakened by her high-souled son, the cowherd girl then beheld her own mother, smiling and radiant with a crown.
Rising up in haste, he scrutinized all of that, seeing himself as if for the first time and the boy as if for the first time.
And seeing her own residence as never seen before, Sītā was overwhelmed with joy upon hearing from the mouth of her son everything regarding the grace of the Lord of Girijā.
He informed the king that he who constantly worships Śiva had arrived suddenly at night, having completed his observances. 57.
He beheld the power of the son of the cowherd woman, born from the gratification of Śiva, as well as a golden abode of Śiva and a linga made of jewels.
And having seen the entire residence of the cowherd women, resplendent with excellent jewels, the lord of the earth, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, [was amazed]. (59)
For a moment, his composure filled with wonder and overflowing with supreme bliss, he embraced that child, shedding tears of love.
Thus, due to the proclamation of the greatness of Śiva in such a most wonderful manner and because of the great excitement of the citizens, that night passed away as if it were a mere moment.
Then at dawn, having besieged the city for battle, the kings heard from the mouths of their spies a most extraordinary report.
Having suddenly abandoned their enmity and being greatly startled, those kings, with their weapons laid down, entered [the city] with the approval of Candrasena.
Having entered that beautiful city and having bowed to Mahākāla, all the kings went to the house of the cowherd woman.
There, having been met and honored by Candrasena, they sat upon costly seats and rejoiced with great joy and wonder.
Beholding the great temple of Śiva and the Liṅga manifested for the grace of Gopasūnu, they fixed their supreme devotion upon Śiva.
All those kings, being pleased with that cowherd boy, gave him garments, gold, jewels, and wealth such as cows, buffaloes, and so forth.
Seeking the grace of Śiva, they gave elephants, horses, golden chariots, umbrellas, vehicles, and furnishings, as well as numerous male and female servants. 68.
All the kings throughout every land appointed him alone as their king, for he was the one who stood as a protector in abundance over them all.
Then, in that interval, the radiant Hanumān, the lord of monkeys, appeared, honored by all the gods of the three worlds.
At his very arrival, the kings, filled with awe, rose up and paid their respects, their bodies bowed low in devotion. (71)
Seated in their midst and honored by them, the Lord of the Monkeys embraced the son of Gopā, looked at the king, and spoke as follows: || 72 ||
Listen all, may it be well with you—both kings and all embodied beings; for there is no other refuge for living creatures apart from the worship of Śiva. (73)
By good fortune, this son of a cowherd, on the evening of a Saturday, attained auspiciousness by worshipping Śiva even without mantras. (74)
This Pradoṣa occurring on a Saturday is difficult for all embodied beings to encounter; it is even more difficult to find when it falls during the dark fortnight.

This most meritorious one in the world, who increases the fame of the cowherds, will have an eighth descendant in his lineage named Nanda of great renown; into his sonship Kṛṣṇa himself, Nārāyaṇa, will enter.
From this day forward, this son of Gopāla shall attain great renown in the world by the name Śrīkara.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus and instructed that son of a cowherd in the conduct of Śiva, the son of Añjanā vanished on the spot.
And all those rulers of the earth, being greatly delighted and duly honored, took leave of Candrasena and returned the way they had come. || 79 ||
The highly effulgent Śrīkara, having been instructed by Hanumān, performed the worship of Śambhu together with Brahmins who were knowers of dharma.
In time, both Śrīkara and King Candrasena, having propitiated Śiva with devotion, attained the supreme abode.

This supreme secret has been narrated—purifying, glorious, meritorious, and increasing great spiritual power; it is a narrative that destroys the flood of sins and increases devotion to the lotus feet of the Lord of Gaurī.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Deeds of the Cowherd Boy," in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa of the third part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: O Sūta, that wonderful great narrative which has been spoken by you—the supreme description of Śambhu’s majesty which removes all sins—is indeed excellent.
Furthermore, with our minds well-composed, we wish to hear once more about how the Lord Śambhu was worshipped by the great-souled ones at dusk.
"O observer of noble vows, tell us what perfection he bestows; for even though we have heard this repeatedly, O Sūta, our thirst for knowledge increases ever further. (3)
Sūta said: Well asked, O highly wise ones, you who are renowned throughout the world! Therefore, I shall fully describe the great fruit of the worship of Śiva.
On the thirteenth lunar day, the evening is proclaimed as Pradoṣa; on that occasion, Mahādeva alone—and no other deity—is to be worshipped by those seeking the fruits [of their devotion].
Who indeed is capable of describing the greatness of the Pradoṣa worship, wherein all the gods remain in the presence of the Lord of the Mountain?
At the time of twilight, the Lord performs a dance on Kailāsa, the silver abode, his rising virtues being praised by the gods.
Therefore, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, discourse on Him, and praise of His qualities must be performed regularly by mortals who desire the fruits of the four aims of life.
For mortals blinded by the darkness of poverty, who fear worldly existence and are submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, this is the raft that leads to the further shore.
For those afflicted by suffering, grief, and fear, and who desire the extinction of their afflictions, worship of the Lord of Pārvatī at twilight is a source of auspiciousness. (10)
Even one of wicked intellect, or low-born, or unfortunate, or even deceitful—by worshipping the Lord of Gods at dusk, he is liberated from calamities. || 11 ||
Even while being struck by enemies, bitten by serpents, crushed by mountains, or fallen into the great ocean; (12)
Even one whose staff of life is pierced, or who is afflicted by various diseases, that mortal does not perish through the worship of Giriśa at twilight. (13)
By worshipping Śiva, one instantly shakes off poverty, death, suffering, and the mountain-like burden of debt, and is honored with all prosperity. (14)
In this regard, I shall relate an ancient history of great merit, hearing which all men attain the fulfillment of their purpose. (15)
In the realm of Vidarbha, there was a king named Satyaratha; he was steadfast, devoted to all duties, virtuous, and true to his promise.
O best of sages, as that high-minded king protected the earth according to dharma, a great length of time passed by in perfect ease.
Then, that sovereign of the earth, King Śālva, had enemies of exalted power, led by Durmarṣaṇa. || 18 ||
Then, on one occasion, those Śālvas, having donned their armor and accompanied by a vast army, reached the city of Vidarbha and besieged it, desiring victory.
Seeing that city being suppressed, the lord of Vidarbha quickly marched forth to fight, surrounded by a great army.
He engaged in battle with those Śālvas, who were arrogant in their strength, just as the lord of serpents in the netherworld fought with the intoxicated Gandharvas.
Then that king of Vidarbha, having waged a most terrible battle, was slain at the head of the fray by the Śālvas, whose great forces had been destroyed.
When that hero, the great chariot-warrior, had been slain along with his ministers, the remaining soldiers who survived the slaughter fled from the battle, broken in spirit.
Then, when the battle had ceased and the enemy ministers were crying out, a tumultuous roar arose as the city itself seemed to be fighting back.
One virtuous wife of that Satyaratha, the lord of Vidarbha, overcome with intense grief, somehow managed to escape from there with great effort. (25)
At the time of nightfall, that pregnant queen, tormented by grief, emerged with great effort and set out toward the western direction.
Then, traveling slowly along the path at dawn, Satī, having traversed a long distance, beheld a stainless lake.
Having arrived there, the beautiful woman, greatly tormented by heat, took refuge at the edge of the lake under a shady tree that was shimmering with radiance.
There, by the power of destiny, the virtuous queen gave birth to a son in a secluded spot on a stone slab beneath a tree, at an hour endowed with auspicious qualities.
Then that queen, struck by intense thirst, descended into the lake with her beautiful limbs, only to be seized once more by a great crocodile.
As soon as he was born, the infant prince, whose father and mother had perished, cried out loudly on the shore of the lake, weak and afflicted by hunger and thirst.
While that newborn boy was thus crying, a certain excellent Brahmin woman arrived quickly by good fortune.
She too, carrying her own infant son who was only one year old, being destitute and bereft of her husband, went begging from house to house.
A Brahmin’s wife named Umā, who had an only daughter, was bereft of kinsmen and had fallen under the power of seeking alms; she beheld the prince.
Seeing the prince, who was like the orb of the sun fallen [from the sky], helpless and crying out, she reflected deeply upon him many times.
"Aha! A truly great marvel has now been seen by me: this infant’s umbilical cord is still uncut; where indeed has the mother gone? (36)
There is no father, nor anyone else, nor even any kinsman; helpless and miserable, the child lies alone upon the bare ground. (37)
"Whether this child be born of a Caṇḍāla, or born of a Śūdra, or even of a Vaiśya; or whether he be the son of a Brāhmaṇa or a king—how can he be identified? (38)
Having rescued this child, I shall certainly nourish him like my own son; however, because his lineage is unknown, I do not venture to touch this most excellent one.
While that most excellent of Brahmin women was thus reflecting, [the following occurred].
Then a certain mendicant arrived, who was Śiva himself in person; that best of mendicants said to her, "O beautiful wife of a brahmin, do not grieve."
"O lady of beautiful brows, cast away this doubt from your heart and protect this boy; for by means of him, you shall indeed attain the highest welfare here before long."
Having said this much, the compassionate monk departed in haste; then, once that monk had gone, the brahmin lady felt confident.
Taking that child with her, the virtuous woman, trusting the words of the mendicant, went to her own home, O King. (44)
Out of compassion, she nurtured him as if he were her own son; having made her dwelling in the beautiful village called Ekacakra.
She nourished her own son and the prince with alms-food; thus did both the Brahmin’s son and the king’s son grow up.
Having undergone the purificatory rites performed by the Brahmins, they grew up highly honored.
Having undergone the initiation ceremony at the proper time, the two boys remained established in their religious observances.
Day after day, they wandered there for alms together with their mother; once, that Brahmin woman was accompanied by those two children.
While wandering for alms, she entered a temple by fate; there, in that temple crowded with aged sages, [she found herself]. (19)
Seeing those two children, the wise sage Śāṇḍilya said: "Aha! How wondrous is the power of destiny; aha! How difficult it is to overcome the force of karma! (50)
This boy, having resorted to another's mother, lives on alms; yet he has obtained this very Brahmin woman as his own excellent mother. (51)
"Having assumed the state of a twice-born along with the son of a twice-born"—having heard these words of the sage Śāṇḍilya, the wife of the twice-born [spoke].
Having bowed down in the midst of the assembly, she asked with amazement: "O Brahmin, this devotee of Śiva was brought to my house by the word of a mendicant. (53)
Even now, his lineage unknown, he is nurtured like a son; in what family was he born, who is his mother, and who is his father? (54)
I wish to know everything from you, whose eye is wisdom.
Thus questioned by the Brahmin woman, that sage, possessing the vision of knowledge, then related the birth and the previous life's deeds of that boy.
The son of the king of Vidarbha, however, reported in its entirety the death of his father in battle and the abduction of his mother by the crocodile. (57)
Then that astonished woman asked the sage again: "How did that king die in battle, having abandoned all worldly enjoyments? (58)
O Great Sage, how did this boy come to poverty? And having shaken off that poverty, how will he obtain a kingdom? (59)
"You ought to instruct me as well, who live on the food of alms given to my son, regarding the means to alleviate this poverty. (60)
Śāṇḍilya said: The father of this boy is that lord of Vidarbha; in a previous birth, he was an excellent king, the ruler of Pāṇḍya.
That king, who knew all dharmas, while protecting the entire earth, once worshipped Śambhu at the time of evening twilight.
As he was worshipping with devotion the God who is the Lord of the three worlds, a great clamor arose everywhere throughout the city.
Hearing that tumultuous sound, the king, having abandoned his worship of Śiva, emerged from the royal palace out of fear of a disturbance in the city.
At that very moment, his minister Mahābala, having captured the enemy vassal, approached the presence of the king. || 65 ||
Seeing that a neighboring enemy, who had been brought by his minister, had become arrogant, the king, out of anger, ordered his head to be cut off.
Having performed the worship of Śiva in that very manner, the protector of the earth, without having completed his personal observances, took his meal at night.
His son also acted in the same way; at the time of evening twilight, that foolish-minded and arrogant youth failed to worship Śiva, and having eaten, he went to sleep. (68)
In another birth, that king became the ruler of Vidarbha; however, due to an interruption in his worship of Śiva, he was slain by enemies in the midst of his enjoyments.
He who was his son in a previous birth became his son in this life, yet fell into poverty due to the neglect of the worship of Śiva.
In a previous birth, his mother killed her co-wife through deceit; because of that great sin, she was killed by a crocodile in this present life. (71)
This conduct of theirs has been described to you: mortals who do not honor Śivā fall into poverty.

I speak the truth; I speak what is beneficial for the world beyond; I speak the essence; I speak the heart of the Upanishads. Having encountered this fierce and pithless cycle of existence, the only essence for a living being is service to the lotus feet of the Lord.

Those fools who do not worship Giriśa at the appointed time of Pradoṣa, nor bow down even to Śiva when he has been worshipped by others, and who do not drink in this story with the vessels of their ears, shall remain poor throughout birth after birth.

Those who, with single-minded devotion, perform the worship of the lotus feet of the Supreme Lord at the time of dusk, shall indeed possess ever-increasing wealth, grain, wife, sons, good fortune, and prosperity in this very world. (75)

When the trident-bearer Śiva, having seated Gaurī—the mother of the three worlds—upon a jeweled throne adorned with gold in his abode on Mount Kailāsa, desires to perform a dance, all the gods attend upon him at the time of twilight.

Vāgdevī holds a lute; Śatakratu (Indra) bears a flute; the lotus-born (Brahmā) has hands raised with cymbals; and the blessed goddess Ramā is engaged in the performance of song. Viṣṇu is expert at playing the deep-toned mṛdaṅga drum, and the gods stand all around, serving that Lord, the husband of Mṛḍānī, at the time of twilight.

The hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Patagas, Uragas, Siddhas, Sādhyas, Vidyādharas, the best of the immortals, and Apsarases, as well as others who dwell in the three worlds together with the classes of spirits, stood at the side of Hara when the time of evening had arrived.

Therefore, at twilight, Śiva alone is to be worshipped, and not others such as Hari or Padmajā; when that Great Lord is worshipped according to the rules, all the lords of the gods become propitiated.
This son of yours was, in a previous birth, an excellent Brāhmaṇa who spent his life accepting gifts rather than through virtuous deeds such as sacrifices and the like.
Therefore, O lady of the twice-born, since your son has fallen into poverty, let him seek refuge with Śaṅkara for the sake of removing that fault.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by the sage, that virtuous Brahmin woman bowed to him once more and then inquired about the sequence of the ritual for the worship of Śiva.
Śāṇḍilya said: When one is fasting on the thirteenth day of either fortnight, one should perform a ritual bath three *ghaṭikās* before sunset.
Wearing white garments, steadfast, restrained in speech, and observant of the rules, having performed the rites of twilight prayers and recitation, he should commence the worship of Śiva.
Having properly smeared the ground with fresh water before the deity and having fashioned a beautiful mandala, the wise one [should prepare] with washed garments and other such items.
Having adorned it with canopies and the like, as well as fruits, flowers, and fresh sprouts, one should draw a multicolored lotus endowed with the five colors.
Having sat there upon a very beautiful, firm seat with devotion, he was pure and had properly prepared all the requisites for worship.

The wise practitioner should consecrate the seat with the mantra as declared in the scriptures; then, he should perform self-purification and the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) in their proper sequence.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the seed-syllables accompanied by the nasal bindu, one should duly perform the placement of the Mātṛkā and meditate upon that supreme deity.
Having completed the Mātṛkā and meditated once more upon Supreme Śiva, one should bow to the Guru on the left side and salute Gaṇapati on the right.

Having placed Dharma and the others on the pair of shoulders and thighs, and Adharma and the others on the navel and the two sides, one should place Ananta and the others in the heart, and then place the mantra upon the pedestal.

Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in due order, beginning from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) up to the self consisting of knowledge (jñānātmā), according to the stated sequence, within the well-purified lotus of the heart; || 11 ||
One should meditate upon the Lord, the consort of Umā, who consists of the nine powers, who is delightful, who resembles ten million moons, who has three eyes, and who bears the moon upon his crest.
With a mass of matted hair tawny at the tips, adorned with a crown of jewels, blue-throated, noble-limbed, and beautified by a necklace of serpents.
He holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and carries an axe; he wears serpent-bracelets, armlets, bracelets, and finger-rings.
Having meditated upon him as wearing a tiger skin and seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, one should contemplate the Daughter of the Mountain at his left side.
She has the luster of a shining hibiscus flower, a radiance equal to the rising sun, and resembles a mass of lightning; she is slender and delights the mind and the eyes.
She has the young moon as her crest-jewel, is tender, and possesses dark, curly locks; she is beautiful with a swarm of bees and adorned by dark tresses.
Her face was radiant with the shimmering luster of jeweled earrings, and her mirror-like cheeks were marked with the impression of fresh saffron paste.
She whose sprout-like lower lip shines with a sweet smile, who possesses a neck like a conch shell, who is auspicious, and whose budding lotus-buds of breasts are emerging. (19)
She has four arms, resplendent with a noose, a goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the granting of desired boons; she is adorned with rings and bracelets shimmering with many jewels.
She was adorned with three folds [on her belly], endowed with a shimmering golden girdle-string, wearing red garlands and garments, and anointed with divine sandalwood paste.
Her lotus feet were bowed upon the crowns of the wives of the world-protectors; she was seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with the king of serpents as her garment.

Having thus meditated upon Mahādeva and the goddess Giri-kanyā, and having worshipped the Lord with perfumes and other offerings in due order according to the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa), [he should proceed].

One should perform [the rite] with the five Brahma-mantras in the prescribed locations or in the heart; one should offer separate handfuls of flowers upon the body, and three times in the heart with the root mantra.
Furthermore, having himself become Śiva, the practitioner should then worship the God on the external pedestal (bāhyapīṭha) again in due order by means of the root mantra (mūlamantra). || 25 ||
Being composed, he should utter the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) at the commencement of the worship; then, with palms joined in reverence, he should meditate upon Śaṅkara within his heart.
For the removal of debt, sin, misfortune, and poverty, and for the destruction of all evil, be gracious to me, O Śaṅkara! (27)
Scorched by the fire of suffering and grief, oppressed by the fear of saṃsāra, distressed by many diseases, and wretched—save me, O Bull-vehicled One! (28)
Come, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Mahādeva, the granter of fearlessness! Accept this worship performed by me together with Pārvatī. (29)
Having thus formed the resolve, one should perform the worship of Brahmā according to the rules; one should likewise worship the Guru and Gaṇapati on the left and right sides respectively.
One should worship Kṣetreśa in the northeast corner of the site, and then worship Vāstoṣpati in due order; one should worship Vāgdevī there, and thereafter worship Kātyāyanī.

One should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya, along with their opposites (Adharma, etc.), in the corners starting from the northeast using the vowels preceded by "namaḥ" and ending with "anta," respectively, as the feet of the pedestal; and one should worship Adharma and the others with these two, namely Bindu and Visarga.
One should place the forms of Sattva in the four directions and Ananta with the stars in the center; then one should assign the three qualities, Sattva and the others, as forms upon the seats.
Above that, on the upper covering, [he should worship] Māyā together with Lakṣmī and Śiva.
At its end, there is again a lotus, encompassing the entire triad of mandalas, pervaded by petals, filaments, and anthers, [inscribed] with the syllables of the stars in their proper order.

Having likewise worshipped the three lotuses with devotion in the center of the mandala, one should worship Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī in the cardinal directions with their respective portions and other offerings.
One should worship the nine Śaktis beginning with Vāmā, conjoined with the nine vowels; one should also worship the Pīṭha-mantra preceded by the three seed-syllables at the heart.
With the five primary limbs returned, with the powers of the forms (mūrtti-śaktis), with others who possess the three powers and forms, and accompanied by the two treasures (nidhis); || 38 ||
They were surrounded by Ananta and the others, as well as the Mothers beginning with Vṛṣā, the supernatural powers beginning with Aṇimā, and Indra and the other gods together with their weapons.
Vṛṣabha, Kṣetrapāla, Caṇḍeśa, Durgā, Skanda, Nandin, Gaṇeśa, and Sainyapa are each characterized by their respective specific attributes.
Aṇimā, mahimā, and likewise garimā, laghimā; as well as īśitva, vaśitva, prāpti, and prākāmya. || 41 ||

And the eight sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvaryāṇi) have been described as consisting solely of the forms of splendor (tejas), preceded by the five Brahmans, beginning with Hṛllekhā and the others, in due order.
The worship with Umā and the others, as well as Indra and the rest, has been described by those sages; one should worship Umā, Caṇḍeśvara, and the others starting from the north.
Thus, one should worship with ritual offerings the god Sadāśiva, whose form is radiant energy and who is endowed with these veils, together with Umā.
Having bathed Mahādeva with the waters of the *supratiṣṭhita-śaṅkha* vessel and with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) using the Rudra-hymns, one should remain concentrated in mind.
One should arrange the various services, beginning with the seat, using diverse mantras; one should prepare a golden seat provided with divine garments. (46)

One should offer the *arghya* endowed with eight qualities, as well as the water for the feet (*pādya*) consisting of pure water; with that same water one should give the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and then the *madhuparka* which abounds in honey.

Having again offered water for sipping (ācamana), one should perform the ritual bath with mantras. One should likewise present the sacred thread (upavīta), garments, and ornaments; one should offer pure sandalwood paste endowed with its eight ingredients.
Then [he offered] bilva, mandāra, kahlāra, and sarasīruha lotuses, as well as dhattūraka, karṇikāra, śaṇa flowers, and mallikā.
The practitioner should take kuśa grass, apāmārga, tulasī, mādhavī, campaka, and so forth, as well as bṛhatī and karavīra, as they may be obtained. (50)
One should offer fragrant garlands of various kinds, as well as incense produced from black aloe-wood and a pure, auspicious lamp.

The Special Section (viśeṣaka): Now, the food offering (naivedya) consists of milk-rice (pāyasa) with ghee and side-dishes (upadaṃśa), combined with sweetmeats (modaka) and cakes (apūpa), and mixed with sugar and jaggery. || 52 ||
One should offer oblations into the fire, which has been consecrated by mantras, using that very sacrificial substance mixed with honey, combined with curd, and accompanied by the drinking of water.
Constrained by the words of his guru, and following the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, he again offered an oblation to Śambhu, as well as excellent betel-leaf.
Having offered incense, the beautiful lustration lamp, the parasol, and the excellent mirror, according to the prescribed rites with Vedic and Tantric mantras.
If one is personally unable or destitute, one should worship according to one's means; for Gaurīśa is satisfied even by a mere flower offered with devotion.
Then the wise devotee should worship all the subsidiary deities, beginning with Gaṇeśa; having praised them with various hymns, he should prostrate himself with the eight limbs touching the ground.
Then, having circumambulated Vṛṣa, Caṇḍeśvara, and the others, and having offered worship according to the rules, one should pray to the Lord of Girijā.
Victory to you, O God, Lord of the World! Victory to you, eternal Śaṅkara! Victory to you, sovereign of all the gods! Victory to you, worshipped by all the gods! 59.
Victory to you who transcend all qualities! Victory to you, the bestower of all boons! Victory to you, the eternal and supportless! Victory to you, the imperishable sustainer of the universe! 60.

Victory to you, Lord of the one object of knowledge for the entire universe; victory to you, adorned with the king of serpents! Victory to you, O Śambhu, Lord of Gaurī; victory to you, whose crest is the crescent moon! 61.
Victory to you who resemble ten million suns; victory to you, the refuge of infinite virtues!

Victory to you, O Rudra, O Virūpākṣa! Victory to you, the inconceivable and stainless one! Victory to you, O Lord, ocean of mercy! Victory to you, the destroyer of the distress of devotees! Victory to you, O Master, who enables the crossing of the difficult-to-traverse ocean of saṃsāra!
Be gracious to me, O Mahādeva, who am afflicted and distressed by the cycle of worldly existence; having removed the fear of all sins, protect me, O Supreme Lord. (64)
For one submerged in great poverty, struck down by great sin, destroyed by great grief, and afflicted by a great disease; || 65 ||
O Śaṅkara, be gracious to me, who am overwhelmed by the burden of debt, consumed by my own actions, and tormented by the planets.
At the conclusion of the worship, a poor man should thus pray to the Lord of Girijā; or even a wealthy man or a king should pray to the divine Īśvara.
O Śaṅkara, by your grace, may there always be long life, constant health, increase of my treasury, and the rise of my strength; may there be eternal bliss for me. 68.
May my enemies go to their destruction; may the planets be propitious to me; may the bandits in the kingdom perish, and may the people be free from calamity. (69)
May the afflictions of famine and pestilence be pacified upon the surface of the earth; may there be an abundance of all crops, and may all directions be filled with happiness. (70)
In this manner, one should propitiate the Lord, the husband of the Mountain-born Goddess, at twilight; thereafter, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and satisfy them with sacrificial fees.
The worship of Śiva, which I have proclaimed, destroys all sins, annihilates all poverty, and bestows the boons of all one's desires. (72)
One should ward off the entire collection of great sins (mahāpātaka), as well as the secondary sins (upapātaka) that exceed them, and everything else except for the theft of Śiva’s property.
In the Purāṇas as well as in the Smṛtis, expiations for sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa are seen, but none for those who steal the property of Śiva. (74)
What is the use of saying much more here? I shall speak in a single half-verse: even a hundred killings of Brahmins the worship of Śiva would destroy. (75)
I have thus described to you this worship of Śiva at dusk; it is a secret for all living beings, of this there is no doubt.
"Let worship be performed in this manner even by these two children; therefore, within just one year, you shall attain supreme perfection."
Having heard these words of Śāṇḍilya, the wife of the twice-born bowed at the feet of the sage together with those two children. (78)
The brahmin’s wife said: "I have attained my life's purpose today merely by the sight of you. O Blessed One, these two boys have come to you alone for refuge. (79)
"O Brahmin, this son of mine is called Śucivrata; this son of the king has been named Dharmagupta by me. (80)
O Blessed One, we and this [child] are your servants; please rescue us who have fallen into this terrible ocean of poverty. (81)
Having thus consoled the brahmin woman who had sought refuge with words like nectar, the sage then instructed the two boys in the mantra-knowledge for the worship of Śiva.
Then, having been instructed by the sage, the two youths and that Brahmin woman bowed to him, took their leave, and departed from the temple of Śiva.
From that time forward, following the instruction of the best of sages, those two boys diligently performed the worship of Pārvatīśa at dusk.
As the prince and the son of the twice-born thus worshipped the God, four months passed for them in perfect ease.
Once, that delight of the twice-born went to the riverbank with the prince to bathe, and he wandered about with great playfulness.
There, upon the paved floor of the embankment, which had been pierced by the force of a mountain torrent, he beheld a large, shimmering treasure jar.
Seeing him, he came running suddenly, overwhelmed with joy and curiosity; considering it a divine providence, he took [the child] upon his head and departed. (88)
Having hurriedly brought and forcibly set down the water-pot, and having placed it at the edge of the house, he addressed his mother.
O Mother, O Mother, behold this grace of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain; by his compassionate nature, he has revealed himself as a treasure in the form of a jar.
Then that virtuous woman, filled with wonder, summoned the prince; honoring the worship of Śiva, she greeted her own son and spoke.
"Listen to my words, my two sons: divide this jar of treasure equally and take it, out of respect for my command. (92)
Having heard these words of his mother, the son of the twice-born was pleased; the prince, confident in his worship of Śaṅkara, replied to her.
"O Mother, this has come about solely through the merit of your son; I do not wish to take a divided share of the accumulated wealth. (94)
May he enjoy by himself what has been obtained through his own good deeds; that very Lord, the Sovereign, will show grace toward me. 95.
As they continued to worship Śambhu in this manner with supreme joy, a full year passed for them in that very house.
Then once, when the spring season had arrived, that prince went out to sport in the forest together with that twice-born man.
Then, having traveled far into a certain forest, the two sons of the brahmin and the king beheld hundreds of gandharva maidens sporting there.
Seeing all of them, beautiful in every limb, sporting enchantingly from afar, the son of the twice-born spoke to the prince.
"You must not go further from here; women are sporting ahead. O wise ones of pure intent, you should avoid the presence of women."
These women, practitioners of deceit, intoxicated by wealth and youth, skilled in the art of persuasion through their speech, delude people when they behold them. (1)
Therefore, O learned one, a practitioner of his own duty—especially a celibate student—should avoid the proximity of women and conversing with them. (3)
"Therefore, I do not venture to go to the pleasure grounds of those fawn-eyed women. Having spoken thus, the son of the twice-born turned back and stood at a distance. || 3 ||
Then that prince, his mind possessed by curiosity, went alone along the path where they were sporting. || 1 ||
There, among the daughters of the Gandharvas, one with a beautiful face, seeing the prince approaching, reflected thus in her mind: || 9 ||
"Aha! Who is this youth of noble form, beautiful in every limb, with the gait of an elephant in rut, an ocean of the nectar of loveliness? (6)"

He possessed large eyes that were restless with playful charm, was exquisite with his sweet smile, bore a beauty of form comparable to the god of love, and was characterized by limbs of delicate tenderness.
Thus, filled with wonder upon seeing the prince from afar, the young girl looked at all her companions and spoke these words: (8)
"O friends, not far from here there is a single, excellent forest, filled with various *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, and *bakula* trees. (9)
"Having gone there to that grove, all of you gather a heap of flowers; then you may return, while I remain here for now. (110)
Thus instructed, the group of friends departed for the interior of the forest; she too, the daughter of a Gandharva, remained there with her gaze fixed upon the prince.
Having beheld that slender-limbed maiden, who was endowed with fresh youth and who, by the perfection of her own beauty, surpassed even Tilottamā; (12)
The prince, having approached her with eyes wide with curiosity, experienced the pain of Love’s arrows through the turn of fate. (13)
When the prince had arrived, that daughter of the Gandharva also rose quickly and offered him a seat of tender leaves.

Having approached him as he sat there after the rites of hospitality had been performed, the slender-waisted woman, her fortitude destroyed and her senses agitated by his beauty and virtues, questioned him.
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one? From what country have you come here? Whose son are you?"—being thus questioned with affection, he reported everything. (16)
[He saw] the son of the King of Vidarbha, whose father and mother had been destroyed, his own position seized by enemies, and himself gone into a foreign kingdom. (17)
Having reported everything once more, the prince asked her: "Who are you, O lady of beautiful thighs? What is your business here, and whose daughter are you? (18)
"What are you contemplating in your heart, or what do you wish to say here? Thus addressed, she spoke again: "Listen, O best of great kings. (19)
There is a leader of the Gandharva clans named Draviṇa; I am his daughter, known by the name Aṃśumatī.
"O high-minded one, seeing you approaching, I am longing for conversation with you; having left all my female companions behind, I am here alone. (21)
"In all the sciences of music, there is none whatsoever other than me; by my yoga alone, even all the celestial women are gratified. (22)
I am proficient in all the arts and understand the gestures of every person; I know your desire, for my mind is united with yours.
Likewise, this longing has been bestowed upon me by fate; henceforth, let no breach of affection between us two prevail. (24)
Having spoken thus, the Gandharva’s daughter, out of love, quickly gave him a pearl necklace that served as an ornament for the space between her breasts.
Taking that wonderful necklace, the prince, overwhelmed by affection for her and overflowing with intense joy, spoke these words to her.
"O timid one, what you have said is true; nevertheless, I shall say this one thing: how can you be dear to me, who am now destitute and have renounced my kingdom? (27)
Being a young woman with a father, how can you, like a fool, disregard your father's command and act according to your own will? (28)
Having heard these words of his, she of the pure smile replied to him: "So be it; I shall do exactly as you say; behold my wonder."
"Go to your own abode, O beloved; however, come back here again on the very morning of the day after tomorrow, for we have a task that is not in vain."
Having spoken thus to the prince, she, whose limbs were beautiful and who was accompanied by her circle of friends, departed; and the son of the king likewise did so.
Approaching the presence of the brahmin’s son with joy, he related everything to him and went to his own home together with him.
And having further gladdened that virtuous Brahmin woman, the prince went to the forest on the day after tomorrow together with that son of a twice-born man.
Having reached the place previously indicated by her, the prince beheld the king of the Gandharvas accompanied by his own daughter.
That lord of the Gandharvas, having greeted the two youths upon their arrival and seating them on a beautiful throne, addressed the prince.
The Gandharva said: O son of the lord of kings, on the previous day I went to Kailāsa; there I beheld the Lord Mahādeva together with Pārvatī.
Having summoned me into the presence of all the inhabitants of heaven, that Lord of Gods, the Blessed One who is an ocean of the nectar of compassion, spoke.
There is a certain prince on earth named Dharmagupta; he is destitute, fallen from his kingdom, and his country has been seized by his enemies. (38)
That boy, by the word of his guru, was always devoted to my worship; today, all his ancestors have reached me through the power of that [devotion]. (39)
O best of Gandharvas, you too should provide him assistance; then, established in his own kingdom, he will have his enemies destroyed.
Thus commanded by Maheśa, he returned to his own abode, having been entreated in many ways by this daughter of mine.
Having understood this entire command of Śambhu, whose nature is compassion, I have taken this daughter and arrived at this forest region.
Therefore, I bestow this daughter, Aṃśumatī, upon you; having slain your enemies, I shall establish you in your own kingdom by the command of Śiva.

Having enjoyed all desired pleasures with her in that city, at the end of ten thousand years you shall go to the abode of Giriśa. There too, this daughter of mine shall attain you alone, in this very divine body, in the presence of Śiva.
Having thus addressed the prince, the king of the Gandharvas had his own daughter take his hand in marriage in that forest.
He gave him as a parting gift loads of brilliantly radiant jewels—a crest-jewel resembling the moon and shining pearl necklaces. (47)
He gave divine ornaments and garments, coverings of gold, ten thousand elephants, and furthermore, a hundred thousand blue horses.
There were thousands of great golden chariots, as well as one divine chariot and a bow resembling the rainbow of Indra.
Thousands of missiles, two quivers with inexhaustible arrows, impenetrable golden armor, and a spear that crushes enemies. (150)
With a joyful heart, he gave him five thousand female slaves for the sake of attending to his daughter, as well as various kinds of wealth.
Furthermore, for the sake of assisting him, the lord of the Gandharvas gave a most formidable Gandharva army, complete with its four divisions.
Thus the son of the lord of kings, having attained supreme fortune and accompanied by his beloved wife, rejoiced in his own prosperity.
Having performed the marriage of his daughter according to the custom of the occasion, the lord of the Gandharvas ascended a celestial chariot and departed for heaven.
Having married Gandharvasenā, Dharmagupta returned once more to his own city and slaughtered the army of his enemies.
Having slain the invincible Durdharṣaṇa in battle with his spear, and having utterly destroyed the enemy forces along with the Gandharva army, he entered his own city.
