Then, consecrated by his ministers and the most eminent brahmins, he ascended the jeweled lion-throne and ruled a kingdom free from all thorns.
The brahmin woman who had previously nourished him like her own son became his mother, and that son of the twice-born became his brother. (58)
The daughter of a Gandharva became his wife; having propitiated Lord Giriśa, Dharmagupta became the sovereign of the city of Vidarbha.
In this way, others who have propitiated the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain at dusk obtain their desired wishes, and at the end of the body, they attain the supreme goal.
Sūta said: This meritorious great vow is the worship of Śaṅkara at dusk; it is the supreme means for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Whoever should hear this meritorious and most wonderful majesty, or should recite it with a concentrated mind at the end of the worship of Śiva during Pradoṣa; || 62 ||
He shall not suffer poverty even in hundreds of future births; endowed with knowledge and sovereignty, he shall go at the end to the city of Śiva.

Blessed indeed are those men who, having obtained this most difficult-to-attain human body, perform worship at the feet of the Supreme Lord; they have conquered the three worlds by their own merit, and the dust of their lotus-feet purifies the entire world. 164.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Pradosha," in the Brahmottara-khanda of the third part of the glorious Skanda Mahapurana, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Sūta said: Those who know the Śiva-principle—which consists of eternal bliss, is peaceful, free from conceptual construction, devoid of affliction, and without beginning or end—have attained the Supreme.
Those wise ones who, being detached from the enjoyment of desires, practice supreme, disinterested devotion toward Śiva—attain liberation; for them there is no further cycle of worldly existence.
Those who, having disregarded sense objects, cultivate devotion to Śiva, are not overcome by sense objects even while enjoying their fruits.
A man endowed with devotion to Śiva by whatever means does not perish through time; he attains the supreme goal. || 4 ||
One who desires to ascend to the supreme station but whose mind is attached to sense objects should worship Śambhu through ritual action; at the end of his enjoyments, he shall attain Śiva.
Most people are unable to abandon the latent impressions of sense objects; therefore, for embodied beings, worship consisting of ritual action is a wish-fulfilling cow.
This dharma has been proclaimed for those who, having dwelt happily for a long time even in this saṃsāra which consists of illusion, desire liberation at the end of the body.
In this world, the worship of Śiva is always the cause of both heaven and liberation, especially on Mondays endowed with the excellence of the time of Pradoṣa and other such qualities.
Even those who perform the worship of Śiva on a Monday alone shall find nothing difficult to attain, either in this world or in the next.
Having fasted, become pure, and subdued his senses on a Monday, he should worship Śiva according to the prescribed rites, whether with Vedic or worldly mantras.
Whether he be a celibate student, a householder, or a maiden—whether with a husband or without a husband—who worships [her], obtains his desired boon. (11)
In this regard, I shall relate a story that captivates the hearts of listeners; by hearing it, they surely attain liberation, and devotion to Śambhu arises.
In the land of Āryāvarta, there was a certain king, the best among the upholders of dharma, renowned as Citravarma; he was a king of righteousness to the wicked. (13)
He is the protector of the bridges of dharma, the teacher of those who travel on wrong paths, the performer of all sacrifices, and the savior of those seeking refuge. (14)
He was the performer of all meritorious deeds, the bestower of all riches, the conqueror of hosts of enemies, and a devotee of Śiva and Mukunda. (15)
Having obtained sons of great prowess from his devoted wives, he finally obtained, after a long time, a single daughter of beautiful countenance whom he had long desired.
Having fortunately obtained a daughter, just as Himavat did Pārvatī, he considered himself equal to a god, his desires fulfilled. (17)

Once, his mind filled with curiosity, he summoned groups of virtuous brahmins who were experts in the knowledge of the marks of birth, and questioned them regarding the fruits resulting from the birth of a daughter.
Then, a certain learned and most excellent brahmin spoke there: "O lord of the earth, this girl is yours by name, Sīmantinī. (19)
She was like Umā in auspiciousness, like Damayantī in beauty, like Sarasvatī in her knowledge of the arts, and like Lakṣmī in her great virtues.

She was like the divine Mother Earth in her noble progeny, like Janaki in her steadfastness to her vows; she possessed a true luster like that of the sun’s radiance and was as enchanting as moonlight.
She shall rejoice with her husband for ten thousand years; having given birth to eight sons, she will attain supreme happiness.
Having honored that brahmin who had spoken thus with wealth, the king attained supreme delight by partaking of the nectar of his words.
Then another twice-born man, steadfast and of immeasurable luster, said: "In her fourteenth year, she shall enter into widowhood. (24)
Having heard those words of his, harsh as the crash of a thunderbolt, the king’s mind became agitated with anxiety for a moment.
Then, having dismissed all the brahmins, the king, who was devoted to the Brahmanas, considered everything to be the work of fate and became free from anxiety.
That young woman Sīmantinī, having gradually passed her childhood, heard from the mouth of her own friend that widowhood was destined to befall her.
Having fallen into great despondency, the young girl reflected and questioned Maitreyī, the wife of the sage Yājñavalkya.
O Mother, I have come for refuge to your lotus feet, overwhelmed by fear; you should instruct me in the rite that increases good fortune.
Thus, O King, the chaste wife of the sage spoke to the princess who had sought refuge: "O slender-limbed one, go for protection to Pārvatī, who is united with Śiva."
On Monday, worship Śiva and Gaurī with a concentrated mind; having fasted, being well-bathed, and wearing stainless garments. (31)
Having restrained his speech and steadied his mind, and having performed the worship as was appropriate, he then fed the Brahmins and properly propitiated Śiva.

The destruction of evil occurs through consecration; sovereignty through the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhas); and complete good fortune and happiness through the offering of perfumes, garlands, and unbroken rice grains.
Through the offering of incense comes fragrance; through the offering of lamps, splendor; through food offerings, great enjoyment; and through the offering of betel-leaf, prosperity.

Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa arise from the offering of salutation; indeed, the recitation [of the mantra] alone is the cause for the attainment of the eightfold sovereign powers and other siddhis. (35)
Through the fire-oblation (homa), the fulfillment of all desires arises; through the feeding of Brahmins, there is satisfaction for all the gods.
In this manner, worship Śiva and also Śivā on Mondays; even if you have fallen into extreme calamity, you shall emerge victorious and overcome all adversity.
"Even though you have encountered a terrible, horrific, and fearsome great affliction, by the power of the worship of Śiva, you shall cross over this great danger."
Having thus properly instructed Sīmantinī, that virtuous woman departed; and the princess of noble form likewise acted accordingly. (39)
To Nala and Damayantī was born a son named Indrasena; and his son was named Candrāṅgada, who was as radiant as the moon.
Citravarmā, the best of kings, having summoned that prince, bestowed his daughter Sīmantinī upon him with the permission of his preceptor.
A great festival took place there at her wedding ceremony, wherein there was a vast assembly of all the kings of the earth.
Having performed the marriage ceremony with her at the proper time, the virtuous Candrāṅgada dwelt for some months right there in his father-in-law's house.
Once, that powerful prince, desiring to cross the Yamunā, boarded a boat playfully along with some of his companions. (44)
While the prince was crossing the Kālindī, by the power of fate, the boat, struck by a whirlpool, sank along with the fishermen.
A very great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose on both its banks; as all the armies looked on, their lamentation reached the heavens.
Some died while struggling; some entered the bellies of crocodiles; and certain princes and others were no longer seen in the great waters.
Having heard that, King Citravarman also became extremely distressed; reaching the bank of the Yamunā, he fell into a state of agitation.
Then, upon hearing this, the king's wives became senseless; and Sīmantinī, having heard it, fell to the ground in a swoon.
Likewise, other chief ministers and leaders, together with the family priests, distressed and tormented by grief, wailed with their hair disheveled.
Indrasena, the lord of kings, having heard the news of his son, was deeply distressed; together with his wives, he fell down, losing consciousness.
His ministers, the citizens, and the inhabitants of that land, including children, the elderly, and women, cried out, overwhelmed with grief. (52)
Out of grief, some beat their chests, and others struck their heads; crying out, "O prince! O father! Where are you? Where are you? they wandered about.
Thus, the city of Indrasena, the lord of the earth, was overwhelmed with grief and wretchedness; likewise, Citravarmapura was suddenly thrown into turmoil.
Then, consoled by the elders, King Citravarmā slowly returned to the city and comforted his daughter.
That king had the funeral rites for his son-in-law, who was submerged in the water, performed in their entirety by the kinsmen who had arrived.
And that virtuous Sīmantinī, being devoted to the world of her husband, was forbidden by her father out of affection; nevertheless, she entered into widowhood.
The auspicious lady of virtuous conduct did not abandon the auspicious Somavāra-vrata, which had been instructed to her by the sage, even though she had fallen into widowhood. (58)
Thus, having experienced most terrible suffering during the fourteenth year, she passed three years meditating upon the lotus feet of Śiva.
His heirs forcibly seized by force the seven constituents of the kingdom from King Indrasena, who was like one driven mad by grief for his son.
Deprived of his throne by his heroic kinsmen, that childless king was seized along with his wife and confined in a prison cell.
His son, Candrāgada, also sank into the waters of the Yamunā; as he was sinking deeper and deeper, he beheld the serpent-maidens.
Seeing that prince intent on water-sports, they were filled with wonder and then led him to Pātāla, the abode of the serpents.
Being led swiftly by the female serpents, the prince entered the beautiful and most wonderful city of Takṣaka.
The prince beheld that place, which resembled the abode of Mahendra and was illuminated by the radiance of rays flashing from great jewels. (65)
It was crowded with hundreds of palaces made of diamonds, lapis lazuli, and other gems; it had gate-towers and doors of rubies, radiant with strings of pearls.
The ground was made of beautiful moonstones, with golden doors and panels, and it shone with hundreds of thousands of jewel-lamps.
There, in the midst of the assembly, he beheld Takṣaka, the lord of the serpents, seated upon a jeweled throne, blazing with hundreds of hoods.
Wearing celestial garments, radiant, adorned with jeweled earrings, and beautified by the luster of a crown encrusted with various gems.
He was attended by countless supreme serpents, rich with the radiance of the jewels on their hoods, who were adorned with variegated gems and stood with palms joined in reverence.
He was surrounded on all sides by a thousand Naga maidens, who were radiant with beauty, youth, sweetness, charm, and graceful gait.
His limbs were radiant with divine ornaments and anointed with divine sandalwood paste; he was as unassailable as the fire of cosmic destruction and resembled the sun in his splendor.
Having seen him, the steadfast prince prostrated himself on the floor of the assembly hall; then, his eyes dazzled by the other's splendor, he stood up with palms joined in reverence.
The Naga king, having seen that charming prince, asked the female serpents: "Who is this, and from where has he come here? (74)
They said, "In the waters of the Yamunā, this man—whose family and name were unknown—was seen by us by chance and brought into your presence. (75)
Then the prince was questioned by the high-souled Takṣaka: "Whose son are you? Who are you? What is your country? And how have you come here? (76)
Having heard these words, the prince spoke this speech to Takṣaka: || 77 ||

The prince said: "There is a certain region on the surface of the earth known as Niṣadha. Its ruler was a king named Nala, possessed of great fame. That auspicious lord of the earth, whose glory was meritorious, was the husband of Damayantī. (78)

From him was born a son of great strength named Indrasena; I am his son, known by the name Candrāṅgada. Having recently married, while sporting in the waters of the Yamunā at my father-in-law’s house, I was impelled by fate and drowned.
I have been brought into your presence by these serpent-women; having beheld your lotus feet through merits accumulated over many previous births. (80)
Today I am blessed, I am blessed; my parents have achieved their purpose, since I have been beheld by you out of compassion and even addressed by you. (81)
Sūta said: Having heard these noble, composed, and exceedingly graceful words, Takṣaka, out of renewed eagerness, spoke again to the prince. (82)
Takṣaka said: "O descendant of a king, do not fear; take courage! Among all the gods, which deity is always worshipped by you? (83)
The prince said: "That god who among all gods is remembered as Mahādeva—he, the Lord of Umā, the Soul of the Universe, is indeed Śiva who is worshipped by us. (84)
He, by even a minute fraction of whose splendor and by whose passion (rajas) the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), having assumed form, created the universe—that Maheśvara is worthy of our worship. 85.
He from whose portion the eternal Viṣṇu, the soul of all beings, bears the divine and sattvic universe—that Śiva is worshipped by us. (86)
From whose tamasic portion Rudra was born, who resembles the fire of cosmic destruction and consumes this entire universe at the end—He, the Lord, is to be worshipped by us. (87)
He who is the creator and the cause even of the Creator, the supreme light among all lights—that Śiva is our ultimate refuge. (88)
Though standing near, he is far away for those whose minds are afflicted by sin; that Śiva, whose splendor is unfathomable, is our supreme refuge. (89)
He who dwells in fire, he who is in the earth, he who is in the wind and in the water, and he who is in space—the Universal Soul, that Sadāśiva is ever to be worshipped by us.
He who is the witness of all beings, who dwells within the self, who is untainted, and under whose will the world is subject—that Śiva is worshipped by us.

He whom some call the one primordial, ancient Puruṣa, divided by the transformation of the qualities (guṇas); whom others call the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), others the Fourth (turīya), and still others the Immutable (kūṭastha)—that Śiva is our refuge. 92.

He whom the mental and vocal functions of embodied beings do not touch—that shrine of inconceivable reality, whose abode is difficult to reach and whose nature is not that [of the mind]—he is this very Supreme Śiva, our object of worship. (93)

Having obtained his grace, the virtuous do not desire even the radiant station of Indra; having crossed over the wheel of time that obstructs the path of karma, they wander fearlessly—he is Śiva, our refuge. (94)

To Him whose remembrance instantly destroys the affliction of all sins even for those born as outcasts (pulkasas), and whose entire nature is sought after by the Vedas—to that Śiva, let us perpetually offer worship. 95.

He upon whose head the celestial river has found her abode, in whose body dwells the Blessed Mother of the Universe, and whose two earrings are indeed Takṣaka and Vāsuki—that Lord who bears the crescent moon upon his crest is our only refuge.

Victorious is that Lord whose lotus feet rest upon the crests of the Vedas, and whose form eternally dwells in the hearts of yogis; victorious is his form which illuminates all principles—he, the Lord who has conquered the creation of the qualities, is worshipped by us.
Sūta said: Having heard these words, Takṣaka, with a delighted mind and having conceived devotion for Mahādeva, spoke to the prince. (98)

Takṣaka said: "I am well-pleased; may it be well with you, O delight of the best of kings! For even though you are but a child, you know the supreme reality, the Śaiva truth that is higher than the highest. (99)
This world is composed of jewels; these women are of lovely countenance; all these are wish-fulfilling trees, and the ponds contain water of the essence of nectar. (100)
Here there is no terrible fear of death, nor the affliction of old age and disease; sport right here as you please and enjoy the pleasures as they are fitting.
Thus addressed by the king of the nāgas, that noble-minded prince, the son of a lord of kings, replied with great affection, his palms joined in reverence.
I have taken a wife at the proper time; she is a virtuous housewife who is constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, and my parents have me as their only son. (3)
Thinking me dead today, they are overwhelmed by great grief; for the most part they are being deprived of their lives, though by fate some still continue to breathe.
Therefore, I must by no means remain here for very long; you ought, out of compassion, to lead me to that very world.

Having spoken thus to the son of the king of men, they refreshed him with divine, excellent food produced from the celestial wish-fulfilling tree, and with choice perfumes, garments, garlands, and various wonderful divine ornaments.
Having gratified him with various enjoyments, the king of serpents spoke again: "Whenever you remember me, I shall manifest myself before you at that very moment."
And again, he gave to the prince Takṣaka’s horse, which travels at will through various islands, oceans, and worlds without obstruction.
The lord of the serpents gave him jeweled ornaments, divine garments, and one Rākṣasa as a mount.
And having appointed one young prince of the serpents as his companion for that purpose, Takṣaka affectionately sent him forth, saying, "Go! (110).
Thus, having gathered various kinds of wealth and mounted his horse Kāmagama, Candrāṅgada set forth together with those two.
Emerging from those very waters as if in an instant, he mounted his divine horse and sported upon the beautiful bank.
Then, at that time, that slender and virtuous Sīmantinī arrived there to bathe, surrounded by her female companions.
She saw the prince sporting on the riverbank, accompanied by a Rākṣasa in human form and the son of a Nāga.
It was strewn with divine jewels and adorned with celestial garlands and ornaments; its divine fragrance was diffused for ten yojanas by its body.
Beholding him of unprecedented form seated upon the divine horse, she stood with her eyes fixed upon him like one who is dazed, mad, or terrified.
And that son of the lord of kings, remembering her as one he had seen before, [beheld her] with her neck-ornaments cast off and devoid of her neck-thread. (17)
Her hair was no longer braided, she was devoid of body-unguents, the dark collyrium had been abandoned from the corners of her eyes, her limbs were emaciated, and she was afflicted by grief.
Having seen her, he dismounted from his horse and sat down on the riverbank; calling that woman of beautiful limbs and seating her there, he spoke as follows.
"Who are you? Whose wife are you, or whose daughter are you, O virtuous one? O lady, why do you display such unbearable signs of grief in your youth? (120)
Thus questioned with affection, that bride, her eyes filled with tears, was too ashamed to speak for herself; her friend then related everything.
This woman named Sīmantinī is the daughter-in-law of the king of Niṣadha, the queen of Candrāṅgada, and the daughter of Citravarmā.
By the turn of fate, her husband was submerged in this great water; consequently, this young woman has met with widowhood and has been withered by sorrow. (23)
In this way, three years were spent under the sway of exceedingly powerful grief; now that the day of Induvāra has arrived, I have come here to bathe.
And her father-in-law, a lord of kings, had been robbed of his kingdom by enemies; he was forcibly seized and bound, remaining under their control along with his wife.
Nevertheless, this woman of virtuous conduct, possessing a pure heart, worships Maheśvara together with Ambikā on Mondays with supreme devotion.
Sūta said: Having thus communicated everything through the mouth of her friend, the virtuous Sīmantinī then spoke herself to the prince.
Who are you, resembling Kandarpa? Who are these two at your side? Are you a god, a lord of men, a perfected being (siddha), a gandharva, or perhaps a kinnara? || 28 ||
"For what reason do you ask about my history as if you were full of affection? Do you know me, O mighty-armed one, or have you seen me somewhere? (29)
"You appear as if seen before, like a kinsman to me; tell me everything according to the truth, for the virtuous have truth as their essence. (130)

Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the daughter of the king wept for a long time with a throat choked by tears; surrounded by her friends, she fainted and fell upon the ground, unable to say anything further.
Having heard all the causes of his beloved's grief, Candrāṅgada remained silent for a moment, himself overwhelmed with sorrow.
Then, having comforted his slender beloved with various skillful words, he said, "We are gods named Siddhas, who travel at will."
Then, having drawn her away by force as she feared the grasping of his hand, he spoke these words into her ear, while her entire body was covered with horripilation.
"O fair-faced one, I have seen your husband somewhere in the world; pleased by the performance of your vow, he will return immediately. (35)
"Within just two or three days, he will surely remove your grief; I have come to tell you this, for I am a friend of your husband. (36)
In this matter, there should be no doubt; I swear it by the feet of Śiva. You must remain within your heart and not reveal this anywhere.
Having heard those words of his, which were sweeter than hundreds of streams of nectar, she, her eyes rolling with agitation, gazed at him again and again.
She spoke words that were an elixir, intensified by the bonds of love, accompanied by graceful gestures and a generous display of charm, along with sweet side-long glances.

Having examined his body, which was covered with horripilation arising from the touch of her own hand, and having scrutinized the marks previously seen on his limbs, as well as his voice and other traits, his age, and his complexion, she reflected upon him.
"He alone shall be my husband, certainly no other; my heart, distressed by love, is attached to him alone. (141)
"How could one who has come here from the other world possess such a form? How could there be a sight of my lost husband for me, so unfortunate? (142)
"Is this a dream, or is it not a dream? Is this an illusion, or is it not an illusion? Or is he some rogue, a yakṣa, or perhaps even a gandharva? (143)
"Whether it be the vow itself or its very fruit, fulfill that which was said to me by the wife of the sage, even though I am fallen into the greatest calamity. (44)
"That best of the twice-born who said, 'Fortune has been mine for ten thousand years'—surely his word is true; for who could know this except for the Lord? (45)
And auspicious omens are seen day after day; when the Lord of Pārvatī is pleased, what is impossible for embodied beings? (46)
Having reflected thus in many ways upon her, who was now freed from doubt, he whispered his own purpose into the ear of her whose face was bowed with shame. (47)
"Let us go to relate this account to her parents, who are tormented by grief; may it be well with you, O blessed lady, for you shall soon regain your husband."
Having spoken thus, the prince mounted his horse and departed; accompanied by those two, he reached his own kingdom at that very moment.
Standing near the city garden, he dispatched that young serpent toward his own kinsmen who were seated upon the royal throne.
Having gone there, he said to them: "Let Indrasena be released quickly; his son Candrāṅgada has arrived here from the abode of the serpents."
"Abandon your royal thrones; let there be no hesitation. Otherwise, the arrows of Candrāgada will swiftly take away your lives. (152)
Having plunged into the waters of the Yamunā and gone to the abode of Takṣaka, and having obtained his assistance, he returned here from that world once more. || 153 ||
Having heard that account related in its entirety, those adversaries, filled with agitation, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! and praised him.
Having quickly informed Indrasena of the reunion with his lost son, and having propitiated him who had regained the throne of a lord of men, the chief heirs fell into a state of fear. (55)
Then all the citizens, having seen the prince in the city garden, quickly informed the king and received great wealth.
Hearing that their son was approaching, the king was bathed in tears of joy, and the queen likewise, with supreme delight, could no longer distinguish this world.
Then all the citizens, the elder ministers, and the family priests went out to meet him, embraced him, and led him into the presence of the king.
Then, having entered his own palace with great celebration, the prince, shedding tears, paid homage to his parents.
The lord of the earth did not recognize his own son for a moment as he fell at his feet; only after being somehow awakened by his ministers, he rose and embraced him with a heart drenched in tears.
Having saluted his mothers in due order and received the blessings increased by them—who were overwhelmed with affection—he, the prince, embraced all the citizens without exception and honored them.
Seated in their midst, he related his entire account to his father, including his friendship with Takṣaka.
He reported everything to his father—the collection of wealth consisting of jewels and other treasures given by the king of serpents, as well as that divine object brought by the Rākṣasa.
Having seen and heard of the prince's conduct, he was overwhelmed; he considered his daughter-in-law’s good fortune to have been earned through the propitiation of Maheśa.
The King of Niṣadha had his spies report this auspicious news to King Citravarman.
Having heard this nectar-like news, he rose up in agitation; after giving abundant wealth to them, he danced, overwhelmed with joy.
Then, having summoned his daughter and embraced her with tearful eyes, he adorned her with ornaments, thereby causing her to cast off the marks of widowhood.
Then there was a great festival in the kingdoms, villages, cities, and so forth; people everywhere praised the auspicious conduct of Sīmantinī.
Then King Citravarmā, having summoned the son of Indrasena, offered his daughter to him again according to the rites of marriage. (69)
Candrāṅgada, moreover, adorned his own wife with jewels and other treasures brought from the abode of Takṣaka—things exceedingly difficult for mortals to obtain. (170)
With a divine body-unguent, shining like molten gold, fragrant and spreading for ten yojanas, she was resplendent.
Adorned with a perpetual garland of unwithered lotus filaments produced from the Kalpa tree, the young and virtuous woman shone resplendently. (72)
And thus, having obtained his wife at an auspicious time, Candrāṅgada returned once more to his own city, permitted by his father-in-law.
Indrasena, the lord of kings, having established his own son in the kingdom and having propitiated Śiva through penance, attained the goal of those who have fully restrained themselves.
For ten thousand years, King Candrāṅgada enjoyed many worldly pleasures together with his wife Sīmantinī.

She gave birth to eight sons and one daughter of beautiful countenance. Sīmantinī took delight with her husband, worshipping Maheśvara; and day by day, she attained good fortune from the lunar day of the Moon (Monday).
Sūta said: This wonderful narrative has been fully described by me; I shall speak further of the majesty arising from the vow of the Monday fast.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Monday Vow," in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The sages said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! This supreme narrative you have told is wonderful; you should now speak of another marvelous account."
Sūta said: Formerly, in the land of Vidarbha, there was a certain preeminent brahmin known as Vedamitra, who was wise and a knower of the meaning of the Vedas and the Śāstras.
He had another brahmin friend named Sārasvata; both of them were extremely affectionate toward one another and lived in the same region.
The son of Vedamitra was named Sumedhas, who was firm in his vows; and the son of Sārasvata was renowned as Somavān. || 4 ||
Both were of the same age, both had similar dress and similar postures; they underwent their purificatory rites together and became equal in their learning. || 5 ||
Having studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches, as well as logic, grammar, the epics, the Purāṇas, and the entire body of Dharmaśāstras, those two—
Skilled in all branches of knowledge and wise even in their childhood, they bestowed incomparable joy upon their parents through all their virtues.
Once, those two excellent Brahmins affectionately called their two sons, who were sixteen years old and possessed auspicious forms, and spoke to them.
"O my two sons, you have both mastered the sciences in your youth and possess great splendor; the time for your marriage has now arrived simultaneously for both of you."
"By pleasing this king, the lord of Vidarbha, with your own skill, you will then obtain abundant wealth and perform the marriage ceremony."
Thus addressed by them, both those sons, the delights of the twice-born, approached the King of Vidarbha and gratified him with their virtues.
To him, who was fully satisfied with their learning, the two young brahmins announced that they were devoid of wealth and had made preparations for marriage.
Having understood the opinion of those two as well, that lord of Vidarbha laughed slightly and spoke, desiring to know the true nature of the world.
The virtuous Sīmantinī, queen of the king of Niṣadha, remains there; on Mondays she worships Mahādeva together with Ambikā.
On that day, having worshipped with supreme devotion the foremost of the twice-born who are most learned in the Vedas along with their wives, he bestows abundant wealth upon them.
Therefore, in this matter, let one of you two, assuming the attire and grace of a woman, and the other becoming her husband, be born as a Brahmin couple. (16)
Having become bride and groom and reached the house of the married woman, and having enjoyed abundant wealth and obtained it, you two have returned once more to my presence. || 17 ||
Thus commanded by the king, the two terrified young brahmins replied: "Fear arises in us to perform this deed. (18)
One who, out of delusion, practices deceit toward the deities, the guru, his parents, or royal families, is instantly destroyed along with his entire lineage. (19)
How may a man enter the inner apartments of kings by means of a disguise? For even a disguise, when it is being concealed, may at some time become known. (20)
Those virtues previously established through moral conduct, right behavior, learning, and so forth, immediately go to ruin for those who walk the path of crookedness. (21)
Sin, censure, fear, and enmity—these four indeed always abide in embodied beings who have entered upon the path of hypocrisy. (22)
Therefore, we two have been born of virtuous conduct in a family of pure people; we never resort to behavior that is praised by deceitful folk. (23)
The king said: "Because the commands of the gods, of gurus, of one's parents, and of a lord of the earth must never be transgressed, there shall be no refusal at any time. (24)
Whatever has been commanded by these, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must certainly be performed by those who are fearful, vigilant, and desirous of prosperity.
"Aha! We are indeed kings, and you are the subjects esteemed by us. For those who act according to the king's command there shall be prosperity; otherwise, there will be fear. (26)
"Therefore, you two must carry out my command without delay. When addressed thus by the king, they both said "So be it," out of fear.
The king made Sāmavanta, the son of Sarasvata, assume the form of a woman, adorning him with garments, ornaments, and other finery.

Having assumed an artificial state of a wife, with earrings and body-unguents applied, his eyes anointed with glossy collyrium and his form becoming desirable, he instantly took on the appearance of a most excellent woman. (29)
Having become a husband and wife, those two sons of a brahmin went to the land of Niṣadha by the king's command, saying, "Let it be as it may."
Having approached the royal palace on a Monday with the best of the twice-born, they both had their feet washed and were received as guests along with their wives.
That queen honored each of those excellent brahmins, together with their wives, as they were seated upon the finest seats.
Seeing those two sons of the Brahmin arrived as a couple who had assumed their roles, and recognizing them for what they were, he then smiled slightly and considered them to be Gaurī and Maheśvara.
Having invoked Sadāśiva, the God of gods, into the foremost of the twice-born, that queen invoked the Goddess, the Mother of the Universe, into their wives.
Having honored the best of the twice-born with fragrant perfumes, garlands, incense, and even the ritual waving of lights (nīrājana), she bowed down to them with a concentrated mind.
In golden vessels, there was milk-rice mixed with ghee, combined with sugar and honey, and served with delightful vegetables. || 36 ||
With fragrant śāli rice, delightful heaps of modakas and apūpas, śaṣkulīs, saṃyāvas, kṛsaras, and cooked mung beans; || 37 ||
Likewise, with other countless delightful foods and edibles, fragrant and delicious soups, and even cool drinks; (38)
She devotedly served the prepared food to the foremost of the twice-born; having offered that incomparable rice with curd, she fully satisfied them. (39)
When the foremost of the twice-born had finished eating and performed their ritual rinsing, the king’s wife bowed down and offered them betel-leaf and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) as was appropriate.
Having given cows, gold, garments, and ornaments of jewels and garlands, and having bowed down once more, he dismissed those best of the twice-born.

Of those two sons of the best of Brahmins, one was honored by her with the thought that he was Himavat’s daughter, and the other was worshipped with the thought that he was Mahādeva; having offered their salutations, they both departed at her command.
Having forgotten her male state, she—intoxicated with passion, overwhelmed by the god of love, and filled with longing for that very best of the twice-born—spoke.
O dear lord, large-eyed one, beautiful in every limb! Stay, stay! Where are you going? Do you not see me, your beloved?
"This forest before us is delightful, with its great trees in full bloom; I wish to sport here with you at your pleasure. (45)
Having heard what she said in this manner, the son of the twice-born went forward; reflecting that her words were spoken in jest, he proceeded just as before.
Again that young woman said: "Stop, stop! Where will you go, having approached me to enjoy me while I am possessed by an irresistible passion of love? (47)
Embrace me, your beloved, and let me drink from your lower lip; I am unable to go, being tormented by the arrows of Love.
Having heard that which had never been heard before, he became apprehensive; seeing her approaching from behind, he was suddenly struck with wonder. (49)
Who is this woman with eyes like lotus petals, with full and elevated breasts, a slender waist, and broad hips, as delicate as a fresh sprout? (50)
"He is indeed my friend; surely he was born as a beautiful woman. Therefore, I shall ask him everything. Having reflected thus, he spoke. (51)
"O friend, why do you speak as if you were someone new in terms of your appearance, qualities, and so forth? You speak words never heard before, like a woman agitated by passion. (52)
How is it that you, who are a knower of the Vedas and Purāṇas, a celibate student with conquered senses, the son of Sārasvata, and peaceful, speak in such a manner?
Thus addressed, she spoke again: "O Lord, I am not a man; I am a young girl named Sāmavatī, here to grant you pleasure. (54)
"If you have any doubt, my dear, look at my limbs. Having been addressed thus, he suddenly looked at her in secret on the path.
Beholding her, who possessed an unartificial braid, who was graced by full breasts, and who was beautiful in form, he became somewhat agitated with desire.
Then, having again restrained the agitation of his mind with effort, the wise man stood for a moment overcome with wonder and said nothing at all.
Sāmavatī said: "Your doubt has now vanished; therefore, come and enjoy me. O beloved, behold this forest, which is suited for dalliance with the wives of others."

Sumedhā said: Do not speak thus; do not transgress the bounds of propriety like one intoxicated with pride. Since both of us have understood the meaning of the scriptures, how can you speak in such a manner? (59)
Is this practice of following the conduct of a paramour consistent with the learning of the scriptures, with discernment, and with noble birth? (60)
"You are neither woman nor man, but a wise one; know the Self by means of the self. This misfortune has been brought about by ourselves through our own actions. (61)
Having deceived his own parents at the command of the rogue king and having performed an improper deed, he now experiences this fruit thereof. (62)
Every improper action destroys the welfare of men; for you, a learned son of a brahmin, have fallen into this contemptible state of womanhood.

Just as a man who leaves the path and goes into the forest might be pierced by thorns, or one who abandons the company of the virtuous might be harmed by violent predators, so too would he perish through the loss of his strength and prosperity.
Thus, resorting to solitude, go home yourself in silence; by the grace of the gods and the twice-born, your womanhood shall dissolve.
Or else, by the turn of fate, if womanhood itself should be yours, you shall be given by my father to sport with me, O lady of excellent complexion.
Oh, how wonderful! Oh, what suffering! Oh, how great is the power of sin! Oh, this is the majesty of the king, accumulated through the propitiation of Śiva!
Although addressed thus by him repeatedly, that bride, being extremely overwhelmed, forcibly embraced him and kissed his sprout-like lower lip.
Although she had tried to seduce him, the steadfast Sumedha brought the young woman with effort to his home and introduced her to him there in its entirety.
Having heard that, the two Brahmins, enraged and overwhelmed with grief, went into the presence of the King of Vidarbha along with those two princes.
Then Sārasvata said to the king regarding the conduct of the rogue: "O King, behold my son, brought under control by your command. (71)
Under the power of your command, these two committed a despicable deed; my son now experiences its fruit, having attained this loathsome female state. (72)
Today my lineage is destroyed; my ancestors have lost all hope. For there is no world for one who is sonless, whose rites such as the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) have been cut off. (73)
Having abandoned the topknot, the sacred thread, the deerskin, the girdle of muñja grass, the staff, and the water-pot—the marks appropriate for a life of celibacy—he has reached this present state.

"O King, tell me, what is the fate of one who has abandoned the Brahmasūtra, the Sāvitrī, ritual bathing, the twilight prayers, and the recitation and worship [of the deity], yet has attained womanhood? (75)
"By you my lineage has been destroyed, and the path of the Vedas has been lost to me. O King, tell me, what is the eternal destiny for me who have but one son? (76)
Having heard these words spoken by Sārasvata, the king was filled with supreme wonder at the power of Sīmantinī.
Then, having summoned all those great seers of immeasurable luster and having propitiated them, the lord of the earth requested his virility.
Then they said: "Who is capable of altering the will of Pārvatī and Śiva, as well as the greatness of their devotees? (79)
Then the king, taking with him Bharadvāja, the bull among sages, accompanied by those two foremost of the twice-born, his sons, set forth.
Having reached the abode of Ambikā according to the instruction of Bharadvāja, he worshipped that goddess during the deep of night with intense observances.

Thus, for three nights, having completely renounced food, that lord of the earth, devoted to the meditation on Pārvatī, gratified Gaurī—the remover of the distress of those who seek refuge—through perfect prostrations and various hymns of praise.
Then that goddess, pleased with the devoted lord of the earth, revealed her own form, which possessed a splendor equal to ten million moons.
Then Gaurī said to the king, "Tell me what you desire. He replied, "By your grace, let manhood be granted to him. (84)
The Great Goddess spoke further: "Whatever deed has been performed by my devotees cannot be undone, even in hundreds of millions of years. (85)
The king said: "This brahmin has but one son, and his lineage has been destroyed by his own actions; how can such a man attain happiness without a son? (86)
The Goddess said: By my grace, he shall have another excellent son, endowed with learning and discipline, long-lived, and pure of heart. (87)
"Let this daughter of that twice-born Sumedhas, named Sāmavatī, having become your wife, be united with the enjoyment of desires. (88)
Having spoken thus, the Goddess vanished; and they, led by the king, all went to their respective homes and remained abiding by her command.
That Brahmin Sārasvata, too, by the grace of the Goddess, obtained an excellent son even before his previous son, in a very short time.
And he gave that daughter Sāmavatī to Sumedhas; that couple enjoyed supreme happiness for a long time.
Sūta said: Thus has been described the power of Sīmantinī, the queen devoted to Śiva, and the majesty of Śambhu has also been recounted. (92)
Furthermore, I shall describe in brief the wondrous power of the devotees of Śiva, which serves as a source of auspiciousness for those who hear it. (93)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Power of Sīmantinī," in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa of the third part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Wondrous is the creation of Śiva; wondrous is the activity of Śiva; wondrous is the majesty of Śiva; and wondrous is the speech of Śiva. || 1 ||
The diverse life-stories of the devotees of Śiva are destroyers of sin; I shall now relate that which is truly the means for attaining both heaven and liberation.
In the region of Avanti, there was a certain Brāhmaṇa named Mandara, who delighted in sensual pleasures, was enslaved by women, and was a hoarder of wealth.
Having abandoned the twilight ablutions, he was fond of perfumes, garlands, and fine clothes; addicted to wicked women and established on an evil path, just like Ajāmila in former times.
Delighting day and night with a courtesan named Piṅgalā, he remained constantly in her house, his senses unsubdued.
Once, while that brahmin was dwelling in her house, a righteous-souled yogi of Śiva devoted to yoga named Ṛṣabha arrived there.
Beholding him arrived and considering their own merit to be exalted, both that courtesan and that brahmin honored him.
Having placed him upon a great throne covered with blankets and cloth, they devoutly washed his feet and placed that water upon their heads.
Having honored them with hospitable offerings, water for the feet, salutations, perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other ritual services, the two of them joyfully fed them.
When he had finished eating and rinsed his mouth, they joyfully seated him upon a couch with a comfortable covering and offered him betel-leaf.
Prompted by destiny, they devotedly massaged his feet; having arranged for his service, they gratified him for a long time.
Thus honored by the two of them, the Śiva-yogin of great luster spent one night there and departed in the morning, being highly esteemed by them.
Thus, when his time had nearly run out, that brahmin met his death; and that courtesan also died in due course and went to the destination earned by her own karma.
Led by his own past actions, that Brahmin entered the womb of Sumati, the wife of Vajrabāhu, the lord of the Daśārṇa kingdom.
Seeing that the king’s senior queen had conceived a child, his co-wives administered poison to her under a pretext.
Having consumed that terrible poison, she did not die due to the turn of fate; instead, she experienced only supreme suffering, which was even more unbearable than death itself.
Then, when the time had arrived, that virtuous woman of excellent complexion, afflicted by great suffering, gave birth to a son.
That prince, having passed the ten-day period and having previously been touched by poison, underwent great suffering, wailing day and night.
The mother of that child, afflicted by wounds on all her limbs, became exceedingly distressed due to the influence of the administration of poison. || 19 ||
Bringing them both together with the king, the physicians administered medicines; yet, despite numerous efforts being applied, they did not regain their health.
That queen, afflicted by great anguish and exceedingly emaciated, found no sleep at night, being deeply distressed by the suffering of her son. (21)
Having thus spent several months, the king, observing that his mother and son were alive yet as good as dead, reflected within himself: ||| 22 ||
"These two, my wife and son, have come here from hell; with their diseases unabated, they cry out and cause the breaking of my sleep. (23)
In this matter, I shall certainly employ a stratagem against these two sinners; whether they die or live, these two enjoyers of evil deeds are no longer capable [of such conduct].
Having thus resolved, the protector of the earth, though attached to his wives and their sons, summoned the charioteer and had his own wife and son carried far away by chariot.
Abandoned by the charioteer in some lonely forest, the two of them, utterly overwhelmed, suffered extreme agony from hunger and thirst.
Carrying her own child, stumbling at every step, sighing as she reproached her own past actions, she was greatly terrified.

In some places her limbs were pierced by thorns and her hair was disheveled as she was overcome with fear; in other places she was terrified by the roars of tigers, and in others she was pursued by serpents.
Being threatened by piśācas, vetālas, and brahmarākṣasas, she ran through great thickets with her feet pierced by razor-sharp stones.
Thus wandering in that terrible great forest, the king’s wife, by fate, reached a merchant's path frequented by cattle, horses, and men.
Traveling along that path for a very long distance with great effort, she beheld a city of Vaiśyas, frequented by many women and men.
The protector of that city is a great Vaiśya of noble standing named Padmākara, who is like another king of kings. || 32 ||
A certain female servant of that lord of the Vaiśyas, seeing the queen approaching from afar, went near her.
That maidservant, having personally learned the circumstances, presented her mistress—the beloved of the king, who was accompanied by her son and severely afflicted—to her master.
Seeing her afflicted by pain and distressed for her son, the lord of the people took her aside and clearly asked about her situation.
Having been informed of the entire account by her, that lord of merchants, realizing "Alas, what misery!", sighed again and again.
Having settled her in a private chamber near his own home, he honored her with equality to a mother, providing her with clothing, food, drink, and bedding.
While the king’s wife lived in that house under strict protection, she found no relief from diseases such as ulcers and consumption.
Then, after a few days, that boy, tormented by his wounds and having disregarded the physician’s efforts, died due to the power of destiny. (39)
When her own son had died, the queen, overwhelmed by great grief, fell unconscious upon the ground like a creeper broken by an elephant. (40)
Then, having somehow regained consciousness by chance, her breasts drenched with tears, she lamented in great distress, even though she was being consoled by the wives of the merchants.
Alas, father, father! Alas, son! Alas, protector of my life! Alas, full moon of the royal family! Alas, increaser of my joy! 42.
"O prince, where have you gone, abandoning your mother—this helpless, pitiable woman who has lost her kinsmen and whose life depends solely on yours? (43)
Who indeed is capable of consoling her as she laments with these uttered words that increase her grief and anxiety, she whose child has died? (44)
At that time, the one previously mentioned as Ṛṣabha, a Śiva-yogin and healer of her suffering and grief, arrived. 45.
That yogi, honored by the Lord of the Vaiśyas who held an arghya offering in his hand, went into her presence as she was grieving and spoke this to her.
Ṛṣabha said: "O child, why do you, with a bewildered mind, cry out so suddenly? Who has been born, who in this world has died? Tell me now. (47)
These entities, such as the body and so forth, share the same nature as water-foam; in some cases there is delusion, in some cases peace, or again, they may even persist.
Therefore, when this body, which resembles a bubble, has reached its dissolution into the five elements, the wise do not grieve, for there is no occasion for sorrow.
Beings are created by the qualities (guṇas), they are made to wander by their own actions (karma), they are dragged along by time (kāla), and they lie within latent impressions (vāsanā).
Through Māyā, the three qualities—sattva and the others—come into manifestation; by them alone bodies are born, and once born, they take refuge in those very characteristics.

Driven by latent impressions and rendered helpless, a living being attains divinity through the quality of goodness (sattva), humanity through passion (rajas), and the state of an animal through darkness (tamas). 52.
While existing in this saṃsāra, a living being, due to the binding force of karma, repeatedly undergoes a state of existence consisting of pleasure and pain that is difficult to discern.
Even for those gods who possess a lifespan of an eon, there is such a reversal of fortune; what then can be said of those with human bodies, who are bound by manifold ailments? 54.
Some say that time alone is indeed the cause of the body; some say it is karma, and others say it is the qualities (guṇas); for this body is common to all these.
Seeing this body, composed of the five elements, born through the influence of time, karma, and the qualities (guṇas), the wise do not rejoice at its birth, nor do they grieve when it has died.
A living being is born in the unmanifest and is dissolved in the unmanifest; in the interim, it appears as if manifest, resembling a bubble on water. || 57 ||
When the destruction of the embodied being while still in the womb is ordained, he may live by chance after birth, or he may die suddenly.
Some perish while still in the womb, others as soon as they are born; some perish in their youth, and some die in old age.
According to the nature of one's past karma, such is the body one obtains; indeed, one experiences joys and sorrows that correspond to it.
From the agitation of sexual union between the parents, impelled by the power of illusion (māyā), a certain body arises, characterized as male, female, or neuter.
A living being is born bearing upon its forehead that which has been inscribed by the Creator: lifespan, happiness, and suffering; merit and sin; learning and wealth. (62)
Because actions cannot be transgressed, because time cannot be bypassed, and because all things are impermanent, you ought not to grieve. (63)
Where is there any certain stability in a dream, or where is there truth in a magician’s illusion? Where is there permanence in an autumn cloud, or where is there eternity in the body? (64)
Hundreds of millions and tens of thousands of your previous births have passed; not knowing the supreme reality, this great exhaustion has been reached.
Whose daughter are you? Whose mother are you? And whose wife are you as you pass through millions of existences? (66)
The body consists of the five elements; it is bound together by skin, blood, and flesh; it is filled with fat, marrow, and bones; and it is a vessel for feces, urine, and phlegm. (67)
O deluded woman, considering this other body to be merely the impurity arising from your own body, you ought not to grieve for your son.
If indeed some person were to overcome death through effort, then how is it that all the ancient sages perished? (69)
Neither by austerity, nor by knowledge, nor by intellect, nor by mantras, herbs, or elixirs, does any wise man whatsoever transcend supreme death.
"O fair-faced one, today one creature dies and tomorrow another; therefore, you ought not to grieve for that which is impermanent by nature."
Death is ever-present; tell me, what happiness can there be for embodied beings? When a tiger stands before them, would prey ever find pleasure in a morsel of food? 72.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, if you desire to conquer birth and old age, go for refuge to the Lord of All, the Conqueror of Death, the Consort of Umā. (73)
So long does the terrible fear of death persist, and so long does the fear of birth and old age remain, as long as the embodied soul does not take refuge at the lotus feet of Śiva.
When the mind becomes detached after having experienced the sufferings here in this exceedingly terrible cycle of existence (saṃsāra), then Maheśvara should be meditated upon.
For a person who drinks with the mind the nectar-essence of meditation upon Śiva, a further thirst for the wine of the objects of worldly existence shall not arise.
When the mind is liberated from all attachments, restrained by dispassion, and immersed in the state of Śiva, then there is no further rebirth.
Therefore, O blessed lady, let this mind be solely devoted to the means of auspicious meditation; do not allow it to be possessed by grief and delusion, but worship Śiva. 78.
Sūta said: Thus enlightened with conciliatory words by the Śiva-yogin, the queen bowed at his lotus feet and replied to that guru.
The queen said: "O Blessed One, for me—who have lost my son, who have been abandoned by my dear kinsmen, and who am afflicted by a great disease—what recourse is there other than death? (80)
Therefore, I wish to die together with this child; for I, who was facing death, have today attained my purpose by beholding you. (81)
Sūta said: Having heard these words of hers, Śivayogī, a treasure-house of compassion, remembered his former service and went into the presence of the deceased.
Then, having taken that ash consecrated with Śiva-mantras and cast it into his split-open mouth, he restored the dead man to life.
That infant, reunited with his life-breaths, slowly opened his eyes; having regained the strength of his former senses, he wept out of longing for breast-milk.
Seeing the resurrection of the dead child, all the people, including those at the head of the cities, were filled with wonder and rejoiced.
Then the queen, overwhelmed with joy, her eyes agitated and wild with emotion, quickly took hold of her son, her own eyes clouded with tears.
Then, embracing him, the slender woman, filled with supreme bliss and tranquility, knew neither herself nor another, like one in deep sleep from exhaustion.
Furthermore, the yogi Ṛṣabha touched the bodies of that mother and son, which were afflicted with poison-wounds, with sacred ashes alone.
Touched by those ashes, the two of them attained divine bodies and assumed a form resembling that of the gods, adorned with splendor. (89)
That queen attained a supreme happiness a hundred times greater than the bliss experienced by those of meritorious deeds when they have obtained sovereignty over the three heavens.
Rṣabha, overwhelmed with love, raised her as she fell at his feet, comforted her who was now freed from her sorrows, and spoke to her.
O dear child, O Great Queen, may you live for eternal years; as long as you live in this world, you shall not reach old age.
"O virtuous lady, this son of yours shall be known in the worlds by the name Bhadrāyu; he shall regain his own kingdom. (93)
O lady of pure smiles, stay in this Vaiśya’s house for as long as it takes for this son of yours to have acquired his learning. (94)
Sūta said: Having thus restored both her and the prince to life by the power of his ashes, the yogi Ṛṣabha departed for whatever lands he desired.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Life of Bhadrāyu by the Yogi Ṛṣabha," within the Bhadrāyu-narrative of the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa, the third part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: The prostitute named Piṅgalā, whom I previously mentioned, cast off her former body due to the merit of worshipping the devotee of Śiva.
She was born again as the daughter of Candrāṅgada and Sīmantinī, endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtue, and known by the name Kīrtimālinī.
There, in the very house of the merchant lord, Prince Bhadrāyu grew like the sun of great heat in the month of Śuci. || 3 ||
That Vaiśyanātha also had one excellent son named Sunaya, who became a friend to the prince.

Both of them, the prince and the son of the merchant, were exceedingly affectionate toward one another; they were adorned with noble bodies and decorated with jeweled ornaments, and they delighted in the game of painting.
The brahmins performed the purificatory rites for that prince, and they also performed them in full detail for the merchant's own son.
Having undergone the initiation ceremony at the proper time, they, devoted to the service of their teacher and endowed with humility, acquired a mastery of all branches of knowledge.
Then, when the prince had reached his sixteenth year, that very same yogi, Ṛṣabha, arrived at his palace.
Both the queen and the prince, having repeatedly prostrated before the arrived Śiva-yogin, joyfully honored him.
Then, honored by those two, that lord of yogis, his mind delighted and his heart moist with compassion, spoke, addressing the prince.
Śivayogin said: "Is all well with you, dear son, and is your mother also free from ailment? And have you completed the acquisition of all the sciences?"
I hope you are constantly devoted to the service of your elders; and do you remember me, O dear one, as your teacher who gave you life? (12)
While the Lord of Yogis was speaking thus, the queen, full of humility, cast her son at his feet and addressed him as follows.
"O Teacher, this is your son; you are his father who gave him life. This disciple, moreover, should be accepted by you, whose nature is compassion. (14)
Therefore, protect this helpless one who has been abandoned by his kinsmen; you ought to properly instruct him in the path of the virtuous.
Thus propitiated by the queen, the high-minded Śivayogin instructed that prince in the true path.
Ṛṣabha said: The eternal dharma, as proclaimed in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, should always be practiced by people in accordance with their caste (varṇa) and stage of life (āśrama). || 17 ||
"O child, follow the path of the virtuous; always practice the conduct of the righteous. Do not transgress the command of the gods, and do not commit an offense against them. (18)
Always be devoted to the gods, the guru, and the brahmins; always honor even a caṇḍāla who has arrived as a guest. (19)
Never abandon the truth under any circumstances, even when faced with a life-threatening crisis; however, you may speak untruth at times for the sake of protecting cows and Brahmins. (20)
O mighty-armed one, abandon craving for the wealth of others, for the wives of others, for the possessions of gods and brahmins, and even for those things that are difficult to obtain. (21)

O Great-minded One, always cultivate a longing for noble discourse, right conduct, virtuous vows, and the authentic scriptures, as well as for the constant accumulation of merit and other such qualities.
O sinless one, be free from laziness in bathing, recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, the libations to the ancestors, and in the worship of cows, deities, and guests. (23)
Diligently avoid anger, hatred, fear, deceit, backbiting, stubborn attachment to the untrue, crookedness, hypocrisy, and agitation. (24)
Though you are devoted to the duty of a warrior, abandon senseless violence; avoid groundless enmity, idle chatter, and the disparagement of others. (25)
Hunting, gambling, drinking, women, and those conquered by women; excessive eating, excessive anger, excessive sleep, and excessive toil. (26)
Always completely avoid excessive conversation and excessive play. || 27 ||
Accomplish supreme knowledge, supreme faith, supreme merit, supreme mindfulness, supreme enthusiasm, supreme renown, and supreme fortitude.
He was full of desire for his own wives, full of anger toward his enemies, full of greed for the accumulation of merit, and indeed full of envy toward those who were unrighteous.
Be full of hatred toward heretics and full of passion for the virtuous; be difficult to understand in the face of evil counsel and deaf to the words of backbiters. (30)
Avoid from afar the rogue, the fierce, the deceitful, the cruel, the gambler, the fickle, the wicked, the fallen, the atheist, and the crooked.
Do not engage in self-praise; remain one who understands through subtle gestures. Always remain free from excessive attachment to wealth and to your entire family.
Always place your trust in the words of your wife who is devoted to her husband, of your mother, of your father-in-law, of the virtuous, and of your guru.
Always intent on self-protection, vigilant, and firm in your vows, you should never place your trust even in your own servants.
O high-minded one, do not kill any thief who has placed his trust in you; do not suspect those who are innocent, and do not waver from the truth.
Protect the helpless, the wretched, the aged, women, children, and the innocent with your wealth, your life, your intellect, your power, and your strength. (36)
Do not kill even an enemy who deserves death if he has come to you for refuge; whether he be unworthy or worthy, low-born or most exalted. (37)
Whoever may beg, give even your head to them; by great effort, always acquire only fame.
For both kings and the learned, fame alone is indeed the ornament; prosperity arises from good fame, and merit is born of good fame. (39)
The world shines with his good reputation, just as the moon shines with its moonlight; he possesses a multitude of elephants, horses, and gold, and a heap of jewels as large as a mountain. (40)
Quickly abandon everything that is ruined by infamy like a blade of grass; [abandon] the anger of your mother, the anger of your father, and the anger of your teacher, which destroys wealth.
O Lord, forgive the transgression of your sons and of the brahmins; act for their welfare in such a way that the favor of the twice-born may be secured.
The best of the twice-born shall rescue the king who is submerged in distress; [they grant] longevity, fame, strength, happiness, wealth, merit, and the prosperity of the subjects. (43)

One should always practice that action by which [the desired result] may arise, taking into account the place, the time, one's own power, and what ought to be done as well as what ought not to be done. (44)
Having investigated thoroughly with diligence, always perform your duties; do not cause harm to anyone, and prevent the suffering of others.
You should restrain thieves and the wicked through sound policy and the exercise of power, during bathing, recitation, and burnt offerings, as well as in rites for the gods and the ancestors.
Be swift in sleep and prompt in eating; be truthful, free from deceit, endowed with courtesy, and pleasing to people. (47)
O Mahāmati, speak words that are concise yet possess infinite meaning; be fearless in all adversities and calamities.
Be afraid of the Brahmin class, not of sinful instruction; be afraid of kinsmen, relatives, Brahmins, wives, and sons. (49)
You should conduct yourself with equanimity in rows of diners, as well as in the beneficial instructions of the virtuous and in meritorious discourses. (50)

In assemblies for the discussion of knowledge that are righteous, never turn your back; [be present] at the edge of pure, meritorious waters, in renowned places crowded with those devoted to the Veda.
"You must always reside in a great land filled with Śiva, wherever unchaste women, courtesans, and lustful men may dwell. (52)
Never dwell, even for a moment, in an ill-fated place crowded with the lowly; rather, take refuge in Śiva alone, the Lord of the three worlds.
You should worship all the gods and honor those days, always pure, always diligent, always peaceful, and always steadfast.

O sinless one, you have always conquered the group of six [internal foes] and have always remained in solitude; you honor the Brahmins who know the Vedas, the peaceful ascetics, and those who are self-restrained and radiant.
A pair [of verses]: [One should see] sacred trees, sacred rivers, a holy pilgrimage site, a great lake, a cow, a bull, a jewel, and a devoted young wife. (56)
Having risen at the Brahma-hour, with a pure heart and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should immediately offer salutations to one's own tutelary deities.
Having paid homage to his own guru, and having meditated upon the Lord who is the consort of Umā, as well as Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī, Brahmā, and Vināyaka; || 58 ||
[He worshipped] Skanda, the goddess Kātyāyanī, Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī, as well as Indra and the other lords of the worlds, and also the sages of meritorious renown.
Having reflected thus, one should always bow to the rising sun, offering perfume, flowers, betel, vegetables, cooked fruits, and so forth.

Having offered it to Śiva, enjoy this dear and fresh food—both that which is chewed and that which is eaten. Whatever has been given, whatever performed, whatever chanted, whatever bathed in, whatever offered in sacrifice, and whatever remembered [is all for his sake].
And whatever austerity you have performed, offer it all unto Śiva. Whether eating, reciting, sleeping, or moving about; whether seeing, hearing, speaking, or grasping—contemplate only Śiva.

With your two hands shining with bracelets of rudrākṣa beads, bearing white ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) between your eyebrows, reciting the five-syllabled supreme king of mantras and constantly meditating on the feet of Paśupati, may you find delight.
Thus, my dear child, this compendium of Dharma has been told in brief; it is proclaimed in detail in other Purāṇas as well. (64)

Now, for your benefit, I shall proclaim the Śaiva armor (kavaca), which is the supreme secret of all Purāṇas, the purifier that removes the entire flood of sins without remainder, bestows victory, and liberates one from all calamities.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of Ṛṣabha’s Instruction to Bhadrāyu," in the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Ṛṣabha said: Having paid homage to Mahādeva, the Lord who pervades the universe, I shall proclaim this armor consisting of Śiva, which provides protection for all men. (1)
Seated in a clean place upon a properly prepared seat, with his senses and vital breaths subdued, he should meditate upon the imperishable Śiva.

One should meditate upon Maheśa, who is composed of supreme bliss, seated within the lotus of the heart, pervading the expanse of the sky with his own splendor, beyond the senses, subtle, infinite, and primordial.

Having shaken off all bonds of karma through meditation, with his mind long immersed in the bliss of consciousness, and with his self composed by the placement of the six-syllable mantra, he should provide protection by means of the Śaiva armor.

May the Lord, the soul of all deities, protect me who have fallen into the deep well of saṃsāra; may His divine name, the root of the most excellent mantra, shake off all the sin residing within my heart.

May the Lord, the one whose form is the universe, who consists of light, who is a mass of bliss, and whose nature is consciousness—He who is subtler than the subtle and possesses great power—protect me everywhere from all fear. 6.
May Giriśa, who sustains the universe in the form of the earth and possesses eight forms, protect me from the earth; may he who provides life to men in the form of water protect me from the waters.

May that Kālarudra, who at the end of the aeon dances with manifold sports after burning all the worlds, protect me from the fear of forest fires, from storms and the like, and from every form of suffering.

Shining with the luster of blazing lightning and gold, holding in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness along with a book and an axe, four-faced, three-eyed, and known as Tatpuruṣa—may he protect me perpetually from the eastern direction. (9)
Holding an axe, a goad, a noose, a trident, a skull, a drum, and a rosary; four-faced, blue-hued, and three-eyed—may Aghora protect in the southern direction. (10)

Resplendent like a jasmine flower, the moon, a conch, or crystal; holding a Veda, a rosary, and bestowing boons and fearlessness; three-eyed, four-faced, and of vast power—may Sadyojāta protect me in the west.

May Vāmadeva protect me in the northern direction—he who holds a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and a ṭaṅka in his hands; whose complexion is like the filaments of a lotus; who possesses three eyes and four beautiful faces. (12)

May Īśāna, who holds in his hands the Vedas, the shield, the goad, the ṭaṅka, the noose, the skull-bowl, the drum, the eye, and the trident; who possesses white luster, five faces, and supreme radiance from above, protect me. (13)

May the moon-crested Lord protect my head; may the one with the eye on his forehead protect my brow; may the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes protect my eyes; and may the Lord of the Universe always protect my nose. (14)
May he whose fame is sung by the Vedas protect my ears; may Kapālī always protect my cheeks; may Pañcavaktra always protect my face; and may Vedajihva always protect my tongue. (15)

May the blue-throated Lord of the Mountains protect my throat; may he who holds the Pināka bow in his hand protect my two hands; may he whose arms are righteousness protect the roots of my arms; and may the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice protect my chest.
May the one whose bow is the king of mountains protect my belly; may the destroyer of Madana protect my waist. May the son of Heraṃba protect my navel, and may the Lord Dhūrjaṭi protect my hips.

May the friend of Kubera protect my two thighs; may the Lord of the World protect my two knees. May he whose banner is the bull protect the pair of my shanks, and may he whose feet are worshipped by the gods protect my feet.

May Maheśvara protect me during the first watch of the day; may Vāmadeva protect me during the middle watch; may Tryambaka protect me during the third watch; and may the Bull-bannered Lord protect me during the final watch of the day. (19)

May the moon-crested Lord protect me at the beginning of the night; may the bearer of the Gaṅgā protect me at midnight; may the husband of Gaurī protect me at the end of the night; and may the Conqueror of Death protect me at all times. (20)

May Śaṅkara protect me while I am within; may Sthāṇu always protect me while I am outside. May the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati) protect me in the space between those two; may Sadāśiva protect me on all sides.

May the sole Lord of the universe protect me while standing; may the Lord of the Pramathas protect me while walking; may He who is known through the Vedāntas protect me while seated; and may the imperishable Śiva protect me while lying down.

May Nīlakaṇṭha protect me on the roads; may the enemy of Tripura protect me in mountain fastnesses and other difficult terrains; and may the noble Mṛgavyādha protect me during great travels such as dwelling in the forest.

May Vīrabhadra protect [us] from the terrible and insurmountable fear arising from the ocean-like army of the enemy—he whose fierce wrath is as intense as the cataclysm at the end of an aeon, and who has caused the cosmic egg to tremble with his manifest, loud laughter. (24)

A fool might cut through a hundred *akṣauhiṇīs* of assassins—terrifying with thousands, lakhs, tens of thousands, and millions of throngs of foot-soldiers, horses, and elephants—with the edge of his terrible axe. (25)

May the trident of the Destroyer of Tripura, blazing with the flames of the fire of universal dissolution, slay the Dasyus; may the Pināka bow of the Lord terrify the predators such as tigers, lions, bears, and wolves.

May the Lord of the worlds destroy for me bad dreams, ill omens, miserable rebirths, dejection, famine, calamities, unbearable infamy, portents, torments, the fear of poison, afflictions by malevolent planets, and diseases. (27)

Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, Sadāśiva, whose essence is all principles (tattvas), who sports in all principles, the sole creator of all worlds, the sole sustainer of all worlds, the sole destroyer of all worlds, the sole teacher of all worlds, the sole witness of all worlds, the secret of all Vedas, the bestower of all boons, the dispeller of all misfortunes and afflictions, the granter of fearlessness to the entire universe, the sole benefactor of all people, he whose crest is the moon, whose self-luminosity is eternal, who is beyond qualities (nirguṇa), incomparable, formless, beyond appearances, free from disease, devoid of phenomenal expansion (niṣprapañca), stainless, free from duality, unattached, pure, without exit [from the world], whose glory is eternal form, whose glory is incomparable, who is without support, the non-dual existence-consciousness-bliss that is eternally pure, awakened, and perfect, whose nature is the light of supreme peace and splendor. Victory! Victory! O Great Rudra, O Great Terrible One, O Auspicious Incarnation, O Dispeller of the Forest Fire of Suffering, O Mahābhairava, O Kālabhairava, O Bhairava of the End of the Kalpa, wearer of the garland of skulls, wielder of the Khaṭvāṅga, sword, shield, noose, goad, hand-drum (ḍamaru), trident, bow, arrow, mace, spear, club, *bhiṇḍipāla*, javelin, pestle, hammer, axe, iron bar, *bhuśuṇḍī*, *śataghnī*, discus, and other weapons; you whose thousand hands are terrifying with these arms, whose face is formidable with tusks, whose loud laughter causes the Brahma-maṇḍala to tremble, whose earrings are lordly serpents, whose necklace is lordly serpents, whose bracelets are lordly serpents, who wears the skin of a lordly serpent, conqueror of Death, three-eyed one, destroyer of Tripura, odd-eyed one, Lord of the Universe, universal form, whose vehicle is the bull, whose ornament is poison, whose faces are everywhere—protect me, protect me! Blaze, blaze! Destroy, destroy the fear of great death and untimely death! Eradicate, eradicate the fear of disease! Pacify, pacify the fear of poisonous snakes! Kill, kill the fear of thieves! Exterminate, exterminate my enemies! Tear apart, tear apart with your trident! Split, split with your axe! Cut, cut with your sword! Crush, crush with your Khaṭvāṅga! Pound, pound with your pestle! Strike, strike with your arrows! Terrify, terrify the Rākṣasas! Put to flight, put to flight the spirits (bhūtas)! Frighten, frighten the Kūṣmāṇḍas, Vetālas, hosts of Mārīs, and Brahmarākṣasas! Grant me fearlessness, grant me fearlessness! Console me, who am terrified, console me! Lift me up, lift me up from the fear of hell! Revive me, revive me! Quench my hunger and thirst, quench them! Delight me, who am afflicted by suffering, delight me! Cover me, cover me with the armor of Śiva! O Three-eyed One, Sadāśiva, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you! Ṛṣabha said: Thus has this armor (kavaca) of Śiva, the bestower of boons, been declared by me; it is the secret of all embodied beings, which pacifies all afflictions. (28)
Whatever mortal should always wear this supreme armor of Śiva, no fear shall ever arise for him by virtue of the grace of Śambhu. (29)
Whether one's lifespan has been exhausted and death has arrived, or one is afflicted by a great disease, one attains immediate happiness and finds long life. (30)
He who wears this armor of Śiva—which pacifies all poverty and increases auspiciousness—is honored even by the gods. (31)
One is liberated from the multitude of great sins (mahāpātaka) as well as the minor sins (upapātaka); at the end of the body, one attains Śiva through the power of the Śivavarman.
O child, you too should wear with faith this supreme armor of Śiva given by me; you shall indeed immediately attain the highest good.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus to that son of the king, the yogi Ṛṣabha gave him a conch of great sound and a sword that destroys enemies.
Furthermore, having consecrated the ashes with mantras, he touched that body on all sides and bestowed upon it twice the strength of six thousand elephants.
Having regained his strength, sovereignty, fortitude, and memory through the power of the ashes, that prince shone with splendor like the autumnal sun.
To him, who stood with palms joined in reverence, that yogi spoke again to the prince: "This sword has been given by me through the power of my asceticism and mantras. (37)
To whomever you clearly show this sharp-edged sword, that enemy shall die instantly, even if he were Death himself in person. (38)
Those enemies of yours who hear the blast of this conch shell will fall down unconscious, their weapons cast aside and deprived of their senses. (39)
These two divine weapons, the sword and the conch, destroy the enemy forces and increase the valor and splendor of one's own army and partisans. (40)
And by the power of these two, as well as by the Śaiva armor and even by the great strength of twelve thousand nāgas— || 41 ||
