By the power of wearing the sacred ash, you shall conquer the enemy army; having attained your father’s throne, you shall protect this earth.
Having thus properly instructed Bhadrāyuṣa along with his mother, the yogi, honored by them both, then departed at his own will.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Śiva-Kavaca" within the Bhadrāyū-pākhyāna of the Sīmantinī-māhātmya, in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa of the third part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 12 ||
Sūta said: Then the powerful king of Magadha became the enemy of that mighty-armed Vajrabāhu, the lord of Daśārṇa.
That powerful one, named Hemaratha, mighty-armed and fierce in battle, surrounded Daśārṇa with a vast force and besieged him.
The invincible commanders of his army, having reached the territory of Daśārṇaka, plundered the finest jewels and others set fire to the houses.
Some seized wealth, others took children and women; some took cattle-wealth, while others took grain and household goods. Some destroyed the crops in the orchards and ruined the domestic gardens.
Having thus destroyed that kingdom, the Magadhas, desiring to seize his women and cattle, surrounded the city of Vajrabāhu.
Seeing the city thus thrown into such turmoil, King Vajrabāhu quickly went forth with his army to do battle.
King Vajrabāhu, along with his ministers and attendants, fought together with the Māgadhas and struck down the enemy host.
Vajrabāhu, the great archer, clad in armor and mounted upon his chariot, wrought a great slaughter, scattering showers of arrows. || 8 ||
Seeing the King of Daśārṇa fighting most unbearably in battle, all the Magadhan soldiers swiftly surrounded him alone.
Having fought for a very long time, the Magadhas of firm prowess destroyed that army and attained the glory of victory.
Some struck his chariot, while others cut that bow; one slew his charioteer, and another severed his sword.
Having seized the king by force while his sword and bow were severed, his chariot destroyed, and his charioteer slain, the powerful warriors bound him in their wrath.
Having conquered his entire assembly of ministers and his army, those Māgadhas, proclaiming their victory, entered his city. (13)
They seized horses, men, elephants, camels, and cattle, as well as wealth, all the young women, and maidens with beautiful limbs. || 14 ||
Those assailants bound the king's queens and thousands of female servants, and they also carried off his treasury, which was filled with jewels.
Having thus destroyed the city and seized the women, cattle, wealth, and other possessions, they forcibly bound Vajrabāhu, placed him upon a chariot, and departed.
When such a clamor arose and a terrible destruction of the kingdom occurred, the powerful Prince Bhadrāyu then heard that news.
Hearing that his father was bound by enemies, that his father’s wives had been carried off, and that the kingdom of Daśārṇa was lost, he roared like a lion.
Taking up his sword and conch, accompanied by the son of a Vaiśya and clad in armor, the prince mounted his horse with the desire for victory.
Having arrived with speed at that region filled with the Māgadhas, which was being consumed by fire, crying out in distress, and deprived of its women, sons, cattle, and wealth; || 20 ||

Seeing the entire royal assembly and the kingdom empty and overwhelmed by fear, his mind swelling with rage, he quickly entered the enemy host; drawing his bow back to his ear, he rained down a continuous stream of arrows.
Being struck by the prince with his arrows, those enemies rushed at him with speed and pierced him with formidable shafts.
Though being struck by a multitude of weapons by enemies intoxicated with battle, the steadfast one did not waver in the fray, protected as he was by the armor of Śiva. || 23 ||
Forcefully entering the fray with the swift gait of an elephant, he quickly struck down chariots, elephants, and foot soldiers in great numbers.

There, having slain a single charioteer along with his driver, the prince, with the son of a Vaiśya as his charioteer, mounted that very same chariot and moved fearlessly through the battle like a lion among a herd of deer. || 25 ||
Then all those powerful heroes, highly enraged and with bows raised high, rushed toward that single commander of the army alone. || 26 ||
Raising his formidable sword before them as they were charging, he advanced against those great heroes, as if displaying his own prowess.
Upon merely seeing his sword, which was as blazingly radiant as the tongue of the formidable God of Death, the kings suddenly perished through its power.
Whosoever beheld that sword flashing upon the field of battle, they all met their end, just as an insect perishes upon encountering a thunderbolt.
Then, for the destruction of all the armies, that mighty-armed one blew his conch with a great roar, as if filling heaven and earth.
By that sound of the conch shell, which was as if heavily smeared with poison, the enemies fell to the ground in a swoon the very moment it was heard.
Those who were mounted on the backs of horses, those in chariots, and those stationed upon elephants, lost consciousness in an instant and fell, their vigor destroyed by the blast of the conch.
Having counted them all as being on the ground, unconscious, disarmed, and resembling corpses, he who was learned in the treatises of dharma did not kill them.
Having liberated his own father who was bound on the field of battle, he immediately freed all his wives who had fallen under the power of the enemy.
He also took the wives of the chief ministers as well as those of other city-dwellers, along with women, children, maidens, and numerous cattle and wealth. (35)
Having liberated him from the fear of his enemies, he comforted the agitated man; then, moving among the enemy forces, he seized their women.
Horses swift as the wind or thought, elephants resembling mountains, golden chariots, and maidservants with beautiful faces.
Having seized all that vast wealth with speed and taken it away, he bound the defeated Hemaratha, the lord of Magadha. || 38 ||
Having swiftly seized his ministers, kings, and the principal leaders there, he bound them and quickly brought them into the city. (39)
Those chief ministers and leaders who had previously been broken and scattered in all directions in battle now returned with full confidence. || 40 ||
Seeing the prowess of the youth, they were all struck with wonder in their minds; they considered him to be the foremost of the gods who had descended to the earth for a specific purpose.
"Oh, what great fortune is ours! Oh, what a fruit of our asceticism! By this certain hero, we who were dead have truly been restored to life! (42)
Is he one perfected through yoga, or perfected through asceticism, or perhaps an immortal? For this great deed which has been performed by him is superhuman.
"Surely his mother must be Gaurī and Śiva his father; for he, possessing infinite power, has conquered nine akṣauhiṇīs. (44)
Thus questioned by the ministers, who were filled with wonder, delighted, and praising one another, he spoke of himself according to the truth.
Overwhelmed with love, he prostrated before his father who had arrived, who was overwhelmed by wonder and joy, and who was shedding tears of bliss. || 46 ||
That king, saluted with affection by his own son, embraced him firmly and quickly spoke, overcome with love.
"O Great-minded One, who are you? Are you a god, a human, or a gandharva? Who is your mother, who is your father, what is your country, and what is your name? (48)
Why did he, having encountered them here along with their wives, release those who had been bound by his enemies—men who were like the dead, their vital energy destroyed out of compassion? (49)
From where have you obtained this valor, this fortitude, this splendor, and this preeminence of strength? You seem as if you wish to conquer the three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
"Even in a thousand births, I am not capable of discharging my debt to you, O one of great majesty, along with these wives and kinsmen. (51)
"Leaving behind these sons, these wives, this kingdom, and this city—everything—my mind is bound to you alone by the ties of love. (52)
Tell me everything, O father, you who protect my life; for the lives of these wives of mine depend entirely upon you.
Sūta said: Thus questioned by his father, Bhadrāyu spoke to him: "O King, this friend of mine is the son of a Vaiśya named Sunaya."
I dwell in this beautiful house together with my mother; my name is Bhadrāyu, and I shall inform you of my history later.
Having entered the city—may prosperity be yours—dwell at ease as you please, together with your wife and friends, having cast off all fear of enemies.
"Do not release these enemies until my return; today I shall go quickly to my own abode. (57)
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the king, Bhadrāyu, the prince, returned to his own abode and reported everything to his mother.
She too, joyful and with eyes full of tears, embraced her son; and that lord of the Vaiśyas, having embraced him with love, honored him.
And Vajrabāhu, the lord of kings, having entered his own palace together with his wives, sons, and ministers, attained incomparable joy.
When that night had dawned, Ṛṣabha, the best among yogins, approached King Candrāṅgada, the husband of Sīmantinī.
Having related in private with affection the birth of Bhadrāyus and his superhuman deeds, [inform me] of your daughter Kīrtimālinī.
Having thus instructed the King of Niṣadha, saying, "Give [the horse] to Bhadrāyus," Ṛṣabha, who knew the true nature of place and time, then departed.
The Special Verse: Then, at an auspicious moment, King Candrāṅgada summoned Bhadrāyus and gave Kīrtimālinī to him.
Having performed the marriage ceremony, that son of the lord of kings, seated upon a golden throne together with his wife, shone like the moon with Rohiṇī.
Having summoned his father Vajrabāhu, that prince of Niṣadha, accompanied by his ministers, entered the city, went out to meet him, and paid him honor.
There he saw Bhadrāyu, the subduer of enemies, who had just been married; falling at his feet out of love, the king embraced him with joy.
"This hero is the giver of my life; he is the destroyer of my enemies. Yet, his lineage is unknown to me, as is his infinite prowess. (68)
"O King, this is your son-in-law, the mighty Candrāṅgada. Now I wish to hear, in accordance with the truth, about his lineage and his birth. (69)
Thus requested by the King of Daśārṇa, the Lord of Niṣadha approached him in private and, smiling, spoke these words: (70)
"O King, this is your son, who in his childhood was afflicted by disease; he was abandoned by you in the forest along with his mother, who was tormented by illness. (71)
Wandering through the forest with this infant, that woman reached the house of a Vaiśya by chance and was protected by that Vaiśya.
Then, that young boy of yours, afflicted by many diseases, died; however, he was brought back to life again by a certain king of yogins.
By the power of that very Śivayogin named Ṛṣabha, the mother and the boy attained forms resembling those of gods.
Protected by the armor of Śiva, he conquered his enemies in battle with that sword and that conch, the slayer of foes, which had been given to him.
He alone possesses the strength of twelve thousand nāgas; proficient in all branches of knowledge, he has become my son-in-law. (76)
Therefore, O King, taking him along with his mother of virtuous vows, go to the city; you shall attain the highest welfare.
Having related all this, Candrāṅgada summoned his chief wife, who was staying within the inner apartments, and showed her to him as she was adorned with ornaments.
Having heard all this and having seen it, that lord of the earth was utterly ashamed; out of folly, he censured his own deed. (79)
Having attained supreme bliss from the curiosity of seeing them both, with his entire body covered in horripilation, he embraced them both.
Thus honored and greeted by the King of Niṣadha, he [Nala], having properly fed him as well as himself along with his ministers, [proceeded]. (81)
Taking her as his own chief queen, along with that son and his daughter-in-law, Vajrabāhu departed for the city accompanied by his entire retinue.
With great excitement, Bhadrāyus reached his father’s palace and brought supreme joy to all the inhabitants of the city.
When his father had ascended to heaven in due time, Bhadrāyus, having reached youth and possessing marvelous prowess, ruled over the entire earth.
Having established a supreme friendship in the presence of the Brahman-sages, he released Hemaratha, the lord of Magadha, from his bonds.

Having thus performed the worship of Śiva, honored by the three worlds, even in his previous birth, that prince—having crossed over a multitude of unbearable calamities and attained his kingdom—joyfully sported with the daughter of Candrāṅgada.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Marriage of Bhadrāyu," in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa of the third part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 13 ||
Sūta said: Having ascended the throne, that heroic lord of the earth, Bhadrāyus, once entered a beautiful forest together with his wife.

In that place, where the blossoms of the *aśoka* tree were in full bloom and its new shoots had sprouted, and which was filled with swarms of humming bees hovering over clusters of fully opened jasmine flowers.
In the midst of a dense thicket of *tamāla* trees where the *aśoka* trees had suddenly burst into bud, there was a festival for those filled with passion by the fragrance of fresh filaments.
In a bower of mādhavī creepers, bent low under the weight of clusters of blossoms, and adorned with mango trees radiant with coral-red flowers; || 4 ||
In the delightful season of spring, resounding with the cries of male cuckoos wandering through the groves of *punnāga* trees, he sported together with his wife.
Then, not far away, that best of kings saw a brahmin couple running and crying out, pursued by a tiger.
"Save us! Save us, O Great King! Alas, O King, treasury of compassion! This tiger of great speed is rushing here to devour us both. (7)
"O King, protect us before this being, who resembles a mountain and strikes fear into all living creatures, reaches us and devours us."
Having heard this lamentation, the king took up his bow; meanwhile, a tiger arrived and seized that bride in the midst.
"O Lord, O Lord! O Beloved! O Śambhu, Lord of the World!"—while she was thus wailing piteously, Bhīṣaṇa seized her.
Then the king struck the tiger with sharp arrows, yet it was not pained by them in the least, like the lord of mountains by showers of rain.
That great being, Śārdūla, unharmed by the king's weapons, forcibly dragged that woman away and departed with haste. (12)
Seeing his wife carried away by a tiger, the Brahmin was deeply distressed and wept, crying out: "Alas, my dear! O young girl! Alas, my beloved! Alas, my devoted wife! (13)
"Having abandoned me here all alone, how have you gone to the other world? Having left her who was dearer to me than my own life, how can I bear to live? (14)
O King, where are your great weapons? Where is your praiseworthy, mighty bow? And where is your strength, which surpasses that of twelve thousand great elephants? (15)
What use have you for the conch or the sword? What use have you for the knowledge of mantras and missiles? And what use is that exertion, or what use is such great power? (16)
All that has become fruitless, as well as whatever else remains in you—you who are incapable of warding off a forest-dwelling creature. (17)
This is the supreme duty of a Kṣatriya: the protection of those who are oppressed. Therefore, when the duty appropriate to your lineage has perished, what is the use of your life?
Kings who know the Dharma provide protection for those who are distressed and seeking refuge with their lives and wealth; those devoid of such protection are like the dead. (19)
For the wealthy who are devoid of charity, the state of a mendicant is better than the life of a householder; for those who lack protection for the distressed, death is better than life. (20)
It is better for a king to suffer the loss of his vigor than to fail to protect those who are helpless, those who have sought refuge, and the miserable. (21)
Having heard his lamentation and his reproach of his own prowess, the king, out of grief, reflected thus within himself: (22)
"Alas! My manliness has perished today due to the reversal of fate; today my fame has vanished, and a most grievous sin has been incurred. (23)
The dharma appropriate for the time has perished for me, unfortunate and evil-minded as I am; surely my wealth, kingdom, and lifespan will come to an end. (24)
The prosperity, enjoyments, sons, wives, and wealth of those lacking merit arise for a moment through destiny and vanish in an instant. (25)
Therefore, by giving up even my own dear life, I shall free this twice-born man, who has lost his wife and is tormented by grief, from his sorrow.
Having thus resolved in his mind, Bhadrāyu, the best of kings, fell at his feet and spoke to him consolingly.
"O Brahmin, have mercy on me, a wretched kshatriya whose vigor has been destroyed; abandon your grief, O one of great intelligence, and I shall give you whatever wealth you desire. (28)
"This kingdom, this queen, and this body of mine—all this is at your disposal; tell me, what is your desire? (29)

The Brāhmaṇa said: What is the use of a mirror to a blind man? What is the use of houses to one who lives on alms? What is the use of a book to a fool? And what is the use of wealth to one who has no wife? (30)
Therefore, being one whose wife has passed away and who has already enjoyed all pleasures, I shall never [seek them again]; let this chief queen of yours be given to me for the sake of desire. (31)
The king said: "O Brahmin, is this your dharma? Is this the command of your preceptor? For violating another's wife leads neither to heaven nor to fame. (32)
There are donors of wealth, of kingdoms, and of elephants and horses; but there is nowhere anyone who gives their own body, and never one who gives their wife. (33)
The sin that has been accumulated through the enjoyment of another's wife cannot be washed away even by hundreds of expiatory rites.

The Brāhmaṇa said: "Even a terrible act such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, or even the consumption of liquor, I shall destroy through ascetic penance; how much more so the sin of adultery? Therefore, give this wife of mine to me; otherwise, it will certainly be so. (35)

"By failing to protect those afflicted by fear, you will certainly go to hell. Terrified by these words of the Brahmin, the king reflected: "Great sin arises from non-protection; therefore, giving away my wife is better. (36)
Therefore, having given my wife to this foremost of the twice-born and being thus freed from sin, I shall immediately enter the fire so that my fame may be established. (37)
Having thus resolved in his mind and kindled the sacrificial fire, he summoned that brahmin and gave him his wife along with the ritual water.
Having bathed himself and become pure, he prostrated before the lords of the gods; having circumambulated that fire twice, he meditated upon Śiva with a concentrated mind.
Then, as he was about to fall into the fire with his mind fixed upon his own feet, the Lord of the Universe, the Master of the World, appeared before him.

That Lord, five-faced and three-eyed, wielder of the Pināka bow, adorned with a digit of the moon, with a mass of tawny matted locks hanging down, standing in the midst [of the assembly], possessing the splendor of ten million suns. || 41 ||

White as a lotus stalk, clad in an elephant hide, with the region of his head sprinkled by the waves of the Gaṅgā, he shone brilliantly with necklaces of lordly serpents, bracelets, rings, the tip of his crown, armlets, and earrings.

The king beheld before him the Lord Śitikaṇṭha, standing upon a bull, holding in his hands a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, an axe, a shield, a deer, the gesture of fearlessness, the gesture of granting boons, and the Pināka bow. 43.
Then, divine showers of flowers fell swiftly from the sky; celestial instruments resounded, and the gods danced and sang.
There, Nārada and others, the celestial sages beginning with Sanaka, the world-protectors headed by Indra, and the stainless brahmin-sages arrived. (45)
Seated in their midst together with Umā, Mahādeva showered a stream of compassion upon the king who was bowed in devotion.

With his heart expanded by the joy of that vision, his limbs drenched by a flood of rising tears, his hair standing on end, and his voice faltering with emotion, he offered praise with words while his hands were joined in the gesture of reverence.

The King said: I bow to the Lord, the protectorless, the imperishable, the primordial, whose qualities are unmanifest, the Great One; the causeless cause of all causes, the supreme Śiva, consisting of consciousness and bliss, the perfectly tranquil. 48.

You are the witness of the universe, the creator of this world, whose splendor has grown great and who is seated within the heart; therefore, the wise, having restrained their minds through various yogic practices, investigate You through meditative inquiry. 49.

To those who meditate upon you as a single essence, you are one; yet to those of diverse intellects, you appear in manifold forms. Your state is beyond the senses, a witness to the arising and the delusion of the mind; it is withdrawn from the path of the mind.

How can my speech, O Aṅgiras, be capable of praising your form—which is difficult to attain, which is free from delusion through both word and thought, and which is the nature of the Supreme Self—while I myself am devoted solely to the qualities of nature and dissolved within it? 51.

Nevertheless, let them take refuge in devotion to Your lotus feet, which destroy the suffering of those who bow before You; tormented by the fierce forest fire of saṃsāra, I worship You constantly for the sake of pacifying the fear of worldly existence. (52)
Salutations to you, the God of gods, the Great God, the Source of Bliss; salutations to him whose form is the triple manifestation, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.
Salutations to the one whose form is the universe, the first witness of the universe; salutations to the reality that is pure existence, and to the mass of consciousness and bliss.
Salutations to you, who dwell in all fields, whose self-power is differentiated according to the field; salutations to you, the powerless one, who appears as power and is the most abundant.
To the one who is without appearance, eternal, whose inner self is true knowledge, who is pure, far-reaching, and liberated from all karma; || 56 ||
Salutations to the one known through Vedānta, who dwells at the root of the Vedas; salutations to the one whose conduct is solitary and whose activity regarding the qualities has ceased.
Salutations to the one of auspicious vigor, the bestower of auspicious fruits; salutations to the infinite, the great, the peaceful, whose form is auspiciousness.

Salutations to the non-terrible and the most terrible, who tears asunder the flood of terrible sins; salutations to Bharga, the most venerable destroyer of the seeds of worldly existence; salutations to him who has dispelled delusion and whose self-attributes are pure. (59)
Protect me, O Lord of the worlds; protect me, O eternal Śaṅkara! Protect me, O Rudra, O Virūpākṣa; protect me, O imperishable Conqueror of Death! 60.

O Śambhu, whose crest is adorned with the moon, O you of peaceful form, O Lord of Gaurī, whose eyes are the sun, the moon, and fire; O bearer of the Gaṅgā, destroyer of Andhaka, O you of holy fame, Lord of beings, whose dwelling is upon the mountain—salutations to you always!
Sūta said: Thus praised by the king, the Lord Maheśvara, the ocean of compassion, being pleased along with Pārvatī, replied: 62.

Īśvara said: O King, I am well-pleased with you because of your devotion and your meritorious hymn of praise; for you have always worshipped me with a mind that was never directed toward anything else.
Having become a brahmin for the sake of testing your disposition, I have come here; she who was seized by the tiger is this very daughter of the Lord of Mountains, born of destiny.
I requested your wife from you, that tiger made of illusion whose body remains unhurt by arrows, desiring to test your fortitude. (65)
O giver of honor, because of her [Kīrtimālinī] and because of your devotion, I am pleased; I grant you a boon—choose one that is difficult to obtain.
The king said: "O Lord, this alone is the boon, that you, the Supreme Lord, have become manifest before me who am overwhelmed by the heat of worldly existence. (67)
"O God, best among the givers of boons, I choose no other boon from you: let him be my father, and let her be that queen, my mother. (68)
The Vaiśya named Padmākara and his son named Sunaya—O Mahādeva, always keep all of these by your side.
Sūta said: Then the highly fortunate queen Kīrtimālinī, having bowed down and propitiated Giriśa with devotion, requested an excellent boon.
The queen said: "O Mahādeva, Candrāṅgada is my father and Sīmantinī is my mother; I pray that they may always remain in your presence. (71)
"So be it," said the Lord of Gaurī, who is gracious and affectionate toward his devotees; having granted them their desired boon, he vanished in an instant. (72)
That king also, having obtained the grace of the Wielder of the Trident along with the gods, enjoyed his beloved sense-objects together with Kīrtimālinī.
Having ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years with unimpeded power and prosperity, he entrusted the realm to his sons and attained the supreme state of Śambhu.
The lord of kings Candrāṅgada and Queen Sīmantinī, having worshipped Giriśa with devotion, went to the abode of Śambhu.

This sacred narrative of Śambhu’s qualities, which destroys great sins, is wonderful, supreme, and a profound secret. He who, being self-restrained, recites it or causes wise people to hear it, attains the splendor of enjoyments and goes to Śiva at the end.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of Bhadrāyu’s Attainment of Śiva’s Grace," in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa of the third part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: This majesty of Ṛṣabha, the Śiva-yogin, has been described; now I shall speak of the power of another Śiva-yogin as well.
I shall also describe, in brief, the majesty of the sacred ash (bhasman), by hearing which even sinful people will become fulfilled in their purpose.
There is a certain Śiva-yogi named Vāmadeva, a man of great austerity; he is free from dualities, devoid of qualities, peaceful, unattached, and possessed of equal vision toward all.
Delighting in the self, having conquered anger, and abandoned home and wood; his movements unobserved, observing silence, contented, and free from possessions. || 4 ||
With his entire body smeared with ashes, adorned with a mass of matted hair, clothed in bark and deerskin, he accepted only alms as his possession.
Once, while wandering through the world intent on bestowing grace upon all beings, he entered by chance the most formidable Krauñca forest.
In that desolate forest devoid of people, there dwells a certain most terrifying brahmarākṣasa, who is constantly tormented by hunger and thirst.
Seeing that the very essence of Śiva had entered him, the Brahmarākṣasa, tormented by hunger, rushed at him with speed, desiring to devour him.
Beholding him approaching—with gaping mouth, massive body, fearsome tusks, and terrifying appearance—the Lord of Yogins did not waver.
Then, rushing forward with speed, that terrible forest-dweller seized the unwavering Śiva-yogin, squeezing him with both his arms.
By the mere touch of his limbs, that terrible Brahmarākṣasa was instantly cleansed of his sins; dejected, he regained his memory.
Just as iron attains the state of gold upon touching the *cintāmaṇi* gem, and just as clay attains the state of gold upon reaching the river Jambūnadī; || 12 ||
Just as crows, having approached the Mānasa lake, attain the state of swans; and just as a man, having drunk the nectar even once, may attain divinity. || 13 ||
For in the same way, great souls immediately purify those possessed by sin through their sight, touch, and so forth; therefore, association with the virtuous is indeed difficult to attain.
He who previously, afflicted by hunger and thirst, roamed the forest with a terrible nature, immediately attained satisfaction and became filled with perfect bliss.

Pierced by the particles of white ash clinging to his body, his nature immediately shaken free from the dense darkness of sin, and having regained the memory of his former birth, he—whose purpose was now urgent—bowed at the pair of his lotus feet and spoke.
The Rākṣasa said: Be gracious to me, O Great Yogin; be gracious, O Ocean of Compassion; be gracious to those tormented by worldly existence, O Ocean of the Nectar of Bliss. (17)
Where am I—wicked-minded, terrible, and a source of fear to all living beings—and where is the vision of you, whose nature is compassion and who possesses great majesty? (18)
Lift me up, lift me up, for I have fallen into a terrible ocean of suffering; by your mere presence, great bliss increases. (19)
Vāmadeva said: Who are you, a terrible forest-dweller; what Rākṣasa is stationed here? How did you attain this most dreadful and painful state?
The Rākṣasa said: "In a previous birth, twenty-five [kalpas] ago, I was a powerful Rākṣasa named Durjaya, the protector of the Yavana kingdom."
Such am I—evil-minded, most sinful, acting according to my own whims, intoxicated with pride, a wielder of the rod of punishment, of wicked conduct, fierce, merciless, and base.
Though young, possessed of many wives, addicted to desire, and having my senses unsubdued, I have once again fallen into this most sinful conduct. (23)
Always intent on enjoying a different woman every day, women were brought from all lands by my servants at my command.
Day after day, having enjoyed one woman and then abandoned her, they kept her within their inner apartments and took up other women once more.

Thus, having brought women from my own kingdom and from foreign lands—from countries, mines, villages, cities, and settlements—I have enjoyed them day after day; yet once I have enjoyed a certain woman, she is never enjoyed by me again.
Furthermore, those women whom I have enjoyed are not enjoyed by others; confined within the inner apartments, they grieve day and night. (27)
When the women of the Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Śūdras were abducted by me, the Brahmins residing in my kingdom fled along with their wives. || 28 ||
Women with husbands, maidens, widows, and those in their courses—having brought them here, I took pleasure with these women, my soul overcome by lust. (29)
There were three hundred wives of the twice-born, four hundred wives of kings, six hundred wives of Vaiśyas, and one thousand wives of Śūdras.
A hundred Caṇḍāla women, a thousand Pulinda women, five hundred Śailūṣī women, and four hundred washerwomen [were swallowed]. (31)
Countless chief courtesans have been enjoyed by me, that evil-souled one; nevertheless, no satiety regarding desire arose within me. (32)
Thus, though he was in the prime of youth, great diseases such as consumption and others entered him, for he was addicted to evil objects, intoxicated, and constantly devoted to drink.
Afflicted by disease, childless, and tormented by enemies, abandoned by both ministers and servants, I died through my own past actions. (34)
The life of a man devoid of dharma is surely destroyed, his infamy increases, his fortune perishes, and he falls into a miserable state; even his ancient ancestors fall from heaven. (35)
Then I was led by the servants of Yama to the abode of Vaivasvata; thereupon, I was cast into that terrible pit in hell.
There, in a terrible hell, for thirty thousand years, I dwelt, being tormented by the servants of Yama while forced to drink semen.
Then, due to the remainder of his sin, he was born as a Piśāca in a desolate forest with a thousand penises, constantly tormented by hunger and thirst.
Having resorted to the state of a Piśāca, a divine hundred autumns were spent; in my second birth here, I was born as a tiger, a source of terror to living beings. (39)
In the third [birth] I was a terrible python; in the fourth birth I was a wolf; in the fifth I was a village pig, and in the sixth I was a chameleon.
In my seventh birth I was a dog, and in the eighth I was a jackal; in the ninth I was a fearsome gavaya, and in the tenth birth I was a deer.
In the eleventh birth I was a monkey, and in the twelfth I was a vulture; in the thirteenth I was a mongoose, and in the fourteenth a crow. (42)
In the fifteenth [birth] I was a bear, in the sixteenth a wild cock; in the seventeenth I was a donkey, and in the eighteenth birth I was a cat. (43)
In the nineteenth [birth] I was a frog; in the twentieth I became a tortoise; in the twenty-first I was a fish; and in the twenty-second I became a mouse. (44)
In the twenty-third birth I was an owl, in the twenty-fourth a forest elephant, and in this twenty-fifth birth I have been born as a Brahmarākṣasa.

Overcome by hunger and deprived of food, I dwell here in this great forest; seeing you arrive now, I am eager to devour you. Yet, by the mere touch of your body, the memory of my former birth has arisen. (46)
Today, in your presence, I remember thousands of past births; supreme world-weariness has arisen within me, and my heart has become serene. (47)
O high-minded one, how was such power as this obtained by you? Was it through intense austerity, or perhaps from frequenting sacred fords? (48)
Tell me the truth, O Blessed One, whether through yoga, divine power, or mantras of infinite potency; I have come to you for refuge. (49)
Vāmadeva said: This is the great power of the ash clinging to my body, that through contact with it, this supreme understanding has arisen in you who were enveloped in darkness.
Who else besides Mahādeva knows the power of the ashes? Just as the majesty of Śambhu is difficult to conceive, so too is that of the ashes. (51)
Formerly, there was a certain Brahmin like you who was devoid of dharma; staying among the Dravidas, that fool attained the status of a Śūdra through his own actions. || 52 ||
A man of thieving habits, deceitful, and excessively lustful for a low-caste woman, once became a paramour and was killed at night by a Śūdra. (53)
When that corpse, having been cast outside the village for the funeral rites, was left there, a dog with ashes on its feet wandered by chance over its body.
Then the servants of Śiva forcibly took him away from the servants of Yama, having placed him upon a celestial chariot, as he had fallen into that terrible hell.
Approaching the messengers of Śiva, Yama also questioned them: "How do you intend to lead this man, who is a perpetrator of great sins?"
Then those messengers of Śiva said: "Behold his corpse-like body; its chest, forehead, and armpits are marked with excellent sacred ash."
Therefore, we have come here by the command of Śiva to bring him back; you are not able to stop us—let there be no doubt in you regarding this. || 58 ||
Having thus addressed Yama, the messengers of Śambhu then led that Brāhmaṇa to the world free from ailment, while all the worlds looked on. (59)
Therefore, the ash that is the ornament of Śambhu is the supreme and immediate purifier of all sins without exception; it is worn by me constantly. (60)
Having thus heard the greatness of the sacred ash, the Brahmarākṣasa spoke out of intense longing to hear it again in detail.
Excellent, excellent, O great yogin! I am blessed by the sight of you. O righteous-souled one, deliver me from this terrible and base birth.
"It appears to me that some merit was performed by me in the past; therefore, O best of the twice-born, I am liberated today through your grace. (63)
In that birth as a king, I gave land endowed with crops and gardens to a certain devotee of Śiva for his livelihood. (99)
At that very moment, Yama also said: "In your twenty-fifth birth, through the company of a certain yogi, you shall be liberated from saṃsāra."
That merit which was acquired in previous lives has now borne fruit; therefore, in this forest devoid of human beings, I have obtained union with you.
Therefore, O ocean of compassion, deliver me, who am wandering through terrible births due to my horrific sins, by granting me the sacred ash along with its mantra. (67)
How is this ash to be worn? What is the mantra? What is the auspicious procedure? What is the proper time and what is the proper place? O Guru, tell me all of this.
Great-souled beings such as you are always devoted to the welfare of the world; like wish-fulfilling trees, they do not desire their own benefit.
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by that terrible forest-dweller, the lord of yogis, the knower of reality, again described the greatness of the sacred ash.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Sacred Ashes," in the Brahmottara Section of the third part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Listen, O best of sages, to the speech of Vāmadeva.
Vāmadeva said: Formerly, on Mandara, the lord of mountains, variegated with various minerals, teeming with diverse creatures, and crowded with many trees and creepers—(2).
Once, the Lord Kālāgnirudra, the Supreme Ruler and Master of Beings, who is adored by the entire universe, arrived there of his own free will.
Hundreds of millions of Rudras stood surrounding him from all sides; seated in their midst was the three-eyed God of gods.
There arrived Purandara, the best of the gods, together with the deities; likewise Agni, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
The Gandharvas, headed by Citrasena; the sky-dwellers, such as the Pannagas; the Vidyādharas, Kimpuruṣas, Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Guhyakas.
The Brahman-sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha, the celestial sages beginning with Nārada, the high-souled ancestors, and the lords of progeny beginning with Dakṣa; || 7 ||
The Apsarases, beginning with Urvaśī; the Mothers, beginning with Caṇḍikā; the Ādityas, the Vasus, the two Dasras, and the Viśvedevas of great power.
Then there were other lords of beings capable of destroying the world: Mahākāla, Nandin, and likewise Śaṅkhapālaka.
Vīrabhadra of great splendor, Śaṅkukarṇa of great strength, the invincible Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Maṇibhadra, and Vṛkodara. || 10 ||
And Kuṇḍodara, as well as Vikaṭa and the powerful Kubhodara; Mandodara, Karṇadhāra, Ketur, and likewise Bhṛṅgiriṭi.
The lords of spirits, as well as others of massive bodies and great majesty—some black in color, some white, and some with the luster of frogs. || 12 ||
Green, grey, smoky, variegated, yellowish-red, with diverse colors and wonderful limbs, they were playful and fierce with intoxication. || 13 ||
With various weapons raised in their hands and adorned with diverse mounts and ornaments, some had the faces of tigers, some the faces of boars, and others the faces of various deer.
Some had the faces of crocodiles, others the faces of dogs; some had the faces of jackals, and others the faces of camels.
Some had the faces of deer, jackals, lions, horses, camels, and cranes; they were single-faced, two-faced, three-faced, or even faceless. || 16 ||
Some had one hand, some three hands, and some five hands; some were handless, some were footless, some had many feet, and some had many ears or only a single ear. (17)
Some with one eye, some with four eyes, some tall and some dwarfish, they attend upon the Lord, the Master of Beings, surrounding him on all sides.
Then the highly effulgent, wise, and righteous Sanatkumāra, the foremost among sages, arrived to behold that Lord of the Universe.

To that God of gods, the Lord of the Universe, whose radiance is equal to ten million suns, and whose deep roar is like the tumultuous sound of the seven oceans at the time of the great dissolution; (20)
Resembling the swelling of the fire of universal destruction, adorned with a circle of matted locks, possessing an unblinking eye in his forehead, and with the luster of his face faded by flames.
He was adorned with the blazing crest-jewel Śaśikhaṇḍa; Takṣaka was on his left ear and Vāsuki on his right.
Wearing a pair of earrings with great blue-gemset jaws, having a blue neck and mighty arms, he was resplendent with a necklace of serpents.
He wore bracelets, armlets, and finger-rings shining with the king of serpents, and his girdle was adorned with thousands of jewels possessing infinite qualities.
Clad in a tiger skin and adorned with bells and mirrors, [he is encircled] by Karkoṭaka, Mahāpadma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Dhanañjaya.
He was resplendent with lotus-like feet echoing with the tinkling of anklets, and he bore a spear, a tomara-weapon, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a trident, a ṭaṅka-axe, and a bow.
The great sage bowed down to the Lord, who is invincible, indefinable, and of inconceivable form, seated upon a lion-throne of jewels.

With his inner self swelling with the weight of devotion, he praised Him with words consistent with the Vedas; then, with palms joined in reverence and his neck bowed in humility, he inquired about all the dharmas that bestow auspiciousness.
The Blessed Lord Rudra explained those various dharmas in their entirety to which the sage had inquired; the sage questioned him further once more.

Sanatkumāra said: "O Blessed One, you have heard from your own lips these dharmas which are the cause of liberation; by means of them, men, freed from sin, shall cross the ocean of worldly existence. (30)
Furthermore, O Lord, out of compassion, tell me another teaching that requires little effort yet yields great fruit, which grants immediate liberation to human beings. (31)
The thousands of teachings seen in the scriptures, when practiced with great assiduity, may or may not grant success in due time if they are not properly cultivated.
Therefore, O Maheśvara, through your grace, I wish to understand the Dharma—the secret benefit for the world and the means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (33)
Śrī Rudra said: Of all religious duties, the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), which is enjoined by the Vedas, is the most excellent; it is a secret for all living beings. (34)
Sanatkumāra said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the worlds, tell me the rule for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra); O Maheśvara, I desire to know it in its true essence through your grace. (35)
How many locations are there? What is the substance? What is the power? And who is the deity? What is the measure? Who is the agent? What are his mantras? And what is the fruit? || 36 ||
O Lord of the worlds, out of a desire to favor the world, tell me in its entirety and without omission all these characteristics of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Śrī Rudra said: O great sage, the ash produced from burnt cow dung is called *āgneya*; that very substance is declared to be the material for the *tripuṇḍra*. (38)
Having taken up [the ashes] with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*, one should consecrate the ashes with the mantras beginning with *agniriti*. (39)

Having cleansed himself with the mantra "Mānastoke," he should smear his head with ashes while reciting the "Tryambaka" mantra; then, with the "Triyāyuṣa" and other mantras, he should apply the water-activated ashes, consecrated by mantras, to his forehead, both arms, and his shoulder.
O bull among sages, three lines appear in these places, beginning from the middle of the eyebrows and extending as far as the ends of the eyebrows.
A line made with the thumb between the middle and ring fingers, drawn in reverse order, is called the *tripuṇḍra*.
For each of the three lines, there are nine deities: the letter *A*, the Gārhapatya fire, the Ṛgveda, the Earth (*bhūrloka*), and likewise Rajas. (43)
The Self, the power of action, and the morning libation (prātaḥsavana) are the deities of the first line of Mahādeva.

The letter *U* is the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, the sky, the quality of *sattva*, and likewise the Yajurveda; it is also the midday libation (*madhyandina-savana*), the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), and the inner self (*antarātman*). (45)
Maheśvara is the deity of the line and the second [vowel]; he is the letter 'ma', the Āhavanīya fire, the Supreme Self, darkness, and heaven. (46)
The power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), the Sāmaveda, the third libation (tṛtīyasavana), and Śiva are the presiding deities of the third line.
Having constantly paid homage to these [deities], the wise man should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra); this is the vow of Maheśvara, celebrated in all the Vedas. (48)
It should be practiced by men desiring liberation, for there is no rebirth for them; he who applies the triple mark with ashes according to the prescribed rule, [attains this]. (49)
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or even an ascetic, he is liberated from the multitude of great sins as well as the minor offenses.
Likewise, one is liberated from other sins such as the killing of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a woman, or a cow, as well as from the killing of a hero or a horse; of this there is no doubt. (51)
Even one who applies the Tripuṇḍra on the surface of the forehead without knowing its greatness or without using a mantra is liberated from all sins. || 52 ||
The seizing of another's property, the violation of another's wife, censuring others, seizing another's field, and causing pain to others; || 53 ||

Stealing crops, gardens, and the like; acts such as setting fire to houses; speaking untruths, backbiting, harsh speech, and selling the Vedas; giving false testimony, abandoning one's vows, gambling, and serving the base. (54)
The acceptance of cows, land, gold, buffaloes, sesame seeds, blankets, garments, food, grain, water, and so forth from low-born persons [is forbidden]. (55)
He has sexual union with female slaves, courtesans, paramours, low-caste women, actresses, as well as with menstruating girls, virgins, and widows. (56)
The sale of meat, hides, juices, salt, and so forth—these and various other such sins are innumerable. (57)
They perish instantly by the wearing of the Tripuṇḍra; likewise, the misappropriation of Śiva’s property and the occasional disparagement of Śiva [are likewise destroyed]. || 58 ||
The censure of Śiva’s devotees is not purified even by penances; yet he upon whose limbs are Rudrākṣas and on whose forehead is the Tripuṇḍra— [is purified]. (59)
Even that Cāṇḍāla is worthy of worship and shall become the highest among all castes; for whatever holy places exist in this world, and whatever rivers there are, such as the Gaṅgā— [60]
He who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on his forehead is considered as having bathed everywhere; [he possesses] the seven crores of great mantras, preceded by the five-syllabled mantra.
Likewise, there are other millions of Śaiva mantras that are the causes of liberation; all of these are as if recited by him who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
He who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) shall uplift a thousand ancestors and a thousand descendants born of his own lineage among mortals.
Having enjoyed all pleasures here, long-lived and free from disease, he meets his death with ease at the end of his life.
Having attained a divine and auspicious body endowed with the eight qualities of sovereignty, he ascends a celestial chariot attended by hundreds of divine women.
And likewise, in the worlds of the Vidyādharas, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas of great luster, and the world-protectors beginning with Indra, in due order.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures in the cities of the lords of subjects, he shall reach the station of Brahmā and rejoice there for a hundred kalpas.
And he rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as three hundred Brahmās.
Then, having reached the world of Śiva, he rejoices for imperishable time; he attains union with Śiva and is not born again. || 69 ||
Having repeatedly reflected upon the essence of all the Upaniṣads, this alone has been determined as the supreme good: the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka).
This majesty of the Tripuṇḍra has been recounted by me in brief; it is a secret of all beings and must be kept hidden by you.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Rudra vanished right there; and the sage Sanatkumāra also went to the abode of Brahmā.
Even for you, a pure intellect has arisen through contact with the ashes; you too, with faith, should wear the meritorious triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, Vāmadeva, the yogi of Śiva and one of great austerity, consecrated with mantras and gave the sacred ash to the terrible Brahma-rākṣasa.
With that, he drew a horizontal triple-mark (tripuṇḍra) on the surface of his forehead; by its power, he immediately abandoned his state as a Brahma-rākṣasa.
He shone like the sun, adorned with a circle of splendor, resplendent with divine limbs and forms, and radiant in celestial garlands and garments.
Having circumambulated that preceptor, the Śiva-yogin, with devotion, he ascended a divine celestial chariot and departed for the worlds of merit.
The great yogi Vāmadeva, having granted him the supreme goal, wandered through the world as one whose soul was deluded, appearing like Śiva himself in person.
The man who hears this greatness of the sacred ash and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), or causes it to be heard, or even reads it, indeed attains the supreme goal. || 79 ||

He proclaims the fame of Śiva as the cause of liberation from saṃsāra; he bows to the lotus-feet of the Lord, which are meditated upon by the yogis of Śiva; and he applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on his forehead, shining with devotion to Śiva—he shall never again experience dwelling in a mother’s womb in this world.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Sacred Ashes," in the Brahmottara Section of the third part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

The sages said: For those men who have received instruction from gurus who are knowers of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas) and who discourse upon Brahman, success indeed arises immediately.
Furthermore, what kind of success is achieved by men who have received instructions from gurus who are experts in ethics yet are common to other people? (2)
Sūta said: Faith alone is exceedingly beneficial for all dharma; through faith alone does the perfection of men arise in both worlds.
For a person who worships with faith, even a stone yields fruit; even a fool, when honored with devotion, becomes a guru who bestows spiritual perfection.
A mantra recited with faith yields fruit even if it is uncomposed; a deity worshipped with faith yields fruit even for one of low birth. (6)
Worship, charity, sacrifice, austerity, and vows performed without faith all go to fruitlessness, like a flower on a barren tree.
Pervaded by doubt in all things, devoid of faith, and exceedingly fickle, he falls away from the supreme goal and is not liberated from the cycle of worldly existence.
In a mantra, a sacred ford, a twice-born, a deity, an astrologer, a medicine, and a guru—whatever one's conviction is in these, such will be the success attained.
Therefore, the universe consists of mental states, and merit and demerit arise from such states; for one devoid of mental states, neither of these two can ever exist.
In this regard, this most wonderful narrative is described, by which the lack of faith of all mortals is instantly dispelled.
The King of the Pañcālas had a son known as Siṃhaketu, who was endowed with all virtues and always devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya. || 11 ||
Once, that mighty one, accompanied by a few servants, went for the sake of hunting to a forest filled with many creatures.
A certain Śabara, his servant, while wandering in the forest on a hunt, saw a dilapidated, cracked, and fallen temple.
There he saw a straight, subtle Śiva-liṅga, its pedestal broken and fallen upon the bare ground, appearing like his own personified good fortune.
Taking it up with speed, impelled by his past karma, he showed it to that wise prince.
"Behold this beautiful Liṅga, O Lord, which has been seen by me here; I shall worship it with devotion according to my means. (16)
Tell me the procedure for his worship, so that the god Maheśvara may be pleased when worshipped by both those who do not know the mantras and those who do. || 17 ||
Thus questioned by that Niṣāda, the son of the king, who was skilled in jesting, laughed and replied to him.

One should always perform the consecration with fresh water while maintaining right resolve. Having seated [the deity] on a pure seat, one should worship with auspicious, fresh perfumes and unbroken grains (akṣata), as well as with wild leaves, flowers, incense, and lamps. (19)
One should first offer an oblation of funeral pyre ashes; the wise one should prepare the food offering with food intended for his own consumption.
Furthermore, one should arrange offerings such as incense and lamps; one should duly provide dances, instrumental music, songs, and so forth. || 21 ||
Having paid homage according to the prescribed rule, the wise man should maintain his composure; this general procedure for the worship of Śiva has been declared to you.
Śaṅkara is instantly gratified by an offering of funeral pyre ashes.
Sūta said: Thus instructed by his master with a spirit of playful jest, that Śabara named Caṇḍaka received those words upon his head.
Then, having reached his own abode, he worshipped Maheśvara in the form of a *liṅga* every day, offering funeral ashes as his oblation.
Whatever object was dear to himself—such as perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth—he would first offer it constantly to Śambhu and only thereafter use it himself.
Thus, with devotion, the Śabara worshipped Maheśvara together with his wife; having attained happiness, he spent several years there.
Once, when the best of Śabaras set out to worship Śiva, he did not see even a tiny bit of funeral-ground ash remaining in his vessel.
Then, searching far and wandering about in haste, he did not find the ashes of the funeral pyre; exhausted, he returned home once more.
Then, having summoned his wife, the Śabara spoke these words: "I have not obtained the ashes of the funeral pyre; tell me, my dear, what shall I do? (30)
"Alas, an obstacle to my worship of Śiva has arisen today due to my sin; without performing worship, I cannot endure to live for even a moment. (31)
I see no other means here when the requisites for worship have been destroyed; nor would the teaching of the Guru, which bestows all goals, be impaired. (32)
Seeing her husband thus distressed, the Śabara woman replied: "Do not fear; I shall tell you a remedy."
Having burned down this very house, which has been maintained for a long time, I shall enter the fire; thereafter, let there be only the ashes of the funeral pyre.
Śabara said: "The body is the supreme means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; why do you abandon that body, which is in the prime of youth, for the sake of [mere] pleasure? (35)
Now, being childless and having not yet tasted the essence of the objects of the senses, why do you wish to burn this body which is fit for enjoyment? (36)
Śabarī said: "The fulfillment of life and birth consists in this alone: that one should sacrifice one's life for the sake of another; how much more so, then, for the sake of Śiva himself? (37)
What terrible austerity was performed, or what gift was given by me in the past? Or what worship of Śambhu was performed during the interval of hundreds of previous births? (38)
What merit shall accrue to my father, or what fulfillment of purpose for my mother, that I cast off this body into the kindled fire for the sake of Śiva? (39)
Having thus observed her firm resolve and her devotion to Śaṅkara, the Śabara, his own determination being likewise firm, honored her in return, saying, "So be it. (40)
Having reached her husband, she bathed, became pure, and adorned herself; then, having set fire to the house, she circumambulated that flame with devotion.
Having paid homage to her own guru and meditated upon Sadāśiva in her heart, she, facing toward the entry into the fire with palms joined in reverence, spoke this: ||| 42 ||

Śabarī said: O Lord, let my senses be your flowers; let this body be your aguru incense, and this heart be your lamp. Let my vital breaths be the oblations and my faculties be your unbroken grains (akṣata); may this very life now attain the fruit of worship.

I do not desire even the sovereignty over all wealth, nor the eternal realm of heaven, nor the station of the Creator; rather, may I, in birth after birth, become a female bee sipping the shimmering nectar from the lotus-feet of You.

O Lord, may I have more than a hundred births; let not delusion, the cause of ignorance, enter my mind. O Lord, may my heart never depart from Your lotus feet for even half a moment; salutations, salutations unto You! 45.
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods, Śabarī, firm in her resolve, entered the blazing fire and was reduced to ashes in an instant.
And that Śabara, having carefully taken up those ashes, performed the worship of Śiva with a concentrated mind near his burnt-out house.
Then, at the conclusion of the worship, he remembered his beloved wife—who was always arriving with palms joined in reverence and full of humility—as she was accustomed to receiving his favor.
As soon as she was remembered, he then beheld her arrived and standing behind him, with her upper body alone visible, bowing with devotion and possessing a pure smile.
Seeing his wife standing as before with palms joined in reverence, and seeing the house reduced to ashes yet standing as it was before, the Śabara [was amazed].
Fire burns with its flames, the sun burns with its rays; the king burns with his rod of punishment, but the Brahmin should burn with his mind alone.
"Is this a dream, or is it an illusion consisting of delusion?"—thus, agitated by wonder, he questioned her further. (52)
Moreover, how did you come to be reduced to ashes in the fire, and how was the burnt palace restored once more to its former state? (53)
Śabarī said: When I entered the fire after setting my house ablaze, at that moment I was not conscious of myself, nor did I see the fire.
Not even a trace of heat remained for me, as if I had entered into water; like one who has slept soundly, I was awakened again in half a moment. (55)
Until now, we have seen this palace as if it were unburnt and well-established; now, at the conclusion of the worship of the deity, we have come to receive your grace.
While the couple was thus conversing with mutual affection, a divine and wonderful celestial chariot appeared before them.

In that celestial chariot, radiant as a hundred moons, four attendants of Īśa, acting as precursors, took the Niṣāda couple by the hand and placed them upon it while they were still clad in their battle attire.
At that very moment, by the touch of the hand of Śiva’s messenger, the bodies of that Niṣāda couple attained a form identical to his.
Therefore, faith alone must be cultivated in all meritorious deeds; even a lowly Śabara attained the state of the yogins through faith.

What is the use of birth as the most excellent among all castes, or what is the use of learning that encompasses the investigation of all scriptures, if one possesses constant devotion to the Supreme Lord in one’s heart? Who else in the three worlds is more blessed than such a person? (61)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Sacred Ashes," in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa of the third part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Now I shall fully describe the vow named Umāmaheśvara, the most excellent among all dharmas, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
There was a certain twice-born man born in Ānarta named Vedaratha, who was learned, born of a noble lineage, and endowed with a wife and sons.
While that brahmin was living thus in the householder stage of life, a lotus-eyed daughter named Śāradā was born to him.
That twice-born man, whose wife had died, requested that twelve-year-old girl, who was endowed with beautiful form and auspicious marks, from the one named Padmanābha.
Out of fear of rejecting his request, the father gave that daughter to him, who was immensely wealthy, tranquil, and always a friend of the king.
Having performed the wedding at midday, that brahmin went to the shore of a lake in his father-in-law's house to perform the evening twilight devotions.
Having performed his twilight devotions according to the rules, he was returning when he was bitten by a serpent on a path shrouded in darkness and died due to his own past karma.
When he had died after the marriage had been performed, his kinsmen, tormented by grief, cried out, as did his father-in-law and his mother-in-law. || 8 ||
Having carried her away, those kinsmen went each to their own home; Śāradā, having attained widowhood, remained in her father’s very abode.
Deprived of her husband who provided her with food and clothing, that young woman spent several months in her father’s house.
Once, a certain very elderly sage named Naidhruva, who was blind and held the hand of his disciple, arrived at his palace.
When that old man had arrived at the house and his kinsmen had gone elsewhere, that young woman approached him as if he were her own manifest destiny.
Welcome to you, O highly fortunate one; please be seated upon this seat. Salutations to you, the Lord of Sages; what pleasing service may I perform for you?
Having spoken thus, and having established devotion, he washed the sage's feet; then, fanning the weary sage, he completely satisfied him.
Having seated the weary sage upon a seat and having massaged him with his own hands, he performed the ritual bath for him and conducted the worship of the deity according to the rules.
Having honored him, who was seated on a comfortable seat, with incense, garlands, and ointments, he respectfully fed him with excellent food.
Having eaten properly and slowly, being fully satisfied and overflowing with joy, the blind sage, well-pleased, bestowed a supreme blessing upon her.

Having lived together with that husband and having swiftly obtained a son most excellent in all virtues, and having attained great fame in the world, may you become worthy of the grace of the gods. (18)
Having heard these words spoken by that sage whose sight had departed, the young woman was struck with wonder and replied with palms joined in reverence.
O Brahman, your word is true and can never be false; yet how shall this bear fruit for one so unfortunate as I? (20)
Just as a good rain on a stone slab, or a hospitable reception for a dog, even the blessing of those who know Brahman is fruitless upon one of meager fortune.
O Brahmin, here I am, a widow who partakes in the fruits of evil deeds; how shall I become worthy of this benediction of yours? (22)
The sage said: "O auspicious one, whatever I have just spoken even in my ignorance because I did not recognize you, I shall now fulfill that; carry out my command."
If you shall observe the vow named Umāmaheśvara, by the power of that vow you will immediately experience spiritual welfare.
Śāradā said: "I shall practice with effort even that which is difficult to perform as instructed by you. O Brāhmaṇa, tell me that vow; explain its procedure in detail. (25)
The Sage said: In the month of Caitra or Mārgaśīrṣa, on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, one should duly commence the vow with the permission of the preceptor.
On the eighth and the fourteenth days of both fortnights, having performed the formal ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the rules, one should perform the morning bath.
Having gratified the ancestors, the gods, and others, and having returned to his own abode, he should construct a divine pavilion adorned with canopies and other ornaments.
Adorned with fruits, sprouts, flowers, and the like, as well as archways, one should draw a lotus in its center using powders of five colors.
On the outside with fourteen petals, within that with twenty-two; within that with sixteen, and within that with eight.
Having thus removed the lotus, one should then construct a beautiful square with five colors, within which there is an excellent circle.
And having placed a heap of rice grains with its husks in the middle of that [area], one should firmly establish a water-filled jar upon a *kūrca* mat.

Having placed a cloth of appropriate color upon the water-pot (kalaśa), and having set down two auspicious golden images of Śiva and Śivā upon it, one should worship them with devotion according to the extent of one's means.
Having bathed [the image] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) as well as pure water, one should recite the eleven Rudra mantras and eight hundred repetitions of the five-syllabled mantra.

Having consecrated it with mantras and established it again, he should likewise worship the pedestal in the center; the wise one himself, having purified his seat and wearing washed white garments, should sit there.
Having addressed the seat with the mantra, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma); there, with palms joined in reverence (añjali) before Śiva, one should utter the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
For the complete destruction of whatever terrible sins I have committed throughout hundreds of previous births, I commence this worship of Śiva.
For the increase of good fortune, victory, health, merit, and sovereignty, and for the attainment of heaven and liberation, I shall perform the worship of Śiva.
Having thus uttered this resolve, being perfectly composed as prescribed, he should then perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and meditate upon the Lord and Pārvatī.
Having a form as white as a jasmine flower or the moon, adorned with serpent ornaments, and bearing in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as an axe and a deer.
Resembling ten million suns, he is the cause of joy for the world; through contact with the waters of the Gaṅgā, he bears long, tawny matted locks.
Adorned with a great crown arising from the hoods of the lord of serpents, he was decorated with a tiara and armlets shining with fragments of the moon.
With his forehead-eye blossoming, likewise with the sun and moon as his eyes, blue-throated, four-armed, and clothed in the skin of a lordly elephant.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with ornaments of serpents, and [beholding] the Goddess, clothed in divine garments, possessing the splendor of ten thousand rising suns. || 44 ||

She has the form of a young girl, with slender limbs, and bears the young moon as her crest; she possesses four arms, holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
[He beheld] his mother, whose face was bright with grace, who sported in the essence of divine play, [surrounded] by radiant kurabaka, aśoka, punnāga, and fresh campaka flowers.
She had fashioned an ear-ornament [from a flower] whose filaments were curled like blossoming jasmine; she was graced by the full expanse of her hips, upon which a girdle of many strings was cast.
Her two feet were adorned with anklets and rows of magnificent small bells, and she was beautified by jeweled earrings resting against the curves of her cheeks.
Her lips were red like the bimba fruit, her budding teeth shone brightly, and she was resplendent with a neck-ornament of precious gems and a pearl necklace.
She wore beautiful bracelets, armlets, and rings made of nine kinds of rubies; she was clothed in red garments and adorned with garlands and ointments of jewels.
Her pair of uplifted, full breasts surpasses the lotus buds; her dark outer corners of the eyes are tremulous with playfulness; she is the bestower of grace upon her devotees.

Having thus meditated upon Śiva and Śivā, the parents of the universe, within the lotus of the heart, and having recited the mantra consisting of their essence, one should then worship them externally at the conclusion.
Having invoked [the deities] into the pair of images, the knower of mantras should provide the seat and other offerings, and present the *arghya* to Śiva and Śivā with this mantra: (53)
Salutations to you, O Lord of Pārvatī, O preeminent bestower of boons upon the three worlds! O Tryambakeśa, O Mahādeva, accept this arghya; salutations be unto you.

Salutations to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods, who removes the fear of those who have sought refuge; O Mother, O bestower of boons, O Goddess beloved of Śiva, accept this water offering (arghya).
Having recited this three times, one should offer the arghya with a concentrated mind; one should properly present perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, incense, and lamps.
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) consisting of milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee; one should perform the oblation (homa) one hundred and eight times with the root mantra.

Then, having offered the food-oblation (naivedya) and performed the incense, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and so forth, and having presented betel-leaf (tāmbūla), one should offer salutation with a concentrated mind.
Then, having honored them with ritual services, one should feed a Brahmin couple.
Having thus performed the evening worship and being approved by the Brahmins, he should eat at night with speech restrained, consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya) prepared with milk.
In this manner, a wise person should observe the vow during both fortnights for one year; then, when the year is complete, he should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the vow.
One should bathe the image with waters consecrated by the recitation of the Śatarudra, having worshipped Girijā and Śiva with the mantra prescribed in the Āgama.

Having given to the great preceptor, who is devoted to virtuous conduct, a water-pot accompanied by cloth and gold, one should feed the Brahmins with devotion, having honored them according to one's capacity. (63)

And one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of cows, gold, garments, and so forth; then, permitted by them, one may enjoy [the feast] together with one's beloved people and kinsmen.
Thus, he who performs this vow, renowned throughout the three worlds, with devotion, uplifts twenty-one generations of his family and, having enjoyed all desired pleasures, [attains liberation].
He dwells eternally in the abodes of the world-protectors, Indra and the others; he rejoices in the world of Brahmā and in the eternal world of Viṣṇu.
Then, having reached the world of Śiva and enjoyed vast pleasures there for a hundred kalpas, he attains Śiva himself once again.
This has been declared as the Great Vow; you too should practice it with faith, and you shall attain even that desire which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Thus instructed by the Lord of Sages, that young woman was exceedingly delighted; full of confidence, she accepted his most enchanting words. (69)
Then her father, mother, and brothers arrived; they saw that sage seated comfortably, having finished his meal.
Having arrived suddenly, they all paid homage to the Great-Souled One; uttering "Be gracious to us! Be gracious!", they worshipped him on every side.
And having heard that the supreme sage had been honored by that virtuous woman, and having heard of his benevolent disposition toward her, they attained the highest joy.
With palms joined in reverence, they all spoke to that bull among sages.
Today we are all blessed simply by your arrival; our entire lineage has been purified and this house has been made fruitful. (74)
And this maiden named Śāradā has fallen into widowhood due to some exceedingly insurmountable force of karma. (75)
This very Satī has today sought refuge at your lotus feet; rescue her from this unbearable and most terrible ocean of suffering.
"You too must remain right here near our house, in this monastery of ours which is well-suited for bathing, worship, and recitation. (77)
O Blessed One, O Great Sage, although she is but a child, while performing the worship of your feet, she shall observe her vow in your very presence.
O Guru, let us dwell right here until her vow reaches its completion in your presence; during that time, make us successful in our purpose.
Thus entreated by all her brothers and kinsmen, that best of sages agreed, saying "So be it," and dwelt there in that auspicious monastery.
Following that path instructed by him, the pure and virtuous woman worshipped Girijā and Śiva and duly observed her vow.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Performance of the Umā-Maheśvara Vow," in the third section, the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Thus, as she was performing that great vow in the presence of her guru, a year passed for her, whose mind was intent upon her religious observances.
At the end of the year, that young woman properly performed the concluding rite (udyāpana) right there in her father's house, preceded by the feeding of Brahmins.
Having given a sacrificial fee to those brahmins according to their merit, and having dismissed them after paying homage, she was congratulated by her parents.
Having fasted herself on that day and observed the prescribed restraints, she recited the supreme mantra imparted by the Great-souled One.
Then, when the time of dusk had arrived, having worshipped Śaṅkara in that small hermitage near the house in the presence of that preceptor, [he remained there]. || 5 ||
Devoted to the recitation of mantras and worship, that virtuous woman meditated upon the Supreme Lord; during that night vigil, she remained seated near Śiva.
During that night, together with her, the sage gratified Pārvatī, the Mother of the World, through recitation, meditation, and ascetic penance. (7)

And by her devotion, purified by her vows, and by the sage’s asceticism, yoga, and meditative absorption, Bhavānī—the sole mother of the world—was pleased and appeared, manifesting her dense, solid form.
When Gaurī, who is identical with the universe, appeared before them, even the blind sage instantly regained his two eyes at that very moment.
Beholding that Mother of the Worlds, who had appeared and stood before them, both the sage and the maiden fell at her feet.

With their pure hearts swelling with devotion and their entire bodies drenched in tears of joy, the two were raised up by the Goddess; overflowing with compassion, she who speaks with soft and charming words addressed them with love. (11)
The Goddess said: "I am pleased with you, O best of sages; I am pleased with you, O sinless child. What desired boon shall I grant you, even if it be difficult for the gods to obtain?"
The sage said: "This maiden, named Śāradā, is indeed widowed; and when my vision had departed, I, being pleased, made a promise to her."
"After you have sported with your husband for a long time, may you obtain an excellent son"—this was said by me; make it true, salutations be unto you! (14)
The illustrious Goddess said: "In a previous birth, this young woman was the second beloved wife of a Dravidian twice-born man, renowned by the name Bhāminī. (15)

Always beloved by her husband and charming with the sweetness of her beauty, she brought her husband under her control through the artifice of "subduing him by means of her form" and other such wiles. (16)
With his heart attached to her and constrained by delusion, that brahmin never once went to his eldest wife, who was devoted to her husband.
Because her husband did not return, that woman, deprived of sons and constantly tormented by grief, met her death in the course of time.
A certain young Brahmin living near her house, seeing this woman of beautiful limbs, was overcome by desire and took her hand.
But that brahmin was restrained by her, whose eyes were copper-red with rage; and remembering her day and night, he met his death.
Having deluded her husband and caused him to turn away from his eldest wife, she became a widow in this very life because of that sin.
Those women in the world who cause discord between husband and wife shall suffer widowhood from their maidenhood for twenty-one births.
Because she performed such great worship of me in her previous birth, by that merit all of her sin was indeed destroyed at that very moment. (23)
That brahmin who, being afflicted by passion and deluded by desire, died while she was still alive, has met his end in this very birth after having taken her hand in marriage. (24)
The husband of this woman in her previous birth was now born in the Pāṇḍya kingdoms as an illustrious and excellent Brahmin, together with his wife and attendants.
May she, united with that husband through love every night, experience in her dreams the highest pleasure of union, even greater than waking. (26)

That best of brahmins, residing three hundred and sixty yojanas away from his home, beheld this bride—who was a delight to the mind—every night in his dreams for a long time, finding great pleasure therein through the course of karma.
Indeed, through her union with her husband during sleep every night, this virtuous woman shall in due time obtain a son who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
In her, he shall behold his own son born from their long-awaited union; that brahmin, too, will constantly see him in dreams, filled with love.
"O Great Sage, having been propitiated by her in a previous birth, I have now appeared for the very purpose of granting her a boon. (30)
Sūta said: Then the Great Goddess spoke with respect to that young girl: "O child, O highly fortunate one, listen to my supreme word. (31)
Whenever and wherever you see your former husband, whom you previously beheld in a dream, you, being wise, will recognize him.
That brahmin will also see you, who possess the auspicious marks of a dream; then a conversation between the two of you will take place.
Then, O blessed lady, give your own highly learned son to him; place the foremost fruit of this vow into his hand.
From that time forward, O slender-waisted one, remain under his very control; let there be no physical union between you two, except as in a dream.
"When that best of Brahmins has met his death in due time, you shall enter the fire and go with him to my own abode."
"O fair-browed one, you shall have a son who will be enchanting to all the world; he shall possess all prosperity and attain the supreme state. (37)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus and having granted her heart's desire, the Mother of the three worlds vanished in an instant while the two of them were still looking on.
That young girl, having obtained the boon from Pārvatī, the ocean of compassion, attained supreme bliss and worshipped that guru.
When that night had passed, that sage, who had attained spiritual vision and knew the dharma, disclosed all of that secret to her parents.
Then, having taken leave of everyone and having bestowed his grace upon the illustrious Śāradā, the sage, moving with unhindered gait, departed.
