As the days passed in this manner, that young woman obtained the company of her husband every moment in her dreams, which increased her happiness.
By virtue of Gaurī’s granting of a boon, Śāradā, whose vows were pure, conceived a child even in a dream through the power of her union with her husband.
Hearing that Śāradā was pregnant while being without her husband, everyone said, "Fie on her! and the people declared her to be an adulteress.
Hearing that unbearable news regarding their husband who had passed away, his kinsmen, relatives, and family members went to his father’s house. (45)
Then all the village elders and learned men arrived; they held a council there together with the family elders.
Having summoned the pregnant Śāradā, whose face was cast down in shame, some, being highly enraged, threatened her, while others turned their faces away.
"O paramour, O evil-minded one, what is this deed you have done? O fool, you have brought a great infamy upon our family! (48)
Thus rebuking him, those wise elders of the village all consulted together, saying, "What shall we do? (49)
There, certain elders spoke mercilessly toward that girl: "This girl is evil-minded and will bring ruin to both families. (50)
Having shaved her hair and cut off her ears and nose, let her be banished from the village and cast out from her own kin.
Having thus deliberated, they all prepared to act accordingly; then, a voice arose from the sky that was beyond the range of hearing.
No sin has been committed by her, nor has she brought disgrace upon her family; there is no violation of her vows, for this woman is of virtuous conduct.
Henceforth, the tongues of those deluded by vice who say that this woman is an adulteress shall instantly split asunder.
Having heard this incorporeal voice produced in the intermediate space, everyone—including her mother, father, and others—rejoiced greatly.
Then all the village elders and the members of the assembly, filled with agitation, remained silent for a moment and stood with their heads bowed in fear.
There, some who were faithless declared it to be a false speech; their tongues split in two, and in an instant they vomited forth worms.
Then her kinsmen and relatives honored that young girl, and the elder women among her kin exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (58).
Some of the best of their lineage shed drops of tears of joy; the women of the family, being overjoyed, offered words of consolation directed toward her.
Then others there said: "The Lord does not speak untruth; how could He have conceived them in the womb? She certainly did not waver from her virtuous conduct. (50)
Thus, observing all the members of the assembly whose minds were possessed by doubt, an elderly man there—omniscient and a knower of the true nature of the world—[spoke].
This entire universe, whatever is seen or heard, is composed of illusion; in this world characterized by momentariness, what is real and what is unreal? 62.
That which is indefinable and unreal in essence clearly arises through *māyā*. *Māyā* is under the control of the Lord; who knows His activity? (23)
It is said that the seed of the royal sage Yūpaketu fell into the water; having drunk that water containing his seed, a courtesan conceived a child.
Having drunk the semen of the sage Vibhāṇḍaka along with water, a doe became pregnant and gave birth to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
Likewise, having touched the hand of King Surāṣṭra, the doe became pregnant at that very moment and gave birth to an ascetic sage.
Likewise, the woman Satyavatī was born from the womb of a Śapharī fish; and in the same way, Mahiṣāsura was born from the womb of a buffalo-cow.
Likewise, in former times there were women who gave birth to children out of compassion; for instance, a son was born to Rohiṇī by Vasudeva.
By the curse or the boon of deities and great sages, even an improper act becomes appropriate; there is no doubt in this matter. (69)
The club was born from the womb of Sāmba due to the curse of the sages; through the power of the sages' mantras, it became the embryo of Yuvanāśva.
Surely this auspicious lady also, through her service at the feet of the great seer and by the power of his great vow, bears a child in her womb, though she was previously barren.
"In this matter, let the women ask her in private about the truth; then the great multitude will have their doubts dispelled. (72)
Then, at those very words, the women questioned her among themselves; she related to them all that most wonderful account of her own life.
Then, recognizing her, they all honored that virtuous woman and, rejoicing and praising her, departed for their respective abodes.
Then, when an auspicious time had arrived, the young Śāradā, whose heart was pure, gave birth to a son whose splendor was equal to the rising sun. (75)
That prince, possessing most noble marks and lotus-like eyes, attained great knowledge while still in his childhood, for he was of vast intelligence. (76)
Then, having been initiated by his preceptor at the proper time, he who was delightful to the world obtained fame in the world as "Śāradvatīputra. (77)
In his eighth year he mastered the Ṛgveda, in the ninth the collection of Yajus formulas, and in the tenth, the Sāmaveda—all with ease, that one of keen intellect. (78)
Then, when the festival of Śiva, honored throughout the three worlds, had arrived, all the people residing everywhere set out for Gokarṇa.
Śāradā also, being virtuous, went to Gokarṇa with her own son.
There she saw her husband from a previous birth, who had been constantly perceived in her dreams, arrived there surrounded by his kinsmen and fellow brahmins.
Seeing him, she stood there, overwhelmed with love, her body covered in horripilation, the flow of her tears checked, her eyes fixed intently upon him.
And that brahmin, too, having seen her—marked with auspicious signs of beauty and providing him delight, as she was always being enjoyed by him in his dreams—[was struck with wonder].
Having seen that prince, born from his own body, even in a dream, he was overcome with wonder upon beholding him and approached his side.
"O blessed lady, I wish to ask you whatever is in your mind. Having spoken thus, he first led her to a secluded place. (85)
"Who are you? Tell me, O lady of beautiful thighs; whose wife are you, O woman of virtuous vows? What is your country, whose daughter are you, and what is your name? Thus he spoke to her. (86)
Thus questioned by him, that woman with tearful eyes related her own history and the cause of her widowhood in childhood.
Again he asked that young woman: "Whose excellent son is this? And how was this boy, who resembles the moon, carried in your womb? (88)
Śāradā said: "O Lord, this is my son, proficient in all branches of knowledge; he has been named Śāradeya, derived from my very name. (69)
Having heard her words, that best of Brahmins laughed and said: "O beautiful lady, your conduct is indeed a hardship upon hardship. (90)
"Having performed only the taking of your hand in marriage, your husband has indeed died; how then was this son born? Let the cause of this be told. (91)
Having heard these words spoken by him, she was deeply ashamed; after remaining with a tearful face for a moment, she spoke thus with fortitude: || 92 ||
Śāradā said: "Enough with these joking words; you know me, O high-minded one, and I know you. In this matter, our own minds are the authority for both of us. (93)
Having spoken thus and reported everything, including the boons granted by the Goddess, he gave half of his vow to that Kumāra who was himself firm in his observance.
That brahmin, also being greatly delighted, accepted the boy and, with the permission of his parents, led him to his own home.
She too, having stayed for many months in the house of that brahmin, entered the fire and followed him when he had come under the power of time.
Then, having become husband and wife, they ascended a divine celestial chariot and, endowed with divine enjoyments, went to the abode of Śiva.
Thus, this meritorious narrative has been fully described by me; it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who read and listen to it correctly.
It increases longevity, health, prosperity, wealth, and power; for women, it is the means for achieving auspiciousness, good fortune, progeny, and happiness. (99)

This great narrative destroys the flood of sins and proclaims the meritorious fame of the vow of Gaurī and Maheśa; he who listens to it even once with devotion or recites it, having enjoyed worldly pleasures, attains the eternal state.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Śāradā," in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa of the third part of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Now, I shall describe in brief the greatness of the rudrākṣa, which causes the destruction of all sins for those who hear it or even read it.
Whether one is a non-devotee or a devotee, whether lowly or even lower than the lowly—whosoever wears Rudrākṣas is liberated from all sins.
With what else could the merit of wearing rudrākṣas be compared? Those sages who perceive the ultimate truth declare this to be a great vow (mahāvrata). || 3 ||
He who, firm in his vows, wears a thousand rudrākṣas, is saluted by all the gods; he is indeed just like Rudra himself.
In the absence of a thousand [repetitions], however, there should be sixteen on each of the two arms; one on the crest-lock, and indeed twelve on each of the two hands.
He who wears thirty-two Rudrākṣas on the neck, forty on the head, one on each ear, six on each [ear], and one hundred and eight on the chest, is honored like Rudra himself.
He who wears Rudrākṣas combined with pearls, coral, crystal, silver, lapis lazuli, and gold shall become Śiva himself.
Even he who wears only rudrākṣas, according to whatever may be available, is not touched by sins, just as darkness does not touch the sun.
A mantra recited with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads bestows infinite fruit; a recitation by men without rudrākṣa yields only a proportionate measure of fruit.
If even a single rudrākṣa, which bestows great merit, is not on one's body, or if one is devoid of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), that person's birth shall be in vain.
He who, having tied a rudrākṣa on his head, performs a head-bath, obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt. || 11 ||
Whoever worships a rudrākṣa even without the sprinkling of water certainly obtains that very same fruit which is gained from the worship of a liṅga. || 12 ||
Some rudrākṣas have one face, some five faces, others eleven faces, and some have fourteen faces; these are worshipped by the world.
The rudrākṣa, which is of the nature of Śaṅkara, when constantly worshipped with devotion, makes even a poor man endowed with the splendor of the king of kings.
In this regard, the wise recount this meritorious narrative, which destroys even great sins through both hearing and reciting it. (15)
There was a king of the land of Kaśmīra known as Bhadrasena; he had a wise and heroic son named Sudharman.
In that city, there was a certain son of a minister named Tāraka, who possessed excellent virtues and was a most distinguished friend of the prince. || 17 ||
Those two princes, exceedingly affectionate toward one another and beautiful in form, devoted themselves to the study of the sciences and engaged in play together during their childhood. (18)
With Rudrākṣa beads serving as ornaments on all their limbs, those two noble-bodied ones constantly wandered about, always smeared with sacred ash.
Having cast aside their ornaments made of gold and gems, such as necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and earrings, the two of them began to wear rudrākṣas.
They always wear rosaries of rudrākṣa beads, they have rudrākṣa bracelets on their hands, they always have rudrākṣa ornaments around their necks, and they always wear rudrākṣa earrings.
Regarding their ornaments of gold, jewels, and the like as mere clods of earth and stones, they did not cast off their rudrākṣa beads even when being exhorted by people.
By chance, the eminent sage Parāśara, who was like the Grandfather (Brahmā) himself, arrived at the house of that king of Kaśmīra. || 23 ||

Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, the king, the best among the upholders of dharma, questioned that great sage—who knows the three periods of time—once he was seated in comfort.
The king said: "O Blessed One, this son of mine and that son of my minister constantly wear rudrākṣas and have no desire for jeweled ornaments."
Even though they were constantly being instructed to accept ornaments made of jewels, they disregarded our words and remained solely intent upon rudrākṣa beads.
These two boys have never been instructed by anyone at any time; how did this natural disposition belong to the two princes? (27)
Parāśara said: Listen, O King, I shall relate to you the wondrous former history of your wise son and the minister’s son. (28)
Formerly, in the village of Nandigrāma, there was a certain courtesan renowned as Mahānandā, whose form was graceful with the charms of love.
An umbrella resembling the full moon, a vehicle resplendent with gold, fly-whisks with beautiful handles, and golden sandals.
There were variegated garments, highly precious and radiant; the beds were like moonbeams, and the couches were made of gold.
Hundreds of cows, hundreds of buffalo-cows, and likewise hundreds of male servants. || 32 ||
The maidservants, in the full bloom of youth, had limbs radiant with all kinds of ornaments, and their priceless jewelry was resplendent with the nine precious gems.
Anointing with perfumes, saffron, musk, camphor, and agallochum; variegated garlands and ear-ornaments; and delicious food according to one's desire. (34)
A house enriched with various variegated canopies, filled with diverse grains, abounding in many thousands of jewels, and possessing wealth exceeding ten million in number. || 35 ||
Thus, though a courtesan endowed with great wealth and living for sensual pleasure, she was constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva and dedicated to truth and righteousness. || 36 ||
She was constantly devoted to the stories of Sadāśiva, eager for discourse on the name of Śiva, bowing at the feet of Śiva’s devotees, and delighting day and night in devotion to Śiva. (37)
For the sake of diversion, that courtesan, having decorated one monkey and one cock with rudrākṣa beads, placed them in the middle of the theater pavilion.
She herself constantly causes [them] to dance with rhythmic clapping and songs; then again, surrounded by her female companions, she laughs loudly. (39)
A pair [of verses]: Adorned with armlets, earrings, and ornaments made of rudrākṣa beads, the monkey, through her instruction, always dances like a child. (40)
With a rudrākṣa bead tied to his crest, the cock, an expert in dancing, danced for a long time with the monkey, bringing wonder to those who watched. (41)
Once, a certain Vaiśya, devoted to the vow of Śiva, wearing rudrākṣa beads and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), free from possessiveness and accomplished in his purpose, came to her abode.
He bore upon his bright forearm a superior bracelet, studded with great jewels, blazing like the rising sun.
When he arrived, that courtesan honored him with supreme joy; seeing the bracelet upon his wrist, she spoke in amazement: || 44 ||
This bracelet, composed of great jewels, rests upon your hand; O virtuous one, it captivates my mind, being worthy of the ornaments of a celestial woman. (45)
Thus, the Vaiśya of noble mind, looking at her who was richly adorned with excellent jewels and longing for his hand-ornament, spoke to her with a smile: (46)
The Vaiśya said: "If your mind is set upon this divine and excellent jewel, then take it with full satisfaction; what price will you give for it? (47)
The courtesan said: "We are indeed courtesans who act according to our own will; we are not devoted wives. There is no doubt that infidelity is the dharma appropriate for our family. (48)
"If you give me this hand-ornament studded with jewels, I shall become your wife for three days and nights. (49)
The Vaiśya said: "So be it, O beloved of the courtesans, if your word is true; I give you this jewel bracelet—be my wife for three nights."
In this legal proceeding, however, the moon and the sun are my witnesses; having said "Truth" three times, touch my heart, O beloved. (51)
The courtesan said: "O Lord, having become your wife for three days and nights, let me practice dharma together with you"—this thought touched his heart. (52)
Then that Vaiśya gave her a jeweled bracelet; having placed a linga made of jewels into her hand, he spoke as follows: || 53 ||
"This Śiva-liṅga made of jewels is like my own life-breath; it must be protected by you, O beloved, for its loss would be my death. (54)
Saying "So be it," that beloved woman took the linga made of jewels, placed it upon a pillar of the dance pavilion, and entered her house.
Having united with that Vaiśya, who acted like a libertine, she slept happily on a couch adorned with a soft mattress during the night.
Then, at the hour of midnight, within the dancing pavilion, a fire suddenly arose and instantly enveloped him.
While the pavilion was burning, that courtesan rose up suddenly in agitation and released the monkey from its bonds there.
Once its bonds were released, that monkey, terrified along with the cock, fled far away, scattering many sparks of fire.
Seeing that linga, which had been burnt along with the pillar and shattered into pieces, the prostitute and the merchant fell into boundless misery.
Having seen that the Liṅga, which was as dear to him as his own life, had been burnt, the lord of the Vaiśyas likewise attained a state of world-weariness and set his mind upon death.
Out of extreme distress and despondency, the Vaiśya spoke to her who was so afflicted: "Now that the Śiva-liṅga has been shattered, I have no desire to live. (62)
"O blessed lady, have a funeral pyre prepared for me by your highly powerful servants; having fixed my mind on Śiva, I shall enter the fire. (63)
Even if Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the others were to come together and restrain me, nevertheless, at this very moment, being firm, I shall enter the fire and abandon my life-breaths.
Perceiving him to be thus firmly bound, she, being deeply distressed, had a funeral pyre prepared by her own servants outside her city.
Then that wise Vaiśya, purified by devotion to Śiva, circumambulated the kindled fire and entered it while the people looked on; and that young woman was overcome with remorse.
Then that distressed woman, remembering the perfectly pure Dharma and looking upon all her kinsmen, spoke these piteous words: || 67 ||
Taking the jeweled bracelet, I spoke the truth: "For three days, I am indeed the esteemed wife of that merchant. (68)

"By my own action, this Vaiśya, a follower of Śiva's vow, has died; therefore, I shall enter the fire along with him. Behold, for this which I have spoken as 'I am his partner in dharma' is indeed the truth. (69)
Through truth, the gods who are lords of the three worlds attain delight; devotion to truth is the supreme dharma, for everything is established in truth.
Through truth one attains heaven and liberation, but through untruth there is no supreme goal; therefore, relying upon truth, I shall enter the fire.
Thus, though restrained by her kinsmen, that woman, being firm in her resolve and fearing the loss of truth, set her mind upon giving up her life.
Having given away her entire possessions to the devotees of Śiva and meditated upon Sadāśiva, she circumambulated that fire three times and stood facing the region.
As she was falling into the kindled fire with her mind fixed upon his own feet, Śiva himself, the soul of the universe, manifested and restrained her.

Beholding that god of all gods, the three-eyed one adorned with the crescent moon, who possesses the brilliance of ten million moons, suns, and fires, she stood there as if paralyzed and as if terrified.
Having comforted her—who was overwhelmed, terrified, trembling, and stunned—and taking her by the hand as her tears flowed, he spoke these words.
Śiva said: "It was to test your truthfulness, your righteousness, your fortitude, and your unwavering devotion to me that I came to your presence having become a Vaiśya. (77)
Having raised a fire by means of illusion, I burned down the theater pavilion; having set it ablaze, I consumed the jeweled linga and entered the sacrificial fire.
Prostitutes are deceitful, wanton, and deceivers of people; yet you, having remembered the truth, have entered the fire along with me. (79)

Therefore, I shall bestow upon you enjoyments difficult even for the gods to obtain, as well as an exceedingly long life, health, and the prosperity of your progeny; whatever you desire, O fair-hipped one, that very thing I grant to you.
Sūta said: While the Lord of Gaurī was speaking thus, that courtesan replied.
The courtesan said: "I have no desire for enjoyments on earth, in heaven, or in the netherworld; other than the touch of your lotus-feet, I truly choose nothing else. (82)
These servants and maidservants, as well as my other kinsmen—all are intent upon worshipping you, having surrendered their livelihoods to you. (83)
Having led all these together with me to your supreme state, release us from the terrible fear of rebirth; salutations be to you! (84)
Saying "So be it," Maheśvara welcomed her words and led them all, together with her, to the supreme abode.
Parāśara said: Those two who formerly fled far away when the theater pavilion was set on fire—the cock and the monkey—remain there even now.
That dancing monkey of hers who met his death in due time became this prince Kuvakuṭa, the son of the minister.
Due to the merit arising from wearing rudrākṣa beads, earned in a previous birth, these two boys have been born into a noble family and now reside here. (88)
Those of pure mind, by virtue of their previous practice, wear rudrākṣas; having worshipped that auspicious world in this very birth, they shall go there.
Thus has the conduct of these two children been described, as well as the story of the devotee of Śiva; what else do you wish to ask? (90)
Sūta said: Having heard these words, which were like nectar, spoken thus by the Brahman-sage, the king was delighted and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke again.
The King said: "Oh, the company of the virtuous is the purifier of all sins for men; it is indeed the destroyer of lust and anger, and the milker of one's desires for people."
The darkness of my illusion has vanished and the vision of knowledge has been illumined; by the mere sight of you, O best of immortals, I have almost become a god myself. (3)
O Sage, I have correctly heard the past deeds of these two children; I now ask you concerning their future conduct as well, and that of my own son.
Tell me, how many years is his lifespan, and what is his fortune like? What are his learning, fame, power, faith, and devotion like? (5)
O Sage, you ought to explain all of this in its entirety; I am your disciple, I am your servant, and I have come to you for refuge.
Parāśara said: "Indeed, there is something here that ought not to be spoken; how could I possibly describe it, hearing which even those possessed of fortitude would fall into despondency?"
Nevertheless, O Lord of the Earth, because you inquire with such sincere intent, I shall speak even that which ought not to be spoken out of affection for you.
Twelve years have passed for this prince of yours; henceforth, he shall meet his death on the seventh day.
Having heard these words of his, which were like the risen Kālakūṭa poison, the king suddenly fell to the ground in a swoon out of grief.
Having raised him up and comforted him, that sage, his mind moistened with compassion, said: "Do not fear, O King; I shall speak again for your benefit."
Prior to creation, that which was one, partless, supreme, and devoid of light—the light consisting of consciousness and bliss—that is the primordial, absolute Śiva.
Having first created Brahmā from himself in the form of *rajas*, he bestowed the Vedas upon him who was appointed to the task of creation.
Furthermore, the Lord gave him the singular compendium of the reality of the Self, and he also gave him the Rudrādhyāya, the essence of all the Upaniṣads.
That which is the one, immutable, eternal light of Brahman, the supreme reality whose nature is Śiva, is established in the Rudrādhyāya. || 15 ||
That Virāṭ, born of himself, created the universe with his four mouths; he produced the four Vedas for the sake of the stability of the worlds.
There, from the mouth of Brahmā facing south, this Rudrādhyāya emerged from among the Yajus-mantras as the essence of all the Upaniṣads. (17)
This very [Veda] was upheld by all the sages, led by Marīci and Atri, together with the gods; and their disciples received it from them.
By his disciples, their disciples, and their sons, who have come down in succession, this essence of the Veda, whose nature is Rudra, has been upheld and propitiated. || 19 ||
This alone is the supreme mantra; this alone is the supreme austerity: the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya is the ultimate means for men to attain liberation.

Those who are declared to be perpetrators of great sins (mahāpātakin) and those who commit minor offenses (upapātakin)—even they immediately attain the supreme goal through the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya.
Furthermore, beings of mixed origins—good and evil—such as gods, animals, humans, and others, were created by Brahmā; by them, the world was then filled.
Their actions are created in accordance with their own births; they proceed through those worlds and indeed experience their fruit.
For the sake of the continuous flow of the world's creation, Prajāpati himself first created dharma and adharma from the front and back parts of his own body.
Those who practice righteousness alone obtain merit and its fruit; those who practice unrighteousness become enjoyers of the fruits of sin.
Heaven is the fruit of meritorious deeds, and hell is the opposite of that; the Creator appointed two sovereigns over these two, namely Indra and Yama.
Lust, anger, greed, and others such as pride and arrogance were the sons of Adharma; they were all the leaders of hell.
Violating the teacher’s bed, drinking liquor, and likewise approaching a Pulkasī woman—these are proclaimed as the primary sons of Kāma. (28)
From anger arose the killing of a father, as well as the killing of a mother; and Brahmahatyā and Kanyā—these are the daughters of Anger. (29)
The seizing of the property of gods, the seizing of the property of Brahmins, and the theft of gold—these are recorded as the sons of Greed. (30)
Having summoned these Cāṇḍālas, the leaders of sinners, Yama established them in lordship over hell for the purpose of its expansion.
Commanded by Yama, those nine leaders of sinners—all those terrible leaders of sinners—once again assembled together.
They guarded the hells through their own servants and minor offenses, even as the Rudrādhyāya—the direct means to liberation—reached the earth.
Terrified, all those leaders of minor sins fled, and together with other secondary sinners, they made a representation to Yama.
Victory to you, O God, Great King! For we are indeed your servants; yet we have been appointed by you with authority for the purpose of increasing Naraka’s power. (35)
O Lord, we are now unable to remain in this world; scorched by the power of the Rudrādhyāya, we have indeed fled.
In every village, on the banks of rivers, and in sacred shrines—if the recitation of the Rudra-hymns were sufficient, how could we ever wander through the world? (37)
We do not count even a thousand atonements; alas, we are unable to endure even the syllables of the Rudra-japa.
For us, the chief perpetrators of great sins and destroyers of the world, the chanting of the Rudra-mantra is a terrible fear; the chanting of the Rudra-mantra is a great poison. (39)
Therefore, you ought to remove this great, terrible, and unbearable calamity that has befallen us through the recitation of the Rudra-hymn. (40)
Thus informed by the leaders of the sinners, Yama himself approached Brahmā and reported everything to him. (41)
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, I have come to you alone for refuge; I have been appointed by you for the restraint of mortals who commit evil deeds.
Now there are no sinful mortals remaining on the surface of the earth; the great multitude of sins has been destroyed by the Rudrādhyāya.
When the lineage of sinners has perished, the hells have become empty; and when the hells have reached emptiness, my kingdom is indeed rendered fruitless. (44)
Therefore, O Blessed One, you yourself must devise a means so that my sovereignty over those embodied in mortal form may not be destroyed. (45)
Thus addressed by Yama, who was distressed, the Creator devised a means for the purpose of preventing the interruption of Rudra’s recitation.
He instilled both lack of faith and dullness of intellect—the two offspring of ignorance—into mortals, which destroy both faith and intelligence. (47)
When the world was thus deluded by those two and turned away from the Rudrādhyāya, Yama, having reached his own abode, felt as though he had achieved his purpose.
People are born short-lived due to sins committed in previous births; those sins perish for men who chant the Rudra-mantra. (49)
When all sins have been exhausted, long life, strength, fortitude, health, knowledge, and sovereignty increase for all embodied beings. (50)
Those who bathe the god Maheśvara with the Rudrādhyāya and perform their own ablutions with that water cross over death.
Those who perform their ablutions with water consecrated by the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya have no fear of death; they are glorified in the world of Śiva.
By the consecration of the Śatarudra, a man becomes long-lived for a hundred years; liberated from all sins without exception, he shall become beloved of Śiva. (53)
"Let this son of yours perform the ritual bath of ten thousand Rudras; he shall rejoice on earth for ten thousand years like Śakra. (94)
Possessing unimpeded power and sovereignty, with his enemies destroyed and free from disease, he—having shaken off the entire flood of sins—is the ruler whose kingdom is free from thorns.

The Brahmins were knowers of the Vedas, tranquil, accomplished, and observers of praised vows; they were established in the sacrifice of knowledge and austerity, and were solely devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Let those of pure intention perform the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya correctly; by the power of their recitation, immediate welfare shall come to pass. (57)

When the great sage had spoken thus, the king chose him alone as his primary preceptor for the rites; then, in an instant, he summoned thousands of other sages who were free from the desire for wealth.
Those sages, tranquil in mind and numbering one thousand, having established a hundred jars filled with the juices of auspicious trees, [proceeded]. (59)
When the seventh day arrived, they bathed that son of the lord of the earth according to the prescribed rites, having first performed the ritual ablution with the Rudrādhyāya.
While being bathed by the sages, that young prince was suddenly seized with terror and fell into a swoon for a moment.
Suddenly awakened and protected by the sages, he spoke: "A certain man has arrived with a staff in his hand. (62)
Intent on striking me, that terrifying one with a formidable staff was himself beaten by other great heroes. (63)
Bound by a great noose, he seemed as if carried far away; this much I beheld while you were providing protection.
When the king’s son had spoken thus, the best of the twice-born honored him with blessings and informed the king of their fear.
Then the best of kings, having honored all the most excellent sages with sacrificial fees and having fed them with choice food out of devotion, [dismissed them]. (66)
Having received the blessings of those sages who discourse on Brahman, he sat down in the assembly hall with his kinsmen out of devotion.
When that heroic king had arrived together with the sages, the great yogi, the celestial sage Nārada himself, came there.

Seeing that the Guru of the sages had arrived together with all the members and the lords of the sages, the king bowed with devotion, seated him upon a throne, performed the rites of hospitality, and spoke.
The king said: "O Brahmin, have you seen anything wonderful in the three worlds? Tell us that, for we are all longing for the nectar of your words. (70)
Nārada said: "Today, O Great King, a great wonder was seen by me as I descended from the sky; listen to that, together with these foremost of sages. (71)
Today Death has arrived here with staff in hand, invincible and constantly oppressing the world, to slay your son. (72)
Lord Śiva also, having learned that he had come to kill your son, dispatched a certain Vīrabhadra along with his attendants.
Having arrived, he seized Mṛtyu—who had come with intent to kill your son—bound him very tightly, and struck him with a staff in his wrath.

Perceiving that he was being led swiftly into the presence of the Lord of the World, the venerable Yama himself, with palms joined in reverence and crying out "Victory to You, O God!", bowed his head and spoke to the Wielder of the Trident.
Yama said: O God of gods, O Mahārudra, O Vīrabhadra, salutations be unto you! How has this anger arisen in you toward Death, who is innocent?
O Lord, tell me, what fault is there when Death, intent on striking down the prince whose life has reached its end through the consequence of his own karma, prepares to strike? (77)
Vīrabhadra said: "How could that prince, whose lifespan was ten thousand years and whose inauspiciousness had been destroyed by bathing in the Rudra-tīrtha, meet with such calamity?"
If you still have doubt regarding my unrefuted words, summon Citragupta this very day and question him without delay.
Nārada said: Then Citragupta, summoned by Yama, arrived suddenly; being questioned regarding the measure of your son's lifespan, he spoke.
Having stated that his lifespan was twelve years and having reflected upon it, he spoke again regarding the written record, saying that he would live for ten thousand years.
Then King Yama, being terrified, bowed down to Vīrabhadra and somehow released Mṛtyu from that difficult-to-avert bondage.
Then, released by Vīrabhadra, Yama went to his own abode; and Vīrabhadra reached Kailāsa, arriving here into my presence.
Therefore, by the power of the recitation of the Rudra-mantra, this son of yours has crossed over the fear of death and become happy for ten thousand years.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the king, when Nārada had departed for heaven, all the brahmins, filled with joy, returned then to their respective hermitages.
Thus, by the power of the Rudrādhyāya, the King of Kaśmīra, together with his sons, crossed over all miseries and attained his life's purpose. (86)

Those men who glorify this majesty of the Supreme Lord and drink it in with the cups of their ears, being liberated from the multitude of sins committed over ten million births, become peaceful and attain the supreme abode of the Moon-crested Lord.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Rudrādhyāya," in the third section, the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
